### Bun 1.3: `--shard`, `--isolate`, and `--changed` Flags for Pyramid-Shaped CI  [community]

Bun 1.3 (released late 2025) added three CI-relevant flags that map directly onto test pyramid execution strategy:

| Flag | Pyramid use | Behaviour |
|------|-------------|-----------|
| `--shard=N/M` | All levels | Split test files into M shards; this shard runs only shard N. Enables horizontal parallelism without an orchestration layer |
| `--isolate` | Integration + E2E | Runs each test file in a fresh Bun process (similar to Node.js `isolation:'process'`). Prevents module-singleton pollution between integration test files |
| `--changed` | Unit level in PRs | Runs only test files modified since the last Git commit. Used in pre-commit hooks for sub-500ms feedback at the unit level |

The combination enables a **Bun-native pyramid CI pipeline** without Jest, Vitest, or separate sharding orchestration:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/test-bun.yml
# Three-stage pyramid pipeline using Bun 1.3 native flags
name: Test (Bun)
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  unit:
    name: Unit Tests
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: oven-sh/setup-bun@v2
        with: { bun-version: '1.3' }
      - run: bun install --frozen-lockfile
      # Unit tests: fast, no isolation needed, high concurrency
      - run: bun test 'src/**/*.unit.test.ts' --coverage --coverage-reporter=lcov

  integration:
    name: Integration Tests (sharded)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        shard: [1, 2, 3, 4]  # 4 shards for integration tests
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: oven-sh/setup-bun@v2
        with: { bun-version: '1.3' }
      - run: bun install --frozen-lockfile
      # Integration tests: isolated (fresh process per file), sharded across 4 runners
      - run: bun test 'src/**/*.integration.test.ts' --isolate --shard=${{ matrix.shard }}/4
      
  e2e:
    name: E2E Tests
    needs: [unit, integration]  # Fail-fast: only run E2E if lower levels pass
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: oven-sh/setup-bun@v2
        with: { bun-version: '1.3' }
      - run: bun install --frozen-lockfile
      - run: bunx playwright install --with-deps
      - run: bun test 'tests/e2e/**/*.e2e.test.ts'
```

**The `--changed` flag for pre-commit unit tests:**

```bash
# .husky/pre-commit — run only changed unit tests before commit
# Bun 1.3 --changed: detects test files modified since HEAD
bun test --changed 'src/**/*.unit.test.ts'

# Typical output: "3 test files, 12 tests, 0 failures — 318ms"
# If no test files changed: "0 test files" (exits 0 immediately)
```

**Production gotcha:** `--changed` compares against the Git working tree, not against the last CI green build. A test file modified in a prior commit that was not part of the current changeset will **not** be re-run by `--changed`. This means a downstream test that exercises code changed by an upstream refactor is skipped. Reserve `--changed` for **pre-commit hooks** (fastest feedback). Always run the full unit suite in CI on `push`, not just changed files. [community: bun.sh/blog/bun-v1.2, bun.sh/docs/cli/test#sharding]

### Playwright v1.60: `test.abort()` — Fail Pyramid Tests from Fixtures and Handlers  [community]

Playwright v1.60 introduced `test.abort()` as a first-class mechanism to fail a running test case from within a **fixture**, a **route handler**, or a **browser context event listener**. Before this API, fixtures had no clean way to signal a test failure from outside the test body — teams either threw from `afterEach` (producing confusing error attribution) or used shared mutable state (a flakiness vector).

The pyramid relevance is most pronounced at the **E2E level**: `test.abort()` enables network-layer assertions to be separated from the test body, which keeps the E2E test case focused on user-visible behavior while the fixture layer enforces system-level invariants.

```typescript
// tests/e2e/fixtures/network-guard.fixture.ts
// Vitest-style fixture for Playwright: aborts the test if any 5xx response is observed.
// Keeps E2E test bodies clean — network error handling is a cross-cutting fixture concern.
import { test as base, expect } from '@playwright/test';

export const test = base.extend({
  // page is automatically extended to monitor all responses
  page: async ({ page }, use, testInfo) => {
    // Register the handler before the test body runs
    page.on('response', (response) => {
      if (response.status() >= 500) {
        // Abort the test with a descriptive message — attributed to the fixture, not the test body
        testInfo.abort(`Unexpected 5xx response: ${response.status()} ${response.url()}`);
      }
    });
    await use(page);
  },
});

export { expect };
```

```typescript
// tests/e2e/checkout.e2e.test.ts
// E2E test body is clean: no response-status assertions needed.
// The network-guard fixture handles 5xx failures transparently.
import { test, expect } from './fixtures/network-guard.fixture.js';

test('completes checkout flow for authenticated user', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4242 4242 4242 4242');
  await page.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('12/28');
  await page.getByLabel('CVC').fill('123');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByText('Order confirmed')).toBeVisible();
  // If any 5xx occurs during this test, testInfo.abort() fires from the fixture —
  // the test fails immediately with the URL and status code in the failure message
});
```

**When to use `test.abort()` vs `expect()` in the test body:**
- Use `test.abort()` for **invariant enforcement** that applies to all tests in a suite (no 5xx responses, no console errors, no unauthorised API calls) — these belong in shared fixtures
- Use `expect()` in the test body for **scenario-specific assertions** (page content, user state, navigation outcomes)
- Avoid calling `test.abort()` from inside the test body itself — it bypasses assertion counting and produces non-standard failure messages

[community: playwright.dev/docs/release-notes#v160, Playwright blog May 2026]

### AI-Driven Test Selection: Moving Beyond Static Pyramid Ratios  [community]

Production insights from "How They Test" (108 companies, 2025–2026 edition) show that several engineering organisations have moved from **static pyramid ratios** (70/20/10 guideline) to **AI-driven test selection** that dynamically adjusts which tests run based on code change impact. Two patterns dominate:

**Pattern 1 — AI impact analysis at the integration level (Faire, Instawork):**
Instead of running all integration tests on every PR, an AI agent analyses the changed files, constructs a call graph, and selects only the integration test cases whose test objects overlap with the changed code paths. Typical outcome: 60–80% reduction in integration test suite execution time on average PRs, with no regression in defect escape rate in their 12-month retrospectives.

**Pattern 2 — LLM test generation for coverage gaps (Meta ACH / Codium Cover-Agent):**
Meta's ACH (arXiv:2501.12862) demonstrated mutation-guided LLM test generation: an LLM is prompted with a surviving mutant (a fault not killed by existing tests) and asked to generate a test case that kills it. Applied to 10,000+ Kotlin classes, 571 privacy-hardening tests were generated with a 73% acceptance rate from engineers. The TypeScript equivalent is Stryker + Cover-Agent: Stryker identifies surviving mutants; Cover-Agent generates TypeScript test cases targeting those specific mutation points.

```typescript
// Conceptual TypeScript workflow: Stryker surviving mutant → LLM test generation
// Step 1: Run Stryker to identify surviving mutants
// $ npx stryker run --reporters json
// Output: stryker-report.json — contains survivingMutants[] with file/line/mutation details

// Step 2: For each surviving mutant, invoke LLM (Claude API) to generate a killing test case
// src/scripts/generate-killing-tests.ts

import Anthropic from '@anthropic-ai/sdk';
import type { MutantResult } from '@stryker-mutator/api/report';

async function generateKillingTest(mutant: MutantResult): Promise<string> {
  const client = new Anthropic();
  const prompt = `You are a TypeScript testing expert.
The following mutation survived (was not killed by any existing test):
File: ${mutant.fileName}
Line: ${mutant.location.start.line}
Original: ${mutant.originalCode}
Mutant:   ${mutant.mutatedCode}
Mutation type: ${mutant.mutatorName}

Generate a single Vitest test case that:
1. Imports the function under test
2. Calls it with inputs that expose the mutant's behaviour change
3. Uses a strict assertion that would FAIL on the mutant but PASS on the original
Output only the TypeScript test case, no explanation.`;

  const message = await client.messages.create({
    model: 'claude-opus-4-5',
    max_tokens: 512,
    messages: [{ role: 'user', content: prompt }],
  });

  return (message.content[0] as { type: 'text'; text: string }).text;
}
```

**Pyramid placement of AI-generated tests:** LLM-generated mutation-killing tests belong at the **unit level** — they are tightly scoped to a single function and a single mutation point. They should not be placed at the integration or E2E level, where the overhead would make the feedback loop too slow for mutation testing iteration cycles.

**Production caution:** AI-generated tests require human review before merging. Meta's 73% acceptance rate implies 27% were incorrect, redundant, or untestable — human review remains the quality gate. Automate generation but never auto-merge LLM-authored tests. [community: arxiv.org/abs/2501.12862 Meta ACH 2025, github.com/Codium-ai/cover-agent, howtheytest abhivaikar.github.io]

55. **Vitest 4.1 `coverage.changed` prevents false "green coverage" on unchanged files in PRs** [community] — The `coverage.changed` option (Vitest 4.1) runs all tests but reports coverage only for files modified in the current branch. Without this option, a PR that adds 50 new lines to `orders.service.ts` but deletes 50 lines from `legacy-billing.service.ts` may show 85% overall coverage while the new `orders.service.ts` code has 0% coverage — the aggregate hides the gap. With `coverage.changed: true`, the coverage report surfaces only the changed files, making PR-level coverage reviews actionable. Combine with `coverage.thresholds` on the changed-only report to enforce per-PR minimums: `{ coverage: { changed: true, thresholds: { lines: 80 } } }`. [community: vitest.dev/blog/vitest-4-1.html, vitest.dev/config/coverage#coverage-changed]

56. **Node.js 26 test runner `isolation: 'none'` reveals hidden shared-state coupling at unit level** [community] — Running `node --test --experimental-test-isolation=none` disables per-file process isolation and runs all test files in the same Node.js process. On a well-isolated test suite, this should produce identical results to the default `'process'` isolation. When results differ (tests pass in isolation but fail together), the discrepancy reveals **module-singleton state leakage** — a module was modified by one test file and the mutation persisted into the next file. Use `isolation: 'none'` as a diagnostic tool: add it to a CI job on a weekly schedule; if results diverge from the main test run, a state-leaking test file has been introduced. The fix is almost always a missing `afterEach(() => jest.resetModules())` or a missing singleton reset in the module's test helpers. [community: nodejs.org/api/test.html#isolation, production debugging patterns TypeScript 2026]

57. **Bun's `--isolate` at the integration level must be combined with explicit `setDefaultTimeout()` or tests time out silently** [community] — When Bun 1.3 spawns a fresh process per test file with `--isolate`, the default test timeout applies to each test *within* that file. Integration tests using Testcontainers or real database connections often exceed Bun's default timeout (5 seconds). Unlike Vitest, which surfaces a clear "Test timed out" message with the test name, Bun's isolated process exits with code 1 and no output when the timeout is hit — the CI log shows a bare process exit, not a named failure. The fix is to call `setDefaultTimeout(60_000)` (or use `jest.setTimeout` for Jest compat) at the top of every integration test file when using Bun `--isolate`, or set it in `bunfig.toml` under `[test] timeout = 60000`. [community: bun.sh/docs/cli/test#timeout, production experience Bun 1.3 --isolate TypeScript 2026]

58. **Playwright `test.abort()` attribution: failures appear as "test interrupted" in reports, not "assertion failed"** [community] — When `testInfo.abort()` is called from a fixture, Playwright reports the test result as `interrupted` in the HTML report and JUnit XML — not `failed`. This distinction matters for CI merge gates that filter on `failedCount > 0`: an `interruptedCount > 0` may not trigger the gate. Teams using `test.abort()` for invariant enforcement (no 5xx responses, no console errors) must update their merge gate condition to treat `interrupted` tests as failures. In GitHub Actions with the official Playwright reporter, add `--reporter=github` and configure the branch protection rule to require the `playwright` check to pass — the GitHub reporter marks interrupted tests as failures in the Actions summary. ### Node.js 26.x `run()` Built-in Sharding and Coverage Thresholds

The Node.js `node:test` `run()` function gained several pyramid-relevant configuration options in the v25–v26 release series that are not widely known. These enable distributing tests across CI shards and enforcing per-metric coverage thresholds entirely within the built-in test runner — no external orchestration layer needed.

**Sharding** (`shard: { index, total }`) splits the test file list across N parallel CI jobs deterministically. Unlike Vitest's `--shard` flag (which is a CLI option), the Node.js `run()` shard option is a programmatic API, suitable for monorepos where a custom test entry-point script controls test discovery.

**Per-metric coverage thresholds** (`lineCoverage`, `branchCoverage`, `functionCoverage`) complement the existing `coverage: true` option and cause the process to exit with code 1 when any threshold is not met — enabling pyramid-level coverage gates without a separate tool.

```typescript
// test-runner.ts — custom entry point using node:test run() API (Node.js 26.x)
// Run with: node --experimental-test-coverage test-runner.ts
import { run } from 'node:test';
import { spec } from 'node:test/reporters';
import { pipeline } from 'node:stream/promises';

const shardIndex = parseInt(process.env.CI_SHARD_INDEX ?? '1', 10);
const shardTotal = parseInt(process.env.CI_SHARD_TOTAL ?? '1', 10);

await pipeline(
  run({
    // Shard: CI_SHARD_INDEX=2 CI_SHARD_TOTAL=4 → this runner processes 1/4 of test files
    shard: { index: shardIndex, total: shardTotal },

    // Coverage thresholds: fail the process (exit code 1) if any metric falls below these values
    coverage: true,
    lineCoverage: 80,
    branchCoverage: 75,
    functionCoverage: 80,
    coverageIncludeGlobs: ['src/**/*.ts'],
    coverageExcludeGlobs: ['src/**/*.d.ts', 'src/**/*.test.ts'],

    // Randomise test order to surface hidden order-dependencies (Node.js 26.1.0)
    randomize: true,

    // Per-test timeout (default: Infinity)
    timeout: 30_000,

    // Persist the list of failed test files for --only-failures reruns
    rerunFailuresFilePath: '.node-test-failures.json',
  }),
  spec,
  process.stdout,
);
```

**Pyramid placement:** the `shard` option operates at the test-file level, not the test-case level — all three pyramid levels (unit, integration, e2e) can be sharded this way. For mixed-suite monorepos, run unit and integration test files in a single sharded job (fast, many files) and keep e2e test files in a separate job so coverage thresholds are computed independently per level.

[official: nodejs.org/api/test.html — run() options v25.6.0–v26.1.0]

### Vitest 4.1 `viteModuleRunner: false` — Production-Parity Test Mode

Vitest's default execution environment runs test files inside Vite's module runner sandbox. This provides features like HMR-aware mocking and path alias transformation but introduces a subtle pyramid risk: **module evaluation semantics in the sandbox can differ from the Node.js production runtime**, particularly around singleton module state, dynamic `import()` timing, and ESM/CJS interop.

Vitest 4.1 introduced the experimental `viteModuleRunner: false` option, which bypasses the Vite sandbox and runs test files with native Node.js imports. This is the closest a Vitest unit or integration test case can get to the same module evaluation environment used in production — a significant confidence gain for tests that rely on module initialisation side effects (e.g., class-based DI containers, database connection singletons, middleware registration).

**Requirements:**
- Node.js 22.15+ (for module mocking support in native-import mode)
- ESM test files (no `require()` calls in test helpers)
- Path aliases must be resolvable by Node.js (`--import ./register-aliases.mjs`) or configured via `tsconfig` `paths` resolved by `--experimental-require-module`

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — enable production-parity mode for integration tests
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // Split test projects: unit tests use default (fast, Vite sandbox),
    // integration tests use native Node.js imports (production parity)
    projects: [
      {
        test: {
          name: 'unit',
          include: ['src/**/*.unit.test.ts'],
          // Default: viteModuleRunner: true — Vite sandbox for fast mocking
        },
      },
      {
        test: {
          name: 'integration',
          include: ['src/**/*.integration.test.ts'],
          // Experimental: native Node.js imports — no Vite sandbox
          // Requires Node.js 22.15+ for vi.mock() support in this mode
          experimentalVmWorkers: false, // deprecated alias; use viteModuleRunner
          // @ts-expect-error — experimental option not yet in types as of 4.1.6
          viteModuleRunner: false,
          environment: 'node',
          pool: 'forks', // forks pool required for native-import isolation
        },
      },
    ],
  },
});
```

**When NOT to use `viteModuleRunner: false`:**
- Test files that rely on Vitest's `vi.mock()` hoisting (hoisting requires Vite transformation) — switch to explicit `vi.doMock()` instead
- Tests using `.vue`, `.jsx`, or `.svelte` imports — Vite transforms are required for framework files
- Rapid TDD loops where the Vite sandbox's HMR-aware caching gives meaningful speedups

**Production gotcha:** `viteModuleRunner: false` silently disables `vi.mock()` calls that were previously hoisted. The mock call still executes but the factory runs *after* module evaluation, meaning the actual module is imported before the mock takes effect. The symptom is a test that passes in CI (where `viteModuleRunner: true`) but fails when `viteModuleRunner: false` is enabled — or vice versa. Always pair the switch with a full `vi.mock()` audit. [official: vitest.dev/blog/vitest-4-1.html#experimental-vmModuleRunner]

### Node.js 26.1.0 Randomization API: The `describe`/`it` Restriction

The `--test-randomize` flag (Node.js 26.1.0) and the `randomize: true` option in `run()` are the canonical tools for detecting **order-dependent test cases** at the unit and integration levels. However, they contain a non-obvious restriction that causes silent no-ops in many codebases:

**Randomization only applies to sibling `describe`/`it` blocks registered in the same event-loop turn.** Sequentially `await`-ed subtests (`await t.test(...)`) are not reordered because the runtime cannot know the full sibling set before the first subtest starts executing.

```typescript
// tests/unit/math.test.ts — Node.js built-in test runner
import { describe, it, test } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

// ✅ These WILL be randomised by --test-randomize
// All siblings are registered synchronously before any runs
describe('addition', () => {
  it('handles zero', () => { assert.equal(0 + 0, 0); });
  it('handles positive', () => { assert.equal(1 + 2, 3); });
  it('handles negative', () => { assert.equal(-1 + -2, -3); });
});

// ❌ These will NOT be randomised — sequential awaiting locks the order
test('sequential subtests', async (t) => {
  // Order is fixed: 'step a' always runs before 'step b'
  // --test-randomize has no effect here
  await t.test('step a', () => { /* ... */ });
  await t.test('step b', () => { /* ... */ });
});

// ✅ Fix: use Promise.all for parallel registration instead
test('parallel subtests — randomisable', async (t) => {
  // Both subtests are enqueued before either runs — eligible for randomisation
  await Promise.all([
    t.test('step a', () => { /* ... */ }),
    t.test('step b', () => { /* ... */ }),
  ]);
});
```

**Diagnostic workflow for hidden order-dependencies:**

```bash
# Step 1: Run with randomisation enabled, capture the seed
node --test --test-randomize 2>&1 | tee test-output.log
# Output includes: "Randomized test order seed: 7483920"

# Step 2: If tests fail, replay with the same seed to reproduce the failure
node --test --test-random-seed=7483920

# Step 3: Identify which test case produced stale state by running singletons
node --test --test-random-seed=7483920 --test-reporter=tap 2>&1 | grep -E 'not ok|ok [0-9]'
```

**Known limitation:** `--test-randomize` is incompatible with `--watch` mode. It also does not randomise test *cases within a single file* when that file uses the low-level procedural API (`test('name', fn)` at top-level) — those are subject to Node.js module evaluation order, not the randomizer. Use `describe`/`it` wrappers at all levels for randomisation to be effective.

[official: nodejs.org/api/test.html#randomization, community: production debugging Node.js 26 order-dependency detection 2026]

59. **Node.js `run()` `rerunFailuresFilePath` used as permanent state accumulates stale failures** [community] — The `rerunFailuresFilePath` option (Node.js 26.x) writes the list of failed test files to a JSON file after each run. On the next `run()` invocation with `--test-only` or a custom script reading this file, only those files are re-executed — a fast "fix and verify" loop. The gotcha: if the failure file is committed to source control or persisted across CI jobs in a shared artifact store, stale failure paths from a previous PR accumulate. The next PR's CI run re-executes those deleted or renamed test files, gets "no tests found" errors, and may silently treat them as passing. Fix: always delete `rerunFailuresFilePath` at the start of each fresh CI run (`rm -f .node-test-failures.json`) and never commit it. [community: nodejs.org/api/test.html — rerunFailuresFilePath, production experience Node.js 26 CI pipelines 2026]

60. **Vitest 4.1 `--detect-async-leaks` at the integration test level identifies container teardown gaps** [community] — The `--detect-async-leaks` flag uses `node:async_hooks` to track async resources (timers, handles, unresolved Promises) that are still active when a test case ends. At the unit level this catches forgotten `setTimeout` calls and unresolved mock Promises. At the integration test level it serves a more valuable purpose: detecting **Testcontainers teardown gaps** — a database container `afterAll()` hook that throws silently leaves the Docker container running, the `DataSource` connection open, and the Vitest worker hanging until the test suite times out. With `--detect-async-leaks`, the worker immediately reports the leaked async resource (the open TCP socket to the container) with its allocation stack trace, pointing directly to the missing `await dataSource.destroy()` call. This transforms a 60-second CI timeout into a 2-second diagnostic. [community: vitest.dev/blog/vitest-4-1.html#detect-async-leaks, production Vitest + Testcontainers TypeScript 2026]

61. **Bun 1.3 `--only-failures` reruns exactly the test cases that failed in the previous run** [community] — Bun persists failed test results in `.bun-test-results` (a JSON file in the project root) and the `--only-failures` flag re-executes only the test cases from that file. Unlike Vitest's `--changed` (which operates on modified *files*) or the Node.js `rerunFailuresFilePath` (which operates on failed *files*), Bun's `--only-failures` operates at the *test case* level — if a file had 100 passing tests and 1 failing test, only the 1 failing test case is re-executed. This dramatically reduces the feedback loop for integration test suites where a single test case failure requires iterating on a slow database fixture: instead of re-running the full integration suite (30+ seconds), the developer re-runs just the failing test case (3–5 seconds). **Pyramid placement:** most valuable at the integration level where test case execution time is asymmetric. At the unit level, the speed difference is negligible (all unit tests run in milliseconds). **Gotcha:** `.bun-test-results` is only updated when `bun test` completes successfully *for at least one test case*. A syntax error that prevents the test file from loading does not update the results file — `--only-failures` will re-run the stale set from the previous valid run, masking the new syntax error. [community: bun.sh/docs/cli/test#only-failures, bun.sh/blog/bun-v1.3]

62. **TypeScript 5.9 `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` default: typed array access in test factories produces `T | undefined` everywhere** [community] — TypeScript 5.9's new `tsc --init` defaults include `noUncheckedIndexedAccess: true`. When a project's `tsconfig.json` inherits from a parent that was regenerated with `tsc --init`, this option silently propagates into the test tsconfig. The result: every array index access in test factories, fixtures, and builders returns `T | undefined` instead of `T`. This breaks typed test object builders that use `items[0]` as an input to `expect()`:

```typescript
// Before TypeScript 5.9 noUncheckedIndexedAccess: error is silent
// After: TS2532 — Object is possibly 'undefined'
const orders = await repo.findAll();
expect(orders[0].id).toBe('order-001'); // TS error: orders[0] is Order | undefined

// Fix option 1: non-null assertion (acceptable in test code — you control the fixture)
expect(orders[0]!.id).toBe('order-001');

// Fix option 2: explicit length assertion before indexed access (preferred for integration tests)
expect(orders).toHaveLength(1);
const [firstOrder] = orders; // destructuring is safe — no undefined risk
expect(firstOrder.id).toBe('order-001');

// Fix option 3: add noUncheckedIndexedAccess: false to test tsconfig.json only
// tsconfig.test.json:
// { "extends": "../tsconfig.json", "compilerOptions": { "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": false } }
// This avoids noise from the noUncheckedIndexedAccess rule in tests while keeping it in src/
```

**Recommended test tsconfig pattern for TypeScript 5.9+ projects:**

```json
{
  "extends": "../tsconfig.json",
  "compilerOptions": {
    "types": ["vitest/globals", "node"],
    "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": false,
    "exactOptionalPropertyTypes": false,
    "module": "nodenext",
    "moduleResolution": "nodenext"
  },
  "include": ["**/*.test.ts", "**/*.spec.ts", "setup.ts"]
}
```

[community: typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-5-9.html, production TypeScript 5.9 test migration experience 2026]

63. **AI test selection (Instawork/Faire pattern) requires pyramid labelling to avoid selecting integration tests when unit tests suffice** [community] — Production implementations of AI-driven test selection (as deployed by Instawork and Faire per "How They Test" 2025–2026 edition) use a call-graph impact analysis to select which tests to run on a PR. The analysis works at the function/module call graph level — a change to `pricing.service.ts` propagates to all callers. Without pyramid-level labelling on test cases, the AI selector cannot distinguish a 2ms unit test case from a 30-second integration test case that happens to import `pricing.service.ts`. The result: the selector correctly identifies all affected tests but includes integration test cases that add 3–5 minutes to the PR feedback loop when a unit test case for the same logic exists.

**Fix: use Vitest test tags as pyramid labels, then configure the AI selector to prefer unit tests when integration tests cover the same test object:**

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — pyramid-level test tags for AI selector compatibility
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    projects: [
      {
        test: {
          name: 'unit',
          include: ['src/**/*.unit.test.ts'],
          // Tag all tests in this project as 'unit' for AI selector filtering
          // AI selector: run unit-tagged tests first; skip integration-tagged if unit coverage > threshold
        },
      },
      {
        test: {
          name: 'integration',
          include: ['src/**/*.integration.test.ts'],
          // AI selector: only run if no unit-tagged test covers the changed module
        },
      },
    ],
  },
});
```

```typescript
// src/pricing/pricing.service.unit.test.ts — explicit pyramid tag via Vitest test tags API
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { calculateDiscount } from './pricing.service.js';

// Tag 'unit' and 'pricing' — AI selector uses tags to classify pyramid level
describe.tags(['unit', 'pricing'])('PricingService — discount calculation', () => {
  it('applies 10% for standard members over $100 threshold', () => {
    expect(calculateDiscount({ tier: 'standard', total: 150 })).toBe(15);
  });
});
```

**Production outcome:** teams using pyramid-labelled tags report 60–80% reduction in average PR test execution time (consistent with Instawork and Faire data), with no regression in defect escape rate over a 12-month period. The key enabler is the label — without it, the AI selector cannot make the unit-before-integration preference decision. [community: howtheytest abhivaikar.github.io — Instawork, Faire case studies 2025-2026]

### 1. Jest 30 Explicit Resource Management — Automatic Spy Cleanup with `using`

Jest 30 (released June 2025) adopts the TC39 Explicit Resource Management proposal (`using` keyword) for spy lifecycle management. Previously, spies required a manual `jest.restoreAllMocks()` call in `afterEach` or relied on the `restoreMocks: true` config option. Forgetting the teardown caused hidden cross-test state contamination — a classic test isolation defect at the unit pyramid level.

With `using`, the spy is restored automatically when the block scope exits (whether normally or via exception), eliminating an entire class of test isolation defects without configuration ceremony.

**Pyramid relevance:** unit test cases must be isolated (FIRST principle: Independent). Leaked spy state caused order-dependent test failures that only appeared in CI batch runs — exactly the class of defect the `using` keyword eliminates.

```typescript
// Jest 30 — automatic spy cleanup with explicit resource management
// Requires Node.js 18+ (Symbol.dispose support) and Jest 30+
import { describe, expect, test, jest } from '@jest/globals';
import { auditLogger } from '../services/audit-logger.js';
import { createOrder } from '../domain/order.js';

describe('Order creation', () => {
  test('emits an audit log entry on success', () => {
    // using keyword: spy is automatically restored when this test scope exits
    // no afterEach(() => jest.restoreAllMocks()) needed
    using logSpy = jest.spyOn(auditLogger, 'log');

    createOrder({ productId: 'p1', quantity: 2, userId: 'u1' });

    expect(logSpy).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
      expect.objectContaining({ action: 'ORDER_CREATED', userId: 'u1' })
    );
    // logSpy.mockRestore() is called automatically here — no afterEach needed
  });

  test('does NOT emit audit log when validation fails', () => {
    // A fresh spy — previous test's spy was already restored
    using logSpy = jest.spyOn(auditLogger, 'log');

    expect(() => createOrder({ productId: '', quantity: -1, userId: 'u1' }))
      .toThrow('ValidationError');

    expect(logSpy).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
  });
});
```

**Migration note:** `jest.SpyInstance` type was removed in Jest 30. Use `jest.Spied<typeof obj.method>` for typed spy references in TypeScript.

[official: jestjs.io/docs/upgrading-to-jest30]

---

### 2. Jest 30 `expect.arrayOf` — Homogeneous Array Assertions at the Unit Level

Jest 30 introduced the `expect.arrayOf(matcher)` asymmetric matcher to validate that every element in an array satisfies a condition. Previously teams either wrote custom array `every()` assertions or accepted the weaker `expect.arrayContaining([...])` check (which only requires at least the listed elements to be present, not that all elements match).

`expect.arrayOf` enforces the constraint cleanly in a single assertion, eliminating the need for a forEach loop in integration test cases that receive paginated responses or collection endpoints.

```typescript
// Jest 30 — expect.arrayOf for homogeneous collection assertions
import { describe, expect, test } from '@jest/globals';
import { fetchProductCatalog } from '../api/catalog.js';

describe('GET /products — catalog endpoint', () => {
  test('returns a list where every item has required product fields', async () => {
    const response = await fetchProductCatalog({ page: 1, limit: 10 });

    // Before Jest 30: you needed a forEach loop or custom matcher
    // After: single assertion, concise and readable
    expect(response.items).toEqual(
      expect.arrayOf(
        expect.objectContaining({
          id: expect.any(String),
          name: expect.any(String),
          priceInCents: expect.any(Number),
          inStock: expect.any(Boolean),
        })
      )
    );

    // Pair with a length assertion to catch empty-list false positives
    // (arrayOf passes on an empty array — no elements to violate the constraint)
    expect(response.items.length).toBeGreaterThan(0);
  });

  test('price is never negative in catalog response', async () => {
    const response = await fetchProductCatalog({ page: 1, limit: 50 });

    // Use expect.arrayOf with a custom predicate via expect.objectContaining
    response.items.forEach(item => {
      expect(item.priceInCents).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(0);
    });

    // Equivalent asymmetric form (preferred for cleaner failure output):
    expect(response.items).toEqual(
      expect.arrayOf(expect.objectContaining({ priceInCents: expect.not.any(NaN) }))
    );
  });
});
```

**Gotcha:** `expect.arrayOf` passes vacuously on an empty array (`[]`) — always pair it with a length assertion when testing endpoints that should return non-empty collections. [community: Jest 30 beta user reports, GitHub jestjs/jest — issue discussions June 2025]

[official: jestjs.io/blog/ — Jest 30 release announcement]

### 3. Jest 30 `globalsCleanup` — Eliminating Memory Leaks Between Test Files

Jest 30 introduced a `globalsCleanup` option to address a chronic memory problem in large test suites: JavaScript globals added by test files (event listeners, timers, custom properties on `globalThis`) were never cleaned up between files in the same worker process. After dozens of test files ran in the same process, memory pressure caused GC pauses that inflated integration test case runtimes by 2–4x compared to running them in isolation.

```typescript
// jest.config.ts — enable globalsCleanup for large suites (Jest 30)
import type { Config } from 'jest';

const config: Config = {
  // 'on' = clean up all globals after each test file
  // 'soft' (default) = warn about uncleaned globals but don't fail
  // 'off' = legacy behavior (no warnings, no cleanup)
  testEnvironmentOptions: {
    globalsCleanup: 'on',
  },

  // Protect globals that are intentionally shared across files
  // (use the protectProperties() API from jest-util in setupFilesAfterEnv)
  setupFilesAfterEnv: ['<rootDir>/jest.setup.ts'],
};

export default config;
```

```typescript
// jest.setup.ts — protect intentional shared globals from cleanup
import { protectProperties } from 'jest-util';

// Protect a custom metric registry that is shared across all test files
// (it's intentionally stateful — a deliberate architectural choice)
protectProperties(globalThis['metrics-registry']);

// Protect MSW server instance shared between integration test files
protectProperties(globalThis['msw-server']);
```

**Pyramid impact:** enabling `globalsCleanup: 'on'` in a 400-file integration test suite reduced total CI run time by 18% in a reported production case, with no test failures introduced. The gotcha: any test code that deliberately pollutes globals for cross-file sharing (a test pyramid anti-pattern, but common with MSW server instances) must be wrapped in `protectProperties()`.

[official: jestjs.io/docs/upgrading-to-jest30 — globalsCleanup section]

### 4. Jest 30 Barrel File Penalty — Unit Test Startup Overhead

One of the most impactful community findings from the Jest 30 migration cycle: **barrel files (`index.ts` re-exporting everything) cause unit test startup time to scale O(N) with the number of exported symbols**, even when the test case only imports one function.

Jest's module resolution loads, transforms, and caches every module transitively imported by the barrel file. A barrel file with 80 re-exports in a medium-size codebase adds 400–800 ms of transform overhead per unit test file. At 200 unit test files, this can add 90+ seconds to the test run — before any test case logic executes.

```typescript
// ANTI-PATTERN: barrel file import in unit tests
// jest.transform must process all 80 modules even though only priceFor is needed
import { priceFor } from '../../services/index.js';

describe('priceFor', () => { /* ... */ });
```

```typescript
// PATTERN: direct import in unit tests — no barrel overhead
// Only pricing.service.ts and its direct dependencies are loaded
import { priceFor } from '../../services/pricing.service.js';

describe('priceFor', () => {
  test('applies volume discount for orders over 100 units', () => {
    expect(priceFor({ unitPrice: 10_00, quantity: 101 })).toBe(8_99);
  });

  test('returns unit price with no discount below threshold', () => {
    expect(priceFor({ unitPrice: 10_00, quantity: 99 })).toBe(10_00);
  });
});
```

**Tooling remedies for large codebases:**
- `babel-jest-boost` — intercepts barrel imports and resolves to direct paths
- `babel-plugin-transform-barrels` — compile-time barrel flattening
- `no-barrel-file` ESLint rule — prevents new barrel files from being introduced
- Vitest is less affected because its module resolution is Vite-based (ESM tree-shaking at the module graph level)

[community: Jest 30 performance analysis by the Jest core team (jestjs.io/blog), production benchmarks from babel-jest-boost GitHub repo, Nergie/no-barrel-file README]

### 5. Vitest 4.1 `aroundEach` / `aroundAll` — Transaction-Wrapped Integration Tests

Vitest 4.1 (March 2026) introduced `aroundEach` and `aroundAll` hooks that wrap test execution inside a user-controlled function. Unlike `beforeEach`/`afterEach` (two separate callbacks with no shared scope), `aroundEach` provides a single callback that calls `runTest()` in the middle — enabling patterns that are structurally impossible with split hooks, such as wrapping each integration test case inside a database transaction that is rolled back after the assertion.

**Pyramid relevance:** the standard integration test pyramid practice for database-touching tests is to run each test inside a rolled-back transaction (the "transactional test case" pattern from xUnit). Previously in Vitest, this required a fixture workaround. `aroundEach` makes it idiomatic.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — aroundEach for database transaction isolation
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    name: 'integration',
    include: ['src/**/*.integration.test.ts'],
    // aroundEach is defined per test file or in test.extend fixtures
  },
});
```

```typescript
// test/setup/db-transaction.ts — reusable aroundEach fixture for integration tests
import { test as baseTest } from 'vitest';
import { db } from '../../src/db/connection.js';

// Extend test with transaction fixture using aroundEach
export const test = baseTest.extend<{ _txIsolation: void }>({
  // aroundEach wraps every test in this extended test's suite
  _txIsolation: [
    async function ({ task }, runTest) {
      // BEGIN TRANSACTION before test
      await db.query('BEGIN');
      try {
        await runTest();
      } finally {
        // ROLLBACK regardless of test outcome — no state leaks between tests
        await db.query('ROLLBACK');
      }
    },
    { auto: true }, // auto-use: no need to declare in each test
  ],
});
```

```typescript
// src/orders/order-repository.integration.test.ts
import { describe, expect } from 'vitest';
import { test } from '../../test/setup/db-transaction.js';
import { OrderRepository } from './order-repository.js';

const repo = new OrderRepository(db);

describe('OrderRepository — write operations', () => {
  test('persists a new order and returns it with a generated id', async () => {
    const saved = await repo.create({ userId: 'u1', total: 99_99 });

    expect(saved.id).toMatch(/^ord_[a-z0-9]{12}$/);
    expect(saved.total).toBe(99_99);
    // Transaction is rolled back after this assertion — DB stays clean
  });

  test('throws NotFoundError when updating a non-existent order', async () => {
    await expect(repo.update('ord_nonexistent', { total: 50_00 }))
      .rejects.toThrow('NotFoundError');
    // Each test gets a fresh transaction — no state from previous test
  });
});
```

[official: vitest.dev/blog/vitest-4-1 — aroundEach/aroundAll hooks]

### 6. Vitest 4.1 `detectAsyncLeaks` — Flaky Test Root Cause Identification

Vitest 4.1 added a `--detect-async-leaks` CLI flag (and `detectAsyncLeaks: true` config option) that uses Node.js `async_hooks` to report leaked async resources with source locations. A "leaked async resource" is any `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, unresolved `Promise`, open file handle, or network socket that was created during a test but not resolved before the test ended.

**Pyramid impact:** async leaks are one of the top 3 root causes of flaky integration tests. They manifest as tests that pass in isolation but fail intermittently in parallel CI runs (a leaked timer from test A fires during test B's assertion phase). `detectAsyncLeaks` converts these invisible failures into actionable source-location warnings.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — enable async leak detection (Vitest 4.1)
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // Enable for integration test project where async leaks are most common
    detectAsyncLeaks: true,

    // Example output when a leak is detected:
    // LEAK: Timer (setTimeout) created at:
    //   at setupRetryPoller (src/infra/retry-poller.ts:42:5)
    //   at RetryService.start (src/domain/retry.service.ts:18:3)
    //   at Object.<anonymous> (src/orders/order.service.integration.test.ts:55:5)
  },
});
```

```typescript
// src/orders/order-service.integration.test.ts — fixing a detected leak
import { describe, it, expect, beforeEach, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { OrderService } from './order-service.js';

let service: OrderService;

beforeEach(() => {
  service = new OrderService();
  service.startRetryPoller(); // creates a setInterval internally
});

afterEach(async () => {
  // Without this, detectAsyncLeaks reports a Timer leak from startRetryPoller
  await service.stopRetryPoller(); // clears the setInterval
});

describe('OrderService retry behavior', () => {
  it('retries a failed delivery after the backoff window', async () => {
    const result = await service.scheduleDelivery({ orderId: 'o1' });
    expect(result.status).toBe('scheduled');
  });
});
```

**Known limitation:** `detectAsyncLeaks` reports warnings, not hard failures. Add `expect.assertions(N)` or a custom post-test checker if you want hard failures on leaks. A future Vitest release is expected to support `detectAsyncLeaks: 'error'` mode. [community: Vitest GitHub issue #7421 — detectAsyncLeaks feature request and design discussion]

[official: vitest.dev/blog/vitest-4-1 — detectAsyncLeaks config]

### 7. Vitest 4.1 Test Tag Filter Syntax — Pyramid-Level Selective Execution

Vitest 4.1 introduced a structured tag filter language for selecting tests by pyramid level (or any other label) during development. The filter supports boolean operators (`and`/`&&`, `or`/`||`, `not`/`!`), wildcard patterns (`*`), and grouping with parentheses — enabling precise test selection without naming convention hacks.

**Before (Vitest 3.x):** teams used file-path patterns or `--grep` regex to filter by pyramid level, which required a strict naming convention and broke when test names contained special characters.

**After (Vitest 4.1):** use `--tags-filter` with declarative boolean logic.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — declare tag metadata for unit and integration projects
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    projects: [
      {
        test: {
          name: 'unit',
          include: ['src/**/*.unit.test.ts'],
          // All tests in this project inherit the 'unit' tag automatically
          // when describe.tags(['unit']) is used at the suite level
        },
      },
      {
        test: {
          name: 'integration',
          include: ['src/**/*.integration.test.ts'],
        },
      },
    ],
  },
});
```

```typescript
// src/pricing/pricing-engine.unit.test.ts — tag declaration
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { applyTieredDiscount } from './pricing-engine.js';

// Pyramid-level tag: 'unit'. Feature area tag: 'pricing'.
// Also tag 'fast' to enable: vitest --tags-filter="unit and fast"
describe.tags(['unit', 'pricing', 'fast'])('PricingEngine', () => {
  it('returns 0% discount below minimum threshold', () => {
    expect(applyTieredDiscount(50_00, 'standard')).toBe(50_00);
  });

  it('returns 10% discount for standard tier above threshold', () => {
    expect(applyTieredDiscount(150_00, 'standard')).toBe(135_00);
  });
});
```

```bash
# Selective execution examples using Vitest 4.1 tag filter language
# Run all unit tests (CI fast path — feedback in < 30s):
vitest --tags-filter="unit"

# Run integration tests excluding slow DB migration tests:
vitest --tags-filter="integration and !db-migration"

# Run all tests tagged pricing OR checkout (feature area regression):
vitest --tags-filter="pricing or checkout"

# Run fast unit tests for CI pre-commit hook (< 5 seconds):
vitest --tags-filter="unit and fast"

# Run all tests except flaky-quarantine:
vitest --tags-filter="!flaky-quarantine"
```

[official: vitest.dev/blog/vitest-4-1 — Test Tags section]

### 8. Vitest 4.0 Browser Mode Stabilized — Pyramid Tier for Component Tests

Vitest 4.0 (October 2025) promoted Browser Mode from experimental to stable. The provider packages were split into separate packages (`@vitest/browser-playwright`, `@vitest/browser-webdriverio`, `@vitest/browser-preview`), reducing the core bundle size and making the browser tier of the test pyramid an explicit, first-class project dependency.

**Pyramid positioning:** Vitest Browser Mode occupies the gap between unit tests (Node.js, jsdom) and full Playwright e2e tests. It renders components in a real browser (Chromium, Firefox, WebKit via Playwright provider) but without the application routing layer. Recommended pyramid tier: **component integration tests** (faster than e2e, higher confidence than jsdom-based tests).

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — three-tier pyramid with Vitest browser mode as middle layer
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
import { playwright } from '@vitest/browser-playwright';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    projects: [
      // Tier 1: Unit tests — Node.js environment, fastest feedback
      {
        test: {
          name: 'unit',
          include: ['src/**/*.unit.test.ts'],
          environment: 'node',
        },
      },

      // Tier 2: Browser component tests — real browser, no server
      // Uses Playwright provider; renders components in Chromium
      {
        test: {
          name: 'browser',
          include: ['src/**/*.browser.test.ts'],
          browser: {
            provider: playwright(),
            enabled: true,
            instances: [{ browser: 'chromium' }],
          },
        },
      },

      // Tier 3: Full e2e tests — handled by Playwright Test directly
      // (separate playwright.config.ts, runs against dev server)
    ],
  },
});
```

```typescript
// src/components/ProductCard.browser.test.ts — browser mode component test
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { mount } from '@vitest/browser/context';
import { ProductCard } from './ProductCard.js';

describe('ProductCard — browser component test', () => {
  it('renders the product name and price', async () => {
    // mount() renders in a real Chromium tab — not jsdom simulation
    const wrapper = await mount(ProductCard, {
      props: {
        name: 'Wireless Keyboard',
        priceInCents: 7999,
        inStock: true,
      },
    });

    // Playwright-backed locators — same API as e2e tests
    await expect.element(wrapper.getByRole('heading')).toHaveText('Wireless Keyboard');
    await expect.element(wrapper.getByTestId('price')).toHaveText('$79.99');
    await expect.element(wrapper.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' }))
      .toBeEnabled();
  });

  it('shows out-of-stock badge and disables cart button when not available', async () => {
    const wrapper = await mount(ProductCard, {
      props: { name: 'Sold Out Item', priceInCents: 1999, inStock: false },
    });

    await expect.element(wrapper.getByText('Out of stock')).toBeVisible();
    await expect.element(wrapper.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' }))
      .toBeDisabled();
  });
});
```

**Visual regression testing:** Vitest 4.0 added `toMatchScreenshot()` for pixel-diff assertions inside browser mode test cases, removing the need for a separate visual regression tool at the component level:

```typescript
it('matches approved design for in-stock state', async () => {
  const wrapper = await mount(ProductCard, {
    props: { name: 'Keyboard', priceInCents: 7999, inStock: true },
  });

  // Generates a baseline screenshot on first run, diffs on subsequent runs
  await expect(wrapper.locator('body')).toMatchScreenshot('product-card-in-stock');
});
```

[official: vitest.dev/blog/vitest-4 — Browser Mode stable, @vitest/browser-playwright package]

### 9. Vitest 3.2 `projects` Replaces `workspace` + `sequence.groupOrder`

Vitest 3.2 (June 2025) deprecated the standalone `vitest.workspace.ts` file in favor of an inline `projects` array in `vitest.config.ts`. The workspace file approach caused naming conflicts with PNPM workspace manifests and other monorepo tools. The `workspace` config key was simultaneously introduced as a compatibility alias, but `projects` is the canonical form.

Additionally, Vitest 3.2 added `sequence.groupOrder` — a number assigned to each project that controls execution order. Projects with the same group number run concurrently; groups run sequentially from lowest to highest. This enables the pyramid's fastest-feedback-first principle without CI parallelization overhead.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — inline projects with sequence.groupOrder (Vitest 3.2+)
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    projects: [
      // Group 1: unit tests — run first, always (fastest, fewest deps)
      {
        test: {
          name: { label: 'unit', color: 'green' },
          include: ['src/**/*.unit.test.ts'],
          environment: 'node',
          sequence: { groupOrder: 1 },
        },
      },

      // Group 2: integration tests — run after group 1 completes
      {
        test: {
          name: { label: 'integration', color: 'yellow' },
          include: ['src/**/*.integration.test.ts'],
          environment: 'node',
          sequence: { groupOrder: 2 },
        },
      },

      // Group 3: browser component tests — run last (slowest startup)
      {
        test: {
          name: { label: 'browser', color: 'blue' },
          include: ['src/**/*.browser.test.ts'],
          sequence: { groupOrder: 3 },
        },
      },
    ],
  },
});
```

**Migration from workspace file:**

```bash
# Before Vitest 3.2 (workspace file approach — now deprecated):
# vitest.workspace.ts exists separately with defineWorkspace([...])

# After Vitest 3.2 (inline projects in root config):
# Delete vitest.workspace.ts, move defineWorkspace content to vitest.config.ts test.projects
```

[official: vitest.dev/blog/vitest-3-2 — Projects Configuration section]

### 10. Vitest 3.2 Scoped Fixtures — `file` and `worker` Scope in `test.extend`

Vitest 3.2 added `scope` options to the `test.extend` fixture API, enabling fixture instances to be shared at the file level or worker level instead of recreated for every test case. This addresses a common integration test performance problem: heavyweight setup (database connection pools, HTTP clients, in-process servers) was being instantiated per test case even when the setup was idempotent.

```typescript
// test/fixtures/db.ts — scoped fixtures for integration test performance
import { test as baseTest } from 'vitest';
import { Pool } from 'pg';
import { buildTestDatabase } from './db-builder.js';

export const test = baseTest.extend<
  { db: Pool; schema: string },
  { dbPool: Pool } // worker-scoped fixtures are typed in the second type param
>({
  // worker-scoped fixture: ONE pool instance shared across all test files
  // in this worker process — avoids creating N pools for N test files
  dbPool: [
    async function (_, use) {
      const pool = new Pool({ connectionString: process.env.TEST_DATABASE_URL });
      await use(pool);
      await pool.end();
    },
    { scope: 'worker' },
  ],

  // file-scoped fixture: ONE schema per test file — avoids schema creation
  // overhead on every test case while still isolating files from each other
  schema: [
    async function ({ dbPool }, use) {
      const schemaName = `test_${Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 10)}`;
      await buildTestDatabase(dbPool, schemaName);
      await use(schemaName);
      await dbPool.query(`DROP SCHEMA ${schemaName} CASCADE`);
    },
    { scope: 'file' },
  ],

  // test-scoped fixture (default): fresh connection per test case
  db: async function ({ dbPool, schema }, use) {
    const client = await dbPool.connect();
    await client.query(`SET search_path TO ${schema}`);
    await use(dbPool);
    client.release();
  },
});
```

```typescript
// src/users/user-repo.integration.test.ts — benefits from scoped fixtures
import { describe, expect } from 'vitest';
import { test } from '../../test/fixtures/db.js';

describe('UserRepository', () => {
  test('creates a user with hashed password', async ({ db }) => {
    // db is a fresh connection; schema was created once for this entire file
    const user = await db.query(
      'INSERT INTO users (email) VALUES ($1) RETURNING *',
      ['alice@example.com']
    );
    expect(user.rows[0].email).toBe('alice@example.com');
  });
});
```

**Performance benchmark:** migrating a 120-test integration suite from test-scoped DB connections to file-scoped schema + worker-scoped pool reduced per-test-file setup time from ~800 ms to ~40 ms per file (the pool is already warm). [community: Vitest 3.2 release discussion, user reports in vitest-dev/vitest GitHub — Scoped fixtures RFC]

[official: vitest.dev/blog/vitest-3-2 — Scoped Fixtures section]

### 11. Playwright Component Testing — `router` Fixture for MSW Integration

Playwright Component Testing (CT) introduced an experimental `router` fixture in v1.46 that enables network interception inside component tests without a running server. The `router.use(handlers)` method accepts Mock Service Worker (MSW) handlers — the same handlers used in unit and integration tests — creating a pyramid-level shared mock layer.

**Pyramid benefit:** sharing MSW handler definitions between unit, component, and integration test cases ensures that the mock contract is consistent across all pyramid levels. A change to the handler automatically propagates to all levels, removing the risk of divergent mocks.

```typescript
// src/mocks/handlers.ts — MSW handlers shared across all pyramid levels
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw';

export const productHandlers = [
  http.get('/api/products/:id', ({ params }) => {
    if (params.id === 'p999') {
      return HttpResponse.json({ error: 'Not Found' }, { status: 404 });
    }
    return HttpResponse.json({
      id: params.id,
      name: 'Test Product',
      priceInCents: 2999,
    });
  }),
];
```

```typescript
// src/components/ProductDetail.ct.test.ts — Playwright CT with router fixture
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/experimental-ct-react';
import { productHandlers } from '../mocks/handlers.js';
import { ProductDetail } from './ProductDetail.js';

test.describe('ProductDetail component', () => {
  test('renders product data from API', async ({ mount, router }) => {
    // Share the same MSW handlers used in unit and integration tests
    await router.use(...productHandlers);

    const component = await mount(<ProductDetail productId="p1" />);

    await expect(component.getByRole('heading')).toContainText('Test Product');
    await expect(component.getByTestId('price')).toHaveText('$29.99');
  });

  test('shows error state when product is not found', async ({ mount, router }) => {
    await router.use(...productHandlers); // p999 returns 404 per handler

    const component = await mount(<ProductDetail productId="p999" />);

    await expect(component.getByRole('alert')).toHaveText('Product not found');
  });
});
```

**Gotcha:** the `router` fixture is component-test-scoped — handlers set in one test case do not leak into the next test case. This differs from the `page.route()` API in e2e tests, where routes persist for the lifetime of the page. [community: Playwright CT users, GitHub microsoft/playwright — CT router fixture PR #27566]

[official: playwright.dev/docs/test-components — router fixture (v1.46+)]

### 12. Playwright `--only-changed` — Pyramid-Aware CI for Affected Test Files

Playwright v1.46 added `--only-changed` (and `--only-changed=<base-branch>`) flags that run only test files that were modified or that import changed source files. This is a pyramid-level CI optimization: instead of running the full e2e suite on every PR commit, only the e2e test cases most likely to catch the regression are executed.

```bash
# CI workflow: run only e2e tests affected by changes on this PR branch
# Compares current branch to origin/main to determine changed files
npx playwright test --only-changed=origin/main

# Local development: run only tests affected by your unstaged/staged changes
npx playwright test --only-changed
```

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — structure for --only-changed to work efficiently
// Tests must import source files directly (not via server URL) for the import
// graph to be traversable. Use importProject from @playwright/test utilities.
import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  testDir: './e2e',
  use: {
    baseURL: 'http://localhost:5173',
    trace: 'on-first-retry',
  },
  projects: [
    {
      name: 'chromium',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] },
    },
  ],
  // Web server must be running for --only-changed to execute the selected tests
  webServer: {
    command: 'npm run dev',
    url: 'http://localhost:5173',
    reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI,
  },
});
```

**Pyramid strategy for `--only-changed`:**

| CI trigger | Recommended test scope |
|------------|----------------------|
| Pre-commit hook | Unit tests only (< 30s) |
| PR push (every commit) | Unit + integration + `--only-changed` e2e |
| PR merge to main | Full unit + integration + full e2e suite |
| Nightly CI | Full suite + performance baseline |

**Gotcha:** `--only-changed` traces the TypeScript/JavaScript import graph. If your e2e tests use page object models that import shared utility modules, a change to one utility may select more e2e test files than expected. Use `--reporter=list` to inspect which files were selected before relying on this in production CI. [community: Playwright GitHub discussions — --only-changed practical usage]

[official: playwright.dev/docs/release-notes — v1.46 --only-changed flag]

### 13. Google TotT: "Construct with Collaborators, Call with Work" — DI Pattern for Testable Units

A May 2026 Google Testing on the Toilet (TotT) post by Shahar Roth articulated a concise design principle for writing testable code at the unit level: **inject complex collaborators at construction time, pass simple value objects at call time.** This principle has direct pyramid implications: it defines the natural seam at which to mock during unit test cases versus integration test cases.

**The principle:**
- **Construct with collaborators:** pass service dependencies (`database`, `emailService`, `clock`) into the constructor or factory function, not into method calls.
- **Call with work:** pass simple, serializable data (`orderId`, `timestamp`, `config`) into method calls, not services.

When a class follows this principle, its unit test cases can inject fake collaborators at construction time (making the class easy to test in isolation), and its integration test cases can inject real collaborators to test the interaction boundary.

```typescript
// ANTI-PATTERN: collaborator passed at call time — hard to unit test
class OrderProcessor {
  async process(order: Order, database: Database, emailer: EmailService): Promise<void> {
    await database.save(order);
    await emailer.sendConfirmation(order.userId, order.id);
  }
}
// Unit test must provide real or mocked Database AND EmailService on every call
```

```typescript
// PATTERN: collaborators injected at construction, work passed at call time
class OrderProcessor {
  constructor(
    private readonly database: Database,
    private readonly emailer: EmailService,
    private readonly clock: Clock = systemClock,
  ) {}

  async process(order: Order): Promise<ProcessResult> {
    const savedOrder = await this.database.save({
      ...order,
      processedAt: this.clock.now(),
    });
    await this.emailer.sendConfirmation(savedOrder.userId, savedOrder.id);
    return { orderId: savedOrder.id, status: 'processed' };
  }
}
```

```typescript
// Unit test: inject fake collaborators at construction — no mocking framework needed
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { OrderProcessor } from './order-processor.js';

const fakeDatabase = {
  save: async (order: Order) => ({ ...order, id: 'ord_test_001' }),
};
const fakeEmailer = {
  sendConfirmation: async () => { /* no-op */ },
};
const fixedClock = { now: () => new Date('2026-01-01T00:00:00Z') };

describe('OrderProcessor.process() — unit', () => {
  it('returns a ProcessResult with the saved order id', async () => {
    const processor = new OrderProcessor(fakeDatabase, fakeEmailer, fixedClock);
    const result = await processor.process({ userId: 'u1', total: 99_99 });
    expect(result).toEqual({ orderId: 'ord_test_001', status: 'processed' });
  });

  it('stamps processedAt with the clock time', async () => {
    const saved: Order[] = [];
    const capturingDatabase = {
      save: async (order: Order) => { saved.push(order); return { ...order, id: 'x' }; },
    };
    const processor = new OrderProcessor(capturingDatabase, fakeEmailer, fixedClock);
    await processor.process({ userId: 'u2', total: 50_00 });
    expect(saved[0].processedAt).toEqual(new Date('2026-01-01T00:00:00Z'));
  });
});
```

**Pyramid corollary:** a class that violates "Construct with Collaborators" by accepting service objects at call time cannot be unit tested without mocking framework involvement — every call site must provide mocked services. This forces test pyramid inflation: developers reach for integration test cases (where real services are available) instead of unit test cases, causing an inverted pyramid. [community: Google Testing Blog TotT series — "Construct with Collaborators, Call with Work" (May 2026), Shahar Roth]

[official: testing.googleblog.com — May 2026 TotT post]

### 14. Jest 30 CLI Migration — `--testPathPatterns` Plural and `--init` Removal

Jest 30 renamed `--testPathPattern` (singular) to `--testPathPatterns` (plural, accepts multiple values) and removed `jest --init` in favor of `npm init jest@latest`. These are breaking changes that affect CI pipeline scripts and `package.json` scripts in any project that upgraded from Jest 29.

```bash
# BEFORE (Jest 29) — singular flag, accepted one regex
jest --testPathPattern="src/unit/.*"

# AFTER (Jest 30) — plural flag, accepts multiple patterns
jest --testPathPatterns "src/unit/.*" "src/integration/.*"

# CI pyramid example: run only unit tests in fast path
jest --testPathPatterns ".*\\.unit\\.test\\.ts$"

# CI pyramid example: run integration tests excluding slow fixtures
jest --testPathPatterns ".*\\.integration\\.test\\.ts$" --testNamePattern="^(?!.*slow).*"
```

```typescript
// package.json scripts migration — Jest 29 → Jest 30
// BEFORE:
{
  "scripts": {
    "test:unit": "jest --testPathPattern='src/.+\\.unit\\.test\\.ts'",
    "test:integration": "jest --testPathPattern='src/.+\\.integration\\.test\\.ts'",
    "test:init": "jest --init"
  }
}

// AFTER (Jest 30):
{
  "scripts": {
    "test:unit": "jest --testPathPatterns 'src/.+\\.unit\\.test\\.ts'",
    "test:integration": "jest --testPathPatterns 'src/.+\\.integration\\.test\\.ts'",
    "test:init": "npm init jest@latest"
  }
}
```

**Additional Jest 30 matcher renames:** all deprecated alias matchers were removed. The `eslint-plugin-jest` `no-alias-methods` rule should be enabled and run as part of the migration to catch any remaining usages automatically:

```typescript
// jest.eslint.config.ts — enable Jest 30 migration rules
import jestPlugin from 'eslint-plugin-jest';

export default [
  {
    plugins: { jest: jestPlugin },
    rules: {
      // Fails on removed Jest 30 aliases: toBeCalled → toHaveBeenCalled, etc.
      'jest/no-alias-methods': 'error',
    },
  },
];
```

[official: jestjs.io/docs/upgrading-to-jest30 — CLI changes section]

### 15. Node.js Test Runner Decision Guide — `node:test` vs Vitest vs Jest (2026)

For teams starting new TypeScript projects in 2026, the choice of test runner has pyramid-level implications: each runner has different strengths at different pyramid levels.

```typescript
// Decision matrix — 2026 test runner selection guide
//
// node:test (Node.js built-in v18+)
//   Unit tests:        ✓ excellent (zero deps, fast startup)
//   Integration tests: ✓ good (async/await native, coverage via --experimental-test-coverage)
//   Component tests:   ✗ not supported (no DOM, no browser)
//   E2E tests:         ✗ not applicable (use Playwright Test)
//   When to choose:    zero-dependency library packages, CLI tools, Node.js microservices
//                      that have no frontend component
//
// Vitest (v3.x/v4.x)
//   Unit tests:        ✓ excellent (HMR-aware watch, Jest-compatible API)
//   Integration tests: ✓ excellent (scoped fixtures, aroundEach, viteModuleRunner:false)
//   Component tests:   ✓ excellent (Browser Mode stable in v4.0, toMatchScreenshot)
//   E2E tests:         ✗ use Playwright Test (separate tool)
//   When to choose:    Vite-based projects, full-stack TypeScript, component libraries,
//                      any project that needs unit + component test levels in one runner
//
// Jest (v30)
//   Unit tests:        ✓ excellent (mature ecosystem, using keyword, globalsCleanup)
//   Integration tests: ✓ good (JSdom v26, async module support)
//   Component tests:   ✓ good (React Testing Library integration)
//   E2E tests:         ✗ not applicable
//   When to choose:    existing Jest projects, React Native (via jest-circus + Metro),
//                      projects that need the broadest ecosystem compatibility
```

```typescript
// Recommended stack for a new TypeScript monorepo (2026):
// Unit + integration tests: Vitest (inline projects, scoped fixtures, tag filtering)
// Component tests:          Vitest Browser Mode (@vitest/browser-playwright)
// E2E tests:                Playwright Test (separate playwright.config.ts)
// Performance tests:        k6 or Locust (separate qa-perf suite)

// vitest.config.ts — full pyramid coverage in one config
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
import { playwright } from '@vitest/browser-playwright';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    projects: [
      { test: { name: 'unit', include: ['src/**/*.unit.test.ts'], environment: 'node', sequence: { groupOrder: 1 } } },
      { test: { name: 'integration', include: ['src/**/*.integration.test.ts'], environment: 'node', sequence: { groupOrder: 2 } } },
      { test: { name: 'browser', include: ['src/**/*.browser.test.ts'], browser: { provider: playwright(), enabled: true, instances: [{ browser: 'chromium' }] }, sequence: { groupOrder: 3 } } },
    ],
  },
});
```

### 16. Jest 30 `jest.onGenerateMock` — Centralized Auto-Mock Customization

Jest 30's `jest.onGenerateMock` global hook fires whenever `jest.createMockFromModule()` or `jest.mock(modulePath)` generates a module mock. This enables centralized, cross-project customization of auto-generated mocks without requiring manual `__mocks__` directories or `moduleNameMapper` entries for every module.

**Pyramid use case:** in large integration test suites, database clients, HTTP clients, and cloud SDKs are auto-mocked for unit tests. Without `onGenerateMock`, teams needed separate `__mocks__` files for each module to provide sensible default implementations. With `onGenerateMock`, a single setup file handles all auto-mock customizations.

```typescript
// jest.setup.ts — centralized auto-mock customization via onGenerateMock
import { jest } from '@jest/globals';

jest.onGenerateMock((modulePath, moduleMock) => {
  // Customize all auto-mocked database clients
  if (modulePath.includes('/db/') || modulePath.endsWith('client.ts')) {
    (moduleMock as Record<string, unknown>).connect = jest.fn().mockResolvedValue(undefined);
    (moduleMock as Record<string, unknown>).disconnect = jest.fn().mockResolvedValue(undefined);
    (moduleMock as Record<string, unknown>).query = jest.fn().mockResolvedValue({ rows: [], rowCount: 0 });
  }

  // Customize all auto-mocked email services
  if (modulePath.includes('email') || modulePath.includes('mailer')) {
    (moduleMock as Record<string, unknown>).send = jest.fn().mockResolvedValue({ messageId: 'test-msg-id' });
  }

  return moduleMock;
});
```

```typescript
// src/users/user-service.unit.test.ts — benefits from onGenerateMock
import { jest, describe, it, expect, beforeEach } from '@jest/globals';

// Auto-mock: jest.onGenerateMock fires and applies the db customization above
jest.mock('../../db/postgres-client.js');

import { PostgresClient } from '../../db/postgres-client.js';
import { UserService } from './user-service.js';

describe('UserService', () => {
  let service: UserService;

  beforeEach(() => {
    jest.clearAllMocks();
    // PostgresClient mock already has sensible defaults from onGenerateMock
    service = new UserService(new PostgresClient());
  });

  it('returns null when user is not found', async () => {
    // query returns { rows: [], rowCount: 0 } by default — no per-test setup needed
    const user = await service.findById('u999');
    expect(user).toBeNull();
  });

  it('overrides the default mock for specific scenarios', async () => {
    const mockClient = new PostgresClient();
    // Override for this test case only
    jest.mocked(mockClient.query).mockResolvedValueOnce({
      rows: [{ id: 'u1', email: 'alice@example.com' }],
      rowCount: 1,
    });
    service = new UserService(mockClient);
    const user = await service.findById('u1');
    expect(user?.email).toBe('alice@example.com');
  });
});
```

[official: jestjs.io/blog/ — Jest 30 release notes, onGenerateMock API]

### 17. Vitest 4.1 Chai-Style Mock Assertions — Sinon Migration Path

Vitest 4.1 added Chai-style mock assertions (`to.have.been.called`, `.calledWith()`, `.returned`, `.callCount(n)`) as an alternative to the Jest-style `toHaveBeenCalled()` API. This enables teams migrating from Sinon + Chai (a common combination in older JavaScript projects) to Vitest without rewriting all assertion styles immediately.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — Chai-style assertions require no special config in Vitest 4.1
// They are available via the same expect() import as Jest-style assertions

import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
export default defineConfig({ test: { globals: true } });
```

```typescript
// JEST-STYLE mock assertions (Vitest 2.x / 3.x / 4.x — all supported):
import { describe, it, expect, vi } from 'vitest';

const emailer = { send: vi.fn<() => Promise<void>>() };

describe('NotificationService', () => {
  it('sends an email on order completion [jest-style]', async () => {
    await notificationService.notifyOrderComplete('o1', emailer);
    expect(emailer.send).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
    expect(emailer.send).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
      expect.objectContaining({ subject: 'Order confirmed' })
    );
  });
});
```

```typescript
// CHAI-STYLE mock assertions (Vitest 4.1+ — migration path from Sinon):
import { describe, it, expect, vi } from 'vitest';

const emailer = { send: vi.fn<() => Promise<void>>() };

describe('NotificationService', () => {
  it('sends an email on order completion [chai-style]', async () => {
    await notificationService.notifyOrderComplete('o1', emailer);

    // Chai-style: matches Sinon spy assertions for migration compatibility
    expect(emailer.send).to.have.been.called;
    expect(emailer.send).to.have.callCount(1);
    expect(emailer.send).to.have.been.calledWith(
      expect.objectContaining({ subject: 'Order confirmed' })
    );
  });
});
```

**Gotcha:** Chai-style and Jest-style assertions can be mixed in the same test file (Vitest supports both on the same `expect` object). However, mixing styles in the same `expect()` chain is not supported — each assertion must be a separate `expect(mock)` call. [community: Vitest GitHub PR adding Chai-style mock assertions — vitest-dev/vitest#7512]

[official: vitest.dev/blog/vitest-4-1 — Chai-style mock assertions section]

### Real-World Gotchas (Cycle 23)  [community]

64. **Jest 30 `expect.arrayOf` passes on empty arrays — always pair with length assertion** [community] — `expect([]).toEqual(expect.arrayOf(expect.any(String)))` passes unconditionally. API tests that expect non-empty collections must add `expect(arr.length).toBeGreaterThan(0)` to catch cases where the endpoint returns an empty list for the wrong reason. [community: Jest 30 beta testing reports, GitHub jestjs/jest discussions]

65. **Vitest `aroundEach` must call `runTest()` exactly once or the test hangs/is skipped** [community] — If `runTest()` is not called (e.g., due to a conditional in the around callback), the test case is silently skipped, not failed. If `runTest()` is called twice, the test runs twice with separate result recording. Add an assertion guard at the end of the `aroundEach` callback that the test completed as expected. [community: Vitest 4.1 alpha user reports, vitest-dev/vitest GitHub issue tracker]

66. **Vitest Browser Mode Playwright provider requires Playwright to be installed separately** [community] — `@vitest/browser-playwright` is a thin wrapper; the actual Playwright chromium/firefox/webkit browsers must still be installed via `npx playwright install chromium`. First-time CI setups that install `@vitest/browser-playwright` without the `playwright install` step silently fail with an opaque "browser not found" error. [community: Vitest Browser Mode GitHub issues, user setup reports May 2026]

67. **Jest 30 `globalsCleanup: 'on'` breaks MSW server instances shared via `globalThis`** [community] — MSW server instances added to `globalThis` in `setupFilesAfterEnv` are cleaned up between test files when `globalsCleanup: 'on'` is enabled. The server receives no requests after the first test file. Fix: wrap the MSW server global with `protectProperties(globalThis['msw-server'])` in the setup file. [community: Jest 30 migration reports, next.js testing setup thread May 2026]

68. **Playwright `--only-changed` traces JavaScript imports, not test IDs — page-level tests are always selected** [community] — If a page object model imports a shared utilities module and that module changes, all e2e test files that use the POM are selected by `--only-changed`. This can select more tests than expected. Use a separate `--project` flag to limit to the relevant test project, and review the selection output with `--reporter=list` before relying on this in production CI. [community: Playwright GitHub discussions — --only-changed practical adoption]

69. **Vitest 3.2 `projects` inline config still inherits root-level `include`/`exclude` patterns if not overridden** [community] — When migrating from `vitest.workspace.ts` to inline `projects` config, the root-level `test.include` glob (if present) acts as a default for any project that does not declare its own `include`. This causes unexpected test discovery: the root pattern matches unit test files inside integration test projects. Always declare explicit `include` in every project object when using inline config. [community: Vitest 3.2 migration thread, vitest-dev/vitest GitHub issue #6231]
