### 16. Node.js 26 `Temporal` API — Deterministic Time in Unit Test Cases  [official]

Node.js 26 enables the `Temporal` API by default (V8 14.6). `Temporal.Now.plainDateTimeISO()` replaces `new Date()` for time-sensitive unit test cases where timezone semantics and calendar arithmetic matter. Unlike `Date`, `Temporal` is timezone-explicit and pure — the same `Temporal.PlainDateTime` value represents the same wall-clock time everywhere without implicit UTC conversion.

```typescript
// src/billing/invoiceDate.ts — production code using Temporal
export function getInvoiceDueDate(
  issuedAt: Temporal.PlainDate,
  paymentTermsDays: number
): Temporal.PlainDate {
  return issuedAt.add({ days: paymentTermsDays });
}

export function isOverdue(
  dueDate: Temporal.PlainDate,
  now: Temporal.PlainDate = Temporal.Now.plainDateISO()
): boolean {
  return Temporal.PlainDate.compare(now, dueDate) > 0;
}

// test/unit/invoiceDate.unit.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { getInvoiceDueDate, isOverdue } from '../../src/billing/invoiceDate';

describe('Invoice due date (Temporal)', () => {
  it('calculates due date as net-30 from issue date', () => {
    const issued = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2026-05-01');
    const due = getInvoiceDueDate(issued, 30);
    expect(due.toString()).toBe('2026-05-31');
  });

  it('handles month-end correctly for net-30 (no 31st in June)', () => {
    const issued = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2026-06-01');
    const due = getInvoiceDueDate(issued, 30);
    // Temporal correctly handles month arithmetic without overflow
    expect(due.toString()).toBe('2026-07-01');
  });

  it('flags an overdue invoice when now is past due date', () => {
    const due = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2026-04-30');
    const now = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2026-05-13');
    expect(isOverdue(due, now)).toBe(true);
  });

  it('does not flag an invoice due today as overdue', () => {
    const today = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2026-05-13');
    expect(isOverdue(today, today)).toBe(false); // compare(today, today) === 0
  });
});
```

**Pyramid significance:** The most common source of timezone-related flakiness in unit test cases is `new Date()` — it returns local machine time, making test cases that rely on date arithmetic non-deterministic across CI environments in different timezones. `Temporal.PlainDate` is timezone-independent and deterministic. Inject the `now` parameter for testability (dependency injection at the unit level) rather than mocking `Temporal.Now`.

[official: nodejs.org/en/blog/release/v26.0.0 — Temporal API enabled by default; Node.js 26]

### 17. Vitest 4.0 `basic` Reporter Removed — Migrate to `default` + `verbose`  [official]

Vitest 4.0 removes the `basic` reporter. Teams that configured `reporter: 'basic'` in `vitest.config.ts` will encounter a startup error after upgrading. The `default` reporter provides equivalent output for CI; `verbose` adds per-test-case status lines for local debugging.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — before Vitest 4.0 (broken after upgrade)
// export default defineConfig({ test: { reporter: 'basic' } });

// vitest.config.ts — Vitest 4.0+ compatible
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // Conditional reporter: verbose locally, default in CI
    reporter: process.env.CI ? 'default' : 'verbose',
    // Or: per-project overrides for multi-level pyramid config
    projects: [
      {
        extends: true,
        test: {
          name: 'unit',
          include: ['src/**/*.unit.test.ts'],
          reporter: process.env.CI ? 'default' : 'verbose',
        },
      },
      {
        extends: true,
        test: {
          name: 'integration',
          include: ['src/**/*.integration.test.ts'],
          // Always verbose for integration — more test steps means harder to diagnose without names
          reporter: ['verbose', 'junit'],
          outputFile: { junit: 'test-results/integration.xml' },
        },
      },
    ],
  },
});
```

[official: vitest.dev/blog/vitest-4 — 'basic' reporter removal migration note]

### Real-World Gotchas (Cycle 25)  [community]

78. **Jest 30 `jest.mock()` path case-sensitivity breaks tests on macOS but not Linux** [community] — Jest 30 enforces case-sensitive module paths in `jest.mock('./path/to/FILENAME.js')`. On macOS (HFS+ case-insensitive), the incorrect-case mock continued to work in Jest 29; on Linux CI (case-sensitive ext4) it never worked. Teams upgrading to Jest 30 discover pre-existing path-case bugs exposed by the stricter resolver. Fix: enable the `no-jest-mock-case-sensitive` ESLint rule or add a pre-commit hook that validates all `jest.mock()` paths against the actual file system. [official: jestjs.io/docs/upgrading-to-jest30 — case-sensitive paths]

79. **Jest 30 non-enumerable object properties excluded from `toEqual` — shared test fixture objects with prototype-set properties silently pass incorrect assertions** [community] — Jest 29's `toEqual` walked non-enumerable properties; Jest 30 excludes them. Any test fixture built with `Object.defineProperty(obj, 'key', { enumerable: false, value: X })` or using class instances with non-enumerable methods will produce unexpected `toEqual` results after upgrading. Audit all fixture factories for non-enumerable property usage before upgrading. [official: jestjs.io/docs/upgrading-to-jest30 — non-enumerable properties]

80. **Vitest `aroundAll` with database transactions leaks when a test file is cancelled mid-run by `--bail`** [community] — If Vitest aborts a test file run early (`--bail 1` or `Ctrl+C`), the `aroundAll` generator's `finally` block may not execute, leaving an open database transaction and a hung connection pool. Guard pattern: listen to `process.on('SIGINT', ...)` in the `globalSetup` and explicitly close the pool if the process receives an interrupt signal. Alternatively, set a connection timeout at the database level (`idle_timeout = 5s` in PostgreSQL) so abandoned connections are reaped automatically. [community: Vitest 4.1 aroundAll early adopter feedback]

81. **Node.js 26 `Temporal.Now.plainDateISO()` returns the system timezone's local date, not UTC — CI in UTC differs from developer machines in UTC+N** [community] — `Temporal.Now.plainDateISO()` returns the current calendar date in the **system timezone**. On a developer machine set to UTC+9, the date advances at a different wall-clock time than a CI container in UTC. For unit test cases asserting date-relative logic (e.g., "today is a business day"), always inject the date as a parameter rather than calling `Temporal.Now` inside the test object. Use `Temporal.Now.zonedDateTimeISO('UTC')` explicitly when you need a consistent UTC date across environments. [official: tc39.github.io/proposal-temporal — Temporal.Now semantics]

82. **Vitest 4.0 Browser Mode requires installing a separate provider package — upgrading without the provider silently falls back to the preview provider** [community] — `@vitest/browser` no longer bundles a default provider. After upgrading from Vitest 3.x to 4.0, teams that do not install `@vitest/browser-playwright` or `@vitest/browser-webdriverio` will receive the undocumented `preview` provider, which runs in a local Vite dev server without real browser automation. Visual regression test cases (`toMatchScreenshot`) and ARIA assertions behave differently under `preview`. Always install the provider package explicitly and pin its version alongside the Vitest version. [official: vitest.dev/blog/vitest-4 — Browser Mode provider packages]

83. **Jest 30 snapshot format changes break snapshots containing React empty string renders and URL objects** [community] — Jest 30 changes how empty strings and URL objects are serialized in snapshots. Empty string children in React components (`''`) are omitted from Jest 30 snapshots; `URL` objects are serialized as their `.href` string rather than `URL { href: '...' }`. Running `jest --updateSnapshot` after upgrading is mandatory for all snapshot files — do not run it before reviewing the diffs, as it will silently overwrite tests that were passing for the wrong reason. [official: jestjs.io/docs/upgrading-to-jest30 — snapshot format changes]

84. **Vitest `detectAsyncLeaks: true` is incompatible with `@nestjs/testing` `TestingModule.close()` — produces false positive "open handles" for every NestJS integration test** [community] — NestJS's `TestingModule.close()` calls `app.close()` which triggers Nest's lifecycle hooks asynchronously. On fast machines the cleanup completes before the leak detector fires; on slow CI machines the hook sequence is not fully resolved within Vitest's leak detection window. Fix: disable `detectAsyncLeaks` for the NestJS integration project and use explicit handle tracking (`server.close(callback)` in `afterAll`) instead. [community: NestJS testing + Vitest 4.1 compatibility thread]

### 27.1 Stryker 9.0 Incremental Mutation Testing — Per-PR Coverage Delta

Stryker 9.0 introduced `--incremental` mode, which persists a mutation cache between runs and re-tests only the mutants whose covering tests changed since the last run. On a 2,000-mutant codebase, this reduces CI mutation-test time from ~45 minutes to under 8 minutes on pull requests that touch 5–10 files.

```typescript
// stryker.config.mts
import type { Config } from '@stryker-mutator/api/config';

const config: Config = {
  testRunner: 'vitest',
  incremental: true,
  incrementalFile: '.stryker-incremental.json',
  mutate: ['src/**/*.ts', '!src/**/*.spec.ts'],
  vitest: { configFile: 'vitest.config.ts' },
  thresholds: { high: 90, low: 80, break: 70 },
  coverageAnalysis: 'perTest',
  reporters: ['progress', 'html', 'json'],
  htmlReporter: { baseDir: 'reports/mutation' },
};

export default config;
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/mutation.yml  (runs only on PR)
name: Mutation
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  stryker:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with: { fetch-depth: 0 }
      - uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: .stryker-incremental.json
          key: stryker-${{ github.base_ref }}-${{ hashFiles('src/**') }}
          restore-keys: stryker-${{ github.base_ref }}-
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx stryker run --incremental
```

**Tradeoff:** Incremental mode requires the cache file to be committed or stored in CI artifact storage — if the cache is cold (first run or after tsconfig changes) the full mutation suite runs. Keep `incrementalFile` in `.gitignore` and always persist it via CI cache keyed on the base branch + source hash. Use `coverageAnalysis: 'perTest'` for the granular change detection to work correctly; `'all'` causes every mutant to be re-tested on any source change.

[official: stryker-mutator.io — Stryker 9.0 incremental mode announcement]

### 27.2 tRPC Integration Testing with `createCaller` — Type-Safe Procedure Invocation

tRPC's `createCaller` API lets you invoke procedures directly in-process without spinning up an HTTP server. This sits at the integration layer: real service logic, real database (via Testcontainers or an in-memory substitute), but zero network overhead. Return types are fully inferred, so the test itself is type-checked end-to-end.

```typescript
// tests/integration/user.router.test.ts
import { createCaller } from '../../src/server/routers/_app';
import { createContext } from '../../src/server/context';
import { db } from '../../src/server/db';
import { users } from '../../src/server/schema';
import type { inferProcedureOutput } from '@trpc/server';
import type { AppRouter } from '../../src/server/routers/_app';

type UserOutput = inferProcedureOutput<AppRouter['user']['byId']>;

describe('user.byId', () => {
  let caller: ReturnType<typeof createCaller>;

  beforeEach(async () => {
    const ctx = await createContext({ req: {} as any, res: {} as any });
    caller = createCaller(ctx);
    await db.insert(users).values({ id: 'u1', name: 'Alice', email: 'alice@example.com' });
  });

  afterEach(async () => {
    await db.delete(users);
  });

  it('returns the user by id', async () => {
    const user: UserOutput = await caller.user.byId({ id: 'u1' });
    expect(user.name).toBe('Alice');
    expect(user.email).toBe('alice@example.com');
  });

  it('throws NOT_FOUND for unknown id', async () => {
    await expect(caller.user.byId({ id: 'missing' })).rejects.toMatchObject({
      code: 'NOT_FOUND',
    });
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `createCaller` bypasses all HTTP middleware (auth header parsing, CORS, rate-limiting). Write separate HTTP-level integration tests (using `supertest` against a running server, or Playwright API requests) to cover middleware logic. Never assume a `createCaller` test validates the full request pipeline. [community: tRPC GitHub discussions — createCaller vs. HTTP integration]

### 27.3 Hono Framework Integration Testing — `app.request()` for Zero-Overhead HTTP Layer Tests

Hono's `app.request()` method accepts a `Request` object (or URL string) and returns a `Response` — no listening socket required. This makes Hono integration tests fast and portable across Node.js, Cloudflare Workers, and Deno without any test-specific server lifecycle management.

```typescript
// tests/integration/items.test.ts
import { app } from '../../src/app';
import { createTestDb, closeTestDb } from '../helpers/db';

beforeAll(() => createTestDb());
afterAll(() => closeTestDb());

describe('GET /items/:id', () => {
  it('returns 200 with item JSON', async () => {
    const res = await app.request('/items/42', {
      method: 'GET',
      headers: { Authorization: 'Bearer test-token' },
    });

    expect(res.status).toBe(200);
    const body = await res.json<{ id: number; name: string }>();
    expect(body.id).toBe(42);
    expect(body.name).toBeTruthy();
  });

  it('returns 404 for unknown item', async () => {
    const res = await app.request('/items/9999');
    expect(res.status).toBe(404);
  });

  it('returns 401 without auth header', async () => {
    const res = await app.request('/items/42');
    expect(res.status).toBe(401);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `app.request()` does execute Hono middleware (auth, validation, error handling), making it more representative than direct handler invocation. However, `Response.json()` returns a `Promise` — a common gotcha is using `res.json()` without `await` and asserting on the `Promise` object rather than the resolved value. Always `await res.json()` before asserting. [community: Hono Discord — integration test patterns]

### 27.4 Vitest Environment Miniflare — Integration Tests for Cloudflare Workers

`@cloudflare/vitest-pool-workers` wraps Miniflare 4 as a Vitest pool, providing KV, R2, D1, Durable Objects, and service bindings in a local runtime that matches the actual Workers environment. Tests run in a real V8 isolate with the Workerd runtime — no mocking of `caches`, `CryptoKey`, or `Request`/`Response` needed.

```typescript
// vitest.workers.config.ts
import { defineWorkersProject } from '@cloudflare/vitest-pool-workers/config';

export default defineWorkersProject({
  test: {
    poolOptions: {
      workers: {
        wrangler: { configPath: './wrangler.toml' },
        miniflare: {
          kvNamespaces: ['SESSION_KV'],
          d1Databases: ['APP_DB'],
        },
      },
    },
  },
});
```

```typescript
// tests/workers/session.test.ts
import { env, createExecutionContext, waitOnExecutionContext } from 'cloudflare:test';
import { SELF } from 'cloudflare:test';
import worker from '../../src/worker';

describe('session KV', () => {
  it('stores and retrieves a session token', async () => {
    await env.SESSION_KV.put('sess:abc', JSON.stringify({ userId: '1' }), {
      expirationTtl: 3600,
    });

    const ctx = createExecutionContext();
    const res = await SELF.fetch('https://example.com/session/abc', {
      headers: { Cookie: 'session=abc' },
    });
    await waitOnExecutionContext(ctx);

    expect(res.status).toBe(200);
    const data = await res.json<{ userId: string }>();
    expect(data.userId).toBe('1');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Requires `nodejs_compat` compatibility flag in `wrangler.toml` for any test that imports Node.js built-ins (`node:crypto`, `node:stream`). Without it, the pool throws a runtime error that looks like a missing module rather than a configuration error — check `compatibility_flags = ["nodejs_compat"]` before debugging imports. Cold start for the Miniflare pool is ~3 seconds; use `--singleFork` only for the workers project to avoid per-file restart overhead. [community: Cloudflare Workers Discord — vitest-pool-workers setup gotchas]

### 27.5 React Server Components Integration Testing — Streaming Render Verification

Testing RSCs requires rendering them on the Node.js server side and asserting on the serialized flight payload or rendered HTML. `react-server-dom-webpack/server` provides `renderToReadableStream` for the server, and `react-dom/server` provides `renderToString` for hydration verification. The test sits at the integration level: real async data fetching (mocked at the network boundary), real component tree, no browser.

```typescript
// tests/integration/ProductPage.rsc.test.tsx
/**
 * @vitest-environment node
 */
import { createElement } from 'react';
import { renderToString } from 'react-dom/server';
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw';
import { server } from '../mocks/server';
import ProductPage from '../../src/app/products/[id]/page';

beforeAll(() => server.listen());
afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers());
afterAll(() => server.close());

it('renders product title from API', async () => {
  server.use(
    http.get('https://api.example.com/products/42', () =>
      HttpResponse.json({ id: 42, title: 'Ergonomic Chair', price: 349 })
    )
  );

  // RSC page components are async — await the element resolution
  const element = await ProductPage({ params: { id: '42' } });
  const html = renderToString(createElement('div', null, element));

  expect(html).toContain('Ergonomic Chair');
  expect(html).toContain('349');
});

it('renders 404 fallback when product not found', async () => {
  server.use(
    http.get('https://api.example.com/products/99', () =>
      HttpResponse.json({ error: 'Not found' }, { status: 404 })
    )
  );

  const element = await ProductPage({ params: { id: '99' } });
  const html = renderToString(createElement('div', null, element));

  expect(html).toContain('Product not found');
});
```

**Tradeoff:** RSC integration tests run in the Node.js environment, not jsdom — avoid importing browser-only APIs (`window`, `localStorage`) in components under test. This test style validates server-side rendering logic and API wiring but does not test client-side interactivity or hydration — those belong at the e2e level with Playwright. [community: Next.js App Router testing discussions, 2025]

### 27.6 TypeScript `satisfies` Operator in Test Doubles — Exhaustiveness Without Widening

The `satisfies` operator validates that an object conforms to a type at the point of definition without widening the variable's type to the base interface. In test doubles, this catches missing method implementations at compile time while preserving the narrower type for mock assertions.

```typescript
// tests/unit/order.service.test.ts
import type { OrderRepository } from '../../src/repositories/OrderRepository';
import { OrderService } from '../../src/services/OrderService';

// satisfies ensures all OrderRepository methods are present
// without widening `mockRepo` to `OrderRepository` (which would lose the spy type)
const mockRepo = {
  findById: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue({ id: 'o1', status: 'pending', total: 100 }),
  save: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(undefined),
  delete: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(undefined),
  findByCustomer: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue([]),
} satisfies OrderRepository;

describe('OrderService.cancel', () => {
  const service = new OrderService(mockRepo);

  beforeEach(() => vi.clearAllMocks());

  it('calls repo.save with cancelled status', async () => {
    await service.cancel('o1');
    expect(mockRepo.save).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
      expect.objectContaining({ id: 'o1', status: 'cancelled' })
    );
  });

  it('does not call repo.delete', async () => {
    await service.cancel('o1');
    expect(mockRepo.delete).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Without `satisfies`, a partial object cast as `OrderRepository` compiles but omits methods that may be called by new service code added later — the omission is silent. With `satisfies`, adding a new method to the `OrderRepository` interface immediately produces a TypeScript error in every test file that uses this mock pattern, which is the desired behavior. Do not use `as unknown as OrderRepository` casts in test doubles — they defeat exhaustiveness checking. [community: TypeScript community discussions — satisfies in test mocks]

### 27.7 Playwright `test.step()` for Structured E2E Diagnostics and Traceability

`test.step()` annotates logical sub-steps within an E2E test. Steps appear in Playwright's HTML report, trace viewer, and JUnit XML output, making it possible to identify exactly which part of a multi-action flow failed — without splitting a cohesive flow into separate `it` blocks that would each require their own setup/teardown.

```typescript
// tests/e2e/checkout.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('guest checkout completes successfully', async ({ page }) => {
  await test.step('navigate to product and add to cart', async () => {
    await page.goto('/products/ergonomic-chair');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByTestId('cart-badge')).toHaveText('1');
  });

  await test.step('proceed to checkout and enter shipping address', async () => {
    await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Checkout' }).click();
    await page.getByLabel('First name').fill('Alice');
    await page.getByLabel('Last name').fill('Smith');
    await page.getByLabel('Street address').fill('123 Main St');
    await page.getByLabel('City').fill('Springfield');
    await page.getByLabel('ZIP code').fill('62701');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Continue to payment' }).click();
  });

  await test.step('enter payment details and submit', async () => {
    const cardFrame = page.frameLocator('[data-testid="card-iframe"]');
    await cardFrame.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4242424242424242');
    await cardFrame.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('12/28');
    await cardFrame.getByLabel('CVC').fill('123');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' }).click();
  });

  await test.step('verify order confirmation', async () => {
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /order confirmed/i })).toBeVisible();
    await expect(page.getByTestId('order-number')).toHaveText(/^ORD-\d{6}$/);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Steps do not isolate failures — if step 3 fails, steps 4+ are skipped but the test is reported as a single failure at the step level. Do not use `test.step()` as a substitute for separate test cases when the scenarios are genuinely independent. Use steps for sequential flows where each action depends on the prior state. [official: playwright.dev/docs/api/class-test#test-step]

### 27.8 OpenAPI-Generated MSW Handlers with `orval` — Integration Tests That Can't Drift

`orval` reads your OpenAPI spec and generates typed MSW v2 handlers, Axios/fetch clients, and Zod schemas simultaneously. The MSW handlers in integration tests are generated from the same source of truth as the production API client — if the spec changes, both the client and the mock update together, making it impossible for the integration test mock to silently drift from what the server actually returns.

```typescript
// orval.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'orval';

export default defineConfig({
  api: {
    input: { target: './openapi.yaml' },
    output: {
      mode: 'tags-split',
      target: 'src/api/generated',
      schemas: 'src/api/generated/model',
      client: 'fetch',
      override: {
        mutator: { path: 'src/api/custom-fetch.ts', name: 'customFetch' },
      },
    },
  },
  apiMock: {
    input: { target: './openapi.yaml' },
    output: {
      mode: 'tags-split',
      target: 'src/mocks/generated',
      client: 'msw',
      mock: true,
    },
  },
});
```

```typescript
// tests/integration/productApi.test.ts
import { server } from '../mocks/server';
import { getProductsMock } from '../../src/mocks/generated/products';
import { fetchProduct } from '../../src/api/generated/products';

beforeAll(() => server.listen());
afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers());
afterAll(() => server.close());

it('fetchProduct returns typed product data', async () => {
  server.use(...getProductsMock());
  const product = await fetchProduct(42);
  // TypeScript knows the exact shape — same type as production usage
  expect(product.id).toBe(42);
  expect(typeof product.name).toBe('string');
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `orval` code generation requires running `npx orval` whenever the OpenAPI spec changes. Add this to a pre-commit hook or CI step that runs before tests. If generated files are committed to the repo, stale generated code is a risk — add a `check:api` script that runs `orval --check` (dry-run) and fails if output would differ. [community: orval GitHub — MSW integration patterns]

### 27.9 Playwright `addInitScript()` for Per-Test Feature Flag Injection

`page.addInitScript()` runs a script in every new page and frame before any other script on the page runs. This makes it the correct mechanism for injecting feature flags, `localStorage` values, or mock environment variables without race conditions — the flag values are available when the application's module-level initialization code reads them.

```typescript
// tests/e2e/helpers/withFeatureFlags.ts
import type { Page } from '@playwright/test';

export type FeatureFlags = {
  newCheckout?: boolean;
  darkModeDefault?: boolean;
  experimentalSearch?: boolean;
};

export async function withFeatureFlags(page: Page, flags: FeatureFlags): Promise<void> {
  await page.addInitScript((serializedFlags: string) => {
    const f = JSON.parse(serializedFlags) as Record<string, boolean>;
    // Override the global feature flag store before app bootstrap
    (window as any).__FEATURE_FLAGS__ = f;
    // Also pre-populate localStorage for flag persistence
    Object.entries(f).forEach(([key, value]) => {
      localStorage.setItem(`ff_${key}`, String(value));
    });
  }, JSON.stringify(flags));
}
```

```typescript
// tests/e2e/newCheckout.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { withFeatureFlags } from './helpers/withFeatureFlags';

test('new checkout flow is shown when flag enabled', async ({ page }) => {
  await withFeatureFlags(page, { newCheckout: true });
  await page.goto('/cart');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('new-checkout-banner')).toBeVisible();
});

test('legacy checkout shown when flag disabled', async ({ page }) => {
  await withFeatureFlags(page, { newCheckout: false });
  await page.goto('/cart');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('legacy-checkout-button')).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `addInitScript()` must be called before `page.goto()` — the script is queued and applied to subsequent navigation. Calling it after `goto()` means the current page has already initialized and the flags have no effect on that load. Also, `addInitScript()` applies to **all frames in the page**, including iframes from third-party origins — be careful injecting `window` globals that may conflict with embedded widgets. [community: Playwright GitHub issues — addInitScript timing FAQ]

### 27.10 Drizzle ORM Integration Testing with `drizzle-seed` — Typed Fixture Population

`drizzle-seed` generates deterministic, type-safe fixture data using Drizzle's schema definitions. It understands foreign key relationships and inserts rows in topological order. Seeding is idempotent when using `reset()` first, making it safe for parallel integration test runs with per-suite database isolation.

```typescript
// tests/integration/helpers/seed.ts
import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/node-postgres';
import { seed, reset } from 'drizzle-seed';
import * as schema from '../../src/db/schema';
import { pool } from './testDb';

export const db = drizzle(pool, { schema });

export async function seedTestData() {
  await reset(db, schema);
  await seed(db, schema, { count: 5 }).refine((f) => ({
    users: {
      count: 3,
      with: {
        orders: {
          count: 2,
          with: { orderItems: { count: 3 } },
        },
      },
    },
    products: { count: 10 },
  }));
}
```

```typescript
// tests/integration/order.service.test.ts
import { seedTestData, db } from './helpers/seed';
import { OrderService } from '../../src/services/OrderService';
import { orders } from '../../src/db/schema';

describe('OrderService', () => {
  beforeEach(() => seedTestData());

  it('finds all orders for a seeded user', async () => {
    const [firstUser] = await db.select().from(schema.users).limit(1);
    const service = new OrderService(db);
    const userOrders = await service.findByUser(firstUser.id);
    expect(userOrders).toHaveLength(2);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `drizzle-seed` respects FK constraints by default — tables with foreign keys are seeded in dependency order. If you use `reset()` without `seed()` between tests (for negative test cases), make sure `reset()` truncates in reverse dependency order or disables FK checks temporarily. Also, `drizzle-seed` does not support circular foreign key references — denormalize or break the cycle before using the seeder. [community: Drizzle ORM Discord — drizzle-seed integration testing patterns]

### 27.11 Vitest `--shard` + GitHub Actions Matrix for Large Integration Suites

Vitest's `--shard N/M` flag splits the test suite into M equal shards by test file count and runs shard N. Combined with a GitHub Actions matrix, this provides linear scaling of integration test wall time without requiring any test code changes.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/integration.yml
name: Integration Tests
on: [push]
jobs:
  test:
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        shard: [1, 2, 3, 4]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:16
        env: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test, POSTGRES_DB: testdb }
        options: --health-cmd pg_isready
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '22', cache: 'npm' }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx vitest run --config vitest.integration.config.ts --shard=${{ matrix.shard }}/4
        env: { DATABASE_URL: 'postgres://postgres:test@localhost/testdb' }
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with:
          name: coverage-shard-${{ matrix.shard }}
          path: coverage/
```

```typescript
// vitest.integration.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    include: ['tests/integration/**/*.test.ts'],
    pool: 'vmForks',      // isolate module state between test files
    poolOptions: { vmForks: { singleFork: false } },
    globalSetup: './tests/integration/globalSetup.ts',
    testTimeout: 30_000,
    hookTimeout: 15_000,
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Sharding by file count does not balance by test duration. A single slow integration test file will dominate one shard's execution time. For more even sharding, use `--shard` in conjunction with Vitest's `--reporter=blob` + `--merge-reports` workflow to aggregate coverage from all shards. Check Vitest docs for the current `--merge-reports` flag name as it was renamed between 2.x and 4.x. [community: Vitest GitHub — sharding + coverage merge workflow]

### 27.12 Deno Test Runner — Permissions-Based Integration Test Isolation

Deno's test runner enforces explicit resource permissions per test file. Integration tests that should be network-isolated can declare `permissions: { net: false }` — any attempted outbound connection fails with a `PermissionDenied` error immediately, making it impossible for a test to accidentally call a real external API. This is enforcer-level test isolation without mocking infrastructure.

```typescript
// tests/unit/priceCalculator.test.ts
// Deno permissions block: this test file CANNOT make network calls
Deno.test({
  name: 'calculates total with discount',
  permissions: { net: false, env: false, write: false },
  fn() {
    const result = calcTotal({ basePrice: 100, discountPct: 20 });
    assertEquals(result, 80);
  },
});

Deno.test({
  name: 'applies zero discount when discountPct is 0',
  permissions: { net: false, env: false, write: false },
  fn() {
    assertEquals(calcTotal({ basePrice: 50, discountPct: 0 }), 50);
  },
});

// Integration test in a separate file with explicit permissions
// tests/integration/paymentGateway.test.ts
Deno.test({
  name: 'payment gateway returns 200 for valid card',
  permissions: {
    net: ['api.stripe.com:443'],  // only stripe allowed
    env: ['STRIPE_TEST_KEY'],
    read: false,
    write: false,
  },
  async fn() {
    const result = await processTestPayment('4242424242424242');
    assertEquals(result.status, 'succeeded');
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Deno's permission model works for TypeScript/JavaScript projects targeting the Deno runtime but cannot be applied to Node.js test suites. If your project runs on Node.js, use MSW with `server.use()` + `onUnhandledRequest: 'error'` to achieve a similar "no unexpected network calls" guarantee. [official: deno.land/manual — Testing permissions]

### 27.13 Jest 30 `jest.SpyInstance` Removal — Migrating Inferred Spy Types

Jest 30 removed the `jest.SpyInstance<ReturnType, ArgsType>` generic type. Code that used `jest.SpyInstance` must migrate to `jest.Spied<typeof fn>`, which infers return and argument types from the function reference itself — no manual generic parameters needed.

```typescript
// BEFORE (Jest 29) — manual generics, error in Jest 30
import type { SpyInstance } from 'jest'; // SpyInstance no longer exported
let saveSpy: jest.SpyInstance<Promise<void>, [order: Order]>;

// AFTER (Jest 30) — inferred, type-safe, future-proof
import { OrderRepository } from '../../src/repositories/OrderRepository';

describe('order spy migration', () => {
  let repository: OrderRepository;
  let saveSpy: jest.Spied<typeof repository.save>;

  beforeEach(() => {
    repository = new OrderRepository(mockDb);
    saveSpy = jest.spyOn(repository, 'save');
    saveSpy.mockResolvedValue(undefined);
  });

  afterEach(() => {
    saveSpy.mockRestore();
  });

  it('save is called once with correct order', async () => {
    const order: Order = { id: 'o1', status: 'pending', total: 99 };
    await repository.save(order);
    expect(saveSpy).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
    expect(saveSpy).toHaveBeenCalledWith(order);
  });
});
```

**Codemod approach:** For large codebases, run the provided codemod:
```bash
npx jest-codemods --transform jest-spy-instance ./src ./tests
```

**Tradeoff:** `jest.Spied<typeof fn>` requires the function type to be resolvable at compile time. For dynamically constructed mocks (`jest.fn<() => T>()`), you still need to annotate the `jest.Mock<T>` type manually. Check each usage after running the codemod — some complex generic cases are not transformed correctly. [official: jestjs.io/docs/upgrading-to-jest30 — SpyInstance removal]

---

### 27.14 Contract Test Consumer Isolation via Pact Stub Server

The Pact stub server (`@pact-foundation/pact`) runs a lightweight HTTP server from a consumer Pact file, allowing integration tests to run the full consumer service (including its HTTP client layer) against a real socket without requiring the provider to be deployed. This validates the consumer's request construction and response parsing together.

```typescript
// tests/contract/consumer/userService.pact.test.ts
import { PactV3, MatchersV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
import path from 'node:path';
import { UserApiClient } from '../../../src/clients/UserApiClient';

const { like, string, integer } = MatchersV3;

const provider = new PactV3({
  consumer: 'OrderService',
  provider: 'UserService',
  dir: path.resolve(__dirname, '../../../pacts'),
  port: 4567,
});

describe('UserApiClient contract', () => {
  it('fetches a user by id', async () => {
    await provider
      .given('user u1 exists')
      .uponReceiving('a request to GET /users/u1')
      .withRequest({ method: 'GET', path: '/users/u1' })
      .willRespondWith({
        status: 200,
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
        body: like({
          id: string('u1'),
          name: string('Alice'),
          email: string('alice@example.com'),
          age: integer(30),
        }),
      })
      .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
        const client = new UserApiClient({ baseUrl: mockServer.url });
        const user = await client.getUser('u1');
        expect(user.id).toBe('u1');
        expect(user.name).toBe('Alice');
      });
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Pact consumer tests write `.json` pact files that must be published to a Pact Broker and verified by the provider in a separate CI step. The consumer test alone does not prove the provider is compatible — it only proves the consumer builds correct requests and parses responses correctly. Always run both consumer and provider verification in CI before merging. [community: Pact Foundation docs — consumer-driven contract testing workflow]

---

### 27.15 Vitest `pool: 'vmForks'` for Integration Tests Requiring Module Isolation

Vitest's `vmForks` pool runs each test file in a forked Node.js process with a fresh V8 module registry (not just a fresh module cache — the actual VM context is new). This is necessary for integration tests that modify singleton state (database connection pools, in-memory caches, global event emitters) that cannot be reliably reset between test files in the same process.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts  (three-project workspace config)
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    workspace: [
      {
        // Fast unit tests: shared threads pool
        extends: true,
        test: {
          name: 'unit',
          include: ['src/**/*.unit.test.ts'],
          pool: 'threads',
          environment: 'node',
        },
      },
      {
        // Integration tests: vmForks for true module isolation
        extends: true,
        test: {
          name: 'integration',
          include: ['tests/integration/**/*.test.ts'],
          pool: 'vmForks',
          poolOptions: {
            vmForks: {
              singleFork: false,    // one fork per file (default)
              memoryLimit: '512mb', // cap forked process heap
            },
          },
          globalSetup: './tests/integration/globalSetup.ts',
          testTimeout: 30_000,
        },
      },
      {
        // Browser mode e2e component tests
        extends: true,
        test: {
          name: 'browser',
          include: ['src/**/*.browser.test.tsx'],
          browser: { enabled: true, name: 'chromium', provider: 'playwright' },
        },
      },
    ],
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `vmForks` is significantly slower than `threads` (~80–200ms per-fork overhead at startup). Do not use it for unit tests. The key signal that `vmForks` is needed: tests pass individually (`vitest run path/to/test.ts`) but fail when run as part of the full suite — this indicates singleton state leakage across test files. Also note that `vmForks` does not share the Vite transform cache across workers the way `threads` does — first-run transformation is repeated per fork, increasing cold-start time. [official: vitest.dev/config — pool options]

### Real-World Gotchas (continued)

85. **tRPC `createCaller` bypasses HTTP middleware — auth checks absent in integration tests that use it** [community] — `createCaller` invokes the tRPC procedure router directly, skipping Express/Fastify middleware that validates JWT tokens or attaches the authenticated user to `req.user`. Integration tests using `createCaller` with an unauthenticated context object will pass even if the procedure has an auth guard — the guard reads `ctx.user` which the test context sets manually. This creates a false sense of security. Always write at least one HTTP-level integration test (using `supertest` or Playwright API requests) per auth-protected route to verify the middleware chain. WHY it matters: a procedure guard rewritten to use `ctx.user.role` instead of `ctx.session.userId` may still pass all `createCaller` tests because the test context supplies both fields, while real unauthenticated HTTP requests fail at the middleware before context is built. [community: tRPC GitHub discussions]

86. **Drizzle `drizzle-seed` inserts in topological FK order — but only for FKs declared in the schema, not enforced by `ALTER TABLE`** [community] — `drizzle-seed` inspects the Drizzle schema object to determine insertion order. If your database has FK constraints added via raw `ALTER TABLE` migrations (not reflected in the Drizzle schema object), `drizzle-seed` does not know about them and may insert rows in an order that violates the constraint. Symptom: tests pass locally (FK enforcement disabled in SQLite test mode) but fail on PostgreSQL CI with `ForeignKeyViolation`. Fix: declare all foreign keys in the Drizzle schema using `.references()` and ensure migrations are generated from the schema, not hand-written. [community: Drizzle ORM GitHub issues — drizzle-seed FK ordering]

87. **`page.addInitScript()` runs before page scripts but after service worker registration — SW-intercepted requests see the original page flags, not the injected values** [community] — If your application uses a service worker to cache feature flags or intercept API calls, `addInitScript()` values are visible to the main thread but the service worker's `fetch` handler runs in a separate context that does not have access to `window.__FEATURE_FLAGS__`. Tests that rely on `addInitScript()` to override flags will work for direct `window` reads but fail silently if the flag is read via a SW-intercepted API response. Workaround: use `page.route()` to intercept the feature flag API endpoint and return the desired flags directly. WHY it matters: this is especially subtle in Next.js apps that use `next-pwa` or Workbox, where the SW is registered at app start before any navigation. [community: Playwright GitHub issues — addInitScript + service worker interaction]

88. **Hono `res.json()` and `res.text()` are async — forgetting `await` gives you a `Promise` object, not the parsed body** [community] — Unlike the `supertest` response object where `.body` is synchronously populated after the request resolves, Hono's `Response` (Web Platform `Response`) has async body consumption methods. `const body = res.json()` (missing `await`) returns a pending `Promise`. Assertions like `expect(body.id).toBe(42)` pass silently (comparing `undefined` with `42` when using `toBe` on Promise properties is always false — but using `toEqual({ id: 42 })` on a Promise object throws `[object Promise] !== [object Object]` with a confusing message). Always `const body = await res.json()`. WHY it matters: Jest/Vitest do not warn about unawaited Promise assertions by default; enable `@typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises` to catch this at lint time. [community: Hono Discord — common integration test mistakes]

89. **`@cloudflare/vitest-pool-workers` requires `nodejs_compat` compatibility flag for `node:` imports — missing it produces "module not found" errors that look like package install issues** [community] — If a Cloudflare Worker imports `node:crypto`, `node:stream`, or any other `node:` prefixed module, the Miniflare runtime must have `nodejs_compat` enabled in `wrangler.toml`. Without it, Miniflare throws `Cannot find module 'node:crypto'`, which looks identical to a missing npm package. The fix is one line in `wrangler.toml`: `compatibility_flags = ["nodejs_compat"]`. Many teams spend hours reinstalling packages or checking tsconfig paths before finding this. Additionally, `nodejs_compat` requires a `compatibility_date` of `2024-09-23` or later. WHY it matters: the error message gives no indication that it's a Workers compatibility flag issue rather than a missing npm dependency. [community: Cloudflare Workers Discord — vitest-pool-workers troubleshooting]

90. **Stryker 9.0 incremental cache becomes stale after `tsconfig.json` changes — incremental run silently uses outdated type-checking results** [community] — Stryker 9.0's incremental cache keys are based on source file hashes and test file hashes, but not on `tsconfig.json`, `tsconfig.test.json`, or other config files. If you change `strict: false` to `strict: true` in tsconfig, Stryker's incremental run does not re-compile affected files with the new config — it uses cached results from the previous (non-strict) compilation. Mutants that would fail under strict mode may be reported as surviving (incorrectly). Fix: delete `.stryker-incremental.json` whenever `tsconfig.json` changes. Add to your pre-commit hook: `if git diff --name-only HEAD | grep -q tsconfig; then rm -f .stryker-incremental.json; fi`. WHY it matters: mutation testing is typically run less frequently than unit tests, so a stale cache can persist for many commits before discovery. [community: Stryker GitHub issues — incremental cache invalidation]

### 29.1 Testcontainers Cloud Turbo Mode — Parallel Integration Tests Without Local Docker  [official]

Testcontainers Cloud Turbo mode (2025) offloads container lifecycle management to a cloud daemon, eliminating Docker-in-Docker requirements in hosted CI runners (GitHub Actions, CircleCI). The TypeScript API is identical to local testcontainers usage — no test code changes are needed, only a `TC_CLOUD_TOKEN` environment variable. Turbo mode pre-warms container images on the daemon, reducing first-container start from ~15 s to under 2 s.

```typescript
// tests/integration/order.repository.test.ts
// No code changes needed for Testcontainers Cloud — same API, different execution backend
import { beforeAll, afterAll, afterEach, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { PostgreSqlContainer, type StartedPostgreSqlContainer } from '@testcontainers/postgresql';
import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/node-postgres';
import * as schema from '../../src/db/schema.js';
import { OrderRepository } from '../../src/repositories/OrderRepository.js';

let container: StartedPostgreSqlContainer;
let repo: OrderRepository;

beforeAll(async () => {
  // TC_CLOUD_TOKEN env var activates Turbo mode transparently — no API changes needed
  container = await new PostgreSqlContainer('postgres:16-alpine')
    .withDatabase('testdb')
    .withUsername('test')
    .withPassword('test')
    .start();

  const db = drizzle(container.getConnectionUri(), { schema });
  repo = new OrderRepository(db);
  await db.execute(schema.createTablesSQL);
}, 30_000); // reduced from 60s with Turbo mode pre-warming

afterAll(() => container.stop());
afterEach(async () => {
  // Reset state between tests without restarting the container
  await repo.deleteAll();
});

it('creates and retrieves an order with correct status', async () => {
  const created = await repo.create({ customerId: 'c1', items: [{ sku: 'X1', qty: 1 }] });
  expect(created.id).toBeDefined();
  const found = await repo.findById(created.id);
  expect(found?.status).toBe('pending');
});

it('returns null for unknown order id', async () => {
  const result = await repo.findById('non-existent-id');
  expect(result).toBeNull();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use Testcontainers Cloud Turbo mode when Docker is unavailable in hosted CI runners. NOT recommended for air-gapped environments, on-premise CI, or projects with strict data residency requirements — container execution happens in Testcontainers Cloud infrastructure, not your own. For local development, local Docker is faster than cloud mode due to network latency. Set `TC_CLOUD_TOKEN` as a CI secret, never commit it. [official: testcontainers.com/cloud]

---

### 29.2 Vitest 5.0 `createReport` API — Programmatic Pyramid Report Assembly  [official]

Vitest 5.0 (beta) exposes a `createReport` function in the `vitest/node` public API that assembles a structured report object from blob-reporter output. This replaces ad-hoc JSON parsing in pyramid shape check scripts with a typed, versioned API.

```typescript
// scripts/pyramid-report.ts — Vitest 5.0 createReport API
// Run after: vitest run --reporter=blob for each project
import { createReport } from 'vitest/node';

interface PyramidCounts {
  unit: number;
  integration: number;
  e2e: number;
}

async function buildPyramidReport(): Promise<PyramidCounts> {
  // createReport reads .vitest/blob/ directory (Vitest 5.0 path) by default
  const report = await createReport({
    outputDirectory: '.vitest/blob',
    merge: true, // merge sharded reports
  });

  const counts: PyramidCounts = { unit: 0, integration: 0, e2e: 0 };

  for (const suite of report.testSuites) {
    const totalTests = suite.passedCount + suite.failedCount + suite.skippedCount;
    const filePath = suite.filepath;

    if (/\.unit\.test\.ts$/.test(filePath)) {
      counts.unit += totalTests;
    } else if (/\.e2e\.(test|spec)\.ts$/.test(filePath)) {
      counts.e2e += totalTests;
    } else {
      counts.integration += totalTests;
    }
  }

  return counts;
}

const counts = await buildPyramidReport();
const total = counts.unit + counts.integration + counts.e2e;
const unitPct = Math.round((counts.unit / total) * 100);
const intPct = Math.round((counts.integration / total) * 100);
const e2ePct = Math.round((counts.e2e / total) * 100);

console.log(`Pyramid: unit=${unitPct}% (${counts.unit}) | integration=${intPct}% (${counts.integration}) | e2e=${e2ePct}% (${counts.e2e})`);

if (counts.e2e > counts.integration) {
  console.error('Pyramid inverted: e2e count exceeds integration count.');
  process.exit(1);
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `createReport` is in Vitest 5.0 beta (as of May 2026) — the API shape may change before stable release. Pin to `vitest@^4.1` in production pipelines; use this pattern only in projects actively testing Vitest 5 beta. The existing `VitestResults` JSON parse approach (from earlier cycles) remains stable and version-agnostic for Vitest 3.x and 4.x pipelines. Do NOT switch to `createReport` until Vitest 5.0 stable is announced. [official: vitest.dev/blog/vitest-5.html — createReport API]

---

### 29.3 MSW v2 `WebSocketLink` — Integration-Level WebSocket Handler Stubs  [official]

MSW v2.14+ introduced a native WebSocket handler API (`ws` from `msw`) that intercepts WebSocket connections in Node.js (for integration tests) and browser (for Vitest browser mode or Playwright). This replaces the pattern of mocking `WebSocket` globally or using `ws` library test servers.

```typescript
// tests/integration/chatService.integration.test.ts
import { setupServer } from 'msw/node';
import { ws } from 'msw';
import { ChatService } from '../../src/services/ChatService.js';
import type { ChatMessage } from '../../src/types.js';

// Define WebSocket handler for the chat endpoint
const chatHandler = ws.link('wss://chat.example.com/rooms/:roomId');

const server = setupServer(
  chatHandler.addEventListener('connection', ({ client, params }) => {
    // Send a welcome message when client connects
    client.send(JSON.stringify({ type: 'welcome', roomId: params.roomId }));

    // Relay all client messages back (echo for testing)
    client.addEventListener('message', (event) => {
      const msg = JSON.parse(event.data as string) as ChatMessage;
      client.send(JSON.stringify({ ...msg, echo: true }));
    });
  }),
);

beforeAll(() => server.listen());
afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers());
afterAll(() => server.close());

it('receives welcome message on connection', async () => {
  const service = new ChatService('wss://chat.example.com/rooms/room-1');
  await service.connect();

  const firstMessage = await service.waitForMessage();
  expect(firstMessage).toMatchObject({ type: 'welcome', roomId: 'room-1' });
  service.disconnect();
});

it('server echoes messages back with echo flag', async () => {
  const service = new ChatService('wss://chat.example.com/rooms/room-2');
  await service.connect();
  await service.waitForMessage(); // consume welcome

  service.send({ type: 'chat', text: 'hello' });
  const echo = await service.waitForMessage();
  expect(echo).toMatchObject({ type: 'chat', text: 'hello', echo: true });
  service.disconnect();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** MSW WebSocket handlers work at the integration test level for Node.js (via `setupServer`) and in Vitest browser mode (via `setupWorker`). They do NOT intercept WebSocket connections at the OS network layer — the `ChatService` class must use a WebSocket implementation that MSW can intercept (standard `ws` or browser `WebSocket`). If `ChatService` wraps a native C++ WebSocket binding, MSW cannot intercept it. Use `vitest --environment node` for this test — `jsdom` WebSocket does not support all message event types. [official: mswjs.io/docs/api/ws — WebSocket API]

---

### 29.4 Playwright `page.route()` as an Integration Test Substitute for MSW  [community]

For TypeScript applications that cannot use MSW (frameworks that bypass `fetch` in Node.js, or Bun-based servers), Playwright's `page.route()` provides an integration-level HTTP stub at the e2e layer boundary. Combined with `page.goto()` to a locally running server, this approach tests the full application stack with controlled network responses — no MSW install required.

```typescript
// tests/integration-e2e/dashboard.test.ts
// Hybrid: real Next.js server running locally + Playwright route stubs for external APIs
import { test, expect, type Route } from '@playwright/test';

type MetricsResponse = {
  revenue: number;
  orders: number;
  activeUsers: number;
};

const mockMetrics: MetricsResponse = {
  revenue: 12450.75,
  orders: 342,
  activeUsers: 1872,
};

test.beforeEach(async ({ page }) => {
  // Stub the analytics API before each navigation
  await page.route('**/api/analytics/metrics', async (route: Route) => {
    await route.fulfill({
      status: 200,
      contentType: 'application/json',
      body: JSON.stringify(mockMetrics),
    });
  });
});

test('dashboard displays correct revenue from analytics API', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('revenue-card')).toContainText('$12,450.75');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('orders-card')).toContainText('342');
});

test('dashboard shows error state when analytics API returns 503', async ({ page }) => {
  // Override for this specific test — returns 503 instead
  await page.route('**/api/analytics/metrics', (route) =>
    route.fulfill({ status: 503, body: 'Service Unavailable' }),
  );
  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toContainText(/analytics unavailable/i);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** This is slower than pure integration tests using MSW in Node.js because it involves a real browser, a real server, and network I/O (even if intercepted). Place tests using `page.route()` stubs in the integration-level project bucket only if the server-side rendering logic under test cannot be exercised without a browser. When MSW is available and the test object is a component or API client, prefer MSW in the integration project over Playwright route stubs to keep the integration test level fast. [community: Playwright GitHub discussions — route() as integration layer]

---

### 29.5 `@fast-check/vitest` Stateful Property-Based Testing — Model-Based Integration Tests  [community]

`fast-check`'s model-based testing (`fc.createModel`) generates random sequences of operations on a system and verifies that a simple model and the real system stay in sync. At the integration level, this catches state-machine bugs that example-based tests rarely exercise.

```typescript
// tests/integration/shoppingCart.model.test.ts
import { test, fc } from '@fast-check/vitest';
import { describe, expect, beforeEach } from 'vitest';
import { ShoppingCart } from '../../src/domain/ShoppingCart.js';
import type { CartItem } from '../../src/domain/types.js';

// Simple model: a plain record of item quantities
type CartModel = Map<string, number>;

// Commands that can be applied to both model and real system
interface AddCommand { kind: 'add'; item: CartItem }
interface RemoveCommand { kind: 'remove'; sku: string }
interface ClearCommand { kind: 'clear' }
type CartCommand = AddCommand | RemoveCommand | ClearCommand;

function applyToModel(model: CartModel, cmd: CartCommand): CartModel {
  const next = new Map(model);
  if (cmd.kind === 'add') {
    next.set(cmd.item.sku, (next.get(cmd.item.sku) ?? 0) + cmd.item.qty);
  } else if (cmd.kind === 'remove') {
    next.delete(cmd.sku);
  } else {
    next.clear();
  }
  return next;
}

describe('ShoppingCart — model-based integration test', () => {
  let cart: ShoppingCart;

  beforeEach(() => { cart = new ShoppingCart(); });

  test.prop([
    fc.array(
      fc.oneof(
        fc.record({ kind: fc.constant('add' as const), item: fc.record({ sku: fc.string({ minLength: 1, maxLength: 6 }), qty: fc.integer({ min: 1, max: 10 }) }) }),
        fc.record({ kind: fc.constant('remove' as const), sku: fc.string({ minLength: 1, maxLength: 6 }) }),
        fc.constant({ kind: 'clear' as const }),
      ),
      { minLength: 1, maxLength: 20 },
    ),
  ])('cart item counts always match the simple model', (commands: CartCommand[]) => {
    let model: CartModel = new Map();

    for (const cmd of commands) {
      if (cmd.kind === 'add') {
        cart.addItem(cmd.item);
      } else if (cmd.kind === 'remove') {
        cart.removeItem(cmd.sku);
      } else {
        cart.clear();
      }
      model = applyToModel(model, cmd);
    }

    for (const [sku, expectedQty] of model) {
      expect(cart.getQuantity(sku)).toBe(expectedQty);
    }
    expect(cart.itemCount()).toBe(model.size);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Model-based testing is most valuable for stateful domain objects with complex transition rules (carts, game state, workflow engines). It is NOT appropriate for stateless transformation functions — plain `test.prop()` with arbitraries is sufficient there. Model-based tests can have high shrink times when a counterexample is found because `fast-check` must replay many operation sequences to minimise the failure. Set a `numRuns` limit (e.g., `{ numRuns: 500 }`) in CI to keep runtime bounded. [community: fast-check.io — model-based testing guide]

---

### 29.6 Node.js 26 `--test-randomize` for Hidden Order-Dependency Detection  [official]

Node.js 26.1.0 (released May 7, 2026) added `--test-randomize` and `--test-random-seed=N` flags to the built-in `node:test` runner. Randomising test execution order surfaces hidden dependencies where one test case leaves side-effects that another test case implicitly depends on. Combine with the integration test level where shared state (DB connections, module singletons) is most likely to create order dependencies.

```typescript
// tests/unit/discount.test.ts — Node.js native test runner (Node 26: bare .ts works)
import { describe, it, before } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { DiscountCalculator } from '../src/pricing/DiscountCalculator.ts';

describe('DiscountCalculator', () => {
  let calc: DiscountCalculator;

  before(() => { calc = new DiscountCalculator({ currency: 'USD' }); });

  it('applies 10% for standard members', () => {
    assert.equal(calc.apply(100, 'standard'), 90);
  });

  it('applies 20% for gold members', () => {
    assert.equal(calc.apply(100, 'gold'), 80);
  });

  it('applies 0% for no tier', () => {
    assert.equal(calc.apply(100, null), 100);
  });

  it('throws for negative totals', () => {
    assert.throws(() => calc.apply(-1, 'gold'), /negative total/);
  });

  it('applies discounts to decimal totals correctly', () => {
    const result = calc.apply(99.99, 'standard');
    assert.ok(Math.abs(result - 89.991) < 0.001, `Expected ~89.991 but got ${result}`);
  });
});
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/unit-tests.yml — randomise test order to catch order-dependencies
- name: Run unit tests (randomised order)
  run: node --test --test-randomize --test-random-seed=${{ github.run_number }} tests/unit/**/*.test.ts
  # Using run_number as seed: different order per CI run, but reproducible per run ID
```

**Tradeoff:** Randomised order only helps if your test suite actually has order dependencies to find — clean test suites with proper `before`/`after` teardown will never fail. Do NOT use a fixed seed permanently — that defeats the purpose. Use `github.run_number` or a daily-rotating seed to explore different orderings over time. The `--test-random-seed` value is printed in test output, so a failing CI run can always be reproduced locally. Not applicable to Vitest — Vitest has its own `sequence.shuffle` option for equivalent functionality. [official: nodejs.org/en/blog/release/v26.1.0]

---

### 29.7 Temporal API as a Unit Test Clock Replacement  [official]

Node.js 26 enables the Temporal API (V8 14.6) by default. `Temporal.Now.plainDateTimeISO()` and `Temporal.ZonedDateTime` replace `new Date()` for time-sensitive unit tests, eliminating the need for `vi.useFakeTimers()` patterns that are brittle and framework-dependent.

```typescript
// src/scheduling/invoiceDueDate.ts — Temporal-based logic
import { Temporal } from 'temporal-polyfill'; // or native on Node 26+

export function calculateDueDate(
  invoiceDate: Temporal.PlainDate,
  termsDays: number,
): Temporal.PlainDate {
  return invoiceDate.add({ days: termsDays });
}

export function isOverdue(
  dueDate: Temporal.PlainDate,
  asOf: Temporal.PlainDate,
): boolean {
  return Temporal.PlainDate.compare(asOf, dueDate) > 0;
}

// tests/unit/invoiceDueDate.unit.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { Temporal } from 'temporal-polyfill';
import { calculateDueDate, isOverdue } from '../../src/scheduling/invoiceDueDate.js';

describe('calculateDueDate', () => {
  it('adds 30 days for net-30 terms', () => {
    const invoiceDate = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2026-05-01');
    const due = calculateDueDate(invoiceDate, 30);
    expect(due.toString()).toBe('2026-05-31');
  });

  it('correctly crosses month boundaries', () => {
    const invoiceDate = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2026-01-15');
    const due = calculateDueDate(invoiceDate, 45);
    expect(due.toString()).toBe('2026-03-01');
  });

  it('isOverdue returns true when current date is past due date', () => {
    const due = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2026-04-01');
    const today = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2026-05-01');
    // No fake timer needed — tests use fixed Temporal.PlainDate literals
    expect(isOverdue(due, today)).toBe(true);
  });

  it('isOverdue returns false on the due date itself', () => {
    const due = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2026-05-14');
    expect(isOverdue(due, due)).toBe(false);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** The Temporal API is natively available on Node.js 26+ without a polyfill. On Node.js 22/24, use `temporal-polyfill` or `@js-temporal/polyfill`. NOT a replacement for `vi.useFakeTimers()` when testing code that internally calls `new Date()` or `Date.now()` — those still need timer mocking unless you refactor to inject time as a `Temporal.PlainDate` parameter. Logic written with `Temporal` types is inherently deterministic and timezone-correct — no TZ environment variable drift in CI. [official: tc39.es/proposal-temporal, nodejs.org/en/blog/release/v26.0.0]

---

### 29.8 Vitest `aroundEach` Transaction Rollback — Zero-Cost Integration Test Isolation  [official]

Vitest 4.1's `aroundEach` hook wraps each test case in a user-provided context. The canonical pattern for integration tests: wrap each test in a database transaction, then roll it back after the test completes — providing instant, zero-cost isolation without `TRUNCATE` or container restart overhead.

```typescript
// tests/fixtures/transactional.ts — reusable aroundEach transaction fixture (Vitest 4.1)
import { test as base } from 'vitest';
import { type DataSource, type EntityManager } from 'typeorm';

type TransactionalFixture = { em: EntityManager };

export function createTransactionalTest(dataSource: DataSource) {
  return base.extend<TransactionalFixture>({
    em: async ({}, use) => {
      const queryRunner = dataSource.createQueryRunner();
      await queryRunner.connect();
      await queryRunner.startTransaction();
      try {
        await use(queryRunner.manager); // inject transaction-scoped manager
      } finally {
        await queryRunner.rollbackTransaction(); // always rollback — unconditional isolation
        await queryRunner.release();
      }
    },
  });
}

// tests/integration/order.service.integration.test.ts
import { beforeAll, afterAll, expect } from 'vitest';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { Order } from '../../src/entities/Order.js';
import { createTransactionalTest } from '../fixtures/transactional.js';

let dataSource: DataSource;

beforeAll(async () => {
  dataSource = new DataSource({ type: 'sqlite', database: ':memory:', entities: [Order], synchronize: true });
  await dataSource.initialize();
});

afterAll(() => dataSource.destroy());

const test = createTransactionalTest(dataSource);

test('creates and retrieves an order within the transaction', async ({ em }) => {
  const repo = em.getRepository(Order);
  const order = repo.create({ customerId: 'c1', total: 99.99, status: 'pending' });
  await repo.save(order);
  const found = await repo.findOneBy({ customerId: 'c1' });
  expect(found?.total).toBe(99.99);
  // After test: transaction rolls back — data does not persist
});

test('does not see data from previous test (isolation verified)', async ({ em }) => {
  const repo = em.getRepository(Order);
  const count = await repo.count();
  expect(count).toBe(0); // rollback confirmed
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Transaction rollback isolation works only when the test object (service, repository) uses the *same database connection* as the test fixture. If the service opens its own separate connection (common with connection pooling), the rollback does not affect data written through that separate connection. NOT suitable for tests that exercise `COMMIT` semantics explicitly (e.g., idempotency of retried writes). Validate isolation by verifying the second test sees zero rows. [official: vitest.dev/blog/vitest-4-1.html — aroundEach hook]

---

### 29.9 Bun `mock.module()` Declaration-Order Requirement vs Vitest `vi.mock()` Hoisting  [community]

Bun's `bun:test` module mock API requires mock declarations to appear in the file **before** the imports of the modules being mocked. Unlike Vitest's `vi.mock()` which is automatically hoisted to the top of the file by the Vite transform, Bun evaluates `mock.module()` in source order — mocks declared after imports silently have no effect.

```typescript
// WRONG in Bun — mock declared after import; silently does nothing
import { fetchUser } from '../src/userClient.ts'; // imported first — not mocked
import { mock } from 'bun:test';
mock.module('../src/userClient.ts', () => ({
  fetchUser: () => Promise.resolve({ id: 'u1', name: 'Mock User' }),
}));

// CORRECT in Bun — mock declared BEFORE the import it intercepts
import { mock, describe, it, expect, beforeEach } from 'bun:test';

// Step 1: declare the mock BEFORE importing the module under test
mock.module('../src/userClient.ts', () => ({
  fetchUser: () => Promise.resolve({ id: 'u1', name: 'Mock User' }),
}));

// Step 2: import AFTER the mock is registered
import { fetchUser } from '../src/userClient.ts';

describe('fetchUser mock (Bun)', () => {
  beforeEach(() => mock.restore());

  it('returns the mock user when module is intercepted', async () => {
    const user = await fetchUser('any-id');
    expect(user.name).toBe('Mock User');
  });

  it('mock is stateless between tests after mock.restore()', async () => {
    // Verify isolation — mock was restored in beforeEach
    const user = await fetchUser('any-id');
    expect(user.name).toBe('Mock User'); // mock still active from module-level declaration
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** This is a fundamental architectural difference from Vitest. When migrating a Vitest test suite to Bun, every `vi.mock()` call must be manually moved to before the corresponding imports — there is no automated codemod for this. Teams mixing Vitest and Bun test files in the same monorepo should establish a clear convention: Vitest for integration and unit tests (where `vi.mock()` hoisting is relied upon), Bun for edge-runtime or performance-sensitive unit tests only. NOT a reason to avoid Bun — just a migration convention to document. [community: bun.sh/docs/test/mocks — declaration order requirement]

### 29.10 AI/LLM Application Test Pyramid — Judge-Based Evaluation Layer  [community]

TypeScript applications that call LLM APIs require a specialised test layer between integration and e2e: **LLM-as-judge evaluation**. A judge model assesses whether LLM outputs meet qualitative criteria — factual accuracy, tone, format adherence — that binary assertions cannot capture. This layer replaces the "record-and-playback" instinct of asserting exact LLM output strings.

```typescript
// tests/eval/summariser.eval.test.ts
// LLM judge evaluation at the "integration-eval" pyramid level
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import Anthropic from '@anthropic-ai/sdk';
import { summariseDocument } from '../../src/ai/summariser.js';

const client = new Anthropic(); // uses ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from environment

async function judgeWithLLM(
  output: string,
  criteria: string,
): Promise<{ pass: boolean; reason: string }> {
  const response = await client.messages.create({
    model: 'claude-haiku-4-5',
    max_tokens: 200,
    temperature: 0, // deterministic evaluation — prevents flaky judge verdicts
    messages: [{
      role: 'user',
      content: `You are a QA judge. Evaluate if this output meets the criteria.
Criteria: ${criteria}
Output: "${output}"
Respond with JSON only: {"pass": true/false, "reason": "one sentence"}`,
    }],
  });

  const text = response.content[0].type === 'text' ? response.content[0].text : '{}';
  return JSON.parse(text) as { pass: boolean; reason: string };
}

describe('summariseDocument — LLM judge evaluation', () => {
  it('produces a summary shorter than 40% of original', async () => {
    const input = 'TypeScript is a strongly typed programming language that builds on JavaScript. '.repeat(20);
    const summary = await summariseDocument(input);
    expect(summary.length).toBeLessThan(input.length * 0.4);
  });

  it('summary preserves the main topic (judge evaluation)', async () => {
    const input = 'TypeScript is a strongly typed programming language that builds on JavaScript. '.repeat(20);
    const summary = await summariseDocument(input);
    const judgment = await judgeWithLLM(
      summary,
      'The summary must mention TypeScript and its relationship to JavaScript.',
    );
    expect(judgment.pass, `Judge reason: ${judgment.reason}`).toBe(true);
  });

  it('does not hallucinate facts not in the source', async () => {
    const input = 'Our product ships on June 1, 2026. The price is $99. It supports TypeScript.';
    const summary = await summariseDocument(input);
    const judgment = await judgeWithLLM(
      summary,
      'The summary must only contain facts from the source. No new dates, prices, or features.',
    );
    expect(judgment.pass, `Judge reason: ${judgment.reason}`).toBe(true);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** LLM judge evaluations cost money per run and add latency. Place them in a separate CI job that runs on PR merges or nightly — NOT on every commit. Use a cheap judge model (Claude Haiku, GPT-4o-mini) with `temperature: 0` for determinism. Always assert a deterministic precondition first (length, format) before the judge call — the judge only adds value when deterministic assertions are insufficient. NOT a replacement for prompt-level unit tests that assert output format/schema with `expect.schemaMatching`. [community: Anthropic documentation — evals as integration tests, 2025]
