### 18. TypeScript 5.9 `verbatimModuleSyntax` Default Breaks Test Import Patterns  [official]

TypeScript 5.9 made `verbatimModuleSyntax: true` a default in `tsc --init`-generated configs. Any test file that imports a symbol used only as a type (without `import type`) now fails type-checking with TS error `TS1484`. This silently breaks test suites that inherit the root `tsconfig.json` — `vitest.config.ts` and test files compiled with `tsconfig.test.json extends: ./tsconfig.json` are affected. The fix requires audit of all test imports, not just source imports.

```typescript
// BEFORE TypeScript 5.9 with verbatimModuleSyntax:true (BREAKS)
// tests/unit/order.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { OrderService }          from '../src/OrderService.js';
import { OrderStatus }           from '../src/order-types.js'; // TS1484: re-exported as type-only

describe('OrderService', () => {
  it('returns PENDING status for new orders', () => {
    const svc = new OrderService();
    const order = svc.create({ customerId: 'c1', total: 100 });
    // OrderStatus used as a value comparison — but it is an enum,
    // and verbatimModuleSyntax requires explicit import type for pure-type uses
    expect(order.status).toBe(OrderStatus.PENDING);
  });
});

// AFTER — explicit import type separation (TypeScript 5.9+ compatible)
import { describe, it, expect }   from 'vitest';
import { OrderService }            from '../src/OrderService.js';
import { OrderStatus }             from '../src/order-types.js';  // enum VALUE — keep as value import
import type { CreateOrderInput }   from '../src/order-types.js';  // type-only — use import type

// Alternatively, use the inline 'type' modifier:
// import { OrderStatus, type CreateOrderInput } from '../src/order-types.js';

describe('OrderService', () => {
  it('returns PENDING status for new orders', () => {
    const input: CreateOrderInput = { customerId: 'c1', total: 100 };
    const svc = new OrderService();
    const order = svc.create(input);
    expect(order.status).toBe(OrderStatus.PENDING);
  });

  it('rejects negative total', () => {
    const svc = new OrderService();
    expect(() => svc.create({ customerId: 'c1', total: -1 }))
      .toThrow('Total must be positive');
  });
});
```

**When to use:** Adopt `verbatimModuleSyntax: true` in all new TypeScript projects (it improves bundler compatibility and makes module semantics explicit); run `tsc --noEmit` as a gate in CI to catch violations before tests run.

**When NOT to use:** Projects using Babel or SWC for transpilation without `tsc` type-checking (the flag is irrelevant at the transpiler level, but you lose type-checking benefits); legacy codebases with hundreds of test files — fix incrementally with `// @ts-expect-error` suppressions and an automated codemod (`npx ts-morph-helpers fix-imports`).

**Alternative:** TypeScript's `--verbatimModuleSyntax` migration codemod (`npx @typescript/codemods add-import-type`); ESLint rule `@typescript-eslint/consistent-type-imports` enforces the same invariant at lint time before `tsc` runs.

### 19. Playwright `tracing.startHar()` for Integration-Level Network Verification  [official]

Playwright v1.60 promotes `tracing.startHar()` to a first-class API. HAR (HTTP Archive) recording captures every network request made during a test run, including headers, bodies, timing, and status codes. At the integration test level this enables **network-layer assertions** without a real backend: record a HAR against the real API once, then replay it in CI with `page.routeFromHAR()`. At the e2e level, HAR replay creates deterministic tests for third-party APIs (payment gateways, OAuth providers) without network flakiness.

```typescript
// e2e/payment-flow.e2e.test.ts — Playwright v1.60 HAR record + replay (TypeScript)
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'node:path';

const HAR_PATH = path.resolve('e2e/fixtures/payment-api.har');

test.describe('Payment flow with HAR replay', () => {
  test('checkout with replayed Stripe HAR', async ({ page, context }) => {
    // Replay HAR for the Stripe domain — all other requests go to real app
    await context.routeFromHAR(HAR_PATH, {
      url: '**/api.stripe.com/**',
      update: process.env['UPDATE_HAR'] === '1', // set env var to re-record
    });

    await page.goto('/checkout');
    await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4242424242424242');
    await page.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('12/30');
    await page.getByLabel('CVC').fill('123');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay' }).click();

    // Assert on the UI response to the replayed Stripe success event
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /payment successful/i })).toBeVisible();

    // HAR tracing: verify Stripe API was called with correct amount
    const har = await context.tracing.stopHar(); // v1.60 API
    const chargeCall = har.entries.find(e => e.request.url.includes('charges'));
    expect(chargeCall?.response?.status).toBe(200);
  });
});
```

**When to use:** E2e tests that must interact with third-party APIs (payment, auth, maps) where network flakiness causes false failures; integration-level network assertions where you need to verify the correct HTTP request was made to an external service; cross-browser testing where real API rate limits are a concern.

**When NOT to use:** Tests against internal APIs you fully control (use MSW or real test environments instead — HAR replay adds a maintenance burden when the API contract changes); HAR files for APIs with rapidly changing response shapes (HAR will go stale quickly); security-sensitive flows where HAR files would contain credential tokens committed to the repo (use `UPDATE_HAR` redaction hooks or `playwright.config.ts` `contextOptions.recordHarOmitContent`).

**Alternative:** MSW (`msw/node` with `setupServer`) for handler-based API mocking at unit/integration level; Nock for Node.js HTTP-level interception; WireMock for Java-adjacent test environments; Playwright `page.route()` for inline request interception without HAR.

### 20. `expect.schemaMatching` with Zod at Integration Level (Vitest 4.0+)  [official]

Vitest 4.0 introduced `expect.schemaMatching(schema)` — a built-in assertion that validates a value against a Zod (or Valibot) schema and produces structured error messages showing exactly which field failed and why. At the integration test level this replaces verbose manual property assertions on API response bodies, enforces the same schema used in production validation, and ensures the test basis stays synchronised with the runtime schema automatically.

```typescript
// tests/integration/users-api.integration.test.ts — Vitest 4.0 expect.schemaMatching + Zod
import { describe, it, expect, beforeAll, afterAll } from 'vitest';
import { z }        from 'zod';
import request      from 'supertest';
import { buildApp } from '../../src/app.js';
import { createTestDb, type TestDb } from '../helpers/db.js';
import type { Express } from 'express';

// Single source of truth: the same Zod schema used in the route handler
const UserResponseSchema = z.object({
  id:        z.string().uuid(),
  email:     z.string().email(),
  createdAt: z.string().datetime(),
  role:      z.enum(['admin', 'member', 'guest']),
});

type UserResponse = z.infer<typeof UserResponseSchema>;

let app: Express;
let db: TestDb;

beforeAll(async () => {
  db = await createTestDb();
  app = buildApp({ db });
});

afterAll(() => db.destroy());

describe('GET /users/:id', () => {
  it('returns a valid user conforming to UserResponseSchema', async () => {
    const userId = await db.seedUser({ email: 'alice@example.com', role: 'member' });

    const res = await request(app).get(`/users/${userId}`).expect(200);

    // expect.schemaMatching validates the entire response body against the Zod schema
    // If role is missing or email is malformed, the error message names the failing field
    expect(res.body).toEqual(expect.schemaMatching(UserResponseSchema));
  });

  it('returns 404 for non-existent user', async () => {
    const res = await request(app).get('/users/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000').expect(404);
    expect(res.body).toEqual(expect.objectContaining({ error: expect.any(String) }));
  });
});
```

**When to use:** Integration tests validating HTTP API response bodies where the Zod schema is already defined in the production code; contract validation between service layers; anywhere you currently write `expect(res.body.id).toBeDefined(); expect(res.body.email).toMatch(/@/)` — collapse into a single `schemaMatching` assertion.

**When NOT to use:** Unit tests for the Zod schema itself (test the schema in isolation with `safeParse` — not through the HTTP layer); responses with highly variable shapes driven by user-controlled data (use partial schema matching with `z.object().partial()`); projects on Vitest 3.x or below where the API is not available (polyfill with `expect.extend` + Zod `safeParse`).

**Alternative:** Manual `expect.objectContaining()` chains; `zod-matcher` npm package for Jest; `supertest-openapi` for schema validation driven directly from the OpenAPI spec without a Zod dependency in tests.

### 21. Playwright Agents Governance: AI-Generated E2E Tests Need Pyramid Triage  [community]

Playwright v1.56+ ships an **Agents** subsystem: a planner agent generates test cases from a natural-language description, a generator agent writes Playwright TypeScript, and a healer agent auto-repairs broken locators after UI changes. Without pyramid governance, teams adopt AI-generated e2e test cases for logic that belongs at the unit or integration level — resulting in an inverted pyramid within weeks. The governance rule: every AI-generated test case must be classified and, if it duplicates integration-level coverage, either deleted or replaced with a lower-level test.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — governance: tag AI-generated tests for triage
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  testDir: './e2e',
  // CI: skip unaudited AI-generated test candidates in the main pipeline
  grep: process.env['CI'] ? /(?!.*\[ai-generated\])/ : undefined,
  use: { trace: 'on' },
  projects: [
    {
      name: 'audited-e2e',
      testMatch: /.*\.e2e\.test\.ts$/,
      // Exclude unaudited AI candidates from the main run
      testIgnore: /.*\.ai-candidate\.ts$/,
    },
    {
      name: 'ai-candidates',
      // Run separately with --project ai-candidates for triage sessions
      testMatch: /.*\.ai-candidate\.ts$/,
    },
  ],
});

// scripts/triage-ai-tests.ts — classify AI-generated tests into pyramid levels
import { readdir } from 'node:fs/promises';
import path from 'node:path';

const candidates = await readdir('./e2e', { recursive: true })
  .then((files: string[]) => files.filter(f => f.endsWith('.ai-candidate.ts')));

for (const file of candidates) {
  console.log(`\nTriaging: ${file}`);
  console.log('  [u] Unit  [i] Integration  [e] E2e (keep)  [d] Delete');
  // Interactive classification logic — assigns the correct test level and renames the file
}
```

**When to use:** Teams adopting Playwright Agents or any AI test-generation tooling (GitHub Copilot workspace, Cursor AI test generation); post-sprint triage sessions to classify the backlog of AI-generated candidates; CI gates that block merging AI-candidate test files without triage approval.

**When NOT to use:** Teams not using any AI test generation (no governance overhead needed); small codebases where a single engineer trivially reviews all tests; teams that already require test-level justification in PR descriptions (the governance hook is redundant).

**Alternative:** Manual PR review checklist requiring test-level justification; Vitest `--tags` filter (`@unit`, `@integration`, `@e2e`) applied to all AI-generated tests with a CI ratio check; `eslint-plugin-playwright` custom rule that rejects test cases with no `page.goto()` calls in `.e2e.test.ts` files (a proxy for "this is not a real e2e test").

### 22. Contract Testing with Pact-JS v16 at the Integration-E2E Boundary  [official]

Pact-JS v16.0 (Oct 2025) introduces the canonical export rename (`Pact` / `Matchers` replace `PactV4` / `MatchersV3`) and adds pending interactions and GraphQL support for V3+V4. Contract tests occupy the boundary between integration and e2e: they verify that a consumer's expectations of a provider match the provider's actual behaviour, without requiring both services to run simultaneously. This is the fourth pyramid layer recommended for microservice meshes.

```typescript
// tests/contract/order-service-consumer.pact.test.ts — Pact-JS v16 consumer contract
import { describe, it, beforeAll, afterAll, expect } from 'vitest';
import { Pact, Matchers } from '@pact-foundation/pact'; // v16 canonical names
import path from 'node:path';
import axios from 'axios';

const { like, term } = Matchers;

const provider = new Pact({
  consumer: 'order-service',
  provider: 'inventory-service',
  port: 1234,
  dir: path.resolve('./pacts'),
  logLevel: 'error',
});

describe('OrderService → InventoryService contract', () => {
  beforeAll(() => provider.setup());
  afterAll(() => provider.finalize());

  it('GET /stock/:sku returns available quantity matching the consumer contract', async () => {
    await provider.addInteraction({
      state: 'SKU A1 has 10 units in stock',
      uponReceiving: 'a request for stock level of SKU A1',
      withRequest: {
        method: 'GET',
        path: '/stock/A1',
        headers: { Accept: 'application/json' },
      },
      willRespondWith: {
        status: 200,
        headers: {
          'Content-Type': term({
            generate: 'application/json',
            matcher: 'application/json.*',
          }),
        },
        body: like({ sku: 'A1', available: 10, reserved: 2 }),
      },
    });

    const res = await axios.get('http://localhost:1234/stock/A1');
    expect(res.data.available).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(0);
    expect(res.data.sku).toBe('A1');

    await provider.verify();
  });
});
```

**When to use:** Microservice architectures where multiple teams own separate services; integrations with third-party APIs where provider-driven tests are not possible; before introducing a breaking API change (consumer pacts fail before the change ships); CI pipelines that need cross-service compatibility checks without a full integration environment.

**When NOT to use:** Monolithic applications where all services share a single deploy (use supertest integration tests directly); teams who cannot enforce that provider services also run the pact verification step (one-sided pact provides false confidence); GraphQL APIs where schema-level contract testing via schema introspection (`graphql-inspector`) is more appropriate.

**Alternative:** OpenAPI schema diffing (`oasdiff`, `swagger-diff`) for REST API contract validation without Pact overhead; Consumer-Driven Contract Testing with Spring Cloud Contract for JVM services; MSW handlers derived from OpenAPI as lightweight consumer-side contract tests.

---

### 23. Property-Based Testing with `@fast-check/vitest` `test.prop()` API  [community]

`@fast-check/vitest` 0.4+ exposes a `test.prop()` API that integrates property-based testing natively into Vitest's test runner — no wrapping `fc.assert(fc.property(...))` boilerplate. Properties run alongside regular unit tests, share `beforeEach`/`afterEach` lifecycle, and appear in the Vitest HTML reporter as individual test cases with their shrunk counter-examples. This is the recommended pattern for testing business rules with large input spaces at the unit level.

```typescript
// src/pricing/discount.property.test.ts — @fast-check/vitest 0.4+ test.prop() API
import { describe, expect } from 'vitest';
import { test } from '@fast-check/vitest';
import fc from 'fast-check';
import { calculateDiscount } from './discount.js';
import type { DiscountInput } from './discount.js';

describe('calculateDiscount properties', () => {
  // Property: discount is always non-negative for any valid input
  test.prop([
    fc.record<DiscountInput>({
      total:          fc.float({ min: 0, max: 100_000, noNaN: true }),
      membershipTier: fc.constantFrom('standard', 'gold', 'platinum'),
    }),
  ])('discount is never negative for any valid input', (input) => {
    expect(calculateDiscount(input)).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(0);
  });

  // Property: gold tier always yields >= standard tier discount for the same total
  test.prop([
    fc.float({ min: 0, max: 100_000, noNaN: true }),
  ])('gold discount >= standard discount for the same total', (total) => {
    const goldDiscount     = calculateDiscount({ total, membershipTier: 'gold' });
    const standardDiscount = calculateDiscount({ total, membershipTier: 'standard' });
    expect(goldDiscount).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(standardDiscount);
  });

  // Property: calculateDiscount is pure — same input always yields same output
  test.prop([
    fc.record<DiscountInput>({
      total:          fc.float({ min: 0, max: 100_000, noNaN: true }),
      membershipTier: fc.constantFrom('standard', 'gold', 'platinum'),
    }),
  ])('calculateDiscount is referentially transparent', (input) => {
    expect(calculateDiscount(input)).toBe(calculateDiscount(input));
  });
});
```

**When to use:** Pure functions with large or unbounded input domains (pricing engines, validators, parsers, encoders); algebraic laws (commutativity, associativity, idempotency, round-trip encoding); regression suites where the bug was triggered by an unusual but valid combination of inputs; after a production bug — formalise the violated invariant as a property.

**When NOT to use:** Tests that verify specific known values (unit examples are more expressive for known input/output pairs); I/O-bound code where arbitrary inputs cannot be trivially constructed without side effects; property tests that rely on external services (use example-based integration tests for those paths).

**Alternative:** `jest-fast-check` for Jest projects; Hypothesis via Python for polyglot projects; manual `fc.assert(fc.property(...))` wrapper when Vitest integration is not desired.

---

### 24. MSW v2 `HttpResponse` Factory Pattern for Typed Integration Mocks  [official]

MSW v2 replaced the `res(ctx.json(...))` builder pattern with `HttpResponse.json(body, init?)` factory methods typed against the `Response` interface. At the integration test level this provides compile-time safety for mock response bodies — if the handler returns a shape that does not match the production type, TypeScript catches the mismatch before the test runs, keeping mock contracts in sync with production types automatically.

```typescript
// tests/integration/msw-handlers.ts — MSW v2 typed HttpResponse factories
import { http, HttpResponse, delay } from 'msw';
import type { OrderResponse, CreateOrderInput, ErrorResponse } from '../../src/types.js';

// Shared handler factory: reusable across unit and integration tests
export function makeOrderHandlers(overrides?: {
  status?: number;
  body?:   Partial<OrderResponse>;
}) {
  return [
    http.post<never, CreateOrderInput>('/api/orders', async ({ request }) => {
      const input = await request.json();

      // Simulate realistic network latency in integration tests
      await delay(20);

      if (overrides?.status && overrides.status >= 400) {
        const errBody: ErrorResponse = { error: 'Simulated server error', code: 'MOCK_ERROR' };
        return HttpResponse.json(errBody, { status: overrides.status });
      }

      const body: OrderResponse = {
        id:         'ord_test_001',
        customerId: input.customerId,
        total:      input.items.reduce((s, i) => s + i.price * i.qty, 0),
        status:     'confirmed',
        createdAt:  new Date().toISOString(),
        ...overrides?.body,
      };

      // HttpResponse.json is generic — TypeScript ensures body satisfies OrderResponse
      return HttpResponse.json<OrderResponse>(body, { status: 201 });
    }),

    http.get('/api/orders/:id', ({ params }) => {
      const body: OrderResponse = {
        id:         params['id'] as string,
        customerId: 'c1',
        total:      99.0,
        status:     'confirmed',
        createdAt:  new Date().toISOString(),
      };
      return HttpResponse.json<OrderResponse>(body);
    }),
  ];
}
```

**When to use:** Integration and unit test suites using MSW v2 where mock response bodies should stay type-aligned with production TypeScript interfaces; handler factories shared across multiple test files; teams migrating from MSW v1 `res(ctx.json(...))` pattern.

**When NOT to use:** Tests that intentionally return malformed bodies to verify client error-handling (use the `overrides.status` escape hatch deliberately); microservices where response types are in a separate package requiring a publish cycle (consider `openapi-typescript` + `orval` to generate both production types and MSW handlers from the OpenAPI spec).

**Alternative:** `orval` OpenAPI codegen generating MSW handlers automatically from the API spec — eliminates manual handler maintenance; `msw-trpc` for tRPC integration tests; `next-router-mock` for Next.js App Router integration tests where MSW does not cover server-side fetching.

---

### 25. Snapshot Testing Anti-Pattern: Snapshot Sprawl at the Integration Layer  [community]

Snapshot tests (`toMatchSnapshot()`, `toMatchInlineSnapshot()`) seem like easy integration coverage but are the leading cause of snapshot sprawl: as the codebase evolves, snapshots are regenerated without review (`--updateSnapshot`), rendering them meaningless as regression guards. At the integration test level the failure mode is worst — a change in a deeply nested component or a DB seed value causes hundreds of snapshot diffs, all legitimate, masking the one actual regression. The rule: snapshots are acceptable for stable serialisation outputs; they are an anti-pattern for dynamic integration test fixtures.

```typescript
// ANTI-PATTERN: snapshot on dynamic integration output (timestamps, generated IDs)
// tests/integration/order-list.snapshot.test.ts
it('renders order list (BAD — snapshot contains timestamps)', async () => {
  const orders = await orderRepo.findAll();
  // Every CI run regenerates this snapshot because createdAt/updatedAt drift
  expect(orders).toMatchSnapshot();
});

// PREFERRED: explicit assertions on fields that matter at the integration level
it('returns orders with correct shape and populated deterministic fields', async () => {
  await db.seedOrders([
    { customerId: 'c1', total: 50,  status: 'pending' },
    { customerId: 'c2', total: 150, status: 'confirmed' },
  ]);

  const orders = await orderRepo.findAll();

  expect(orders).toHaveLength(2);
  expect(orders[0]).toMatchObject({ customerId: 'c1', total: 50,  status: 'pending' });
  expect(orders[1]).toMatchObject({ customerId: 'c2', total: 150, status: 'confirmed' });
  // Verify shape structure without pinning dynamic runtime values
  expect(orders[0]).toMatchObject({ id: expect.any(String), createdAt: expect.any(String) });
});

// ACCEPTABLE: snapshot on a stable serialised format (generated OpenAPI schema)
it('generates stable OpenAPI schema (snapshot acceptable — output is deterministic)', () => {
  const schema = generateOpenApiSchema(app);
  expect(schema).toMatchInlineSnapshot(`
    "openapi: 3.1.0
    info:
      title: Orders API
      version: 1.0.0"
  `);
});
```

**When to use:** Snapshots are appropriate for stable serialisation outputs: generated GraphQL schemas, OpenAPI specs, CSS-in-JS static outputs, compiler error messages, and rendered HTML when the test is specifically a rendering regression guard (Storybook screenshot tests).

**When NOT to use:** Any output containing timestamps, runtime-generated IDs, random values, or environment-specific paths; integration tests where the snapshot encompasses data from a real database or HTTP response with variable fields; tests expected to fail legitimately as features evolve (snapshot updates mask intentional changes).

**Alternative:** `expect.objectContaining()` for partial structure assertions; `expect.schemaMatching(zodSchema)` (Vitest 4.0+) for contract-level shape validation; `toMatchObject()` for explicit field-level integration assertions; Playwright ARIA snapshots (`expect(page).toHaveAriaSnapshot()`) for UI accessibility regression testing (stable against style changes).

### 26. Bun `bun:test` Pyramid Configuration with `bunfig.toml`  [official]

Bun 1.2+ supports `bunfig.toml` for configuring the `bun:test` runner — analogous to `vitest.config.ts`. For pyramid-level organisation, `bunfig.toml` defines separate test patterns per level and exposes flags like `--rerun-each` for flakiness detection at the integration level and `--randomize` for order-dependency detection at the unit level. TypeScript files run natively without transpiler configuration.

```toml
# bunfig.toml — pyramid-level test configuration for Bun 1.2+
[test]
# Default: unit tests only (fast, no I/O)
include  = ["src/**/*.unit.test.ts"]
timeout  = 5000    # 5 s per unit test — fails fast for runaway async
bail     = 5       # stop after 5 failures to keep the feedback loop short

[test.integration]
include  = ["tests/integration/**/*.integration.test.ts"]
timeout  = 30000   # 30 s for real DB/container I/O
preload  = ["tests/helpers/testcontainers-setup.ts"]

[test.e2e]
include  = ["e2e/**/*.e2e.test.ts"]
timeout  = 120000  # 2 min for full browser flows
```

```typescript
// tests/helpers/testcontainers-setup.ts — preloaded for integration level in Bun
// Bun 1.2+: testcontainers works without Node.js compatibility flag
import { PostgreSqlContainer } from '@testcontainers/postgresql';
import type { StartedPostgreSqlContainer } from '@testcontainers/postgresql';

let container: StartedPostgreSqlContainer;

export async function setup(): Promise<void> {
  container = await new PostgreSqlContainer('postgres:16')
    .withDatabase('testdb')
    .start();
  process.env['TEST_DB_URL'] = container.getConnectionUri();
}

export async function teardown(): Promise<void> {
  await container?.stop();
}
```

```bash
# Pyramid-level CI commands
bun test                                    # unit level (default config)
bun test --config bunfig.toml:integration   # integration level
bun test --config bunfig.toml:e2e           # e2e level
bun test --rerun-each=3                     # flakiness detection (3 runs per test)
bun test --randomize --seed=42              # order-dependency detection
```

**When to use:** Projects using Bun as the primary runtime for both development and testing; greenfield TypeScript services where Bun's native TypeScript execution eliminates transpiler configuration overhead; teams wanting a zero-config pyramid setup without a Vitest or Jest dependency.

**When NOT to use:** Projects requiring Vitest browser mode, Playwright integration, or `expect.schemaMatching`; monorepos using Turborepo with Vitest project references (Bun lacks equivalent workspace-level test orchestration as of Bun 1.3); NestJS projects using decorator support (Bun's decorator implementation may cause issues with `reflect-metadata`).

**Alternative:** Vitest with `defineProject` inline workspace config for equivalent pyramid-level separation; Jest with `projects` configuration; Node.js 26 `node:test` with `--test-name-pattern` filtering as a zero-dependency option.

---

### 27. OpenTelemetry Trace-Based Integration Testing  [community]

Trace-based integration testing uses OpenTelemetry spans emitted by the system under test to assert on the *causal chain* of a request — verifying not just the HTTP response but that the correct downstream services were called, in the correct order, with the correct attributes. This is the integration-level equivalent of a contract test but for observability: if a service call is short-circuited by a cache or config change, the trace assertion fails even if the HTTP response is identical.

```typescript
// tests/integration/trace-based.integration.test.ts — OTel InMemorySpanExporter + Vitest
import { describe, it, beforeAll, afterAll, expect } from 'vitest';
import { NodeSDK }               from '@opentelemetry/sdk-node';
import { InMemorySpanExporter }  from '@opentelemetry/sdk-trace-base';
import { SimpleSpanProcessor }   from '@opentelemetry/sdk-trace-node';
import { HttpInstrumentation }   from '@opentelemetry/instrumentation-http';
import request                   from 'supertest';
import { buildApp }              from '../../src/app.js';
import { createTestDb }          from '../helpers/db.js';

const exporter = new InMemorySpanExporter();
const sdk = new NodeSDK({
  spanProcessors:  [new SimpleSpanProcessor(exporter)],
  instrumentations: [new HttpInstrumentation()],
});

let app: ReturnType<typeof buildApp>;
let db: Awaited<ReturnType<typeof createTestDb>>;

beforeAll(async () => {
  sdk.start();
  db = await createTestDb();
  app = buildApp({ db });
});

afterAll(async () => {
  await sdk.shutdown();
  await db.destroy();
});

describe('POST /orders — trace-based causal assertions', () => {
  it('emits a DB span and an event span in the correct order', async () => {
    exporter.reset(); // clear spans from setup

    await request(app)
      .post('/orders')
      .send({ customerId: 'c1', items: [{ sku: 'A1', qty: 1, price: 50 }] })
      .expect(201);

    const spans     = exporter.getFinishedSpans();
    const spanNames = spans.map(s => s.name);

    // Assert that both the DB write and the event publication spans were emitted
    expect(spanNames).toContain('INSERT orders');
    expect(spanNames).toContain('publish order.created');

    // Assert correct causal ordering: DB write must complete before event fires
    const dbSpan    = spans.find(s => s.name === 'INSERT orders')!;
    const eventSpan = spans.find(s => s.name === 'publish order.created')!;
    expect(dbSpan.endTime[0]).toBeLessThanOrEqual(eventSpan.startTime[0]);
  });
});
```

**When to use:** Event-driven microservices where the integration test must verify both the HTTP response *and* downstream effects (event published, cache written, metric emitted); distributed systems where a service call may be silently swallowed by a circuit breaker; tests that supplement contract tests — contract tests verify shape, trace tests verify causality.

**When NOT to use:** Simple CRUD services where the HTTP response is sufficient evidence of correctness; tests that need to assert on spans from *other* services in a mesh (use a dedicated tracing backend like Tracetest or Jaeger for cross-service span assertions, not in-process `InMemorySpanExporter`); unit test level (span emission is an integration concern).

**Alternative:** Tracetest (tracetest.io) for distributed trace-based testing with YAML assertions; Jaeger + `opentelemetry-js` for manual span inspection; direct event store assertion for event-sourced systems (assert on the event log rather than spans).

---

### 28. Node.js 26 Temporal API for Deterministic Time-Sensitive Unit Tests  [official]

Node.js 26 enables the TC39 Temporal API by default (V8 14.6). `Temporal.Now.plainDateTimeISO()` and `Temporal.ZonedDateTime` replace `new Date()` for time-sensitive unit tests — they are immutable, timezone-explicit, and arithmetic-safe, eliminating the most common class of flaky unit tests: tests that assert on date strings derived from `new Date()` and fail at midnight, on DST changeover days, or in CI workers running in a different timezone.

```typescript
// src/billing/invoice.ts — production code using Temporal (Node 26 / temporal-polyfill)
import { Temporal } from 'temporal-polyfill';

export interface Invoice {
  id:        string;
  amount:    number;
  issuedAt:  string;
  dueDate:   string;
}

export function buildInvoice(orderId: string, amount: number): Invoice {
  return {
    id:       `inv_${orderId}`,
    amount,
    // Explicit UTC — no implicit local-timezone offset ambiguity
    issuedAt: Temporal.Now.plainDateTimeISO('UTC').toString(),
    dueDate:  Temporal.Now.plainDateTimeISO('UTC').add({ days: 30 }).toString(),
  };
}

// tests/unit/invoice.unit.test.ts — Temporal + Vitest fake timers for determinism
import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { Temporal } from 'temporal-polyfill';
import { buildInvoice } from '../../src/billing/invoice.js';

const FIXED_ISO = '2026-05-14T12:00:00';

describe('buildInvoice', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    vi.useFakeTimers();
    vi.setSystemTime(new Date('2026-05-14T12:00:00.000Z'));
  });

  afterEach(() => { vi.useRealTimers(); });

  it('sets issuedAt to the pinned UTC datetime', () => {
    const invoice = buildInvoice('ord_001', 100);
    expect(invoice.issuedAt).toBe(FIXED_ISO);
  });

  it('sets dueDate to exactly 30 days after issuedAt', () => {
    const invoice = buildInvoice('ord_001', 100);
    const due    = Temporal.PlainDateTime.from(invoice.dueDate);
    const issued = Temporal.PlainDateTime.from(invoice.issuedAt);
    // Temporal.compare returns -1 | 0 | 1 — use toBe(0) for equality, not toBe(true)
    expect(Temporal.PlainDateTime.compare(due, issued.add({ days: 30 }))).toBe(0);
  });

  it('invoice id contains the order id', () => {
    const invoice = buildInvoice('ord_xyz', 200);
    expect(invoice.id).toContain('ord_xyz');
  });
});
```

**When to use:** Any unit test that asserts on date/time values, especially relative ones (due dates, expiry, token TTL); CI pipelines running in multiple timezones or workers with system-clock drift; replacing `new Date()` in domain model code to gain timezone-explicit semantics.

**When NOT to use:** Tests that interact with external APIs returning ISO 8601 strings from `Date.toISOString()` (convert to Temporal at the boundary); Node.js 24 and below without `temporal-polyfill`; performance-critical tight loops where `Temporal` object allocation overhead is measurably slower than raw `Date` arithmetic.

**Alternative:** `vi.useFakeTimers()` + `vi.setSystemTime()` with `new Date()` (works but timezone semantics stay implicit); `date-fns` with explicit UTC functions (`formatISO`, `addDays`); `luxon` DateTime for timezone-explicit arithmetic without Temporal dependency.

### 29. Vitest 4.1 `coverage.changed` for Per-PR Coverage Delta  [official]

Vitest 4.1 introduces `coverage.changed` — a flag that restricts coverage reporting to files changed in the current PR (using `git diff` under the hood). Running `--coverage --coverage.changed` on a PR that touches 3 files generates a focused coverage report for those 3 files only, reducing CI runtime from minutes to seconds for large codebases and making coverage gates actionable at the PR level rather than the whole-repo level.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — coverage.changed for PR-level gates (Vitest 4.1+)
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      reporter: ['text', 'html', 'lcov'],
      // In CI: compare changed files against the main branch merge-base
      // Locally: run full coverage (changed:false skips the git diff)
      changed: process.env['CI'] ? { base: 'main' } : false,
      // Thresholds apply only to the changed files when 'changed' is enabled
      thresholds: {
        lines:      80,
        branches:   75,
        functions:  80,
        statements: 80,
      },
      // Exclude test files and infrastructure from the coverage report
      exclude: ['**/*.test.ts', '**/*.spec.ts', 'tests/**', 'e2e/**', 'scripts/**'],
    },
  },
});
```

```bash
# CI PR coverage gate
npx vitest run --coverage --coverage.changed

# Local: targeted coverage for a specific module being developed
npx vitest run --coverage src/orders/order.service.ts
```

**When to use:** Large monorepos where full coverage runs take more than 5 minutes; PRs touching 1–10 files that need targeted coverage gates without waiting for the entire suite; teams enforcing "no new uncovered code" without addressing existing legacy coverage gaps; replacing fragile diff-based coverage scripts (`diff-cover`, `lcov-to-cobertura`).

**When NOT to use:** Greenfield projects where full coverage is fast (< 60 s) — no benefit over standard `--coverage`; PRs that delete code (coverage.changed may report 0% on deleted files, triggering false threshold failures — exclude deleted files explicitly); projects on Vitest 4.0.x or below (flag not available).

**Alternative:** `diff-cover` CLI for LCOV-based PR diff coverage; GitHub Actions `codecov` action with per-PR patch coverage; Nx `affected` targeting to run tests only for affected projects in a monorepo.

### 30. Ice Cream Cone Anti-Pattern: Diagnosing and Inverting an Over-E2E Suite  [community]

The **ice cream cone** is the inverted test pyramid: a codebase with 70%+ e2e, 20% integration, 10% unit. Symptoms include CI runs taking 45+ minutes, a single deployment blocked on a browser test, flaky tests normalised as background noise, and "fix the tests" becoming a full-time job. The inversion happens gradually — teams add Playwright tests for every bug because "e2e proved the fix" — and goes unnoticed until CI is unusable. The fix is a structured **pyramid audit** followed by incremental refactoring.

```typescript
// scripts/pyramid-audit.ts — count test cases per level and report the ratio
// Usage: npx tsx scripts/pyramid-audit.ts
import { readdir, readFile } from 'node:fs/promises';
import path from 'node:path';

interface PyramidStats {
  unit:        number;
  integration: number;
  e2e:         number;
}

async function countTests(dir: string, pattern: RegExp): Promise<number> {
  let count = 0;
  try {
    const entries = await readdir(dir, { recursive: true, withFileTypes: true });
    for (const entry of entries) {
      if (!entry.isFile() || !pattern.test(entry.name)) continue;
      const content = await readFile(
        path.join(entry.parentPath ?? entry.path, entry.name),
        'utf8',
      );
      const matches = content.match(/^\s*(it|test)\s*\(/gm);
      count += matches?.length ?? 0;
    }
  } catch {
    // Directory may not exist in all projects
  }
  return count;
}

const stats: PyramidStats = {
  unit:        await countTests('./src',   /\.unit\.test\.ts$/),
  integration: await countTests('./tests', /\.integration\.test\.ts$/),
  e2e:         await countTests('./e2e',   /\.e2e\.test\.ts$/),
};

const total = stats.unit + stats.integration + stats.e2e || 1;
const pct = (n: number) => `${((n / total) * 100).toFixed(1)}%`;

console.log('=== Pyramid Audit ===');
console.log(`Unit        : ${stats.unit}  (${pct(stats.unit)})`);
console.log(`Integration : ${stats.integration}  (${pct(stats.integration)})`);
console.log(`E2E         : ${stats.e2e}  (${pct(stats.e2e)})`);

if (stats.e2e > stats.unit) {
  console.warn('\nWARNING: Ice cream cone detected — e2e > unit. Target: 70/20/10.');
  process.exit(1); // CI gate: fail if the pyramid is inverted
}
```

**When to use:** Quarterly pyramid health audits; CI gates that block new e2e tests when the e2e ratio exceeds 25%; post-incident reviews where a bug slipped through a green CI (the audit often reveals an empty integration layer); new team members joining a project to understand the testing culture.

**When NOT to use:** Projects in early development (< 50 test cases total — ratio auditing is premature); projects where the correct shape is intentionally different (a pure-UI Storybook library with mostly visual regression tests); teams using Testing Trophy where integration > unit is expected.

**Alternative:** Vitest's JSON reporter (`--reporter=json`) with a post-processing script for test counts; `jest --listTests --json` in Jest; Sonarqube test quality gates with pyramid-shape rules; PR review checklist asking "which pyramid level does this test belong to?"

---

### Real-World Gotchas (Cycle 31)

102. **Vitest 5.0 `createReport` API silently produces an empty merged report when per-level JSON result files were written by a Vitest 4.x run** [community] — WHY: The JSON result schema changed between Vitest 4.x and 5.0. The `meta.vitestVersion` field and the `results[].tasks` shape differ. Passing a Vitest 4.x JSON blob to the Vitest 5.0 `createReport` API does not throw; it silently discards incompatible entries and produces a report showing zero tests. Teams running a mixed Vitest 4/5 pipeline (unit on an older worker image, browser on a newer image) are most affected. Fix: ensure all pyramid-level runners use the same Vitest version (`pnpm dedupe vitest`); add a schema version assertion at the top of the merge script before calling `createReport`.

103. **Node.js 26 `--test-randomize` only randomises within a single file — cross-file order-dependencies are not detected** [community] — WHY: `node:test`'s `--test-randomize` flag shuffles `it()`/`test()` order within one file but runs test *files* in the same filesystem enumeration order every time. A test in `file-b.test.ts` that depends on module-level state mutated by `file-a.test.ts` will always pass because `file-a.ts` loads first. Fix: vary which file runs first using `--test-shard` with different assignments, or script multiple runs with randomised file lists. Vitest `--sequence.shuffle` does shuffle across files as well, making it more thorough for cross-file order-dependency detection.

104. **TypeScript 5.9 `noUncheckedIndexedAccess: true` new `tsc --init` default makes every integration test fixture array access type `T | undefined`, causing `Object is possibly 'undefined'` errors in existing test helpers** [community] — WHY: When `tsconfig.json` is regenerated with `tsc --init` under TypeScript 5.9, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess: true` is included. Test helper files doing `const first = orders[0]` now have `first: Order | undefined`, and subsequent accesses (`first.id`, `first.total`) are type errors. Fix for seeded arrays of known length: use TypeScript tuple destructuring — `const [first, second] = orders as [Order, Order]` — to preserve element types without `| undefined`. For general helpers, use `orders.at(0)!` with an explicit non-null assertion after a length guard.

105. **`@fast-check/vitest` 0.4+ is ESM-only — projects with a CommonJS `vitest.config.ts` that use `require('@fast-check/vitest')` break with `ERR_REQUIRE_ESM` after upgrading** [community] — WHY: `@fast-check/vitest` 0.4 exports only an `"import"` entry in `package.json#exports` with no `"require"` field. Projects where the Vitest config file uses `module.exports = defineConfig(...)` (CJS syntax) and `require()` for test framework imports hit the ESM-only boundary immediately. Fix: convert `vitest.config.ts` to ESM (`export default defineConfig(...)`); ensure `package.json` has `"type": "module"` or rename the config file to `vitest.config.mts`.

106. **MSW `setupServer` from `msw/node` does not intercept `fetch()` calls inside Bun 1.x test files — Bun's native `fetch` bypasses MSW's Node.js HTTP interceptor patches** [community] — WHY: MSW v2 uses `@mswjs/interceptors` to patch Node.js's `http`/`https` modules and the WHATWG `fetch` global. Bun provides its own native `fetch` that does not route through Node.js HTTP internals, so the interceptor patches have no effect. `fetch()` calls in Bun test files reach real network endpoints, making tests non-deterministic in CI. Fix: use Bun's native `mock.module()` to replace the `fetch` global with a stub, or keep MSW-dependent integration tests running under Node.js and restrict Bun to unit-only runs.

107. **Playwright HAR replay via `context.routeFromHAR()` fails silently for HTTP/2 requests — the HAR file records the request but the route handler never fires, so the real network is hit in CI** [community] — WHY: Playwright's HAR replay matches requests by URL and method for browser-initiated requests. HTTP/2 requests made by backend server-side fetch (e.g., Next.js Server Components calling an API) use a different protocol stack that Playwright's browser-context routing does not intercept. The HAR file contains the frame but `routeFromHAR` silently falls through to real network. Fix: use `page.route()` with manual response objects for server-side requests rather than HAR replay; or configure the application under test to use HTTP/1.1 in test mode.

## Cycle 32 — 2026-05-14

### 31. Vitest 5.0 Inline `expect` Package for Cross-Framework Assertions  [official]

Vitest 5.0 extracts its assertion engine into a standalone `@vitest/expect` package that can run outside Vitest — in Node.js `node:test`, Bun's `bun:test`, or any test runner that just calls the assertions directly. This unlocks a **shared assertion vocabulary** across pyramid levels: the same `expect(value).toMatchObject(shape)` call runs in a Vitest unit test, a `node:test` integration test, and a Playwright custom helper without importing three different assertion libraries. The package is tree-shakeable and has no dependency on the Vitest runner itself.

```typescript
// tests/integration/order-api.integration.test.ts
// Using @vitest/expect in a bare node:test integration test — no Vitest runner needed
import { test } from 'node:test';
import { expect } from '@vitest/expect';
import { buildTestApp } from '../helpers/app-factory.js';
import type { OrderResponse } from '../../src/orders/order.types.js';

// The assertion API is identical to Vitest unit tests, making
// the cognitive load across pyramid levels uniform.
test('POST /orders returns 201 and the created order shape', async () => {
  const app = await buildTestApp();
  const response = await app.inject({
    method: 'POST',
    url: '/orders',
    payload: { productId: 'SKU-001', quantity: 2 },
  });

  expect(response.statusCode).toBe(201);

  const body = response.json<OrderResponse>();
  expect(body).toMatchObject({
    id:        expect.any(String),
    status:    'pending',
    productId: 'SKU-001',
    quantity:  2,
  });
  expect(body.createdAt).toMatch(/^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}T/);
});
```

**When to use:** Monorepos or polyglot test pipelines where different pyramid levels run under different test runners (Vitest for unit, `node:test` for integration, Playwright for e2e); teams migrating away from Jest who want assertion compatibility without migrating test runners at every layer; library authors publishing shared test utilities consumed by downstream projects on arbitrary runners.

**When NOT to use:** Single-runner projects where all levels use Vitest (no benefit — just use Vitest's built-in `expect`); projects that rely on Jest-specific matchers not ported to `@vitest/expect` (e.g., `expect.assertions(n)` counting semantics differ slightly); codebases still on Vitest 4.x (the standalone package is only stable in Vitest 5.0+).

**Alternative:** `chai` for a cross-runner assertion library with a longer ecosystem history; `jest-circus` as the assertion + runner combo for pure-Jest stacks; keeping each pyramid level in Vitest with `--project` flags for environment isolation.

---

### 32. Playwright `testProject.teardown` for Deterministic E2E Cleanup  [official]

Playwright v1.51+ introduces `testProject.teardown` — a named project that runs *after* a specific test project completes, regardless of pass/fail status. This solves a longstanding e2e anti-pattern: database cleanup code embedded in `afterAll` hooks inside test files, which fails to run when a test crashes hard (process exit, timeout abort). Moving cleanup to a dedicated teardown project ensures it always runs, keeps the main test files focused on assertions, and makes teardown visible in the HTML reporter as a first-class project step.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — teardown project pattern for deterministic cleanup
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  projects: [
    // 1. Setup: provision test data in the real (or staging) database
    {
      name:  'setup-db',
      testMatch: /global-setup\.ts/,
    },
    // 2. Main e2e tests — depend on setup, trigger cleanup on finish
    {
      name:      'e2e-chrome',
      use:       { browserName: 'chromium' },
      dependencies: ['setup-db'],
      teardown:     'cleanup-db',   // <-- always runs after e2e-chrome
      testDir:   './e2e',
      testMatch: /\.e2e\.spec\.ts$/,
    },
    // 3. Teardown: delete provisioned test data
    // Runs even if e2e-chrome tests crash or are aborted
    {
      name:      'cleanup-db',
      testMatch: /global-teardown\.ts/,
    },
  ],
});

// e2e/global-teardown.ts
import { test as teardownTest } from '@playwright/test';
import { deleteTestTenant } from '../helpers/db-admin.js';

// This file receives the same test-scoped fixtures as the main test project
teardownTest('delete test tenant', async ({ request }) => {
  const tenantId = process.env['TEST_TENANT_ID'];
  if (tenantId) {
    await deleteTestTenant(tenantId);
  }
});
```

**When to use:** E2e suites that provision real database rows, S3 objects, or third-party API test accounts; CI pipelines where a flaky test aborting the runner would otherwise leave stale test data; multi-project Playwright configs where one project's cleanup must not block another project's run; regulated environments requiring evidence that test data is deleted after each run.

**When NOT to use:** Projects using ephemeral databases (Testcontainers, Neon branch-per-run) where the container/branch is deleted at the infrastructure level — teardown projects add overhead without benefit; local development where `afterAll` cleanup is acceptable; suites with fewer than 20 e2e tests where the complexity of a teardown project outweighs its benefit.

**Alternative:** Vitest's `globalTeardown` option for integration-level cleanup; Testcontainers `container.stop()` in `afterAll`; Docker Compose `--abort-on-container-exit` with a cleanup service defined in `docker-compose.test.yml`.

---

### 33. Node.js 26 `--test-randomize` + `--test-random-seed` for Order-Dependency Detection at Unit Level  [official]

Node.js 26.1.0 adds `--test-randomize` and `--test-random-seed=N` flags to `node:test`. Running the unit test suite with `--test-randomize` each CI push surfaces **hidden order-dependencies** — test cases that pass only because a previous test left module-level state (a singleton, a cached value, an uncleared mock) in a specific configuration. The seed flag makes failures reproducible: once a failure is found at seed 42, subsequent runs with `--test-random-seed=42` reproduce it deterministically until the root cause is fixed.

```typescript
// scripts/test-order-check.ts — CI script to detect order-dependencies
// Run with: npx tsx scripts/test-order-check.ts
import { execSync } from 'node:child_process';

const SEEDS_TO_TRY = 5;
const failures: number[] = [];

for (let seed = 1; seed <= SEEDS_TO_TRY; seed++) {
  console.log(`Running unit tests with --test-random-seed=${seed}...`);
  try {
    execSync(
      `node --test --test-randomize --test-random-seed=${seed} src/**/*.unit.test.ts`,
      { stdio: 'pipe' },
    );
    console.log(`  Seed ${seed}: PASS`);
  } catch {
    console.error(`  Seed ${seed}: FAIL — order-dependency detected`);
    failures.push(seed);
  }
}

if (failures.length > 0) {
  console.error(`\nOrder-dependencies detected at seeds: ${failures.join(', ')}`);
  console.error('Fix: isolate module-level state in beforeEach / using Symbol.dispose');
  process.exit(1);
}

console.log('\nNo order-dependencies detected across all seeds.');
```

**When to use:** Any `node:test` unit suite with more than 30 test cases; CI pipelines where flaky tests are normalised as "just re-run it" (randomisation forces root-cause analysis); projects that share module singletons across tests (connection pools, caches, event emitters); onboarding audits for legacy codebases where test isolation discipline is unknown.

**When NOT to use:** Integration test suites that intentionally share a database transaction across tests for speed (the randomised order would break the shared transaction strategy — use Vitest `sequence.concurrent:false` instead); suites that are already fully isolated and have been proven so by prior randomisation passes (re-running adds CI time without new signal); Vitest-based projects where `--sequence.shuffle` already covers cross-file shuffling more thoroughly.

**Alternative:** Vitest `--sequence.shuffle` (covers both within-file and cross-file order shuffling, more thorough than `node:test`'s within-file-only randomisation); Jest `--randomize` flag (same semantics as `node:test`); `jest-circus` with `randomize: true` in Jest config for teams on Jest.

---

### 34. MSW v2 WebSocket Handler with `ws.onUpgrade` at the Integration Layer  [official]

MSW v2.14+ adds a `ws.onUpgrade` interceptor that intercepts the WebSocket protocol upgrade handshake before the connection is established. This enables integration tests to assert on the upgrade headers (JWT in `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`, tenant in a custom header) without spinning up a real WebSocket server. Combined with MSW's existing `ws.addEventListener('connection', ...)` API, teams can test the full WebSocket lifecycle — upgrade auth, message exchange, and graceful close — entirely within the integration test level, removing the need for e2e browser tests for WebSocket auth flows.

```typescript
// tests/integration/ws-auth.integration.test.ts
import { describe, beforeAll, afterAll, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { setupServer } from 'msw/node';
import { ws } from 'msw';

// The handler intercepts WS connections at the Node HTTP layer
// — no browser required, runs at integration level
const wsHandler = ws.link('ws://localhost:3001/live');

const server = setupServer(
  wsHandler.addEventListener('connection', ({ client }) => {
    // Mirror the auth token back as the first message for test assertion
    const upgradeHeaders = client.socket.upgradeRequest?.headers ?? {};
    const token = upgradeHeaders['sec-websocket-protocol'] as string | undefined;
    client.send(JSON.stringify({ type: 'auth-echo', token: token ?? 'missing' }));
  }),
);

beforeAll(() => server.listen({ onUnhandledRequest: 'error' }));
afterAll(() => server.close());

describe('WebSocket auth integration', () => {
  it('echoes the JWT from the upgrade handshake on connect', async () => {
    const socket = new WebSocket('ws://localhost:3001/live', ['Bearer.test-jwt-abc123']);
    const firstMessage = await new Promise<string>((resolve) => {
      socket.onmessage = (ev) => resolve(ev.data as string);
    });
    socket.close();

    const parsed = JSON.parse(firstMessage) as { type: string; token: string };
    expect(parsed.type).toBe('auth-echo');
    expect(parsed.token).toContain('test-jwt-abc123');
  });
});
```

**When to use:** Services with WebSocket auth that previously required full browser e2e tests (JWT in upgrade headers, session cookie validation, per-tenant routing); real-time notification systems where the connection establishment is more valuable to test than the message content; teams trying to migrate WebSocket e2e tests down to the integration level to reduce CI runtime.

**When NOT to use:** WebSocket tests that specifically need to validate browser rendering on receipt of a message (push notification UI, live data chart updates) — those belong at the e2e level; gRPC-Web or Server-Sent Events connections (different protocol — MSW handles `http.EventSource` separately); test environments using Bun 1.x where MSW's Node interceptor does not patch Bun's native WebSocket (see Gotcha #106).

**Alternative:** `jest-websocket-mock` for Jest-based integration suites; `ws` npm package with a real test server in `beforeAll`; Vitest's `vi.fn()` mock on `WebSocket` constructor at the unit level for connection-establishment-only tests.

---

### 35. Testcontainers Reuse Mode (`TESTCONTAINERS_REUSE_ENABLE`) for Fast Local Integration Loops  [community]

Testcontainers' container reuse feature (`withReuse()` on `GenericContainer`) keeps the database container running between test runs when the developer is iterating locally. The first run starts the container; subsequent `npm test` invocations skip container startup and connect directly to the running instance — reducing local integration test startup from 15–30 s to under 1 s. In CI, the `TESTCONTAINERS_REUSE_ENABLE` env var is omitted (defaults to off), so each CI job gets a fresh container. This pattern eliminates the common trade-off between "fast tests with mocks" and "slow tests with real containers."

```typescript
// tests/helpers/db-container.ts
// Shared container helper — reuse enabled for local, disabled in CI
import { GenericContainer, type StartedTestContainer } from 'testcontainers';

let _container: StartedTestContainer | null = null;

export async function getPostgresContainer(): Promise<StartedTestContainer> {
  if (_container) return _container; // already started in this process

  const reuseEnabled = process.env['TESTCONTAINERS_REUSE_ENABLE'] === 'true';

  const builder = new GenericContainer('postgres:16-alpine')
    .withEnvironment({
      POSTGRES_DB:       'testdb',
      POSTGRES_USER:     'test',
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: 'test',
    })
    .withExposedPorts(5432);

  if (reuseEnabled) {
    builder.withReuse(); // keeps container alive between process restarts locally
  }

  _container = await builder.start();

  if (!reuseEnabled) {
    // In CI: register a process exit handler to stop the container
    process.once('exit', () => { _container?.stop().catch(() => {}); });
  }

  return _container;
}

// Usage in integration test:
// import { getPostgresContainer } from '../helpers/db-container.js';
// beforeAll(async () => {
//   const container = await getPostgresContainer();
//   const port = container.getMappedPort(5432);
//   process.env['DATABASE_URL'] = `postgresql://test:test@localhost:${port}/testdb`;
// });
```

**When to use:** Developer-inner-loop integration tests where container startup latency discourages running the suite locally; teams where integration tests are run frequently (TDD at the integration level, not just in CI); monorepos where multiple integration test suites share the same Postgres/Redis/Kafka image version.

**When NOT to use:** CI pipelines — always use fresh containers in CI to avoid test pollution between PR builds; tests that require a clean initial database state (no seed data, schema migrations applied from scratch) — reused containers carry previous test data; tests that test the database migration path itself (the container must start from scratch each time).

**Alternative:** Docker Compose `--abort-on-container-exit` with a shared network for local integration test runs; Neon database branching (branch-per-test-run) where container startup is not relevant; `vitest --pool=forks` with a shared in-memory SQLite instance for integration tests that do not require Postgres-specific features.

---

### 36. Playwright `page.pickLocator()` for Locator Discovery in Test Maintenance  [official]

Playwright v1.60 introduces `page.pickLocator()` — an interactive method that returns the best-practice locator for an element at a given coordinate. In test maintenance workflows (fixing a broken locator after a UI refactor), `page.pickLocator()` can be called from a `--debug` session to discover the current resilient locator without manually inspecting the DOM. Unlike the Playwright Inspector's codegen mode, `pickLocator()` is programmable — it can be called in a script that iterates over a locator audit list and emits updated locator strings as TypeScript source.

```typescript
// scripts/audit-locators.ts
// Run with: npx playwright test --headed --debug scripts/audit-locators.ts
// Produces updated locators for known-fragile selectors
import { chromium } from 'playwright';

interface LocatorAuditEntry {
  label: string;
  oldSelector: string;
}

const FRAGILE_SELECTORS: LocatorAuditEntry[] = [
  { label: 'submit-button',     oldSelector: '#btn-submit-order' },
  { label: 'order-total-badge', oldSelector: '.order-summary > span:last-child' },
  { label: 'error-alert',       oldSelector: '[data-test="error"]' },
];

const browser = await chromium.launch({ headless: false });
const page    = await browser.newPage();
await page.goto('http://localhost:3000/checkout');

for (const { label, oldSelector } of FRAGILE_SELECTORS) {
  const element = page.locator(oldSelector).first();
  if (await element.count() === 0) {
    console.warn(`${label}: OLD selector not found — needs manual investigation`);
    continue;
  }
  const box = await element.boundingBox();
  if (!box) continue;
  const cx = box.x + box.width / 2;
  const cy = box.y + box.height / 2;
  const picked = await page.pickLocator({ x: cx, y: cy });
  console.log(`${label}: NEW locator = ${JSON.stringify(picked)}`);
}

await browser.close();
```

**When to use:** Post-refactor locator audits where tens of e2e selectors break simultaneously; teams inheriting legacy Playwright suites that use brittle CSS selectors (`.class > span:nth-child(2)`) rather than role-based locators; dedicated "locator health" CI checks that flag selectors not using `getByRole`, `getByLabel`, or `getByTestId` conventions.

**When NOT to use:** Automated test execution (not interactive mode — `pickLocator()` requires a headed browser with user interaction capability); replacing the discipline of writing resilient locators from the start (treat `pickLocator` as a repair tool, not a generation tool); projects where all locators already use semantic `data-testid` attributes and role-based selectors (no benefit).

**Alternative:** Playwright Codegen (`npx playwright codegen`) for generating locators interactively; `@testing-library/dom` `getByRole` utilities at the component integration level to enforce accessible locators by convention; Storybook interaction tests with `screen.getByRole` to verify component locators before Playwright e2e is written.

---

### 37. Vitest `aroundEach` / `aroundAll` Hooks for Symmetric Setup-Teardown  [official]

Vitest 4.0 introduces `aroundEach` and `aroundAll` hooks — generator-based hooks that wrap setup *and* teardown in a single function using `yield`. This eliminates the anti-pattern of `beforeEach` and `afterEach` referencing a shared mutable variable (`let container: StartedTestContainer`). With `aroundEach`, the resource is declared, used, and cleaned up in a single lexical scope — making it impossible to forget teardown and impossible for the teardown to reference an uninitialised variable.

```typescript
// tests/integration/user-service.integration.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, aroundEach } from 'vitest';
import { startPostgresContainer } from '../helpers/containers.js';
import { UserService }             from '../../src/users/user.service.js';
import { createTestDataSource }    from '../helpers/datasource-factory.js';

describe('UserService integration', () => {
  // aroundEach: setup BEFORE yield, teardown AFTER yield — single function
  aroundEach(async function* (use) {
    // --- SETUP ---
    const container  = await startPostgresContainer();
    const dataSource = await createTestDataSource(container.getMappedPort(5432));
    await dataSource.runMigrations();

    await use({ container, dataSource }); // <-- test runs here

    // --- TEARDOWN (always runs, even if test throws) ---
    await dataSource.destroy();
    await container.stop();
  });

  it('creates a user and finds them by email', async ({ container: _c, dataSource }) => {
    const service = new UserService(dataSource.getRepository('User'));
    const created  = await service.create({ email: 'alice@example.com', name: 'Alice' });
    const found    = await service.findByEmail('alice@example.com');

    expect(found).not.toBeNull();
    expect(found?.id).toBe(created.id);
    expect(found?.name).toBe('Alice');
  });

  it('throws when creating a duplicate email', async ({ dataSource }) => {
    const service = new UserService(dataSource.getRepository('User'));
    await service.create({ email: 'bob@example.com', name: 'Bob' });

    await expect(
      service.create({ email: 'bob@example.com', name: 'Bob Again' }),
    ).rejects.toThrow(/duplicate key/i);
  });
});
```

**When to use:** Integration tests that start/stop Testcontainers containers, open/close database connections, or acquire/release any resource that must be cleaned up; teams where `afterEach` teardown bugs (forgot to call `container.stop()`, `afterEach` referencing an uninitialised `let container`) are a recurring issue; any test that currently uses a `beforeEach`/`afterEach` pair to manage the same resource.

**When NOT to use:** Simple unit tests where `beforeEach` resetting a local variable is idiomatic and sufficient; test suites on Vitest 3.x or below (not available — use `beforeEach`/`afterEach` pair); tests that need *conditional* teardown depending on test outcome (aroundEach always resumes after yield — use `onTestFailed()` for conditional-only teardown).

**Alternative:** Vitest `test.extend` with a fixture function (similar generator-based pattern, scoped to a test context object); `using` keyword (explicit resource management, TypeScript 5.2+, requires `Symbol.asyncDispose` on the resource — more idiomatic for single resources but requires polyfilling pre-ES2026 runtimes).

---

### 38. Contract Testing with Pact-JS v16 at the Integration Pyramid Layer  [official]

Pact-JS v16.0 (Oct 2025) stabilises the V4 Pact specification with `Pact` (renamed from `PactV4`) as the canonical export, adds GraphQL support, and ships pending/comment/test-name annotations on interactions. Contract tests sit between integration and e2e on the pyramid: they verify the *interface contract* between a consumer and a provider without requiring both services to run simultaneously. Each pyramid level has a distinct role — unit tests verify the consumer serialisation logic, contract tests verify the provider honours the contract, integration tests verify the consumer can reach a real endpoint, e2e tests verify the user journey.

```typescript
// tests/contract/order-consumer.contract.test.ts
// Consumer side — Pact-JS v16 canonical API (Pact + Matchers)
import { Pact, Matchers } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
import path from 'node:path';

const { like, string, integer, datetime } = Matchers;

const provider = new Pact({
  consumer: 'OrderService',
  provider: 'InventoryService',
  dir:      path.resolve('./pacts'),
  logDir:   path.resolve('./logs'),
});

describe('Order → Inventory contract (Pact-JS v16)', () => {
  beforeAll(() => provider.setup());
  afterAll(() => provider.finalize());
  afterEach(() => provider.verify());

  it('gets stock level for a product', async () => {
    await provider.addInteraction({
      state:          'product SKU-001 has 50 units in stock',
      uponReceiving:  'a GET request for stock level of SKU-001',
      withRequest: {
        method:  'GET',
        path:    '/inventory/SKU-001',
        headers: { Accept: 'application/json' },
      },
      willRespondWith: {
        status: 200,
        body: like({
          productId: string('SKU-001'),
          quantity:  integer(50),
          updatedAt: datetime("yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss", '2026-05-14T00:00:00'),
        }),
      },
    });

    const { InventoryClient } = await import('../../src/inventory/client.js');
    const client = new InventoryClient({ baseUrl: provider.mockService.baseUrl });
    const stock  = await client.getStock('SKU-001');
    expect(stock.quantity).toBe(50);
  });
});
```

**When to use:** Microservice architectures where consumer and provider are deployed independently; teams that have experienced production incidents caused by undiscovered API contract drift (provider changed a field name, consumer broke silently); pipelines where running both services simultaneously is expensive or unreliable; GraphQL API evolution where breaking changes in a schema must be detected before deployment.

**When NOT to use:** Monoliths where consumer and provider share the same TypeScript types and compile together (TypeScript already enforces the contract at compile time — Pact adds no new signal); third-party APIs you do not control (Pact requires the provider team to run provider verification — use MSW mock handlers instead); contract tests as a substitute for integration tests (they verify *shape*, not *behaviour* — a provider can pass contract tests while returning wrong business logic).

**Alternative:** OpenAPI contract testing with `openapi-backend` or `schemathesis`; type-safe gRPC with Protobuf definitions as the contract (enforced by the TypeScript protobuf codegen); `prism` (Stoplight) for provider mock and contract validation from an OpenAPI schema.

---

### 39. Vitest 4.1 `vi.defineHelper` for Clean Custom Assertion Stack Traces  [official]

Vitest 4.1 introduces `vi.defineHelper` — a wrapper for custom assertion utility functions that marks the helper's internal frames as non-user code. Without it, when a custom `expectValidOrder(order)` helper fails, the stack trace points *inside* the helper at the `expect` call, not at the test case that called `expectValidOrder`. With `vi.defineHelper`, Vitest strips the helper frames and the stack trace points directly to the test case line, drastically reducing time-to-diagnosis for integration test failures.

```typescript
// tests/helpers/order-assertions.ts
// Custom assertions wrapped with vi.defineHelper for clean stack traces
import { expect, vi } from 'vitest';
import type { Order, OrderStatus } from '../../src/orders/order.types.js';

// Without vi.defineHelper: failure stack points inside this function body
// With vi.defineHelper:    failure stack points to the test file call site
export const expectValidOrder = vi.defineHelper(
  function expectValidOrder(order: unknown): asserts order is Order {
    expect(order).toMatchObject({
      id:        expect.any(String),
      status:    expect.stringMatching(/^(pending|confirmed|shipped|delivered|cancelled)$/),
      createdAt: expect.any(String),
      total:     expect.any(Number),
    });
  },
);

export const expectOrderStatus = vi.defineHelper(
  function expectOrderStatus(order: Order, expectedStatus: OrderStatus): void {
    expect(order.status).toBe(expectedStatus);
    if (expectedStatus === 'shipped') {
      expect(order.trackingId).not.toBeNull();
      expect(order.shippedAt).not.toBeNull();
    }
    if (expectedStatus === 'cancelled') {
      expect(order.cancellationReason).not.toBeNull();
    }
  },
);

// Usage in integration test:
// it('order flow: pending → confirmed → shipped', async () => {
//   const order = await orderService.create(payload);
//   expectValidOrder(order);              // stack trace → this line if it fails
//   expectOrderStatus(order, 'pending'); // stack trace → this line if it fails
// });
```

**When to use:** Any Vitest project (unit or integration level) with shared assertion helpers called from multiple test files; teams spending significant time diagnosing "which test called the helper that failed" by manually tracing stack frames; helpers that perform multi-step assertions where the failing sub-assertion is not immediately obvious from the stack.

**When NOT to use:** Assertions used only once (no need for a helper wrapper); projects on Vitest 4.0.x or below (not available); helpers that intentionally show their internal frames for debugging (e.g., a helper that logs intermediate state — `vi.defineHelper` hides those frames from the stack view).

**Alternative:** Vitest `extend` matchers (`expect.extend({ validOrder(received) {...} })`) for custom `toBeValidOrder()` matcher syntax — slightly more ergonomic at the call site but more boilerplate to write; `chai`-style plugin API for projects mixing chai assertions.

---

### 40. TypeScript 5.9 `import defer` for Expensive Test Setup Modules  [official]

TypeScript 5.9 stabilises the TC39 `import defer` proposal — a lazy module evaluation syntax that defers execution of a module's top-level code until the first property access. At the integration test level, this solves a specific problem: setup files that `import` a database client or HTTP adapter at the top level incur startup cost even in test files that stub or mock that module. With `import defer`, the real module only initialises when the test actually calls into it, making module-load time for the mocked path nearly zero.

```typescript
// tests/integration/order-processor.integration.test.ts
// import defer: the EmailClient module-level code does not execute unless the
// test actually accesses a property on it (which this file does, but via mock)
import defer * as EmailClientModule from '../../src/notifications/email-client.js';
import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach }  from 'vitest';
import { OrderProcessor }   from '../../src/orders/order-processor.js';
import { createInMemoryDb }  from '../helpers/in-memory-db.js';

// vi.mock hoisting still fires before any import — mock takes effect correctly
vi.mock('../../src/notifications/email-client.js', () => ({
  EmailClient: vi.fn().mockImplementation(() => ({
    sendOrderConfirmation: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue({ messageId: 'mock-001' }),
  })),
}));

describe('OrderProcessor integration (EmailClient deferred + mocked)', () => {
  let processor: OrderProcessor;

  beforeEach(() => {
    const db = createInMemoryDb();
    // First property access on EmailClientModule triggers deferred init,
    // but vi.mock already replaced the module — real SMTP client never connects
    processor = new OrderProcessor(db, new EmailClientModule.EmailClient());
  });

  it('processes a valid order and returns confirmed status', async () => {
    const result = await processor.process({
      orderId: 'ORD-001', productId: 'SKU-002', quantity: 3,
    });
    expect(result.status).toBe('confirmed');
    expect(result.confirmationId).toMatch(/^CONF-/);
  });

  it('rejects orders with zero quantity', async () => {
    await expect(
      processor.process({ orderId: 'ORD-002', productId: 'SKU-002', quantity: 0 }),
    ).rejects.toThrow('Quantity must be greater than zero');
  });
});
```

**When to use:** Integration test files that import modules with expensive side-effectful initialisation (DB connection pool, Redis client, SMTP transport); test suites where module load time contributes meaningfully to CI startup overhead; files where the import is sometimes mocked and sometimes real, and mocked paths should have near-zero overhead.

**When NOT to use:** Simple modules with no side effects at the top level (no startup benefit from deferring); projects on TypeScript 5.8 or below (the `import defer` syntax is not available — use dynamic `import()` inside the function instead); modules that must initialise synchronously for correct typing behaviour.

**Alternative:** Dynamic `import()` inside `beforeAll` for manually-lazy module loading; Vitest's `vi.mock()` hoisting for stubbing expensive modules without changing the import syntax; `vi.importActual()` + `vi.importMock()` for selective real/mock module evaluation.

---

### 41. React Testing Library v16 Auto-`act()` Wrap for Async Component Integration Tests  [official]

React Testing Library v16 (Dec 2024), compatible with React 19, removes the need for manual `await act(async () => {...})` wrappers around RTL events and queries. RTL v16 automatically wraps all interactions in `act()` internally. This eliminates a widespread TypeScript integration test pattern where tests wrapped every `userEvent` and `fireEvent` call in an explicit `act()`, producing noisy async syntax that obscured the actual test intent. Tests now read as near-synchronous assertions even when testing components with async state updates, suspense boundaries, or concurrent rendering.

```typescript
// tests/integration/checkout-form.integration.test.tsx
// RTL v16 + React 19: no explicit act() needed — RTL wraps internally
import { render, screen, waitFor } from '@testing-library/react';
import userEvent from '@testing-library/user-event';
import { CheckoutForm } from '../../src/components/CheckoutForm.js';
import { server }       from '../mocks/server.js'; // MSW server
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw';

describe('CheckoutForm integration', () => {
  it('submits the form and shows the confirmation message', async () => {
    server.use(
      http.post('/api/checkout', () =>
        HttpResponse.json({ orderId: 'ORD-123', status: 'confirmed' }),
      ),
    );

    // No act() wrapper: RTL v16 handles it internally with React 19 scheduler
    render(<CheckoutForm productId="SKU-001" quantity={2} />);

    await userEvent.type(screen.getByLabelText(/shipping address/i), '123 Main St');
    await userEvent.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: /place order/i }));

    await waitFor(() => {
      expect(screen.getByRole('alert')).toHaveTextContent('Order confirmed: ORD-123');
    });

    expect(screen.getByLabelText(/shipping address/i)).toHaveValue('');
  });

  it('shows an error message when the API returns 422', async () => {
    server.use(
      http.post('/api/checkout', () =>
        HttpResponse.json({ error: 'Invalid address' }, { status: 422 }),
      ),
    );

    render(<CheckoutForm productId="SKU-001" quantity={2} />);
    await userEvent.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: /place order/i }));

    await waitFor(() =>
      expect(screen.getByRole('alert')).toHaveTextContent('Invalid address'),
    );
  });
});
```

**When to use:** Any React/Next.js TypeScript project that has upgraded to RTL v16 and React 19; teams with existing test files full of `await act(async () => {...})` wrappers that should be removed as a cleanup pass; component integration tests with suspense boundaries, deferred state updates, or React 19 `use()` hook usage that required complex act orchestration.

**When NOT to use:** Projects still on React 17/18 with RTL v14/v15 — the auto-wrapping behaviour is React 19-specific and relies on new scheduler signals; tests that need explicit `act()` to control the exact timing of state flushes (rare but valid for testing transition states); tests that import `act` from `react` directly for low-level imperative control.

**Alternative:** Vue Testing Library v2 for Vue 3 + Composition API component integration tests (same auto-act pattern); Svelte Testing Library for Svelte 5 runes; `@testing-library/angular` v17 for Angular 17+ standalone component integration tests.
