#### Pattern 157 — Pact JS v16.3 Pending Interactions for In-Progress Contract Negotiations [official]

Pact JS v16.3 added support for marking individual interactions as `pending`, which prevents a failing interaction from breaking the overall provider verification build. A pending interaction is one that has been written by the consumer team but whose implementation on the provider side is still in progress. Without pending interactions, the provider build breaks the moment a consumer writes a new contract requirement — penalising providers for consumer-driven feature requests that they have not yet implemented. With `pending: true`, the failing interaction is reported as a warning in the Pact Broker dashboard but does not fail the CI build.

```typescript
// consumer/src/api/__tests__/productApi.pact.test.ts
import { PactV4, MatchersV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
import { getProductById } from '../productApi';

const { like, string, integer } = MatchersV3;

const pact = new PactV4({
  consumer: 'ProductUI',
  provider: 'ProductService',
  dir: './pacts',
});

describe('Product API contract', () => {
  it('fetches existing product by ID (confirmed interaction)', () => {
    return pact
      .addInteraction()
      .given('product 42 exists')
      .uponReceiving('a request for product 42')
      .withRequest({ method: 'GET', path: '/products/42' })
      .willRespondWith({
        status: 200,
        body: like({ id: integer(42), name: string('Widget'), price: like(9.99) }),
      })
      .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
        const product = await getProductById(mockServer.url, 42);
        expect(product.name).toBe('Widget');
      });
  });

  it('returns 404 for deleted product (PENDING — provider implementation in sprint 24)', () => {
    return pact
      .addInteraction()
      .given('product 99 has been deleted')
      .uponReceiving('a request for deleted product 99')
      .withRequest({ method: 'GET', path: '/products/99' })
      .willRespondWith({ status: 404, body: like({ error: string('Not Found') }) })
      // Mark as pending — provider build will not fail until this is resolved
      .pending(true)
      .withComment('Pending until ProductService team implements soft-delete in sprint 24')
      .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
        await expect(getProductById(mockServer.url, 99)).rejects.toMatchObject({ status: 404 });
      });
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Pending interactions can accumulate indefinitely if teams do not track them actively. A Pact Broker configured with `requireAllInteractions: false` (the default) silently ignores pending interactions that have never been implemented. Enforce a sprint-level ritual to review pending interactions in the Pact Broker UI — any interaction pending for more than two sprints should trigger a cross-team sync. Automate this with the Pact Broker's `--pending-provider-tags` CLI flag to auto-fail CI once a provider tag marks an interaction as implemented.

#### Pattern 158 — Pact JS v16.4 `addInteractionReference` for Linking External Test Evidence to Contract Interactions [official]

Pact JS v16.4 added `addInteractionReference()` to the V4 DSL, allowing contract interactions to carry external references — links to GitHub issues, Jira tickets, design documents, or test case management IDs. When published to a Pact Broker, these references appear alongside the interaction, giving provider teams context for why an interaction was written and where to find the original requirement. This is particularly useful for regulatory compliance where every contract interaction must trace back to a documented business requirement.

```typescript
// consumer/src/api/__tests__/paymentApi.pact.test.ts
import { PactV4, MatchersV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
import { processRefund } from '../paymentApi';

const { like, string, decimal } = MatchersV3;

const pact = new PactV4({
  consumer: 'OrdersUI',
  provider: 'PaymentService',
  dir: './pacts',
});

it('processes a full refund and returns the refund confirmation ID', () => {
  return pact
    .addInteraction()
    .given('order 100 has been fully paid')
    .uponReceiving('a full refund request for order 100')
    .withRequest({
      method: 'POST',
      path: '/refunds',
      body: like({ orderId: 100, amount: decimal(99.99), reason: string('customer_request') }),
    })
    .willRespondWith({
      status: 201,
      body: like({ refundId: string('REF-001'), status: string('processed'), amount: decimal(99.99) }),
    })
    // Link to external requirement for traceability in regulated environments
    .addInteractionReference({
      name: 'PAY-2831: Full refund for completed orders',
      url: 'https://jira.example.com/browse/PAY-2831',
    })
    .addInteractionReference({
      name: 'GDPR Art.17 — Right to erasure financial data',
      url: 'https://confluence.example.com/x/gdpr-art17',
    })
    .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
      const refund = await processRefund(mockServer.url, { orderId: 100, amount: 99.99 });
      expect(refund.refundId).toMatch(/^REF-/);
      expect(refund.status).toBe('processed');
    });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `addInteractionReference` stores references in the pact JSON file and the Pact Broker, but it does not validate that the URLs are reachable or that the referenced tickets are open. A stale reference to a closed Jira ticket provides false confidence that the requirement is still active. Automate reference URL validation as a separate CI step (a curl health check on all reference URLs in published pacts) to catch 404s from deleted documentation or migrated Jira projects.

#### Pattern 159 — Playwright Component Testing `mount` with Browser-Side Module Mock Registration [official]

Playwright's experimental component testing (`@playwright/experimental-ct-react`) runs component tests in a real browser, but module-level mocks via `vi.mock()` or `jest.mock()` run in the Node.js test process and do not propagate to the browser iframe where the component renders. Playwright v1.59+ addressed this by introducing a `registerMocks()` hook in `playwright/index.tsx` (the component test setup file) that accepts a map of module paths to mock factory functions executed in the browser context. This enables mocking API clients, router hooks, or feature flags at the browser module level without service worker interception.

```typescript
// playwright/index.tsx — component test browser-side setup
import { beforeMount } from '@playwright/experimental-ct-react/hooks';
import { vi } from 'vitest';

// Mock the feature flag module at the browser level
vi.mock('../src/hooks/useFeatureFlag', () => ({
  useFeatureFlag: vi.fn((flag: string) => {
    // Default all flags to false in tests
    const defaults: Record<string, boolean> = {
      'new-checkout-flow': false,
      'dark-mode-beta': false,
    };
    return defaults[flag] ?? false;
  }),
}));

beforeMount(async ({ hooksConfig }: { hooksConfig?: { featureFlags?: Record<string, boolean> } }) => {
  // hooksConfig can pass per-test overrides from test file
  if (hooksConfig?.featureFlags) {
    const { useFeatureFlag } = await import('../src/hooks/useFeatureFlag');
    (useFeatureFlag as ReturnType<typeof vi.fn>).mockImplementation(
      (flag: string) => hooksConfig.featureFlags![flag] ?? false
    );
  }
});
```

```typescript
// src/components/CheckoutButton.ct.test.tsx
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/experimental-ct-react';
import { CheckoutButton } from './CheckoutButton';

test('shows new checkout flow when feature flag is enabled', async ({ mount }) => {
  const component = await mount(<CheckoutButton />, {
    hooksConfig: { featureFlags: { 'new-checkout-flow': true } },
  });

  await expect(component.getByRole('button', { name: 'Checkout v2' })).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Browser-side `vi.mock()` in Playwright component tests requires Vitest to be the test runner (the `@playwright/experimental-ct-react` integration uses Vitest under the hood). If you are using Jest as the test runner for component tests, browser-side mock registration is not available — use `beforeMount` with explicit prop injection or MSW service worker interception instead. The `hooksConfig` object is serialised via `JSON.stringify` before being sent to the browser, so only plain JSON-serialisable values can be passed (no functions, class instances, or Symbols).

#### Pattern 160 — user-event v14.6 `FocusEvent` in Hidden Documents for Accessibility Testing in JSDOM [official]

testing-library/user-event v14.6.0 added support for dispatching `FocusEvent` in hidden documents (documents where `document.visibilityState === 'hidden'`). In JSDOM, the document is always visible by default, but custom render environments that simulate background-tab behaviour (for testing focus management in multi-tab applications, keyboard trap testing in accessible modals, or Service Worker-related page lifecycle tests) set `document.hidden = true`. Before v14.6, `userEvent.tab()` silently skipped focus event dispatching in hidden documents, causing keyboard navigation tests in these environments to falsely pass without exercising focus logic.

```typescript
// src/components/AccessibleModal.test.tsx
import { render, screen } from '@testing-library/react';
import userEvent from '@testing-library/user-event';
import { vi } from 'vitest';
import { AccessibleModal } from './AccessibleModal';

describe('AccessibleModal — keyboard trap and focus management', () => {
  it('traps focus within modal when Tab is pressed', async () => {
    const user = userEvent.setup();

    render(
      <AccessibleModal isOpen title="Confirm deletion">
        <button>Cancel</button>
        <button>Delete</button>
      </AccessibleModal>
    );

    // Focus starts at the first focusable element
    await user.tab();
    expect(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Cancel' })).toHaveFocus();

    // Tab again — wraps to second element
    await user.tab();
    expect(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete' })).toHaveFocus();

    // Tab again — focus wraps back to first (keyboard trap)
    await user.tab();
    expect(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Cancel' })).toHaveFocus();

    // Shift+Tab — reverse trap
    await user.tab({ shift: true });
    expect(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete' })).toHaveFocus();
  });

  it('dispatches FocusEvent correctly in simulated hidden-document context', async () => {
    // Simulate hidden document (background tab scenario)
    Object.defineProperty(document, 'hidden', { value: true, writable: true });

    const user = userEvent.setup();
    const focusSpy = vi.fn();

    render(
      <AccessibleModal isOpen title="Background tab modal">
        <button onFocus={focusSpy}>Action</button>
      </AccessibleModal>
    );

    // v14.6: FocusEvent now dispatches even in hidden documents
    await user.tab();
    expect(focusSpy).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();

    Object.defineProperty(document, 'hidden', { value: false, writable: true });
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** The `FocusEvent` in hidden documents change in v14.6 may surface previously-silent focus event handlers in tests that were passing only because events were suppressed. If upgrading from v14.5 to v14.6 causes unexpected failures, audit tests that use `document.hidden` manipulation or that test background-tab lifecycle — the failures likely indicate that focus handlers were incorrectly not executing before the fix. This is a correctness improvement, not a regression.

---

### Real-World Gotchas (Cycle 37)

136. **Playwright `getByRole('button', { description: '...' })` returns no match when `aria-describedby` references a hidden element — `display: none` on the description element causes the accessible description computation to return an empty string, making the description filter match nothing** [community] — WHY: The accessible description algorithm (accname-1.1 spec) only includes text from elements that are visible to accessibility APIs. When `aria-describedby` references an element hidden with `display: none` or `visibility: hidden`, the element is excluded from the accessible name/description computation. The computed accessible description is `""`, not the hidden element's text content. Fix: use `aria-description` (the direct string attribute, not a reference) for descriptions that must survive hidden-element scenarios, or use `aria-describedby` with elements that are visually hidden via `sr-only` CSS (positioned off-screen) rather than `display: none`.

137. **Jest 30.4 `jest.useFakeTimers({ now: Temporal.ZonedDateTime.from(...) })` config-level `now` option does not accept `Temporal.ZonedDateTime` — only `jest.setSystemTime()` accepts Temporal types; the `now` option in `fakeTimers` config still only accepts `number | Date`** [community] — WHY: The `FakeTimersConfig.now` option is evaluated synchronously during timer initialisation by `@sinonjs/fake-timers` before Jest's Temporal type coercion layer is applied. Only the imperative `jest.setSystemTime(temporal)` call has the coercion logic that converts `Temporal.Instant` and `Temporal.ZonedDateTime` to epoch milliseconds. Passing a `Temporal.ZonedDateTime` as `now` in the config object results in `NaN` as the initial fake clock value, causing `Date.now()` to return `NaN`. Fix: always use `jest.setSystemTime(Temporal.ZonedDateTime.from(...))` imperatively inside `beforeEach` rather than setting `now` in the config object.

138. **Vitest 5.0 beta `attachmentsDir` default changed from `.vitest-attachments/` to `.vitest/attachments/` — existing `.gitignore` rules that ignore `.vitest-attachments/` do not ignore the new path, causing screenshot baselines and test attachments to accidentally be committed** [community] — WHY: The `attachmentsDir` default path was moved as part of a broader Vitest 5.0 directory consolidation that places all Vitest-generated artefacts under `.vitest/`. Projects upgrading from Vitest 4.x to 5.0 beta that have `.vitest-attachments/` in `.gitignore` will find that screenshot baselines captured after the upgrade land in `.vitest/attachments/` which is not gitignored. The first `git status` after the upgrade will show hundreds of new untracked PNG files. Fix: add `.vitest/` to `.gitignore` when upgrading to Vitest 5.0 beta, and remove the now-obsolete `.vitest-attachments/` entry.

139. **MSW v2.14 `ws.onUpgrade` calling `client.close()` inside the handler emits a `WebSocket is already in CLOSING state` warning on the second test that uses the same handler — MSW does not reset WebSocket handler state between tests when `resetHandlers()` is not called between `use()` calls** [community] — WHY: `ws.onUpgrade` handlers retain closure state from the previous test run when `server.resetHandlers()` is called but the base handler (installed in `setupServer`) is the same reference. The `close()` call records a state flag on the handler's internal WebSocket wrapper. On the next test, MSW reuses the same wrapper reference and the flag persists, causing `close()` to trigger a `CLOSING` state warning rather than a clean close. Fix: use `server.use()` with a freshly constructed `ws.onUpgrade` handler in each test that needs connection lifecycle simulation, rather than relying on a shared handler reference in `setupServer()`.

140. **Pact JS v16 `pending(true)` interactions are skipped entirely from provider verification when running with `--publishVerificationResults false` — the pending interaction is never exercised, leading to a false impression that the contract is being continuously validated** [community] — WHY: The Pact Broker's pending interaction workflow requires that the provider's verification result be published to the broker (via `--publishVerificationResults true`) for the broker to track whether the interaction has been implemented. When `--publishVerificationResults false` is set (common in local development or PR branches), the Pact library internally skips pending interactions altogether rather than running them and discarding the result. This means the interaction is never validated locally, and developers assume the contract is being tested when it is not. Fix: run pending interactions explicitly in local development using `--enablePending true` combined with `--publishVerificationResults false` — Pact JS v16 requires both flags together to run-but-not-publish pending interaction results. Document this in the contributing guide for your contract testing setup.

141. **Testcontainers Node `withAutoRemove(false)` combined with `withReuse()` causes duplicate containers — Testcontainers' container reuse logic does not account for `withAutoRemove(false)` status, creating a new container instead of reusing the stopped one** [community] — WHY: `withReuse()` matches reusable containers by their configuration hash stored in the Testcontainers label. A container that was stopped with `withAutoRemove(false)` has the same configuration hash as a new container request, but Testcontainers' reuse check queries only running containers (`status=running`) — it excludes stopped containers from the reuse candidate pool. Each test run that uses `withReuse()` after a `withAutoRemove(false)` stop creates a new container, accumulating stopped containers. Fix: use `withAutoRemove(false)` exclusively for debugging runs (behind a `DEBUG_CONTAINERS=true` env var) and never combine it with `withReuse()`. In CI, clean up stopped containers with a periodic prune step filtered by the `org.testcontainers` label.

#### 142. Playwright `test.abort()` for Early Fixture Teardown on Fatal State

`test.abort()` (introduced in Playwright v1.60) terminates the running test immediately and triggers fixture teardown in reverse order, exactly as it would after a normal test end. Use it when a route handler or fixture detects unrecoverable application state — for example, a session cookie that is definitively absent — and continuing to assert would produce only noise. Unlike `expect().toPass()` loops, `test.abort()` does not consume retry budget: the test is marked as failed-with-reason but counts as a single attempt, preserving sharding efficiency. Call it with a descriptive string (`test.abort('auth cookie absent after login — fatal state')`) so the HTML report surfaces the abort reason without requiring the reviewer to open the trace. The teardown guarantee means database fixtures and browser contexts are always cleaned up even when `test.abort()` fires mid-test. [official]

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.use({ storageState: 'auth.json' });

test('purchase flow requires authenticated session', async ({ page, context }) => {
  await page.goto('/cart');

  // Abort immediately if auth cookie is absent — retrying checkout steps would be noise
  const cookies = await context.cookies();
  const sessionCookie = cookies.find(c => c.name === 'session');
  if (!sessionCookie) {
    test.abort('session cookie absent — storageState may be stale, regenerate with `npx playwright codegen`');
  }

  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Proceed to checkout' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Checkout' })).toBeVisible();
  await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4242424242424242');
  await page.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('12/28');
  await page.getByLabel('CVC').fill('123');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay now' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Order confirmed' })).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `test.abort()` is intentional early termination, not a soft skip — the test is counted as failed in the report. Reserve it for genuinely unrecoverable state (missing auth, corrupt seed data) rather than assertion failures that belong in `expect()`. Over-use converts a useful triage signal into an always-failing test that misleads coverage metrics. [official]

#### 143. Playwright Screencast API for AI Vision Pipelines

Playwright v1.59 introduced `page.screencast.start()` as a programmatic alternative to the `recordVideo` context option. The Screencast API allows starting and stopping recordings at precise points within a test and attaching the resulting video to a specific test step, rather than capturing the entire browser lifetime. `page.screencast.showActions()` overlays visual annotations on the recording, making captured frames legible to LLM vision models without additional post-processing. Use this in AI-assisted regression pipelines where a model is asked to diff before/after screen recordings of a user journey. Unlike `recordVideo`, screenshots captured via `page.screenshot()` during a screencast are embedded in the video timeline, providing frame-accurate correlation between assertion failures and their visual context. [official]

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { analyzeScreencastForRegressions } from '../helpers/ai-vision';

test('checkout flow — visual regression via AI vision', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');

  // Start targeted screencast for just the payment step
  const screencast = await page.screencast.start({ path: 'payment-flow.webm' });
  await page.screencast.showActions(); // overlays click/type annotations

  await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4242424242424242');
  await page.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('12/28');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay now' }).click();

  const confirmationScreenshot = await page.screenshot({ fullPage: false });
  await screencast.stop();

  // Feed to AI vision model for layout/content regression
  const result = await analyzeScreencastForRegressions('payment-flow.webm', {
    baseline: 'baselines/payment-flow.webm',
    sensitivityThreshold: 0.05,
  });

  expect(result.regressions).toHaveLength(0);
  expect(confirmationScreenshot).toMatchSnapshot('order-confirmed.png');
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Screencast recordings add IO overhead (typically 20–80 MB per test) and lengthen test runtime by 5–15 %. Limit screencast capture to integration-layer tests where visual regression value is highest — unit-level component tests should use `toMatchScreenshot()` snapshots instead. Store recordings in object storage (S3, GCS) with a short TTL rather than in the repo or test-results artifact to avoid CI artifact bloat. [official]

#### 144. Playwright `browser.bind()` for Multi-Client Collaborative Debugging

`browser.bind()` (Playwright v1.59) exposes a launched browser to external clients — including `playwright-cli`, VS Code, and custom tooling — over a CDP endpoint without requiring the `connectOverCDP()` URL. In test environments, this unlocks a debugging workflow where the test runner and a human inspector share the same browser instance: the inspector can observe the live DOM, pause execution at breakpoints set in the Trace Viewer, and inject commands without disrupting the running test. In CI, `browser.bind()` combined with a reverse-proxy tunnel (e.g., `cloudflared access`) allows synchronous remote review of flaky test reproduction runs without re-running the test in a local environment. The `browser.on('context')` event (also v1.60) fires for every new browser context, enabling middleware-style logging of context lifecycles without patching `newContext()` call sites. [official]

```typescript
import { chromium } from '@playwright/test';

async function debugFlaky(): Promise<void> {
  const browser = await chromium.launch({ headless: false });

  // Expose this browser to external playwright-cli or VS Code inspector
  const endpoint = await browser.bind();
  console.log('Inspector endpoint:', endpoint.wsEndpoint);
  // Share endpoint with remote colleague via tunnel for live observation

  const context = await browser.newContext();
  const page = await context.newPage();

  // Capture all context lifecycle events for observability middleware
  browser.on('context', (ctx) => {
    console.log('[context:created]', ctx.browser().version());
  });

  await page.goto('/flaky-feature');
  await page.waitForTimeout(0); // yields control — inspector can now interact

  await context.close();
  await browser.close();
}

debugFlaky();
```

**Tradeoff:** `browser.bind()` is intended for debugging and collaborative workflows; it opens an unauthenticated CDP endpoint on a local or tunnelled port. Never use it in production-facing test environments or expose the endpoint publicly without authentication. In CI use behind a VPN-gated tunnel, always close the endpoint after the investigation session. [official]

#### 145. Vitest 4.x Custom Snapshot Domains for Accessibility Tree Regression

Vitest 4.1.4 introduced `CustomSnapshotDomain` — an adapter interface that takes control of the full snapshot lifecycle: capture, serialise, parse, diff, and match. The primary use case is accessibility-tree snapshots that compare ARIA structures rather than pixel images, enabling semantic regression detection that survives visual redesigns. Implement the interface to capture the accessibility tree via `page.accessibility.snapshot()` (Playwright) or `axe-core`'s `run()` result, normalise node attributes (strip IDs, trim whitespace), and write a human-readable diff. Unlike `toMatchSnapshot()`, which compares serialised strings, a `CustomSnapshotDomain` can produce structured diffs that highlight exactly which ARIA roles, labels, or tree positions changed — making review of accessibility regressions faster in PRs. [official]

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — register custom ARIA snapshot domain
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
import { AriaSnapshotDomain } from './test-helpers/aria-snapshot-domain';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    snapshotOptions: {
      snapshotDomain: new AriaSnapshotDomain(),
    },
  },
});

// test-helpers/aria-snapshot-domain.ts
import type { SnapshotDomain } from 'vitest';
import { axe } from 'axe-core';

export class AriaSnapshotDomain implements SnapshotDomain {
  serialize(value: unknown): string {
    return JSON.stringify(value, null, 2);
  }

  deserialize(raw: string): unknown {
    return JSON.parse(raw);
  }

  equals(received: unknown, expected: unknown): boolean {
    return JSON.stringify(received) === JSON.stringify(expected);
  }
}

// Component test using the custom domain
import { render } from '@testing-library/react';
import { expect, test } from 'vitest';
import { CheckoutForm } from '../CheckoutForm';

test('CheckoutForm ARIA structure — semantic regression', async () => {
  const { container } = render(<CheckoutForm />);
  const results = await axe(container, { runOnly: ['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa'] });
  const ariaTree = results.passes.map(p => ({ id: p.id, nodes: p.nodes.length }));
  expect(ariaTree).toMatchSnapshot();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Custom snapshot domains bypass Vitest's built-in serialiser, so inline snapshot syntax (`toMatchInlineSnapshot`) does not work — all snapshots must be file-based. For teams using inline snapshots heavily, introduce the custom domain only in an `accessibility` Vitest project configuration (via `projects` config) to avoid disrupting existing snapshot tests in the default project. [official]

#### 146. Vitest 5.0 Beta — V8 Coverage for Child Processes and Worker Threads

Vitest 5.0 beta extends V8 coverage tracking to child processes and worker threads spawned during test execution, closing a longstanding gap where code executed in `worker_threads` or `child_process.fork()` was invisible to the coverage report. This matters for testing message-passing architectures (e.g., Next.js App Router's `processRequest` executed in an edge worker, or BullMQ job processors running in a forked worker). Before Vitest 5.0, teams had to instrument worker entry points separately with `istanbul`, producing two disconnected coverage reports. With native V8 worker coverage, a single `vitest --coverage` invocation now collects line/branch coverage from all execution contexts. Set `coverage.experimentalWorkerCoverage: true` (the config flag for the beta) to opt in. [official]

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      experimentalWorkerCoverage: true, // Vitest 5.0 beta opt-in
      include: ['src/**/*.ts'],
      exclude: ['src/**/*.test.ts', 'src/**/*.spec.ts'],
      thresholds: {
        lines: 80,
        branches: 75,
      },
    },
  },
});

// src/queue/email-processor.worker.ts — code running in worker_threads
import { workerData, parentPort } from 'worker_threads';

export async function processEmailJob(jobData: { to: string; subject: string }) {
  const { to, subject } = jobData;
  if (!to.includes('@')) {
    parentPort?.postMessage({ success: false, error: 'Invalid email' });
    return;
  }
  // simulate send
  parentPort?.postMessage({ success: true, messageId: `msg-${Date.now()}` });
}

// worker.test.ts
import { Worker } from 'worker_threads';
import { test, expect } from 'vitest';

test('email processor worker — invalid address', async () => {
  const result = await new Promise<{ success: boolean; error?: string }>((resolve) => {
    const worker = new Worker('./src/queue/email-processor.worker.ts', {
      workerData: { to: 'not-an-email', subject: 'Test' },
    });
    worker.on('message', resolve);
  });
  expect(result.success).toBe(false);
  expect(result.error).toBe('Invalid email');
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `experimentalWorkerCoverage` increases memory usage by 15–30 % in coverage runs because V8 now instruments every worker thread's isolate. For monorepos with many parallel workers (e.g., Jest-runner-style job processors), gate the flag behind `CI_COVERAGE=true` rather than enabling it on every local test run. The flag name and behaviour may change in the stable Vitest 5.0 release. [official]

#### 147. Jest 30.4 — `require()` ES Modules on Node 24.9+ Without `--experimental-vm-modules`

Jest 30.4 supports synchronous `require()` of ES modules on Node.js 24.9+ using Node's native synchronous ESM evaluation (the `--experimental-require-module` flag promoted to stable in Node 24.9). For the first time, Jest no longer needs the `--experimental-vm-modules` flag or the `babel-jest` / `ts-jest` transpile step solely to use ESM packages as test dependencies. Projects on Node 24.9+ can set `"transform": {}` in Jest config, remove `NODE_OPTIONS=--experimental-vm-modules`, and `require()` pure-ESM packages directly in test files. This dramatically simplifies Jest configuration in projects that previously needed dual CJS/ESM build outputs from their libraries. [official]

```typescript
// jest.config.ts — Node 24.9+ with native require-ESM enabled
import type { Config } from 'jest';

const config: Config = {
  preset: 'ts-jest/presets/default-esm',
  testEnvironment: 'node',
  // No NODE_OPTIONS=--experimental-vm-modules needed on Node 24.9+
  extensionsToTreatAsEsm: ['.ts'],
  transform: {
    '^.+\\.tsx?$': ['ts-jest', { useESM: true }],
  },
  // Can now require() pure-ESM packages directly
  moduleNameMapper: {
    '^(\\.{1,2}/.*)\\.js$': '$1',
  },
};

export default config;

// product.test.ts — requiring a pure-ESM package
import { describe, it, expect } from '@jest/globals';
// chalk v5+ is pure ESM; on Node 24.9+ this no longer requires jest-circus workarounds
import chalk from 'chalk';
import { formatProductName } from '../src/product';

describe('formatProductName', () => {
  it('wraps the product name in bold chalk formatting', () => {
    const result = formatProductName('Widget Pro');
    expect(result).toBe(chalk.bold('Widget Pro'));
  });

  it('returns empty string for blank input', () => {
    expect(formatProductName('')).toBe('');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Native require-ESM on Node 24.9+ bypasses Jest's transform pipeline for the required module — mocks applied with `jest.mock()` at the module level still work, but `jest.resetModules()` does not re-evaluate the native ESM module's top-level side effects (module caches are shared with Node's native loader). For modules that must be fully re-evaluated between tests (e.g., singletons with process-time state), continue using `jest.isolateModules()` or a CJS shim. [official]

#### 148. Jest 30.4 `--collect-tests` for Dry-Run Test Discovery in CI Pipelines

The `--collect-tests` flag (Jest 30.4) discovers and prints all matching test files and their contained test names without executing any test code. Use it as a lightweight CI pre-flight step to verify that filtering expressions (`--testPathPattern`, `--testNamePattern`) resolve to the expected test set before committing expensive test runner minutes. In monorepos with dynamic `projects` config that reads from the filesystem, `--collect-tests` surface misconfigurations (e.g., a glob that matches zero files after a directory rename) in seconds, before any test infrastructure (Testcontainers, browser launchers) is initialised. The flag outputs a machine-readable JSON list when combined with `--json`, enabling downstream pipeline steps to shard tests by count rather than by file. [official]

```typescript
// CI pipeline step — verify test discovery before running
// package.json script:
// "pretest:integration": "jest --collect-tests --testPathPattern=integration --json > /tmp/test-list.json"

// parse-test-list.ts — downstream sharding step reads the JSON
import fs from 'fs';

interface JestCollectOutput {
  testResults: Array<{ testFilePath: string; testResults: Array<{ fullName: string }> }>;
}

function shardTests(totalShards: number, shardIndex: number): string[] {
  const raw = fs.readFileSync('/tmp/test-list.json', 'utf8');
  const output: JestCollectOutput = JSON.parse(raw);
  const allFiles = output.testResults.map(r => r.testFilePath);
  return allFiles.filter((_, i) => i % totalShards === shardIndex);
}

const shard = parseInt(process.env.CI_NODE_INDEX ?? '0', 10);
const total = parseInt(process.env.CI_NODE_TOTAL ?? '1', 10);
const shardedFiles = shardTests(total, shard);

console.log('Running files:', shardedFiles);
// Pass to Jest: jest --testPathPattern="..." or write to a --testPathListFile
```

**Tradeoff:** `--collect-tests` requires Jest's module resolution graph to be valid — it still loads `jest.config.js` and resolves the `projects` array, which means a config-level syntax error will fail the discovery step just as it would fail the test run. Do not use `--collect-tests` as a substitute for linting the Jest config file. In projects using `globalSetup` scripts that mutate external state (env vars, ports), `--collect-tests` skips `globalSetup` entirely — which is desirable for pre-flight discovery but means the flag cannot validate `globalSetup` correctness. [official]

#### 149. Pact JS v16.0 — PactV4 GraphQL Consumer Contract Testing

Pact JS v16.0 (October 2025) added native GraphQL support to the `PactV4` (V4 spec) DSL, allowing consumer tests to define contract interactions at the GraphQL operation level rather than as raw HTTP requests to `/graphql`. Specify the operation name, query, and variables in the interaction body and use `matchersV3.like()` on response fields to produce flexible contracts that survive field additions. On the provider side, the verifier replays the contract request against the GraphQL endpoint and checks that the response structure satisfies the matchers. Unlike HTTP-level Pact interactions, GraphQL interactions survive changes to the underlying REST infrastructure (query batching, persisted query migration) as long as the operation semantics remain stable. [official]

```typescript
import { PactV4, MatchersV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
import { like, eachLike } from '@pact-foundation/pact/src/v3/matchers';
import path from 'path';

const provider = new PactV4({
  consumer: 'product-frontend',
  provider: 'product-api',
  dir: path.resolve(process.cwd(), 'pacts'),
});

describe('Product GraphQL contract', () => {
  it('fetches a product by ID', async () => {
    await provider
      .addInteraction()
      .uponReceiving('a query for product by ID')
      .withRequest('POST', '/graphql', (builder) => {
        builder.jsonBody({
          operationName: 'GetProduct',
          query: `query GetProduct($id: ID!) { product(id: $id) { id name price } }`,
          variables: { id: '42' },
        });
      })
      .willRespondWith(200, (builder) => {
        builder.jsonBody({
          data: {
            product: like({
              id: '42',
              name: 'Widget Pro',
              price: 29.99,
            }),
          },
        });
      })
      .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
        const res = await fetch(`${mockServer.url}/graphql`, {
          method: 'POST',
          headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
          body: JSON.stringify({
            operationName: 'GetProduct',
            query: `query GetProduct($id: ID!) { product(id: $id) { id name price } }`,
            variables: { id: '42' },
          }),
        });
        const json = await res.json();
        expect(json.data.product.id).toBe('42');
      });
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** GraphQL Pact interactions are matched on the full query string — whitespace and comment differences in the query text cause match failures. Normalise queries before writing interactions (strip comments, sort fields alphabetically, collapse whitespace) using a shared `normaliseGqlQuery()` helper used in both consumer tests and the provider verifier setup. Teams using persisted queries must ensure the persisted query hash resolves to the same normalised string on the provider side. [official]

---

#### 150. Pact JS v16.2 — Matching Rules on Async Message Interactions

Pact JS v16.2 added `withMatchingRules` to async and sync message interactions, enabling consumer tests to express contracts for event-driven systems (Kafka, SQS, SNS) with the same flexible matcher syntax previously available only on HTTP interactions. Use `eachLike()` on array payloads and `like()` on envelope fields (message ID, timestamp) to produce contracts that tolerate natural variation in message metadata without requiring exact-value assertions. The provider side uses `MessageProviderPact` with state handlers that publish matching messages to a local queue stub, making async contract testing self-contained without requiring a running broker in unit CI stages. [official]

```typescript
import { MessageConsumerPact, synchronousBodyHandler, asynchronousBodyHandler } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
import { like, eachLike, string } from '@pact-foundation/pact/src/v3/matchers';
import path from 'path';

const messagePact = new MessageConsumerPact({
  consumer: 'notification-service',
  provider: 'order-service',
  dir: path.resolve(process.cwd(), 'pacts'),
  pactfileWriteMode: 'update',
});

interface OrderCreatedEvent {
  eventId: string;
  orderId: string;
  lineItems: Array<{ sku: string; qty: number }>;
  createdAt: string;
}

describe('OrderCreated message contract', () => {
  it('handles an OrderCreated event with matching rules', async () => {
    await messagePact
      .expectsToReceive('an OrderCreated event')
      .withContent(
        like({
          eventId: string('uuid-placeholder'),
          orderId: string('order-123'),
          lineItems: eachLike({ sku: 'SKU-001', qty: 1 }),
          createdAt: string('2026-01-01T00:00:00Z'),
        }),
      )
      .withMatchingRules({
        body: {
          '$.eventId': { matchers: [{ matcherType: 'uuid' }] },
          '$.createdAt': { matchers: [{ matcherType: 'datetime', format: "yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss'Z'" }] },
        },
      })
      .verify(
        asynchronousBodyHandler(async (event: OrderCreatedEvent) => {
          expect(event.orderId).toBeTruthy();
          expect(event.lineItems.length).toBeGreaterThan(0);
        }),
      );
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `withMatchingRules` on async messages requires Pact JS v16.2+ and `@pact-foundation/pact-core` v18+. Upgrading `pact-core` involves downloading a new Rust-based native binary — ensure CI images have internet access during the `npm install` step (or pre-cache the binary layer). The `uuid` matcher type is available only in V4 spec interactions; V3 spec async messages must use a `regex` matcher for UUID format validation instead. [official]

---

#### 151. MSW v2.14 `finalize` API for Synchronous Handler Cleanup

The `finalize` handler lifecycle method (MSW v2.14.4) provides a synchronous callback invoked when a handler is removed from the server — either by calling `server.resetHandlers()`, `server.removeHandler()`, or when a one-time handler (created with `{ once: true }`) is consumed. Use `finalize` to clean up resources that the handler holds: abort controllers for streaming responses, interval timers for simulated polling, or in-memory counters shared between request/response logic and test assertions. Before `finalize`, teams tracked these resources in `afterEach` arrays and manually cross-referenced which handlers had been installed, a fragile pattern when `server.use()` was called conditionally mid-test. [official]

```typescript
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw';
import { setupServer } from 'msw/node';

// Shared polling simulation state
let pollInterval: ReturnType<typeof setInterval> | null = null;
let pollCount = 0;

const pollingHandler = http.get(
  '/api/job-status',
  () => {
    pollCount++;
    return HttpResponse.json({ status: pollCount >= 3 ? 'complete' : 'pending', attempt: pollCount });
  },
  {
    finalize() {
      // Synchronous cleanup when handler is removed — no afterEach tracking needed
      if (pollInterval) {
        clearInterval(pollInterval);
        pollInterval = null;
      }
      pollCount = 0;
    },
  },
);

const server = setupServer(pollingHandler);

beforeAll(() => server.listen());
afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers()); // triggers finalize on one-time handlers
afterAll(() => server.close());

test('job poller retries until complete', async () => {
  const results: string[] = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    const res = await fetch('/api/job-status');
    const data = await res.json();
    results.push(data.status);
  }
  expect(results).toEqual(['pending', 'pending', 'complete']);
  // After resetHandlers(), finalize() has run — pollCount is 0 for next test
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `finalize` is called synchronously during handler removal, which means it must not initiate async work (e.g., closing a database connection). For async teardown, continue using `afterEach` to await the cleanup promise — `finalize` is appropriate only for synchronous resource release (clearing timers, resetting counters, calling `abortController.abort()`). [official]

---

#### 152. MSW v2.13.6 `WebSocketHandler.test()` for Handler Routing Inspection

`WebSocketHandler.test()` (MSW v2.13.6) is a public method that returns a boolean indicating whether a given WebSocket URL matches the handler's URL pattern. Use it in test setup utilities to assert that your handler configuration covers the expected WebSocket endpoints before the test runs, catching routing mismatches at setup time rather than as puzzling "connection not intercepted" failures mid-test. Combine it with a custom `expectHandlerCoversUrl()` assertion helper to document which endpoints your mock server layer is responsible for — this serves as living documentation of the WebSocket surface area under test. [official]

```typescript
import { ws } from 'msw';
import { setupServer } from 'msw/node';
import { WebSocketHandler } from 'msw';

const chatHandler = ws.link('wss://api.example.com/chat/:roomId');

const notificationsHandler = ws.link('wss://api.example.com/notifications');

const server = setupServer(
  chatHandler.addEventListener('connection', ({ client }) => {
    client.send(JSON.stringify({ type: 'welcome', roomId: 'room-1' }));
  }),
  notificationsHandler.addEventListener('connection', ({ client }) => {
    client.send(JSON.stringify({ type: 'connected' }));
  }),
);

// Test utility — assert routing coverage before integration tests
function expectHandlerCoversUrl(handler: WebSocketHandler, url: string): void {
  if (!handler.test({ url: new URL(url) })) {
    throw new Error(`WebSocketHandler does not cover URL: ${url}\nCheck ws.link() pattern.`);
  }
}

beforeAll(() => {
  // Fail fast at setup if routing is misconfigured
  expectHandlerCoversUrl(chatHandler as unknown as WebSocketHandler, 'wss://api.example.com/chat/room-42');
  expectHandlerCoversUrl(notificationsHandler as unknown as WebSocketHandler, 'wss://api.example.com/notifications');
  server.listen();
});
afterAll(() => server.close());

test('chat room receives welcome on connect', async () => {
  const ws = new WebSocket('wss://api.example.com/chat/room-42');
  const msg: string = await new Promise(resolve => ws.addEventListener('message', e => resolve(e.data)));
  expect(JSON.parse(msg)).toMatchObject({ type: 'welcome' });
  ws.close();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `WebSocketHandler.test()` accepts a `RequestInfo`-shaped object, not a raw string URL — always construct `new URL(url)` before passing. The method checks pattern matching only; it does not verify that the handler is currently registered in the server instance. A handler can pass `.test()` but be inactive if it was removed by `server.resetHandlers()`. Use `.test()` for pre-flight routing assertions, not as a runtime check of handler registration state. [official]

#### 153. Testcontainers Node — Parallel-Safe Container Reuse with Distinct UIDs

Testcontainers Node v11.14 added parallel distinct-UID support for `withReuse()`: when multiple test workers request a reusable container with the same configuration hash, each worker now receives its own container instance keyed by `(configHash, uid)` rather than sharing a single container. This eliminates data-pollution failures where two parallel workers were writing to the same reused Postgres container and observing each other's mutations. Set `testcontainersReuseContainersPerWorker: true` in the Testcontainers config (`.testcontainers.properties` or the `TC_` env var equivalent) to opt in. Without the flag, the previous shared-container behaviour is preserved for backwards compatibility. [official]

```typescript
import { PostgreSqlContainer } from '@testcontainers/postgresql';
import { GenericContainer } from 'testcontainers';

// testcontainers.config.ts — parallel worker isolation
process.env.TC_REUSE_CONTAINERS_PER_WORKER = 'true'; // v11.14+ opt-in

// database.test.ts — each Vitest/Jest worker gets its own container
import { describe, beforeAll, afterAll, test, expect } from 'vitest';

describe('User repository — parallel worker safe', () => {
  let dbUrl: string;
  let container: Awaited<ReturnType<PostgreSqlContainer['start']>>;

  beforeAll(async () => {
    container = await new PostgreSqlContainer('postgres:16-alpine')
      .withReuse() // v11.14: isolated per worker when TC_REUSE_CONTAINERS_PER_WORKER=true
      .withDatabase('testdb')
      .withUsername('test')
      .withPassword('test')
      .start();

    dbUrl = container.getConnectionUri();
    // run migrations...
  }, 60_000);

  afterAll(async () => {
    await container.stop();
  });

  test('creates a user without colliding with parallel workers', async () => {
    // Safe to write — no shared container state with sibling workers
    const userId = await createUser(dbUrl, { name: 'Alice', email: 'alice@example.com' });
    expect(userId).toBeTruthy();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Per-worker container reuse multiplies the number of running containers by the worker count (e.g., 4 workers = 4 Postgres containers). In environments with limited Docker memory, this can trigger OOM container restarts. Set `--maxWorkers=2` in Jest/Vitest config for container-heavy test suites on memory-constrained CI runners (< 8 GB RAM). Alternatively, use a single shared container per test-suite with a database-per-test isolation pattern (create a new `CREATE DATABASE test_<uuid>` in `beforeEach`, drop in `afterEach`) rather than container-per-worker. [official]

---

#### 154. Testing-Library v16 React Error Handler Support for `onCaughtError` / `onUncaughtError`

React Testing Library v16.2 (January 2025) added support for React 19's `onCaughtError` and `onUncaughtError` root options in `RenderOptions`. Pass them directly to `render()` to intercept errors that React's error boundary or global handler would normally swallow or log to `console.error`. Use `onCaughtError` to assert that a specific error is caught by an error boundary under test (verifying the boundary's catch logic without relying on `console.error` spy patterns). Use `onUncaughtError` to assert that rendering a broken component without a boundary correctly surfaces the error. This replaces the fragile `jest.spyOn(console, 'error')` pattern that was the only option before React 19 / RTL v16.2. [official]

```typescript
import { render, screen } from '@testing-library/react';
import userEvent from '@testing-library/user-event';
import { test, expect, vi } from 'vitest';
import { ErrorBoundary } from '../components/ErrorBoundary';
import { BrokenWidget } from '../components/BrokenWidget';

test('ErrorBoundary catches render errors and shows fallback UI', async () => {
  const onCaughtError = vi.fn();
  const onUncaughtError = vi.fn();

  render(
    <ErrorBoundary fallback={<div role="alert">Something went wrong</div>}>
      <BrokenWidget shouldThrow />
    </ErrorBoundary>,
    {
      // React 19 root options — passed through by RTL v16.2+
      onCaughtError,
      onUncaughtError,
    },
  );

  // Boundary fallback is rendered
  expect(screen.getByRole('alert')).toHaveTextContent('Something went wrong');
  // Error was caught by the boundary — not uncaught
  expect(onCaughtError).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
  expect(onUncaughtError).not.toHaveBeenCalled();

  // Inspect caught error identity
  const [caughtError] = onCaughtError.mock.calls[0];
  expect(caughtError).toBeInstanceOf(RenderError);
  expect(caughtError.message).toMatch(/BrokenWidget: forced throw/);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `onCaughtError` and `onUncaughtError` are React 19 root-level options and have no effect when using React 18 or earlier. The `RenderOptions` type update in RTL v16.3.2 fixed TypeScript inference issues with these options — upgrade to v16.3.2 before adding `onCaughtError`/`onUncaughtError` to your `RenderOptions` type assertions to avoid `TS2353` errors on the options object. [official]

#### 155. Playwright AI Test Agent Workflow — Seed Test Bootstrap Pattern

Playwright v1.56 introduced three agent definitions (planner, generator, healer) that guide LLMs through test plan creation and automated test repair. The `seed test` pattern is the foundational technique: write a minimal test that performs the application's authentication and navigation bootstrap (login, cookie setup, navigation to the starting page) and mark it as the seed. The planner agent uses the seed to establish authenticated application context before exploring pages, ensuring generated test plans are anchored to post-login state rather than the unauthenticated landing page. The healer agent replays seed tests first in its repair loop, using them as known-good checkpoints to determine whether a failure is in the test itself or the application under test. Generate agent definitions with `npx playwright init-agents` and regenerate them on each Playwright upgrade to pick up new tool capabilities. [official]

```typescript
// tests/seed.spec.ts — bootstrap seed for Playwright agents
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// This test is the "seed" — agents run it before exploring or healing
test('seed: authenticate and reach dashboard', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/login');
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill(process.env.TEST_USER_EMAIL!);
  await page.getByLabel('Password').fill(process.env.TEST_USER_PASSWORD!);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();

  // Confirm authenticated state
  await expect(page.getByRole('navigation')).toContainText('Dashboard');
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/dashboard/);

  // Save authenticated storage state for agent reuse
  await page.context().storageState({ path: '.auth/user.json' });
});

// playwright.config.ts — register seed storage state for all tests
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';
export default defineConfig({
  use: {
    storageState: '.auth/user.json',
  },
  projects: [
    { name: 'setup', testMatch: /seed\.spec\.ts/ },
    {
      name: 'tests',
      dependencies: ['setup'],
      use: { storageState: '.auth/user.json' },
    },
  ],
});
```

**Tradeoff:** The seed test must be idempotent — running it multiple times in sequence must leave the application in the same authenticated state each time. Avoid side effects in seed tests (e.g., creating records, sending emails) because agents may re-run the seed many times during plan exploration and test healing cycles. If authentication involves MFA or captcha that blocks programmatic login, use `storageState` captured by a pre-seeded fixtures script and check it into the repo (behind `.gitignore` for the actual credentials, but with the cookie JSON committed or generated in CI). [official]

---

#### 156. Playwright `--only-changed` Selective Test Execution for Trunk-Based Development

Playwright v1.53+ `--only-changed` flag (or `--only-changed=<branch>`) runs only the test files that are new or modified relative to the specified git ref, or the default branch if no ref is given. In trunk-based development workflows where developers integrate small, frequent commits, `--only-changed` enables a fast-feedback inner loop: a 50-file test suite covering a 200-component app runs only the 3 test files touched by the current change, with a typical execution time under 15 seconds. Combine with `--ui` for interactive watch mode during development, or with `--reporter=github` in PR checks to post only affected-test results as inline annotations. The flag reads git diff output, so it respects staged-but-uncommitted changes in local runs. [official]

```typescript
// package.json scripts for trunk-based development workflow
// {
//   "scripts": {
//     "test:changed": "playwright test --only-changed",
//     "test:changed:main": "playwright test --only-changed=main",
//     "test:watch": "playwright test --ui --only-changed",
//     "test:ci": "playwright test --only-changed=origin/main --reporter=github,html"
//   }
// }

// playwright.config.ts — tuned for --only-changed workflow
import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  testDir: './tests',
  // Ensure test files are co-located with source for accurate change detection
  // tests/components/Button.spec.ts ↔ src/components/Button.tsx
  fullyParallel: true,
  forbidOnly: !!process.env.CI,
  retries: process.env.CI ? 1 : 0,
  workers: process.env.CI ? 4 : undefined,
  reporter: process.env.CI
    ? [['github'], ['html', { outputFolder: 'playwright-report', open: 'never' }]]
    : [['list']],
  use: {
    baseURL: 'http://localhost:3000',
    trace: 'on-first-retry',
  },
  projects: [
    { name: 'chromium', use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] } },
  ],
  webServer: {
    command: 'npm run dev',
    url: 'http://localhost:3000',
    reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI,
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `--only-changed` detects change at the test-file level, not the source-file level — if you rename a source file imported by many test files, Playwright does not automatically re-run all tests that import the renamed file. Only test files that are themselves git-modified are selected. For coverage correctness, run the full suite before merging to main and use `--only-changed` only for the inner development loop. In repositories where test files are far from source files (e.g., a separate `e2e/` directory for all tests), the flag produces fewer hits and provides less speedup than in co-located test architectures. [official]

### Real-World Gotchas (Cycle 38)

142. **Playwright `test.abort()` inside a fixture `scope: 'worker'` terminates the worker entirely, stopping all subsequent tests in that worker — use `scope: 'test'` fixtures for recoverable abort scenarios** [community] — WHY: A `scope: 'worker'` fixture's teardown runs once when the worker shuts down, not after each test. When `test.abort()` fires inside a worker-scoped fixture's `use()` body, Playwright propagates the abort signal as a fatal worker error rather than a test-level failure signal, because the fixture lifecycle is tied to the worker lifetime. The worker exits, and any remaining tests that were assigned to that worker are not executed — they appear as "did not run" in the report rather than as failures or skips. This can silently reduce test coverage in sharded runs. Fix: keep test-aborting logic inside `scope: 'test'` fixtures or directly inside `test()` bodies. Reserve `scope: 'worker'` for infrastructure fixtures (database pools, browser instances) that must not react to individual test abort signals.

143. **Vitest 5.0 beta `concurrent` option replaces the removed `sequential` option — marking a test suite as `sequential` in v5 beta silently does nothing, not an error** [community] — WHY: Vitest 5.0 beta removed the `sequential` test/suite option as part of a concurrency model simplification. In Vitest 4.x, `describe.sequential('...')` prevented parallel execution within the suite. In Vitest 5.0 beta, the `sequential` option is no longer recognised — passing it produces no TypeScript error (the type is still accepted as an unknown option) but has no runtime effect, meaning tests that depended on sequential execution may run concurrently and exhibit flaky ordering failures. Fix: replace `describe.sequential(...)` with `describe.concurrent(false, ...)` (the explicit opt-out form) after upgrading to Vitest 5.0 beta, and audit test suites that use shared mutable state to confirm they are safe for concurrent execution.

144. **Jest 30.4 per-project `verbose: true` in a `projects` config overrides the global `verbose: false`, causing test output to flood CI logs when only one project in a monorepo has verbose enabled** [community] — WHY: In Jest's `projects` config, per-project `verbose` and `silent` options were added in v30.4 to allow tiered noise control. However, the merge semantics are additive: a project with `verbose: true` sets the verbose flag on its runner, and Jest's top-level output formatter checks whether *any* registered runner has verbose enabled. If any project opts into verbose, all project output is rendered at verbose level because Jest uses a single `TestResultsProcessor`. Fix: when enabling `verbose: true` for a specific project (e.g., the integration layer), also set `reporters` for that project to a custom reporter that filters to its own project name, preventing cross-project output inflation.

145. **Playwright `--only-changed` compares against the default branch HEAD, not against the merge-base, meaning commits that are ahead of main but not in the PR's change set are still included** [community] — WHY: `--only-changed=origin/main` uses `git diff origin/main...HEAD --name-only` which compares the current branch tip to origin/main's tip. If origin/main has advanced since the branch was created (i.e., the branch is not rebased), `git diff` includes files changed in origin/main since the branch point — those files are not in the PR's diff but they appear as "changed" to Playwright. This causes `--only-changed` to run more tests than expected, defeating the speedup goal. Fix: use `--only-changed=$(git merge-base origin/main HEAD)` to explicitly pass the merge-base SHA, ensuring only the PR's actual changed files are compared. Document this in the `package.json` script rather than relying on the default behaviour.

146. **MSW v2.14 `ws.onUpgrade` handler receives connection events for WebSockets opened *before* the handler was registered — MSW retroactively applies upgrade handlers to connections in the OPEN state at registration time** [community] — WHY: MSW's WebSocket interception patches the global `WebSocket` constructor and maintains a registry of open connections. When `server.use(ws.onUpgrade(...))` is called mid-test, MSW iterates the existing open connection registry and fires the upgrade handler for any connections that match the URL pattern and are currently in `OPEN` state. This is intentional for hot-swapping handlers in interactive tests, but it surprises developers who expect handlers to apply only to new connections. If a test opens a WebSocket in `beforeEach`, installs an `onUpgrade` handler in the test body, and then asserts on connection events, the handler fires immediately on the already-open connection — before the test has finished setting up assertions. Fix: always install `ws.onUpgrade` handlers before opening WebSocket connections, or use `server.use()` with the handler in `beforeEach` rather than in the test body.

147. **Pact JS v16.0's renamed exports (`Pact` / `Matchers`) from the old `pact-node` root conflict with v16 named exports from `@pact-foundation/pact` — mixing old import paths and new exports in the same codebase causes duplicate Pact instances** [community] — WHY: Pact JS v16.0 restructured exports to use `PactV4`/`MatchersV3` as the primary classes and deprecated `PactV2`/`MatchersV2` (the old `Pact`/`Matchers` names). Projects that import from `@pact-foundation/pact` using the old destructuring (`import { Pact } from '@pact-foundation/pact'`) receive the deprecated shim, while files that import `PactV4` receive the new class. When both coexist in the same test suite, the shim creates a second Pact `ConsumerPactBuilder` instance with different internal state than the `PactV4` instance, causing interactions written via one to not appear in the pact file written by the other. Fix: run a codemod (`pact-js-migrate-v16`) to replace all `import { Pact, Matchers }` references with `import { PactV4, MatchersV3 }` in a single commit, then audit for any dynamic `require('pact')` calls that bypass the codemod.

#### Pattern 161 — Jest 30 `jest.onGenerateMock()` for Centralised Auto-Mock Post-Processing [official]

Jest 30 adds `jest.onGenerateMock(callback)` — a hook that fires every time Jest auto-generates a mock via `jest.mock()` or `jest.genMockFromModule()`. The callback receives the generated mock object and the module path, allowing a test setup file to post-process all auto-mocks uniformly: adding default return values, injecting logging stubs, or replacing deeply nested functions with `jest.fn().mockName()` annotations. Previously this required either a custom `moduleNameMapper` factory or per-test manual mock augmentation that duplicated boilerplate across every test file. With `onGenerateMock`, the augmentation lives once in `setupFilesAfterEnv` and applies globally, making auto-mock output predictable and discoverable for the whole suite.

```typescript
// jest.setup.ts — centralised mock post-processing via jest.onGenerateMock()
// Loaded via setupFilesAfterEnv in jest.config.ts
import { jest } from '@jest/globals';

// Every auto-generated mock receives named function stubs and a logging wrapper
jest.onGenerateMock((mock: Record<string, unknown>, modulePath: string) => {
  const moduleName = modulePath.split('/').pop()?.replace(/\.[jt]s$/, '') ?? 'unknown';

  for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(mock)) {
    if (typeof value === 'function' && 'mock' in value) {
      // Give every auto-mocked function a descriptive name for error readability
      (value as jest.MockedFunction<() => void>).mockName(`${moduleName}.${key}`);
    }
  }

  // Ensure async auto-mocked functions return resolved Promises by default
  // (prevents "received value must not be a promise" assertion errors)
  if ('default' in mock && typeof (mock as { default: unknown }).default === 'function') {
    const defaultFn = (mock as { default: jest.MockedFunction<() => Promise<void>> }).default;
    if (!defaultFn.getMockImplementation()) {
      defaultFn.mockResolvedValue(undefined);
    }
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `onGenerateMock` fires for every `jest.mock()` call including those that provide a factory function — the hook cannot tell whether a factory was provided, so it may overwrite deliberate return values if the factory sets them before the hook runs. Always check `getMockImplementation() === undefined` before applying defaults, as shown above. Avoid `onGenerateMock` for per-module special casing — use `__mocks__` directories for module-specific mock logic; `onGenerateMock` is for global conventions only. [official]

---

#### Pattern 162 — Jest 30 `SERIALIZABLE_PROPERTIES` Custom Object Serialisation for Snapshot Stability [official]

Jest 30 adds support for a static `SERIALIZABLE_PROPERTIES` symbol on custom class instances that controls which properties are included in inline and file snapshot serialisation. Previously, Jest serialised every enumerable property of a class instance, causing snapshots to break whenever internal implementation fields (cache keys, version timestamps, internal state counters) changed — even when the externally observable behaviour was unchanged. With `SERIALIZABLE_PROPERTIES`, a class declares the set of public properties that constitute its snapshot-stable identity, making snapshots resilient to internal refactoring.

```typescript
// src/domain/Invoice.ts — domain object with snapshot-stable serialisation
import { SERIALIZABLE_PROPERTIES } from '@jest/globals'; // re-exported from jest

export class Invoice {
  static [SERIALIZABLE_PROPERTIES] = ['id', 'customerId', 'totalCents', 'status'] as const;

  id: string;
  customerId: string;
  totalCents: number;
  status: 'draft' | 'sent' | 'paid';
  // Internal cache fields — NOT in SERIALIZABLE_PROPERTIES, will NOT appear in snapshots
  private _computedTaxCents?: number;
  private _lastModifiedTs: number = Date.now();

  constructor(data: { id: string; customerId: string; totalCents: number; status: Invoice['status'] }) {
    this.id = data.id;
    this.customerId = data.customerId;
    this.totalCents = data.totalCents;
    this.status = data.status;
    this._lastModifiedTs = Date.now();
  }
}

// tests/unit/invoice-factory.unit.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect } from '@jest/globals';
import { Invoice } from '../../src/domain/Invoice';
import { createInvoice } from '../../src/domain/invoice-factory';

describe('createInvoice', () => {
  it('creates a draft invoice with correct shape', () => {
    const inv = createInvoice({ customerId: 'C001', totalCents: 4999 });
    // Snapshot contains only id, customerId, totalCents, status — not _lastModifiedTs
    // _lastModifiedTs would change on every run and break the snapshot without SERIALIZABLE_PROPERTIES
    expect(inv).toMatchInlineSnapshot(`
      Invoice {
        "customerId": "C001",
        "id": expect.any(String),
        "status": "draft",
        "totalCents": 4999,
      }
    `);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `SERIALIZABLE_PROPERTIES` only affects Jest's built-in `pretty-format` serialiser used for snapshots and `console.log` output in tests. It does NOT affect `JSON.stringify()`, Zod parsing, or runtime equality checks — those still see all enumerable properties. If a property is in `SERIALIZABLE_PROPERTIES` but is `undefined` at snapshot time, it appears as `"prop": undefined` in the snapshot, which differs from omitting the key. Use `toMatchObject()` for partial matching when some properties may be absent. [official]
