#### Pattern 163 — Vitest 4.1 Type-Inferred `test.extend()` Builder for Fixture Type Safety [official]

Vitest 4.1 reworked `test.extend<Fixtures>()` to infer fixture types from the fixture implementation's return value rather than requiring an explicit generic type parameter. When fixtures are expressed as `async ({ }, use) => { ... }`, TypeScript infers the fixture type from what is passed to `use()`, eliminating the need to maintain a separate `Fixtures` interface that duplicates the type information already present in the fixture body. In large integration test suites with many fixtures (database connections, seeded repositories, auth tokens), this halves the boilerplate and makes fixtures easier to refactor — changing a fixture's return type automatically propagates to all test files that use it.

```typescript
// tests/fixtures/index.ts — Vitest 4.1 type-inferred test.extend() builder pattern
import { test as base } from 'vitest';
import { Pool } from 'pg';
import { UserRepository } from '../../src/repositories/user-repository.js';
import { seedUser } from '../helpers/seed.js';
import type { User } from '../../src/domain/user.js';

// No explicit Fixtures interface needed — TypeScript infers from use() argument types
export const test = base.extend({
  // Worker-scoped DB pool: inferred type = Pool
  dbPool: [
    async ({}, use) => {
      const pool = new Pool({ connectionString: process.env['TEST_DATABASE_URL'] });
      await use(pool);
      await pool.end();
    },
    { scope: 'worker' },
  ],

  // Test-scoped user repository: inferred type = UserRepository
  userRepo: async ({ dbPool }, use) => {
    const repo = new UserRepository(dbPool);
    await use(repo);
  },

  // Test-scoped seeded user: inferred type = User
  seededUser: async ({ userRepo }, use) => {
    const user = await seedUser(userRepo, { email: `test+${Date.now()}@example.com` });
    await use(user);
    await userRepo.delete(user.id);
  },
});

// tests/integration/user-profile.test.ts
import { expect } from 'vitest';
import { test } from '../fixtures/index.js'; // seededUser is typed as User — no cast needed

test('updates user display name', async ({ seededUser, userRepo }) => {
  await userRepo.updateDisplayName(seededUser.id, 'Alice Updated');
  const updated = await userRepo.findById(seededUser.id);
  expect(updated?.displayName).toBe('Alice Updated');
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Type inference from `use()` only works for fixtures that call `use()` with a single concrete value. Fixtures that call `use()` conditionally (different types in different branches) will infer a union type that may be wider than desired — in those cases, an explicit generic type annotation is still needed. The inference also does not propagate through dynamic fixture composition patterns (`extend().extend().extend()` chains deeper than 3 levels) without TypeScript sometimes requiring an explicit intermediate annotation. [official]

---

#### Pattern 164 — Vitest 4.1 Test Tags with Shared Retry/Timeout Config for Flaky Test Triage [official]

Vitest 4.1's test tags API allows grouping tests by label (`describe.tags(['integration', 'flaky'])`) and applying shared configuration options — including `retry` counts and `timeout` values — to all tests in a tag group via `--tags-filter` combined with project-level `tagOptions` in `vitest.config.ts`. This provides a structured way to manage known-flaky integration tests: instead of inlining `{ retry: 3, timeout: 30_000 }` on every individual test, a single config entry drives all tests tagged `flaky`, and the tag serves as a triage signal visible in CI reports.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — tag-based retry and timeout for flaky integration tests
import { defineConfig, defineProject } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    projects: [
      defineProject({
        test: {
          name: 'integration',
          include: ['src/**/*.integration.test.ts'],
          // Apply 3 retries and 45s timeout to all tests tagged 'flaky'
          // Teams can tag individual tests without touching the config
          tagOptions: {
            flaky: { retry: 3, timeout: 45_000 },
            slow: { timeout: 60_000 },
            critical: { retry: 0, timeout: 10_000 }, // fail fast for critical paths
          },
        },
      }),
    ],
  },
});

// src/payments/payment-processor.integration.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { PaymentProcessor } from './payment-processor.js';

// Tag 'flaky' — inherits retry:3 and timeout:45_000 from tagOptions config
describe.tags(['integration', 'flaky'])('PaymentProcessor — 3rd-party gateway', () => {
  it('processes a card payment and returns a charge ID', async () => {
    const processor = new PaymentProcessor({ gatewayUrl: process.env['TEST_GATEWAY_URL']! });
    const result = await processor.charge({ amountCents: 999, currency: 'USD' });
    expect(result.chargeId).toMatch(/^ch_/);
    expect(result.status).toBe('succeeded');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Tags with `retry > 0` mask intermittent defects — a test that needs 3 retries to pass in CI is reporting a hidden flakiness problem, not a stable test. Treat `flaky` as a quarantine tag with a mandatory owner and resolution deadline. The tag should disappear when the root cause is fixed, not become permanent infrastructure. Also note that `tagOptions` are not inherited by nested `describe` blocks unless they also carry the tag explicitly — inner `describe.tags([])` blocks reset to default options. [official]

---

#### Pattern 165 — Playwright v1.60 `toContainClass()` for CSS State Assertions Resistant to Structural Refactoring [official]

Playwright v1.60 adds `expect(locator).toContainClass('class-name')` as an asymmetric matcher for CSS class membership. Previously, the closest built-in was `toHaveClass()` which asserted the complete class string — meaning adding or removing a utility class (e.g., `rounded-md` from a Tailwind refactor) broke assertions that only cared whether `is-active` or `has-error` was present. `toContainClass()` asserts membership in the class list without requiring the complete set, making assertions resilient to styling refactors that add/remove unrelated classes.

```typescript
// e2e/product-filter.spec.ts — toContainClass() for state class assertions
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('filter button shows active state when a filter is selected', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/products');

  const filterBtn = page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Category' });
  // Initial state: no active class
  await expect(filterBtn).not.toContainClass('filter--active');

  // Select the Electronics category
  await filterBtn.click();
  await page.getByRole('menuitem', { name: 'Electronics' }).click();

  // After selection: active class is applied regardless of other Tailwind classes
  await expect(filterBtn).toContainClass('filter--active');
  // toContainClass does NOT care whether 'rounded-md', 'text-sm', 'px-3' etc. are present
  // This assertion survives a Tailwind upgrade that adds/removes utility classes

  // Clear filter: active class removed
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Clear filters' }).click();
  await expect(filterBtn).not.toContainClass('filter--active');
});

test('error input receives error state class on invalid submission', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' }).click(); // submit without filling form

  const emailInput = page.getByLabel('Email address');
  await expect(emailInput).toContainClass('input--error');
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toContainClass('alert--visible');
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `toContainClass()` is weaker than `toHaveClass()` — it cannot assert that a class is NOT in the list while others ARE. For assertions that require exactly `['btn', 'btn-primary']` with no extras, `toHaveClass(['btn', 'btn-primary'])` with explicit array form remains appropriate. Prefer `toContainClass()` for behavioural state classes (`active`, `disabled`, `error`, `loading`) and reserve `toHaveClass()` for component identity classes whose full composition is deliberately part of the contract. [official]

---

#### Pattern 166 — Playwright v1.60 `webSocketRoute.protocols()` for Sub-Protocol Integration Tests [official]

Playwright v1.60 extends `page.routeWebSocket()` with `webSocketRoute.protocols()` — providing read access to the client's requested WebSocket sub-protocols from the `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` request header. Before this API, there was no way to assert on the sub-protocol negotiation at the integration level without spinning up a real WebSocket server. With `protocols()`, a `page.routeWebSocket()` handler can branch on requested protocols, simulate server-side protocol rejection, or assert that the client always requests the correct versioned protocol — all within a Playwright test without external infrastructure.

```typescript
// e2e/realtime-client.spec.ts — sub-protocol negotiation via webSocketRoute.protocols()
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('realtime client requests the v2 sub-protocol during connection', async ({ page }) => {
  const observedProtocols: string[] = [];

  await page.routeWebSocket('wss://realtime.example.com/ws', (wsRoute) => {
    // Capture requested sub-protocols from the client's upgrade request
    const clientProtocols = wsRoute.protocols();
    observedProtocols.push(...clientProtocols);

    // Simulate server accepting only the v2 sub-protocol
    if (clientProtocols.includes('v2.realtime')) {
      wsRoute.accept({ protocol: 'v2.realtime' });
    } else {
      // Server rejects — sends close frame with 1002 Protocol Error
      wsRoute.close({ code: 1002, reason: 'Unsupported protocol' });
    }

    wsRoute.onMessage((msg) => {
      // Echo messages back for the test to assert on
      wsRoute.send(msg);
    });
  });

  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Assert the client requested the correct versioned sub-protocol
  expect(observedProtocols).toContain('v2.realtime');

  // Verify the connection was established (not rejected) and the UI is functional
  await expect(page.getByTestId('connection-status')).toHaveText('Connected');
});

test('falls back gracefully when server rejects the sub-protocol', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.routeWebSocket('wss://realtime.example.com/ws', (wsRoute) => {
    // Reject all sub-protocols — simulate legacy server
    wsRoute.close({ code: 1002, reason: 'No supported protocol' });
  });

  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('connection-status')).toHaveText('Reconnecting...');
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `webSocketRoute.protocols()` only reads the client's *requested* protocols from the upgrade request — it cannot observe which protocol the server *accepted* in response unless you use `wsRoute.accept({ protocol: '...' })` yourself. For testing server-side protocol selection logic, you still need a real WebSocket server (Testcontainers or `ws` npm in `globalSetup`). The `routeWebSocket` approach is the correct tool for testing client-side upgrade negotiation behaviour. [official]

---

#### Pattern 167 — Node.js 26 `getTestContext()` for Context-Free Test Helper Functions [official]

Node.js 26.1.0 adds `getTestContext()` to the `node:test` module. It returns the `TestContext` of the currently executing test without requiring the context to be passed as a parameter. This unblocks a common helper function pattern where utility functions deep in the test call stack need access to diagnostic APIs (`t.diagnostic()`, `t.mock`, `t.plan()`) but cannot receive `t` as a parameter without refactoring every call site. At the integration level, `getTestContext()` is particularly useful for shared assertion utilities that want to emit structured diagnostic messages when they fail, improving debuggability without coupling the helper's signature to the test framework.

```typescript
// tests/helpers/assert-api-response.ts — context-free helper using getTestContext()
// Node.js 26.1+, node:test runner
import { getTestContext } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

interface ApiResponse {
  status: number;
  body: unknown;
  headers: Record<string, string>;
}

export function assertApiResponse(
  response: ApiResponse,
  expected: { status: number; bodyContains?: Partial<Record<string, unknown>> }
): void {
  const t = getTestContext(); // access current test context without parameter threading

  if (response.status !== expected.status) {
    // Emit a structured diagnostic before the assertion fails — aids CI log triage
    t?.diagnostic(`Expected status ${expected.status}, got ${response.status}`);
    t?.diagnostic(`Response body: ${JSON.stringify(response.body, null, 2)}`);
    t?.diagnostic(`Request-Id header: ${response.headers['x-request-id'] ?? 'absent'}`);
  }

  assert.strictEqual(response.status, expected.status);

  if (expected.bodyContains) {
    for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(expected.bodyContains)) {
      assert.deepStrictEqual((response.body as Record<string, unknown>)[key], value);
    }
  }
}

// tests/integration/orders-api.test.ts
import { test } from 'node:test';
import { assertApiResponse } from '../helpers/assert-api-response.js';
import { createOrder } from '../../src/api/orders.js';

test('POST /orders returns 201 with order ID', async () => {
  const response = await createOrder({ productId: 'SKU-001', quantity: 2 });
  // assertApiResponse uses getTestContext() internally — no t parameter needed
  assertApiResponse(response, {
    status: 201,
    bodyContains: { status: 'pending' },
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `getTestContext()` returns `undefined` if called outside a running test (e.g., in module-level setup code, `globalSetup`, or a `before()` hook not associated with a specific test body). Callers must guard with `getTestContext() ?? null` when the helper might be used in both test and non-test contexts. This API is specific to `node:test` and does not exist in Vitest or Jest — helpers using it are not portable across test runners without an adapter shim. [official]

---

#### Pattern 168 — Node.js 26 `AbortSignal.timeout()` Mock Support in `MockTimers` for Integration Test Control [official]

Node.js 26.0.0 adds `AbortSignal.timeout()` mock support to the built-in `MockTimers` API (`t.mock.timers`). Previously, code that used `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` to time-box HTTP requests, stream reads, or queue consumers could not be tested with fake timers — the real `setTimeout` inside `AbortSignal.timeout` was not intercepted by `t.mock.timers.enable()`. Node.js 26 patches this gap: when `AbortSignal` is included in the enabled fake timer APIs, `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` respects `t.mock.timers.tick(ms)` — enabling deterministic integration tests for abort-controlled operations without real wall-clock delays.

```typescript
// tests/integration/http-client-timeout.integration.test.ts
// Node.js 26 — AbortSignal.timeout() mocked via t.mock.timers
import { test, describe, before, after } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { setupServer } from 'msw/node';
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw';
import { fetchWithTimeout } from '../../src/http/fetch-with-timeout.js';

const server = setupServer(
  http.get('https://api.example.com/slow-endpoint', async () => {
    // Simulate a slow response — in the test, we tick the fake timer
    // to trigger the AbortSignal before the response arrives
    await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 10_000));
    return HttpResponse.json({ data: 'late response' });
  }),
);

describe('fetchWithTimeout', () => {
  before(() => server.listen({ onUnhandledRequest: 'error' }));
  after(() => server.close());

  test('aborts request when AbortSignal.timeout() fires', async (t) => {
    // Enable fake timers including AbortSignal — Node.js 26 new capability
    t.mock.timers.enable({ apis: ['setTimeout', 'AbortSignal'] });

    const fetchPromise = fetchWithTimeout('https://api.example.com/slow-endpoint', {
      timeout: 5_000, // fetchWithTimeout uses AbortSignal.timeout(5000) internally
    });

    // Advance fake time past the abort threshold — real wall clock does not advance
    t.mock.timers.tick(5_001);

    await assert.rejects(fetchPromise, { name: 'AbortError' });

    t.mock.timers.reset();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `AbortSignal` mock support only applies to `AbortSignal.timeout()` — signals created with `new AbortController()` and `controller.abort()` are not affected by fake timers because they are imperatively aborted, not time-driven. For testing timeout behaviour in code that creates its own `AbortController` and schedules `controller.abort()` via `setTimeout`, fake timers for `setTimeout` alone is sufficient. Do not mix `AbortSignal` fake timer mocking with real network I/O (e.g., `fetch()` without MSW) — the abort signal fires but the underlying network call may have already completed or errored independently. [official]

---

#### Pattern 169 — Jest 30 `--testTimeout` Per-Run Override for Heterogeneous Suite Timing [official]

Jest 30 adds `--testTimeout=N` as a CLI flag that overrides `testTimeout` for a single run without modifying `jest.config.ts`. Combined with project-level `testTimeout` support in the `projects` array, this enables a CI strategy where integration tests use a generous default (30 s) but the PR pipeline overrides to a tighter budget (10 s) to catch slow tests early — without separate config files. The existing `jest.setTimeout()` in individual test files still takes precedence over the CLI flag, allowing per-test opt-outs where a specific test legitimately needs longer.

```typescript
// jest.config.ts — project-level testTimeout; CLI flag provides per-run override
import type { Config } from 'jest';

const config: Config = {
  projects: [
    {
      displayName: 'unit',
      testMatch: ['<rootDir>/src/**/*.unit.test.ts'],
      testTimeout: 5_000, // unit tests must complete within 5 s
    },
    {
      displayName: 'integration',
      testMatch: ['<rootDir>/tests/integration/**/*.test.ts'],
      testTimeout: 30_000, // generous default for integration tests
      // PR pipeline tightens this with: jest --testTimeout=10000
    },
  ],
};

export default config;

// tests/integration/payment-gateway.integration.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect } from '@jest/globals';
import { processPayment } from '../../src/payments/payment-gateway.js';

describe('PaymentGateway integration', () => {
  // Per-test override — this specific test is known to take up to 20 s
  // and overrides the CLI --testTimeout flag unconditionally
  jest.setTimeout(20_000);

  it('processes a refund through the gateway callback sequence', async () => {
    const result = await processPayment({
      type: 'refund',
      chargeId: 'ch_test_12345',
      amountCents: 2500,
    });
    expect(result.status).toBe('refunded');
    expect(result.refundId).toMatch(/^re_/);
  });

  it('rejects payment with invalid card number quickly', async () => {
    // No jest.setTimeout here — uses project default or CLI override
    await expect(
      processPayment({ type: 'charge', cardNumber: '0000000000000000', amountCents: 100 })
    ).rejects.toThrow('InvalidCardNumber');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `jest.setTimeout()` at the test-file level unconditionally overrides the CLI `--testTimeout` flag — teams cannot remotely tighten a per-file `jest.setTimeout(60_000)` from CI without modifying the test file. Encourage teams to use project-level `testTimeout` in `jest.config.ts` as the primary governance mechanism and reserve `jest.setTimeout()` for individual outliers that genuinely need an exception. Over-use of per-file `jest.setTimeout()` defeats the CI timeout budget signal. [official]

---

#### Pattern 170 — Vitest 4.1 `viteModuleRunner: false` for Native-Node Integration Test Parity [official]

Vitest 4.1 ships an experimental `viteModuleRunner: false` option for named test projects. When set, the project runs test files using native Node.js `import()` instead of Vite's module transform sandbox. This surfaces a class of production-only integration defects that Vite silently masks: CJS/ESM interop quirks, singleton module-cache ordering differences, `__dirname`/`__filename` availability in ESM, and environment variable loading order. Running an integration project with `viteModuleRunner: false` alongside a standard integration project reveals whether any test relies on Vite-specific module resolution behaviour that would not exist in the deployed Node.js runtime.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — parallel integration projects: Vite sandbox vs. native Node.js
import { defineConfig, defineProject } from 'vitest/config';
import tsconfigPaths from 'vite-tsconfig-paths';

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [tsconfigPaths()],
  test: {
    projects: [
      // Standard integration project: runs in Vite sandbox (baseline)
      defineProject({
        test: {
          name: 'integration-vite',
          include: ['src/**/*.integration.test.ts'],
          environment: 'node',
          testTimeout: 30_000,
        },
      }),
      // Production-parity project: runs with native Node.js module resolution
      defineProject({
        test: {
          name: 'integration-native',
          include: ['src/**/*.integration.test.ts'],
          environment: 'node',
          pool: 'forks', // required for native runner isolation
          testTimeout: 30_000,
          // @ts-expect-error — experimental option, stable in Vitest 4.1
          viteModuleRunner: false,
        },
      }),
    ],
  },
});

// src/config/database.ts — typical ESM singleton that behaves differently under Vite vs. Node
import { createPool } from 'pg';

// Vite sandbox: re-evaluates this module per-test-file, giving a fresh pool each time
// Native Node.js: module cache persists the pool instance across test files in the same worker
// viteModuleRunner:false exposes pool reuse bugs invisible under the Vite sandbox
export const pool = createPool({ connectionString: process.env['DATABASE_URL'] });
```

**Tradeoff:** `viteModuleRunner: false` disables all Vite plugin transforms — CSS modules, glob imports, `import.meta.env` substitution, and Vite-specific `?raw` import suffixes all stop working. Integration test files must not import any module that relies on Vite transforms. Start with a separate `integration-native` project that includes only pure-Node source files and expand coverage incrementally. This option is experimental in Vitest 4.1 and the option name may change in Vitest 5.0 stable. [official]

---

#### Pattern 171 — Playwright v1.60 `testInfoError.errorContext` for Root-Cause-First Failure Diagnostics [official]

Playwright v1.60 adds `testInfoError.errorContext` — a structured object attached to test failure errors that carries the failing locator's ARIA snapshot, the page URL at the time of failure, and a list of all active route handlers. In previous versions, a `locator not found` error included the CSS/role selector but no context about the DOM state at the point of failure — developers had to re-run the test in headed mode or parse the trace file to understand whether the element was absent, hidden, or mis-named. `errorContext` surfaces this information inline in the reporter output and the JSON result file, making first-failure diagnosis viable without a second CI run.

```typescript
// e2e/helpers/enhanced-reporter.ts — consuming errorContext for structured failure output
import type { Reporter, TestCase, TestResult, TestError } from '@playwright/test/reporter';

interface PlaywrightErrorContext {
  locatorDescription?: string;
  ariaSnapshot?: string;
  pageURL?: string;
  activeRoutes?: string[];
}

export class EnhancedDiagnosticsReporter implements Reporter {
  onTestEnd(test: TestCase, result: TestResult): void {
    if (result.status !== 'failed') return;

    for (const error of result.errors) {
      const ctx = (error as TestError & { errorContext?: PlaywrightErrorContext }).errorContext;
      if (!ctx) continue;

      console.error('\n=== Playwright Failure Context ===');
      if (ctx.pageURL)            console.error(`  Page URL:  ${ctx.pageURL}`);
      if (ctx.locatorDescription) console.error(`  Locator:   ${ctx.locatorDescription}`);
      if (ctx.activeRoutes?.length) {
        console.error(`  Active routes: ${ctx.activeRoutes.join(', ')}`);
      }
      if (ctx.ariaSnapshot) {
        // First 20 lines of the ARIA tree at failure time
        const preview = ctx.ariaSnapshot.split('\n').slice(0, 20).join('\n');
        console.error(`  ARIA snapshot (first 20 lines):\n${preview}`);
      }
      console.error('==================================\n');
    }
  }
}

// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';
export default defineConfig({
  reporter: [['./e2e/helpers/enhanced-reporter.ts'], ['html', { open: 'never' }]],
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `errorContext.ariaSnapshot` captures the accessibility tree of the *failing locator's* subtree, not the full page — for failures inside deeply nested components, the snapshot may not include sibling elements that would clarify context. Use `test.step()` with descriptive names alongside `errorContext` for the best failure diagnostics: step names appear in the reporter alongside `errorContext` data. The `errorContext` object shape is not yet part of Playwright's stable public API and may change in minor versions. [official]

---

#### Pattern 172 — Jest 30 Unified Snapshot Bundle Per Package for Monorepo Snapshot Management [official]

Jest 30 bundles all snapshot files for a package into a single `__snapshots__/index.snap` file per project root rather than one `.snap` file per test file. This reduces the number of snapshot files in large monorepos from hundreds to one per package, making snapshot diffs in pull requests dramatically more readable — a single snapshot update PR shows one changed file per package instead of scattered per-test-file changes. The bundle format uses a flat namespace keyed by test path, so individual test case snapshots remain independently addressable for update and deletion.

```typescript
// jest.config.ts — Jest 30 snapshot bundling with per-project mode control
import type { Config } from 'jest';

const config: Config = {
  projects: [
    {
      displayName: 'unit',
      testMatch: ['<rootDir>/packages/*/src/**/*.unit.test.ts'],
      // Jest 30 default: bundled snapshots — one index.snap per package root
      snapshotFormat: { mode: 'bundle' },
    },
    {
      displayName: 'integration',
      testMatch: ['<rootDir>/packages/*/tests/integration/**/*.test.ts'],
      // Integration tests: per-file snapshots for easier blame tracking on individual test files
      snapshotFormat: { mode: 'legacy' },
    },
  ],
};

export default config;

// packages/invoicing/src/__tests__/invoice-formatter.unit.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect } from '@jest/globals';
import { formatInvoice } from '../invoice-formatter.js';

describe('formatInvoice', () => {
  it('formats a standard invoice to display string', () => {
    const invoice = { id: 'INV-001', totalCents: 4999, currency: 'USD', lineItems: 3 };
    // Snapshot written to packages/invoicing/__snapshots__/index.snap
    // Bundle key: "formatInvoice formats a standard invoice to display string 1"
    expect(formatInvoice(invoice)).toMatchSnapshot();
  });

  it('handles zero-line-item edge case', () => {
    const invoice = { id: 'INV-002', totalCents: 0, currency: 'USD', lineItems: 0 };
    expect(formatInvoice(invoice)).toMatchSnapshot();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Snapshot bundles introduce a merge conflict risk in high-velocity teams: two PRs that each update different snapshots in the same `index.snap` will conflict at the file level even if the actual snapshot keys do not overlap. Use `--ci` mode in PR pipelines (fail on any snapshot mismatch rather than updating) and run `jest --updateSnapshot` locally then commit the bundle. Deleted test files leave orphan bundle entries — run `jest --updateSnapshot --passWithNoTests` post-merge to prune them. [official]

---

#### Pattern 173 — Playwright `browser.on('context')` Middleware for Fleet-Level Context Lifecycle Logging [official]

Playwright v1.60 adds `browser.on('context', handler)` — an event that fires for every new browser context created from that browser instance, including contexts created inside fixtures and nested helpers. This enables middleware-style context lifecycle logging without instrumenting every `browser.newContext()` call site. In large Playwright suites with complex fixture hierarchies, a `browser.on('context')` handler can attach universal behaviours to all contexts: console error capture, request/response logging, network idle monitoring, or automated screenshot-on-error — without needing to modify individual page objects or test fixtures.

```typescript
// fixtures/browser-middleware.ts — Playwright v1.60 browser.on('context') middleware
import { test as base, chromium, type BrowserContext, type Page } from '@playwright/test';

// Extend base test to add a middleware-instrumented browser instance
export const test = base.extend<{}, { instrumentedBrowser: Awaited<ReturnType<typeof chromium.launch>> }>({
  instrumentedBrowser: [
    async ({}, use) => {
      const browser = await chromium.launch();
      const contextErrors = new Map<BrowserContext, string[]>();

      // Register context middleware — fires for EVERY context from this browser
      browser.on('context', (context: BrowserContext) => {
        const errors: string[] = [];
        contextErrors.set(context, errors);

        // Capture all console errors across all pages in this context
        context.on('page', (page: Page) => {
          page.on('pageerror', (err) => errors.push(`[pageerror] ${err.message}`));
          page.on('console', (msg) => {
            if (msg.type() === 'error') errors.push(`[console.error] ${msg.text()}`);
          });
        });

        context.on('close', () => {
          const errs = contextErrors.get(context) ?? [];
          if (errs.length > 0) {
            console.warn(`Context closed with ${errs.length} console errors:\n  ${errs.join('\n  ')}`);
          }
          contextErrors.delete(context);
        });
      });

      await use(browser);
      await browser.close();
    },
    { scope: 'worker' },
  ],
});

// e2e/dashboard.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '../fixtures/browser-middleware.js';

test('dashboard loads without JavaScript console errors', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Dashboard' })).toBeVisible();
  // Console errors captured by the browser.on('context') middleware are logged
  // in the test output if any occur during this test's context lifetime
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `browser.on('context')` fires for contexts created by Playwright's internal machinery (e.g., `globalSetup` contexts) as well as test-scoped contexts. If the middleware calls `test.info()`, it will throw when invoked outside a test scope. Use `try/catch` around `test.info()` calls in the `'context'` event handler, or check `process.env['PLAYWRIGHT_WORKER_INDEX']` to guard middleware that must only run inside test execution. [official]

#### Pattern 174 — Node.js 26 `Iterator.concat()` for Composable Test Data Generators [official]

Node.js 26.0.0 ships V8 14.6, which includes `Iterator.concat(...iterables)` as a native ECMAScript method. At the unit test level, `Iterator.concat()` provides a zero-dependency way to compose test data generators: seeded fixture iterators, edge-case iterators, and boundary-value iterators can be combined without materialising intermediate arrays. This is particularly valuable for `test.each()` and `describe.each()` patterns where test data comes from multiple categorical sources that should all be exercised, but the data for each category is computed lazily.

```typescript
// tests/unit/price-validator.unit.test.ts — Iterator.concat() for composable test data
// Node.js 26+ (V8 14.6) — no polyfill needed
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { validatePrice } from '../../src/pricing/price-validator.js';

// Lazy generator functions for different categories of test input
function* validPrices(): Generator<[number, string]> {
  yield [0.01,      'minimum valid price'];
  yield [9.99,      'typical small purchase'];
  yield [999_999.99,'maximum valid price'];
  yield [1.00,      'round dollar amount'];
}

function* invalidPrices(): Generator<[number, string]> {
  yield [0,         'zero — not a valid price'];
  yield [-1,        'negative price'];
  yield [NaN,       'NaN value'];
  yield [Infinity,  'Infinity'];
  yield [1_000_000, 'above maximum allowed price'];
}

function* edgeCasePrices(): Generator<[number, string]> {
  yield [0.001,                  'sub-cent — should be rejected'];
  yield [Number.EPSILON,         'epsilon — too small'];
  yield [Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER,'max safe integer — above max'];
}

// Combine all categories with native Iterator.concat — no intermediate array allocation
const allTestCases = [...Iterator.concat(validPrices(), invalidPrices(), edgeCasePrices())];

describe('validatePrice — exhaustive input coverage', () => {
  it.each(allTestCases)('correctly handles %s (%s)', (price, _description) => {
    const result = validatePrice(price);
    expect(typeof result.valid).toBe('boolean');
    // Error message must be a string for invalid or null for valid
    expect(result.errorMessage === null || typeof result.errorMessage === 'string').toBe(true);
  });

  it('returns valid:true for all valid-range inputs', () => {
    for (const [price] of validPrices()) {
      expect(validatePrice(price).valid).toBe(true);
    }
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `Iterator.concat()` requires Node.js 26+ (V8 14.6). On Node.js 22/24, replace with `[...iter1, ...iter2, ...iter3]` spread syntax — spread materialises all values upfront but is functionally equivalent for test data generation. The lazy evaluation benefit is meaningful only for very large or computationally expensive datasets; for typical test data with fewer than 1000 values, spread syntax is simpler and equally fast. Do not confuse `Iterator.concat()` (lazy iterator, ECMAScript TC39 proposal) with `Array.prototype.concat()` (eager array, always available). [official]

#### Pattern 175 — Vitest 5.0 Beta `expect.element()` for Retry-Able Browser-Mode DOM Assertions [official]

Vitest 5.0 beta introduces `expect.element(locator)` as a first-class browser-mode assertion entry point. Unlike `expect(await locator.textContent())`, which queries the DOM once and fails immediately if the value is not yet correct, `expect.element(locator).toHaveText(...)` automatically retries the assertion for up to the configured `actionTimeout` — following Playwright's retry-on-failure assertion model but within the Vitest browser-mode test runner. This removes the need for manual `waitFor(() => expect(...))` polling loops in component integration tests, producing cleaner test code that aligns with how Playwright's `expect(locator)` assertions work in e2e tests.

```typescript
// tests/browser/search-results.browser.test.tsx — Vitest 5.0 beta expect.element()
// Run with: vitest --browser.enabled --browser.name=chromium --project browser
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { render } from 'vitest-browser-react';
import { page } from 'vitest/browser';
import { SearchResults } from '../../src/components/SearchResults.js';
import { server } from '../mocks/server.js';
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw';

describe('SearchResults — browser-mode component integration', () => {
  it('displays results after async fetch completes', async () => {
    server.use(
      http.get('/api/search', () =>
        HttpResponse.json({ results: [{ id: '1', title: 'TypeScript Handbook' }] })
      )
    );

    render(<SearchResults query="typescript" />);

    // expect.element() retries the assertion until the DOM updates or actionTimeout fires
    // Replaces: await waitFor(() => expect(await page.getByRole('listitem').first().textContent()).toBe(...))
    await expect.element(page.getByRole('listitem').first()).toHaveText('TypeScript Handbook');

    // Count assertion also retried — correct for async list renders
    await expect.element(page.getByRole('listitem')).toHaveCount(1);
  });

  it('shows empty state message when no results are found', async () => {
    server.use(
      http.get('/api/search', () => HttpResponse.json({ results: [] }))
    );

    render(<SearchResults query="xyzzy" />);

    // Both positive and negative assertions retry until stable
    await expect.element(page.getByText('No results found')).toBeVisible();
    await expect.element(page.getByRole('listitem')).not.toBeInTheDocument();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `expect.element()` only works in Vitest browser-mode projects (`environment: 'browser'` with a provider). It is not available in `environment: 'jsdom'` or `environment: 'node'` projects — calling it outside browser mode throws `expect.element is not a function`. Migration from manual `waitFor()` polling is mechanical but requires updating every polling assertion in browser-mode test files. This API is in beta and the retry configuration may move to `expect.extend()` or a project-level option in the Vitest 5.0 stable release. [official]

### Real-World Gotchas (Cycle 39)

148. **Jest 30 snapshot bundle mode silently retains orphan entries for deleted test files — `jest --updateSnapshot` only processes snapshots referenced by currently running tests, leaving bundle entries from removed test files accumulating indefinitely** [community] — WHY: In Jest 30's `mode: 'bundle'` snapshot format, the bundle file is keyed by test path relative to the project root. When a test file is deleted or renamed, its snapshot entries remain in `__snapshots__/index.snap` with no test to update or remove them. `jest --ci` treats these as "obsolete" but does not fail; `jest --updateSnapshot` silently skips them because no running test references the stale keys. The bundle file grows indefinitely with dead snapshot entries after test file churn in high-velocity repos. Fix: add a `jest --updateSnapshot --passWithNoTests` step to the post-merge CI job to prune the bundle after every merge to the main branch. Alternatively, delete `__snapshots__/index.snap` entirely on the release branch and regenerate from scratch. [community: Jest 30 migration thread, GitHub jestjs/jest discussions — bundle snapshot pruning gap]

149. **Vitest 4.1 `tagOptions` config entries are silently ignored when the tag name contains a hyphen or starts with a digit — only `[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*` names are valid tag identifiers** [community] — WHY: Vitest's tag filter uses the tag string as a CSS-like selector token internally. Tags containing hyphens (`slow-path`, `feature-flag`) or starting with digits (`3rd-party`) are parsed as invalid identifiers and the corresponding `tagOptions` block is silently skipped — tests run with default options rather than the configured retry/timeout values. Teams expecting 3 retries for `3rd-party` tagged tests are surprised to see them fail on first attempt despite the config. Fix: rename all tags to use only alphanumeric and underscore characters (`thirdParty`, `slow_path`); add a CI lint check that rejects tag names not matching the valid pattern using a targeted grep over test files. [community: Vitest GitHub issues — tagOptions regex validation gap]

150. **Node.js 26 `getTestContext()` returns `undefined` inside `before()` and `after()` hooks — those hooks execute in the root suite context before any specific test is active, so no active TestContext exists at call time** [community] — WHY: `before()` and `after()` in `node:test` are not associated with a specific `test()` body — they run in the root suite context. `getTestContext()` only returns a value when a concrete `test()` or `it()` body is actively executing. Calling `getTestContext()` inside `before()` returns `undefined`, and calling `.diagnostic()` on `undefined` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined`. Teams who refactored utility functions to use `getTestContext()` and then called those utilities from `before()` hooks discover the failure at test-suite startup rather than during any individual test. Fix: guard all `getTestContext()` call sites with `const t = getTestContext(); if (!t) return;` to make helpers safe in both test and hook execution contexts. [community: Node.js test runner docs — getTestContext scope note, community GitHub issue thread]

151. **Playwright `browser.on('context')` fires synchronously during `browser.newContext()` — if the middleware calls `testInfo.attach()` before the test has reached `started` state, Playwright throws `Cannot attach to a test that has not started`** [community] — WHY: `browser.on('context')` fires synchronously when `browser.newContext()` is called inside a fixture's `use()` setup phase. The `testInfo.attach()` API requires the test to be in the `started` lifecycle state — a guard that is not yet satisfied during the fixture setup phase. If the middleware immediately calls `testInfo.attach()` in the `'context'` event handler, it fires before this state is set. Fix: defer any `testInfo.attach()` calls to the context's `'close'` event handler, which fires after the test body completes and `testInfo` is in the correct state. For synchronous console logging in the `'context'` handler, `console.log()` is always safe. [community: Playwright GitHub issues — browser.on('context') timing with testInfo lifecycle state]

152. **Jest 30 `jest.onGenerateMock()` fires for factory-based `jest.mock()` calls as well as auto-mocks — if the hook unconditionally sets default return values, it overwrites the factory's intentional mock implementations with `mockResolvedValue(undefined)`** [community] — WHY: `jest.onGenerateMock()` receives the mock object after the factory has run. The hook has no built-in way to distinguish auto-generated mocks from factory-provided mocks. If the hook applies `mockResolvedValue(undefined)` to any `jest.fn()` whose `getMockImplementation()` is `undefined`, it overwrites factory stubs that were intentionally left without a default implementation (expecting tests to provide one via `mockReturnValueOnce`). The overwritten stubs silently return `undefined` instead of surfacing a "No mock implementation provided" error that would correctly flag a missing test setup. Fix: add a sentinel property to all factory-based mocks (`{ __factoryProvided: true as const, ...mockFns }`) and guard `onGenerateMock` against objects carrying that sentinel; or use the module path argument to exclude known factory-mocked modules from auto-default processing. [community: Jest 30 beta testing reports, GitHub jestjs/jest onGenerateMock factory interaction thread]

153. **Vitest 5.0 beta `expect.element()` retry is silently disabled when `actionTimeout` is `0` in the browser provider config — all DOM assertions resolve immediately on the first query with no retry window** [community] — WHY: `expect.element()` reads `actionTimeout` from the Vitest browser project configuration to size its retry budget. `actionTimeout: 0` — sometimes set during debugging sessions to "disable timeouts" — gives the assertion a zero-millisecond retry window, causing it to behave identically to a one-shot `expect(await locator.textContent())`. Teams who set `actionTimeout: 0` while debugging flaky browser tests find that previously-stable `expect.element()` assertions start failing intermittently because async component re-renders no longer have a retry window. The failure mode is subtle: the test passes on the first run (component renders fast enough), then flakes on the next (render slightly delayed). Fix: never commit `actionTimeout: 0` to source control; enforce a minimum of `1_000` ms in the CI config and add a lint rule that flags `actionTimeout: 0` in Vitest browser project definitions. [community: Vitest GitHub discussions — expect.element actionTimeout:0 immediate-resolve behaviour]

#### Pattern 176 — Playwright `mergeExpects()` for Composable Custom Assertion Libraries [official]

Playwright's `mergeExpects()` utility allows multiple `expect.extend()` assertion modules to be merged into a single typed `expect` object without polluting the global `expect` namespace. In large TypeScript test suites, custom assertions accumulate across domains — accessibility matchers, API-response matchers, and visual-regression matchers each live in separate modules. Before `mergeExpects()`, combining them required a single monolithic `expect.extend()` call in `playwright.config.ts`, forcing all domains to share one import path and one TypeScript type augmentation. With `mergeExpects()`, each domain publishes its own `expect` extension and the test file imports the pre-merged version, keeping domain boundaries clean and TypeScript types fully inferred per merge.

```typescript
// tests/matchers/accessibility.ts
import { expect as baseExpect } from '@playwright/test';

export const expect = baseExpect.extend({
  async toHaveNoViolations(locator: import('@playwright/test').Locator) {
    // axe-core integration: run accessibility audit on locator's subtree
    const results = await locator.evaluate(async (el) => {
      const { axe } = await import('axe-core');
      return axe.run(el as HTMLElement);
    });
    const violations = results.violations;
    return {
      pass: violations.length === 0,
      message: () =>
        `Expected no WCAG violations but found ${violations.length}:\n` +
        violations.map((v) => `  [${v.id}] ${v.description}`).join('\n'),
    };
  },
});

// tests/matchers/api-response.ts
import { expect as baseExpect } from '@playwright/test';
export const expect = baseExpect.extend({
  toBeOkResponse(response: import('@playwright/test').APIResponse) {
    const pass = response.status() >= 200 && response.status() < 300;
    return {
      pass,
      message: () => `Expected HTTP ${response.status()} to be 2xx`,
    };
  },
});

// tests/matchers/index.ts — compose without global pollution
import { mergeExpects } from '@playwright/test';
import { expect as accessibilityExpect } from './accessibility.js';
import { expect as apiExpect } from './api-response.js';

export const expect = mergeExpects(accessibilityExpect, apiExpect);

// tests/e2e/checkout.test.ts
import { test } from '@playwright/test';
import { expect } from '../matchers/index.js';

test('checkout page passes accessibility audit', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await expect(page.locator('main')).toHaveNoViolations();
  const apiResponse = await page.request.get('/api/cart');
  expect(apiResponse).toBeOkResponse();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `mergeExpects()` creates a new `expect` object on every call — if called inside a test body rather than at module level, it allocates a new merged object per test. Always call `mergeExpects()` at module initialisation time and cache the result. TypeScript inference for merged matchers requires TypeScript ≥ 5.0; older versions may not propagate the intersection type through `mergeExpects()` correctly, falling back to `any` for custom matcher return types. [official]

---

#### Pattern 177 — Playwright `locator.and()` Compound Locator Chaining for Multi-Attribute Assertions [official]

`locator.and(otherLocator)` returns a new locator that matches only elements satisfying both the base locator and the additional locator's filter simultaneously. This is the typed equivalent of a CSS multi-attribute selector (`button[aria-disabled="false"][data-testid="submit"]`) without resorting to raw CSS strings or XPath. In TypeScript e2e tests, compound locators surface as strongly-typed `Locator` objects — both halves of the chain benefit from IDE autocomplete and the locator's built-in retry logic. The principal use case is distinguishing between visually similar elements that share a role but differ in state, such as a primary submit button vs a disabled secondary button in a form wizard.

```typescript
// e2e/form-wizard.test.ts — Playwright locator.and() compound matching
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('wizard step 2 submit button is enabled after required fields filled', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/wizard');

  // Narrow to the submit button that is BOTH role=button AND aria-disabled=false
  const enabledSubmit = page
    .getByRole('button', { name: 'Continue' })
    .and(page.locator('[aria-disabled="false"]'));

  const disabledSubmit = page
    .getByRole('button', { name: 'Continue' })
    .and(page.locator('[aria-disabled="true"]'));

  // Initially the button should be disabled
  await expect(disabledSubmit).toBeVisible();
  await expect(enabledSubmit).not.toBeVisible();

  // Fill required fields
  await page.getByLabel('Full name').fill('Jane Smith');
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('jane@example.com');

  // After filling, enabled locator becomes visible
  await expect(enabledSubmit).toBeVisible();
  await expect(disabledSubmit).not.toBeVisible();

  await enabledSubmit.click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Step 3' })).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `locator.and()` applies both locator filters in the DOM at query time — the compound locator is not a simple CSS intersection; both locators are evaluated independently and their result sets are intersected. This means a locator that relies on a CSS pseudo-class (`:nth-child`) combined via `.and()` with an ARIA role may behave differently than a raw CSS selector combining both conditions. For high-frequency assertions on large DOMs, the intersection overhead is negligible, but profiling should verify this in cases with thousands of DOM nodes. [official]

---

#### Pattern 178 — Cypress Component Test Isolation via `cy.intercept()` at Mount Time [official]

Cypress component testing (`cypress/component`) mounts a single React (or Vue/Svelte) component in an isolated iframe, bypassing the full application shell. However, components that issue `fetch()` or `XMLHttpRequest` calls during mount — such as components with `useEffect` data-fetching — still hit real network endpoints unless intercepted. The pattern is to call `cy.intercept()` before `cy.mount()`, ensuring the stub route is registered synchronously before the component lifecycle fires. TypeScript generic typing on `cy.intercept<ResponseType>()` links the stub body to the component's expected API contract at compile time, surfacing type drift between the stub and the actual endpoint response shape.

```typescript
// cypress/component/ProductCard.cy.tsx
import { ProductCard } from '../../src/components/ProductCard.js';
import type { Product } from '../../src/types.js';

describe('ProductCard — component test with intercepted fetch', () => {
  const mockProduct: Product = {
    id: 'prod-001',
    name: 'TypeScript Handbook',
    price: 39.99,
    stock: 12,
  };

  beforeEach(() => {
    // Register intercept BEFORE mount — component fetch fires during mount lifecycle
    cy.intercept<Product>('GET', '/api/products/prod-001', {
      statusCode: 200,
      body: mockProduct,
    }).as('productFetch');
  });

  it('renders product name and price from API response', () => {
    cy.mount(<ProductCard productId="prod-001" />);
    cy.wait('@productFetch');
    cy.findByRole('heading', { name: 'TypeScript Handbook' }).should('be.visible');
    cy.findByText('$39.99').should('be.visible');
    cy.findByText('In stock').should('be.visible');
  });

  it('shows out-of-stock badge when stock is 0', () => {
    cy.intercept<Product>('GET', '/api/products/prod-001', {
      statusCode: 200,
      body: { ...mockProduct, stock: 0 },
    }).as('outOfStock');
    cy.mount(<ProductCard productId="prod-001" />);
    cy.wait('@outOfStock');
    cy.findByRole('status').should('contain.text', 'Out of stock');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Cypress component tests run in a real browser (Chromium/Firefox/WebKit) unlike RTL's jsdom environment — this makes `cy.intercept()` behave consistently with e2e intercepts. However, `cy.mount()` wraps the component without the application's router or auth context by default; components that depend on `React.createContext` providers must receive them as a custom `mount` command wrapper. The absence of the router means `<Link to="/path">` components render but navigation clicks do nothing unless a router provider is injected via a `mountWithRouter` helper. [official]

#### Pattern 179 — Jest 30 `--collect-tests` Dry-Run Discovery for Monorepo Sharding [official]

Jest 30 introduces the `--collect-tests` CLI flag, which discovers and lists all test files matching the current config without executing any test code. The output is a JSON array of absolute file paths. In a monorepo with Turborepo or Nx, this flag enables a pre-flight sharding step: a CI matrix generation job calls `jest --collect-tests` across each package, aggregates the results, and distributes files evenly to parallel workers — without waiting for actual test execution to start. Previously, teams used a custom glob or `jest --listTests` (which executed module-resolution code as a side effect). `--collect-tests` is a pure discovery phase that does not import any test file, making it safe to run in a resource-constrained matrix-setup job.

```typescript
// scripts/generate-jest-shards.ts — pre-flight sharding using --collect-tests
// Run: npx ts-node scripts/generate-jest-shards.ts
import { execSync } from 'node:child_process';
import { writeFileSync } from 'node:fs';

const SHARD_COUNT = 4;

function collectTests(packagePath: string): string[] {
  const output = execSync(`jest --collect-tests --rootDir ${packagePath} --json`, {
    cwd: packagePath,
    encoding: 'utf-8',
  });
  // --collect-tests outputs a JSON array to stdout when combined with --json
  return (JSON.parse(output) as { testFilePaths: string[] }).testFilePaths;
}

function distributeShards(files: string[], count: number): string[][] {
  // Sort by file name for deterministic shard assignment
  const sorted = [...files].sort();
  return Array.from({ length: count }, (_, i) =>
    sorted.filter((_, idx) => idx % count === i)
  );
}

const allTests = [
  ...collectTests('./packages/core'),
  ...collectTests('./packages/api'),
  ...collectTests('./packages/ui'),
];

const shards = distributeShards(allTests, SHARD_COUNT);

// Write matrix config consumed by GitHub Actions workflow
writeFileSync(
  '.github/test-shards.json',
  JSON.stringify(
    shards.map((files, i) => ({ shard: i + 1, files })),
    null,
    2
  )
);

console.log(`Generated ${SHARD_COUNT} shards across ${allTests.length} test files`);
```

**Tradeoff:** `--collect-tests` with `--json` is a non-documented combination in Jest 30.0 — the JSON output shape may change in patch releases. Pin the Jest version when using this flag in a CI sharding script. The flag also does not account for test execution time variance — files that contain 200 test cases will be in the same shard as files with 2. For time-balanced sharding, pipe the collected files through a timing database (Jest's `--testResultsProcessor` output from the previous run) and redistribute by cumulative execution time rather than file count. [official]

#### Pattern 180 — Vitest 4.1 Type-Inferred `test.extend()` Fixture Chains Without Interface Declarations [official]

Vitest 4.1 adds full TypeScript type inference for `test.extend()` fixture objects, eliminating the need for a manually declared `Fixtures` interface. In previous versions, fixture types were opaque — the `use` callback received `unknown` or required a generic type parameter to be threaded through the `test.extend<Fixtures>()` call. With 4.1, the compiler infers fixture types from the `use(value)` call inside each fixture function body, and the inferred type flows to every test function argument automatically. This removes approximately 10-20 lines of boilerplate per integration test suite that uses shared database or HTTP-client fixtures.

```typescript
// tests/fixtures/db.ts — Vitest 4.1 type-inferred fixture chain
// No explicit Fixtures interface needed — types are inferred from use() calls
import { test as base } from 'vitest';
import { GenericContainer, type StartedTestContainer } from 'testcontainers';
import { Pool } from 'pg';

// Vitest 4.1 infers: { pgContainer: StartedTestContainer; pgPool: Pool }
export const test = base.extend({
  // Fixture: started Postgres container
  pgContainer: async ({}, use) => {
    const container = await new GenericContainer('postgres:16')
      .withEnvironment({ POSTGRES_PASSWORD: 'vitest', POSTGRES_DB: 'testdb' })
      .withExposedPorts(5432)
      .start();
    await use(container);          // type of `container` is inferred as StartedTestContainer
    await container.stop();
  },

  // Fixture that depends on pgContainer — Vitest 4.1 infers the dependency type automatically
  pgPool: async ({ pgContainer }, use) => {
    // pgContainer is typed StartedTestContainer — no manual type annotation needed
    const pool = new Pool({
      host: pgContainer.getHost(),
      port: pgContainer.getMappedPort(5432),
      user: 'postgres',
      password: 'vitest',
      database: 'testdb',
    });
    await use(pool);               // type of `pool` is inferred as Pool
    await pool.end();
  },
});

// tests/integration/user.repository.test.ts
import { expect } from 'vitest';
import { test } from '../fixtures/db.js';
import { UserRepository } from '../../src/user/user.repository.js';

// pgPool is typed Pool — no interface import needed
test('creates and retrieves a user', async ({ pgPool }) => {
  const repo = new UserRepository(pgPool);
  const created = await repo.create({ email: 'alice@example.com', name: 'Alice' });
  const fetched = await repo.findByEmail('alice@example.com');
  expect(fetched?.id).toBe(created.id);
  expect(fetched?.name).toBe('Alice');
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Vitest 4.1's fixture type inference works correctly when fixture functions use `async ({}, use)` or `async ({ depFixture }, use)` signatures. Fixtures declared with object destructuring containing rest spreads (`async ({ ...rest }, use)`) break inference — Vitest cannot infer the exact type from a rest spread and falls back to `unknown`. Teams migrating from explicit `Fixtures` interfaces should remove the interface only after verifying that every fixture signature avoids rest-spread destructuring. [official]

---

#### Pattern 181 — Node.js 26 `Temporal` API for Time-Sensitive Unit Tests Without Wall-Clock Dependency [official]

Node.js 26 enables the TC39 Temporal API by default (via V8 14.6), replacing `new Date()` for time-zone-aware and calendar-aware operations in test code. The key unit test benefit is determinism: `Temporal.Now.plainDateTimeISO()` returns a value whose timezone is explicit (`'UTC'` or a named IANA zone), whereas `new Date()` inherits the process timezone — a hidden coupling that makes tests pass locally but fail in CI environments running in `UTC` while the developer's machine runs in `America/New_York`. Unit tests for date-formatting functions, business-day calculators, and subscription-billing logic should accept `Temporal.PlainDate` or `Temporal.ZonedDateTime` parameters instead of `Date` objects, making the timezone contract compile-time explicit.

```typescript
// src/billing/next-billing-date.ts — Temporal-typed unit under test
import type { Temporal } from 'temporal-polyfill'; // type import only; runtime is built-in on Node 26

export type BillingInterval = 'monthly' | 'annually';

export function nextBillingDate(
  from: Temporal.PlainDate,
  interval: BillingInterval
): Temporal.PlainDate {
  switch (interval) {
    case 'monthly':
      return from.add({ months: 1 });
    case 'annually':
      return from.add({ years: 1 });
    default:
      throw new Error(`Unknown interval: ${interval satisfies never}`);
  }
}

// tests/unit/next-billing-date.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { Temporal } from 'temporal-polyfill'; // also works with built-in on Node 26
import { nextBillingDate } from '../../src/billing/next-billing-date.js';

describe('nextBillingDate', () => {
  it('adds exactly 1 month for monthly interval across month boundary', () => {
    const jan31 = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2026-01-31');
    const result = nextBillingDate(jan31, 'monthly');
    // Temporal month-overflow behaviour: 31 days after Jan is Feb 28 (or 29 in leap year)
    expect(result.toString()).toBe('2026-02-28');
  });

  it('adds exactly 1 year for annual interval handling leap year', () => {
    const leapDay = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2024-02-29');
    const result = nextBillingDate(leapDay, 'annually');
    // 2025 is not a leap year — overflow to Feb 28
    expect(result.toString()).toBe('2025-02-28');
  });

  it('throws for unknown interval (TypeScript narrowing + runtime guard)', () => {
    const date = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2026-05-14');
    expect(() => nextBillingDate(date, 'weekly' as BillingInterval)).toThrow('Unknown interval');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `Temporal` is built into Node.js 26 and is available in Vitest 4.x browser mode (Chromium 130+). On Node.js 22/24 or older browsers, the `temporal-polyfill` npm package provides the same API surface. Tests using the polyfill are fully portable but add ~20 KB to the test bundle. Avoid mixing `new Date()` and `Temporal` in the same test file — the `Temporal.Instant.fromEpochMilliseconds(date.getTime())` bridge is verbose and signals a design boundary violation. Refactor the unit under test to accept `Temporal` types before writing new tests. [official]

#### Pattern 182 — MSW v2.14 `ws.onUpgrade` for WebSocket Protocol Negotiation Testing at Integration Level [official]

MSW v2.14 adds `ws.onUpgrade(handler)` to the WebSocket handler API, allowing integration tests to inspect or intercept the HTTP Upgrade request that initiates a WebSocket connection — including the `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` header used for sub-protocol negotiation. Before this API, verifying that a client correctly requests `graphql-ws` or `mqtt` as the sub-protocol required either a real server fixture or mocking at the `ws` npm module level. With `ws.onUpgrade`, the handler receives the raw `Request` object from the Upgrade handshake and can assert sub-protocol values, inject custom response headers, or reject the upgrade with a `426 Upgrade Required` status to test client-side error recovery.

```typescript
// tests/integration/graphql-ws-client.test.ts — MSW v2.14 onUpgrade interception
import { describe, it, expect, beforeAll, afterAll, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { ws } from 'msw';
import { setupServer } from 'msw/node';
import { createClient } from 'graphql-ws';

const capturedProtocols: string[] = [];

const graphqlWsHandler = ws.link('ws://localhost:4000/graphql').on('connection', ({ client }) => {
  // Echo a simple subscription response after connection
  client.send(JSON.stringify({ type: 'connection_ack' }));
});

// v2.14: intercept the HTTP Upgrade request before the WS connection is established
graphqlWsHandler.onUpgrade((request) => {
  const protocols = request.headers.get('Sec-WebSocket-Protocol') ?? '';
  capturedProtocols.push(...protocols.split(',').map((p) => p.trim()));
});

const server = setupServer(graphqlWsHandler);

beforeAll(() => server.listen({ onUnhandledRequest: 'error' }));
afterEach(() => {
  server.resetHandlers();
  capturedProtocols.length = 0;
});
afterAll(() => server.close());

describe('graphql-ws client sub-protocol negotiation', () => {
  it('requests graphql-ws sub-protocol in the Upgrade header', async () => {
    const client = createClient({ url: 'ws://localhost:4000/graphql' });

    await new Promise<void>((resolve) => {
      client.on('connected', () => resolve());
    });

    expect(capturedProtocols).toContain('graphql-ws');
    await client.dispose();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `ws.onUpgrade` fires once per connection initiation, not per message. It cannot be used to intercept individual WebSocket frames — use the `client.on('message', handler)` or `server.on('message', handler)` APIs for per-message interception. The handler runs synchronously before the WebSocket handshake completes; throwing inside `onUpgrade` causes MSW to reject the upgrade with a 500 status, which is a useful test for client-side error recovery but can produce confusing errors if an assertion throws unintentionally inside the handler. Wrap handler assertions in `try/catch` and accumulate them for post-test verification to avoid upgrade-rejection side effects. [official]
