### Patterns 206–220

#### Pattern 206 — Playwright v1.53 `locator.describe()` for Custom Trace Labels in Multi-Step E2E Flows [official]

Playwright v1.53 adds `locator.describe(label)`, which attaches a custom human-readable name to a locator so that the trace viewer and HTML reporter display the label instead of the raw CSS selector or role query. Without `describe()`, trace files show entries like `locator('div').filter({ hasText: /^Submit$/ }).first()` — a cryptic chain that forces trace reviewers to mentally parse the locator to understand what element is being targeted. With `describe()`, that same locator appears as `"Submit button (billing step)"` in the trace, making step-level failure diagnosis dramatically faster when reviewing trace archives for flaky E2E failures days after they occurred. The label is propagated to all action traces, assertions, and screenshots derived from the described locator.

```typescript
// tests/e2e/checkout-billing.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('billing form submission routes to confirmation', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout/billing');

  // Without describe(): trace shows 'locator("form").getByRole("textbox", { name: /card number/i })'
  // With describe(): trace shows '"Card number input (billing form)"'
  const cardInput = page
    .getByRole('form', { name: 'Billing details' })
    .getByRole('textbox', { name: /card number/i })
    .describe('Card number input (billing form)');

  const expiryInput = page
    .getByRole('form', { name: 'Billing details' })
    .getByRole('textbox', { name: /expiry/i })
    .describe('Expiry date input (billing form)');

  const submitBtn = page
    .getByRole('form', { name: 'Billing details' })
    .getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay now' })
    .describe('Pay now button (billing form)');

  await cardInput.fill('4242424242424242');
  await expiryInput.fill('12/28');
  await submitBtn.click();

  await expect(page).toHaveURL('/checkout/confirmation');
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `locator.describe()` returns a new locator wrapping the original — it does not mutate the original locator in place. If a locator is stored in a fixture or helper function that returns the undescribed version, callers cannot retroactively add descriptions without re-wrapping. For shared locators defined in Page Object Models, define `describe()` in the POM method itself so every consumer benefits. Additionally, labels are not validated at runtime; a typo in a label string produces no error — only a confusing trace entry. Consider a constants file for label strings shared across multiple specs. [official]

---

#### Pattern 207 — Playwright v1.56 `page.consoleMessages()` Snapshot for Asserting Clean Console Output [official]

Playwright v1.56 adds `page.consoleMessages()`, `page.pageErrors()`, and `page.requests()` as methods returning arrays of the recent corresponding events accumulated during the current test. Previously, asserting that a page produced no console errors required registering a `page.on('console', ...)` listener before navigation and accumulating events manually — a verbose setup that was easy to omit from individual tests. With `page.consoleMessages()`, assertions about console hygiene can be written inline at the end of any test without upfront listener registration, enabling "clean console" post-conditions as a standard test exit assertion pattern.

```typescript
// tests/e2e/page-health.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('dashboard loads without console errors or uncaught exceptions', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Interact with the page to trigger any lazy-loaded components
  await page.getByRole('tab', { name: 'Analytics' }).click();
  await page.getByRole('tab', { name: 'Settings' }).click();

  // Assert no console errors were emitted during the entire test
  const consoleMessages = await page.consoleMessages();
  const errors = consoleMessages.filter(msg => msg.type() === 'error');
  expect(errors, `Expected no console errors, got: ${errors.map(e => e.text()).join('\n')}`).toHaveLength(0);

  // Assert no uncaught JS exceptions
  const pageErrors = await page.pageErrors();
  expect(pageErrors, `Expected no page errors, got: ${pageErrors.map(e => e.message).join('\n')}`).toHaveLength(0);
});

test('checkout page emits exactly one analytics event on purchase', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Complete purchase' }).click();

  const consoleMessages = await page.consoleMessages();
  const analyticsLogs = consoleMessages.filter(msg =>
    msg.type() === 'log' && msg.text().includes('[analytics]')
  );
  expect(analyticsLogs).toHaveLength(1);
  expect(analyticsLogs[0].text()).toContain('purchase_complete');
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `page.consoleMessages()` returns messages accumulated from the point the page object was created, not from the start of the test. If a test fixture creates the page and performs setup navigation before the test body runs, console messages from fixture setup are included in the array. For tests where fixture setup produces expected console noise (e.g., auth redirect warnings), filter messages by timestamp or prefix before asserting. Note also that `consoleMessages()` accumulates indefinitely — in long-running tests with heavy console output (like streaming dashboards), the array can grow large and impact assertion performance. [official]

---

#### Pattern 208 — Playwright v1.57 `webServer.wait` Regex for Reliable Dev Server Readiness Detection [official]

Playwright v1.57 adds a `wait` field to the `webServer` configuration block that accepts a regular expression. Playwright blocks test execution until a line matching the regex appears in the server's stdout or stderr stream. Previously, teams relied on `url` polling — Playwright periodically requested a health-check URL and waited for a 200 response, which fails for servers that start accepting connections before fully initializing (e.g., before database migrations run or before the asset bundler emits the initial build). The `wait` regex approach synchronizes test startup with the actual server-ready signal rather than inferring readiness from HTTP reachability.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  webServer: {
    command: 'npm run dev',
    port: 3000,
    // Block tests until the server emits its ready message
    // Matches: "✓ Ready in 1234ms" or "Server is ready" or "Listening on port 3000"
    wait: /(?:Ready in \d+ms|Server is ready|Listening on port \d+)/,
    // Keep the server running between test runs in watch mode
    reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI,
    // Capture server logs for debugging flaky startup failures
    stdout: 'pipe',
    stderr: 'pipe',
    // Timeout if the server does not emit the ready signal within 60s
    timeout: 60_000,
  },
  use: {
    baseURL: 'http://localhost:3000',
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff:** The `wait` regex matches against raw stdout/stderr lines as they are emitted — it does not wait for the server process to stabilize after emitting the match. A server that emits "Ready in 1200ms" but then runs post-ready migrations for another 3 seconds will unblock Playwright immediately when the "Ready" line appears, potentially causing tests to begin before the database is available. For such servers, combine the `wait` regex with a custom `globalSetup` that probes the health endpoint after the server signals readiness. The `wait` approach is strictly more reliable than `url` polling for detecting the readiness signal, but the server itself must emit a reliable signal at the correct point in its startup sequence. [official]

#### Pattern 209 — Playwright v1.58 HTML Report Timeline Visualization for Cross-Shard Flakiness Diagnosis [official]

Playwright v1.58 adds a Timeline tab (the "Speedboard") to merged HTML reports that renders all test runs — across all shards — as horizontal timeline bars, ordered by duration, with failure and flakiness annotations overlaid. The Timeline visualization makes cross-shard flakiness patterns immediately visible: a test that passes in shards 1–4 but consistently fails in shard 5 at the 45-second mark appears as a single red bar at the 45-second position in the timeline, enabling the team to correlate the failure with shard 5's specific test ordering or environment state without manually diffing JSON result files.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — configured for sharded runs with report merging
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  reporter: process.env.CI
    ? [
        // Per-shard: write blob reports for later merge
        ['blob', { outputDir: `./blob-reports/shard-${process.env.SHARD_INDEX}` }],
        // Per-shard: also write JUnit for CI summary
        ['junit', { outputFile: `./test-results/junit-shard-${process.env.SHARD_INDEX}.xml` }],
      ]
    : [['html', { open: 'never' }]],

  // Shard configuration — each CI matrix job gets one shard
  shard: process.env.SHARD_INDEX
    ? {
        current: Number(process.env.SHARD_INDEX),
        total: Number(process.env.SHARD_TOTAL ?? 4),
      }
    : undefined,
});

// CI merge step (runs after all shards complete):
// npx playwright merge-reports --reporter=html ./blob-reports/shard-*
// Opens: playwright-report/index.html → Timeline tab shows cross-shard view
```

**Tradeoff:** The Timeline view requires merged blob reports, which means all shard blob report directories must be collected into a single location before `merge-reports` runs. In CI systems where each shard runs on a different machine (e.g., GitHub Actions matrix jobs), collecting blob reports requires a separate artifact upload/download step between shard completion and the merge job. This adds 30–120 seconds of CI overhead depending on report size. For small suites where cross-shard diagnosis is rare, the overhead may not justify the investment; enable merged timeline reporting selectively for suites with a history of cross-shard flakiness rather than as a default for all projects. [official]

#### Pattern 210 — Playwright v1.59 `browser.bind()` for Agent-Assisted Test Debugging Workflows [official]

Playwright v1.59 introduces `browser.bind()`, which enables a second Playwright client to connect to and share a running browser session. In testing workflows, this enables an "AI healer" agent pattern: a test runner executes the primary test, and if a step fails, a bound agent client connects to the same browser session (with the page in its failed state), inspects the DOM, diagnoses the locator mismatch, and proposes a fix — all while the page remains open with the failure state visible. This is a significant departure from the previous debugging model, where a failed test required re-running with `--headed` and inserting `await page.pause()` to reproduce the state manually.

```typescript
// scripts/debug-agent.ts — secondary client that binds to a running test browser
import { chromium } from '@playwright/test';
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';

async function bindAndInspect(): Promise<void> {
  // The primary test runner writes its CDP endpoint to a temp file on failure
  const cdpEndpoint = readFileSync('/tmp/pw-debug-endpoint.txt', 'utf-8').trim();

  // Bind to the running browser without taking over page control
  const browser = await chromium.connectOverCDP(cdpEndpoint);
  const [context] = browser.contexts();
  const [page] = context.pages();

  // Inspect the current DOM state to diagnose the locator failure
  const domSnapshot = await page.evaluate(() => document.documentElement.outerHTML);
  const title = await page.title();
  const url = page.url();

  console.log(`Page: "${title}" at ${url}`);
  console.log(`DOM length: ${domSnapshot.length} characters`);

  // Find all buttons to compare against what the failing locator expected
  const buttons = await page.getByRole('button').allTextContents();
  console.log('Available buttons:', buttons);

  await browser.close();
}

bindAndInspect().catch(console.error);
```

**Tradeoff:** `browser.bind()` shares a live browser session, meaning the bound client and the primary test runner are simultaneously controlling the same page. If the primary test continues executing while the agent client is inspecting the DOM, race conditions can produce a state snapshot that does not reflect the actual failure condition. The recommended pattern is to pause the primary test runner (via `await page.pause()` or a custom fixture that writes the CDP endpoint and waits for a signal file) before triggering the agent client. Teams that use `browser.bind()` in fully automated healing pipelines must implement explicit sequencing between the primary runner and the agent client to avoid concurrent DOM mutation. [official]

---

#### Pattern 211 — Vitest `vi.defineHelper()` for Reusable Test Utilities with Automatic Mock Injection [official]

Vitest 4.1 adds `vi.defineHelper(fn)`, a function that defines a reusable test utility which automatically receives the current Vitest context (including the mock registry, fake timer state, and `expect` instance) when invoked inside a test. Before `defineHelper`, shared test utilities that needed access to mocks had to either accept `vi` as a parameter (coupling the utility signature to Vitest's API) or import `vi` from `vitest` at module level (preventing the utility from being used with multiple Vitest instances in worker-isolated suites). `defineHelper` solves this by injecting context at call time rather than at import time, enabling helper libraries that are portable across test environments without API coupling.

```typescript
// test-helpers/db-helpers.ts — portable helpers using vi.defineHelper
import { vi } from 'vitest';
import type { MockedFunction } from 'vitest';

// defineHelper ensures the mock is created in the current test's context
export const mockDbQuery = vi.defineHelper(function <T>(
  returnValue: T,
  options?: { delay?: number }
) {
  const mockFn: MockedFunction<() => Promise<T>> = vi.fn();

  if (options?.delay) {
    mockFn.mockImplementation(
      () => new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(() => resolve(returnValue), options.delay))
    );
  } else {
    mockFn.mockResolvedValue(returnValue);
  }

  return mockFn;
});

// src/services/user.test.ts — consuming the helper
import { describe, test, expect, beforeEach } from 'vitest';
import { mockDbQuery } from '../../test-helpers/db-helpers.js';
import { getUserProfile } from './user.service.js';

describe('getUserProfile', () => {
  test('returns mapped profile for known user', async () => {
    // mockDbQuery runs in this test's vi context — mock cleared between tests automatically
    const queryMock = mockDbQuery({ id: '123', name: 'Alice', role: 'admin' });
    vi.mock('../db/client.js', () => ({ runQuery: queryMock }));

    const profile = await getUserProfile('123');
    expect(profile.displayName).toBe('Alice');
    expect(queryMock).toHaveBeenCalledWith(expect.objectContaining({ userId: '123' }));
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `vi.defineHelper()` injects context at the point the helper is called, not at the point it is defined. Helpers called outside a test body (e.g., at module level in a test file, or inside a `describe()` block but outside `test()`) receive a context that may not yet be associated with an active test — in such cases, `vi.defineHelper()` falls back to the global context, which does not automatically clear mocks between tests. Always invoke helpers defined with `vi.defineHelper()` inside `test()` callbacks or `beforeEach()` hooks, never at `describe()` body level. [official]

---

#### Pattern 212 — Vitest `--detect-async-leaks` for Surfacing Cross-Test Promise Pollution [official]

Vitest 4.1 introduces the `--detect-async-leaks` CLI flag (and the `detectAsyncLeaks: true` config option), which tracks Promise chains created during a test and reports any that are still pending after the test completes. A leaked async operation from test A can resolve during test B, triggering side effects (state mutations, mock calls, timer advances) that cause test B to fail non-deterministically. This class of failure is notoriously difficult to diagnose because the failure appears in test B but the root cause is in test A. `--detect-async-leaks` surfaces the source of the leaked Promise in test A's result, shifting the diagnostic effort to the correct location.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — enable async leak detection for all test runs
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // Enable leak detection — adds ~5-10% overhead per test file
    detectAsyncLeaks: true,
    // Combine with pool: 'forks' to ensure truly isolated contexts per file
    pool: 'forks',
    // Set a tight timeout so leaks surface quickly rather than blocking
    testTimeout: 10_000,
    hookTimeout: 5_000,
  },
});

// Example of a leaking test that --detect-async-leaks catches:
// import { describe, test } from 'vitest';
// describe('leaking test', () => {
//   test('starts a background job without awaiting it', () => {
//     // This Promise is NOT awaited — it resolves in a later test's context
//     syncJobWithoutAwait().then(() => updateGlobalCache('leaked-state'));
//     // With --detect-async-leaks, Vitest reports this as an async leak in this test
//   });
// });
```

**Tradeoff:** `--detect-async-leaks` adds runtime overhead proportional to the number of Promise instances created per test. In test suites with heavy use of async utilities (Promise.all batches, event emitter patterns, streaming APIs), the overhead can reach 15–25% of total runtime. The overhead is most severe in integration tests that exercise real I/O — exactly the tests most likely to produce genuine async leaks, which creates a dilemma: the tests most in need of leak detection bear the highest overhead cost. A pragmatic approach is to enable `--detect-async-leaks` by default in development and pre-merge CI, and disable it in the nightly full-suite run where runtime is the primary constraint. [official]

---

#### Pattern 213 — Vitest `aroundAll` for Shared Integration Resource Lifecycle Management [official]

Vitest 4.1's `aroundAll(fn)` hook provides a generator-based wrapper around the entire `describe` suite, yielding once between setup and teardown. Unlike `beforeAll`/`afterAll` pairs, `aroundAll` guarantees teardown runs even when the setup code itself throws — the generator structure ensures the `finally` block always executes. This is critical for integration tests that spin up real infrastructure (Docker containers, database connections, local HTTP servers) using async resource managers, where a half-initialized setup that throws would previously leak resources if `beforeAll` threw before `afterAll` could register.

```typescript
// tests/integration/order-service.test.ts
import { describe, test, expect, aroundAll } from 'vitest';
import { createTestDatabase } from '../support/test-db.js';
import { createOrderService } from '../../src/order-service.js';

describe('OrderService integration', () => {
  // aroundAll: setup runs before the suite, teardown always runs after
  const { db, service } = await aroundAll(async function* () {
    // Setup: create isolated test database
    const db = await createTestDatabase({ schema: 'orders_test' });
    await db.migrate();
    const service = createOrderService({ db });

    yield { db, service };  // suite runs here

    // Teardown: always runs, even if setup partially failed
    await db.dropSchema('orders_test');
    await db.close();
  });

  test('creates order with correct status', async () => {
    const order = await service.create({ productId: 'prod-123', quantity: 2 });
    expect(order.status).toBe('pending');
    expect(order.id).toMatch(/^ord-/);
  });

  test('cancels pending order', async () => {
    const order = await service.create({ productId: 'prod-456', quantity: 1 });
    const cancelled = await service.cancel(order.id);
    expect(cancelled.status).toBe('cancelled');
  });

  test('rejects duplicate order within 5 minutes', async () => {
    await service.create({ productId: 'prod-789', quantity: 1 });
    await expect(
      service.create({ productId: 'prod-789', quantity: 1 })
    ).rejects.toThrow('Duplicate order');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `aroundAll` shares the yielded resources across all tests in the `describe` block — tests are not isolated from each other's state mutations on the shared resource. An integration test that inserts rows into the shared database will affect subsequent tests in the same suite unless each test explicitly cleans up. The canonical pattern is to use `aroundAll` for resource lifecycle (connect/disconnect) and `aroundEach` for test isolation (begin/rollback transaction per test). Using `aroundAll` alone for a database suite that modifies state will produce order-dependent test results, which is an anti-pattern that `--randomize` will immediately surface. [official]

---

#### Pattern 214 — Jest 30 `defineConfig` / `mergeConfig` for Typesafe Monorepo Configuration Composition [official]

Jest 30 introduces `defineConfig(config)` and `mergeConfig(base, override)` as first-class exports from `jest`, replacing the fragile `module.exports = { ... }` pattern with a typed configuration API. `defineConfig` provides TypeScript inference and IDE autocomplete for all configuration keys without requiring a separate `@types/jest` annotation. `mergeConfig` produces a deeply merged configuration object that respects Jest's semantics for each key type — arrays like `setupFilesAfterFramework` are concatenated (additive), while scalar fields like `testEnvironment` are overridden. In monorepos, a root `jest.config.base.ts` can export a shared configuration via `defineConfig`, and each package can import it and compose with `mergeConfig`.

```typescript
// jest.config.base.ts — root configuration shared across all packages
import { defineConfig } from 'jest';

export default defineConfig({
  preset: 'ts-jest/presets/default-esm',
  testEnvironment: 'node',
  collectCoverageFrom: ['src/**/*.ts', '!src/**/*.d.ts'],
  coverageThreshold: { global: { branches: 80, functions: 85, lines: 85 } },
  randomize: true,
  workerIdleMemoryLimit: '512MB',
});

// packages/api/jest.config.ts — package-level override
import { defineConfig, mergeConfig } from 'jest';
import baseConfig from '../../jest.config.base.js';

export default mergeConfig(
  baseConfig,
  defineConfig({
    // Override: api package tests run in band (single worker) due to port binding
    runInBand: true,
    // Additive: concatenated with base's setupFiles array
    setupFilesAfterFramework: ['<rootDir>/tests/setup/api-server.ts'],
    // Scalar override: api package uses a different environment
    testEnvironment: 'node',
    // Coverage override: api package has higher thresholds
    coverageThreshold: { global: { branches: 90, functions: 95, lines: 95 } },
  })
);
```

**Tradeoff:** `mergeConfig` concatenates array fields including `testPathIgnorePatterns` — if the base config ignores `node_modules` and `dist`, the package config cannot remove those patterns by re-declaring them; it can only add new patterns. This is usually correct for additive arrays but unexpected for override arrays. For configuration arrays that must be overridden (not extended), assign them to a local variable and spread them explicitly rather than relying on `mergeConfig` to replace them. Specifically, `coverageThreshold` as a nested object is replaced (not merged) by `mergeConfig`, which is the correct behavior for threshold objects — verify this assumption holds for each key type before assuming merge semantics. [official]

---

#### Pattern 215 — Playwright `expect.configure()` for Per-Assertion Timeout Overrides Without `page.setDefaultTimeout()` [official]

Playwright v1.60 adds `expect.configure({ timeout, soft })`, which returns a pre-configured `expect` instance with custom defaults applied only to assertions made through that instance — without changing the global assertion timeout for the entire test. Previously, overriding timeout for a single slow assertion required either `expect(locator).toBeVisible({ timeout: 30_000 })` (verbose, repeated for every assertion) or `page.setDefaultTimeout(30_000)` (global, risks masking other timeouts). `expect.configure()` enables named assertion presets that express intent clearly: `slowExpect` for operations expected to take up to 30 seconds, `immediateExpect` for operations that should complete within 500ms.

```typescript
// tests/e2e/report-generation.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// Named expect presets — scoped to this test file
const slowExpect = expect.configure({ timeout: 30_000 });
const immediateExpect = expect.configure({ timeout: 500 });
const softExpect = expect.configure({ soft: true, timeout: 5_000 });

test('report generation completes and shows download link', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/reports/generate');

  await page.getByRole('combobox', { name: 'Report type' }).selectOption('quarterly-summary');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Generate report' }).click();

  // Fast assertion: the loading indicator should appear immediately
  await immediateExpect(page.getByRole('progressbar')).toBeVisible();

  // Slow assertion: report generation may take up to 30s
  await slowExpect(page.getByRole('link', { name: /Download .* report/ })).toBeVisible();

  // Soft assertions for non-critical UI details — test continues on failure
  await softExpect(page.getByText('Generated at')).toBeVisible();
  await softExpect(page.getByText(/\d+ rows/)).toBeVisible();
  await softExpect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Share report' })).toBeEnabled();

  // Hard assertion: the download link must have the correct file extension
  const downloadLink = page.getByRole('link', { name: /Download .* report/ });
  await expect(downloadLink).toHaveAttribute('href', expect.stringMatching(/\.pdf$/));
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `expect.configure()` creates a new `expect` function object with pre-applied defaults — it does not register globally or affect assertions made through the default `expect` import. In tests that mix the pre-configured instance with the default `expect`, it is easy to accidentally use the wrong instance, applying a 500ms timeout to an assertion that requires 30 seconds. A linting rule (`no-restricted-imports` or a custom ESLint plugin) can enforce that specific assertion variable names are always used for specific operation types. Additionally, `soft: true` in a configured instance applies to all assertions made through that instance — if the test shares a `softExpect` instance across test files (e.g., via a fixture), a soft failure accumulates across the entire fixture lifecycle, not just the current test's soft assertion scope. [official]

---

#### Pattern 216 — Subcutaneous Testing: Service-Layer E2E Without Browser Overhead [community]

The subcutaneous test pattern — coined by Martin Fowler — places tests just below the UI layer, exercising the application through its service or API boundary rather than through a rendered browser interface. For web applications, subcutaneous tests call the HTTP API layer (or the service layer directly in a test harness) and assert on structured responses rather than visual output. This occupies the upper-middle zone of the test pyramid: broader than narrow integration tests (they exercise the full request/response pipeline including middleware, auth, and serialization) but far faster and more reliable than browser-based E2E tests. Subcutaneous tests are the natural home for critical user workflow validation that does not require visual assertion.

```typescript
// tests/subcutaneous/checkout-workflow.test.ts
import { describe, test, expect, beforeAll, afterAll } from 'vitest';
import { buildApp } from '../../src/app.js';
import type { FastifyInstance } from 'fastify';
import { createTestUser, createTestProduct, cleanupTestData } from '../support/fixtures.js';

describe('Checkout workflow (subcutaneous)', () => {
  let app: FastifyInstance;
  let authToken: string;

  beforeAll(async () => {
    app = await buildApp({ env: 'test' });
    await app.ready();
    const user = await createTestUser({ role: 'customer' });
    const loginRes = await app.inject({
      method: 'POST',
      url: '/api/auth/login',
      payload: { email: user.email, password: 'test-password-123' },
    });
    authToken = loginRes.json<{ token: string }>().token;
  });

  afterAll(async () => {
    await cleanupTestData();
    await app.close();
  });

  test('completes purchase end-to-end through API', async () => {
    const product = await createTestProduct({ price: 49_99, stock: 10 });

    // Add to cart
    const cartRes = await app.inject({
      method: 'POST',
      url: '/api/cart/items',
      headers: { authorization: `Bearer ${authToken}` },
      payload: { productId: product.id, quantity: 2 },
    });
    expect(cartRes.statusCode).toBe(201);

    // Checkout
    const orderRes = await app.inject({
      method: 'POST',
      url: '/api/orders',
      headers: { authorization: `Bearer ${authToken}` },
      payload: { cartId: cartRes.json().cartId, paymentMethodId: 'pm_test_visa' },
    });
    expect(orderRes.statusCode).toBe(201);
    expect(orderRes.json()).toMatchObject({
      status: 'confirmed',
      total: 99_98,
      items: [{ productId: product.id, quantity: 2 }],
    });
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Subcutaneous tests validate application logic and API contracts but cannot detect UI regressions — a broken checkout button, a missing form field, or a CSS layout that renders a form unclickable will all pass subcutaneous tests cleanly. The correct pairing is: subcutaneous tests for business logic and workflow coverage, plus a small number of Playwright tests for critical UI interaction paths (form submission, navigation) and visual regression snapshots. Teams that replace all Playwright tests with subcutaneous tests discover this gap the hard way when a UI deployment breaks visual components without touching API behavior. [community]

---

#### Pattern 217 — Property-Based Testing with `fast-check` for Boundary Condition Discovery [community]

Property-based testing generates hundreds of randomized inputs matching a specification and asserts that a property (a logical invariant) holds for all of them. Unlike example-based testing where the developer selects specific inputs, property-based testing explores the input space automatically and reports the minimal failing case (the "shrunk" input) when a property violation is found. `fast-check` is the dominant property-based testing library for TypeScript, integrating with Vitest and Jest via `fc.assert()`. Properties are particularly valuable for encoding edge cases that developers systematically overlook: off-by-one errors at integer boundaries, Unicode normalization in string processing, floating-point precision in price calculations, and ordering invariants in sort functions.

```typescript
// src/utils/price-calculator.test.ts
import { describe, test, expect } from 'vitest';
import * as fc from 'fast-check';
import { calculateDiscountedPrice } from './price-calculator.js';

describe('calculateDiscountedPrice — property-based', () => {
  test('discounted price is always non-negative', () => {
    fc.assert(
      fc.property(
        fc.integer({ min: 0, max: 1_000_000 }), // price in cents
        fc.float({ min: 0, max: 1, noNaN: true }),  // discount rate 0-100%
        (priceInCents, discountRate) => {
          const result = calculateDiscountedPrice(priceInCents, discountRate);
          expect(result).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(0);
        }
      ),
      { numRuns: 1000 }
    );
  });

  test('applying 0% discount returns original price', () => {
    fc.assert(
      fc.property(
        fc.integer({ min: 0, max: 1_000_000 }),
        (priceInCents) => {
          expect(calculateDiscountedPrice(priceInCents, 0)).toBe(priceInCents);
        }
      )
    );
  });

  test('applying 100% discount returns zero', () => {
    fc.assert(
      fc.property(
        fc.integer({ min: 0, max: 1_000_000 }),
        (priceInCents) => {
          expect(calculateDiscountedPrice(priceInCents, 1)).toBe(0);
        }
      )
    );
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Property-based tests are excellent for discovering input boundary failures but require careful property formulation — a vague property (e.g., "result is a number") passes trivially and provides no value. The most common mistake is writing oracle properties that require the developer to re-implement the function under test in the test itself (asserting `result === refImpl(input)`) — this merely ensures the implementation and reference behave identically without validating whether either is correct. Focus properties on invariants that are easy to specify but hard to violate: non-negativity, idempotence, commutativity, symmetry, and range constraints. Property-based tests complement, rather than replace, example-based tests — use them together. [community]

---

#### Pattern 218 — Mutation Testing with StrykerJS for Validating Test Suite Effectiveness [community]

Mutation testing measures whether your tests can detect intentional code defects. StrykerJS systematically introduces small mutations (e.g., `>` to `>=`, `+` to `-`, `true` to `false`, removing a function body) into the source code and runs the test suite against each mutant. A mutant that makes a test fail is "killed" — the tests detect the defect. A mutant that causes no test failure "survives" — indicating a gap in test coverage even if line coverage is 100%. The mutation score (killed / total mutants) is a more meaningful quality signal than code coverage because it measures behavioral coverage rather than execution coverage.

```typescript
// stryker.config.mjs — StrykerJS configuration for a TypeScript project
/** @type {import('@stryker-mutator/api/core').PartialStrykerOptions} */
export default {
  packageManager: 'npm',
  reporters: ['html', 'clear-text', 'progress', 'dashboard'],
  testRunner: 'vitest',
  // Only mutate source files, not tests or generated code
  mutate: ['src/**/*.ts', '!src/**/*.test.ts', '!src/**/*.spec.ts', '!src/generated/**'],
  vitest: {
    configFile: 'vitest.config.ts',
  },
  // Incremental mode: only re-run mutants affected by changed source files
  incremental: true,
  incrementalFile: '.stryker-tmp/incremental.json',
  // Threshold: fail CI if mutation score drops below 75%
  thresholds: {
    high: 90,
    low: 75,
    break: 70,
  },
  // Limit parallel mutant runners to avoid port conflicts in integration tests
  concurrency: 4,
  timeoutMS: 30_000,
};
```

**Tradeoff:** Mutation testing is computationally expensive: for N mutants and a test suite with runtime T, the total mutation testing time approaches N x T. A TypeScript project with 500 source lines might generate 2,000 mutants; if the unit test suite runs in 10 seconds, the full mutation run takes approximately 5 hours. Incremental mode (enabled above) dramatically reduces this by only re-evaluating mutants in files changed since the last run. Reserve full mutation testing for pre-release quality gates rather than per-commit CI; run incremental mutation testing on changed files in PR pipelines. A pragmatic adoption strategy: start with a `break: 50` threshold to baseline the mutation score without failing CI, then progressively raise the threshold as the team improves test quality. [community]

---

#### Pattern 219 — Consumer-Driven Contract Testing with Pact for Independent Service Deployment [community]

Consumer-Driven Contracts (CDC) testing, implemented with Pact, allows the consumer team to encode its API expectations as an executable contract, which the provider team verifies independently without running the consumer application. In a microservices architecture, this eliminates the need for full integration environment deployments to verify that a provider change does not break a consumer. The consumer writes a Pact test that records interactions (request/expected-response pairs) to a pact file; the provider runs the pact file against its implementation to verify all interactions. The Pact Broker centrally publishes and version-controls pact files, enabling the "can I deploy?" query: the CI pipeline checks whether the current consumer version's pact is satisfied by the current provider version before allowing deployment.

```typescript
// consumer/src/api-client.pact.test.ts — consumer side
import { PactV3, MatchersV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
import { describe, test, expect, beforeAll, afterAll } from 'vitest';
import { UserApiClient } from './user-api-client.js';

const { like, string, integer } = MatchersV3;

const provider = new PactV3({
  consumer: 'UserDashboard',
  provider: 'UserService',
  dir: './pacts',
  logLevel: 'warn',
});

describe('UserApiClient — Pact consumer contract', () => {
  test('returns user profile for valid user ID', async () => {
    await provider
      .given('user with ID user-123 exists')
      .uponReceiving('a GET request for user profile user-123')
      .withRequest({ method: 'GET', path: '/users/user-123' })
      .willRespondWith({
        status: 200,
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
        body: {
          id: string('user-123'),
          name: string('Alice'),
          email: string('alice@example.com'),
          role: string('admin'),
          createdAt: string('2025-01-15T10:00:00Z'),
          loginCount: integer(42),
        },
      })
      .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
        const client = new UserApiClient({ baseUrl: mockServer.url });
        const profile = await client.getUser('user-123');

        expect(profile.id).toBe('user-123');
        expect(profile.name).toBe('Alice');
        expect(profile.role).toBe('admin');
      });
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Pact CDC tests require both the consumer and provider teams to adopt the Pact workflow and maintain a Pact Broker instance (or use PactFlow). The setup overhead is significant — teams that deploy fewer than 3–4 service versions per week are unlikely to recoup the investment in reduced integration environment failures. The primary value of CDC emerges in organizations with multiple consumer teams per provider: a provider team can confidently refactor its API when the Pact Broker shows that all registered consumers' contracts are satisfied by the new implementation, without coordinating with each consumer team individually. For single-consumer, single-provider relationships, the simpler approach is a shared integration test suite with a contract-test annotation convention. [community]

---

#### Pattern 220 — Test Data Builders with the Fluent Interface Pattern for Maintainable Test Fixtures [community]

The Test Data Builder pattern provides a fluent interface for constructing domain objects used in tests, with sensible defaults for all fields and `with*` methods for overriding specific fields. This approach separates two concerns that become tangled in inline test fixtures: declaring the shape of valid domain objects (handled by the builder's defaults) and specifying which fields are relevant to a particular test scenario (handled by `with*` method calls). A test that only cares about a user's role can call `userBuilder().withRole('admin').build()` without specifying email, password, name, or any other field — the builder provides valid defaults. When the domain model evolves (e.g., a required `tenantId` field is added), only the builder needs updating, not every test that constructs a user.

```typescript
// tests/support/builders/user.builder.ts
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';
import type { User, UserRole } from '../../../src/domain/user.js';

interface UserOverrides {
  id?: string;
  email?: string;
  name?: string;
  role?: UserRole;
  tenantId?: string;
  emailVerified?: boolean;
  createdAt?: Date;
}

class UserBuilder {
  private overrides: UserOverrides = {};

  withId(id: string): this { this.overrides.id = id; return this; }
  withEmail(email: string): this { this.overrides.email = email; return this; }
  withName(name: string): this { this.overrides.name = name; return this; }
  withRole(role: UserRole): this { this.overrides.role = role; return this; }
  withTenantId(tenantId: string): this { this.overrides.tenantId = tenantId; return this; }
  withEmailVerified(verified: boolean): this { this.overrides.emailVerified = verified; return this; }
  withCreatedAt(date: Date): this { this.overrides.createdAt = date; return this; }

  build(): User {
    const id = this.overrides.id ?? `user-${randomUUID()}`;
    return {
      id,
      email: this.overrides.email ?? `test-${id}@example.com`,
      name: this.overrides.name ?? 'Test User',
      role: this.overrides.role ?? 'viewer',
      tenantId: this.overrides.tenantId ?? 'tenant-default',
      emailVerified: this.overrides.emailVerified ?? true,
      createdAt: this.overrides.createdAt ?? new Date('2025-01-01T00:00:00Z'),
    };
  }
}

export const userBuilder = () => new UserBuilder();

// Usage in tests:
// const adminUser = userBuilder().withRole('admin').build();
// const unverifiedUser = userBuilder().withEmailVerified(false).build();
// const tenantUser = userBuilder().withTenantId('tenant-acme').withRole('member').build();
```

**Tradeoff:** Test Data Builders require upfront investment to write and ongoing maintenance as the domain model evolves. In small, stable codebases, inline object literals with spread overrides (`{ ...defaultUser, role: 'admin' }`) achieve the same goal with less ceremony. The builder pattern pays off at scale: when domain objects have 15+ fields, when multiple teams share builders, and when domain objects have invariants that cannot be expressed as plain object literals (e.g., a `User` whose `passwordHash` must be derived from a `password` field). Avoid over-engineering builders for simple value objects; reserve the pattern for aggregate roots and entities with complex construction invariants. [community]

### Real-World Gotchas (Cycle 43)

166. **Playwright v1.57 `webServer.wait` regex silently falls back to URL polling if the `reuseExistingServer: true` condition is met and an existing server is already running — meaning the regex is never evaluated when a server is reused** [community] — WHY: When `reuseExistingServer` is `true` and Playwright detects that the configured port is already accepting connections, it skips the server startup sequence entirely (including the `wait` regex evaluation) and proceeds immediately to test execution. If the existing server is mid-initialization (e.g., a previous test run left a half-started server that accepts TCP connections but has not finished loading routes), tests begin against an incompletely initialized server without triggering the regex guard. This failure mode is indistinguishable from a healthy reused server. Fix: in CI, always set `reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI` to disable reuse, ensuring the `wait` regex is always evaluated in automated runs. In development, add an explicit `/health` endpoint check after the `wait` regex fires to confirm full initialization before tests begin. [community: Playwright GitHub discussions — reuseExistingServer interaction with webServer.wait regex]

167. **Vitest `aroundAll` generator is not re-entered if a test file is re-run via `--reporter=verbose --rerun-on-failure=3` — the second and third run attempts execute tests against an already-torn-down resource from the first run's `aroundAll` `finally` block** [community] — WHY: Vitest's file-level retry mechanism (`rerunFailedTests`/`--rerun-on-failure`) re-runs the entire test file when any test fails. The `aroundAll` generator is designed as a suite-level lifecycle hook — it is executed once when the describe block is entered and torn down when the describe block exits. On a file re-run triggered by retry, the describe block is re-entered, but if the first run's `finally` block already closed the database connection or stopped the test server, the second run's `aroundAll` setup receives an already-closed resource. Fix: use `beforeAll`/`afterAll` pairs for resources that must survive across file retries, and reserve `aroundAll` for non-retriable contexts where the guarantee that `finally` always runs is the priority over reusability across retries. [community: Vitest GitHub issues — aroundAll interaction with file-level retry]

168. **StrykerJS incremental mode regenerates the full mutant corpus when the source file's AST changes — including changes to comments, whitespace, or type annotations — because the incremental cache key is the file's content hash, not a semantic hash of the code's behavior** [community] — WHY: StrykerJS incremental mode stores a mapping of `{ fileHash → [mutantResults] }`. Any change to the file — including adding a comment, reformatting whitespace, or updating a JSDoc annotation — produces a new content hash, invalidating the entire cached mutation result set for that file. A developer who reformats a 500-line file with Prettier will trigger a full re-mutation of all mutants in that file on the next run, adding minutes to the pipeline even though no behavioral change occurred. Fix: configure Prettier (or Biome) to run as a pre-commit hook so files are always committed in formatted form — incremental caches stay valid between commits because reformatting does not happen mid-development. Alternatively, switch to `eslint --fix` + `tsc` as the mutation cache key when StrykerJS adds semantic hashing support in future versions. [community: StrykerJS GitHub issues — incremental cache invalidation on non-behavioral changes]

169. **`fast-check` property tests that use `fc.date()` arbitraries without bounding the range produce timestamps in years 0001–9999, causing failures in application code that uses `toLocaleDateString()` with locale-sensitive formatting for dates outside the Unix epoch range** [community] — WHY: `fc.date()` without `{ min, max }` constraints generates `Date` objects across the full valid JavaScript date range: from approximately 100,000,000 days before the Unix epoch to 100,000,000 days after, which includes dates in years well outside the supported range of many locale-aware date formatting APIs. `Intl.DateTimeFormat` implementations in Node.js and browsers often throw `RangeError` for dates before year 100 CE, and some throw for dates after year 9999. A property test that calls `formatDate(fc.date())` will produce intermittent `RangeError` failures on roughly 0.01% of generated samples — rare enough to be missed in development but occurring regularly in CI with `numRuns: 1000`. Fix: always bound `fc.date()` to a realistic application range, e.g., `fc.date({ min: new Date('1970-01-01'), max: new Date('2099-12-31') })`, and add a comment explaining the constraint's rationale. [community: fast-check GitHub issues — fc.date() locale formatting edge cases]

170. **Test Data Builders with `randomUUID()`-based default IDs cause snapshot tests to fail on every run because the default ID changes between runs, making the snapshot file meaningless as a regression signal** [community] — WHY: Builders that generate unique IDs by default (a good practice for avoiding test pollution in a live database) produce different object hashes on each run. When a test that builds a default user passes the result to `expect(user).toMatchSnapshot()`, the snapshot captures the randomly generated `id` field. The next test run generates a new UUID, the snapshot comparison fails, and the developer runs `--update-snapshots` — silently destroying the snapshot's ability to catch actual regressions. The builder's randomness and snapshot testing's determinism requirement are fundamentally incompatible without explicit coordination. Fix: never use builders with random default IDs in snapshot tests — either call `userBuilder().withId('fixed-id-for-snapshot').build()` explicitly, or use a deterministic ID generator seeded by the test name (`createHash('sha1').update(expect.getState().currentTestName!).digest('hex').slice(0, 8)`). [community: Testing Library GitHub discussions — random test data builder IDs in snapshot tests]
