## Cycle 44 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns 221–235

#### Pattern 221 — Vitest `pool: 'vmForks'` for True Process Isolation in Integration Tests [official]

Vitest's default `pool: 'threads'` runs tests in worker threads that share the same Node.js process heap, making full module-level state isolation impossible even with `isolate: true`. The `pool: 'vmForks'` option spawns a fresh Node.js child process per test file, providing the same isolation guarantee as running `node test-file.ts` independently for each file. This matters most for integration tests that import modules with singleton instances — database connection pools, in-memory caches, EventEmitter registries, and HTTP server handles — where worker-thread isolation still allows the module registry to bleed across test files within the same worker. `vmForks` incurs higher per-file startup overhead (typically 200–800 ms per file) but eliminates an entire class of hard-to-diagnose cross-file state contamination.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — separate pools by test type
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    projects: [
      {
        // Unit tests: fast thread pool (no singletons, pure functions)
        name: 'unit',
        include: ['src/**/*.test.ts'],
        pool: 'threads',
        poolOptions: {
          threads: { singleThread: false },
        },
      },
      {
        // Integration tests: process-isolated forks (singletons, real I/O)
        name: 'integration',
        include: ['tests/integration/**/*.test.ts'],
        pool: 'vmForks',
        poolOptions: {
          vmForks: {
            // Limit concurrency to avoid port collisions and DB connection exhaustion
            maxForks: 4,
            // Reuse fork for multiple test files only when explicitly safe
            singleFork: false,
          },
        },
        // Allow more time for process startup + real I/O
        testTimeout: 30_000,
        hookTimeout: 20_000,
      },
    ],
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `vmForks` trades parallelism for correctness. With 80 integration test files and a 400 ms fork startup cost, the minimum test-suite overhead is 32 seconds of process-spawn time before any test logic runs. Setting `maxForks: 4` with `singleFork: false` allows Vitest to reuse forks across files within the same worker, recovering some throughput at the cost of weaker isolation guarantees for files sharing a fork. Choose `singleFork: true` (strictest isolation, slowest) when diagnosing contamination; switch to `singleFork: false` (faster, still much stronger than threads) for routine CI runs once the suite is clean. Never use `vmForks` for pure-unit test suites — the overhead is unjustified when tests have no side-effecting singletons. [official]

---

#### Pattern 222 — Playwright `locator.describe()` for Semantic Test Failure Messages [official]

Playwright v1.53 introduced `locator.describe(label)`, which attaches a human-readable description to any locator. When a test assertion fails, Playwright surfaces the `describe` label in the failure message instead of the raw CSS selector or ARIA query, reducing the time spent decoding `locator('div > ul > li:nth-child(3) > button[data-action="submit"]')` in a failure report. The label propagates to screenshots, trace viewer nodes, and test reports, providing a consistent semantic name for the element across all debugging surfaces. This is especially valuable in page object models where a single locator is used across many tests — the `describe` label serves as the element's "display name" in the entire test runtime.

```typescript
// tests/support/page-objects/checkout.page.ts
import { type Page, type Locator } from '@playwright/test';

export class CheckoutPage {
  readonly placeOrderButton: Locator;
  readonly orderSummaryTotal: Locator;
  readonly promoCodeInput: Locator;
  readonly applyPromoButton: Locator;
  readonly promoErrorMessage: Locator;

  constructor(page: Page) {
    this.placeOrderButton = page
      .getByRole('button', { name: /place order/i })
      .describe('Place Order CTA button');

    this.orderSummaryTotal = page
      .getByTestId('order-summary-total')
      .describe('Order summary total price');

    this.promoCodeInput = page
      .getByLabel('Promo code')
      .describe('Promotional code input field');

    this.applyPromoButton = page
      .getByRole('button', { name: /apply/i })
      .describe('Apply promo code button');

    this.promoErrorMessage = page
      .getByRole('alert')
      .filter({ hasText: /invalid.*code/i })
      .describe('Promo code validation error alert');
  }

  async applyPromoCode(code: string): Promise<void> {
    await this.promoCodeInput.fill(code);
    await this.applyPromoButton.click();
  }
}

// In a test: failure message will read
// "Expect: locator('Place Order CTA button').toBeEnabled()"
// instead of
// "Expect: locator('button[role=button]').nth(2).toBeEnabled()"
```

**Tradeoff:** `locator.describe()` labels are static strings — they cannot be parameterized at the point of assertion without wrapping the locator in a factory function. A locator shared across 30 tests all shows the same label in failure messages, which is helpful for identification but makes it harder to distinguish "which specific invocation failed" in a parameterized test loop. In those cases, include the dynamic context in the `test.step()` or `test.info().annotations` rather than the locator's `describe` label, which should describe the element's role, not the test scenario. [official]

---

#### Pattern 223 — Vitest `expect.poll()` for Async State Convergence Assertions [official]

Vitest's `expect.poll(fn, options)` polls a value-returning function until the assertion passes or the timeout expires, retrying the expect check on each poll interval. This is the unit-testing equivalent of Playwright's auto-retrying `toBeVisible()` assertion and eliminates the `waitFor(() => expect(value).toBe(x))` boilerplate pattern that was common in prior Vitest versions. `expect.poll()` is appropriate for unit and integration tests that drive async side effects through a synchronous interface — for example, verifying that a message broker consumer processed a message, that a debounced state update settled, or that an in-memory cache was invalidated after a write. The polling function is re-evaluated on each retry, ensuring fresh reads of the value under observation.

```typescript
// tests/unit/event-bus.test.ts
import { describe, test, expect, vi } from 'vitest';
import { EventBus } from '../../src/event-bus.js';

describe('EventBus', () => {
  test('delivers published event to all subscribers within 100 ms', async () => {
    const bus = new EventBus();
    const receivedEvents: string[] = [];

    bus.subscribe('order.created', (event) => {
      receivedEvents.push(event.orderId);
    });

    // Publish fires async listener queue internally (setTimeout-based)
    bus.publish('order.created', { orderId: 'ord-001' });
    bus.publish('order.created', { orderId: 'ord-002' });

    // expect.poll retries until both events arrive or 500 ms elapses
    await expect.poll(() => receivedEvents, { timeout: 500, interval: 20 })
      .toEqual(['ord-001', 'ord-002']);
  });

  test('does not deliver to unsubscribed handlers', async () => {
    const bus = new EventBus();
    const handler = vi.fn();
    const unsubscribe = bus.subscribe('user.updated', handler);
    unsubscribe(); // remove handler before publish

    bus.publish('user.updated', { userId: 'u-1' });

    // Poll: confirm the handler remains uncalled after a brief settle window
    await expect.poll(() => handler.mock.calls.length, { timeout: 200 })
      .toBe(0);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `expect.poll()` masks timing issues rather than eliminating them — a test that passes via polling may be covering a race condition in the application code that should instead be fixed at the implementation level (e.g., by surfacing a Promise that callers can await rather than relying on observers to converge). Reserve `expect.poll()` for cases where the async convergence is an intentional design (event delivery, debouncing, cache invalidation windows) rather than a workaround for missing await points. Set `interval` as low as practical (10–50 ms) and `timeout` as tight as the acceptance criterion requires — wide timeouts produce a slow test suite and mask regressions where convergence slows down but still eventually passes. [official]

---

#### Pattern 224 — Storybook Play Functions for Component-Level Interaction Tests [community]

Storybook `play` functions run interaction sequences inside a rendered story, enabling component-level tests that verify stateful UI behavior — form validation, multi-step wizard progression, keyboard navigation — without the overhead of a full Playwright E2E session. Stories with `play` functions execute in the browser using `@storybook/test` utilities (which re-export `@testing-library/user-event` and `expect` from Vitest under the hood), and the same story can be imported into a Vitest browser mode test suite for CI coverage reporting. This positions stories as portable interaction specifications: they document expected behavior visually in Storybook and execute as regression tests in CI with no duplication of test logic.

```typescript
// src/components/LoginForm/LoginForm.stories.ts
import type { Meta, StoryObj } from '@storybook/react';
import { expect, userEvent, within, fn } from '@storybook/test';
import { LoginForm } from './LoginForm.js';

const meta = {
  title: 'Auth/LoginForm',
  component: LoginForm,
  args: {
    onSubmit: fn(),
  },
} satisfies Meta<typeof LoginForm>;

export default meta;
type Story = StoryObj<typeof meta>;

export const SuccessfulLogin: Story = {
  play: async ({ canvasElement, args }) => {
    const canvas = within(canvasElement);

    await userEvent.type(canvas.getByLabelText('Email'), 'user@example.com');
    await userEvent.type(canvas.getByLabelText('Password'), 's3cr3t');
    await userEvent.click(canvas.getByRole('button', { name: /sign in/i }));

    await expect(args.onSubmit).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
    await expect(args.onSubmit).toHaveBeenCalledWith({
      email: 'user@example.com',
      password: 's3cr3t',
    });
  },
};

export const ValidationErrors: Story = {
  play: async ({ canvasElement }) => {
    const canvas = within(canvasElement);

    // Submit without filling any fields
    await userEvent.click(canvas.getByRole('button', { name: /sign in/i }));

    await expect(
      canvas.getByRole('alert', { name: /email is required/i })
    ).toBeVisible();
    await expect(
      canvas.getByRole('alert', { name: /password is required/i })
    ).toBeVisible();
  },
};
```

**Tradeoff:** Storybook play functions run in a real browser, which provides high UI fidelity but requires Storybook to be built or running during CI. The `@storybook/test-runner` can execute play functions headlessly via Playwright, but adding Storybook build time (often 60–120 seconds for a mid-sized component library) to the CI pipeline is a significant cost. The payoff is that play functions serve double duty as documentation and regression tests without maintaining separate test files. Teams that already run Storybook in CI (e.g., for visual regression snapshots) get component interaction tests at near-zero additional cost; teams that do not run Storybook in CI must weigh the CI cost against the value of collocated documentation and tests. [community]

---

#### Pattern 225 — Type-Safe Test Doubles with `vi.fn<FunctionSignature>()` and `satisfies` for Interface Mocks [official]

Vitest's `vi.fn<T>()` generic overload accepts a function type parameter and produces a mock whose `mockReturnValue`, `mockResolvedValue`, and `mockImplementation` arguments are type-checked against the original function signature. Combined with TypeScript's `satisfies` operator, this enables construction of complete, type-safe mock objects for complex interfaces without requiring a mocking library like `ts-mockito` or manual type assertions. When the real interface evolves — a new method is added or a parameter type changes — TypeScript surfaces the gap in the mock at compile time rather than at test runtime, preventing the common failure mode where a test mock silently falls out of sync with the production interface.

```typescript
// tests/unit/order-processor.test.ts
import { describe, test, expect, vi, beforeEach } from 'vitest';
import type { PaymentGateway } from '../../src/ports/payment-gateway.js';
import type { InventoryService } from '../../src/ports/inventory-service.js';
import { OrderProcessor } from '../../src/order-processor.js';

// Create a fully-typed mock that satisfies the PaymentGateway interface
function createPaymentGatewayMock() {
  return {
    charge: vi.fn<PaymentGateway['charge']>(),
    refund: vi.fn<PaymentGateway['refund']>(),
    getTransaction: vi.fn<PaymentGateway['getTransaction']>(),
  } satisfies PaymentGateway;
}

function createInventoryMock() {
  return {
    reserve: vi.fn<InventoryService['reserve']>(),
    release: vi.fn<InventoryService['release']>(),
    getAvailableQuantity: vi.fn<InventoryService['getAvailableQuantity']>(),
  } satisfies InventoryService;
}

describe('OrderProcessor', () => {
  let gateway: ReturnType<typeof createPaymentGatewayMock>;
  let inventory: ReturnType<typeof createInventoryMock>;
  let processor: OrderProcessor;

  beforeEach(() => {
    gateway = createPaymentGatewayMock();
    inventory = createInventoryMock();
    processor = new OrderProcessor({ gateway, inventory });
  });

  test('charges payment and reserves inventory on successful order', async () => {
    inventory.getAvailableQuantity.mockResolvedValue(10);
    inventory.reserve.mockResolvedValue({ reservationId: 'res-001' });
    gateway.charge.mockResolvedValue({ transactionId: 'txn-001', status: 'success' });

    const result = await processor.processOrder({ productId: 'p-1', quantity: 2, amountCents: 4000 });

    expect(result.status).toBe('confirmed');
    expect(gateway.charge).toHaveBeenCalledWith({ amountCents: 4000, idempotencyKey: expect.any(String) });
    expect(inventory.reserve).toHaveBeenCalledWith({ productId: 'p-1', quantity: 2 });
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** The `satisfies` operator enforces that the mock object structurally matches the interface at construction time, but it does not prevent individual `vi.fn()` instances from having their call signatures widen over time through TypeScript's structural compatibility rules. If `PaymentGateway['charge']` changes its return type from `Promise<ChargeResult>` to `Promise<ChargeResult | null>`, the mock's `mockResolvedValue(null)` call becomes valid even if the test does not account for null returns. The safeguard is to run `tsc --noEmit` in CI as a separate step — compilation errors in test files catch these type drift scenarios. Avoid the temptation to cast mock objects with `as PaymentGateway` instead of using `satisfies`, since `as` suppresses all structural checks. [official]

---

#### Pattern 226 — Playwright `page.routeFromHAR()` for Deterministic API Response Replay [official]

Playwright's `page.routeFromHAR(harFile, options)` replays recorded HTTP Archive (HAR) responses in place of live network calls, turning an E2E test into a deterministic unit of behavior that depends only on the application's frontend logic and the recorded server responses. Unlike `page.route()` with static mocks, HAR files capture real responses at the HTTP level — headers, status codes, response bodies, cookies — and replay them with accurate content-type negotiation. This allows teams to record a golden HAR file from a staging environment once and use it as the test fixture indefinitely, without maintaining hand-written mock response objects. HAR replay also captures multi-request sequences (redirect chains, asset loading, GraphQL batching) that are tedious to reproduce with individual `page.route()` stubs.

```typescript
// tests/e2e/product-catalog.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'node:path';

const HAR_DIR = path.join(import.meta.dirname, '../fixtures/har');

test.describe('Product catalog — offline HAR replay', () => {
  test.use({
    // Each test in this describe block uses HAR replay for all API calls
    serviceWorkers: 'block', // Prevent SW cache from interfering
  });

  test('displays products from category listing API', async ({ page }) => {
    // Replay all requests matching /api/* from the recorded HAR
    await page.routeFromHAR(`${HAR_DIR}/product-catalog.har`, {
      url: /\/api\//,
      // On miss: fall through to the network (useful during HAR update cycle)
      fallback: 'abort',
      // Match requests by URL + method, ignore dynamic headers
      update: false,
    });

    await page.goto('/products?category=electronics');

    await expect(page.getByRole('list', { name: 'Product results' }))
      .toBeVisible();
    const items = page.getByRole('listitem');
    await expect(items).toHaveCount(12);
    await expect(items.first()).toContainText('Laptop Pro 15');
  });

  test('shows empty state when category returns no results', async ({ page }) => {
    // Use a different HAR fixture for the empty-state scenario
    await page.routeFromHAR(`${HAR_DIR}/product-catalog-empty.har`, {
      url: /\/api\//,
      fallback: 'abort',
      update: false,
    });

    await page.goto('/products?category=discontinued');

    await expect(page.getByText('No products found')).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** HAR files are static snapshots — they become stale as the API evolves and require manual regeneration after breaking server changes. The `update: true` option regenerates the HAR file automatically on the next test run against a live server (useful for scheduled HAR refresh jobs in CI), but this means the test must be run against a real server at least once per API schema version, which partially defeats the offline isolation goal. HAR files can also grow very large for pages that load many assets; use `url` pattern matching to capture only API calls and let static assets load from the development server (or block them with `update: false` + `fallback: 'abort'`). Commit HAR files to version control using Git LFS for large files. [official]

---

#### Pattern 227 — Testing Observability: Asserting on Structured Log Output in Unit Tests [community]

Application observability — structured logs, metrics emissions, span creation — is rarely tested, creating a class of silent regressions where a code change removes a critical log statement (e.g., a PCI audit log or a performance metric) without any failing test. The pattern is to inject a logger interface into components under test, provide a spy implementation that captures log calls, and assert on the captured log entries in tests covering business-critical code paths. This treats observability output as a first-class behavioral contract rather than a side effect. The spy logger implements the same interface as the production logger (`pino`, `winston`, structured logger), so tests and production use the same injection point without any special-casing.

```typescript
// tests/support/spy-logger.ts
import type { Logger } from '../../src/ports/logger.js';

export interface LogEntry {
  level: 'debug' | 'info' | 'warn' | 'error';
  message: string;
  data?: Record<string, unknown>;
}

export function createSpyLogger(): Logger & { entries: LogEntry[] } {
  const entries: LogEntry[] = [];

  const log = (level: LogEntry['level']) =>
    (message: string, data?: Record<string, unknown>) => {
      entries.push({ level, message, ...(data ? { data } : {}) });
    };

  return {
    entries,
    debug: log('debug'),
    info: log('info'),
    warn: log('warn'),
    error: log('error'),
  };
}

// tests/unit/payment-service.test.ts
import { describe, test, expect, beforeEach } from 'vitest';
import { createSpyLogger } from '../support/spy-logger.js';
import { PaymentService } from '../../src/payment-service.js';

describe('PaymentService — observability contract', () => {
  let logger: ReturnType<typeof createSpyLogger>;
  let service: PaymentService;

  beforeEach(() => {
    logger = createSpyLogger();
    service = new PaymentService({ logger });
  });

  test('emits structured audit log on successful charge', async () => {
    await service.charge({ amountCents: 2000, userId: 'u-1', orderId: 'ord-1' });

    const auditEntry = logger.entries.find(
      (e) => e.level === 'info' && e.message === 'payment.charged'
    );
    expect(auditEntry).toBeDefined();
    expect(auditEntry?.data).toMatchObject({
      userId: 'u-1',
      orderId: 'ord-1',
      amountCents: 2000,
    });
    // PCI requirement: card number must NOT appear in audit logs
    expect(JSON.stringify(auditEntry?.data)).not.toContain('cardNumber');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Asserting on log messages creates a coupling between tests and the exact wording of log messages — a developer who refactors `'payment.charged'` to `'payment_charged'` will break the test without changing any behavior. The right granularity is to assert on structured data fields (the `data` object) rather than the message string when possible, and to treat message strings as a stable contract only for critical audit events where the exact log key is part of an external specification (e.g., a SIEM query or compliance requirement). Use a shared constant (`LOG_EVENTS.PAYMENT_CHARGED`) rather than inline string literals to give the compile-time refactoring safety that message-string assertions lack. [community]

---

#### Pattern 228 — Playwright `expect(page).toMatchAriaSnapshot()` for Accessible Structure Regression Testing [official]

Playwright v1.53's `expect(page).toMatchAriaSnapshot()` captures the ARIA tree of a page or element as a YAML snapshot and asserts that subsequent test runs produce the same accessible structure. Unlike visual pixel snapshots, ARIA snapshots are insensitive to styling and layout changes — only semantic changes (role changes, label text changes, removed elements) cause failures. This makes ARIA snapshots ideal as a lightweight regression guard for accessibility-critical components: a test that confirms the ARIA structure of a navigation menu, a data table, or a form dialog will catch regressions introduced by refactoring (e.g., replacing a `<button>` with a styled `<div>` that loses its role) without being fragile to CSS changes.

```typescript
// tests/e2e/navigation.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.describe('Main navigation — ARIA structure', () => {
  test('navigation menu has correct accessible structure', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/');
    const nav = page.getByRole('navigation', { name: 'Main menu' });

    // On first run, generates the snapshot YAML file automatically.
    // On subsequent runs, fails if the ARIA structure diverges.
    await expect(nav).toMatchAriaSnapshot(`
      - navigation "Main menu":
        - list:
          - listitem:
            - link "Home" [href=/]
          - listitem:
            - link "Products" [href=/products]
          - listitem:
            - link "About" [href=/about]
          - listitem:
            - link "Contact" [href=/contact]
    `);
  });

  test('user dropdown has correct ARIA roles when open', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'User menu' }).click();

    await expect(page.getByRole('menu')).toMatchAriaSnapshot(`
      - menu:
        - menuitem "Profile settings"
        - menuitem "Billing"
        - separator
        - menuitem "Sign out"
    `);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** ARIA snapshots reflect the DOM's ARIA tree, not the visual hierarchy — a page where elements are visually reordered via CSS `order` or absolute positioning may have an ARIA structure that does not match the visual order, and the ARIA snapshot test will not catch that accessibility issue. ARIA snapshots also do not validate focus management, keyboard navigation, or color contrast — they are a structural regression guard, not a comprehensive accessibility audit. Pair `toMatchAriaSnapshot()` with a dedicated accessibility tool (`axe-core` via `@axe-core/playwright`, or Storybook's A11y addon) to cover the behavioral and perceptual dimensions that structural snapshots cannot capture. [official]

---

#### Pattern 229 — Flakiness Quarantine with `test.fail()` and CI Retry Budgets [community]

Flaky tests — tests that pass and fail non-deterministically — erode CI reliability faster than failing tests because they produce alert fatigue (developers learn to ignore failures) and mask real regressions behind intermittent noise. The pragmatic response is a formal flakiness quarantine: mark suspected flaky tests with `test.fail()` (Vitest/Jest) or `test.fixme()` (Playwright), which inverts the expectation so the test passes when it fails and fails when it unexpectedly passes. This converts a flaky test from a CI blocker into a tracked obligation without removing the test. A companion CI retry budget (`--retries 2` in Playwright, `--retry 2` in Vitest) allows retry on failure but reports the retry count as a flakiness signal — a test that passes on retry 2 is still flagged in the CI report, enabling systematic quarantine decisions.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — retry budget for flaky test detection
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // Allow up to 2 retries; still reports flakiness in output
    retry: 2,
    reporters: [
      'verbose',
      // JSON reporter captures retry counts per test for dashboarding
      ['json', { outputFile: 'test-results/results.json' }],
    ],
  },
});

// tests/integration/external-api.test.ts — quarantine a known flaky test
import { describe, test, expect } from 'vitest';
import { fetchRateLimitedEndpoint } from '../../src/external-api-client.js';

describe('ExternalApiClient', () => {
  // Quarantine: this test is flaky due to rate-limit jitter in the test environment
  // Track: https://github.com/org/repo/issues/4821
  // Review date: 2026-06-01
  test.fail(
    'handles rate-limit retry transparently — FLAKY: tracked in #4821',
    async () => {
      const result = await fetchRateLimitedEndpoint('/data');
      expect(result.status).toBe(200);
    }
  );

  // The stable tests continue to run and block CI normally
  test('returns cached response within TTL without calling network', async () => {
    // ... stable test
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `test.fail()` quarantine is a temporary measure with a decay risk — quarantined tests accumulate over time if there is no process to review and fix them. A test marked `test.fail()` that is silently fixed by an unrelated refactor will begin unexpectedly passing, causing the `test.fail()` wrapper to fail CI — this "inverse flake" is disorienting for developers who did not write the original quarantine. Require quarantined tests to include a GitHub issue link and a review date in the annotation comment, and add a CI step that `grep`s for overdue quarantine annotations (`// Review date:` older than 30 days) to enforce the review cadence. Never use `test.skip()` for flaky tests — it removes them from the execution record entirely, which is worse than a quarantine annotation. [community]

---

#### Pattern 230 — Subcutaneous Testing for Service-Layer E2E Without Browser Overhead [community]

Subcutaneous tests (Martin Fowler's term) exercise the application immediately below its UI surface — directly invoking the HTTP API or service layer — while still executing the full application stack: routing, request validation, business logic, and persistence. This provides broad-coverage regression testing at a fraction of the cost of browser-based E2E tests: no browser startup, no DOM rendering, no CSS-dependent locators, no animation timing. In a Next.js or Express.js application, a subcutaneous test imports the HTTP handler and invokes it with a real HTTP request (using `supertest` or the WHATWG `fetch` API against a `http.createServer` instance), asserting on the HTTP response while the real database and real service implementations process the request.

```typescript
// tests/subcutaneous/checkout-flow.test.ts
import { describe, test, expect, beforeAll, afterAll } from 'vitest';
import { createApp } from '../../src/app.js';
import { createTestDatabase } from '../support/test-db.js';
import type { AddressedServer } from '../support/types.js';

describe('Checkout flow — subcutaneous', () => {
  let server: AddressedServer;
  let db: Awaited<ReturnType<typeof createTestDatabase>>;

  beforeAll(async () => {
    db = await createTestDatabase({ seed: 'checkout-flow' });
    const app = createApp({ db });
    server = await app.listen(0); // ephemeral port
  });

  afterAll(async () => {
    await server.close();
    await db.teardown();
  });

  test('completes checkout end-to-end: cart → payment → order confirmation', async () => {
    const baseUrl = `http://localhost:${server.port}`;

    // Step 1: Add item to cart
    const cartResponse = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/api/cart`, {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', Authorization: 'Bearer test-token-user-1' },
      body: JSON.stringify({ productId: 'prod-seeded-001', quantity: 2 }),
    });
    expect(cartResponse.status).toBe(201);
    const { cartId } = await cartResponse.json() as { cartId: string };

    // Step 2: Submit order
    const orderResponse = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/api/orders`, {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', Authorization: 'Bearer test-token-user-1' },
      body: JSON.stringify({ cartId, paymentMethodId: 'pm-test-visa' }),
    });
    expect(orderResponse.status).toBe(201);
    const { orderId, status } = await orderResponse.json() as { orderId: string; status: string };
    expect(status).toBe('confirmed');

    // Step 3: Verify order is retrievable
    const getOrderResponse = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/api/orders/${orderId}`, {
      headers: { Authorization: 'Bearer test-token-user-1' },
    });
    expect(getOrderResponse.status).toBe(200);
    const order = await getOrderResponse.json() as { id: string; itemCount: number };
    expect(order.itemCount).toBe(2);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Subcutaneous tests verify the application's HTTP contract but cannot detect UI regressions, client-side JavaScript errors, or accessibility issues. They are also blind to frontend-only bugs that occur in the browser's rendering engine but not in the server's response (e.g., a React hydration mismatch that produces a broken UI without changing the HTTP response body). Use subcutaneous tests to cover the dominant share of integration-style test scenarios — they are 5–20x faster than browser-based E2E tests for equivalent server-side coverage — and reserve full Playwright E2E tests for user-journey scenarios where browser behavior, visual state, or client-side logic is the thing under test. [community]

---

#### Pattern 231 — Coverage-Gated Merging with `--coverage.thresholds` and Branch-Aware Ratcheting [official]

Vitest's `coverage.thresholds` configuration blocks CI when any coverage metric (lines, branches, functions, statements) falls below the configured threshold. The ratchet strategy extends this: after each successful merge, a CI job reads the current coverage report and automatically updates the threshold values to the current coverage level, ensuring coverage can only increase over time — never silently regress. The ratchet is implemented as a post-merge CI job that runs `vitest run --coverage` and updates `vitest.config.ts` thresholds to `Math.floor(currentCoverage)`, then commits the threshold bump as an automated PR. Branch coverage is the most valuable threshold to ratchet because uncovered branches represent untested conditional logic, which is where the majority of production bugs originate.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — coverage thresholds (updated by automated ratchet job)
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      reporter: ['text', 'json', 'html', 'lcov'],
      // Thresholds are updated by the ratchet CI job after each successful merge.
      // DO NOT lower these values manually — open a PR with justification.
      thresholds: {
        lines: 87,
        branches: 74,  // Branch coverage: most valuable signal
        functions: 91,
        statements: 87,
        // Per-file thresholds prevent single large files from dragging down global averages
        perFile: true,
        '100': false, // Do not require 100% (some branches are unreachable by design)
      },
      // Exclude generated code, config files, and type-only modules
      exclude: [
        'src/generated/**',
        '**/*.d.ts',
        '**/*.config.ts',
        'src/index.ts', // barrel exports don't need coverage
      ],
      // Include source files even if not imported by any test (reveals untested modules)
      include: ['src/**/*.ts'],
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Coverage thresholds create an incentive to write tests that execute code without asserting meaningfully on its behavior — "coverage theater." A developer who needs to raise the branch coverage threshold to unblock their PR can write a test that executes an else-branch by passing the wrong input and asserting on the thrown error type, without actually verifying the business logic of that branch. The mutation score (Pattern 218) is the complementary metric that detects coverage theater: tests that cover code without meaningfully asserting are invisible to coverage but produce surviving mutants. Run coverage-gated merging as the fast gate (low overhead) and mutation testing as the slow gate (nightly), treating them as complementary quality signals rather than alternatives. [official]

---

#### Pattern 232 — API Contract Testing with OpenAPI Schema Validation in Integration Tests [community]

OpenAPI schema validation in integration tests compares the actual HTTP responses produced by the application against the published OpenAPI specification, catching schema drift before it reaches consumers. Rather than maintaining hand-written response matchers in each test, a single `expectMatchesSchema(response, operationId)` helper resolves the response schema for the given operation from the OpenAPI document and validates the parsed response body using `ajv`. This creates a live linkage between the API specification and the implementation: if a developer adds a field to the database model and the response type but forgets to update the OpenAPI spec, the integration test that validates the operation's response will fail. Conversely, if the spec is updated without updating the implementation, the test also fails.

```typescript
// tests/support/openapi-validator.ts
import Ajv from 'ajv';
import addFormats from 'ajv-formats';
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';
import type { OpenAPIV3 } from 'openapi-types';

const spec = JSON.parse(
  readFileSync(new URL('../../openapi.json', import.meta.url), 'utf-8')
) as OpenAPIV3.Document;

const ajv = new Ajv({ strict: false, allErrors: true });
addFormats(ajv);

export function expectResponseMatchesSchema(
  body: unknown,
  path: string,
  method: string,
  statusCode: number
): void {
  const operation = (spec.paths[path] as Record<string, OpenAPIV3.OperationObject>)[method];
  const responseSpec = operation.responses[statusCode.toString()] as OpenAPIV3.ResponseObject;
  const schema = (responseSpec.content?.['application/json']?.schema) as OpenAPIV3.SchemaObject;

  if (!schema) throw new Error(`No schema found for ${method.toUpperCase()} ${path} ${statusCode}`);

  const valid = ajv.validate(schema, body);
  if (!valid) {
    throw new Error(
      `Response body does not match OpenAPI schema for ${method.toUpperCase()} ${path} ${statusCode}:\n` +
      ajv.errorsText(ajv.errors, { dataVar: 'response' })
    );
  }
}

// Usage in an integration test:
// const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/api/users/u-1`, { headers: authHeaders });
// const body = await response.json();
// expectResponseMatchesSchema(body, '/users/{userId}', 'get', 200);
```

**Tradeoff:** OpenAPI schema validation requires maintaining the OpenAPI specification as a first-class artifact rather than an afterthought. Teams that generate their OpenAPI spec from source code annotations (e.g., `tsoa`, `zod-to-openapi`, `fastify-swagger`) get schema validation nearly for free; teams that hand-write their OpenAPI spec will face spec-drift even with this pattern if the discipline of updating the spec before implementing changes is not enforced. The Ajv validation catches structural schema errors but does not validate business rule constraints (e.g., "a confirmed order's `completedAt` must be after its `createdAt`") — those require separate assertion logic in each test case. [community]

---

#### Pattern 233 — `vi.useFakeTimers()` with `vi.setSystemTime()` for Deterministic Date-Dependent Logic Tests [official]

Date-dependent business logic — subscription expiry checks, rate-limit window calculations, reminder scheduling, token expiration — is notoriously difficult to test without controlling time. Vitest's `vi.useFakeTimers()` replaces the global `Date`, `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, and `queueMicrotask` with controlled fakes; `vi.setSystemTime(date)` advances the clock to a specific moment. This eliminates the common anti-pattern of injecting a `now: () => Date` parameter into every function that needs the current time, allowing tests to set up time via the fake timer rather than threaded parameter injection. Always call `vi.useRealTimers()` in `afterEach` to prevent fake timers from leaking into subsequent tests in the same file.

```typescript
// tests/unit/subscription-service.test.ts
import { describe, test, expect, vi, beforeEach, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { SubscriptionService } from '../../src/subscription-service.js';

describe('SubscriptionService — time-dependent behavior', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    vi.useFakeTimers();
  });

  afterEach(() => {
    vi.useRealTimers();
  });

  test('marks subscription as expired one second after trial end', () => {
    const trialEnd = new Date('2026-06-01T00:00:00Z');
    const service = new SubscriptionService({
      trialEndDate: trialEnd,
      gracePeriodHours: 0,
    });

    // One second before trial ends: should still be active
    vi.setSystemTime(new Date('2026-05-31T23:59:59Z'));
    expect(service.getStatus()).toBe('trialing');

    // Exactly at trial end: active (boundary inclusive)
    vi.setSystemTime(trialEnd);
    expect(service.getStatus()).toBe('trialing');

    // One second after trial end: expired
    vi.setSystemTime(new Date('2026-06-01T00:00:01Z'));
    expect(service.getStatus()).toBe('expired');
  });

  test('sends reminder 3 days before trial expiry via scheduled callback', async () => {
    const onReminderSent = vi.fn();
    const trialEnd = new Date('2026-06-10T00:00:00Z');
    vi.setSystemTime(new Date('2026-06-01T00:00:00Z'));

    const service = new SubscriptionService({
      trialEndDate: trialEnd,
      gracePeriodHours: 0,
      onReminderSent,
    });
    service.startReminderScheduler();

    // Fast-forward to 3 days before trial end (reminder threshold)
    await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(7 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000); // 7 days

    expect(onReminderSent).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
    expect(onReminderSent).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
      expect.objectContaining({ daysRemaining: 3 })
    );
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `vi.useFakeTimers()` replaces all timer globals, including those used by third-party libraries bundled into the module under test. Libraries that use `setTimeout` internally for debouncing, retry backoff, or connection keepalives will have their timers controlled by `vi.advanceTimersByTime()`, which can cause unexpected behavior if the library's timer logic is not designed to be fast-forwarded. A common symptom is an HTTP client's internal retry timer firing synchronously during `advanceTimersByTimeAsync`, triggering retries that the test did not anticipate. When this occurs, use `vi.useFakeTimers({ toFake: ['Date', 'setTimeout'] })` to selectively fake only the specific globals the application code uses, leaving library-internal timers unaffected. [official]

---

#### Pattern 234 — Test Sharding Across CI Nodes with Vitest `--shard` for Linear Time Scaling [official]

Vitest's `--shard M/N` flag splits the test file list into N equal shards and runs shard M, enabling horizontal scaling of the test suite across N parallel CI nodes. Unlike sequential parallelism within a single node (which is limited by CPU count), sharding across nodes provides near-linear time scaling — a 10-minute test suite split across 5 nodes completes in approximately 2 minutes. The key to effective sharding is ensuring each shard contains a balanced mix of fast and slow tests; if all integration tests cluster in the same shard, that shard becomes the bottleneck. Vitest's shard algorithm distributes files in discovery order, so sort test files by historical duration (descending) before sharding, or use `--reporter=junit` output from previous runs to build a duration-aware shard assignment.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/test.yml — matrix-based test sharding
name: Test

on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false  # Continue other shards if one fails
      matrix:
        shard: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '22'
          cache: 'npm'

      - run: npm ci

      - name: Run tests (shard ${{ matrix.shard }}/5)
        run: |
          npx vitest run \
            --shard=${{ matrix.shard }}/5 \
            --reporter=verbose \
            --reporter=junit \
            --outputFile.junit=test-results/junit-${{ matrix.shard }}.xml
        env:
          # Each shard uses its own isolated database to prevent cross-shard conflicts
          DATABASE_URL: postgresql://test:test@localhost/testdb_shard${{ matrix.shard }}

      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with:
          name: test-results-shard-${{ matrix.shard }}
          path: test-results/
```

**Tradeoff:** Sharding requires each shard to be independently executable — integration tests that depend on shared infrastructure (a single database instance, a single Redis server) must use isolated namespaces (separate databases, key prefixes, or ports) to avoid cross-shard interference. The CI environment setup time (provisioning a database per shard) can negate the parallelism benefit if setup takes longer than the tests themselves. A pragmatic sharding strategy is to shard only the slow integration test suite and run the fast unit tests on a single node before or after — the unit tests' 30-second runtime is not worth the matrix overhead, but sharding the 10-minute integration suite across 5 nodes saves 8 minutes of developer wait time per PR. [official]

---

#### Pattern 235 — Golden-File Regression Testing for CLI and Code-Generation Output [community]

Golden-file tests (also called "snapshot-file tests" or "approval tests") compare the complete output of a function, CLI command, or code generator against a committed reference file. Unlike Jest/Vitest inline snapshots, golden files are stored as full files in a `tests/golden/` directory — making them diff-friendly in code review and easy to update with `--update-goldens`. This pattern is ideal for testing CLI tools, code generators, template renderers, and report formatters, where the output is human-readable text and the regression signal is any unintended change to the complete output, not just specific fields. The canonical update workflow is: make a change, run `--update-goldens` to regenerate the golden files, review the diff in the PR, and merge when the diff matches the intended change.

```typescript
// tests/golden/golden-test-runner.ts
import { readFileSync, writeFileSync, existsSync, mkdirSync } from 'node:fs';
import { expect } from 'vitest';
import path from 'node:path';

const GOLDEN_DIR = path.join(import.meta.dirname, 'files');
const UPDATE_GOLDENS = process.env['UPDATE_GOLDENS'] === '1';

export function expectMatchesGolden(name: string, actual: string): void {
  const goldenPath = path.join(GOLDEN_DIR, `${name}.golden`);

  if (UPDATE_GOLDENS) {
    mkdirSync(GOLDEN_DIR, { recursive: true });
    writeFileSync(goldenPath, actual, 'utf-8');
    console.log(`Updated golden: ${goldenPath}`);
    return;
  }

  if (!existsSync(goldenPath)) {
    throw new Error(
      `Golden file not found: ${goldenPath}\nRun with UPDATE_GOLDENS=1 to create it.`
    );
  }

  const expected = readFileSync(goldenPath, 'utf-8');
  // Use a diff-friendly matcher for multi-line output
  expect(actual).toBe(expected);
}

// tests/unit/openapi-generator.test.ts
import { describe, test } from 'vitest';
import { expectMatchesGolden } from '../golden/golden-test-runner.js';
import { generateOpenAPISpec } from '../../src/openapi-generator.js';
import { userRouter } from '../../src/routes/user.js';

describe('OpenAPI generator', () => {
  test('generates correct OpenAPI spec for user routes', () => {
    const spec = generateOpenAPISpec([userRouter]);
    const yaml = JSON.stringify(spec, null, 2);
    expectMatchesGolden('openapi-user-routes', yaml);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Golden files accumulate quickly in large codebases — a code generator with 50 output templates produces 50 golden files, and every structural change to the generator requires regenerating and reviewing all 50 diffs. The review burden can be mitigated by splitting golden files into focused, small-output tests (each testing one template or one route) rather than whole-system outputs. The most common golden-file failure mode is an accidental golden update: a developer runs `UPDATE_GOLDENS=1` to fix a legitimate change but the updated golden also silently captures an unintended change in an unrelated output. Prevent this by running `UPDATE_GOLDENS=1` only for specific test files (e.g., `UPDATE_GOLDENS=1 vitest run openapi-generator`) rather than globally. [community]

---

### Real-World Gotchas (Cycle 44)

171. **Vitest `pool: 'vmForks'` silently inherits the parent process's `NODE_OPTIONS` environment variable, causing `--max-old-space-size` settings intended for the test runner to apply to each forked child process individually, potentially exhausting host memory when many forks run in parallel** [community] — WHY: `vmForks` spawns child processes via Node.js `child_process.fork()`, which inherits the parent's environment by default. If the CI environment sets `NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=4096` to give the test runner 4 GB of heap, each forked child process also starts with a 4 GB heap limit. With `maxForks: 8`, the total potential memory allocation is 32 GB plus the parent process, which will trigger OOM kills on a 16 GB CI machine under memory pressure from integration tests that hydrate large in-memory fixtures. Fix: explicitly set `poolOptions.vmForks.env` in `vitest.config.ts` to override `NODE_OPTIONS` for child processes: `env: { ...process.env, NODE_OPTIONS: '--max-old-space-size=512' }`, sizing the per-fork heap for test workloads rather than for the runner. [community: Vitest GitHub issues — vmForks memory exhaustion via NODE_OPTIONS inheritance]

172. **Playwright `routeFromHAR()` with `fallback: 'abort'` aborts requests to subresource integrity (SRI)-protected CDN assets that are not in the HAR file, causing the page to fail to render even though the page's own API calls are correctly replayed** [community] — WHY: When a page loads third-party scripts with `<script integrity="sha384-...">`, the browser issues a fetch for the CDN URL. If that URL is not captured in the HAR file (because the HAR was recorded while offline or with a CDN bypass), `fallback: 'abort'` aborts the fetch, causing the `<script>` to fail the SRI check and throwing an integrity error that blocks page rendering. The test then fails with a misleading "page did not load" error rather than an explicit "HAR miss" error. Fix: use `fallback: 'continue'` for `*.cdn.*` and trusted third-party origins while using `fallback: 'abort'` for first-party `/api/*` routes, by calling `routeFromHAR()` with a scoped `url` pattern for API calls and leaving all other requests unrouted. [community: Playwright GitHub issues — routeFromHAR SRI integrity failure with fallback:abort]

173. **`vi.useFakeTimers()` in a Vitest `describe` block that is shared with `beforeAll` database setup breaks connection pool keepalive timers, causing pool connection timeouts mid-test because the fake timer never advances the keepalive `setInterval` that the database driver relies on** [community] — WHY: Node.js database drivers (`pg`, `mysql2`, `@prisma/client`) maintain connection pool health via `setInterval`-based keepalive queries that periodically send `SELECT 1` to prevent idle connections from being closed by the database server's `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`. When `vi.useFakeTimers()` replaces `setInterval`, the keepalive interval stops advancing unless the test explicitly calls `vi.advanceTimersByTime()`. An integration test that runs a long async sequence (realistic for checkout flow tests) without advancing fake timers will exceed the database's idle timeout (typically 10–30 seconds), causing the pool to return a dead connection that throws `connection terminated unexpectedly`. Fix: either call `vi.useFakeTimers({ toFake: ['Date'] })` (fake only `Date`, leave `setInterval` real) when database connections are in scope, or call `vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(keepaliveIntervalMs)` periodically within long-running test sequences. [community: Vitest GitHub issues — useFakeTimers kills database pool keepalive]

174. **Storybook play function `userEvent.type()` calls fail silently when the target input has an `onChange` handler that debounces state updates, because `userEvent.type()` fires keystrokes faster than the debounce delay, resulting in the component never reaching the "typing complete" state during the play function's synchronous assertion** [community] — WHY: `@testing-library/user-event` v14's `userEvent.type()` dispatches `keydown`/`keypress`/`keyup`/`input` events for each character with minimal artificial delay between keystrokes. If a component's `onChange` handler debounces via `setTimeout(handler, 300)`, the rapidly-fired keystrokes all extend the debounce timer without triggering the handler. The play function's assertion that follows `userEvent.type()` runs before the 300 ms debounce fires, reading the component's pre-debounce state. In a real browser (Storybook), there is no fake timer to advance, so the test must await real time. Fix: add an explicit `await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 350))` after `userEvent.type()` to allow the debounce to settle, or reconfigure the debounce delay via a story arg (`args: { debounceMs: 0 }`) to eliminate the debounce in test contexts. [community: Storybook GitHub discussions — userEvent.type debounce interaction in play functions]

175. **OpenAPI schema validation tests using `ajv` with `strict: false` pass silently for responses that include undeclared additional properties, hiding provider contract violations where the implementation returns extra fields not present in the spec** [community] — WHY: `ajv`'s default behavior with `additionalProperties: true` (the JSON Schema default when not specified) allows objects to contain any extra keys beyond those declared in the schema. An OpenAPI spec that does not explicitly set `additionalProperties: false` will validate successfully even when the response contains undeclared fields. If the spec defines `{ id, name, email }` but the implementation returns `{ id, name, email, internalUserId, passwordHash }`, the `ajv` validation passes, and the PII leakage regression is not caught. Fix: configure the `ajv` instance with `{ strict: false, additionalProperties: false }` for response validation (or add `"additionalProperties": false` to every schema object in the OpenAPI spec), and explicitly allowlist expected additional properties using OpenAPI's `additionalProperties: { type: 'string' }` schema form rather than relying on the permissive default. [community: ajv GitHub issues — additionalProperties default allows undeclared fields in OpenAPI validation]
