### Pattern 261 — Playwright `page.route()` with `route.continue({ headers })` for Auth Token Injection Without Login UI [official]

`route.continue({ headers })` intercepts outgoing requests and augments their headers before allowing them to proceed to the server, enabling tests to inject authentication tokens (Bearer tokens, API keys, CSRF headers) without executing the login UI flow or relying on `storageState`. This pattern is particularly useful for testing pages that require authentication when the login flow itself is not the subject of the test and when the `storageState` approach cannot be used (e.g., the token is issued by an external IdP that cannot be reliably scripted against in CI). The header injection happens transparently from the application's perspective — the app receives an authenticated request and renders the protected page normally.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// Fixture that injects a valid test token into every outgoing request
const authenticatedTest = test.extend<{ authToken: string }>({
  authToken: async ({}, use) => {
    // Fetch a short-lived test token from a dedicated test-token endpoint
    const resp = await fetch(`${process.env.BASE_URL}/api/test-tokens`, {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: { 'X-Test-Key': process.env.TEST_API_KEY! },
      body: JSON.stringify({ role: 'admin', expiresIn: 300 }),
    });
    const { token } = await resp.json();
    await use(token);
  },
});

authenticatedTest('admin can access billing settings', async ({ page, authToken }) => {
  await page.route('**/*', async (route) => {
    await route.continue({
      headers: {
        ...route.request().headers(),
        Authorization: `Bearer ${authToken}`,
      },
    });
  });

  await page.goto('/settings/billing');
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Billing Settings' })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('plan-name')).toHaveText('Enterprise');
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Header injection via `page.route()` intercepts every request on the page, including third-party analytics, CDN asset requests, and browser-initiated prefetch requests. Adding `Authorization` headers to third-party requests may expose tokens to unintended recipients and will cause CORS errors if the third-party server's CORS policy rejects the additional header. Scope the route interceptor to first-party origins only: replace `'**/*'` with `new RegExp('^' + process.env.BASE_URL)` to match only requests to the application under test and let third-party requests proceed unmodified.

---

### Pattern 262 — Vitest `vi.useFakeTimers({ shouldAdvanceTime: true })` for Real-Time-Proportional Fake Clocks [official]

`vi.useFakeTimers({ shouldAdvanceTime: true })` activates Vitest's fake timer infrastructure while still advancing the fake clock in proportion to real elapsed wall-clock time. This mode is useful for testing components that combine real async I/O (network requests, database calls) with timer-dependent logic (debouncing, polling, countdown displays) — the fake clock advances alongside real time, but individual timers can still be manually fast-forwarded with `vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync()`. Without `shouldAdvanceTime: true`, code that awaits `Promise.resolve()` in a loop while waiting for a `setTimeout` to fire will deadlock because the fake clock does not advance while awaiting real microtasks.

```typescript
import { vi, describe, it, expect, beforeEach, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { render, screen } from '@testing-library/react';
import { CountdownTimer } from './CountdownTimer';

describe('CountdownTimer', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    // Real time advances the fake clock proportionally — avoids deadlocks
    // with async code that awaits real I/O and also uses setTimeout
    vi.useFakeTimers({ shouldAdvanceTime: true });
  });

  afterEach(() => {
    vi.useRealTimers();
  });

  it('counts down from 60 and shows "Time is up!" at zero', async () => {
    vi.setSystemTime(new Date('2026-05-14T10:00:00.000Z'));
    render(<CountdownTimer durationSeconds={60} />);

    expect(screen.getByText('0:60')).toBeInTheDocument();

    // Fast-forward the fake clock 30 seconds
    await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(30_000);
    expect(screen.getByText('0:30')).toBeInTheDocument();

    // Fast-forward the remaining 30 seconds
    await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(30_000);
    expect(screen.getByText('Time is up!')).toBeInTheDocument();
  });

  it('pauses countdown correctly', async () => {
    render(<CountdownTimer durationSeconds={10} />);
    await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(3_000);
    screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pause' }).click();
    await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(5_000); // 5s passes while paused
    expect(screen.getByText('0:07')).toBeInTheDocument(); // still at 7s remaining
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `shouldAdvanceTime: true` makes test execution slower because the fake clock only advances as fast as real time — a test that needs to advance 30 seconds of fake time still waits 30 real seconds unless `vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync()` is called to fast-forward. In practice, use `shouldAdvanceTime: true` only during the transition period when debugging deadlocks caused by mixed async/timer code, then switch to `shouldAdvanceTime: false` (the default) with explicit `vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync()` calls for production test suites. Always call `vi.useRealTimers()` in `afterEach` — lingering fake timers from a failed test that skipped teardown cause hard-to-diagnose interference with subsequent tests in the same worker.

### Pattern 263 — Playwright `webServer` Configuration for Zero-Config Local Dev Server Startup in CI [official]

Playwright's `webServer` configuration option in `playwright.config.ts` launches the application's dev or preview server automatically before tests start and tears it down after the suite completes. This eliminates CI pipeline steps that separately start and stop the application, reducing the risk of tests running against a stale or missing server process and the risk of port conflicts when multiple CI jobs run on the same machine. The `reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI` flag allows local developers to run their own dev server (reusing it if already running) while ensuring CI always starts a fresh server from the committed build artifact.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  testDir: './tests/e2e',
  webServer: [
    {
      // Primary app server
      command: 'npm run build && npm run preview',
      url: 'http://localhost:4173',
      reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI,
      timeout: 120_000,
      stdout: 'pipe',
      stderr: 'pipe',
      env: {
        DATABASE_URL: process.env.TEST_DATABASE_URL!,
        NODE_ENV: 'test',
      },
    },
    {
      // Mock external payment provider server
      command: 'node test/servers/mock-payment-provider.js',
      url: 'http://localhost:9090/health',
      reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI,
      timeout: 10_000,
    },
  ],
  use: {
    baseURL: 'http://localhost:4173',
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff.** The `command` in `webServer` runs in a child process that inherits the environment of the Playwright process but does not use the shell's PATH expansion — commands like `npm run build` that invoke other tools must be available in the absolute PATH or invoked as `npx vite build` to avoid "command not found" errors in CI containers. When `webServer.command` fails before the `url` becomes reachable, Playwright emits a generic "Error: Failed to start..." message without showing the server's stderr output, even with `stderr: 'pipe'` — add explicit startup logging to the server's startup script to aid CI diagnosis. Always set `timeout` explicitly; the default timeout (60 s) is too short for `npm run build` steps that compile large TypeScript projects.

---

### Pattern 264 — Vitest `pool: 'forks'` with `singleFork: true` for Serial Integration Tests That Share a Single Database Connection [official]

`pool: 'forks'` with `poolOptions.forks.singleFork: true` runs all tests within a given Vitest project in a single forked child process sequentially, rather than spawning one fork per test file. This mode is intended for integration test suites that require a single shared stateful resource — a database transaction that wraps all tests, an in-process server started once, or a Testcontainers-managed PostgreSQL instance that is too expensive to spin up per file. Unlike `pool: 'vmThreads'` (which shares the same V8 context across test files, causing module-state leakage), `singleFork` gives a clean Node.js process while still allowing shared infrastructure lifecycle across all test files.

```typescript
// vitest.config.integration.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    include: ['tests/integration/**/*.test.ts'],
    pool: 'forks',
    poolOptions: {
      forks: {
        singleFork: true, // All integration tests run in one process, sequentially
      },
    },
    // Global setup/teardown for the shared DB container
    globalSetup: ['tests/integration/setup/start-postgres.ts'],
    setupFiles: ['tests/integration/setup/transaction-wrapper.ts'],
    testTimeout: 30_000,
    hookTimeout: 60_000,
  },
});

// tests/integration/setup/transaction-wrapper.ts
import { beforeEach, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { db } from '../../src/db';

// Each test runs inside a transaction that is rolled back — no state leakage
beforeEach(async () => {
  await db.query('BEGIN');
});

afterEach(async () => {
  await db.query('ROLLBACK');
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `singleFork: true` serializes all integration tests, eliminating the parallelism benefits that normally make Vitest fast. A 200-test integration suite that previously ran across 4 forks in 45 seconds will now run serially in ~3 minutes. Mitigate by splitting integration tests into logical groups (user-domain, payment-domain, notification-domain) and running each group as a separate Vitest project with its own `singleFork` configuration — enabling cross-project parallelism while maintaining intra-project serializability. Always pair `singleFork: true` with `--reporter=verbose` in CI so sequential test output is clearly attributed to individual test files.

---

### Pattern 265 — Playwright `expect(page).toMatchAriaSnapshot()` for Semantic Accessibility Structure Assertions [official]

`toMatchAriaSnapshot()` asserts on the accessibility tree structure of a page or locator — the semantic representation that screen readers use — rather than on visual DOM properties. This means tests catch regressions like role attribute removal, landmark hierarchy changes, and missing ARIA labels that would be invisible to CSS-selector-based assertions but that break screen reader navigation. Unlike `@axe-core/playwright`, which reports rule violations, `toMatchAriaSnapshot()` asserts on the specific semantic structure expected for a feature, making it a precision tool for accessibility regression testing on individual components or page regions.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('navigation menu has correct ARIA structure', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');

  // Assert on the exact ARIA tree for the primary navigation
  await expect(page.getByRole('navigation', { name: 'Primary' })).toMatchAriaSnapshot(`
    - navigation "Primary":
      - list:
        - listitem:
          - link "Home"
        - listitem:
          - link "Products"
          - list:
            - listitem:
              - link "All Products"
            - listitem:
              - link "Featured"
        - listitem:
          - link "Contact"
  `);

  // Assert modal has correct accessible structure when open
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Open cart' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('dialog', { name: 'Shopping Cart' })).toMatchAriaSnapshot(`
    - dialog "Shopping Cart":
      - heading "Shopping Cart" [level=2]
      - list:
        - /listitem .+/:
      - button "Checkout"
      - button "Close"
  `);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** ARIA snapshot strings are brittle when navigational content is dynamic (e.g., a navigation menu whose items are fetched from a CMS). A snapshot that includes the exact link text of menu items will fail whenever content editors update navigation labels — even though the accessibility structure is correct. Use regex patterns (`/listitem .+/`) in ARIA snapshot assertions for content areas whose text changes, and reserve exact-text assertions for structural elements (headings, landmark names, button labels) that are controlled by code rather than content. Run `npx playwright test --update-snapshots` to regenerate baselines after deliberate accessibility structure changes.

---

### Real-World Gotchas (Cycle 46)

181. **Playwright `expect.soft()` assertions that are never followed by a `test.info().errors` check or a hard assertion allow tests to "pass" in Playwright's exit code while containing failed soft assertions — the test is marked as "failed" in Playwright's report but the `playwright test` command exits with code 0 if all other hard assertions passed, causing CI to green-light a broken test suite** [official] — WHY: Playwright's exit code reflects whether the test *run* encountered hard failures (tests that aborted mid-execution). A test that uses only `expect.soft()` and whose soft assertions all fail will still complete to the end of the test body without throwing. If the test body has no hard assertion after the soft ones, the test function returns normally. Playwright marks the test as "failed" in its HTML report (because soft assertion errors are attached to `testInfo.errors`), but the process exit code is determined by whether any test threw an unhandled exception or was explicitly marked as failed — and soft-only failures do not cause a throw. Fix: always add `expect(test.info().errors).toHaveLength(0)` as the final statement of any test that uses `expect.soft()`, or add at least one hard assertion that gates on the previous soft assertions having passed. [official: Playwright soft assertions docs]

182. **Vitest `toMatchInlineSnapshot()` tests fail in CI with "Missing snapshot" errors even though the snapshot string is present in the test file — this occurs when the test file uses Windows-style line endings (CRLF) while the CI environment uses Unix-style (LF), because Vitest's snapshot comparison normalizes the stored snapshot to LF but does not normalize the inline snapshot string extracted from the source file, causing a character-level mismatch** [community] — WHY: When Vitest reads an inline snapshot from a test file, it extracts the string literal as-is from the source text. On Windows, if the test file was committed with CRLF line endings (`\r\n`), the extracted snapshot string contains `\r\n` within multi-line snapshot values. Vitest's snapshot comparison normalizes the *expected* value by stripping `\r` characters for comparison, but the normalization only applies to the serialized-then-compared value — not to the raw string extracted from the source. The actual snapshot (computed by serializing the test value) uses `\n`, so the comparison fails on `\r\n` vs `\n`. Fix: add `.gitattributes` with `*.test.ts text=auto eol=lf` to enforce LF line endings in committed test files, and run `git add --renormalize .` on existing files. [community: Vitest GitHub issues — inline snapshot CRLF failures in CI]

183. **Playwright `.or()` locators used in `expect(locator).toBeVisible()` assertions report a misleading timeout message ("locator resolved to N elements") when both alternatives become simultaneously visible due to a rendering bug — the assertion passes (because at least one element is visible) but masks the fact that both the success banner and the error banner are rendered at the same time** [official] — WHY: `.or()` returns a locator that matches *any* element satisfying either condition. When `expect(successBanner.or(errorBanner)).toBeVisible()` is evaluated, Playwright checks whether the resolved locator contains at least one visible element — it does not assert that exactly one is visible. If a rendering bug causes both banners to appear simultaneously, the assertion passes silently. The test was designed to verify "the page reached a terminal state" but the `.or()` assertion cannot distinguish "one of two states" from "both states simultaneously." Fix: follow `.or()` visibility assertions with `await expect(successBanner.or(errorBanner)).toHaveCount(1)` to assert mutual exclusivity, or use explicit conditional logic: `const isSuccess = await successBanner.isVisible(); const isError = await errorBanner.isVisible(); expect(isSuccess).not.toBe(isError)`. [official: Playwright locator combinators docs]

184. **Vitest `bench()` benchmarks that are placed in the same file as regular `test()` and `it()` tests cause the entire file to require `vitest bench` instead of `vitest run` — running `vitest run` on a file that contains `bench()` calls throws "bench is not defined" because the `bench` global is only injected when Vitest is started in benchmark mode** [official] — WHY: Vitest initializes a different global context for benchmark runs (`vitest bench`) versus test runs (`vitest run`). In benchmark mode, Vitest injects `bench`, `describe`, and `beforeAll`/`afterAll` from the Tinybench integration. In test mode, `bench` is not injected into the global scope. If a test file imports from `vitest` (`import { bench, describe } from 'vitest'`) the missing global is a TypeScript type issue, not a runtime one; but if it uses Vitest's auto-injected globals (via `globals: true` in config), `bench` is undefined at runtime. Fix: always co-locate `bench()` calls in dedicated `.bench.ts` files (named convention: `*.bench.ts`) and configure `include` in `vitest.config.ts` to separate benchmark patterns from test patterns. Use `benchmarkReporter` settings in a dedicated vitest benchmark config. [official: Vitest benchmarking docs]

185. **Playwright `storageState` files generated with JWTs that encode the user's timezone or locale silently break tests in CI environments running in UTC when the application renders dates relative to the authenticated user's stored timezone — the test asserts "Today at 2:00 PM" but the application renders "Today at 9:00 PM" because the CI server's system clock is UTC while the storage state was generated in GMT-7** [community] — WHY: Storage state captures browser state (cookies, localStorage, sessionStorage) but does not capture the browser's timezone setting. When a session cookie or JWT payload contains a `timezone: 'America/Denver'` claim that the application reads to render localized timestamps, and the test was authored in the Denver timezone (UTC-7), the inline expected values in the test encode Denver-time strings. In CI (UTC), the same authentication token causes the application to render the same UTC-7 timezone offset but the test's expected strings were written against the developer's local time. This creates CI-only test failures that pass locally. Fix: always use UTC-relative or locale-neutral date assertions in E2E tests (`expect(dateCell).toHaveText(/\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}/)`), set `TZ=UTC` in the CI environment, and store the timezone explicitly in test fixtures rather than relying on developer machine timezone during storage state generation. [community: Playwright GitHub discussions — storageState JWT timezone mismatch]

| Vitest per-file coverage thresholds | official-docs | https://vitest.dev/config/#coverage-thresholds | Per-glob threshold overrides, `thresholdAutoUpdate`, `/* v8 ignore next */` directives |
| Playwright `serviceWorkers` config | official-docs | https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browser#browser-new-context-option-service-workers | `'block'` vs `'allow'` semantics, MSW interference prevention |

## Cycle 47 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 266 — Playwright `expect(locator).toContainClass()` for Ergonomic Individual Class Assertions [official]

`toContainClass()` asserts that a DOM element's `class` attribute contains one or more specific CSS class names without requiring the full class string to match. Prior to this assertion, teams used `toHaveClass(/class-name/)` with a regex, which is fragile when class ordering changes, or `toHaveAttribute('class', expect.stringContaining('class-name'))`, which is verbose. `toContainClass()` accepts a single string, an array of strings, or a regex, retries automatically, and produces a clear diff on failure that shows which expected classes are missing from the actual class list. It treats the class attribute as a set of tokens rather than a substring, so `toContainClass('done')` passes for `class="item done highlighted"` but would fail for `toHaveClass('done')` if the full class string differs.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('task item reflects completion state with correct CSS class', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/tasks');

  const taskItem = page.getByRole('listitem', { name: 'Ship v1.52' });

  // Before completion: item should NOT have 'done' class
  await expect(taskItem).not.toContainClass('done');

  await page.getByRole('checkbox', { name: 'Ship v1.52' }).check();

  // After completion: assert the 'done' class was added (other classes are irrelevant)
  await expect(taskItem).toContainClass('done');

  // Assert multiple classes together — all must be present
  await expect(taskItem).toContainClass(['done', 'visible']);

  // Regex form — matches any class starting with 'state-'
  await expect(taskItem).toContainClass(/state-\w+/);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `toContainClass()` is strictly more readable than `toHaveClass(/regex/)` for presence checks, but it cannot assert the *exact* full class string when that is intentional (e.g., asserting no unexpected classes were added). Use `toHaveClass('exact-string')` when the full class list must match exactly, and `toContainClass()` when you only care that a specific class is present among others. Avoid mixing both in the same test as it signals unclear intent about which invariant is being tested.

### Pattern 267 — Playwright ARIA Snapshot `/children: equal` for Strict Child Count Assertions [official]

ARIA snapshots added a `/children: equal` property modifier in Playwright 1.52 that changes child matching from the default "partial" mode (where extra children beyond those listed are allowed) to "strict" mode (where the snapshot must account for every child element in the tree). Without `/children: equal`, an ARIA snapshot passes even if new menu items, list items, or sidebar links are added — because the snapshot only asserts the listed items are present somewhere in the subtree. With `/children: equal`, adding or removing any child causes the snapshot to fail, making it a precise regression guard for navigation menus, tab bars, or step indicators where the exact item count is a product requirement. The modifier applies to the node it is placed on and does not propagate to descendant nodes unless each descendant also specifies `/children: equal`.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('tab bar has exactly four tabs — no tabs added or removed', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Without /children: equal, extra tabs would silently pass
  await expect(page.getByRole('tablist')).toMatchAriaSnapshot(`
    - tablist:
      /children: equal
      - tab "Overview" [selected]
      - tab "Analytics"
      - tab "Reports"
      - tab "Settings"
  `);

  // Assert a nav link href using /url modifier
  await expect(page.getByRole('navigation', { name: 'Breadcrumb' })).toMatchAriaSnapshot(`
    - navigation "Breadcrumb":
      - list:
        - listitem:
          - link "Home" /url: /\\/$/
        - listitem:
          - link "Dashboard" /url: /\\/dashboard/
        - listitem "Reports"
  `);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `/children: equal` makes ARIA snapshots as brittle as exact DOM structure assertions — any new feature flag that conditionally adds a tab will break every test using this modifier. Reserve it for structural invariants that are explicit product requirements (e.g., "checkout has exactly 3 steps"), and prefer the default partial mode for navigations whose items may grow with content. When using `/url`, remember that the pattern is matched against the resolved `href` value, not the link text, so relative paths require anchored regex patterns.

### Pattern 268 — Playwright `testProject.workers` for Per-Project Concurrency Control [official]

The `workers` property on `testProject` (introduced in Playwright 1.52) allows individual test projects within a `playwright.config.ts` to declare their own worker concurrency limits, overriding the global `workers` config while still being capped by it. This solves the problem of mixed test suites where E2E tests against a shared staging database must run serially (to avoid data conflicts) while isolated component tests can run fully parallel. Previously, teams worked around this by splitting into separate config files run in CI sequence, or by abusing `test.describe.serial()` throughout test files. With per-project `workers: 1`, the constraint is declared once at the project level and applies uniformly to all test files in that project without test-file modifications.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  workers: 4, // global ceiling — no project can exceed 4 workers

  projects: [
    {
      name: 'component-tests',
      testMatch: '**/*.spec.tsx',
      // inherits global workers: 4 — run maximally parallel
    },
    {
      name: 'api-integration',
      testMatch: '**/api/**/*.spec.ts',
      workers: 2, // limit to 2 workers for API rate-limit compliance
    },
    {
      name: 'e2e-shared-db',
      testMatch: '**/e2e/**/*.spec.ts',
      workers: 1, // serial execution — shared staging DB with no test isolation
    },
  ],
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Per-project `workers` solves data-contention problems at the configuration level, but it does not solve them definitively — tests within a project still run concurrently by default if multiple spec files exist and `workers > 1`. A project with `workers: 2` that has 10 spec files will run 2 files in parallel. If tests within a single file create conflicting database state, use `test.describe.serial()` or the `singleFork` pool option in addition to project-level `workers`. The `workers` ceiling is the global config value, so setting a project's `workers` higher than the global value silently uses the global value.

### Pattern 269 — Playwright `testConfig.failOnFlakyTests` to Enforce Test Suite Stability in CI [official]

`failOnFlakyTests: true` in `playwright.config.ts` causes the overall test run to exit with a failure code if any test passed on a retry after initially failing — regardless of whether the test ultimately passed. Without this option, a test suite that relies on `retries: 2` may silently accumulate flaky tests: individual tests fail on the first attempt, pass on the second, and the CI job shows green. Over time, the suite becomes unreliable because engineers have no signal that tests are non-deterministic. With `failOnFlakyTests: true`, even a test that passes on its final retry causes the run to fail, forcing the team to fix the underlying flakiness rather than papering over it with retries. Retries remain useful for the test output to show that a test was indeed flaky rather than permanently broken.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // Allow retries so we can observe flaky behavior
  retries: process.env.CI ? 2 : 0,

  // But fail the build if anything needed a retry to pass
  // This enforces zero-tolerance for flakiness in CI
  failOnFlakyTests: process.env.CI ? true : false,

  reporter: [
    ['html'],
    // Optional: also emit a JSON report to track flaky test trends over time
    ['json', { outputFile: 'test-results/results.json' }],
  ],

  projects: [
    {
      name: 'chromium',
      use: { browserName: 'chromium' },
    },
  ],
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `failOnFlakyTests` is appropriate for mature test suites where flakiness has been systematically eliminated. Enabling it immediately in a suite with known flakiness will break every CI run until all flaky tests are fixed or quarantined (via `test.skip(condition)` or a dedicated quarantine project). A pragmatic rollout strategy is to enable it only for a project containing the most stable tests (e.g., `e2e-critical-path`) while leaving it disabled globally, then expand coverage as stability improves. Never use `retries: 0` with `failOnFlakyTests: true` — with no retries, Playwright cannot distinguish a flaky test from a consistently failing one, so the `failOnFlakyTests` option has no meaningful effect.

### Pattern 270 — Playwright `storageState({ indexedDB: true })` for IndexedDB-Backed Authentication [official]

Playwright's `storageState()` method added an `indexedDB: true` option in v1.51 that captures the browser context's IndexedDB contents alongside cookies and localStorage in the saved state file. Authentication systems that store tokens in IndexedDB (including Firebase Authentication, Supabase Auth, and any app using `idb-keyval` or `localforage` with IndexedDB as the backend) would previously require re-authentication on every test run because `storageState()` without `indexedDB: true` only preserved cookies and localStorage. With this option enabled during the auth setup phase in `globalSetup`, subsequent tests that restore the storage state have a fully authenticated context without any network round-trips to the authentication provider.

```typescript
// global-setup.ts
import { chromium, FullConfig } from '@playwright/test';

async function globalSetup(config: FullConfig) {
  const browser = await chromium.launch();
  const context = await browser.newContext();
  const page = await context.newPage();

  await page.goto('/login');
  await page.fill('[name="email"]', process.env.TEST_USER_EMAIL!);
  await page.fill('[name="password"]', process.env.TEST_USER_PASSWORD!);
  await page.click('[type="submit"]');

  // Wait for Firebase to finish writing tokens to IndexedDB
  await page.waitForURL('/dashboard');
  await page.waitForTimeout(500); // Allow async IndexedDB write to complete

  // Capture auth state INCLUDING IndexedDB (required for Firebase Auth)
  await context.storageState({
    indexedDB: true,
    path: 'playwright/.auth/user.json',
  });

  await browser.close();
}

export default globalSetup;
```

**Tradeoff.** `indexedDB: true` captures a point-in-time snapshot of the entire IndexedDB for the origin. If the application writes large datasets to IndexedDB (e.g., offline-first apps that cache API responses), the `storageState` file can become very large (tens of megabytes), slowing test startup because Playwright must deserialize and restore all captured records. Scope the captured origin carefully — if only `https://app.example.com` needs IndexedDB restoration, confirm that no other origin in the context has large IndexedDB contents. The `waitForTimeout` before capture is required because IndexedDB writes are asynchronous; capturing state immediately after navigation can result in partially-written token entries that cause silent auth failures.

### Pattern 271 — Playwright `locator.filter({ visible: true })` for Visibility-Scoped Locator Narrowing [official]

`locator.filter({ visible: true })` narrows a multi-match locator to only elements that are currently visible in the viewport (not `display: none`, `visibility: hidden`, or `opacity: 0`). Before this option, teams chained `.filter({ has: page.locator(':visible') })` or used custom JavaScript predicates inside `locator.filter()` callbacks, both of which are semantically unclear and incompatible with Playwright's automatic retry logic. The `visible` option integrates with Playwright's actionability polling: if no visible element matches at assertion time, the locator retries until the timeout, rather than immediately failing. It complements `{ visible: false }` for asserting that all matched elements are hidden.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('dropdown menu shows only visible options', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/products');

  // Some filters may be hidden until a category is selected
  const filterOptions = page.getByRole('checkbox');

  // Only assert on checkboxes that are currently visible to the user
  const visibleFilters = filterOptions.filter({ visible: true });

  // Assert count of currently-visible filter options
  await expect(visibleFilters).toHaveCount(5);

  // Select a sub-category to reveal more options
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Electronics' }).click();

  // Re-evaluate visible filters after expansion
  await expect(visibleFilters).toHaveCount(12);

  // Verify hidden options still exist in DOM but are not visible
  const hiddenFilters = filterOptions.filter({ visible: false });
  await expect(hiddenFilters).not.toHaveCount(0);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `filter({ visible: true })` reflects CSS visibility at the moment Playwright resolves the locator during the retry loop. It does not account for elements that are *present in the viewport* but behind an overlay (which are "visible" in CSS terms but not actually interactable). For actionability — whether a click would succeed — use `element.isVisible()` combined with `element.isEnabled()`, or simply attempt the action and let Playwright's built-in actionability checks surface the error. Do not use `filter({ visible: true })` as a substitute for explicit waits; if an element animates from hidden to visible, the filter may resolve before the animation completes, yielding a partially-rendered element.

### Pattern 272 — Playwright `expect(locator).toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage()` for ARIA Error Message Validation [official]

`toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage()` asserts that a form field or interactive element exposes a specific accessible error message via the `aria-errormessage` attribute, as computed by the accessibility tree. Unlike `toHaveAttribute('aria-errormessage', 'error-id')`, which only asserts the attribute value (a DOM ID), `toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage()` resolves the referenced element's text content and asserts on the human-readable message — the same string a screen reader would announce to a user. This catches broken error associations where the `aria-errormessage` ID is set but points to an element that doesn't exist or has empty text, which `toHaveAttribute` would pass silently.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('email field exposes accessible error message on invalid input', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/signup');

  const emailInput = page.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Email address' });

  // Submit without filling the required field
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Create account' }).click();

  // Assert the accessible error message (resolved text, not the DOM ID)
  await expect(emailInput).toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage('Email address is required.');

  // Regex form for partial matching
  await expect(emailInput).toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage(/required/i);

  // Fill with invalid format
  await emailInput.fill('not-an-email');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Create account' }).click();

  await expect(emailInput).toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage('Please enter a valid email address.');

  // Fill with valid input — error message should disappear
  await emailInput.fill('user@example.com');
  await expect(emailInput).not.toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage()` requires a correct ARIA implementation: the element must have both `aria-invalid="true"` and `aria-errormessage="<id>"` where `<id>` references a live element with the error text. If the component uses a custom pattern (e.g., `aria-describedby` instead of `aria-errormessage`, or a tooltip that appears on hover), this assertion will fail even though an error is visually communicated. Before adopting this assertion, audit the component's ARIA attributes — mixing `aria-describedby` and `aria-errormessage` on the same element is valid per ARIA spec, but screen readers handle them differently, and `toHaveAccessibleErrorMessage()` exclusively checks the `aria-errormessage` association.

---

### Pattern 273 — Playwright `test.step()` with `timeout` Option for Granular Step-Level Timeout Management [official]

`test.step()` accepts a `timeout` option (introduced in Playwright 1.50) that sets a maximum duration for that individual step independently of the overall test timeout. When a step's timeout fires, it throws a `TimeoutError` scoped to that step, not to the entire test — subsequent steps still execute unless the test body rethrows the error. The `box: true` option (also available on steps) redirects error stack traces to the step call site rather than the internal frame where the failure occurred, which improves debuggability when steps are defined in shared page object utilities. Together, these options enable step-level SLA assertions: a "page load" step with `timeout: 3000` fails fast if a page regression causes load times to exceed 3 seconds, without requiring a low global test timeout.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('checkout flow completes within per-step SLA budgets', async ({ page }) => {
  await test.step('navigate to cart', async () => {
    await page.goto('/cart');
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Your Cart' })).toBeVisible();
  }, { timeout: 3000 }); // Page must be interactive within 3 seconds

  await test.step('proceed to checkout', async () => {
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Proceed to Checkout' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Shipping' })).toBeVisible();
  }, { timeout: 5000 }); // Shipping page (heavier) gets 5 seconds

  await test.step('submit order', async (stepInfo) => {
    // stepInfo.skip() can conditionally skip the step at runtime
    if (!process.env.PAYMENT_GATEWAY_LIVE) {
      stepInfo.skip();
      return;
    }
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place Order' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Order Confirmed' })).toBeVisible();
  }, { timeout: 10000, box: true }); // Payment calls get 10s; box=true for cleaner stack traces
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Step-level timeouts create two independent timeout clocks: the step timeout and the test timeout. A test with `timeout: 30000` and three steps each with `timeout: 15000` could theoretically run for 45 seconds if each step approaches its limit — the test timeout is not a sum-of-steps ceiling. Always set step timeouts conservatively below the test timeout divided by the number of steps, and treat step timeout failures as performance regression signals rather than just flakiness. The `stepInfo.skip()` pattern is useful for optional steps (e.g., payment steps behind a feature flag) but produces a "step skipped" annotation in the HTML report that can be confusing — add a step comment explaining the skip condition.

---

### Pattern 274 — Playwright `testConfig.updateSnapshots: "changed"` for Selective Snapshot Baseline Updates [official]

The `updateSnapshots` config option gained a third value `"changed"` in Playwright 1.50, alongside the existing `"all"` (rewrite every snapshot) and `"none"` (never rewrite, CI default). `"changed"` mode updates only snapshots whose underlying test output has actually changed since the last run, leaving unchanged snapshots untouched. This is the correct mode for routine maintenance: when a component's visual design changes intentionally, running `npx playwright test --update-snapshots=changed` rewrites only the affected screenshot baselines, rather than `--update-snapshots` (which is equivalent to `"all"` and rewrites all baselines — silently accepting any regressions that happened to exist in the same run). It pairs with `updateSourceMethod: "3-way"` to apply snapshot updates as a three-way merge rather than an overwrite when source-controlled baselines have local conflicts.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // Default: never auto-update in CI
  updateSnapshots: 'none',

  // Run locally with: npx playwright test --update-snapshots=changed
  // Or set in a dedicated "update" config file:
  // updateSnapshots: 'changed',
  // updateSourceMethod: '3-way', // merge-friendly baseline updates

  projects: [
    {
      name: 'visual-regression',
      testMatch: '**/*.visual.spec.ts',
      snapshotPathTemplate: '{testDir}/__snapshots__/{testFilePath}/{arg}-{projectName}{ext}',
    },
  ],
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `"changed"` mode compares the new output against the stored baseline to determine "changed" status — so it requires a stored baseline to exist. On a CI branch that adds new screenshot tests for the first time, there are no baselines, and all new screenshots are created (equivalent to `"all"` for the new tests). This is correct behavior, but it means a PR that adds new visual tests and modifies existing components will update both new baselines and changed existing ones in a single `--update-snapshots=changed` run. Review the git diff of `__snapshots__` carefully after such a run to confirm only intentional baseline changes were committed.

---

### Pattern 275 — Playwright Component Testing `hooksConfig` for Test-Scoped Router and Provider Setup [official]

Playwright Component Testing's `hooksConfig` option in `mount()` passes test-specific configuration to the `beforeMount` hook defined in `playwright/index.ts`, bridging the Node/browser boundary for provider setup. The standard pattern for mounting a component that depends on a React Router, Vuex store, or i18n provider is to define the provider wrapping in `beforeMount` (which runs in the browser context) and pass the test-specific configuration (initial route, mock store state) as a serializable `hooksConfig` object from the test (which runs in Node). This avoids the fundamental constraint of Playwright CT: test code in Node cannot directly import or instantiate browser-side modules like `createMemoryRouter`.

```typescript
// playwright/index.tsx  (browser-side — runs in the real browser)
import { beforeMount } from '@playwright/experimental-ct-react/hooks';
import { MemoryRouter } from 'react-router-dom';

export type HooksConfig = {
  initialRoute?: string;
};

beforeMount<HooksConfig>(async ({ App, hooksConfig }) => {
  return (
    <MemoryRouter initialEntries={[hooksConfig?.initialRoute ?? '/']}>
      <App />
    </MemoryRouter>
  );
});
```

```typescript
// ProductDetail.spec.tsx  (Node-side — test code)
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/experimental-ct-react';
import ProductDetail from './ProductDetail';

test('renders product detail at /products/42', async ({ mount }) => {
  const component = await mount<{ initialRoute: string }>(
    <ProductDetail productId="42" />,
    {
      hooksConfig: { initialRoute: '/products/42' },
    }
  );

  await expect(component.getByRole('heading', { level: 1 })).toContainText('Product 42');
  await expect(component.getByRole('link', { name: 'Back to catalog' })).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `hooksConfig` must be fully serializable (JSON-safe), because it is passed across the Node/browser boundary via Playwright's serialization layer. Passing functions, class instances, Symbols, or `Date` objects will either throw a serialization error or silently produce `{}` on the browser side. For complex test setups (e.g., a mock store with thunk middleware), define the shape of the mock state as a plain object in `hooksConfig` and reconstruct the store instance inside `beforeMount` — never pass the store object itself. This constraint also means `hooksConfig` cannot carry callbacks that the component would invoke synchronously; use `component.evaluate()` for post-mount assertions on component internals instead.

---

### Pattern 276 — Vitest Browser Mode `userEvent` Hover State Persistence Between Tests [official]

Vitest Browser Mode's `userEvent` instance (imported from `vitest/browser`) maintains pointer and keyboard state across calls within the same test and, critically, across tests if the state is not explicitly reset. The hover state in particular is not automatically cleared between tests: if a test ends while the pointer is positioned over an element (after `userEvent.hover(el)`), the next test starts with the hover state active, causing hover-triggered effects (tooltips, dropdown reveals, CSS `:hover` styles) to be visible from the first assertion. This is a systemic difference from `@testing-library/user-event` in jsdom mode, where the DOM is reconstructed between tests and hover state is implicitly reset. The fix is to call `userEvent.unhover(el)` in an `afterEach` hook, or call `userEvent.unhover(document.body)` as a general reset.

```typescript
import { describe, test, expect, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { userEvent, page } from 'vitest/browser';
import { render } from 'vitest-browser-react';
import { DropdownMenu } from './DropdownMenu';

describe('DropdownMenu', () => {
  // Reset hover state after every test to prevent state leakage
  afterEach(async () => {
    await userEvent.unhover(document.body);
  });

  test('shows tooltip on hover', async () => {
    const { getByRole, getByText } = render(<DropdownMenu />);
    const trigger = getByRole('button', { name: 'Options' });

    await userEvent.hover(trigger);
    await expect.element(getByText('Click to expand options')).toBeVisible();
    // hover state left active — afterEach will clear it
  });

  test('tooltip is not visible when not hovering', async () => {
    // Without afterEach cleanup, hover state from previous test
    // would cause this assertion to fail
    const { getByRole, queryByText } = render(<DropdownMenu />);
    await expect.element(getByRole('button', { name: 'Options' })).toBeVisible();
    // tooltip should NOT be visible — verifies clean state
    expect(queryByText('Click to expand options')).toBeNull();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** The `userEvent` instance from `vitest/browser` is a shared singleton within a test worker, not a per-test instance like `userEvent.setup()` in `@testing-library/user-event`. Creating a "fresh" instance via `userEvent.setup()` does not reset the physical pointer position in Browser Mode — only `userEvent.unhover()` or `userEvent.pointer('[PointerLeave]')` resets the pointer. Teams migrating from jsdom will discover this at the integration stage because local development often masks the issue (tests run in sequence and hover state happens to reset via page reload between test files), while parallel runs surface it as intermittent ordering-dependent failures.

---

### Pattern 277 — Vitest Browser Mode `vi.mock()` with `{ spy: true }` for Module Namespace Spying [official]

In Vitest Browser Mode, ES module namespaces are sealed — the module namespace object cannot be reconfigured after import, which means `vi.mock('module', factory)` with a custom factory that replaces exports causes an error because the namespace is read-only in the browser's module registry. The `{ spy: true }` option in `vi.mock('module', { spy: true })` works around this by wrapping the real module's exports in spy functions rather than replacing the module with a factory. This allows `vi.spyOn()` behavior (observe calls, assert arguments, optionally override return values) while keeping the original module implementation active by default. It is the only supported mocking strategy for modules in Vitest Browser Mode; `vi.mock('module', () => ({ fn: vi.fn() }))` throws.

```typescript
import { describe, test, expect, vi, beforeEach } from 'vitest';
import { render } from 'vitest-browser-react';
import { userEvent, page } from 'vitest/browser';
import * as analyticsModule from '../lib/analytics';
import { SignupForm } from './SignupForm';

// Browser mode: use { spy: true } — factory-based vi.mock() is not supported
vi.mock('../lib/analytics', { spy: true });

describe('SignupForm analytics', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    vi.clearAllMocks();
  });

  test('tracks signup_started event on form submission', async () => {
    const trackSpy = vi.spyOn(analyticsModule, 'track');

    render(<SignupForm />);
    await userEvent.fill(page.getByLabelText('Email'), 'user@example.com');
    await userEvent.click(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign up' }));

    expect(trackSpy).toHaveBeenCalledWith('signup_started', {
      email: 'user@example.com',
    });

    // Real implementation still runs — no behavioral side effects from mocking
    expect(trackSpy).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `{ spy: true }` retains the real module implementation, which means side effects (network calls, localStorage writes, timer registrations) still execute unless individually overridden with `vi.spyOn(module, 'fn').mockImplementation(...)`. For tests that must prevent all side effects (e.g., preventing analytics data from being sent to a real endpoint during testing), you still need to mock each exported function individually after the `{ spy: true }` import. This is more verbose than a factory mock but is the only correct approach in browser mode. Never use `vi.mock()` with a factory function in browser mode test files — the error message ("module namespace is sealed") is often confusing because it appears to implicate the module being mocked rather than the test's mocking strategy.

---

### Pattern 278 — Vitest Browser Mode `expect.element()` vs Standard `expect()` for Browser Locator Assertions [official]

Vitest Browser Mode introduces `expect.element(locator)` as the async-aware assertion wrapper for browser locators, distinct from standard `expect(value)`. The difference is that `expect.element(locator)` polls the locator with automatic retries (like Playwright's `expect(locator).toBeVisible()`), while `expect(locator)` treats the locator object itself as a plain value and asserts synchronously on its reference — which always passes for non-null locators regardless of DOM state. Teams migrating from JSDOM tests to browser mode frequently use `expect(el).toBeTruthy()` and find tests pass even when elements are absent, because `el` is a locator object (always truthy) rather than a DOM element reference. Always use `expect.element(locator).toBeVisible()` or `await expect.element(locator).toBeInTheDocument()` for browser mode DOM presence assertions.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from 'vitest';
import { page } from 'vitest/browser';
import { render } from 'vitest-browser-react';
import { Toast } from './Toast';

test('success toast appears after form submission', async () => {
  const { getByRole } = render(
    <Toast trigger={<button>Submit</button>} message="Saved!" />
  );

  // WRONG: synchronous expect on a locator object — always passes, tests nothing
  // expect(page.getByText('Saved!')).toBeTruthy();  // ← silent false positive

  // CORRECT: expect.element() polls with retry until timeout
  const submitBtn = getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' });
  await expect.element(submitBtn).toBeVisible();
  await submitBtn.click();

  // Asserts 'Saved!' text appears in the DOM, with automatic retry
  await expect.element(page.getByText('Saved!')).toBeVisible();

  // After the toast auto-dismisses, assert it is gone
  await expect.element(page.getByText('Saved!')).not.toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `expect.element()` is Vitest Browser Mode's equivalent to Playwright's `expect(locator)`, but the two APIs have different assertion method names. `expect.element(locator).toBeVisible()` in Vitest Browser Mode corresponds to `expect(locator).toBeVisible()` in Playwright. Teams using both Playwright CT and Vitest Browser Mode in the same monorepo will encounter assertion method mismatches because Playwright's assertions are on the locator directly while Vitest's are on the `expect.element()` wrapper. Establish a project-level convention: if using Playwright CT, use Playwright assertions throughout; if using Vitest Browser Mode, use `expect.element()` throughout — do not mix in the same test file.

---

### Pattern 279 — Playwright `testConfig.captureGitInfo` for Contextual Test Report Metadata [official]

`captureGitInfo: true` in `playwright.config.ts` (introduced in v1.51) instructs Playwright to capture the current Git commit hash, branch name, and optionally the commit message into test result metadata, making it available in the HTML report and JSON results. Test reports without this context are ambiguous when reviewing historical results — a "failing authentication test" could refer to any of dozens of commits. With `captureGitInfo`, every test run is anchored to the exact code snapshot it tested, enabling the report viewer to link failures to specific code changes. The captured data is available in `testResult.annotations` and in the HTML reporter's run summary, and is written into the JSON results file for ingestion by external dashboards.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // Capture git metadata for traceable test reports
  captureGitInfo: { commit: true, diff: false },
  // 'diff: true' would capture the full git diff — useful for PR-level testing
  // but creates very large report files for large changesets

  reporter: [
    ['html', { open: 'never', outputFolder: 'playwright-report' }],
    ['json', { outputFile: 'test-results/playwright-results.json' }],
  ],

  // Use --only-changed flag in CI to run only tests affected by the current diff
  // npx playwright test --only-changed=origin/main
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `captureGitInfo` requires the test to run inside a Git repository with a clean working tree — in detached-HEAD states (common in some CI systems that do a shallow clone), the branch name captured may be `HEAD` or empty rather than the PR branch name. Configure your CI to either do a full clone (`fetch-depth: 0` in GitHub Actions) or set the branch name explicitly via `process.env.GITHUB_HEAD_REF` in a custom reporter. The `diff: true` option captures the full `git diff` output, which can be megabytes for large refactors — only enable it if your test dashboard genuinely consumes the diff data, otherwise it bloats every test results artifact unnecessarily.

### Pattern 280 — Playwright `route.continue()` No Longer Accepts Cookie Header Overrides [official]

A breaking change in Playwright 1.52 prevents `route.continue({ headers: { Cookie: '...' } })` from overriding Cookie headers in continued requests. Previously, teams used this to inject test-specific session tokens into specific requests without modifying the browser context's cookie jar. The new behavior enforces that cookie management flows through `browserContext.addCookies()` / `browserContext.clearCookies()` rather than through header manipulation on individual routes, which aligns with browser security models (Cookie headers are "forbidden headers" in the Fetch spec and cannot be set by scripts in real browsers). Additionally, glob URL patterns in `page.route()` no longer accept `?` or `[]` characters — these must be replaced with regular expression route matchers.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('authenticated API call uses context cookies, not header injection', async ({ page, context }) => {
  // BROKEN in Playwright 1.52+: Cookie header override in route.continue()
  // await page.route('/api/user', async route => {
  //   await route.continue({ headers: { ...route.request().headers(), Cookie: 'session=abc123' } });
  // });

  // CORRECT: Set cookies via browserContext before navigating
  await context.addCookies([
    {
      name: 'session',
      value: 'abc123',
      domain: 'localhost',
      path: '/',
    },
  ]);

  await page.goto('/profile');
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Your Profile' })).toBeVisible();

  // BROKEN in 1.52+: glob pattern with ? or []
  // await page.route('/api/items?page=*', handler);  // ? in glob no longer works

  // CORRECT: use regex for query string patterns
  await page.route(/\/api\/items\?page=\d+/, async route => {
    await route.fulfill({ json: { items: [], total: 0 } });
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** This breaking change requires audit of any test that used `route.continue()` with Cookie header manipulation. The migration to `context.addCookies()` is straightforward for simple session tokens but requires more care for complex multi-cookie auth flows where different routes needed different cookie values. If you need per-request cookie values (e.g., testing CSRF token rotation), the correct approach is to use multiple browser contexts (one per auth state) rather than per-request cookie injection. The glob `?` and `[]` restriction only affects URL patterns passed as strings to `page.route()` — regex patterns are unaffected and are now the recommended approach for URL patterns containing query strings or character sets.

### Real-World Gotchas (Cycle 47)

186. **Playwright `toContainClass()` passes when the element's `className` is not a DOMTokenList — in React's JSDOM test environment, synthetic DOM elements sometimes expose `className` as a plain string rather than a space-delimited token list, and `toContainClass('done')` will match as a substring check rather than a token check, causing `toContainClass('don')` to incorrectly pass for elements with `class="done"` because the assertion falls back to string containment** [official] — WHY: Playwright's `toContainClass()` is designed for the real browser where `classList` is a native `DOMTokenList`, and the assertion tokenizes the class string by splitting on whitespace. In environments where the DOM implementation deviates from the browser spec (JSDOM versions before 20.x), the tokenization may behave differently for Unicode class names or class names with leading/trailing spaces. Fix: always run `toContainClass()` assertions against real browser contexts (using Playwright's actual browser, not JSDOM), and validate that your element's class attribute is space-normalized before asserting. This is not an issue in production Playwright E2E tests but can appear in Playwright CT tests running against a synthetic DOM.

187. **Playwright ARIA snapshot `/children: equal` causes every test to fail after a feature-flag-gated UI item is added to a list — the team adds an "Admin" tab behind a `FEATURE_FLAG_ADMIN=true` environment variable, but all ARIA snapshot tests in the PR fail in CI because CI does not set the flag, yet the developer who wrote the tests had the flag enabled locally and committed a snapshot that includes the Admin tab** [official] — WHY: `/children: equal` records the exact children present at snapshot-generation time. If the developer generated the snapshot with the feature flag enabled, the baseline includes the "Admin" tab. In CI without the flag, only N-1 tabs exist, which fails the strict child count. The snapshot update flow (`--update-snapshots=changed`) only helps if the CI environment runs the update — it won't help if the mismatch is environmental (flag-dependent), because there is no single "correct" baseline. Fix: never generate ARIA snapshots (or visual screenshots) in developer environments where feature flags differ from CI. Use a dedicated `playwright.config.snapshot.ts` that forces all flags to their CI values before snapshot generation.

188. **Vitest Browser Mode `userEvent.type()` and `userEvent.fill()` behave identically for inputs with `maxlength` in jsdom but diverge in Browser Mode — `fill()` bypasses `maxlength` enforcement in some browser versions (it sets the value programmatically via the CDP `Input.insertText` protocol, which does not fire the browser's native truncation logic), while `type()` respects `maxlength` because it simulates individual keystrokes that trigger the native input event handler** [community] — WHY: `userEvent.fill()` in Vitest Browser Mode maps to Playwright's `locator.fill()` under the hood when using the Playwright provider, which uses the Chrome DevTools Protocol `Input.insertText` command. CDP's `insertText` bypasses the browser's native form validation event chain, including `maxlength` truncation. The `maxlength` attribute is enforced by the browser's native keypress handler, not by the `input` event listener — so any method that sets the value without simulating keystrokes will bypass it. Fix: use `userEvent.type()` in tests that assert `maxlength` enforcement, and add an explicit assertion (`expect(input.value.length).toBeLessThanOrEqual(maxLength)`) to make the constraint visible in the test.

189. **Playwright `test.step()` with `timeout` set lower than the time required for a locator's automatic retry can cause confusing "step timed out" errors that appear to indicate a missing element when the element is actually present but slow to appear — the step timeout fires before Playwright's locator retry logic completes, and the error message reports the locator assertion's last-known state (element not found) rather than "step timed out"** [official] — WHY: Playwright's locator retry loop uses the remaining time in the assertion's timeout configuration, not the test timeout. When a step has its own `timeout`, the step's timer does not automatically propagate into the locator assertions inside it as an updated `{ timeout }` option. The locator assertion uses its own configured timeout (from `expect.configure({ timeout })` or from `test.use({ actionTimeout })`), which may exceed the step timeout. Result: the step timer fires mid-assertion-retry, aborting the retry loop with a step timeout error. Fix: always set locator assertion timeouts within a step to be less than the step timeout, either by passing `{ timeout }` explicitly to each `expect()` call or by using `test.use({ expect: { timeout: N } })` in the step scope with the step timeout minus a safety margin.

190. **Playwright `storageState({ indexedDB: true })` captures the IndexedDB snapshot asynchronously but returns the captured state synchronously via the resolved promise — if the application has an in-flight IndexedDB `put()` operation at the moment `storageState()` is called (e.g., because the login response triggers a background token refresh that writes to IndexedDB), the captured state may contain the pre-refresh token, causing auth tests to fail with 401 responses after restoration because the expired token was captured** [official] — WHY: IndexedDB transactions are atomic but asynchronous — a `put()` call submits a transaction that may not be committed to the IndexedDB store by the time Playwright reads the store for `storageState()`. Playwright reads the IndexedDB state at a moment in time via CDP, and if a write transaction is open but uncommitted, the CDP read sees the pre-transaction state. The restored context therefore has the pre-write token value. Fix: add `await page.waitForFunction(() => !window._pendingIndexedDBWrite)` (or equivalent application-specific signal) before calling `storageState()`, and consider adding a deliberate `waitForTimeout(200)` as a last resort if no application-level signal is available. The root cause is the application's failure to expose an observable "auth ready" state — file this as an application bug as well as a test setup concern.
