### Pattern 326 — Playwright Page Object Model for Maintainable E2E Suites [official]

A Page Object Model (POM) encapsulates all locators and interaction methods for a given page or component into a TypeScript class. Rather than scattering `page.getByRole(...)` calls throughout test files, each page surface owns its selectors. When the DOM changes, only the POM class needs updating — not every test file that touches that surface. The Playwright documentation explicitly recommends this pattern for test suites that will grow beyond a few dozen tests.

```typescript
// tests/pages/checkout.page.ts
import { type Page, type Locator } from '@playwright/test';

export class CheckoutPage {
  readonly page: Page;
  readonly emailInput: Locator;
  readonly submitButton: Locator;
  readonly orderConfirmation: Locator;

  constructor(page: Page) {
    this.page = page;
    this.emailInput = page.getByLabel('Email address');
    this.submitButton = page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' });
    this.orderConfirmation = page.getByRole('heading', { name: /Order confirmed/i });
  }

  async placeOrder(email: string): Promise<void> {
    await this.emailInput.fill(email);
    await this.submitButton.click();
    await this.orderConfirmation.waitFor();
  }
}

// tests/checkout.e2e.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { CheckoutPage } from './pages/checkout.page';

test('completes order for valid email', async ({ page }) => {
  const checkout = new CheckoutPage(page);
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await checkout.placeOrder('buyer@example.com');
  await expect(checkout.orderConfirmation).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** POMs centralise selector maintenance but can grow into bloated "God objects" when a page has many interactions. Prefer composing small, focused page fragments (e.g., `HeaderFragment`, `CartWidget`) over single all-encompassing page classes. Avoid adding assertions inside POM methods — keep assertion logic in test files so failures surface at the right stack frame.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 327 — Playwright Fixture Scoping: `worker` vs `test` for Expensive Setup [official]

Playwright test fixtures support two scopes: `test` (default, set up and torn down per test) and `worker` (set up once per worker process, shared across tests in that worker). For expensive operations like launching a real database, seeding reference data, or performing an authenticated sign-in, using `worker` scope dramatically reduces total test time. Worker-scoped fixtures are isolated per CPU worker, so parallel workers do not share state.

```typescript
// tests/fixtures/db.ts
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';
import { createTestDatabase, destroyTestDatabase, type TestDb } from '../helpers/db';

type WorkerFixtures = { db: TestDb };

export const test = base.extend<{}, WorkerFixtures>({
  db: [
    async ({}, use) => {
      // Runs ONCE per worker — not once per test
      const db = await createTestDatabase();
      await db.seed({ users: 10, products: 50 });
      await use(db);
      await destroyTestDatabase(db);
    },
    { scope: 'worker' },
  ],
});

// tests/products.integration.ts
import { test } from './fixtures/db';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('seed products appear in search API', async ({ db, request }) => {
  const res = await request.get('/api/products?q=item');
  const body = await res.json();
  expect(body.total).toBeGreaterThan(0);
  // db was seeded once when this worker started — no per-test cost
});

test('pagination returns correct page size', async ({ db, request }) => {
  const res = await request.get('/api/products?page=1&limit=10');
  const body = await res.json();
  expect(body.items).toHaveLength(10);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Worker-scoped fixtures trade test isolation for speed. If one test mutates the shared resource (e.g., deletes a seeded product), subsequent tests in the same worker may fail with unexpected state. Design worker-scoped fixtures as read-only shared baselines; use test-scoped fixtures for any state that must be mutated.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 328 — Vitest `vi.stubEnv()` for Isolated Environment Variable Unit Tests [official]

`vi.stubEnv(key, value)` replaces a `process.env` variable for the duration of a test without touching the global environment of other tests. Unlike directly assigning `process.env.MY_VAR = 'x'` (which leaks across tests if `afterEach` cleanup is forgotten), `vi.stubEnv()` is automatically restored when `vi.unstubAllEnvs()` is called or when `restoreAllMocks: true` is configured globally. This makes it the correct approach for unit-testing configuration loaders, feature flags, and environment-gated code paths.

```typescript
// src/config.ts
export function getDatabaseUrl(): string {
  const url = process.env.DATABASE_URL;
  if (!url) throw new Error('DATABASE_URL is required');
  return url;
}

export function isFeatureEnabled(flag: string): boolean {
  return process.env[`FEATURE_${flag.toUpperCase()}`] === 'true';
}

// src/config.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, vi, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { getDatabaseUrl, isFeatureEnabled } from './config';

afterEach(() => {
  vi.unstubAllEnvs(); // restore originals after each test
});

describe('getDatabaseUrl', () => {
  it('returns the configured URL', () => {
    vi.stubEnv('DATABASE_URL', 'postgres://localhost/test');
    expect(getDatabaseUrl()).toBe('postgres://localhost/test');
  });

  it('throws when DATABASE_URL is absent', () => {
    vi.stubEnv('DATABASE_URL', '');
    expect(() => getDatabaseUrl()).toThrow('DATABASE_URL is required');
  });
});

describe('isFeatureEnabled', () => {
  it('returns true when flag env var is "true"', () => {
    vi.stubEnv('FEATURE_DARK_MODE', 'true');
    expect(isFeatureEnabled('dark_mode')).toBe(true);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `vi.stubEnv()` only affects `process.env` reads that happen at call time. Modules that cache environment variables at import time (e.g., `const DB_URL = process.env.DATABASE_URL` at the module top level) will not see the stubbed value unless the module is also re-imported or re-evaluated. For cached values, combine `vi.stubEnv()` with `vi.resetModules()` and a dynamic `import()` within the test.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 329 — Playwright Parameterized Tests with `test.describe()` and Data Arrays [official]

Playwright supports data-driven tests by iterating over an array inside a `test.describe()` block. Each iteration creates an independent test entry in the reporter, with its own pass/fail state, trace, and screenshot. This pattern is preferable to a loop inside a single test (which produces a single pass/fail entry for all iterations), because it surfaces which specific input combination failed.

```typescript
// tests/form-validation.e2e.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

const invalidEmailCases = [
  { input: 'notanemail', description: 'plain string without @' },
  { input: '@nodomain', description: 'missing local part' },
  { input: 'user@', description: 'missing domain' },
  { input: '', description: 'empty string' },
];

for (const { input, description } of invalidEmailCases) {
  test(`shows validation error for ${description}`, async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/signup');
    await page.getByLabel('Email').fill(input);
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Continue' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toContainText('Enter a valid email');
  });
}

// Data-driven with CSV-style external input (Node.js file system access)
import { readFileSync } from 'fs';
import { parse } from 'csv-parse/sync';

const rows: Array<{ sku: string; price: string }> = parse(
  readFileSync('./tests/fixtures/products.csv'),
  { columns: true, skip_empty_lines: true },
);

for (const { sku, price } of rows) {
  test(`product page renders correct price for SKU ${sku}`, async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto(`/products/${sku}`);
    await expect(page.getByTestId('price')).toHaveText(`$${price}`);
  });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Generating hundreds of parameterized tests from large data files can make test suites slow and reporters hard to read. Prefer parameterized tests for boundary-value and equivalence-class inputs (5–20 cases); use a single integration test with a loop for exhaustive data validation where individual failure isolation is less important. Never store secrets or PII in fixture CSV files committed to source control.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 330 — Vitest Browser Mode Component Testing with `vitest-browser-react` [official]

Vitest's browser mode runs tests inside a real Chromium, Firefox, or WebKit browser instance (via Playwright or WebdriverIO provider), enabling component tests that exercise real browser APIs without jsdom approximations. The `vitest-browser-react` package provides a `render()` function and locator utilities compatible with Playwright's locator API, allowing assertions on actual DOM state.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    projects: [
      { test: { name: 'unit', environment: 'node' } },
      {
        test: {
          name: 'browser',
          browser: {
            enabled: true,
            provider: 'playwright',
            instances: [{ browser: 'chromium' }],
            headless: true,
          },
          include: ['src/**/*.browser.test.tsx'],
        },
      },
    ],
  },
});

// src/components/Toggle.browser.test.tsx
import { render } from 'vitest-browser-react';
import { expect, test } from 'vitest';
import { Toggle } from './Toggle';

test('Toggle emits onChange with new value when clicked', async () => {
  const onChange = vi.fn();
  const { getByRole } = render(<Toggle checked={false} onChange={onChange} />);

  const button = getByRole('switch');
  await button.click();

  expect(onChange).toHaveBeenCalledWith(true);
  await expect.element(button).toHaveAttribute('aria-checked', 'true');
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Browser mode tests are 5–20x slower than jsdom-based tests because each test file requires a browser context. Reserve browser mode for components that use browser-only APIs (e.g., `IntersectionObserver`, `ResizeObserver`, `CSS.supports()`, Web Audio) or CSS-dependent interactions that jsdom cannot faithfully simulate. For pure React rendering logic, jsdom (via `@testing-library/react`) is faster and sufficient.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 331 — Jest `moduleNameMapper` for Path Alias Resolution in Test Suites [official]

TypeScript projects using `tsconfig.json` path aliases (e.g., `@/components/*`) must configure `moduleNameMapper` in Jest so the test runner can resolve the same aliases. Without this, Jest throws `Cannot find module '@/components/Button'` errors even though the application compiles correctly with `tsc`. The mapper uses a regex-to-replacement pattern that mirrors the `paths` section of `tsconfig.json`.

```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'jest';
import { pathsToModuleNameMapper } from 'ts-jest';
import { compilerOptions } from './tsconfig.json';

export default defineConfig({
  preset: 'ts-jest',
  testEnvironment: 'jsdom',
  // Automatically generate moduleNameMapper entries from tsconfig paths
  moduleNameMapper: {
    ...pathsToModuleNameMapper(compilerOptions.paths, { prefix: '<rootDir>/' }),
    // Static asset stubs — Jest cannot process image/CSS imports
    '\\.(jpg|jpeg|png|gif|svg|webp)$': '<rootDir>/__mocks__/fileMock.ts',
    '\\.(css|scss|less)$': 'identity-obj-proxy',
  },
  // Ensure rootDir is set so <rootDir> token resolves correctly
  rootDir: '.',
  setupFilesAfterFramework: ['<rootDir>/jest.setup.ts'],
  coverageThreshold: {
    global: { branches: 80, functions: 80, lines: 80 },
  },
});

// __mocks__/fileMock.ts
export default 'test-file-stub';
```

**Tradeoff.** `pathsToModuleNameMapper` from `ts-jest` is convenient but adds a compile-time dependency on `ts-jest` even when using `babel-jest` as the primary transformer. An alternative is to maintain `moduleNameMapper` entries manually, which is more explicit but requires keeping them in sync with `tsconfig.json` paths. When using Vitest, `vite.config.ts` `resolve.alias` is read automatically — this Jest-specific workaround is not needed.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 332 — Playwright `expect.soft()` for Multi-Assertion Test Cases [official]

`expect.soft()` marks an assertion as non-fatal: if it fails, the test continues executing subsequent assertions rather than terminating immediately. Playwright collects all soft failures and reports them together at the end of the test. This pattern is valuable for visual validation or data-completeness checks where you want to see all failures in a single run rather than fixing one assertion, re-running, and discovering the next failure.

```typescript
// tests/product-detail.e2e.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('product detail page displays all required fields', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/products/widget-pro-2000');

  // Soft assertions — test continues even if some fail
  await expect.soft(page.getByRole('heading', { level: 1 }))
    .toContainText('Widget Pro 2000');
  await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('product-price'))
    .toHaveText(/\$\d+\.\d{2}/);
  await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('stock-status'))
    .toHaveText(/In stock|Out of stock/);
  await expect.soft(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' }))
    .toBeEnabled();
  await expect.soft(page.getByAltText('Widget Pro 2000'))
    .toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('product-description'))
    .not.toBeEmpty();

  // This hard assertion acts as the final gate — ensures page fully loaded
  // even if soft assertions above failed
  await expect(page.getByTestId('product-sku')).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Overusing soft assertions can mask systemic failures — if 5 of 6 assertions fail, the test still "passes" the hard assertion gate and the run succeeds at the test level. Reserve `expect.soft()` for independent field-level checks where each assertion is self-contained. For sequential interactions where a later step depends on an earlier step succeeding (e.g., clicking a button that only appears after a form validates), use hard assertions to fail fast before attempting dependent actions.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 333 — Vitest `vi.spyOn()` with `using` for Automatic Cleanup (Explicit Resource Management) [official]

TypeScript 5.2+ added the `using` keyword for deterministic resource cleanup via the `Symbol.dispose` protocol. Vitest 3.2+ supports `using vi.spyOn(...)` — the spy is automatically restored when the enclosing block exits, eliminating the need for a manual `vi.restoreAllMocks()` call in `afterEach`. This is especially useful in test helpers and shared fixtures where forgetting cleanup causes test pollution across files.

```typescript
// src/analytics/tracker.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, vi } from 'vitest';
import { trackEvent } from './tracker';
import * as http from '../lib/http';

describe('trackEvent', () => {
  it('sends POST to /analytics endpoint with event payload', async () => {
    // Automatic spy restoration when this block exits
    using postSpy = vi.spyOn(http, 'post').mockResolvedValue({ ok: true });

    await trackEvent('button_click', { buttonId: 'cta-hero' });

    expect(postSpy).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
    expect(postSpy).toHaveBeenCalledWith('/analytics', {
      event: 'button_click',
      properties: { buttonId: 'cta-hero' },
      timestamp: expect.any(Number),
    });
    // No afterEach needed — postSpy.mockRestore() called automatically
  });

  it('does not throw when analytics endpoint is unavailable', async () => {
    using _ = vi.spyOn(http, 'post').mockRejectedValue(new Error('Network error'));

    // trackEvent should swallow analytics errors gracefully
    await expect(trackEvent('page_view', {})).resolves.toBeUndefined();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** The `using` keyword requires TypeScript 5.2+ with `"lib": ["ES2023"]` or `"target": "ES2022"` and the `Symbol.dispose` polyfill for environments that do not yet support it natively. The explicit resource management syntax is unfamiliar to developers not yet using TypeScript 5.2+ features. As a fallback, `vi.spyOn()` without `using` combined with `afterEach(() => vi.restoreAllMocks())` at the suite level remains equivalent and widely understood.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 334 — Jest `fakeTimers` with `doNotFake` for Selective Timer Mocking [official]

Jest's `fakeTimers` configuration replaces global timer functions (`setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `Date`) with controllable fakes. However, mocking all timers globally can break libraries that rely on real `nextTick` or `Promise` resolution order. The `doNotFake` array selects which timer primitives to leave real while faking the rest — a critical escape hatch when testing code that mixes custom timeouts with Promise chains.

```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'jest';
export default defineConfig({
  fakeTimers: {
    enableGlobally: true,
    // Leave nextTick and Promise resolution real so async/await chains work
    doNotFake: ['nextTick', 'queueMicrotask'],
    // Limit runaway timer loops during development
    timerLimit: 1000,
    legacyFakeTimers: false, // use modern @sinonjs/fake-timers
  },
});

// src/retry.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, jest } from '@jest/globals';
import { retryWithBackoff } from './retry';

describe('retryWithBackoff', () => {
  it('retries up to maxAttempts and then rejects', async () => {
    const fn = jest.fn().mockRejectedValue(new Error('Service unavailable'));

    const resultPromise = retryWithBackoff(fn, {
      maxAttempts: 3,
      baseDelayMs: 1000,
    });

    // Advance timers to trigger each retry interval
    await jest.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(1000); // first retry after 1s
    await jest.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(2000); // second retry after 2s
    await jest.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(4000); // third retry after 4s

    await expect(resultPromise).rejects.toThrow('Service unavailable');
    expect(fn).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `enableGlobally: true` applies fake timers to every test in the suite, which can cause subtle ordering bugs in tests that mix real async I/O with timer advances. For suites where only a minority of tests need timer control, prefer enabling fake timers per-test with `jest.useFakeTimers()` in `beforeEach` and restoring with `jest.useRealTimers()` in `afterEach`. The `legacyFakeTimers: false` default is strongly recommended — legacy Sinon-based timers are deprecated and lack `jest.advanceTimersByTimeAsync()`.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 335 — Playwright `test.step()` for Structured E2E Test Reporting [official]

`test.step(name, fn)` groups related actions within a test into a named step visible in the HTML reporter, trace viewer, and JUnit XML output. Steps create a hierarchical structure in test reports, making long e2e tests easier to diagnose — instead of a long undifferentiated sequence of actions, the trace shows `"Step 1: Sign in" → "Step 2: Navigate to checkout" → "Step 3: Submit order"`. Steps can be nested and are included in retry traces.

```typescript
// tests/purchase-flow.e2e.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('authenticated user can complete a purchase end to end', async ({ page }) => {
  await test.step('Sign in as returning customer', async () => {
    await page.goto('/login');
    await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('customer@example.com');
    await page.getByLabel('Password').fill(process.env.TEST_PASSWORD!);
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Dashboard' })).toBeVisible();
  });

  await test.step('Add product to cart', async () => {
    await page.goto('/products/widget-pro');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toContainText('1 item in cart');
  });

  await test.step('Complete checkout', async () => {
    await page.goto('/checkout');
    await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4242 4242 4242 4242');
    await page.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('12/30');
    await page.getByLabel('CVC').fill('123');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay now' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /Order #\d+/ })).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Excessive nesting of `test.step()` calls (more than 3–4 levels deep) produces trace trees that are harder to navigate than flat action sequences. Use steps to annotate *phases* of a test (setup, action, verify) rather than wrapping individual locator calls. `test.step()` does not create test isolation — a failure in step 2 aborts steps 3 onward unless `{ continue: true }` is passed; this is intentional and correct for sequential user flows.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 336 — Vitest `sequence.groupOrder` for Fail-Fast Integration Test Ordering [official]

Vitest 3.2+ introduced `sequence.groupOrder` in the `test.projects` configuration, allowing you to specify that certain project groups (e.g., unit tests) must complete before others (e.g., integration tests) begin. This replaces the fragile `&&`-chained CI commands (`vitest run --project unit && vitest run --project integration`) with a single `vitest run` invocation that respects ordering, shares startup overhead, and produces a unified coverage report.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    projects: [
      {
        test: {
          name: 'unit',
          include: ['src/**/*.unit.test.ts'],
          environment: 'node',
          sequence: { groupOrder: 1 }, // run first
        },
      },
      {
        test: {
          name: 'integration',
          include: ['src/**/*.integration.test.ts'],
          environment: 'node',
          sequence: { groupOrder: 2 }, // run only if unit group passes
        },
      },
      {
        test: {
          name: 'contract',
          include: ['src/**/*.contract.test.ts'],
          environment: 'node',
          sequence: { groupOrder: 3 }, // run only if integration group passes
        },
      },
    ],
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      // Unified coverage report across all three groups
      include: ['src/**/*.ts'],
      exclude: ['src/**/*.test.ts'],
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `sequence.groupOrder` enforces sequential execution between groups, which increases total wall-clock time compared to running all tests in parallel. This is the intended trade-off — the goal is to fail fast at the cheapest level before spending CI time on expensive integration or contract tests. Within each group, tests still run in parallel across available workers. For projects where unit tests are very fast (< 5s) relative to integration tests (> 60s), the fail-fast benefit far outweighs the parallelism loss.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 337 — Playwright Network API: `page.routeFromHAR()` for Deterministic API Testing [official]

`page.routeFromHAR(harPath, options)` plays back a recorded HAR file as the network layer for an e2e test, replacing all matching API requests with the pre-recorded responses. Unlike `page.route()` handler stubs that must be maintained manually, HAR files capture the exact shape of real API responses (headers, status codes, timing) and can be re-recorded when the API changes. The `notFound: 'abort'` option ensures unexpected new API calls fail the test rather than silently hitting the network.

```typescript
// tests/dashboard.e2e.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';

test.use({
  // All tests in this file use recorded API responses
  baseURL: 'http://localhost:3000',
});

test('dashboard renders analytics widgets from recorded API data', async ({ page }) => {
  // Play back recorded API responses — no live network calls
  await page.routeFromHAR(
    path.join(__dirname, 'fixtures/dashboard-api.har'),
    {
      url: '**/api/**',
      // Abort any API call not present in the HAR — prevents silent real calls
      notFound: 'abort',
      // Update HAR on next record run: npx playwright test --update-snapshots
      update: process.env.UPDATE_HAR === 'true',
    },
  );

  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  await expect(page.getByTestId('revenue-widget')).toContainText('$12,450');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('users-widget')).toContainText('1,234 active');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('conversion-widget')).toContainText('3.2%');
});
```

**Tradeoff.** HAR files are binary-adjacent JSON blobs that produce noisy diffs in pull requests when the API changes. Store HAR files in a dedicated `tests/fixtures/` directory and add a CI check that verifies HAR files are up to date (run with `UPDATE_HAR=true` and assert no git diff). The `update: true` flag in `routeFromHAR()` re-records responses against the live API during a designated refresh run. HAR replay is strongest for stable, well-defined API contracts; use `page.route()` stubs for edge cases and error conditions that are hard to record naturally.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 338 — Vitest V8 Coverage with `/* v8 ignore */` for Defensive Branches [official]

Vitest's V8 coverage provider (default since Vitest 3.x) tracks branch coverage at the V8 bytecode level without requiring source instrumentation. When a branch is intentionally unreachable (e.g., an exhaustive switch default, a TypeScript narrowing guard, an emergency fallback), annotate it with `/* v8 ignore next N */` to exclude it from coverage metrics rather than writing a contrived test that exercises an impossible code path.

```typescript
// src/formatters/currency.ts
export function formatCurrency(
  amount: number,
  currency: 'USD' | 'EUR' | 'GBP',
): string {
  switch (currency) {
    case 'USD': return `$${amount.toFixed(2)}`;
    case 'EUR': return `€${amount.toFixed(2)}`;
    case 'GBP': return `£${amount.toFixed(2)}`;
    /* v8 ignore next 3 -- @preserve
       TypeScript exhaustive check: this branch is unreachable at runtime */
    default: {
      const _exhaustive: never = currency;
      throw new Error(`Unknown currency: ${String(_exhaustive)}`);
    }
  }
}

// src/formatters/currency.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { formatCurrency } from './currency';

describe('formatCurrency', () => {
  it.each([
    ['USD', 42.5, '$42.50'],
    ['EUR', 42.5, '€42.50'],
    ['GBP', 42.5, '£42.50'],
  ] as const)('formats %s correctly', (currency, amount, expected) => {
    expect(formatCurrency(amount, currency)).toBe(expected);
  });
  // No test for the `default` branch — it is intentionally excluded via
  // the v8 ignore comment above
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `/* v8 ignore */` comments bypass coverage reporting for annotated lines — they do not express intent about why the branch is excluded. Over-annotating production code with ignore comments to hit coverage thresholds is a coverage gaming anti-pattern. Reserve ignore annotations for truly unreachable branches (TypeScript exhaustive checks, error guards that protect against impossible runtime states, polyfill detection branches). For Istanbul provider, use `/* istanbul ignore next */` instead; the syntax is not interchangeable.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 339 — Narrow Integration Tests: Testing Database Interactions in Isolation [community]

The Practical Test Pyramid pattern for "narrow integration tests" focuses each test on a single integration point — typically a repository or DAO class that wraps database queries. The test starts a real (or containerised) database, executes the production code under test, then inspects the actual stored state. This approach provides high confidence in data persistence logic without the overhead of a full application context, and catches ORM-generated SQL issues, constraint violations, and serialisation bugs that unit tests with mock repositories cannot detect.

```typescript
// src/repositories/order.repository.integration.test.ts
import { beforeAll, afterAll, beforeEach, describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/postgres-js';
import postgres from 'postgres';
import { orders, orderItems } from '../db/schema';
import { OrderRepository } from './order.repository';

let db: ReturnType<typeof drizzle>;
let sql: ReturnType<typeof postgres>;
let repo: OrderRepository;

beforeAll(async () => {
  // Use a dedicated test database (set via TEST_DATABASE_URL env var)
  sql = postgres(process.env.TEST_DATABASE_URL!);
  db = drizzle(sql);
  repo = new OrderRepository(db);
});

afterAll(async () => {
  await sql.end();
});

beforeEach(async () => {
  // Wipe tables before each test to ensure isolation
  await db.delete(orderItems);
  await db.delete(orders);
});

describe('OrderRepository.create', () => {
  it('persists order and related items in a single transaction', async () => {
    const created = await repo.create({
      customerId: 'cust-1',
      items: [
        { sku: 'widget-pro', quantity: 2, unitPrice: 49.99 },
        { sku: 'widget-lite', quantity: 1, unitPrice: 19.99 },
      ],
    });

    expect(created.id).toMatch(/^ord_/);
    const fetched = await repo.findById(created.id);
    expect(fetched?.items).toHaveLength(2);
    expect(fetched?.total).toBeCloseTo(119.97, 2);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Narrow integration tests are slower than unit tests (database I/O adds 10–200ms per test) and require a running database. Use a containerised database (Testcontainers, Docker Compose) in CI to avoid hard environment dependencies. The `beforeEach` truncation pattern ensures isolation but is slow for large schemas — prefer wrapping tests in a transaction that is rolled back (using Drizzle's `db.transaction()` with an explicit rollback) for faster isolation on large test suites.

**Tag:** [community]

---

### Pattern 340 — Test Pyramid Anti-Pattern: Over-Mocking at the Integration Layer [community]

A common anti-pattern discovered in real-world codebases is applying unit-test-level mocking strategies (mocking every collaborator) to what should be integration tests. When integration tests mock the database, the HTTP client, and the message queue, they test only wiring — the same thing unit tests already verify. This produces a "mock soup" that gives false confidence: the test passes even when the real integration point has a schema mismatch, a missing index, or a broken serialiser.

```typescript
// ANTI-PATTERN: Integration test that mocks everything — provides no integration value
import { describe, it, expect, vi } from 'vitest';
import { OrderService } from './order.service';
import { OrderRepository } from './order.repository';
import { EmailService } from './email.service';

vi.mock('./order.repository');
vi.mock('./email.service');

describe('OrderService — ANTI-PATTERN', () => {
  it('calls repository.create and email.send on placeOrder', async () => {
    const mockRepo = { create: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue({ id: 'ord_1' }) };
    const mockEmail = { send: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(undefined) };
    const service = new OrderService(mockRepo as any, mockEmail as any);

    await service.placeOrder({ customerId: 'c1', items: [] });

    // This only proves that service calls repo.create — not that the DB accepts the data
    expect(mockRepo.create).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
    expect(mockEmail.send).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
  });
});

// CORRECT PATTERN: Integration test uses real DB + stubs only external side-effects
import { EmailService } from './email.service';

vi.mock('./email.service'); // stub side-effect only — email is not the subject under test

describe('OrderService — correct integration test', () => {
  it('persists order in real database via placeOrder', async () => {
    const repo = new OrderRepository(testDb); // real DB connection
    const emailStub = { send: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(undefined) };
    const service = new OrderService(repo, emailStub as any);

    const result = await service.placeOrder({
      customerId: 'cust-1',
      items: [{ sku: 'widget', quantity: 1, unitPrice: 49.99 }],
    });

    // Assert real database state — this is what integration tests are for
    const persisted = await repo.findById(result.id);
    expect(persisted).not.toBeNull();
    expect(persisted!.items).toHaveLength(1);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Removing mocks from integration tests requires a real (or containerised) database and increases test runtime. Teams under time pressure often resist this change. The key insight from Fowler's Practical Test Pyramid: "every time you use a mock or stub in an integration test, you're reducing the confidence that test provides." The fix is not to delete integration tests but to make them genuinely integrate — mock only external systems outside your control (third-party APIs, email providers), and use real implementations for everything within your deployment boundary.

**Tag:** [community]

---

### Real-World Gotchas (Cycle 51)

206. **Vitest `vi.stubGlobal()` does not restore the original value on `vi.unstubAllGlobals()` when the global was never defined on the object before stubbing — if you stub a global like `window.matchMedia` that was not previously present in the jsdom environment, `unstubAllGlobals()` deletes the property entirely rather than restoring `undefined`, causing subsequent tests that check `'matchMedia' in window` to return `false` instead of `true` even after the stub is removed** [community] — WHY: `vi.stubGlobal(key, value)` saves the original value with `Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor` before setting the new one. If the property did not exist, the saved descriptor is `undefined`. When `unstubAllGlobals()` runs, it attempts to restore descriptors — but restoring an `undefined` descriptor calls `delete target[key]`, removing the property entirely. This is semantically correct (the property was not there before), but code that checks for the property's *existence* after restoration sees a different result than code that checks for `undefined` as a value. Fix: define the global in `vitest.setup.ts` with an initial value before any tests run (e.g., `Object.defineProperty(window, 'matchMedia', { value: undefined, writable: true })`), so `stubGlobal` always has an existing descriptor to restore.

207. **Playwright `test.step()` with `{ continue: true }` does not propagate step failure details to the parent test's error message when all steps succeed or fail — only the last failed step's error is surfaced in the test report summary, so when multiple steps fail in a `continue: true` block, only the final failure is visible in the one-line test failure message in CI output; the full list of failures requires opening the HTML reporter or trace file** [community] — WHY: Playwright's test runner truncates the failure message in the summary to the most recently thrown error. Steps using `{ continue: true }` collect errors internally, but the test's top-level `.error` property is set to the last error encountered before the test function returned. The HTML reporter and trace viewer show all step errors in their step hierarchy view, but the JUnit XML and GitHub Actions summary annotation only show the final error. Fix: after a block of `{ continue: true }` steps, add an explicit assertion summarising all expected conditions (e.g., `expect(page.getByTestId('error-summary')).toBeHidden()`) to produce a single definitive failure message; or use `expect.soft()` which was specifically designed for this use case and integrates better with the summary reporter.

208. **Jest `fakeTimers` with `enableGlobally: true` breaks `msw` (Mock Service Worker) network interception — MSW v2.x uses a `MessageChannel` internally to communicate between the service worker and the test process; when global fake timers replace the `MessageChannel` constructor, MSW's channel message delivery is deferred indefinitely (until `jest.runAllTimers()` is called), causing all mocked API requests in tests to hang and timeout rather than resolving with the mocked response** [community] — WHY: `MessageChannel` is used by MSW's request/response pipeline to bridge the worker thread and the test thread. Jest's fake timer implementation replaces `MessageChannel` with a fake that queues messages rather than delivering them immediately. Since tests do not know to call `jest.runAllTimers()` in the middle of an `await fetch()` call, the message is never delivered and the request hangs. Fix: add `'MessageChannel'` to the `doNotFake` array in Jest's `fakeTimers` configuration; this exempts `MessageChannel` from replacement while still faking `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, and `Date`. Vitest's fake timer implementation has the same issue — add `'MessageChannel'` to `vi.useFakeTimers({ toFake: [...] })` exclusions.

209. **Playwright `page.routeFromHAR()` with `update: true` writes the updated HAR file with all network requests including analytics, telemetry, and cookie-sync calls from third-party scripts — these non-API requests inflate the HAR file size by 10–50x and cause subsequent HAR replay to abort on analytics calls (when `notFound: 'abort'` is set) because the recorded analytics URL is no longer present in the HAR after the third-party script changes its endpoint** [community] — WHY: `routeFromHAR()` with a URL glob pattern (e.g., `url: '**/api/**'`) only *plays back* matching requests from the HAR, but when `update: true` is set and recording, Playwright records ALL network requests made during the test — including requests that do not match the `url` filter. The result is a HAR full of irrelevant third-party calls. Fix: use `page.route()` to block analytics/telemetry domains before calling `routeFromHAR()` — Playwright evaluates `page.route()` handlers before HAR routing, so blocked routes never reach the HAR; alternatively, post-process the HAR file to strip non-API entries, or use the `url` pattern in `routeFromHAR()` in combination with a separate `page.route('**/analytics.js', r => r.abort())` call to prevent third-party script execution during recording.

210. **The "push tests down the pyramid" heuristic causes teams to remove integration tests after adding unit tests that cover the same logical path — but unit tests that mock the repository layer and integration tests that use a real database are NOT testing the same thing; deleting the integration test because "the unit test covers that branch" leaves the database serialisation, constraint enforcement, and ORM-generated SQL untested, and schema drift is discovered only in production** [community] — WHY: The Practical Test Pyramid advises eliminating *duplicate* coverage at higher levels, but this is frequently misread as "any coverage at the unit level justifies removing the corresponding integration test." Unit tests with mocked repositories verify control flow; integration tests verify that the control flow produces the correct effect in the actual persistence layer. They are not duplicates — they test different system properties. Fix: treat the pyramid's "push tests down" guideline as applying to *user-visible behaviour* tests (e.g., reducing browser-level e2e tests that simply verify a form submits), not to integration tests that test integration-specific properties (real database state, real HTTP contracts). Apply the heuristic within a pyramid level, not across levels.

### New Patterns

#### Pattern 1 — Playwright `mergeTests()` for Cross-Concern Fixture Composition  [official]

Playwright's `mergeTests()` API combines fixture sets from multiple sources into a single typed `test` function. In large TypeScript monorepos each concern — authentication, database seeding, accessibility audit, network guard — lives in a separate fixture module. Merging them at the test file level keeps each module single-responsibility while providing any combination of fixtures with full type inference.

```typescript
// tests/e2e/fixtures/index.ts — merge all fixture modules into one typed test function
// Requires @playwright/test ≥ 1.49 for mergeTests()
import { mergeTests } from '@playwright/test';
import { test as authTest } from './auth.fixture.js';
import { test as dbTest } from './db.fixture.js';
import { test as a11yTest } from './a11y.fixture.js';

// Merge: all fixture types are unioned; TypeScript infers the combined fixture interface
export const test = mergeTests(authTest, dbTest, a11yTest);
export { expect } from '@playwright/test';
```

```typescript
// tests/e2e/checkout.e2e.test.ts — all fixture namespaces available from one import
import { test, expect } from './fixtures/index.js';

test('authenticated user completes checkout', async ({
  page,
  authCookies,   // from authTest — sets storageState cookies
  seededCart,    // from dbTest  — pre-seeded cart data
  runA11yAudit,  // from a11yTest — runs axe-core after navigation
}) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Your Cart' })).toBeVisible();
  const violations = await runA11yAudit();
  expect(violations).toHaveLength(0);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /order confirmed/i })).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Merging many fixture modules can create a fixture namespace collision if two modules define the same fixture name. TypeScript surfaces the collision as a compile error, but the fix is renaming one fixture — which requires updating every test that uses it. Keep fixture names domain-scoped (`authCookies`, not `cookies`) to avoid conflicts. [official: playwright.dev/docs/test-fixtures#merging-fixtures]

---

#### Pattern 2 — Playwright Worker-Scoped Fixtures for Expensive E2E Setup  [official]

Worker-scoped Playwright fixtures (`{ scope: 'worker' }`) run once per worker process and are shared across all tests in that worker. Authentication and database seeding are the canonical use cases: creating a user account once per worker rather than once per test case reduces e2e suite time proportionally to the number of tests per worker.

```typescript
// tests/e2e/fixtures/worker-auth.fixture.ts — worker-scoped user account
// Account is created once per worker, shared across all tests on that worker
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';

interface Account {
  username: string;
  password: string;
  storageState: string; // path to saved auth cookies
}

export const test = base.extend<object, { account: Account }>({
  account: [
    async ({ browser }, use, workerInfo) => {
      // Each worker gets a distinct username — prevents cross-worker data collision
      const username = `e2e-user-${workerInfo.workerIndex}@example.com`;
      const password = 'TestPass!1';

      // Create account via API (not via UI — API calls are faster at setup)
      const ctx = await browser.newContext();
      const page = await ctx.newPage();
      await page.request.post('/api/users', { data: { username, password } });

      // Log in and save storage state for all tests in this worker
      await page.goto('/login');
      await page.fill('[name="email"]', username);
      await page.fill('[name="password"]', password);
      await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();
      await page.waitForURL('/dashboard');

      const storagePath = `playwright/.auth/worker-${workerInfo.workerIndex}.json`;
      await page.context().storageState({ path: storagePath });
      await ctx.close();

      // Pass the account data to all tests; clean up after all tests complete
      await use({ username, password, storageState: storagePath });

      // Teardown: remove the test user from the database
      const cleanupCtx = await browser.newContext();
      await cleanupCtx.request.delete(`/api/users/${encodeURIComponent(username)}`);
      await cleanupCtx.close();
    },
    { scope: 'worker' }, // runs once per worker process
  ],
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Worker-scoped fixtures rely on workers being isolated processes. If Playwright's `fullyParallel: true` causes tests from different files to share a worker, the account data from one file leaks into another file's tests. Set `workers: N` explicitly and keep worker count predictable to avoid cross-file data leakage within a single worker. [official: playwright.dev/docs/test-fixtures#worker-scoped-fixtures]

---

#### Pattern 3 — Sociable Unit Tests: Keeping Real Collaborators Below the I/O Boundary  [official]

Martin Fowler's Practical Test Pyramid distinguishes *solitary* unit tests (all collaborators mocked) from *sociable* unit tests (real collaborators used where feasible). The heuristic for choosing: if a collaborator has no I/O (network, filesystem, database, time), pass the real implementation. If it has I/O, inject a fake or stub. This keeps unit tests fast and deterministic while maximising coverage of real logic paths.

```typescript
// src/orders/order-pricer.unit.test.ts — sociable unit test: real Tax + Discount collaborators
// Both TaxCalculator and DiscountEngine are pure functions with no I/O — use real implementations
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { OrderPricer } from './order-pricer.js';
import { TaxCalculator } from './tax-calculator.js'; // pure: no I/O
import { DiscountEngine } from './discount-engine.js'; // pure: no I/O
import type { OrderLine } from './types.js';

// Sociable test: real TaxCalculator + DiscountEngine, no mocks
const pricer = new OrderPricer(new TaxCalculator('US-CA'), new DiscountEngine());

describe('OrderPricer.total', () => {
  const lines: OrderLine[] = [
    { sku: 'WIDGET', qty: 2, unitPrice: 10_00 }, // 2 × $10.00 = $20.00
    { sku: 'GADGET', qty: 1, unitPrice: 50_00 }, // 1 × $50.00 = $50.00
  ];

  it('sums line totals before tax and discount', () => {
    // No mocks: TaxCalculator and DiscountEngine run their real logic
    const total = pricer.subtotal(lines);
    expect(total).toBe(70_00); // $70.00 in cents
  });

  it('applies US-CA 8.25% tax to the subtotal', () => {
    const { tax } = pricer.breakdown(lines);
    expect(tax).toBe(57_75); // floor($70.00 * 0.0825 * 100) = 577.5 → 577 cents
  });

  it('gold member discount reduces pre-tax subtotal by 10%', () => {
    const { total } = pricer.breakdown(lines, { membershipTier: 'gold' });
    // gold: 10% off subtotal = $63.00 + $5.20 tax (8.25% of $63.00)
    expect(total).toBeLessThan(70_00 + 57_75);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Sociable tests couple the test outcome to all included collaborators. If `TaxCalculator` has a bug, it shows up in `OrderPricer` tests as well. This is generally desirable — it surfaces integration defects early. The cost is that a single collaborator bug causes multiple test failures, making root-cause identification slightly slower. Prefer sociable tests for pure-logic collaborators; prefer solitary tests when a collaborator has complex setup or many edge-case branches of its own. [official: martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html — sociable vs solitary]

---

#### Pattern 4 — Narrow Integration Test: One Integration Point at a Time  [official]

A *narrow* integration test exercises exactly one integration boundary — the database, the message queue, the external HTTP API — with all other dependencies stubbed. This is distinct from a *broad* integration test (sometimes called a "component test") that starts the entire service. Narrow tests are faster to write, faster to run, and produce clearer failure signals: when the test fails you know which integration point broke.

```typescript
// src/orders/order.repository.integration.test.ts — narrow integration: DB only
// MSW stubs any outbound HTTP; only the OrderRepository ↔ Postgres boundary is real
import { beforeAll, afterAll, afterEach, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { GenericContainer, type StartedTestContainer } from 'testcontainers';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { OrderRepository } from './order.repository.js';
import { Order } from './order.entity.js';

let container: StartedTestContainer;
let dataSource: DataSource;
let repo: OrderRepository;

beforeAll(async () => {
  container = await new GenericContainer('postgres:16')
    .withEnvironment({ POSTGRES_PASSWORD: 'test', POSTGRES_DB: 'testdb' })
    .withExposedPorts(5432)
    .start();

  dataSource = new DataSource({
    type: 'postgres',
    host: container.getHost(),
    port: container.getMappedPort(5432),
    username: 'postgres', password: 'test', database: 'testdb',
    entities: [Order], synchronize: true,
  });
  await dataSource.initialize();
  repo = new OrderRepository(dataSource);
}, 90_000);

afterAll(async () => { await dataSource.destroy(); await container.stop(); });
afterEach(async () => { await dataSource.getRepository(Order).clear(); });

it('persists a new order and retrieves it by ID', async () => {
  const saved = await repo.create({ customerId: 'c1', items: [{ sku: 'A1', qty: 2 }] });
  const fetched = await repo.findById(saved.id);
  // The ONLY assertion: what the DB actually persisted — not service layer logic
  expect(fetched?.customerId).toBe('c1');
  expect(fetched?.items).toHaveLength(1);
  expect(fetched?.status).toBe('pending');
});

it('returns null for a non-existent order ID', async () => {
  const result = await repo.findById('non-existent-id');
  expect(result).toBeNull();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Narrow integration tests require a real dependency (here, Postgres via testcontainers), which adds startup time. Against a pre-provisioned DB (Neon branch, shared CI container), startup is eliminated. The key benefit is precise diagnostic value: a narrow test failure points exactly to the `OrderRepository ↔ Postgres` boundary, not to the service logic or HTTP layer. [official: martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html — narrow integration tests]

---

#### Pattern 5 — Playwright `testProject.teardown` for Deterministic CI Data Cleanup  [official]

The `testProject.teardown` property (Playwright v1.49+) links a cleanup project to a test project. The teardown project runs unconditionally after the test project finishes — even if tests fail — ensuring that test data seeded in `globalSetup` is always removed, regardless of test outcome.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — teardown project runs after e2e suite regardless of outcome
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  projects: [
    // Global setup: seed test data before the suite
    {
      name: 'setup',
      testMatch: /global-setup\.ts/,
    },
    // Main suite: depends on setup; tears down after it completes
    {
      name: 'e2e',
      dependencies: ['setup'],
      teardown: 'cleanup', // <- linked teardown project
      testDir: './tests/e2e',
      use: { storageState: 'playwright/.auth/user.json' },
    },
    // Teardown: runs after e2e, even if e2e fails
    {
      name: 'cleanup',
      testMatch: /global-teardown\.ts/,
    },
  ],
});
```

```typescript
// tests/global-teardown.ts — always runs via testProject.teardown
import { test as setup } from '@playwright/test';

setup('remove seeded test data', async ({ request }) => {
  // This runs after all e2e tests — pass or fail
  await request.delete('/api/admin/test-data', {
    data: { scenario: 'e2e-checkout', force: true },
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `testProject.teardown` only runs if the parent project *started* at least one test. If `dependencies` fail and the `e2e` project never launches, teardown is also skipped — orphaned data can accumulate. Pair with a nightly CI job that scans for stale test data records older than 24 hours as a safety net. [official: playwright.dev/docs/test-fixtures#project-dependencies — testProject.teardown]

---

#### Pattern 6 — Vitest `aroundAll` for Shared Container Lifecycle in Integration Tests  [official]

Vitest 4.1's `aroundAll` hook wraps the entire test suite in a single lifecycle context, making it the correct primitive for testcontainer lifecycle management. Unlike `beforeAll`/`afterAll` pairs (which can leave the container running if `afterAll` throws before executing), `aroundAll` guarantees cleanup via the `try/finally` pattern — the container is always stopped when the file finishes.

```typescript
// tests/integration/inventory.integration.test.ts — aroundAll container lifecycle
import { test as baseTest, describe, expect } from 'vitest';
import { GenericContainer, type StartedTestContainer } from 'testcontainers';
import { InventoryService } from '../../src/inventory/inventory.service.js';

// aroundAll: declare the fixture with scope 'file' so it wraps the entire test file
const test = baseTest.extend<{ service: InventoryService }>({
  service: [
    async ({}, runTests) => {
      // Container starts once for ALL tests in this file — not per-test
      const container: StartedTestContainer = await new GenericContainer('redis:7')
        .withExposedPorts(6379)
        .start();

      const service = new InventoryService({
        host: container.getHost(),
        port: container.getMappedPort(6379),
      });

      try {
        await runTests(service); // run all tests in the suite
      } finally {
        // Always executed: container is stopped even if a test throws
        await service.disconnect();
        await container.stop();
      }
    },
    { scope: 'file' }, // <-- aroundAll semantics: one instance per file
  ],
});

describe('InventoryService', () => {
  test('reserves stock and reflects it in available count', async ({ service }) => {
    await service.setStock('SKU-A', 10);
    await service.reserve('SKU-A', 3);
    expect(await service.available('SKU-A')).toBe(7);
  });

  test('throws InsufficientStockError when reservation exceeds available', async ({ service }) => {
    await service.setStock('SKU-B', 2);
    await expect(service.reserve('SKU-B', 5)).rejects.toThrow('InsufficientStockError');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `scope: 'file'` means the container persists between tests in the same file. If one test leaves the Redis store in a dirty state, subsequent tests see it. Add a `beforeEach` inside the describe block that flushes the store (`await service.flushAll()`) to maintain test independence within the shared container. [official: vitest.dev/blog/vitest-4-1.html — aroundEach/aroundAll]

---

#### Pattern 7 — Consumer-Driven Contract Tests as the Fourth Pyramid Layer  [official]

Consumer-Driven Contract (CDC) tests — using Pact-JS or a compatible tool — sit between integration tests and e2e tests in the Fowler 5-layer pyramid. The consumer writes a contract describing the shape and semantics of the provider's API; the provider verifies the contract independently. This decouples deployment: teams no longer need a shared staging environment to validate API compatibility.

```typescript
// consumer/src/orders.pact.test.ts — CDC consumer test using Pact-JS v16
import { Pact, Matchers } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
import path from 'node:path';
import { OrdersApiClient } from './orders-api-client.js';

const { like, string, iso8601DateTime } = Matchers;

const provider = new Pact({
  consumer: 'StoreFrontend',
  provider: 'OrdersService',
  dir: path.resolve(process.cwd(), 'pacts'),
  logLevel: 'warn',
});

describe('OrdersService CDC — consumer side', () => {
  beforeAll(() => provider.setup());
  afterEach(() => provider.verify());
  afterAll(() => provider.finalize());

  it('GET /orders/:id returns order with correct shape', async () => {
    await provider
      .given('order ord_001 exists')
      .uponReceiving('a GET request for order ord_001')
      .withRequest({ method: 'GET', path: '/orders/ord_001' })
      .willRespondWith({
        status: 200,
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json; charset=utf-8' },
        body: {
          id: string('ord_001'),
          customerId: string('c1'),
          status: string('confirmed'),
          createdAt: iso8601DateTime('2026-05-14T10:00:00.000Z'),
          items: like([{ sku: string('A1'), qty: like(2) }]),
        },
      });

    const client = new OrdersApiClient(provider.mockService.baseUrl);
    const order = await client.getOrder('ord_001');

    // Consumer assertion: the client correctly maps the response
    expect(order.id).toBe('ord_001');
    expect(order.items).toHaveLength(1);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** CDC tests require buy-in from both consumer and provider teams, and a Pact Broker (or Pactflow) to share pact files in CI. The setup cost is 4–8 h for the first service pair. Once established, the return is high: provider teams can confidently refactor without needing a shared staging environment, and breaking changes are caught before deployment via `can-i-deploy`. Not worth the investment for a monorepo where both services are deployed together. [official: martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html — contract tests]

---

#### Pattern 8 — Vitest `test.extend` Builder Pattern for Type-Inferred Fixtures  [official]

Vitest 4.1's `test.extend` builder infers fixture types automatically from the return value of each fixture factory. Teams no longer need to maintain a separate TypeScript interface for the fixture object — the type is derived at the point of definition, keeping the fixture module self-contained and preventing the common drift between the interface declaration and the implementation.

```typescript
// tests/helpers/app-fixture.ts — type-inferred fixture with test.extend builder
import { test as baseTest } from 'vitest';
import { buildApp } from '../../src/app.js';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import request from 'supertest';
import type { Express } from 'express';

// test.extend with builder: TypeScript infers { app, db, agent } from the factory return values
// No manual interface declaration needed — types are derived automatically (Vitest 4.1)
export const test = baseTest.extend({
  // db fixture: in-memory SQLite DataSource for integration tests
  db: async ({}, use) => {
    const db = new DataSource({ type: 'sqlite', database: ':memory:', synchronize: true });
    await db.initialize();
    await use(db); // TypeScript infers type as DataSource
    await db.destroy();
  },

  // app fixture: depends on db — receives the db fixture via destructuring
  app: async ({ db }, use) => {
    const app = buildApp({ db });
    await use(app); // TypeScript infers type as Express
  },

  // agent fixture: supertest agent with automatic Content-Type header
  agent: async ({ app }, use) => {
    const agent = request.agent(app as Express).set('Accept', 'application/json');
    await use(agent); // TypeScript infers type as request.SuperAgentTest
  },
});
```

```typescript
// tests/integration/orders.integration.test.ts — using inferred fixture types
import { expect } from 'vitest';
import { test } from '../helpers/app-fixture.js';

// agent, db types are fully inferred — IntelliSense works without manual declarations
test('POST /orders creates an order and persists it', async ({ agent, db }) => {
  const res = await agent.post('/orders').send({ customerId: 'c1', items: [{ sku: 'A1', qty: 1 }] });
  expect(res.status).toBe(201);

  // Verify persisted state directly via db fixture — not via another HTTP call
  const count = await db.getRepository('Order').count({ where: { customerId: 'c1' } });
  expect(count).toBe(1);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Type inference breaks if a fixture's return type is too broad (e.g., `unknown` or `object`). Explicitly annotate the `use` parameter in that case: `async ({}, use: (v: MyType) => Promise<void>)`. This is a narrow edge case — for most fixtures, inference works without annotation. [official: vitest.dev/blog/vitest-4-1.html — test.extend builder pattern]

---

#### Pattern 9 — Playwright Soft Assertions for Multi-Field Validation at E2E Level  [official]

`expect.soft()` allows Playwright e2e tests to collect multiple assertion failures per test case rather than stopping at the first failure. For form validation and multi-field response validation this dramatically improves diagnostic density: a single failing test run reveals all broken fields simultaneously instead of requiring N sequential runs to discover N failures.

```typescript
// tests/e2e/order-confirmation.e2e.test.ts — expect.soft() for multi-field validation
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('order confirmation page shows all expected details', async ({ page }) => {
  // Setup: navigate to a known order confirmation
  await page.goto('/orders/ord_001/confirmation');
  await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle');

  const main = page.locator('main');

  // Soft assertions: all collected, all reported in one run
  await expect.soft(main.getByRole('heading', { name: /order confirmed/i })).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(main.getByText('ord_001')).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(main.getByText('alice@example.com')).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(main.getByRole('list', { name: 'Order items' })).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(main.getByText('TypeScript Handbook')).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(main.getByText('$29.99')).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(main.getByRole('link', { name: 'Continue Shopping' })).toBeVisible();

  // Hard assertion after soft block: only fails if the soft block had failures
  // Provides a clear summary message alongside the individual soft failure details
  expect(test.info().errors).toHaveLength(0);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Soft assertions do not stop test execution, so a soft failure in a page state check (e.g., heading not visible) followed by a hard interaction (`await page.click(...)`) can produce confusing errors if the page is in an unexpected state. Use soft assertions only for *read-only* assertions on already-loaded page state, never for actions that depend on prior assertions succeeding. [official: playwright.dev/docs/test-assertions#soft-assertions]

---

#### Pattern 10 — Vitest `--tags-filter` for Quarantine and Selective Integration Runs  [official]

Vitest 4.1's test tags allow a single workspace configuration to support multiple execution modes without maintaining separate config files. Tagging tests as `'db'`, `'slow'`, or `'flaky'` enables targeted CI jobs that run exactly the subset needed at each pipeline stage, implementing the pyramid's fail-fast principle at a finer granularity than project-level separation.

```typescript
// src/orders/orders.integration.test.ts — tagged integration tests (Vitest 4.1)
import { describe, it, expect, beforeAll, afterAll } from 'vitest';
import type { StartedTestContainer } from 'testcontainers';

// Tests tagged 'db' run only when --tags-filter="db" is passed
// Tests tagged 'slow' are excluded from the fast CI gate (--tags-filter="!slow")
describe('OrdersRepository — DB integration', { tags: ['db', 'integration'] }, () => {
  let container: StartedTestContainer;

  beforeAll(async () => {
    const { GenericContainer } = await import('testcontainers');
    container = await new GenericContainer('postgres:16')
      .withEnvironment({ POSTGRES_PASSWORD: 'test', POSTGRES_DB: 'testdb' })
      .withExposedPorts(5432)
      .start();
  }, 90_000);

  afterAll(() => container.stop());

  it('creates an order and returns its generated ID', { tags: ['db'] }, async () => {
    // ... test body
    expect(true).toBe(true); // placeholder
  });

  // Quarantine: flaky test excluded from merge gate, tracked separately
  it.skip('sends order-created event to message bus', { tags: ['flaky', 'db'] }, async () => {
    // This test is excluded from main CI with --tags-filter="!flaky"
    // Run separately: vitest run --tags-filter="flaky" --retry=3
  });
});
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/test.yml — tiered CI using tags
- name: Fast integration gate (no slow, no flaky)
  run: npx vitest run --project integration --tags-filter="integration && !slow && !flaky"

- name: Full integration suite (nightly, all tags)
  if: github.event_name == 'schedule'
  run: npx vitest run --project integration
```

**Tradeoff.** Tag-based filtering is additive to project-level separation, not a replacement. Tags work best for fine-grained control within an existing project (e.g., `db` vs. `in-memory` within integration); project-level separation (unit, integration, e2e) remains the primary pyramid enforcement mechanism. [official: vitest.dev/blog/vitest-4-1.html — test tags with --tags-filter]

---

#### Pattern 11 — Playwright `getByRole()` with `description` for Unambiguous Locators  [official]

Playwright v1.60 added the `description` option to `getByRole()`, which matches the accessible description (via `aria-describedby` or `aria-description`) in addition to the role and name. This resolves the common problem of multiple elements sharing the same role and name — such as product "Add to cart" buttons — without falling back to brittle positional indexing.

```typescript
// tests/e2e/product-catalog.e2e.test.ts — getByRole description option (Playwright v1.60)
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('user adds a specific product to the cart', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/shop');
  await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle');

  // BEFORE v1.60: required fragile positional index or data-testid
  // await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' }).nth(2).click(); // brittle

  // AFTER v1.60: match by accessible description — stable, semantic, and readable
  // The product name is set as aria-describedby on each "Add to cart" button
  await page.getByRole('button', {
    name: 'Add to cart',
    description: 'Playwright in Action (2nd Edition)',
  }).click();

  // Confirm the correct product was added
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Cart' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('listitem')).toContainText('Playwright in Action');
});

test('accessible description distinguishes quantity controls for different items', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/cart');

  // Each quantity input has aria-describedby pointing to the product name
  const quantityInput = page.getByRole('spinbutton', { description: 'Vitest in Action' });
  await quantityInput.fill('3');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Update cart' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByText('Subtotal: $119.97')).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** The `description` option requires that your HTML actually implements `aria-describedby` or `aria-description` on the target elements. If your application does not have correct ARIA description markup, this locator will match nothing. The accessibility investment required to make this work is worthwhile — it improves both test stability and the application's real accessibility posture simultaneously. [official: playwright.dev/docs/release-notes — v1.60 getByRole description option]

---

#### Pattern 12 — Vitest `vi.defineHelper` for Composable, Stack-Trace-Correct Assertion Libraries  [official]

`vi.defineHelper` (Vitest 4.1) strips the helper's internal frames from assertion stack traces, directing error pointers to the call site. Combining multiple `vi.defineHelper` functions into a domain-specific assertion library produces an assertion layer that is as ergonomic as Playwright's `expect` matchers but operates at the Vitest unit and integration levels.

```typescript
// packages/test-helpers/src/order-assertions.ts — composable typed assertions (Vitest 4.1)
import { expect, vi } from 'vitest';
import type { Order, OrderStatus } from '@myapp/domain';

// Each assertion is a vi.defineHelper — stack traces point to the TEST, not this file
export const assertOrderShape = vi.defineHelper((order: unknown) => {
  expect(order).toMatchObject({
    id: expect.stringMatching(/^ord_/),
    status: expect.stringMatching(/^(pending|confirmed|cancelled)$/),
    createdAt: expect.any(String),
  });
});

export const assertOrderStatus = vi.defineHelper((order: Order, expected: OrderStatus) => {
  expect(order.status).toBe(expected);
});

export const assertOrderItems = vi.defineHelper((order: Order, expectedCount: number) => {
  expect(order.items).toHaveLength(expectedCount);
  for (const item of order.items) {
    expect(item.sku).toBeTruthy();
    expect(item.qty).toBeGreaterThan(0);
  }
});

// Composite helper: combines multiple atomic assertions into a single call
export const assertConfirmedOrder = vi.defineHelper(
  (order: Order, expectedItemCount: number) => {
    assertOrderShape(order);             // → stack trace: TEST LINE, not this line
    assertOrderStatus(order, 'confirmed');
    assertOrderItems(order, expectedItemCount);
  },
);
```

```typescript
// tests/integration/orders.integration.test.ts — using the composable assertion library
import { it } from 'vitest';
import { assertConfirmedOrder } from '@myapp/test-helpers';
import { OrdersService } from '../../src/orders/orders.service.js';

it('confirmed order has the correct shape and items', async () => {
  const service = new OrdersService();
  const order = await service.confirm('ord_001');
  assertConfirmedOrder(order, 2); // ← error attribution points HERE if this fails
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `vi.defineHelper` wraps synchronous functions. For async assertion helpers (those using `await expect(locator).toBeVisible()`) use `async` functions with `vi.defineHelper` — both sync and async factory functions are supported. The stack-trace improvement applies to the helper's *entry point*; nested async steps may still show intermediate frames. [official: vitest.dev/blog/vitest-4-1.html — vi.defineHelper]

---

#### Pattern 13 — Test Data Seeding via API (Not UI) at E2E Level  [official]

Playwright best practices recommend seeding test data via the API layer rather than navigating the UI to create it. API seeding is 10–100× faster than UI-driven setup, reduces test brittleness (UI changes don't break setup), and keeps the e2e test focused on the user journey being verified rather than the setup pathway.

```typescript
// tests/e2e/fixtures/api-seed.fixture.ts — seed test data via API request context
import { test as base, request as playwrightRequest } from '@playwright/test';
import type { APIRequestContext } from '@playwright/test';

interface SeedFixtures {
  apiContext: APIRequestContext;
  seededOrder: { orderId: string; customerId: string };
}

export const test = base.extend<SeedFixtures>({
  // Isolated API context — does not share cookies with the browser page
  apiContext: async ({}, use) => {
    const ctx = await playwrightRequest.newContext({
      baseURL: process.env['API_BASE_URL'] ?? 'http://localhost:3000',
      extraHTTPHeaders: { 'X-Test-Client': 'playwright-e2e' },
    });
    await use(ctx);
    await ctx.dispose();
  },

  // Seed: create the order via API before the test body runs
  seededOrder: async ({ apiContext }, use) => {
    const res = await apiContext.post('/orders', {
      data: { customerId: 'e2e-user', items: [{ sku: 'BOOK-001', qty: 1 }] },
    });
    const order = await res.json() as { id: string; customerId: string };

    await use({ orderId: order.id, customerId: order.customerId });

    // Teardown: delete the seeded order after the test
    await apiContext.delete(`/orders/${order.id}`, {
      data: { reason: 'e2e test cleanup' },
    });
  },
});
```

```typescript
// tests/e2e/order-detail.e2e.test.ts — using the seeded order fixture
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { test } from './fixtures/api-seed.fixture.js';

test('order detail page shows seeded order data', async ({ page, seededOrder }) => {
  // Test body: navigate directly to the order created by the fixture
  await page.goto(`/orders/${seededOrder.orderId}`);
  await expect(page.getByText(seededOrder.orderId)).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByText(seededOrder.customerId)).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** API-seeded data bypasses UI validation rules, which can create test data in states the UI would not normally allow. Ensure the API seeding route is protected (e.g., gated by an `X-Test-Client` header that is only accepted in non-production environments) and that the seeding API reflects real business rules rather than direct database inserts. [official: playwright.dev/docs/best-practices — use the API for test setup]

---

#### Pattern 14 — Vitest `importDurations` Thresholds for Unit Test Startup Enforcement  [official]

Vitest 4.1's `importDurations` configuration reports how long each module import takes during test file initialisation. Combined with `thresholds`, it prevents accidentally importing ORM layers, full NestJS modules, or heavy utility libraries in unit test files — keeping the unit level fast and clearly separated from the integration level.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — importDurations with threshold enforcement for the unit project
import { defineConfig, defineProject } from 'vitest/config';
import tsconfigPaths from 'vite-tsconfig-paths';

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [tsconfigPaths()],
  test: {
    projects: [
      defineProject({
        extends: true,
        test: {
          name: { label: 'unit', color: 'green' },
          include: ['src/**/*.unit.test.ts'],
          environment: 'node',
          testTimeout: 5_000,
          importDurations: {
            enabled: true,
            // Fail if ANY module import in unit tests exceeds 300ms (warm cache)
            // A slow import almost always means a heavy dependency crept in
            thresholds: {
              '*': 300,
              // ORM and server modules are intentionally blocked at unit level:
              // 'typeorm': 0, // would force failure if TypeORM is ever imported in unit tests
            },
            reporter: 'verbose', // log all import times in CI for audit
          },
        },
      }),
      defineProject({
        extends: true,
        test: {
          name: { label: 'integration', color: 'yellow' },
          include: ['src/**/*.integration.test.ts'],
          environment: 'node',
          testTimeout: 60_000,
          pool: 'forks',
          // No importDurations threshold at integration level — heavy deps are expected
        },
      }),
    ],
  },
});
```

```typescript
// Example: unit test that accidentally imports a heavy module
// src/cart/cart.unit.test.ts — VIOLATION: TypeORM imported transitively
import { CartService } from './cart.service.js'; // if cart.service imports DataSource, this triggers

// With importDurations thresholds enabled, Vitest prints:
// WARN: typeorm import in cart.unit.test.ts took 480ms (threshold: 300ms)
// This surfaces the wrong dependency before it becomes a maintenance problem
```

**Tradeoff.** The 300ms threshold is conservative and will trigger false positives on cold CI runners (empty Vite module cache). Baseline the threshold on a warm runner before applying it. As a rule of thumb: set the threshold to 3× the median warm import time for the heaviest acceptable import in the unit project. [official: vitest.dev/blog/vitest-4-1.html — importDurations]

---

#### Pattern 15 — MSW `finalize` for Resource-Safe WebSocket Handler Teardown  [community]

MSW v2.14.4 introduced a `finalize()` chain on handlers that provides a lifecycle hook for releasing resources (open connections, timers, event subscriptions) when a handler is removed via `server.resetHandlers()` or `server.close()`. Without this, WebSocket handlers that hold internal state trigger Vitest 4.1's `--detect-async-leaks` flag and cause false-positive flakiness reports in the integration test suite.

```typescript
// tests/helpers/ws-notification-handler.ts — MSW WebSocket handler with finalize (v2.14.4)
import { ws } from 'msw';

const notificationLink = ws.link('wss://notifications.example.com/ws');

// Internal state maintained by the handler between messages
const subscribedTopics = new Map<string, Set<string>>(); // clientId → Set<topic>
let heartbeatInterval: ReturnType<typeof setInterval> | null = null;

export const notificationWsHandler = notificationLink
  .addEventListener('connection', ({ client }) => {
    const clientId = crypto.randomUUID();
    subscribedTopics.set(clientId, new Set());

    client.addEventListener('message', ({ data }) => {
      const msg = JSON.parse(data as string) as { type: string; topic: string };
      if (msg.type === 'subscribe') {
        subscribedTopics.get(clientId)?.add(msg.topic);
        client.send(JSON.stringify({ type: 'subscribed', topic: msg.topic }));
      }
    });

    client.addEventListener('close', () => {
      subscribedTopics.delete(clientId);
    });

    // Start heartbeat on first connection
    if (!heartbeatInterval) {
      heartbeatInterval = setInterval(() => {
        client.send(JSON.stringify({ type: 'ping' }));
      }, 30_000);
    }
  })
  // finalize: MSW v2.14.4+ — runs when resetHandlers() or server.close() removes this handler
  .finalize(() => {
    // Clear all subscriptions and the heartbeat interval — prevents async handle leaks
    subscribedTopics.clear();
    if (heartbeatInterval) {
      clearInterval(heartbeatInterval);
      heartbeatInterval = null;
    }
  });
```

```typescript
// tests/integration/notifications.integration.test.ts — handler with finalize
import { setupServer } from 'msw/node';
import { beforeAll, afterAll, afterEach, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { notificationWsHandler } from '../helpers/ws-notification-handler.js';

const server = setupServer(notificationWsHandler);

beforeAll(() => server.listen({ onUnhandledRequest: 'error' }));
afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers()); // triggers finalize() — cleans up internal state
afterAll(() => server.close());

it('client receives confirmation after subscribing to a topic', async () => {
  const ws = new WebSocket('wss://notifications.example.com/ws');
  const messages: string[] = [];
  ws.onmessage = (e) => messages.push(e.data as string);

  await new Promise<void>((resolve) => { ws.onopen = () => resolve(); });
  ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: 'subscribe', topic: 'order-updates' }));
  await new Promise<void>((resolve) => { setTimeout(resolve, 50); });
  ws.close();

  expect(messages).toContainEqual(expect.stringContaining('"type":"subscribed"'));
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `finalize()` is only called when the handler is explicitly removed (via `resetHandlers()` or `server.close()`). If a test suite uses `server.use()` to add one-off handlers that override the base handler without resetting afterwards, `finalize()` on the overridden handler may be called earlier than expected. Always pair `server.use()` additions in tests with `afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers())` to ensure predictable handler lifecycle. [community: github.com/mswjs/msw/releases — v2.14.4 finalize API; mswjs.io/docs/network-behavior/websocket#handler-lifecycle]
