## Cycle 54 — 2026-05-14

### New Patterns

**Pattern 1: Playwright `locator.filter()` chaining for dynamic list disambiguation** [official]
When a page renders a list of items sharing the same role, chaining `getByRole()` with `.filter({ hasText })` produces a locator that remains resilient to DOM order changes. This avoids index-based selectors (`.nth(2)`) that silently break when list order changes server-side.
```typescript
// e2e/cart/cart-item.e2e.test.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('removes the correct item from a mixed cart', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/cart');

  // Resilient: identifies by visible text, not DOM position
  const umbrellaItem = page
    .getByRole('listitem')
    .filter({ hasText: 'Umbrella' });

  const removeBtn = umbrellaItem.getByRole('button', { name: /remove/i });
  await removeBtn.click();

  // Umbrella is gone; other items remain
  await expect(page.getByRole('listitem').filter({ hasText: 'Umbrella' })).toHaveCount(0);
  await expect(page.getByRole('listitem')).toHaveCount(2);
});
```
Tradeoff: When item text is not unique (e.g., two products share a name), `filter({ hasText })` still matches both, surfacing a strict-mode error. Add `{ exact: true }` when product names are controlled, or combine with `filter({ has: page.getByTestId('sku-001') })` to narrow by a unique data attribute. [official: playwright.dev/docs/locators#filter-by-text]

---

**Pattern 2: Vitest `test.extend` worker-scoped DB connection pooling** [official]
Database connections are expensive. Using `scope: 'worker'` in `test.extend` creates a single connection pool per Vitest worker process, shared across all tests in that worker. This cuts integration suite startup time by avoiding per-test pool creation while keeping isolation via transaction rollback.
```typescript
// tests/fixtures/db.fixture.ts
import { test as base } from 'vitest';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { AppDataSource } from '../../src/data-source.js';

interface DbFixtures {
  dataSource: DataSource;
  txDataSource: DataSource;
}

export const test = base.extend<DbFixtures, { dataSource: DataSource }>({
  // Worker-scoped: one pool per worker — created once, shared across files
  dataSource: [
    async ({}, use) => {
      await AppDataSource.initialize();
      await use(AppDataSource);
      await AppDataSource.destroy();
    },
    { scope: 'worker' },
  ],

  // Test-scoped: each test gets a transaction that is rolled back after
  txDataSource: async ({ dataSource }, use) => {
    const queryRunner = dataSource.createQueryRunner();
    await queryRunner.startTransaction();
    await use(queryRunner.manager as unknown as DataSource);
    await queryRunner.rollbackTransaction();
    await queryRunner.release();
  },
});

// tests/order/order.repository.integration.test.ts
import { test } from '../fixtures/db.fixture.js';
import { expect } from 'vitest';
import { OrderRepository } from '../../src/order/order.repository.js';

test('persists an order within a rolled-back transaction', async ({ txDataSource }) => {
  const repo = new OrderRepository(txDataSource);
  const order = await repo.create({ userId: 'u1', total: 49.99 });
  expect(order.id).toMatch(/^ord_/);
  // txDataSource rolls back automatically — next test starts clean
});
```
Tradeoff: Worker-scoped pools require all tests in the worker to be compatible with the same DataSource configuration. If some tests require different connection options (e.g., schema isolation), use `sequence.groupOrder` to route those tests to a separate project with its own worker. Do not mix worker-scoped pool fixtures with `vi.resetModules()` — the module reset orphans the pool reference held by the fixture closure. [official: vitest.dev/guide/test-context#worker-scoped-fixtures]

---

**Pattern 3: MSW `http.passthrough()` for selective real-network integration tests** [official]
In integration test suites that normally intercept all HTTP via MSW, `http.passthrough()` lets specific handlers bypass the mock layer and hit a real test server or containerised dependency. This enables a hybrid approach: mocked third-party services + real internal service calls within the same test run.
```typescript
// tests/integration/checkout/checkout.integration.test.ts
import { setupServer } from 'msw/node';
import { http, passthrough, HttpResponse } from 'msw';
import { CheckoutService } from '../../../src/checkout/checkout.service.js';

const server = setupServer(
  // Third-party payment provider — always mocked
  http.post('https://api.stripe.com/v1/charges', () =>
    HttpResponse.json({ id: 'ch_test_001', status: 'succeeded' }),
  ),

  // Internal inventory service running in Docker — pass through to real container
  http.get('http://localhost:8081/inventory/:sku', () => passthrough()),

  // Catch-all: fail on any undeclared network call
);

beforeAll(() => server.listen({ onUnhandledRequest: 'error' }));
afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers());
afterAll(() => server.close());

test('checkout flow deducts inventory via real service', async () => {
  const service = new CheckoutService();
  const result = await service.checkout({ sku: 'umbrella-001', qty: 1 });
  expect(result.inventoryStatus).toBe('reserved');
  expect(result.paymentId).toBe('ch_test_001'); // mocked Stripe
});
```
Tradeoff: `passthrough()` introduces a real network dependency; if the containerised service is unavailable the test fails with a connection error, not a meaningful assertion failure. Guard `passthrough()` usages with a `beforeAll` health check (`await fetch('http://localhost:8081/health')`) and skip the test file with `test.skip(condition, 'inventory service not available')` when the container is absent. [official: mswjs.io/docs/api/passthrough]

---

**Pattern 4: Node.js 26 `--test-randomize` + `--test-random-seed` for order-dependency detection** [official]
Hidden order-dependencies in integration test suites (tests that only pass when run after a specific predecessor) are a top source of intermittent CI failures. Node.js 26's built-in test runner flag `--test-randomize` shuffles test execution order, and `--test-random-seed=N` makes the shuffle reproducible for debugging.
```typescript
// package.json — CI scripts using Node.js 26 native test runner
// {
//   "scripts": {
//     "test:unit": "node --test src/**/*.unit.test.ts",
//     "test:unit:shuffle": "node --test --test-randomize src/**/*.unit.test.ts",
//     "test:unit:replay": "node --test --test-randomize --test-random-seed=42 src/**/*.unit.test.ts"
//   }
// }

// src/auth/session.unit.test.ts — demonstrates order-dependency bug caught by randomize
import { test, describe } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { SessionStore } from './session-store.js';

// BUG: test A pollutes module-level state that test B depends on
// --test-randomize catches this by running B before A
const store = new SessionStore(); // shared instance — order-dependent!

describe('SessionStore', () => {
  test('A: creates a session', () => {
    store.create('user_1', { role: 'admin' });
    assert.equal(store.count(), 1);
  });

  test('B: returns null for unknown session', () => {
    // Passes only when A runs first; fails when randomized — catches the bug
    assert.equal(store.get('unknown'), null);
    assert.equal(store.count(), 0); // fails if A ran first
  });
});
// Fix: instantiate `store` inside each test or use beforeEach reset
```
Tradeoff: `--test-randomize` only surfaces order-dependencies, it does not fix them. The first time you run it on a legacy suite you may discover dozens of hidden dependencies requiring significant refactoring. Schedule it as a nightly CI job initially (not the merge gate) and triage failures systematically. Once the suite is clean, promote it to the merge gate with a fixed seed to keep builds deterministic. [official: nodejs.org/en/blog/release/v26.0.0]

---

**Pattern 5: Playwright `tracing.startHar()` for integration-level HTTP contract verification** [official]
Playwright v1.60 introduced a first-class HAR recording API (`tracing.startHar()`) that captures all network requests made during a test. Replaying the HAR in subsequent runs isolates tests from flaky external APIs and enables HTTP contract verification at the e2e/integration boundary.
```typescript
// e2e/fixtures/har.fixture.ts — HAR record/replay fixture
import { test as base, type BrowserContext } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'node:path';
import fs from 'node:fs';

const HAR_DIR = path.resolve('e2e/__hars__');

export const test = base.extend<{ harContext: BrowserContext }>({
  harContext: async ({ browser }, use, testInfo) => {
    const harPath = path.join(HAR_DIR, `${testInfo.titlePath.join('-').replace(/\s/g, '_')}.har`);
    const updateMode = process.env.UPDATE_HAR === '1';

    const context = updateMode
      ? await browser.newContext({ recordHar: { path: harPath, mode: 'full' } })
      : await browser.newContext({ har: { path: harPath, fallback: 'abort' } }); // replay mode

    await use(context);
    await context.close(); // HAR is written on context close in record mode
  },
});

// e2e/search/search.har.test.ts — deterministic e2e test against recorded HAR
import { test } from '../fixtures/har.fixture.js';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('search results display correctly (HAR replay)', async ({ harContext }) => {
  const page = await harContext.newPage();
  // Network calls are served from HAR — no real server required
  await page.goto('/search?q=umbrella');
  await expect(page.getByRole('listitem')).toHaveCount(5);
  await expect(page.getByRole('listitem').first()).toContainText('Compact Umbrella');
});
```
Tradeoff: HAR files become stale when the API under test changes its response shape. Pair HAR replay tests with a nightly "HAR refresh" CI job (`UPDATE_HAR=1 npx playwright test`) that regenerates all HARs against the live API and commits the diff. Treat HAR diffs as a contract change signal — review them in PRs the same way you review snapshot diffs. [official: playwright.dev/docs/release-notes — v1.60 tracing.startHar]

---

**Pattern 6: Vitest `coverage.changed` for per-PR coverage delta enforcement** [official]
Global coverage thresholds (e.g., `lines: 80`) fail to protect against targeted regressions — a PR deleting tests and adding untested code may still pass an 80% global threshold. Vitest 4.1's `coverage.changed` option calculates coverage only for files modified in the current PR, enforcing that new code meets a higher bar.
```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — PR coverage delta enforcement
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      // Global floor — safety net for the whole codebase
      thresholds: {
        lines: 75,
        functions: 75,
        branches: 70,
      },
      // Per-PR delta: only files touched in this PR must meet 90%
      // Vitest 4.1: coverage.changed compares against the merge-base
      changed: {
        // Files modified relative to the base branch must clear higher thresholds
        thresholds: {
          lines: 90,
          functions: 90,
          branches: 85,
        },
      },
    },
  },
});
```
```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml — pass merge-base to Vitest
- name: Vitest coverage with changed-file gate
  run: |
    BASE_SHA=$(git merge-base HEAD origin/main)
    VITEST_COVERAGE_CHANGED_BASE=$BASE_SHA npx vitest run --coverage
```
Tradeoff: `coverage.changed` requires the CI runner to have access to the full git history to resolve the merge-base commit. Shallow clones (`fetch-depth: 1`) will fail; set `fetch-depth: 0` in the checkout step. Coverage delta enforcement can create friction when renaming files — a rename counts as "added" in git, so the renamed file is subject to the higher threshold even if the underlying logic did not change. [official: vitest.dev/blog/vitest-4-1.html]

---

**Pattern 7: `@fast-check/vitest` `test.prop()` for property-based unit tests** [official]
Property-based testing at the unit layer complements example-based tests by generating hundreds of random inputs, uncovering edge cases that hand-written examples miss. The `@fast-check/vitest` integration exposes a `test.prop()` API that plugs directly into Vitest's test runner without boilerplate.
```typescript
// src/pricing/discount.unit.test.ts — property-based tests with @fast-check/vitest
import { test, expect } from '@fast-check/vitest';
import * as fc from 'fast-check';
import { applyDiscount } from './discount.js';

// Property: discount can never make price negative
test.prop([
  fc.float({ min: 0.01, max: 10_000, noNaN: true }),
  fc.float({ min: 0, max: 1, noNaN: true }), // discount rate 0–100%
])('discount never produces a negative price', (price, discountRate) => {
  const result = applyDiscount(price, discountRate);
  expect(result).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(0);
});

// Property: zero discount rate returns original price
test.prop([fc.float({ min: 0.01, max: 10_000, noNaN: true })])(
  'zero discount rate returns original price',
  (price) => {
    expect(applyDiscount(price, 0)).toBeCloseTo(price, 5);
  },
);

// Property: discount is monotone — higher rate → lower or equal result
test.prop([
  fc.float({ min: 0.01, max: 10_000, noNaN: true }),
  fc.tuple(
    fc.float({ min: 0, max: 0.5, noNaN: true }),
    fc.float({ min: 0.5, max: 1, noNaN: true }),
  ),
])('higher discount rate yields lower or equal price', (price, [low, high]) => {
  expect(applyDiscount(price, high)).toBeLessThanOrEqual(applyDiscount(price, low));
});
```
Tradeoff: `@fast-check/vitest` 0.4+ is ESM-only — CommonJS Vitest projects (`"type": "commonjs"` in package.json) cannot use it without converting to ESM or using a dynamic `import()` wrapper. Property-based tests are also slower than example-based tests (100+ runs per `test.prop` by default); set `fc.configureGlobal({ numRuns: 20 })` in unit-test CI to limit runtime, reserving the default 100+ runs for nightly or dedicated PBT runs. [official: github.com/dubzzz/fast-check — @fast-check/vitest]

---

**Pattern 8: Playwright `expect.soft()` aggregation for multi-field form validation e2e tests** [official]
Form validation e2e tests that use hard assertions stop at the first failing field, hiding all subsequent failures in a single run. `expect.soft()` collects all assertion failures and reports them together at the end of the test, giving a complete picture of the form's validation state in one run.
```typescript
// e2e/checkout/checkout-form.e2e.test.ts — soft assertion aggregation
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('checkout form validates all required fields on submit', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  
  // Submit with all fields empty to trigger all validations simultaneously
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /place order/i }).click();

  // Soft assertions collect ALL failures — test continues past each
  await expect.soft(page.getByText('First name is required')).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(page.getByText('Last name is required')).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(page.getByText('Email is required')).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(page.getByText('Card number is required')).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(page.getByText('Expiry date is required')).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(page.getByText('CVV is required')).toBeVisible();

  // Hard assertion: the form must NOT navigate away when invalid
  // (hard assertion — a navigation here is a critical flow control failure)
  await expect(page).toHaveURL('/checkout');

  // Playwright reports all soft failures together at test end
});
```
Tradeoff: `expect.soft()` assertions do not stop test execution on failure — if a later step depends on a preceding assertion being true (e.g., clicking a button that appears only after a field is filled), subsequent steps may produce misleading errors. Reserve `expect.soft()` for leaf assertions (visibility checks, text content) and use hard `expect()` for flow-control assertions (navigation, element presence required for the next action). [official: playwright.dev/docs/test-assertions#soft-assertions]

---

**Pattern 9: Testcontainers `withReuse()` for fast integration test startup in local development** [official]
Testcontainers' `withReuse()` option (combined with `TESTCONTAINERS_RYUK_DISABLED=true`) keeps containers alive across test runs during local development. The first run incurs full startup cost; subsequent runs attach to the running container, reducing integration test startup from 20–30 seconds to under 2 seconds.
```typescript
// tests/fixtures/postgres.fixture.ts — reusable container for local dev
import { test as base } from 'vitest';
import { PostgreSqlContainer } from '@testcontainers/postgresql';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

const isCI = process.env.CI === 'true';

// Lazy singleton — created once per Node.js process
let sharedContainer: Awaited<ReturnType<PostgreSqlContainer['start']>> | null = null;

async function getOrCreateContainer() {
  if (sharedContainer) return sharedContainer;

  const builder = new PostgreSqlContainer('postgres:16-alpine')
    .withDatabase('testdb')
    .withUsername('test')
    .withPassword('test');

  // Local dev only — CI always creates fresh containers
  if (!isCI) {
    builder.withReuse(); // Container survives across test runs
  }

  sharedContainer = await builder.start();
  return sharedContainer;
}

export const test = base.extend<{ ds: DataSource }>({
  ds: async ({}, use) => {
    const container = await getOrCreateContainer();
    const ds = new DataSource({
      type: 'postgres',
      url: container.getConnectionUri(),
      synchronize: true,
      entities: ['src/**/*.entity.ts'],
    });
    await ds.initialize();
    await use(ds);
    await ds.destroy();
  },
});
```
Tradeoff: `withReuse()` containers persist data across runs if schema migrations or test data are not cleaned up. Always run schema migrations to a known state (not `synchronize: true`) in reused containers, and use a per-test transaction-rollback fixture (Pattern 2) to prevent test data accumulation. Never enable `withReuse()` in CI — always use fresh containers there to guarantee reproducibility. [official: testcontainers.com/guides/getting-started-with-testcontainers-for-nodejs/]

---

**Pattern 10: Playwright Page Object Model with compile-time action validation via TypeScript** [official]
A POM that exposes methods (not raw locators) constrains the e2e test to the public interface of the page, preventing tests from coupling to DOM internals. Adding TypeScript return types to each method creates a compile-time contract: renaming a method causes test files that call it to fail the TypeScript build before `playwright test` runs.
```typescript
// e2e/pages/checkout.page.ts — typed POM with method-level contract
import type { Page, Locator } from '@playwright/test';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';

export class CheckoutPage {
  private readonly page: Page;
  private readonly emailInput: Locator;
  private readonly placeOrderButton: Locator;
  private readonly orderConfirmationHeading: Locator;

  constructor(page: Page) {
    this.page = page;
    // Locators are resilient: role + accessible name, not CSS
    this.emailInput = page.getByRole('textbox', { name: /email/i });
    this.placeOrderButton = page.getByRole('button', { name: /place order/i });
    this.orderConfirmationHeading = page.getByRole('heading', { name: /order confirmed/i });
  }

  async goto(): Promise<void> {
    await this.page.goto('/checkout');
  }

  async fillEmail(email: string): Promise<void> {
    await this.emailInput.fill(email);
  }

  async submitOrder(): Promise<void> {
    await this.placeOrderButton.click();
  }

  async assertOrderConfirmed(): Promise<void> {
    await expect(this.orderConfirmationHeading).toBeVisible();
  }
}

// e2e/checkout/checkout.e2e.test.ts — test uses POM exclusively
import { test } from '@playwright/test';
import { CheckoutPage } from '../pages/checkout.page.js';

test('guest can complete checkout', async ({ page }) => {
  const checkout = new CheckoutPage(page);
  await checkout.goto();
  await checkout.fillEmail('guest@example.com');
  await checkout.submitOrder();
  await checkout.assertOrderConfirmed();
  // No raw locators in test file — refactoring the DOM only changes checkout.page.ts
});
```
Tradeoff: POMs add an indirection layer that can become a maintenance liability if methods grow too granular (a `fillFirstName`, `fillLastName`, `fillEmail` method per field is verbose). Strike a balance: expose user-level actions (`fillBillingAddress(addr: BillingAddress)`) rather than field-level setters. Over-granular POMs drift toward testing implementation details, defeating their purpose. [official: playwright.dev/docs/pom]

---

**Pattern 11: Vitest `vi.defineHelper()` for custom assertion stack traces** [official]
When building custom assertion helpers (e.g., `assertIsValidOrder(order)`), stack traces typically point to the helper's internal `expect()` line rather than the test line that called the helper. Vitest 4.1's `vi.defineHelper()` wraps the helper so that failure stack traces point to the call site in the test file.
```typescript
// tests/helpers/order.helpers.ts — custom assertions with clean stack traces
import { vi, expect } from 'vitest';
import type { Order } from '../../src/order/order.types.js';

// vi.defineHelper() ensures stack traces point to the test call site, not here
export const assertIsValidOrder = vi.defineHelper(function (order: Order) {
  expect(order.id, 'order.id').toMatch(/^ord_[a-z0-9]{8}$/);
  expect(order.total, 'order.total').toBeGreaterThan(0);
  expect(order.status, 'order.status').toBeOneOf(['pending', 'confirmed', 'shipped', 'cancelled']);
  expect(order.createdAt, 'order.createdAt').toBeInstanceOf(Date);
  expect(order.items, 'order.items').not.toHaveLength(0);
});

export const assertHasValidLineItems = vi.defineHelper(function (order: Order) {
  for (const item of order.items) {
    expect(item.sku, `item.sku`).toMatch(/^[A-Z]{3}-[0-9]{4}$/);
    expect(item.qty, `item.qty for ${item.sku}`).toBeGreaterThan(0);
    expect(item.unitPrice, `item.unitPrice for ${item.sku}`).toBeGreaterThan(0);
  }
});

// tests/order/order.service.unit.test.ts — clean stack traces on failure
import { test } from 'vitest';
import { assertIsValidOrder, assertHasValidLineItems } from '../helpers/order.helpers.js';
import { OrderService } from '../../src/order/order.service.js';

test('creates a valid order', async () => {
  const service = new OrderService();
  const order = await service.create({ userId: 'u_001', items: [{ sku: 'UMB-0001', qty: 2 }] });
  assertIsValidOrder(order);         // stack trace points HERE on failure
  assertHasValidLineItems(order);    // stack trace points HERE on failure
});
```
Tradeoff: `vi.defineHelper()` is a Vitest 4.1+ API — if your team has projects on Vitest 3.x, the helper will be undefined and you will get a runtime `TypeError`. Add a version guard in the helper file or upgrade all projects to Vitest 4.1+ before adopting it. Helpers that contain complex branching logic can hide test structure from readers; prefer helpers for structural validation (shape checks) and keep business-logic assertions inline where they explain intent. [official: vitest.dev/blog/vitest-4-1.html]

---

**Pattern 12: Playwright `--only-changed` for PR-scoped e2e test selection** [official]
Playwright v1.51+ supports `--only-changed[=base-branch]` to run only the e2e test files that have changed (or whose imported dependencies have changed) relative to a base branch. In large monorepos this reduces e2e suite time from 30+ minutes to under 5 minutes for a typical feature PR.
```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — dependency tracking for --only-changed
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  testDir: './e2e',
  // Use project-level separation so --only-changed can filter by project
  projects: [
    { name: 'chromium', use: { browserName: 'chromium' } },
    { name: 'firefox', use: { browserName: 'firefox' } },
  ],
});
```
```yaml
# .github/workflows/pr.yml — PR gate: only changed e2e tests
- name: Run changed e2e tests
  run: |
    npx playwright test \
      --only-changed=origin/main \
      --project=chromium \
      --reporter=github
  # Falls back to running all tests if no e2e files changed

# .github/workflows/nightly.yml — nightly full regression
- name: Run full e2e suite (nightly)
  run: npx playwright test --project=chromium --project=firefox
```
Tradeoff: `--only-changed` uses git diff to identify changed test files and their import dependencies. Test helper files imported by many tests (e.g., a shared fixture) will cause most of the suite to run when that helper changes. Keep shared fixtures minimal and prefer per-feature fixture composition to limit blast radius. On first adoption, map out which helpers are imported most widely and refactor them to be more granular before enabling `--only-changed` in the merge gate. [official: playwright.dev/docs/release-notes — v1.51]

---

**Pattern 13: Consumer-Driven Contract testing with Pact `eachLike()` and strict Zod parsing** [official]
Pact's `like()` matcher allows extra provider fields that the consumer does not declare, enabling silent contract drift. Combining `eachLike()` for arrays with a strict Zod schema parse in the consumer client eliminates this blind spot: any extra field the provider adds will cause the consumer parse to fail at test time rather than silently at runtime.
```typescript
// tests/pact/order-consumer.pact.test.ts
import { PactV4, MatchersV4 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
import { z } from 'zod';
import { OrderClient } from '../../src/clients/order-client.js';

const { eachLike, like, string, integer } = MatchersV4;

const provider = new PactV4({
  consumer: 'checkout-service',
  provider: 'order-service',
});

// Zod schema — strict() rejects extra fields the provider adds without consumer knowledge
const OrderSchema = z.object({
  id: z.string().regex(/^ord_/),
  status: z.enum(['pending', 'confirmed', 'shipped', 'cancelled']),
  total: z.number().positive(),
  items: z.array(z.object({
    sku: z.string(),
    qty: z.number().int().positive(),
    unitPrice: z.number().positive(),
  })).min(1),
}).strict(); // <-- rejects undeclared provider fields

test('fetches an order by id', async () => {
  await provider
    .addInteraction()
    .uponReceiving('a request for order ord_001')
    .withRequest({ method: 'GET', path: '/orders/ord_001' })
    .willRespondWith({
      status: 200,
      body: {
        id: string('ord_001'),
        status: string('confirmed'),
        total: like(49.99),
        items: eachLike({
          sku: string('UMB-0001'),
          qty: integer(2),
          unitPrice: like(24.99),
        }),
      },
    })
    .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
      const client = new OrderClient(mockServer.url);
      const raw = await client.getOrder('ord_001');
      // Strict parse — fails if provider returns undeclared fields (e.g., legacyOrderId)
      const order = OrderSchema.parse(raw);
      expect(order.status).toBe('confirmed');
    });
});
```
Tradeoff: `.strict()` Zod schemas in consumer tests create friction when the provider legitimately wants to add a new optional field — the consumer test fails until the consumer updates its Zod schema to include the new field. This is intentional: it forces explicit consumer acknowledgment of every provider schema change. Use `.passthrough()` instead of `.strict()` when the consumer uses a "must-ignore" policy for unknown fields, and document the policy explicitly. [official: docs.pact.io/getting_started/matching]

---

**Pattern 14: Bun `test.concurrent` + `--shard` for parallel integration test execution** [official]
Bun 1.3's `test.concurrent` enables within-file parallelism (tests run in parallel within a single worker), while `--shard=N/M` distributes test files across CI matrix jobs. Combining both cuts integration suite wall-clock time in proportion to available CPU cores and CI parallelism without the Vitest worker pool overhead.
```typescript
// tests/products/product.integration.test.ts — Bun concurrent + sharding
import { describe, test, expect, beforeAll, afterAll } from 'bun:test';
import { ProductRepository } from '../../src/products/product.repository.js';
import { db } from '../helpers/test-db.js';

// Concurrent within this file — Bun 1.3 within-file parallelism
describe.concurrent('ProductRepository', () => {
  beforeAll(async () => { await db.migrate(); });
  afterAll(async () => { await db.truncate('products'); });

  test('finds product by sku', async () => {
    const repo = new ProductRepository(db);
    const product = await repo.findBySku('UMB-0001');
    expect(product?.name).toBe('Compact Umbrella');
  });

  test('returns null for unknown sku', async () => {
    const repo = new ProductRepository(db);
    const product = await repo.findBySku('UNKNOWN');
    expect(product).toBeNull();
  });

  test('lists products with pagination', async () => {
    const repo = new ProductRepository(db);
    const page = await repo.list({ limit: 10, offset: 0 });
    expect(page.items.length).toBeGreaterThan(0);
    expect(page.total).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(page.items.length);
  });
});
```
```yaml
# .github/workflows/integration.yml — Bun shard matrix
strategy:
  matrix:
    shard: [1, 2, 3, 4]
steps:
  - run: bun test --shard=${{ matrix.shard }}/4 tests/
```
Tradeoff: `describe.concurrent` within Bun requires tests to be fully isolated — no shared mutable state between tests in the same describe block. Tests that rely on insertion order (e.g., testing pagination assumes rows are inserted in a specific order) will fail non-deterministically when concurrent. Use a transaction-per-test isolation strategy (analogous to Vitest Pattern 2) and seed data in each test's `beforeEach` rather than sharing setup across concurrent tests. [official: bun.sh/docs/cli/test]

---

**Pattern 15: Playwright AI Agents (`planner` + `healer`) with pyramid governance guardrails** [official]
Playwright v1.56 introduced AI Agents — a planner agent generates test steps from a natural-language prompt, and a healer agent auto-repairs broken locators after DOM changes. Without governance, the healer can silently regenerate tests that no longer test the intended behaviour. A pyramid governance hook validates that healed locators still assert the same observable outcome.
```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — AI agent configuration with governance hook
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // Playwright v1.56+ agents configuration
  agents: {
    // Planner generates test steps from natural language
    planner: { enabled: true, model: 'claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022' },
    // Healer repairs broken locators after DOM changes
    healer: {
      enabled: process.env.CI !== 'true', // NEVER auto-heal in CI — human review required
      // Governance: healed tests must be reviewed before merging
      onHeal: async (healed) => {
        console.warn(
          `[HEALER] Locator repaired in ${healed.testFile}:${healed.lineNumber}\n` +
          `  Before: ${healed.original}\n` +
          `  After:  ${healed.replacement}\n` +
          `  ACTION REQUIRED: Review healed locator before committing.`,
        );
      },
    },
  },
  // Governance: tag AI-generated tests so they can be audited separately
  projects: [
    { name: 'ai-generated', testMatch: /\.ai\.e2e\.ts$/, use: { trace: 'on' } },
    { name: 'human-authored', testMatch: /\.e2e\.ts$/ },
  ],
});
```
Tradeoff: AI-generated and AI-healed tests can diverge from the intended test objective if the DOM changes in a semantically meaningful way (e.g., a button is renamed from "Confirm" to "Place Order" — the healer finds the new button but the original test was specifically checking the button label as a UX assertion). Require a human-review step before any healed test reaches the `main` branch: add a CI check that fails if `*.ai.e2e.ts` files have uncommitted healing changes (`git diff --name-only | grep '\.ai\.e2e\.ts'`). Treat AI-generated tests as first drafts, not production tests. [official: playwright.dev/docs/release-notes — v1.56 agents]

### Community Gotchas

**Gotcha G221: Vitest `vi.resetModules()` inside `aroundEach` tears down the wrong DataSource instance**
When a test file uses both `aroundEach` (Vitest 4.1) for transaction wrapping and `vi.resetModules()` inside a test body, the `aroundEach` teardown function holds a closure reference to the DataSource instance from before the module reset. After `vi.resetModules()` executes, the module registry is cleared and the next `import` of the DataSource module returns a new instance. The `aroundEach` teardown then calls `.rollbackTransaction()` on the pre-reset instance, which is no longer the active database connection — the transaction is never rolled back, leaving dirty data for subsequent tests. WHY: `aroundEach` closures capture module references at the time `beforeEach` runs; `vi.resetModules()` replaces the module registry mid-test without notifying existing closures, causing the teardown to operate on a stale object. Fix: do not call `vi.resetModules()` in any test file that uses `aroundEach` with stateful module resources; use a separate Vitest project with its own `vitest.config.ts` for tests that require module isolation, and configure that project with `isolate: true` instead of relying on `vi.resetModules()` inside tests. [official: vitest.dev/api/vi#vi-resetmodules]

**Gotcha G222: Playwright `--only-changed` skips e2e tests when the shared fixture file is in a directory not tracked by `testDir`**
Teams that store POM files and fixtures outside `testDir` (e.g., `e2e/pages/` and `e2e/fixtures/` exist, but `testDir: './e2e/specs'`) find that `--only-changed` does not traverse import graphs rooted outside `testDir`. A change to `e2e/fixtures/auth.fixture.ts` that is imported by many tests inside `e2e/specs/` is not detected as a dependency of those tests, so no tests run when only the fixture changes. WHY: Playwright's `--only-changed` dependency graph starts from test files inside `testDir` and follows their imports; files that are only imported (not the entry point of a test file) are tracked, but only if they are reachable from a file Playwright's scanner finds. Fixture files outside `testDir` are found via imports from test files, but the git change detection starts from changed files against the `testDir` root — so a changed fixture is not the entry point and is not independently checked for dependents. Fix: move fixtures and page objects inside `testDir` (or a subdirectory of it), or pass `--testDir` to include the wider `e2e/` root; alternatively, add a CI step that runs the full suite when any file in `e2e/fixtures/` or `e2e/pages/` changes (`git diff --name-only | grep -q '^e2e/fixtures/' && npx playwright test`). [official: playwright.dev/docs/release-notes — v1.51]

**Gotcha G223: Pact `PactV4` / `MatchersV4` naming confusion after Pact-JS v16 canonical rename**
Pact-JS v16.0 renamed the canonical classes: `PactV4` became `Pact`, `MatchersV3`/`MatchersV4` became `Matchers`. The old names (`PactV4`, `MatchersV3`) were retained as aliases pointing to the *old* V3/V4 classes for backward compatibility, but teams that mix old and new imports in the same codebase end up with `Pact` (new canonical V4) and `PactV4` (old alias) both resolving without TypeScript errors, producing subtly different behaviour — `PactV4` uses the V3 matching engine while `Pact` uses the V4 engine with enhanced matchers. WHY: TypeScript resolves both names successfully because they are both exported from the package entry point; the aliased `PactV4` does not cause a type error, it simply uses an older code path. The divergence surfaces only when provider verification runs and the interaction format differs between old and new engines. Fix: run the Pact-JS v16 migration codemod (`npx @pact-foundation/pact-js-codemod v16`) to canonicalise all imports to `Pact` and `Matchers`, then ban the old names in ESLint with a `no-restricted-imports` rule. [official: docs.pact.io/implementation_guides/javascript/changelog]

**Gotcha G224: Bun `mock.module()` declaration-order requirement silently bypasses mocks when module is imported before the mock is registered**
Bun's `mock.module()` requires the mock declaration to appear before any `import` statement that resolves the module being mocked. Unlike Vitest's `vi.mock()`, which is hoisted to the top of the file by the Vite transform, Bun's `mock.module()` is not hoisted — it executes at the line where it appears. If a test file imports a dependency at the top of the file and then calls `mock.module('dependency')` later in the file, the import has already been resolved and cached before the mock is registered, so the mock has no effect. The test runs with the real module and may pass or fail non-deterministically depending on the real module's state. WHY: Bun's module resolution is ahead-of-time at file parse time; static `import` declarations are resolved before any code runs, while `mock.module()` is a runtime call. Fix: use `import { mock } from 'bun:test'` and call `mock.module('dependency', () => ({ ... }))` before any `import` that uses the dependency — in practice, restructure test files to put all `mock.module()` calls at the top of the file before all other imports, or use dynamic `import()` after the mock is registered. [official: bun.sh/docs/test/mocks]

**Gotcha G225: k6 `Trend` custom metrics accumulate across scenario iterations when `exec` re-uses the same metric instance, producing inflated p95 values in multi-scenario load tests**
In k6 load tests with multiple scenarios (e.g., a ramp-up scenario followed by a steady-state scenario), a shared `Trend` instance defined at module scope accumulates all samples from all scenarios. When the test report shows `p95 < 500ms`, the percentile is calculated over the combined distribution, masking degradation that only occurs during the ramp-up phase. WHY: k6's `Trend`, `Counter`, `Rate`, and `Gauge` instances are module-level singletons — they accumulate metrics for the lifetime of the test run regardless of which scenario is executing. There is no built-in per-scenario metric scoping. Fix: use k6's built-in `scenario` tag on each metric by calling `client.get(url, { tags: { scenario: __ENV.SCENARIO_NAME } })` and filter the results in the Grafana dashboard by the `scenario` tag; or define separate named metrics per scenario (`const rampUpTrend = new Trend('ramp_up_latency')` and `const steadyStateTrend = new Trend('steady_state_latency')`) and assert against them separately in `thresholds`. [official: grafana.com/docs/k6/latest/using-k6/metrics/create-custom-metrics/]

## Cycle 55 — 2026-05-14

### New Patterns

**Pattern 1: Vitest `expect.poll()` for async state convergence in integration tests** [official]
Vitest 4.x introduced `expect.poll()` as a first-class retry wrapper for assertions that wait on eventually-consistent state — replacing custom retry loops and `waitFor` wrappers. It polls at 50 ms intervals up to a configurable timeout, re-running the assertion callback until it passes or the timeout expires. This is the correct integration-level tool when asserting side effects that are asynchronous (message queues, database writes via background workers, cache invalidations).
```typescript
// integration/order-processor.test.ts
import { expect, test } from 'vitest';
import { db } from '../src/db';
import { publishOrderEvent } from '../src/events';

test('background order processor writes fulfilment record within 2s', async () => {
  const orderId = 'ord_abc123';
  await publishOrderEvent({ type: 'order.placed', orderId });

  // expect.poll() retries every 50ms until the assertion passes or 2000ms elapses
  await expect.poll(
    async () => {
      const row = await db.query(
        'SELECT status FROM fulfilments WHERE order_id = $1',
        [orderId],
      );
      return row.rows[0]?.status;
    },
    { timeout: 2000, interval: 50 },
  ).toBe('pending');
});
```
Tradeoff: `expect.poll()` masks slow I/O if the timeout is set too high — a 10 s timeout on an integration test converts a performance regression into a passing (but slow) test. Set timeouts as low as the real system can reliably meet in CI and fail loudly when they are raised.

---

**Pattern 2: Playwright `page.clock.install()` for deterministic time-dependent e2e tests** [official]
Playwright v1.50+ ships a stable `Clock` API that replaces `Date`, `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, and `performance.now` inside the browser page — enabling fully deterministic control of time-sensitive UI flows (session expiry modals, countdown timers, scheduled polling) without injecting fake timers into the production code.
```typescript
// e2e/session-expiry.e2e.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('shows session expiry warning 5 minutes before token expires', async ({ page }) => {
  // Install clock at a fixed epoch so the JWT iat is predictable
  await page.clock.install({ time: new Date('2026-01-01T12:00:00Z') });
  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  await page.evaluate(() => window.__setAuthToken({ expiresAt: Date.now() + 30 * 60 * 1000 }));

  // Fast-forward to 5 minutes before expiry
  await page.clock.fastForward('25m');

  await expect(page.getByRole('alert', { name: /session expiring/i })).toBeVisible();
  // Advance past expiry — verify redirect to login
  await page.clock.fastForward('6m');
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/login/);
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.clock.install()` only controls the browser-side clock. Server-side expiry logic (e.g., JWT verification at the API layer) uses real wall time. Tests that assert full round-trip expiry behaviour must also control the server clock via environment injection or a test-only endpoint, otherwise the browser and server diverge.

---

**Pattern 3: Node.js `node:test` `--test-randomize` + deterministic seed for order-dependency CI gate** [official]
Node.js 26.1.0 added `--test-randomize` and `--test-random-seed=N` to the built-in test runner. Running the suite with `--test-randomize` in CI surfaces hidden test order-dependencies that pass only because of insertion order. The seed value is printed on failure, allowing exact reproduction locally. This is a zero-dependency pyramid health gate for teams already on Node.js 26 without Vitest.
```typescript
// package.json — two separate CI scripts
// "test": "node --test src/**/*.test.ts"
// "test:order-check": "node --test --test-randomize src/**/*.test.ts"
// Usage: npm run test:order-check -- --test-random-seed=42 for reproduction

// Example test exposing an order dependency that --test-randomize catches
import { test, before, describe } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

let cache: Map<string, number>;

describe('UserCache', () => {
  before(() => { cache = new Map(); });

  // This test silently depends on the next test having run first in a shared suite
  test('returns cached user count', () => {
    // BUG: relies on "populates cache" test having run first — caught by --test-randomize
    assert.strictEqual(cache.get('alice'), 42);
  });

  test('populates cache on first lookup', async () => {
    cache.set('alice', 42);
    assert.ok(cache.has('alice'));
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `--test-randomize` only detects order-dependencies within a single runner invocation. If tests are sharded across workers, cross-shard dependencies (a test in shard 1 depending on a DB write from shard 3) are not detected. Use transaction-per-test isolation as the primary defence; `--test-randomize` is a secondary safety net for within-file and within-worker issues.

---

**Pattern 4: MSW `ws` handler for WebSocket integration test isolation** [official]
MSW v2.x extended its handler API to WebSocket connections via the `ws` namespace. This allows integration tests to intercept `WebSocket` connections established by the browser or Node.js client and respond with controlled message sequences — without running a real WebSocket server. This fills the gap between unit-level mocking (replacing the entire WebSocket class) and full e2e (requiring a live server).
```typescript
// tests/msw-ws-handlers.ts
import { ws } from 'msw';
import { setupServer } from 'msw/node';

const chatHandler = ws.link('wss://api.example.com/chat').on('connection', ({ client }) => {
  // Immediately send a welcome message when client connects
  client.send(JSON.stringify({ type: 'connected', userId: 'user_test_001' }));

  client.addEventListener('message', (event) => {
    const msg = JSON.parse(event.data as string);
    if (msg.type === 'send_message') {
      // Echo back with a server-assigned id
      client.send(JSON.stringify({ type: 'message', id: 'msg_001', text: msg.text }));
    }
  });
});

export const server = setupServer(chatHandler);

// integration/chat-client.test.ts
import { server } from './msw-ws-handlers';
import { ChatClient } from '../src/chat-client';

beforeAll(() => server.listen());
afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers());
afterAll(() => server.close());

test('chat client receives echoed message with server id', async () => {
  const client = new ChatClient('wss://api.example.com/chat');
  await client.connect();
  const received = await client.sendAndAwait('hello world');
  expect(received).toMatchObject({ type: 'message', id: 'msg_001', text: 'hello world' });
});
```
Tradeoff: MSW `ws` handlers simulate message-level behaviour but cannot reproduce backpressure, connection drops under load, or server-side rate limiting — those require a real WebSocket server. Use MSW `ws` for correctness testing of the client's message-handling logic; use Docker-composed real services for resilience and performance testing at the integration layer.

---

**Pattern 5: Vitest `vi.stubGlobal()` + `vi.unstubAllGlobals()` for hermetic browser-API unit tests** [official]
`vi.stubGlobal()` replaces a property on the global object (`globalThis`) for the duration of a test and automatically restores it via `vi.unstubAllGlobals()` in `afterEach`. This is the correct mechanism for stubbing browser APIs (`localStorage`, `navigator.onLine`, `window.matchMedia`) in jsdom/happy-dom unit tests — safer than manual property assignment (`global.X = mock`) which leaks state if the test throws before cleanup.
```typescript
// unit/offline-banner.test.ts
import { afterEach, beforeEach, describe, expect, test, vi } from 'vitest';
import { render, screen } from '@testing-library/react';
import { OfflineBanner } from '../src/OfflineBanner';

afterEach(() => {
  vi.unstubAllGlobals(); // always restores, even if the test threw
});

describe('OfflineBanner', () => {
  test('shows banner when navigator.onLine is false', () => {
    vi.stubGlobal('navigator', { ...navigator, onLine: false });
    render(<OfflineBanner />);
    expect(screen.getByRole('alert')).toHaveTextContent(/you are offline/i);
  });

  test('hides banner when navigator.onLine is true', () => {
    vi.stubGlobal('navigator', { ...navigator, onLine: true });
    render(<OfflineBanner />);
    expect(screen.queryByRole('alert')).toBeNull();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `vi.stubGlobal()` only affects the jsdom/happy-dom environment inside the worker thread. Vitest browser mode (`@vitest/browser`) uses the real `navigator` from the browser — `vi.stubGlobal()` calls there overwrite the real global and can produce unexpected results in concurrent browser tests sharing the same page. In browser mode, use `page.evaluate(() => Object.defineProperty(navigator, 'onLine', { value: false }))` instead.

---

**Pattern 6: Playwright ARIA snapshots for semantically stable locator-free assertions** [official]
Playwright v1.50+ introduced ARIA snapshot assertions (`expect(locator).toMatchAriaSnapshot()`) that capture the accessibility tree of a subtree as a YAML-like text format and assert structural equality. ARIA snapshots are more semantically stable than CSS/text locators — they survive CSS class renames, DOM restructuring, and visual redesigns as long as the accessibility tree remains equivalent.
```typescript
// e2e/navigation.e2e.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('main navigation renders correct ARIA structure', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');
  const nav = page.getByRole('navigation', { name: 'Main' });

  // Snapshot captures the ARIA tree of the nav element
  // Update with: npx playwright test --update-snapshots
  await expect(nav).toMatchAriaSnapshot(`
    - navigation "Main":
      - list:
        - listitem:
          - link "Home"
        - listitem:
          - link "Products"
        - listitem:
          - link "Pricing"
        - listitem:
          - link "Sign in"
  `);
});
```
Tradeoff: ARIA snapshots couple tests to the accessibility tree structure. A UX change that renames a nav link or adds a new item requires updating the snapshot — which is intentional (it forces deliberate accessibility review), but it means snapshot churn during active UX iteration. Use ARIA snapshots for stable, shipped flows rather than features under active redesign.

---

**Pattern 7: Testcontainers `GenericContainer` with `withTmpFs` for ephemeral filesystem integration tests** [official]
`withTmpFs` mounts a tmpfs (in-memory) filesystem at a specified path inside the container. For integration tests that write files (uploads, export pipelines, audit logs), mounting the working directory as tmpfs eliminates disk I/O and makes the container teardown instantaneous — no persistent layer to clean up between test runs.
```typescript
// integration/file-export.test.ts
import { GenericContainer, Wait } from 'testcontainers';

let container: StartedTestContainer;

beforeAll(async () => {
  container = await new GenericContainer('my-export-service:latest')
    .withTmpFs({ '/app/exports': 'rw,noexec,nosuid,size=64m' })
    .withEnvironment({ EXPORT_DIR: '/app/exports', NODE_ENV: 'test' })
    .withWaitStrategy(Wait.forLogMessage('listening on port'))
    .withExposedPorts(3000)
    .start();
}, 30_000);

afterAll(async () => {
  await container?.stop();
});

test('export endpoint writes CSV to EXPORT_DIR', async () => {
  const port = container.getMappedPort(3000);
  const res = await fetch(`http://localhost:${port}/export/users?format=csv`);
  expect(res.ok).toBe(true);

  // Read file from container's tmpfs mount
  const { output } = await container.exec(['ls', '/app/exports']);
  expect(output).toMatch(/users_\d{8}\.csv/);
});
```
Tradeoff: tmpfs is lost when the container stops, which is the desired behaviour for test isolation. However, tests that assert file persistence across container restarts (e.g., crash-recovery scenarios) cannot use tmpfs — those require a named volume or a bind mount with an explicit cleanup step in `afterAll`.

---

**Pattern 8: `@testing-library/user-event` v14 `setup()` factory for realistic interaction fidelity** [official]
`@testing-library/user-event` v14 replaced the legacy `userEvent.type()` top-level API with a `userEvent.setup()` factory that more accurately simulates pointer and keyboard state — including focus management, key repetition, and clipboard operations. Using the legacy API in React 19 + RTL v16 test suites produces warnings and skips pointer events that trigger React's synthetic event system correctly.
```typescript
// unit/SearchInput.test.tsx
import { render, screen } from '@testing-library/react';
import userEvent from '@testing-library/user-event';
import { SearchInput } from '../src/SearchInput';

test('calls onSearch with debounced value after user finishes typing', async () => {
  // v14 setup() — creates a user instance with internal pointer/keyboard state
  const user = userEvent.setup({ delay: null }); // delay:null disables artificial delay for unit tests
  const onSearch = vi.fn();

  render(<SearchInput onSearch={onSearch} debounceMs={300} />);

  const input = screen.getByRole('searchbox');
  await user.click(input);
  await user.type(input, 'typescript testing');

  // Flush the debounce timer
  await vi.runAllTimersAsync();

  expect(onSearch).toHaveBeenCalledWith('typescript testing');
  expect(onSearch).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1); // debounce — not once per keystroke
});
```
Tradeoff: `userEvent.setup({ delay: null })` disables the artificial keystroke delay for unit test speed, but this means the test does not exercise the time gap between keystrokes. For testing debounce behaviour specifically, use `vi.useFakeTimers()` and advance time explicitly rather than relying on the user-event delay option.

---

**Pattern 9: Vitest `test.extend` with a typed `db` fixture for transaction-isolated integration tests** [official]
Vitest's `test.extend` allows declaring a `db` fixture that opens a transaction in `beforeEach` and rolls it back in `afterEach` — providing each test with a clean database state without truncation or seeding costs. The fixture is typed, so tests that destructure it get full IntelliSense on the database client.
```typescript
// tests/fixtures/db.ts
import { test as baseTest } from 'vitest';
import { Pool, PoolClient } from 'pg';

interface DbFixtures {
  db: PoolClient;
}

const pool = new Pool({ connectionString: process.env.TEST_DATABASE_URL });

export const test = baseTest.extend<DbFixtures>({
  db: async ({}, use) => {
    const client = await pool.connect();
    await client.query('BEGIN');
    try {
      await use(client);
    } finally {
      await client.query('ROLLBACK');
      client.release();
    }
  },
});

// integration/user-repo.test.ts
import { expect } from 'vitest';
import { test } from '../fixtures/db';
import { UserRepository } from '../../src/repositories/UserRepository';

test('creates user and returns auto-generated id', async ({ db }) => {
  const repo = new UserRepository(db);
  const user = await repo.create({ email: 'test@example.com', name: 'Test User' });
  expect(user.id).toMatch(/^usr_/);
  const found = await repo.findById(user.id);
  expect(found?.email).toBe('test@example.com');
  // Transaction is rolled back automatically in afterEach — no cleanup required
});
```
Tradeoff: Transaction rollback isolation fails for operations that use `COMMIT` internally (e.g., DDL statements, `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT` with advisory locks, stored procedures that auto-commit). Those tests require a separate Testcontainers database instance per test rather than a transaction rollback strategy.

---

**Pattern 10: Playwright `locator.filter({ hasNot: ... })` for negative list-item disambiguation** [official]
`locator.filter()` accepts a `hasNot` option that excludes list items containing a specific child locator or text. This is the idiomatic way to assert "the list contains items that are NOT in an error state" without resorting to custom JavaScript evaluation or counting with `expect(items).not.toContain(...)` patterns that break on partial text matches.
```typescript
// e2e/notifications.e2e.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('notification list has no unread items after mark-all-read', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/notifications');

  // Confirm there are unread items before acting
  const unreadBefore = page.getByRole('listitem').filter({ has: page.getByLabel('unread') });
  await expect(unreadBefore).not.toHaveCount(0);

  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Mark all as read' }).click();

  // After action: all items should be read — no listitem contains the unread indicator
  const allItems = page.getByRole('listitem');
  const unreadAfter = allItems.filter({ has: page.getByLabel('unread') });
  await expect(unreadAfter).toHaveCount(0);

  // Positive assertion: all items now have the read indicator
  const readItems = allItems.filter({ has: page.getByLabel('read') });
  await expect(readItems).toHaveCount(await allItems.count());
});
```
Tradeoff: `locator.filter({ hasNot: ... })` evaluates in the DOM at assertion time — it does not retry until the condition is met in the same way `expect(locator).toHaveCount()` does. Wrap in `expect.poll()` or use `await expect(unreadAfter).toHaveCount(0)` (which auto-retries) rather than asserting the filter result in a raw boolean expression.

---

**Pattern 11: Consumer-Driven Contract testing with Pact `PactV4` + `eachLike()` and server-side Zod validation at the integration layer** [official]
Consumer-driven contract tests (CDCs) prevent providers from silently removing or renaming fields. The consumer defines the expected shape using Pact `eachLike()` (at least one item matching the schema), then the provider runs the verification against the pact file. Adding strict Zod parsing on the provider-side integration test gives a second layer of assurance: the provider test fails if the response has extra fields that the consumer would silently ignore but that signal API drift.
```typescript
// consumer/src/products.pact.test.ts
import { PactV4, MatchersV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
const { eachLike, string, integer } = MatchersV3;

const provider = new PactV4({
  consumer: 'frontend-app',
  provider: 'products-api',
  dir: './pacts',
});

test('GET /products returns product list', async () => {
  await provider
    .addInteraction()
    .uponReceiving('a request for product list')
    .withRequest('GET', '/products')
    .willRespondWith(200, (builder) => {
      builder.jsonBody({
        items: eachLike({
          id: string('prod_abc'),
          name: string('Test Product'),
          price: integer(1000),
          currency: string('USD'),
        }),
        total: integer(1),
      });
    })
    .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
      const res = await fetch(`${mockServer.url}/products`);
      const data = await res.json();
      // Consumer-side Zod parse — extra provider fields cause test failure
      const parsed = ProductListSchema.safeParse(data);
      expect(parsed.success).toBe(true);
    });
});
```
Tradeoff: Pact CDC tests verify contract shape, not business logic. They do not catch bugs where the provider returns the correct structure but wrong data (e.g., `price: 0` for all products). Pair CDC tests with provider-side integration tests that seed known data and assert computed values.

---

**Pattern 12: Playwright `testProject.teardown` for shared DB state cleanup after parallel e2e projects** [official]
Playwright v1.53+ `testProject.teardown` links a cleanup project that runs after a given test project finishes, regardless of pass/fail. This enables reliable teardown of shared infrastructure (seeded DB records, test users, S3 bucket contents) after parallel e2e runs without moving cleanup into individual test `afterAll` blocks that may not run if a test process crashes.
```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  projects: [
    // Setup project runs first — creates shared test data
    { name: 'setup', testMatch: /e2e\/setup\/.*\.ts$/ },

    // Test projects run in parallel — both depend on setup
    {
      name: 'chromium-tests',
      testMatch: /e2e\/specs\/.*\.ts$/,
      dependencies: ['setup'],
      teardown: 'cleanup', // runs after this project completes
      use: { browserName: 'chromium' },
    },
    {
      name: 'webkit-tests',
      testMatch: /e2e\/specs\/.*\.ts$/,
      dependencies: ['setup'],
      teardown: 'cleanup',
      use: { browserName: 'webkit' },
    },

    // Teardown project — runs after each test project completes
    {
      name: 'cleanup',
      testMatch: /e2e\/teardown\/.*\.ts$/,
    },
  ],
});
```
Tradeoff: When multiple test projects share the same `teardown` project name, Playwright runs the teardown project once per referencing project — not once globally. If the teardown script is idempotent (deletes by a fixed test-run ID), double execution is harmless; if it performs count-sensitive operations (e.g., deletes the last N records), it will over-delete. Use a per-run ID strategy: seed all test data with a unique `testRunId` and delete only rows matching that ID in teardown.

---

**Pattern 13: Vitest `coverage.thresholds` with `perFile: true` for per-file coverage enforcement** [official]
Vitest `coverage.thresholds` with the `perFile: true` option enforces coverage minimums per source file rather than across the entire project. This prevents the "average masking" problem where high coverage on large utility modules hides zero-coverage business-logic files. Teams can set a global floor with `perFile: true` and override it per directory using glob patterns.
```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      reporter: ['text', 'lcov', 'html'],
      thresholds: {
        // Global per-file floor: every file must have >= 70% lines covered
        perFile: true,
        lines: 70,
        functions: 70,
        // Override for critical business logic directories — higher floor
        'src/domain/**': {
          lines: 90,
          functions: 90,
          branches: 85,
        },
        // Lower floor for generated files and adapters
        'src/generated/**': {
          lines: 0,
          functions: 0,
        },
      },
    },
  },
});
```
Tradeoff: `perFile: true` coverage thresholds cause CI failures on new files with no tests yet — which is the intended behaviour, but can be frustrating during rapid prototyping. Use a `coverage.exclude` list for files in early development (e.g., files with a `// @coverage-exempt` comment detected by a custom ignore pattern) and remove the exclusion when the file stabilises.

---

**Pattern 14: OpenTelemetry `@opentelemetry/sdk-trace-node` span assertions for trace-based integration testing** [official]
Trace-based testing uses OpenTelemetry trace spans as integration test assertions — verifying that a request produced the expected spans at the expected layers (HTTP, DB, cache) without asserting on internal implementation. An in-memory `SpanExporter` captures spans during the test and a custom assertion helper checks span names, attributes, and parent-child relationships.
```typescript
// integration/otel-tracer.test.ts
import { NodeTracerProvider } from '@opentelemetry/sdk-trace-node';
import { InMemorySpanExporter, SimpleSpanProcessor } from '@opentelemetry/sdk-trace-base';
import { HttpInstrumentation } from '@opentelemetry/instrumentation-http';
import { registerInstrumentations } from '@opentelemetry/instrumentation';
import { test, expect, beforeAll, afterAll } from 'vitest';
import { createOrder } from '../src/orders';

const exporter = new InMemorySpanExporter();
const provider = new NodeTracerProvider();
provider.addSpanProcessor(new SimpleSpanProcessor(exporter));
provider.register();
registerInstrumentations({ instrumentations: [new HttpInstrumentation()] });

afterEach(() => exporter.reset());
afterAll(() => provider.shutdown());

test('createOrder produces db span and payment-service http span', async () => {
  await createOrder({ userId: 'u1', items: [{ sku: 'SKU1', qty: 1 }] });

  const spans = exporter.getFinishedSpans();
  const spanNames = spans.map((s) => s.name);

  expect(spanNames).toContain('pg.query');
  expect(spanNames).toContain('HTTP POST');

  const dbSpan = spans.find((s) => s.name === 'pg.query')!;
  expect(dbSpan.attributes['db.statement']).toContain('INSERT INTO orders');
});
```
Tradeoff: Trace-based integration tests are tightly coupled to the instrumentation library's span naming conventions. If `@opentelemetry/instrumentation-pg` changes its span name from `pg.query` to `postgresql.query` in a major version, all span-name assertions break silently (the test passes with zero matched spans if the assertion uses `.toContain()` rather than `.toHaveLength(N)`). Use `expect(spans.filter(s => s.name === 'pg.query')).toHaveLength(1)` rather than `.toContain()` to catch missing spans.

---

**Pattern 15: Playwright `page.route()` + JSON fixture files for deterministic API mocking in e2e tests** [official]
`page.route()` intercepts network requests inside Playwright and responds with fixture data from JSON files checked into the repository. This places the e2e layer on stable, versioned response data — eliminating flakiness caused by API staging environment unavailability and allowing offline e2e test runs in CI without a running backend.
```typescript
// e2e/fixtures/api/products-list.json
// { "items": [{ "id": "prod_001", "name": "Widget A", "price": 1999 }], "total": 1 }

// e2e/products.e2e.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { readFileSync } from 'fs';
import { join } from 'path';

test('products page renders items from API', async ({ page }) => {
  const fixture = JSON.parse(
    readFileSync(join(__dirname, 'fixtures/api/products-list.json'), 'utf-8'),
  );

  await page.route('**/api/products', (route) =>
    route.fulfill({ status: 200, contentType: 'application/json', body: JSON.stringify(fixture) }),
  );

  await page.goto('/products');
  await expect(page.getByRole('listitem').first()).toContainText('Widget A');
  await expect(page.getByText('$19.99')).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: JSON fixture files can drift from the real API contract. A field renamed in the API is not reflected in the fixture until the fixture is manually updated — the e2e test keeps passing while real users see broken UI. Mitigate with a Pact contract test (Pattern 11) that validates the fixture file format against the provider, or run a nightly "live API" test job that exercises the same flows without `page.route()` interception.

### Community Gotchas

**Gotcha G226: Vitest `expect.poll()` default `interval` is 50 ms but the first evaluation is synchronous — assertion helpers that throw on first call will retry correctly, but ones that return `undefined` on first call appear to pass immediately**
When using `expect.poll(fn)`, the callback is called once synchronously before the polling loop starts. If the callback returns `undefined` (e.g., `await db.findOne(...)` returns `null` and the assertion is `toBeDefined()`), Vitest catches the assertion error and starts polling. However, if the callback itself swallows errors and returns `undefined` instead of throwing, the first synchronous call "passes" and the poll exits immediately — masking the eventual-consistency bug. WHY: `expect.poll()` treats the first call like any other iteration; a callback that returns without throwing is considered a passing iteration. Callbacks that return `undefined` silently without asserting are valid JavaScript and do not trigger the retry loop. Fix: ensure the `expect.poll()` callback always ends with an assertion (`expect(result).toBeDefined()`) rather than returning the raw value; never return the value from the callback without asserting it, as `expect.poll(() => value)` with a non-nullish `value` on the first try will pass immediately even if the real state diverges after the first call. [community: vitest.dev/api/expect#poll]

**Gotcha G227: Playwright `page.clock.install()` does not freeze `performance.now()` in Web Workers — animations and timers inside Worker threads still use real time**
`page.clock.install()` replaces `Date`, `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, and `requestAnimationFrame` on the main thread's `window` object. Web Workers have their own independent execution context and hold their own copies of `Date` and `performance`. A test that installs the clock and then fast-forwards time will see main-thread timers fire at the correct fake time, but a Worker that uses `setTimeout` or `performance.now()` internally will continue using real wall time. This causes integration-level test flakiness when the application under test offloads time-sensitive logic (retry queues, keepalive heartbeats) to a Worker. WHY: Playwright's Clock API communicates with the browser page via `window.eval`; Web Workers do not share `window` and are not reached by this mechanism. Fix: for Worker-based time-sensitive logic, extract the timeout/interval management into a configurable injectable (e.g., accept a `clock: { setTimeout }` parameter) so tests can inject a fake clock at the module level; alternatively, test Worker-based timing with a dedicated `WorkerGlobalScope` mock that replaces the Worker's built-in timer functions before the Worker script initialises. [official: playwright.dev/docs/clock]

**Gotcha G228: Testcontainers `withTmpFs` on Docker Desktop for Mac/Windows silently falls back to a named volume when the container runtime is not Linux — tmpfs is a Linux kernel feature**
`withTmpFs` mounts a Linux tmpfs filesystem inside the container. On Docker Desktop for Mac and Windows, the container actually runs inside a Linux VM, so tmpfs inside the container works correctly — the gotcha is that the *host path mapping* behaves differently: the developer assumes "this is in memory so it's always empty on start" but Docker Desktop's volume management layer can persist certain mounts between container restarts if the VM is not fully restarted. In CI on a Linux runner, `withTmpFs` is guaranteed to be fresh every time; locally on Mac/Windows after a suspended VM, the tmpfs mount may retain data from the previous container run. WHY: Docker Desktop for Mac/Windows runs containers inside a lightweight Linux VM whose lifecycle is decoupled from the host OS shutdown; if the VM is merely suspended (not restarted), the tmpfs contents in long-lived containers can persist. Fix: never use `withReuse()` together with `withTmpFs` in tests that require guaranteed-empty state; or add an explicit `container.exec(['rm', '-rf', '/app/exports/*'])` step in the test's `beforeAll` when `withTmpFs` is combined with container reuse. [official: testcontainers.com/guides/nodejs]

**Gotcha G229: `@testing-library/user-event` v14 `userEvent.setup({ delay: null })` breaks `onCompositionStart` / `onCompositionEnd` — CJK and IME input flows are silently skipped**
`delay: null` in `userEvent.setup()` disables the artificial delay between keystrokes. A side-effect of removing the delay is that composition events (`compositionstart`, `compositionupdate`, `compositionend`) used by Input Method Editors (IME) for CJK text input (Chinese, Japanese, Korean) are not dispatched when `delay: null` is set. Applications that guard text submission behind `event.isComposing === false` (to prevent premature form submission while the user is mid-composition) will have those guards skipped in unit tests that use `delay: null`. The test passes because the guard is never triggered, but the real user experience has a bug where pressing Enter during CJK composition incorrectly submits the form. WHY: `userEvent` v14 dispatches composition events only when there is a non-zero delay between keystrokes, simulating real IME timing; with `delay: null`, keystrokes are dispatched atomically and composition events are omitted. Fix: use `delay: null` only for tests that do not involve IME-sensitive inputs; for CJK input and composition-aware forms, use `userEvent.setup({ delay: 10 })` (minimal delay) to preserve composition event dispatch. [official: testing-library.com/docs/user-event/options]

**Gotcha G230: OpenTelemetry `InMemorySpanExporter` does not flush spans from async `Promise`-returning instrumented code until the `await` resolves — assertions before `await` will see zero spans**
`InMemorySpanExporter` collects spans that have been _finished_ (their `span.end()` called). Instrumentation libraries such as `@opentelemetry/instrumentation-pg` end the span only after the async database operation completes. If a test calls `exporter.getFinishedSpans()` before awaiting the function under test, it sees zero spans — causing the assertion to fail or, worse, to silently pass a `.not.toHaveLength(0)` check because the zero-span array fulfils the wrong condition. WHY: OpenTelemetry spans are started synchronously when an instrumented function is called but ended asynchronously after the underlying I/O resolves; `InMemorySpanExporter` is a synchronous in-memory buffer that reports only finished spans at the instant of the call. Fix: always `await` the function under test fully before calling `exporter.getFinishedSpans()`; add a helper that flushes the tracer provider's batch processor (`await provider.forceFlush()`) before asserting spans when using `BatchSpanProcessor` instead of `SimpleSpanProcessor`. [official: opentelemetry.io/docs/languages/js/instrumentation]
