**Pattern 53: Testcontainers `reuse` + `TESTCONTAINERS_RYUK_DISABLED` for shared integration containers across multiple test file runs in monorepo CI** [official]
```typescript
// test/helpers/shared-postgres.ts
import { PostgreSqlContainer, StartedPostgreSqlContainer } from '@testcontainers/postgresql';

let sharedContainer: StartedPostgreSqlContainer | null = null;

export async function getSharedPostgres(): Promise<StartedPostgreSqlContainer> {
  if (sharedContainer) return sharedContainer;

  // TESTCONTAINERS_RYUK_DISABLED=true in CI env prevents Ryuk from cleaning
  // containers between test file invocations — combined with reuse: true,
  // the container survives across vitest worker restarts.
  sharedContainer = await new PostgreSqlContainer('postgres:16-alpine')
    .withReuse()     // reuse: container is matched by label and reused if already running
    .withDatabase('testdb')
    .withUsername('test')
    .withPassword('test')
    .start();

  return sharedContainer;
}

// vitest.config.ts — ensure globalSetup controls container lifecycle
export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    globalSetup: ['./test/global-setup.ts'],
    globalTeardown: ['./test/global-teardown.ts'],
    poolOptions: { threads: { singleThread: false } },
  },
});
```
Tradeoff: Container reuse cuts integration test cold-start time by 40-70% in monorepo CI pipelines where 20+ test files all need a Postgres instance, but reuse introduces state leakage risk — every test file must clean up its own rows (or use schema-isolated fixtures) since the container persists between runs; always use `TESTCONTAINERS_RYUK_DISABLED=false` in local development where fresh containers per run is preferable.

**Pattern 54: Playwright `test.abort()` for immediate e2e test termination on unrecoverable application state** [official]
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// A fixture that monitors the app's error boundary and aborts the test
// immediately if a React error boundary renders — no point continuing.
const testWithErrorGuard = test.extend<{ guardErrors: void }>({
  guardErrors: [
    async ({ page }, use, testInfo) => {
      // Set up before test body
      const errorMessages: string[] = [];
      page.on('console', (msg) => {
        if (msg.type() === 'error') errorMessages.push(msg.text());
      });

      await use();

      // Evaluated after test body — abort if unhandled JS errors fired
      if (errorMessages.some((m) => m.includes('Uncaught Error'))) {
        // test.abort() stops the test from further retries and marks it as aborted,
        // not failed — useful for "environment broken" vs "assertion failed" distinction
        await test.abort(`Unhandled JS error during test: ${errorMessages[0]}`);
      }
    },
    { auto: true },
  ],
});

testWithErrorGuard('checkout flow completes without JS errors', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Proceed to payment' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByText('Payment step')).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `test.abort()` cleanly separates "the app is broken" (abort) from "the assertion is wrong" (fail), improving signal quality in e2e suites and preventing retry loops on fundamentally broken states, but overuse of abort in fixtures makes it hard to distinguish genuine flakiness from real bugs — reserve `test.abort()` for non-recoverable conditions (error boundaries, auth failures, network down) and use normal assertion failures for all functional checks.

**Pattern 55: Node.js 26 `Temporal.Now.plainDateTimeISO()` as the standard time source for time-sensitive unit tests** [official]
```typescript
// src/subscription/billing-cycle.ts
import { Temporal } from 'temporal-polyfill'; // or built-in on Node 26

export function isTrialExpired(
  trialStartISO: string,
  nowFn: () => Temporal.PlainDateTime = () => Temporal.Now.plainDateTimeISO(),
): boolean {
  const trialStart = Temporal.PlainDateTime.from(trialStartISO);
  const trialEnd = trialStart.add({ days: 14 });
  return Temporal.PlainDateTime.compare(nowFn(), trialEnd) > 0;
}

// src/subscription/billing-cycle.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { Temporal } from 'temporal-polyfill';
import { isTrialExpired } from './billing-cycle';

describe('isTrialExpired', () => {
  it('returns false when 13 days have elapsed', () => {
    const start = '2026-05-01T00:00:00';
    const fakNow = () => Temporal.PlainDateTime.from('2026-05-14T00:00:00');
    expect(isTrialExpired(start, fakNow)).toBe(false);
  });

  it('returns true when exactly 14 days have elapsed', () => {
    const start = '2026-05-01T00:00:00';
    const fakeNow = () => Temporal.PlainDateTime.from('2026-05-15T00:00:00');
    expect(isTrialExpired(start, fakeNow)).toBe(true);
  });

  it('handles timezone-ambiguous DST boundaries correctly via PlainDateTime', () => {
    // PlainDateTime has no timezone — DST transitions do not affect the comparison
    const start = '2026-03-08T01:30:00'; // DST transition day in US/Eastern
    const fakeNow = () => Temporal.PlainDateTime.from('2026-03-22T01:30:00');
    expect(isTrialExpired(start, fakeNow)).toBe(false); // exactly 14 days
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Injecting `nowFn` as a parameter with `Temporal.PlainDateTime` as the type makes time-sensitive unit tests deterministic and timezone-safe without relying on `vi.useFakeTimers()` or `Date` manipulation, but `Temporal` API requires Node 26 built-in or a polyfill on Node 22/24 — add `temporal-polyfill` as a dev dependency and conditionally use the polyfill until Node 26 is your minimum supported runtime.

**Pattern 56: Vitest `mockThrow` / `mockThrowOnce` for concise error-path unit tests** [official]
```typescript
import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach } from 'vitest';
import { processOrder } from './order-processor';
import { inventoryService } from './inventory-service';

vi.mock('./inventory-service');

describe('processOrder — error paths', () => {
  beforeEach(() => vi.resetAllMocks());

  it('throws OrderUnavailableError when inventory check fails with a transient error', () => {
    // mockThrowOnce — throws only for the first call, subsequent calls use default mock
    vi.mocked(inventoryService.checkStock).mockThrowOnce(
      new Error('inventory service timeout'),
    );

    expect(() => processOrder({ sku: 'ABC-1', qty: 2 })).toThrow(
      'inventory service timeout',
    );
  });

  it('propagates unknown errors from inventory service unchanged', () => {
    // mockThrow — throws on every call
    vi.mocked(inventoryService.checkStock).mockThrow(
      new RangeError('unexpected SKU format'),
    );

    expect(() => processOrder({ sku: '!INVALID', qty: 1 })).toThrow(RangeError);
    expect(() => processOrder({ sku: '!INVALID', qty: 1 })).toThrow(RangeError);
  });

  it('returns fallback result after first transient failure via mockThrowOnce chain', () => {
    vi.mocked(inventoryService.checkStock)
      .mockThrowOnce(new Error('transient'))
      .mockReturnValue({ available: true, quantity: 5 });

    expect(() => processOrder({ sku: 'ABC-1', qty: 1 })).toThrow('transient');
    const result = processOrder({ sku: 'ABC-1', qty: 1 }); // second call succeeds
    expect(result).toMatchObject({ status: 'accepted' });
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `mockThrow` and `mockThrowOnce` are syntactically equivalent to `mockReturnValue`/`mockReturnValueOnce` and slot naturally into chained mock setup, eliminating the previous pattern of `mockImplementation(() => { throw new Error(...) })`, but they are Vitest 4.1-specific — projects on Vitest 3.x or Jest must continue using `mockImplementation` for thrown errors.

**Pattern 57: Playwright `toMatchAriaSnapshot()` on the full page for structural regression testing of dynamic content** [official]
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.describe('dashboard layout — ARIA structural regression', () => {
  test('renders navigation, main, and aside regions with expected roles', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/dashboard');
    await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle');

    // Page-level ARIA snapshot: captures the entire accessible tree.
    // On first run, Playwright writes the snapshot to __snapshots__/dashboard.aria.txt.
    // On subsequent runs it diffs against the saved baseline.
    await expect(page).toMatchAriaSnapshot(`
      - navigation "Main navigation":
        - link "Home"
        - link "Reports"
        - link "Settings"
      - main:
        - heading "Dashboard" [level=1]
        - region "Metrics summary"
        - region "Recent activity"
      - complementary "Sidebar":
        - heading "Quick links" [level=2]
    `);
  });

  test('search result list renders accessible item count', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/dashboard?q=invoice');
    await page.waitForSelector('[data-testid="results-count"]');

    // Scoped to the results region to avoid full-page snapshot noise
    const results = page.getByRole('region', { name: 'Search results' });
    await expect(results).toMatchAriaSnapshot(`
      - region "Search results":
        - status: /\\d+ results found/
        - list:
          - listitem /Invoice .*/
    `);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Page-level `toMatchAriaSnapshot()` provides structural regression coverage that catches accessibility regressions (removed landmarks, renamed links) without the fragility of CSS selector snapshots, but ARIA snapshots are sensitive to text content changes — use regex patterns (`/Invoice .*/`) for dynamic content and commit snapshot files in the same PR as the UI change they validate.

**Pattern 58: TypeScript 5.9 `verbatimModuleSyntax: true` safe migration pattern for test files using type-only imports** [official]
```typescript
// tsconfig.test.json — safe test tsconfig inheriting from root after TS 5.9 upgrade
{
  "extends": "./tsconfig.json",
  "compilerOptions": {
    // TS 5.9 sets verbatimModuleSyntax: true by default in tsc --init output.
    // Test files frequently import type-only symbols without 'import type'.
    // Override explicitly to avoid breaking existing test files en masse.
    "verbatimModuleSyntax": false,
    // Alternatively, keep verbatimModuleSyntax: true and run the codemod:
    // npx @typescript/codemod verbatim-module-syntax --files "src/**/*.test.ts"
    "types": ["vitest/globals", "node"],
    "include": ["src/**/*.test.ts", "src/**/*.spec.ts", "test/**/*.ts"]
  }
}

// Before codemod — causes TS error under verbatimModuleSyntax: true:
import { UserService, UserCreatedEvent } from '../user-service'; // UserCreatedEvent is type-only

// After codemod — explicit import type for the type symbol:
import { UserService } from '../user-service';
import type { UserCreatedEvent } from '../user-service';

// Or combined import (also valid under verbatimModuleSyntax):
import { UserService, type UserCreatedEvent } from '../user-service';
```
Tradeoff: Explicitly overriding `verbatimModuleSyntax: false` in the test tsconfig is the safest short-term migration path after a `tsc --init`-triggered TS 5.9 upgrade, but it leaves a permanent drift between the production tsconfig and test tsconfig — the correct long-term fix is to run the TypeScript `verbatim-module-syntax` codemod on test files and then enable the setting uniformly.

**Pattern 59: Vitest `test.extend` builder pattern with inferred types for zero-annotation fixture typing** [official]
```typescript
// test/fixtures/api-fixtures.ts
import { test as base } from 'vitest';
import { createServer } from '../src/server';
import type { Server } from 'node:http';
import type { AddressInfo } from 'node:net';

// Vitest 4.1 builder pattern: return value type is inferred —
// no explicit generic annotation on test.extend() required.
export const test = base.extend({
  // The fixture factory's return type is inferred from the value passed to `use()`
  server: async ({}, use) => {
    const app = createServer();
    const server = await new Promise<Server>((resolve) => {
      const s = app.listen(0, () => resolve(s));
    });
    const { port } = server.address() as AddressInfo;
    await use({ server, port, baseUrl: `http://localhost:${port}` });
    await new Promise<void>((resolve) => server.close(() => resolve()));
  },

  // Dependent fixture: `server` is injected automatically
  apiClient: async ({ server }, use) => {
    const { default: fetch } = await import('node-fetch');
    await use({
      get: (path: string) => fetch(`${server.baseUrl}${path}`).then((r) => r.json()),
      post: (path: string, body: unknown) =>
        fetch(`${server.baseUrl}${path}`, {
          method: 'POST',
          body: JSON.stringify(body),
          headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
        }).then((r) => r.json()),
    });
  },
});

// test/api/health.test.ts — full TypeScript inference, zero type annotations:
import { test } from '../fixtures/api-fixtures';
import { expect } from 'vitest';

test('GET /health returns 200', async ({ apiClient }) => {
  const data = await apiClient.get('/health');
  expect(data).toMatchObject({ status: 'ok' });
});
```
Tradeoff: The Vitest 4.1 builder pattern eliminates the verbose `base.extend<{ server: ServerFixture; apiClient: ApiClientFixture }>({...})` generic annotation that was required in 3.x, reducing fixture boilerplate by ~40%, but auto-inference can produce overly narrow types (e.g., literal string types instead of `string`) for fixtures that return primitive values — add an explicit type annotation on the `use` parameter only where inference produces an unexpectedly narrow type.

**Pattern 60: Node.js `node:test` `getTestContext()` for context-aware assertion helpers without parameter threading** [official]
```typescript
// test/helpers/db-assert.ts — uses getTestContext() to access the current test
// without needing every helper to accept a TestContext parameter
import { getTestContext } from 'node:test';
import { db } from '../src/db';

export async function assertRowExists(
  table: string,
  where: Record<string, unknown>,
): Promise<void> {
  const ctx = getTestContext(); // returns the currently executing TestContext
  const rows = await db.query(`SELECT 1 FROM ${table} WHERE ?`, where);
  if (rows.length === 0) {
    // ctx.assert.fail() attaches the failure to the correct test node in the report
    ctx.assert.fail(
      `Expected at least one row in '${table}' matching ${JSON.stringify(where)} but found none`,
    );
  }
}

// test/users.test.ts — assertRowExists reads its own test context internally
import { describe, it, before, after } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { assertRowExists } from '../helpers/db-assert';
import { createUser } from '../src/users';

describe('createUser', () => {
  it('persists user to the database', async () => {
    await createUser({ name: 'Bob', email: 'bob@example.com' });
    // No context parameter needed — getTestContext() resolves it internally
    await assertRowExists('users', { email: 'bob@example.com' });
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `getTestContext()` (Node.js 26.1) allows deeply nested helper functions to report failures against the correct test node without threading a `TestContext` parameter through every call site, but it only works within the synchronous or async call stack of a running test — calling it outside a test (e.g., in a `globalSetup` or a `setTimeout` callback) throws `ERR_TEST_OUTSIDE_OF_TEST`; guard with a try/catch in shared utility code.

### Community Gotchas

**G241: Vitest `aroundEach` DB transaction rollback conflicts with Prisma's connection pool `BEGIN` / `COMMIT` lifecycle**
Why this matters: Prisma's default connection pool wraps every query in its own transaction scope internally. When a test wraps the entire test body in an outer `BEGIN` (via `aroundEach`) and then passes a Prisma client to the test, Prisma may issue a nested `BEGIN` which PostgreSQL promotes to a savepoint. If the outer transaction is rolled back by throwing after `runTest()`, Prisma's connection pool marks the connection as broken because it did not receive an explicit `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK` from its own transaction management layer. The pool then attempts to reset the connection and may log spurious "connection terminated" errors in CI, causing flaky test output even when all tests pass.
Fix: Use `prisma.$transaction(async (tx) => { ... throw new Error('__rollback__') })` inside the `aroundEach` body and pass the transaction-scoped `tx` client to fixtures instead of the global `prisma` instance. Alternatively, replace transaction-rollback isolation with per-test schema isolation using Testcontainers snapshots, which avoids the nested transaction problem entirely.

---

**G242: Playwright `toMatchAriaSnapshot()` baseline divergence when headless Chromium ARIA tree generation differs from headed mode between CI and local environments**
Why this matters: Chromium's accessibility tree computation differs subtly between headless (`--headless=new` mode, default since Playwright v1.49) and headed mode. Some ARIA properties — particularly computed `aria-label` values derived from CSS `content: attr(data-label)` and `aria-describedby` resolution across shadow DOM boundaries — produce different string values in headless vs headed Chromium. When a developer updates an ARIA snapshot baseline locally in headed mode and commits it, CI running in headless mode fails the structural regression test with a diff that cannot be reproduced locally, causing a "works on my machine" deadlock.
Fix: Enforce a single rendering mode for snapshot baseline generation using `DISPLAY=:99 xvfb-run` (Linux CI) or always generating baselines from the headless CI environment via `npx playwright test --update-snapshots` in the CI pipeline rather than locally. Document in the test README that ARIA baselines must be updated from the CI environment, not local headed browsers.

---

**G243: Node.js 26 removal of `--experimental-transform-types` breaks CI scripts that passed the flag explicitly on Node 22/24**
Why this matters: Node.js 22.x and 24.x required `--experimental-transform-types` to strip TypeScript type annotations and run `.ts` files natively. Many teams added the flag explicitly to CI scripts (`node --experimental-transform-types server.ts`) after the feature was first announced in Node 22.6. Node.js 26 stabilised type stripping and silently removed the flag — it is now an unrecognised option. CI pipelines that upgraded Node.js 26 without auditing their script flags begin failing with `node: bad option: --experimental-transform-types` before any test runs, which is misdiagnosed as a test framework failure rather than a flag deprecation.
Fix: Remove `--experimental-transform-types` from all CI scripts and `package.json` invocations when upgrading to Node 26. Use a search-and-replace across the repo: `grep -r "experimental-transform-types" .` then remove the flag. On Node 22/24 compatibility branches, keep the flag conditionally via `node$(node --version | cut -d. -f1 | tr -d 'v') >= 26 || --experimental-transform-types`.

---

**G244: Vitest `coverage.changed` reports zero coverage when the diff base branch is not fetched in a shallow CI clone**
Why this matters: `coverage.changed: 'origin/main'` computes the file diff by running `git diff origin/main...HEAD --name-only` internally. In shallow CI clones (`git checkout --depth=1`), the `origin/main` ref is either absent or points to a single commit without the full commit history needed for diff computation. Vitest silently falls back to full-suite coverage when the diff fails, or in some configurations throws `fatal: 'origin/main' is not a commit` and exits the coverage step with an error. The result is that per-PR delta coverage either always shows 0% (silent fallback) or breaks the CI step entirely on the first PR after adopting `coverage.changed`.
Fix: Add `git fetch --depth=1 origin main` as a step before `vitest run --coverage` in the CI workflow. For GitHub Actions, use `fetch-depth: 0` in the `actions/checkout` step to ensure a full history is available for diff computation, or explicitly fetch the base ref: `git fetch origin ${{ github.base_ref }}`.

---

**G245: MSW WebSocket handler `ws.link()` URL must exactly match the protocol scheme — `ws://` and `wss://` handlers do not cross-match**
Why this matters: MSW's WebSocket handler `ws.link('ws://localhost:3000/chat')` only intercepts connections made using the `ws://` scheme. In local development, the app connects using `ws://` (no TLS) but in staging/production it uses `wss://` (TLS). Integration test environments that configure the WebSocket URL via an environment variable (e.g., `WS_URL=wss://localhost:3000/chat`) will find that MSW's `ws://` handler never fires, resulting in real WebSocket connection attempts that fail because no WebSocket server is running in the test environment. The failure manifests as a `WebSocket connection refused` error, which is easily misattributed to port conflicts or missing server setup rather than a scheme mismatch.
Fix: Register both `ws://` and `wss://` variants of the handler, or normalise the WebSocket URL scheme in the test environment to always use `ws://` by setting `WS_URL=ws://localhost:3000/chat` in the test `.env` file. When using a dynamic URL, extract the scheme normalisation into a utility: `const wsUrl = url.replace(/^wss:\/\//, 'ws://')` applied before passing the URL to `ws.link()`.

### Patterns

**Pattern 61: Vitest `test.override()` scoping fixture values to nested describe blocks without re-declaring the fixture** [official]
```typescript
// test/payment.test.ts — uses test.override() (Vitest 4.1) to scope a timeout
// value to the slow describe block without re-extending the test fixture
import { test as baseTest } from 'vitest';
import { createPaymentClient } from '../src/payment';

const test = baseTest.extend<{ paymentClient: ReturnType<typeof createPaymentClient> }>({
  paymentClient: async ({ use }) => {
    const client = createPaymentClient({ endpoint: process.env.PAYMENT_URL! });
    await use(client);
    await client.close();
  },
});

describe('payment fast paths', () => {
  test('validates card number format', ({ paymentClient }) => {
    expect(paymentClient.validateCard('4111111111111111')).toBe(true);
    expect(paymentClient.validateCard('0000000000000000')).toBe(false);
  });
});

describe('payment slow paths', () => {
  // override timeout only for this describe block — no fixture re-declaration needed
  const slowTest = test.override({ timeout: 30_000 });

  slowTest('processes a 3DS2 challenge flow', async ({ paymentClient }) => {
    const result = await paymentClient.charge({
      amount: 1000,
      currency: 'EUR',
      cardToken: 'tok_visa_3ds2_required',
    });
    expect(result.status).toBe('succeeded');
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `test.override()` (Vitest 4.1) enables per-block option scoping without forking the fixture chain, reducing boilerplate in test files that share fixtures but differ on timeout or retry settings, but overrides apply to all tests lexically within the describe scope including nested describes — be explicit with block boundaries to avoid unintentionally inheriting a 30-second timeout in a nested fast-path block.

**Pattern 62: Node.js 26 `it.expectFailure` with regex `match` for testing known-broken third-party integrations** [official]
```typescript
// test/vendor-compat.test.ts — uses it.expectFailure to document and track
// known failures in a third-party SDK until the vendor ships a fix
import { describe, it } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { VendorClient } from '../src/vendor-client';

const client = new VendorClient({ apiKey: process.env.VENDOR_KEY! });

describe('VendorClient known regressions', () => {
  // Documents that this specific call fails with the known vendor error message.
  // The test suite stays green while the failure is tracked in the issue tracker.
  it('pagination cursor expires before the second page fetch', {
    expectFailure: {
      label: 'Vendor bug #VP-4821 — cursor TTL is 30s, not 5min as documented',
      match: /cursor.*expired/i,
    },
  }, async () => {
    const page1 = await client.listItems({ limit: 10 });
    // Artificial delay that exceeds the undocumented 30-second cursor TTL
    await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 35_000));
    const page2 = await client.listItems({ cursor: page1.nextCursor, limit: 10 });
    assert.ok(page2.items.length > 0, 'Expected page 2 to have items');
  });

  it('bulk delete returns 204 as documented', async () => {
    const resp = await client.deleteItems(['id-1', 'id-2']);
    assert.strictEqual(resp.statusCode, 204);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `it.expectFailure` with a `match` regex (Node.js 25.5+) turns known vendor regressions into green CI entries that document the expected failure message, preventing alert fatigue while keeping the team aware of the bug, but if the vendor silently changes the error message the test unexpectedly passes (the regex no longer matches the new error) and the expectFailure wrapper causes the test to fail again — review `match` patterns when updating vendor SDKs.

**Pattern 63: Vitest `vi.setTimerTickMode('nextTimerAsync')` for async timer chains that require automatic advancement** [official]
```typescript
// test/retry-queue.test.ts — uses vi.setTimerTickMode('nextTimerAsync') so that
// chained setTimeout callbacks (retry backoff) advance automatically after each
// async operation without manual vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync() calls
import { describe, it, beforeEach, afterEach, expect, vi } from 'vitest';
import { RetryQueue } from '../src/retry-queue';

describe('RetryQueue exponential backoff', () => {
  let queue: RetryQueue;

  beforeEach(() => {
    vi.useFakeTimers();
    // After each macrotask completes, automatically advance to the next queued timer
    vi.setTimerTickMode('nextTimerAsync');
    queue = new RetryQueue({ maxRetries: 4, baseDelayMs: 100 });
  });

  afterEach(() => {
    vi.useRealTimers();
  });

  it('retries with exponential backoff and eventually succeeds', async () => {
    let callCount = 0;
    const task = vi.fn(async () => {
      callCount++;
      if (callCount < 4) throw new Error(`attempt ${callCount} failed`);
      return 'ok';
    });

    // nextTimerAsync mode auto-advances through the 100ms, 200ms, 400ms delays
    const result = await queue.enqueue(task);

    expect(result).toBe('ok');
    expect(task).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(4);
    // Confirm the backoff delays were honoured (total elapsed: 100+200+400 = 700ms)
    expect(vi.getMockedSystemTime()).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(700);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `vi.setTimerTickMode('nextTimerAsync')` (Vitest 4.1) eliminates the fragile `vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(n)` calls that require knowing every delay value in advance, making tests resilient to backoff tuning, but the mode will auto-advance through all pending timers including ones set by third-party libraries running in the same event loop tick — use `vi.setTimerTickMode('manual')` for tests where you need to assert intermediate timer states.

**Pattern 64: Playwright component test `mount()` with `hooksConfig` for providing React context without wrapping the component under test** [official]
```typescript
// test/checkout-summary.spec.tsx — mounts a React component and provides
// context (cart, theme) via hooksConfig rather than wrapping in a test Provider
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/experimental-ct-react';
import { CheckoutSummary } from '../src/components/CheckoutSummary';
import type { CartItem } from '../src/types';

const mockItems: CartItem[] = [
  { id: '1', name: 'Widget', price: 999, qty: 2 },
  { id: '2', name: 'Gadget', price: 4999, qty: 1 },
];

test('CheckoutSummary displays correct totals with tax', async ({ mount, page }) => {
  const component = await mount(<CheckoutSummary />, {
    hooksConfig: {
      // playwright-ct uses the project's playwright/index.tsx router hook
      // to inject context — no wrapper component needed in the test itself
      cart: { items: mockItems, currency: 'USD' },
      theme: 'light',
    },
  });

  await expect(component.getByTestId('subtotal')).toContainText('$69.97');
  await expect(component.getByTestId('tax')).toContainText('$5.95');
  await expect(component.getByTestId('total')).toContainText('$75.92');

  // Verify accessibility of the summary region
  await expect(component.getByRole('region', { name: 'Order summary' })).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `mount()` with `hooksConfig` keeps test files free of `<CartProvider>` / `<ThemeProvider>` boilerplate by delegating context injection to the `playwright/index.tsx` beforeMount hook, making tests read as pure component interactions, but the `hooksConfig` shape is not statically typed by default — add a `HooksConfig` interface to `playwright/index.tsx` and use the `@playwright/test` generic parameter `mount<HooksConfig>()` to catch shape mismatches at compile time.

**Pattern 65: Node.js `node:test` `run()` with `isolation: 'process'` for per-file environment variable isolation in integration test suites** [official]
```typescript
// scripts/run-integration-tests.ts — uses run() with process isolation so each
// test file sees its own DATABASE_URL pointing to a dedicated test database schema
import { run } from 'node:test';
import { tap } from 'node:test/reporters';
import { pipeline } from 'node:stream/promises';
import { glob } from 'node:fs/promises';
import path from 'node:path';

async function main() {
  const testFiles: string[] = [];
  for await (const file of glob('test/integration/**/*.test.ts')) {
    testFiles.push(path.resolve(file));
  }

  let schemaIndex = 0;
  const stream = run({
    files: testFiles,
    isolation: 'process',   // each file spawns its own Node.js worker process
    concurrency: 4,
    env: (file) => {
      // Assign a dedicated schema slot per file to prevent DB state bleed-over
      const schema = `test_${++schemaIndex}`;
      return {
        ...process.env,
        DATABASE_URL: `postgresql://localhost/testdb?search_path=${schema}`,
        TEST_SCHEMA: schema,
      };
    },
  });

  await pipeline(stream, tap(), process.stdout);
}

main().catch(err => { console.error(err); process.exit(1); });
```
Tradeoff: `isolation: 'process'` with a per-file `env` factory function (Node.js 22+) completely eliminates global state bleed between integration test files by running each in a fresh worker process with its own database schema, but the per-process startup cost is significant (typically 300–800ms per file depending on module graph size) — mitigate with `concurrency: N` and reserve `isolation: 'process'` for integration suites; use the default thread isolation for fast unit test suites.

**Pattern 66: Vitest `vi.mockObject()` with `spy: true` for partially overriding a real service class without manual method wrappers** [official]
```typescript
// test/notification-service.test.ts — uses vi.mockObject({ spy: true }) to spy
// on all methods of a real NotificationService instance, then selectively
// override only the sendEmail method to avoid real network calls
import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach } from 'vitest';
import { NotificationService } from '../src/notification-service';
import { UserRepository } from '../src/user-repository';

describe('NotificationService', () => {
  let service: NotificationService;
  let spiedService: ReturnType<typeof vi.mockObject<NotificationService>>;

  beforeEach(() => {
    const realService = new NotificationService({
      repo: new UserRepository({ dsn: process.env.DATABASE_URL! }),
    });
    // spy: true preserves real implementations; only sendEmail is overridden below
    spiedService = vi.mockObject(realService, { spy: true });
    vi.spyOn(spiedService, 'sendEmail').mockResolvedValue({ messageId: 'mock-id-001' });
    service = spiedService as unknown as NotificationService;
  });

  it('sends a welcome email after a new user is created', async () => {
    await service.handleUserCreated({ userId: 'usr-42', email: 'new@example.com' });

    expect(spiedService.sendEmail).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
    expect(spiedService.sendEmail).toHaveBeenCalledWith({
      to: 'new@example.com',
      template: 'welcome',
      data: expect.objectContaining({ userId: 'usr-42' }),
    });
    // Real logAudit implementation ran — verify via the database
    expect(spiedService.logAudit).toHaveBeenCalledWith('user.created', 'usr-42');
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `vi.mockObject(instance, { spy: true })` (Vitest 3.2+) wraps every method in a spy automatically, letting you assert call counts on all methods while only overriding the ones you need to stub, but it only wraps own-enumerable methods and prototype methods one level deep — methods from abstract base classes or mixins more than one prototype hop away are not wrapped; use explicit `vi.spyOn` for those.

**Pattern 67: Playwright `page.routeFromHAR()` for replaying recorded network traffic in flaky integration environments** [official]
```typescript
// test/dashboard.spec.ts — records a HAR file on first run, then replays it
// on subsequent runs to eliminate external API flakiness in the dashboard test
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'node:path';

const harPath = path.join(__dirname, 'fixtures', 'dashboard-api.har');

test.use({
  // In CI always replay; locally set UPDATE_HAR=1 to re-record
  serviceWorkers: 'block',
});

test('dashboard loads recent activity feed from HAR replay', async ({ page, context }) => {
  const updateHar = process.env.UPDATE_HAR === '1';

  if (updateHar) {
    await context.recordHar({ path: harPath, urlFilter: '**/api/**' });
  } else {
    await page.routeFromHAR(harPath, {
      url: '**/api/**',
      // notFound: 'abort' ensures unexpected URLs fail fast rather than hitting network
      notFound: 'abort',
      update: false,
    });
  }

  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('activity-feed')).toContainText('Last 7 days');
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="feed-item"]')).toHaveCount(10);

  if (updateHar) {
    await context.closeHar();
  }
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.routeFromHAR()` with `notFound: 'abort'` converts network-dependent Playwright tests into deterministic replays that never hit real APIs in CI, eliminating a large class of token-expiry and rate-limit flakes, but HAR files can grow large (megabytes) and become stale when API response shapes change — use `UPDATE_HAR=1` as a deliberate developer action, add the HAR files to `.gitattributes` as binary LFS assets, and lint for stale HARs older than 30 days in the PR pipeline.

**Pattern 68: Node.js 26 `node:test` `globalSetup` / `globalTeardown` for provisioning a shared Postgres container before all integration test files** [official]
```typescript
// test/global-setup.mts — provisions a Postgres Testcontainer once before all
// integration test files and tears it down cleanly after the full run
import { GenericContainer, Wait } from 'testcontainers';
import { execSync } from 'node:child_process';

let container: Awaited<ReturnType<typeof GenericContainer.prototype.start>>;

export async function globalSetup() {
  container = await new GenericContainer('postgres:16-alpine')
    .withEnvironment({ POSTGRES_PASSWORD: 'test', POSTGRES_DB: 'testdb' })
    .withWaitStrategy(Wait.forLogMessage('database system is ready to accept connections'))
    .withExposedPorts(5432)
    .start();

  const host = container.getHost();
  const port = container.getMappedPort(5432);
  const dsn = `postgresql://postgres:test@${host}:${port}/testdb`;

  // Expose DSN to all test worker processes via environment variable
  process.env.TEST_DATABASE_URL = dsn;

  // Run migrations against the shared container
  execSync(`DATABASE_URL=${dsn} npx prisma migrate deploy`, { stdio: 'inherit' });

  console.log(`[globalSetup] Postgres container ready at ${dsn}`);
}

export async function globalTeardown() {
  if (container) {
    await container.stop();
    console.log('[globalTeardown] Postgres container stopped');
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: Node.js 26 `globalSetup` / `globalTeardown` (v24.0.0, early development) runs exactly once before and after the entire test run regardless of `concurrency` or `isolation` settings, making it ideal for expensive shared infrastructure like database containers, but `process.env` mutations in `globalSetup` are only visible to child worker processes spawned after the setup function completes — workers spawned before (e.g., pre-forked workers in watch mode) will not see the mutated env; always use `globalSetup` rather than a top-level `before()` for infrastructure setup.

**Pattern 69: Vitest `test.each` table-driven tests with `%j` JSON formatting for object parameters in test names** [official]
```typescript
// test/price-calculator.test.ts — uses test.each with %j formatting so that
// failing test names display the full parameter object rather than [Object object]
import { describe, test, expect } from 'vitest';
import { calculatePrice } from '../src/price-calculator';

type PriceCase = {
  input: { basePrice: number; qty: number; discount: number; taxRate: number };
  expected: { subtotal: number; tax: number; total: number };
};

const cases: PriceCase[] = [
  {
    input: { basePrice: 100, qty: 2, discount: 0.1, taxRate: 0.2 },
    expected: { subtotal: 180, tax: 36, total: 216 },
  },
  {
    input: { basePrice: 50, qty: 1, discount: 0, taxRate: 0.1 },
    expected: { subtotal: 50, tax: 5, total: 55 },
  },
  {
    input: { basePrice: 200, qty: 3, discount: 0.25, taxRate: 0.15 },
    expected: { subtotal: 450, tax: 67.5, total: 517.5 },
  },
];

describe('calculatePrice', () => {
  // %j serialises the full object — test name becomes: "input=%j" → "input={"basePrice":100,...}"
  test.each(cases)('input=%j → total=$expected.total', ({ input, expected }) => {
    const result = calculatePrice(input);
    expect(result.subtotal).toBeCloseTo(expected.subtotal, 2);
    expect(result.tax).toBeCloseTo(expected.tax, 2);
    expect(result.total).toBeCloseTo(expected.total, 2);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `%j` in `test.each` names (supported in both Vitest and Jest) inlines the full JSON object into the test name so that failure reports immediately show which parameter set failed without needing to open the test runner output — the name becomes unreadable for deeply nested objects; flatten parameter objects to one level and use `%j` for leaf-level structures to keep names under ~120 characters.

**Pattern 70: Playwright `test.step()` with `{ box: true }` for cleaner failure reporting in multi-step e2e user flows** [official]
```typescript
// test/checkout-flow.spec.ts — wraps logical phases of a checkout e2e test in
// test.step({ box: true }) so that failure reports show the step name rather
// than the internal line number deep inside a helper function
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('user can complete a full checkout', async ({ page }) => {
  await test.step('sign in as returning customer', async () => {
    await page.goto('/login');
    await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('alice@example.com');
    await page.getByLabel('Password').fill('s3cr3t!');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();
    await expect(page).toHaveURL('/dashboard');
  });

  await test.step('add product to cart', async () => {
    await page.goto('/products/widget-pro');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByTestId('cart-count')).toContainText('1');
  });

  await test.step('complete checkout', { box: true }, async () => {
    // { box: true } collapses the internal steps into a single reporter entry
    // — on failure, the report shows "complete checkout" not line 37 of helpers.ts
    await page.goto('/checkout');
    await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4111111111111111');
    await page.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('12/28');
    await page.getByLabel('CVV').fill('123');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay now' }).click();
    await expect(page).toHaveURL('/order-confirmation');
    await expect(page.getByTestId('order-id')).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `test.step({ box: true })` (Playwright 1.44+) condenses nested step trees into a single line in the HTML report and trace viewer, making the failure location immediately obvious for product-level QA reports, but the box boundary hides internal step details that are valuable for diagnosing failures within the boxed section — attach a trace or screenshot inside the boxed step to preserve debugging context when a step is boxed for reporting purposes.

**Pattern 71: Vitest `test.for()` with destructured TestContext for concurrent table-driven tests with per-test snapshot isolation** [official]
```typescript
// test/serialiser.test.ts — uses test.for() instead of test.each() because
// test.for() passes the TestContext as the second argument, enabling concurrent
// snapshot assertions that are safely isolated per test instance
import { describe, test } from 'vitest';

type SerialiseCase = { format: 'json' | 'csv' | 'xml'; rows: object[]; };

const cases: SerialiseCase[] = [
  { format: 'json', rows: [{ id: 1, name: 'Alice' }, { id: 2, name: 'Bob' }] },
  { format: 'csv',  rows: [{ id: 1, name: 'Alice' }, { id: 2, name: 'Bob' }] },
  { format: 'xml',  rows: [{ id: 1, name: 'Alice' }, { id: 2, name: 'Bob' }] },
];

describe('DataSerialiser', () => {
  // test.for() passes { expect } from the per-test context so snapshots
  // are isolated even when tests run concurrently (unlike test.each)
  test.for(cases)(
    'serialises rows to $format',
    async ({ format, rows }, { expect }) => {
      const { DataSerialiser } = await import('../src/data-serialiser');
      const output = new DataSerialiser(format).serialise(rows);
      // Using context-bound expect avoids the "snapshot file not found" race condition
      // that occurs when concurrent tests share the module-level expect
      expect(output).toMatchSnapshot();
    },
  );
});
```
Tradeoff: `test.for()` passes the `TestContext` as the second destructured argument, enabling concurrent table-driven tests to safely use snapshot assertions without the snapshot-file race condition that affects `test.each()` with `concurrent` because `test.each` shares the module-level `expect` — the trade-off is that `test.for()` does not support the printf-style `%s`/`%i`/`%j` name interpolation of `test.each`; use `$propertyName` template syntax instead.

**Pattern 72: Node.js `node:test` snapshot testing with `--test-update-snapshots` for pure-function golden-master regression tests** [official]
```typescript
// test/report-generator.test.ts — uses node:test's built-in snapshot API to
// create golden-master regression tests for a report-generation function
// whose expected output is stable enough to commit as a snapshot
import { describe, it } from 'node:test';
import { generateMonthlyReport } from '../src/report-generator';

const FIXED_DATE = new Date('2026-03-31T23:59:59Z');

describe('generateMonthlyReport', () => {
  it('produces a stable HTML report for March 2026 data', (t) => {
    const report = generateMonthlyReport({
      month: 3,
      year: 2026,
      asOf: FIXED_DATE,
      entries: [
        { category: 'Revenue', amount: 120_000 },
        { category: 'Expenses', amount: 84_500 },
        { category: 'Net', amount: 35_500 },
      ],
    });
    // First run (no snapshot file): fails with instructions to run --test-update-snapshots
    // Subsequent runs: diffs against the committed snapshot
    t.assert.snapshot(report);
  });

  it('omits the "previous period" section when priorMonth data is absent', (t) => {
    const report = generateMonthlyReport({
      month: 1, year: 2026, asOf: new Date('2026-01-31T00:00:00Z'), entries: [],
    });
    t.assert.snapshot(report);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Node.js's built-in `t.assert.snapshot()` (stable in v23.4) eliminates the Jest/Vitest snapshot plugin dependency for projects that only need golden-master output comparisons, and snapshot files are co-located with the test file (same directory, `.test.ts.snap` suffix) making diffs easy to review in PRs, but the snapshot serialisation format is a plain string (no structured serialiser registry like Jest's `addSnapshotSerializer`) — for complex objects, serialise to a deterministic string before passing to `t.assert.snapshot()` to avoid non-deterministic key ordering in JSON.

**Pattern 73: Playwright `locator.filter()` chaining for drilling into a specific table row without fragile XPath index selectors** [official]
```typescript
// test/users-table.spec.ts — uses locator.filter() chaining to target a specific
// table row by content rather than by row index, making the test resilient to
// row order changes caused by pagination or sort order differences
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('admin can deactivate a specific user account', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/admin/users');

  // Wait for the table to be populated
  await expect(page.getByRole('table')).toBeVisible();

  // Drill to the row containing 'alice@example.com' without using nth() or XPath
  const aliceRow = page
    .getByRole('row')
    .filter({ hasText: 'alice@example.com' });

  // Confirm the row exists and shows Active status
  await expect(aliceRow.getByTestId('status-badge')).toContainText('Active');

  // Open the actions menu within the filtered row only
  await aliceRow.getByRole('button', { name: 'Actions' }).click();

  await page.getByRole('menuitem', { name: 'Deactivate' }).click();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Confirm' }).click();

  // Assert the same row now shows Inactive
  await expect(aliceRow.getByTestId('status-badge')).toContainText('Inactive');
});
```
Tradeoff: `locator.filter({ hasText })` chaining produces self-documenting selectors that survive column reorders and row reorders, and Playwright auto-retries the entire chain including re-evaluating the filter — the trade-off is that `filter({ hasText })` matches any row containing the string anywhere in the row, so if two rows share a substring (e.g., `alice` matches both `alice@example.com` and `alice.admin@example.com`) the locator will match multiple elements and the subsequent action will fail with a strict-mode violation; use a unique cell value or combine with `filter({ has: page.getByTestId('email').filter({ hasText: /^alice@example\.com$/ }) })` for exact matching.

**Pattern 74: Vitest workspace `projects` array for co-locating unit and browser component tests in a single `vitest.workspace.ts` config** [official]
```typescript
// vitest.workspace.ts — defines two projects in one workspace: a fast Node unit
// project and a browser component project, sharing the same tsconfig and fixtures
import { defineWorkspace } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineWorkspace([
  {
    // --- Unit test project: runs in Node, no browser startup overhead ---
    test: {
      name: 'unit',
      include: ['src/**/*.test.ts', '!src/**/*.browser.test.ts'],
      environment: 'node',
      globals: false,
      coverage: {
        provider: 'v8',
        include: ['src/**/*.ts'],
        exclude: ['src/**/*.browser.test.ts', 'src/**/*.spec.ts'],
        thresholds: { lines: 85, functions: 90, branches: 80 },
      },
    },
  },
  {
    // --- Browser component project: runs in Chromium via @vitest/browser ---
    test: {
      name: 'browser',
      include: ['src/**/*.browser.test.ts'],
      browser: {
        enabled: true,
        provider: 'playwright',
        instances: [{ browser: 'chromium' }],
      },
    },
  },
]);
```
Tradeoff: A single `vitest.workspace.ts` with separate `unit` and `browser` projects lets `vitest run` execute both suites in one command and report combined coverage, which is essential for coverage gates in CI that need to account for both Node and DOM code paths, but the workspace `coverage` config is per-project and totals are not automatically merged — use `vitest run --coverage --reporter=json` for each project separately and merge with `nyc merge` or a custom script if you need a unified coverage report.

**Pattern 75: TypeScript `satisfies` operator in test fixture factories for type-safe partial overrides without losing the concrete type** [official]
```typescript
// test/factories/order.factory.ts — uses the TypeScript `satisfies` operator so
// that the factory function's return type is the concrete object type (not the
// interface type), enabling destructuring and property access on the result
// without additional type assertions in test files
import type { Order, OrderStatus, OrderItem } from '../../src/types';

const defaultItem = {
  id: 'item-default',
  sku: 'SKU-001',
  name: 'Default Widget',
  qty: 1,
  unitPrice: 999,
} satisfies OrderItem;

export function createOrder(overrides: Partial<Order> = {}): Order {
  const base = {
    id: `order-${Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 9)}`,
    status: 'pending' as OrderStatus,
    createdAt: new Date('2026-01-01T00:00:00Z'),
    items: [{ ...defaultItem }],
    total: defaultItem.unitPrice * defaultItem.qty,
    customerId: 'cust-001',
    shippingAddress: {
      line1: '1 Test Street',
      city: 'Testville',
      postcode: 'TE1 1ST',
      country: 'GB',
    },
  } satisfies Order;

  return { ...base, ...overrides };
}

// test/order-service.test.ts — usage: TypeScript knows the exact shape
import { createOrder } from './factories/order.factory';
const o = createOrder({ status: 'shipped', total: 5000 });
// o.shippingAddress.postcode is accessible without a cast — satisfies preserved the type
```
Tradeoff: Using `satisfies` in factory definitions ensures that the object literal is validated against the interface at the point of definition rather than at the assignment target, which catches missing required properties in the factory itself (not at the call site), and preserves the narrow literal type of the object so that TypeScript can infer exact property shapes downstream — the trade-off is that `satisfies` does not widen the type to the interface, so if you later add a required field to the interface, the factory will error at the `satisfies` expression (good!) rather than silently returning a structurally incompatible object, but this means every factory must be updated when the source type changes.

### Community Gotchas

**G246: Vitest `test.override()` silently ignores overrides applied outside a `describe()` block scope**
Why this matters: `test.override()` is designed to scope option overrides to a describe block's child tests. When developers call `const slowTest = test.override({ timeout: 60_000 })` at the top level of a test file (outside any `describe`), the override appears to work in isolation but the scoping semantics apply globally — in a workspace run where test files are collected across multiple workers, the global override can leak into other describe blocks within the same worker process that processes the file sequentially. This causes intermittent timeout values in CI that differ from local runs depending on which worker happens to process the affected file.
Fix: Always call `test.override()` inside a `describe()` block and assign the result to a block-scoped `const`. Never use `test.override()` at file scope — use `test.extend()` with a shared fixture file or configure per-file timeout in `vitest.config.ts` under `test.testTimeout` for file-wide settings.

---

**G247: Node.js `--experimental-test-coverage` `--test-coverage-include` globs are relative to CWD, not to the test file location, causing missed coverage on monorepo sub-packages**
Why this matters: When running `node --test --experimental-test-coverage --test-coverage-include="src/**"` from a monorepo root, the glob `src/**` resolves relative to the current working directory (the monorepo root), not relative to each sub-package where the source files actually live. Sub-packages with sources at `packages/api/src/**` are silently excluded from coverage because their paths do not match the root-relative `src/**` pattern. The coverage report shows 0% for all sub-package code and the overall line-coverage figure is artificially high because the denominator (tracked files) is much smaller than expected.
Fix: Pass absolute glob patterns that match all relevant source trees: `--test-coverage-include="packages/*/src/**"` from the monorepo root, or invoke `node --test --experimental-test-coverage` per package from each package's directory using `npm workspaces run test:coverage`. Document the chosen approach in the root `package.json` test script comments to prevent future regressions.

---

**G248: Playwright `routeFromHAR()` silently serves stale 401 responses when session tokens embedded in HAR headers expire**
Why this matters: HAR files recorded with Playwright capture the exact HTTP response including authentication headers and `Set-Cookie` values from the recording session. When a HAR is replayed, Playwright serves the recorded responses verbatim — including any `Authorization: Bearer <token>` headers the app might echo back and any `Set-Cookie` headers with expiry dates. If the app performs a client-side check of the `expires` field in the session cookie during replay, or if any inline token in a recorded response body has an `exp` claim that has passed, the app silently fails its auth flow with a 401 that is served from the HAR rather than triggering a real network request. Developers debugging the flake will observe the 401 in DevTools but misattribute it to the test setup rather than the stale HAR.
Fix: Record HAR files with short-lived test accounts using non-expiring API tokens, or strip authentication headers from recorded HARs using a post-processing script: `jq 'del(.log.entries[].response.headers[] | select(.name | ascii_downcase | test("authorization|set-cookie")))' raw.har > clean.har`. Add a CI lint step that rejects HARs containing headers matching `authorization` or `set-cookie`.

---

**G249: Vitest workspace `coverage` totals are per-project — running `vitest run --coverage` on a workspace silently reports project-level coverage, not aggregate coverage**
Why this matters: When a `vitest.workspace.ts` defines multiple projects (e.g., `unit` and `browser`), running `vitest run --coverage` generates a separate coverage report for each project. The terminal output shows the unit project's coverage thresholds and the browser project's thresholds separately. Teams that set `thresholds` in only the unit project's config believe they have a repository-wide coverage gate, but the browser component code (in `src/**/*.browser.ts`) is excluded from the unit project's `coverage.include` and tracked only by the browser project. A bug that drops browser component branch coverage below the threshold will pass the unit project threshold check and silently ship.
Fix: Add explicit `coverage.thresholds` to every project in the workspace config, or add a post-test script that merges coverage JSON reports from all projects using `nyc merge coverage-reports/ merged-coverage.json && nyc report --reporter=text-summary` and fails if the merged total is below the repository threshold. Document that `--coverage` in a workspace context is always per-project in the contributing guide.

---

**G250: Playwright component `hooksConfig` values are not reset between tests — mutations in one test's `beforeMount` hook bleed into subsequent tests in the same file**
Why this matters: In Playwright component tests, the `playwright/index.tsx` `beforeMount` hook receives `hooksConfig` from the `mount()` call and typically uses it to initialise React context providers. If the `beforeMount` hook uses a module-level variable to store the injected config (a common pattern for providing a writable store), mutations made to that variable inside one test's component callbacks persist across tests because the browser page is reused within a test file. A test that expects an empty cart may receive the cart state left by a previous test that added items, producing intermittent assertion failures that only appear when test execution order changes.
Fix: Always reset module-level state at the start of each `beforeMount` hook invocation by deep-cloning the incoming `hooksConfig` values: `const config = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(hooksConfig ?? {}))`. Alternatively, use `test.use({ storageState: 'empty.json' })` to isolate browser storage between tests, and prefer passing immutable config objects through `hooksConfig` rather than mutable stores. Add a `afterEach` hook in `playwright/index.tsx` that calls `cleanup()` and resets module-level context variables.

## Cycle 60 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 76** — Vitest V8 AST-Based Coverage Remapping for Accurate Branch Counts
```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — enable V8 provider with AST remapping (Vitest ≥3.2.0)
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',            // AST-based remapping active since v3.2.0
      include: ['src/**/*.ts'],
      exclude: ['src/**/*.d.ts', 'src/**/__mocks__/**'],
      thresholds: {
        lines: 85,
        branches: 80,
        functions: 90,
        statements: 85,
        perFile: true,           // enforce threshold per file, not only aggregate
      },
      reportOnFailure: true,     // emit report even when thresholds fail, for CI artefacts
      reportsDirectory: 'coverage',
      reporter: ['text', 'lcov', 'html'],
    },
  },
});
```
Tradeoff: Enabling `perFile: true` thresholds catches files with 0% coverage that would otherwise be hidden by a healthy aggregate, but it means any new utility file with untested exports immediately fails the coverage gate even before an integration test can reasonably cover it — teams must pair this with `coverage.exclude` patterns for generated code and a short grace period via a separate `thresholds.autoUpdate` workflow that commits baseline updates, otherwise every scaffold-generated file blocks CI until tests are written.

---

**Pattern 77** — Playwright `route.fallback()` Chained Handler Priority for Partial API Mocking
```typescript
// tests/checkout.spec.ts — mock only the payment endpoint, pass everything else through
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('checkout page renders with mocked payment intent', async ({ page }) => {
  // Handler 1: mock only the payment-intent creation endpoint
  await page.route('**/api/payment-intents', async route => {
    await route.fulfill({
      status: 200,
      contentType: 'application/json',
      body: JSON.stringify({ clientSecret: 'pi_test_secret_abc123' }),
    });
  });

  // Handler 2: registered after Handler 1; runs first (LIFO order)
  // Use fallback() so subsequent (earlier-registered) handlers can still match
  await page.route('**/api/**', async route => {
    const url = route.request().url();
    if (url.includes('feature-flags')) {
      await route.fulfill({ status: 200, body: JSON.stringify({ checkout_v2: true }) });
    } else {
      await route.fallback(); // pass to Handler 1 or real network if no match
    }
  });

  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="pay-button"]')).toBeEnabled();
});
```
Tradeoff: Using `route.fallback()` enables a layered mocking strategy where each handler is responsible for a single concern (payment, flags, auth), which keeps handlers small and composable — but because Playwright executes route handlers in reverse registration order (LIFO), adding a new broad `**/api/**` catch-all after narrower handlers reverses the expected priority, so teams must document registration order explicitly and prefer registering broad handlers first (so they execute last via LIFO) to avoid accidentally intercepting requests intended for narrower handlers.

---

**Pattern 78** — Node.js `--test-shard` CI Matrix Parallelism with GitHub Actions
```typescript
// node test runner — programmatic equivalent for understanding shard semantics
// package.json script: "test:shard": "node --test --test-shard=$SHARD_INDEX/$SHARD_TOTAL src/**/*.test.ts"

// test-shard-helper.ts — shows how sharding affects file selection
import { run } from 'node:test';

const shardIndex = parseInt(process.env.SHARD_INDEX ?? '1', 10);
const shardTotal = parseInt(process.env.SHARD_TOTAL ?? '1', 10);

const runner = run({
  files: await collectTestFiles('src'),  // your file-glob utility
  shard: { index: shardIndex, total: shardTotal },
  concurrency: true,
  coverage: shardIndex === 1,            // only collect coverage on shard 1 to avoid merge
  lineCoverage: 80,
  branchCoverage: 75,
});

runner.on('test:fail', () => { process.exitCode = 1; });
runner.compose(await import('node:test/reporters').then(m => m.spec)).pipe(process.stdout);
```
Tradeoff: Node.js native sharding with `shard: { index, total }` splits test files deterministically by index — files are distributed in declaration order, not by estimated duration — so if the slowest integration tests happen to cluster in the same shard, CI wall time is uneven; to balance shards, sort `files` by historical duration data stored in a JSON artefact and pass the sorted array to `run()`, accepting the maintenance cost of keeping the duration data up to date.

---

**Pattern 79** — Vitest `vi.mock()` with `vi.importActual()` for Selective Module Substitution
```typescript
// src/services/__tests__/email.service.test.ts
import { vi, describe, it, expect, beforeEach } from 'vitest';
import type { Transporter } from 'nodemailer';

// vi.mock is hoisted — the factory runs before imports resolve
vi.mock('nodemailer', async importOriginal => {
  const actual = await importOriginal<typeof import('nodemailer')>();
  return {
    ...actual,                        // keep createTransport, Mail, etc.
    createTransport: vi.fn(() => ({
      sendMail: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue({ messageId: 'test-id-001' }),
      verify:   vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(true),
    } satisfies Partial<Transporter>)),
  };
});

import { EmailService } from '../email.service';
import { createTransport } from 'nodemailer';

describe('EmailService', () => {
  let service: EmailService;
  beforeEach(() => {
    vi.clearAllMocks();
    service = new EmailService();
  });

  it('sends a welcome email and returns the message ID', async () => {
    const result = await service.sendWelcome('user@example.com', 'Alice');
    expect(result.messageId).toBe('test-id-001');
    expect(vi.mocked(createTransport)).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Using `importOriginal` in the `vi.mock` factory preserves non-mocked exports (types, enums, helper functions) so tests that import them do not get `undefined` — but this means the actual module code runs during the factory evaluation phase, which can trigger side effects like file-system reads or environment variable checks that happen at module load time; modules with heavy constructor-time side effects must be fully replaced rather than partially spread, requiring duplication of the type surface in the factory.

---

**Pattern 80** — Playwright Worker-Scoped Database Fixture with Unique Schema Isolation
```typescript
// tests/fixtures/db.fixture.ts — worker-scoped DB fixture for parallel safety
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';
import { Pool } from 'pg';

type DbFixtures = { db: Pool; schemaName: string };

export const test = base.extend<object, DbFixtures>({
  schemaName: [
    async ({ workerIndex }, use) => {
      const schema = `test_worker_${workerIndex}_${Date.now()}`;
      await use(schema);
    },
    { scope: 'worker' },
  ],

  db: [
    async ({ schemaName }, use) => {
      const pool = new Pool({ connectionString: process.env.TEST_DATABASE_URL });
      await pool.query(`CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS "${schemaName}"`);
      await pool.query(`SET search_path TO "${schemaName}"`);
      // run migrations against the worker-specific schema
      await runMigrations(pool, schemaName);
      await use(pool);
      await pool.query(`DROP SCHEMA "${schemaName}" CASCADE`);
      await pool.end();
    },
    { scope: 'worker' },
  ],
});

async function runMigrations(pool: Pool, schema: string): Promise<void> {
  // apply schema DDL scoped to this worker's search_path
  await pool.query(`CREATE TABLE "${schema}".users (id uuid PRIMARY KEY, email text NOT NULL)`);
}
```
Tradeoff: Worker-scoped fixtures create one schema per worker process rather than one per test, which dramatically reduces migration overhead and connection pool churn in high-concurrency suites — but it means tests sharing a worker also share schema state, so any test that writes data without cleanup contaminates subsequent tests in the same worker; enforce row-level cleanup via `afterEach` hooks or wrap every write in a transaction that is rolled back, not committed, to maintain isolation without repeating schema creation costs.

**Pattern 81** — Vitest `toMatchFileSnapshot()` for HTML and JSON Output Regression
```typescript
// src/renderers/__tests__/invoice-renderer.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { renderInvoiceHtml } from '../invoice-renderer';
import { createOrder } from '../../test/factories/order.factory';

describe('InvoiceRenderer', () => {
  it('renders a standard invoice to stable HTML', async () => {
    const order = createOrder({
      id:        'ord-snapshot-001',
      createdAt: new Date('2026-01-15T10:00:00Z'),  // fixed date for determinism
      total:     12500,
    });

    const html = await renderInvoiceHtml(order);

    // snapshot stored in __file_snapshots__/invoice-renderer.test.ts.snap.html
    // allows syntax-highlighted review in IDEs and PR diff tools
    await expect(html).toMatchFileSnapshot(
      './__file_snapshots__/invoice-standard.snap.html'
    );
  });

  it('stores API response shape for contract regression', async () => {
    const payload = buildApiPayload(createOrder());
    await expect(JSON.stringify(payload, null, 2)).toMatchFileSnapshot(
      './__file_snapshots__/invoice-api-payload.snap.json'
    );
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `toMatchFileSnapshot()` stores snapshots as real files with the correct extension, enabling IDE syntax highlighting and readable PR diffs for HTML/JSON/YAML output — unlike `.snap` files which store all snapshots in a single serialised file — but every snapshot file is an additional committed artefact that must be updated with `-u` on intentional changes; teams that regenerate output frequently (e.g., design system token changes) will accumulate large PR diffs composed mostly of snapshot updates, which reviewers tend to rubber-stamp, reducing the protective value of the regression check.

**Pattern 82** — Node.js `t.plan()` for Asserting Callback-Based Code Executes All Branches
```typescript
// src/event-bus/__tests__/event-bus.test.mts
import { test, describe } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { EventBus } from '../event-bus.mjs';

describe('EventBus', () => {
  test('emits order.created to all registered subscribers', async t => {
    t.plan(3); // exactly 3 assertions must run — catches subscribers that are never called

    const bus = new EventBus();
    const received: string[] = [];

    bus.on('order.created', payload => {
      assert.ok(payload.orderId, 'subscriber A: orderId must be truthy');
      t.diagnostic(`subscriber A received orderId=${payload.orderId}`);
      received.push('A');
    });

    bus.on('order.created', payload => {
      assert.equal(payload.status, 'pending', 'subscriber B: initial status must be pending');
      received.push('B');
    });

    await bus.emit('order.created', { orderId: 'ord-001', status: 'pending' });

    assert.deepEqual(received.sort(), ['A', 'B'], 'both subscribers must have run');
    // t.plan(3): 2 inline assertions + 1 deepEqual = exactly 3; test fails if any subscriber is skipped
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `t.plan(n)` provides a strong guarantee that async callbacks and event listeners actually fire — a test without a plan can pass vacuously if an event is never emitted — but maintaining the count is a manual bookkeeping task; adding an assertion inside a subscriber without incrementing `t.plan()` causes the test to fail with a confusing "plan count mismatch" error rather than a descriptive assertion message, so teams should document the plan count in a comment and update it whenever assertions are added or removed.

**Pattern 83** — Playwright `test.describe.configure({ mode: 'serial' })` for Stateful E2E Flows
```typescript
// tests/e2e/checkout-flow.spec.ts — serial mode for multi-step stateful flow
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// serial: tests run in order, failure stops the suite (no orphaned state)
test.describe.configure({ mode: 'serial' });

test.describe('Full checkout flow', () => {
  let orderId: string;

  test('Step 1 — add item to cart', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/products/widget-pro');
    await page.click('[data-testid="add-to-cart"]');
    await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="cart-count"]')).toHaveText('1');
  });

  test('Step 2 — proceed to checkout and enter address', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/cart');
    await page.click('[data-testid="checkout-button"]');
    await page.fill('[name="address"]', '42 Elm Street');
    await page.click('[data-testid="continue"]');
    await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/checkout\/payment/);
  });

  test('Step 3 — submit payment and capture order ID', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.fill('[name="card-number"]', '4111111111111111');
    await page.click('[data-testid="place-order"]');
    const confirmEl = page.locator('[data-testid="order-id"]');
    await expect(confirmEl).toBeVisible();
    orderId = (await confirmEl.textContent()) ?? '';
    expect(orderId).toMatch(/^ORD-/);
  });

  test('Step 4 — verify order appears in account history', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/account/orders');
    await expect(page.locator(`text=${orderId}`)).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `mode: 'serial'` ensures multi-step flows execute in order and stops the suite on first failure, preventing subsequent steps from running with corrupted state — but it disables within-describe parallelism, meaning the entire four-step suite blocks one worker for its full duration; in large suites with many serial describes, overall wall time increases proportionally; prefer serial mode only for genuinely stateful flows and decompose independent assertions into separate `test.describe` blocks that can run in parallel.

**Pattern 84** — Vitest `vi.stubEnv()` with Automatic Restore for Environment-Dependent Branches
```typescript
// src/config/__tests__/app-config.test.ts
import { vi, describe, it, expect, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { resolveConfig } from '../app-config';

// vi.stubEnv automatically restores original value after each test
// when paired with vi.unstubAllEnvs() in afterEach
afterEach(() => {
  vi.unstubAllEnvs(); // restore process.env to pre-stub values
});

describe('resolveConfig', () => {
  it('uses REDIS_URL from environment when present', () => {
    vi.stubEnv('REDIS_URL', 'redis://localhost:6379/1');
    vi.stubEnv('NODE_ENV', 'production');

    const config = resolveConfig();

    expect(config.redis.url).toBe('redis://localhost:6379/1');
    expect(config.redis.tls).toBe(true); // production forces TLS
  });

  it('falls back to in-memory cache when REDIS_URL is absent', () => {
    vi.stubEnv('REDIS_URL', '');  // explicitly empty — removes the env key
    vi.stubEnv('NODE_ENV', 'development');

    const config = resolveConfig();

    expect(config.cache.strategy).toBe('memory');
    expect(config.redis).toBeNull();
  });

  it('throws when NODE_ENV is production and no REDIS_URL is set', () => {
    vi.stubEnv('REDIS_URL', '');
    vi.stubEnv('NODE_ENV', 'production');

    expect(() => resolveConfig()).toThrowError(/REDIS_URL is required in production/);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `vi.stubEnv()` provides a clean, side-effect-free way to test environment-dependent config branches without mutating `process.env` directly — which can bleed across tests when `afterEach` cleanup is missed — but it only stubs string values; environment variables that other modules read at module-load time (not at function-call time) are not affected by `stubEnv()` because those modules have already captured the value in a module-level constant; such modules must be re-imported inside the test using `vi.resetModules()` + `await import(...)` to pick up the stub.

**Pattern 85** — Playwright `locator.getByRole()` ARIA-Semantic Assertions Over CSS Selectors
```typescript
// tests/e2e/dashboard.spec.ts — ARIA-semantic selectors resist style refactors
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('dashboard navigation is accessible and functional', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Prefer getByRole over CSS — survives className/structure refactors
  const nav = page.getByRole('navigation', { name: 'Main navigation' });
  await expect(nav).toBeVisible();

  // Heading hierarchy — verifies semantic structure, not just visual text
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { level: 1 })).toHaveText('Dashboard');

  // Button with accessible name — catches mis-labelled icon buttons
  const exportButton = page.getByRole('button', { name: /export/i });
  await expect(exportButton).toBeEnabled();

  // Table with caption — validates data grid semantics
  const table = page.getByRole('table', { name: 'Recent transactions' });
  const rows = table.getByRole('row');
  await expect(rows).toHaveCount(6); // 1 header row + 5 data rows

  // Dialog — verifies modal is announced to screen readers
  await exportButton.click();
  const dialog = page.getByRole('dialog', { name: 'Export data' });
  await expect(dialog).toBeVisible();
  await expect(dialog.getByRole('button', { name: 'Cancel' })).toBeFocused();
});
```
Tradeoff: ARIA-role selectors directly verify accessibility semantics — a button rendered as a `<div>` with a click handler will fail `getByRole('button')` — which catches accessibility regressions that CSS selectors would silently pass, but ARIA queries are more strict about the presence of correct roles and labels, meaning that legitimate UI refactors (renaming a button, restructuring a nav) will break tests even when the feature still works correctly; teams must budget time for test updates whenever intentional UI copy changes occur and avoid using `getByRole` for elements whose accessible name is expected to change frequently.

**Pattern 86** — Vitest Browser Mode Component Integration Test in a Real Browser
```typescript
// src/components/__tests__/combobox.browser.test.tsx
import { describe, it, expect, vi } from 'vitest';
import { render } from 'vitest-browser-react';
import { page } from '@vitest/browser/context';
import { Combobox } from '../Combobox';

const options = ['Apple', 'Banana', 'Cherry', 'Date', 'Elderberry'];

describe('Combobox — browser integration', () => {
  it('filters options on keyboard input and selects on Enter', async () => {
    const onSelect = vi.fn();
    render(<Combobox options={options} onSelect={onSelect} placeholder="Search fruit" />);

    const input = page.getByRole('combobox');
    await input.click();
    await input.fill('an');

    // real browser — options filtered by actual DOM mutation
    const listbox = page.getByRole('listbox');
    await expect.element(listbox).toBeVisible();

    const visibleOptions = listbox.getByRole('option');
    await expect.element(visibleOptions).toHaveCount(2); // Banana, Elderberry contains 'an' — adjust for your data

    await input.press('ArrowDown');
    await input.press('Enter');

    expect(onSelect).toHaveBeenCalledWith('Banana');
    await expect.element(input).toHaveValue('Banana');
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Running component tests in a real browser via Vitest Browser Mode catches CSS-visibility issues, scroll-into-view behaviour, and focus management that jsdom silently passes — because jsdom does not implement layout — but browser mode tests are roughly 3-5x slower than jsdom tests and require a Playwright or WebdriverIO install, increasing CI setup time; the correct split is to use browser mode only for components whose correctness depends on layout, focus order, or native browser input handling, and keep pure logic tests in jsdom for speed.

**Pattern 87** — Node.js `run()` `isolation: 'process'` with Per-File Environment Variables
```typescript
// scripts/run-isolated-tests.mts — per-file process isolation for integration tests
import { run } from 'node:test';
import { spec } from 'node:test/reporters';
import { glob } from 'node:fs/promises';

// collect integration test files
const integrationFiles: string[] = [];
for await (const f of glob('src/**/*.integration.test.ts', { cwd: process.cwd() })) {
  integrationFiles.push(f);
}

const runner = run({
  files: integrationFiles,
  isolation: 'process',         // each file runs in a fresh Node.js child process
  concurrency: 4,               // up to 4 parallel child processes
  env: {
    ...process.env,
    NODE_ENV:     'test',
    DATABASE_URL: process.env.TEST_DATABASE_URL ?? 'postgresql://localhost/test',
    LOG_LEVEL:    'error',      // suppress noise in CI output
  },
  timeout: 30_000,              // per-test timeout in ms
});

runner.on('test:fail', () => { process.exitCode = 1; });
runner
  .compose(spec)
  .pipe(process.stdout);
```
Tradeoff: `isolation: 'process'` guarantees that module-level state (singleton connections, cached config, static class fields) cannot bleed between test files because each file executes in a fresh OS process — eliminating an entire class of order-dependent test failures — but process startup overhead means a suite with 200 integration files takes noticeably longer than thread-based isolation; profile your suite before switching from `isolation: 'none'` and consider reserving process isolation for files that are known to have module-level singletons, using thread isolation for the rest.
