**Pattern 88** — Playwright `expect.soft()` Accumulating Non-Blocking Assertion Failures
```typescript
// tests/e2e/product-listing.spec.ts — soft assertions for exhaustive validation
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('product card displays all required information', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/products');

  const firstCard = page.locator('[data-testid="product-card"]').first();

  // soft assertions: all are evaluated even if one fails
  await expect.soft(firstCard.getByRole('img')).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(firstCard.getByRole('img')).toHaveAttribute('alt', /.+/); // non-empty alt
  await expect.soft(firstCard.getByTestId('product-name')).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(firstCard.getByTestId('product-price')).toHaveText(/\$[\d,.]+/);
  await expect.soft(firstCard.getByTestId('product-rating')).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(firstCard.getByTestId('add-to-cart')).toBeEnabled();

  // hard assertion at the end — fails immediately, aggregates all soft failures above
  await expect(firstCard.getByTestId('product-name')).not.toBeEmpty();

  // testInfo.errors will list ALL soft failures if any exist
  // useful for design QA runs where you want a full inventory of gaps
});
```
Tradeoff: `expect.soft()` accumulates all assertion failures in a single test run rather than stopping at the first failure — giving a complete picture of what is broken on a page in one pass — but it requires discipline to place a hard `expect()` at the end of the test to ensure the test actually fails when soft assertions fail; a test composed entirely of `expect.soft()` calls with no final hard assertion will report as passed even when every soft check failed, which defeats the purpose of the test.

**Pattern 89** — Vitest `describe.concurrent` with `expect.hasAssertions()` for Async Race Validation
```typescript
// src/queue/__tests__/job-processor.concurrent.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, vi } from 'vitest';
import { JobProcessor } from '../job-processor';

// describe.concurrent: all it() blocks in this describe run in parallel
describe.concurrent('JobProcessor — concurrent processing', () => {
  it('processes a fast job within 100ms', async ({ expect }) => {
    expect.hasAssertions(); // guard: test must make at least one assertion
    const processor = new JobProcessor({ maxRetries: 1, timeoutMs: 500 });
    const result = await processor.process({ type: 'ping', payload: {} });
    expect(result.status).toBe('completed');
    expect(result.durationMs).toBeLessThan(100);
  });

  it('retries a failing job up to maxRetries times', async ({ expect }) => {
    expect.hasAssertions();
    const processor = new JobProcessor({ maxRetries: 2, timeoutMs: 500 });
    const failingJob = { type: 'flaky', payload: { failUntilAttempt: 2 } };
    const result = await processor.process(failingJob);
    expect(result.attempts).toBe(2);
    expect(result.status).toBe('completed');
  });

  it('marks a job as failed after exhausting retries', async ({ expect }) => {
    expect.hasAssertions();
    const processor = new JobProcessor({ maxRetries: 1, timeoutMs: 500 });
    const alwaysFailJob = { type: 'flaky', payload: { failUntilAttempt: 99 } };
    const result = await processor.process(alwaysFailJob);
    expect(result.status).toBe('failed');
    expect(result.attempts).toBe(2); // 1 initial + 1 retry
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `describe.concurrent` runs all sibling `it()` blocks simultaneously in the same worker, reducing wall time for independent async tests — but each test receives its own `expect` via the TestContext argument (`{ expect }`) rather than from the top-level import, because concurrent tests share the same execution context and assertions from one test could otherwise be attributed to another; forgetting to destructure `{ expect }` from the test callback arguments will cause assertion failures in one concurrent test to be reported against a different test, producing misleading failure messages that are very difficult to debug.

**Pattern 90** — Playwright `context.storageState()` Snapshot and Restore for Session Reuse
```typescript
// tests/auth.setup.ts — global setup: authenticate once, save session
import { test as setup, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'node:path';

const AUTH_FILE = path.join(__dirname, '../.playwright/auth/user.json');

setup('authenticate and save session', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/login');
  await page.fill('[name="email"]',    'test@example.com');
  await page.fill('[name="password"]', process.env.TEST_PASSWORD!);
  await page.click('[type="submit"]');
  await expect(page).toHaveURL('/dashboard');

  // Serialize cookies + localStorage + sessionStorage to a JSON file
  await page.context().storageState({ path: AUTH_FILE });
});

// playwright.config.ts — restore session in every test project
// projects: [{ name: 'authenticated', use: { storageState: AUTH_FILE } }]

// tests/dashboard.spec.ts — test runs with pre-authenticated session
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('authenticated user sees personal greeting', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  // No login steps needed — session restored from storageState file
  await expect(page.getByTestId('user-greeting')).toContainText('Welcome back');
});
```
Tradeoff: Saving and restoring `storageState` amortises login cost across the entire test suite — a single authentication is performed in global setup and all tests reuse the session snapshot — but the saved state includes expiring session cookies; if the token TTL is shorter than the total suite duration, tests run late in the suite will silently receive 401 responses or be redirected to login, producing hard-to-diagnose failures that only appear in long CI runs; mitigate by using long-lived test API tokens instead of session cookies, or by refreshing the `storageState` file partway through the suite via a periodic re-authentication step.

### Community Gotchas

**G251: Vitest `describe.concurrent` with shared `expect` import causes assertion attribution to wrong test**
Why this matters: When using `describe.concurrent`, all `it()` blocks run simultaneously in the same worker. Vitest tracks which test is "current" via an internal context stack, but concurrent tests interleave execution — when two concurrent tests both call `expect()` from the top-level import at the same moment, Vitest can attribute the assertion result to whichever test happens to be on top of the context stack at that instant. A passing assertion in test A can be counted against test B, and a failure in test B can cause test A to be marked as failed. The failure message will reference the wrong test name, making it appear random and intermittent.
Fix: Always destructure `expect` from the TestContext argument in concurrent tests: `it('name', async ({ expect }) => { ... })`. This gives each concurrent test its own isolated assertion context. Never use the top-level `expect` import inside `describe.concurrent` blocks. Add an ESLint rule (`vitest/prefer-expect-resolves` or a custom rule) that flags top-level `expect` usage inside `describe.concurrent` callbacks.

---

**G252: Playwright `page.route()` handler registered inside `test.beforeEach` is not automatically unregistered — it accumulates across retries**
Why this matters: When a route handler is registered inside `test.beforeEach`, Playwright does not automatically remove it at the end of each test. If a test is retried (due to `--retries` in `playwright.config.ts`), `beforeEach` runs again, registering a second identical handler on the same page. Because Playwright executes route handlers in LIFO order, the second handler runs first and calls `route.fulfill()`, then the first handler also matches the same request and attempts to call `route.fulfill()` again on an already-handled route, throwing an unhandled error: `"Route is already handled"`. This surfaces as a confusing secondary failure on the retry pass that obscures the original test failure.
Fix: Always call `await page.unroute(pattern)` in `test.afterEach` for every pattern registered in `beforeEach`, or register routes inside the test body (not in `beforeEach`) so they are scoped to a single test invocation. Alternatively, use `page.route(pattern, handler, { times: 1 })` to auto-unregister the handler after its first invocation.

---

**G253: Node.js `--test-randomize` combined with `t.plan()` causes plan-count failures when randomized order changes async interleaving**
Why this matters: When test execution order is randomised with `--test-randomize`, tests that use `t.plan(n)` to assert a fixed number of async callbacks can fail non-deterministically. If test A uses `t.plan(3)` and registers three async event listeners, and randomised ordering causes test B to start executing concurrently before test A's event loop has processed all three callbacks, the plan check fires at test A's natural completion boundary — but some callbacks may still be pending in the event queue and attributed to the next test's execution context. The test fails with `plan: 3, actual: 2` on some seeds and passes on others, making the root cause invisible unless the failing seed is preserved.
Fix: Pair `t.plan()` with `await` on all async operations within the test body to ensure all callbacks have resolved before the plan check fires. If using an event emitter, wrap the callback registration in a `Promise` that resolves after all expected events have been received: `await Promise.all([onceEvent(bus, 'a'), onceEvent(bus, 'b'), onceEvent(bus, 'c')])` and then assert. Store the `--test-random-seed` value from failing CI runs in a dedicated issue comment for reproducibility.

---

**G254: Vitest `vi.stubEnv()` does not re-trigger module-level config evaluation — modules that read `process.env` at import time cache the value forever**
Why this matters: Many configuration modules follow the pattern `const redisUrl = process.env.REDIS_URL ?? 'redis://localhost:6379'` at the top level of the module file. When Vitest loads such a module, the assignment runs once and the value is captured in a module-level constant. Calling `vi.stubEnv('REDIS_URL', 'redis://remote:6379')` after the module has been imported does nothing to the already-evaluated constant — `redisUrl` retains its original value for all subsequent calls within the same test file. Tests that expect `stubEnv` to affect module-level config variables will silently test the default value regardless of the stub, producing false confidence.
Fix: Call `vi.resetModules()` before re-importing the config module inside the test that needs a different environment value: `vi.stubEnv('REDIS_URL', 'redis://remote:6379'); vi.resetModules(); const { resolveConfig } = await import('../app-config');`. Mark such tests with a `@module-reload` JSDoc comment so reviewers know the import must remain inside the test body and must not be moved to the top-level import.

---

**G255: Playwright `context.storageState()` silently includes `HttpOnly` cookies that cannot be read by `document.cookie` — leading to false trust in restored session validity**
Why this matters: `HttpOnly` cookies are excluded from JavaScript's `document.cookie` API by design, but Playwright's `context.storageState()` serializes them into the saved JSON because Playwright has privileged CDP access to the full cookie jar. When the saved state is restored via `use: { storageState }`, the `HttpOnly` cookies are correctly replayed. However, if a developer writes a session-validity check in the test setup using `page.evaluate(() => document.cookie)` to verify the auth cookie is present, this check will always return an empty string for `HttpOnly` cookies, causing the setup assertion to fail even though the session is fully valid. Teams misdiagnose this as a broken auth setup and add workarounds that inadvertently bypass the security property.
Fix: Validate restored session state by navigating to a protected route and asserting on a page-level indicator (e.g., `await expect(page).toHaveURL('/dashboard')`) rather than by inspecting `document.cookie`. To enumerate all cookies including `HttpOnly`, use `await context.cookies()` which returns the full CDP cookie list, not `page.evaluate(() => document.cookie)`. Document the distinction in the auth setup file with an inline comment.

## Cycle 61 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 91** — Vitest fixture builder pattern with `onCleanup` for auto-teardown resource lifecycle
```typescript
import { test as baseTest } from 'vitest';
import fs from 'node:fs/promises';
import path from 'node:path';

const test = baseTest.extend<{ tempDir: string }>({
  tempDir: async ({}, { onCleanup }) => {
    const dir = path.join('/tmp', `vitest-${Date.now()}-${Math.random().toString(36).slice(2)}`);
    await fs.mkdir(dir, { recursive: true });
    onCleanup(async () => {
      await fs.rm(dir, { recursive: true, force: true });
    });
    return dir;
  },
});

test('writes and reads file in isolated temp directory', async ({ tempDir }) => {
  const filePath = path.join(tempDir, 'output.json');
  await fs.writeFile(filePath, JSON.stringify({ ok: true }));
  const data = JSON.parse(await fs.readFile(filePath, 'utf8'));
  expect(data.ok).toBe(true);
});
```
Tradeoff: The builder pattern's `onCleanup` callback guarantees teardown even when a test throws mid-execution, preventing orphaned temp directories from accumulating across flaky or interrupted runs — but `onCleanup` can only be registered once per fixture invocation; if the fixture's internal setup requires multiple cleanup steps (e.g., closing a server AND deleting a directory), all teardown logic must be composed into a single callback or the second registration will be silently ignored in versions prior to Vitest 3.x, leaving resources open.

**Pattern 92** — Vitest `file`-scoped fixture for shared database connection across a test file
```typescript
import { test as baseTest } from 'vitest';
import { Pool } from 'pg';

interface FileFixtures {
  pool: Pool;
  uniqueSchema: string;
}

const test = baseTest.extend<object, FileFixtures>({
  pool: [
    async ({}, use) => {
      const pool = new Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL });
      await use(pool);
      await pool.end();
    },
    { scope: 'file' },
  ],
  uniqueSchema: [
    async ({ pool }, use) => {
      const schema = `test_${Date.now()}`;
      await pool.query(`CREATE SCHEMA ${schema}`);
      await use(schema);
      await pool.query(`DROP SCHEMA ${schema} CASCADE`);
    },
    { scope: 'file' },
  ],
});

test('inserts a row', async ({ pool, uniqueSchema }) => {
  await pool.query(`CREATE TABLE ${uniqueSchema}.items (id serial PRIMARY KEY)`);
  const res = await pool.query(`INSERT INTO ${uniqueSchema}.items DEFAULT VALUES RETURNING id`);
  expect(res.rows[0].id).toBe(1);
});
```
Tradeoff: File-scoped fixtures open a single database connection and a single schema for all tests in the file, cutting connection-establishment overhead to one round-trip per file instead of one per test — but all tests in the file share the same connection pool, so a test that holds a transaction open across an `await` without explicitly committing or rolling back will block subsequent tests in the file on row-level locks, producing serialisation deadlocks that appear intermittent because they only surface when the preceding test's async continuation has not yet flushed.

**Pattern 93** — Vitest `test.override()` for per-describe environment configuration without re-importing modules
```typescript
import { test as baseTest } from 'vitest';

interface Config { apiBase: string; timeout: number }
const test = baseTest.extend<{ config: Config }>({
  config: { apiBase: 'http://localhost:3000', timeout: 5000 },
});

describe('staging environment', () => {
  test.override({ config: { apiBase: 'https://staging.api.example.com', timeout: 15000 } });

  test('health endpoint responds within timeout', async ({ config }) => {
    const controller = new AbortController();
    const id = setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), config.timeout);
    const res = await fetch(`${config.apiBase}/health`, { signal: controller.signal });
    clearTimeout(id);
    expect(res.ok).toBe(true);
  });
});

describe('local environment', () => {
  test('health endpoint uses default config', async ({ config }) => {
    expect(config.apiBase).toBe('http://localhost:3000');
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `test.override()` (introduced in Vitest 4.1.0) allows fixture values to be replaced for a specific `describe` block without re-extending the test object or rewriting the fixture factory, making multi-environment test suites concise — but `test.override()` only works with value-type fixtures (objects, primitives) and cannot override async factory fixtures that perform side effects such as starting servers; attempting to override an async factory fixture with `test.override()` will apply only to the resolved value returned by the factory, not to any side effects already performed by the original factory, leading to resource leaks if teardown depended on state captured during setup.

**Pattern 94** — Playwright `--shard` with blob reporter and `merge-reports` for distributed CI artifact consolidation
```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  fullyParallel: true,
  reporter: process.env.CI
    ? [['blob', { outputDir: './blob-report' }]]
    : [['html', { open: 'never' }]],
  use: { baseURL: 'https://staging.example.com' },
});
```
```yaml
# .github/workflows/playwright.yml (excerpt)
jobs:
  playwright-tests:
    strategy:
      matrix:
        shard: [1, 2, 3, 4]
    steps:
      - run: npx playwright test --shard=${{ matrix.shard }}/4
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: blob-report-${{ matrix.shard }}
          path: blob-report/

  merge-reports:
    needs: [playwright-tests]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with: { path: all-blob-reports, pattern: blob-report-* }
      - run: npx playwright merge-reports --reporter html ./all-blob-reports
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with: { name: html-report, path: playwright-report/ }
```
Tradeoff: Blob-reporter sharding with post-merge HTML generation produces a single cohesive report across all CI shards without requiring a live Playwright server, and `fullyParallel: true` ensures individual tests (not just files) are distributed evenly across shards so no shard idles while another runs a large file — but the blob files include absolute paths baked in at report generation time; if the merge job downloads artifact archives into a different directory structure than the shard jobs used, `merge-reports` will fail to resolve source-map file paths in the HTML report, showing raw minified stack traces instead of source-mapped lines; mitigate by normalising the working directory in both the test and merge jobs.

**Pattern 95** — Playwright `fullyParallel: true` with `test.describe.configure({ mode: 'serial' })` for mixed parallelism strategies
```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
export default defineConfig({ fullyParallel: true });

// tests/checkout-flow.spec.ts — serial block within a globally parallel suite
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.describe.configure({ mode: 'serial' });

let orderId: string;

test('add item to cart', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/shop');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' }).first().click();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('cart-count')).toHaveText('1');
});

test('checkout and confirm order', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/cart');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Checkout' }).click();
  await page.fill('[name="card"]', '4242424242424242');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay now' }).click();
  const id = await page.getByTestId('order-id').textContent();
  orderId = id!;
  expect(orderId).toMatch(/^ORD-\d+/);
});

test('order appears in history', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/orders');
  await expect(page.getByText(orderId)).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `test.describe.configure({ mode: 'serial' })` scopes sequential execution to the describe block without disabling parallelism globally, allowing the rest of the suite to run at full concurrency while stateful flows execute in order — but serial mode serialises re-runs as well; when Playwright's `--retries` flag retries the second test in a serial block after a failure, it re-runs the entire describe block from the first test, duplicating side effects (such as repeated cart additions or order submissions) unless each test defensively checks preconditions and skips already-completed setup.

**Pattern 96** — Node.js `context.mock.timers` with selective API mocking for async retry-loop unit tests
```typescript
import { test, describe } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

async function retryWithBackoff<T>(
  fn: () => Promise<T>,
  maxAttempts = 3,
  baseDelayMs = 1000,
): Promise<T> {
  for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= maxAttempts; attempt++) {
    try { return await fn(); }
    catch (err) {
      if (attempt === maxAttempts) throw err;
      await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, baseDelayMs * 2 ** (attempt - 1)));
    }
  }
  throw new Error('unreachable');
}

describe('retryWithBackoff', () => {
  test('resolves on third attempt after mocked delays', async (t) => {
    t.mock.timers.enable({ apis: ['setTimeout'] });
    let calls = 0;
    const fn = async () => {
      if (++calls < 3) throw new Error('transient');
      return 'success';
    };
    const resultPromise = retryWithBackoff(fn, 3, 100);
    t.mock.timers.tick(100);   // first backoff: 100ms
    t.mock.timers.tick(200);   // second backoff: 200ms
    const result = await resultPromise;
    assert.equal(result, 'success');
    assert.equal(calls, 3);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `context.mock.timers.enable({ apis: ['setTimeout'] })` replaces only `setTimeout` while leaving `setInterval`, `Date`, and `Promise` microtask queues on real clocks, making the mock surgical enough not to disturb the async scheduler — but because only `setTimeout` is replaced, `tick()` advances the mocked timer queue synchronously and then returns control; if `retryWithBackoff` awaits a real `Promise` that resolves via microtask between ticks, the microtask may not have flushed by the time the next `tick()` call fires, causing the timer to advance past the point where the promise was expected to resolve and producing an `await` that hangs; always interleave `tick()` calls with `await Promise.resolve()` to flush pending microtasks between timer advances.

**Pattern 97** — Node.js `run()` with `coverage: true` and `lcov` reporter for CI coverage gating
```typescript
// scripts/run-tests.mts
import { run } from 'node:test';
import { lcov } from 'node:test/reporters';
import { createWriteStream } from 'node:fs';

const stream = run({
  files: ['./src/**/*.test.ts'],
  coverage: true,
  coverageExcludeGlobs: ['**/*.d.ts', '**/generated/**'],
  concurrency: true,
});

stream
  .compose(lcov)
  .pipe(createWriteStream('./coverage/lcov.info'));

stream.on('test:coverage', (data) => {
  const { coveredLinePercent, coveredBranchPercent } = data.summary.totals;
  if (coveredLinePercent < 80 || coveredBranchPercent < 70) {
    console.error(
      `Coverage gates failed: lines=${coveredLinePercent.toFixed(1)}% branches=${coveredBranchPercent.toFixed(1)}%`
    );
    process.exitCode = 1;
  }
});
```
Tradeoff: Programmatic `run()` with a `'test:coverage'` event listener allows coverage thresholds to be enforced in the same process as the test runner without shelling out to a separate coverage tool, and the `lcov` reporter output is directly consumable by Codecov and Coveralls CI integrations — but Node.js's built-in coverage instrumentation uses V8's block coverage, which counts executed AST nodes rather than logical branches; ternary expressions with `||` / `&&` short-circuit evaluation are counted as a single AST node, so a branch where the right-hand operand is never reached will not reduce `coveredBranchPercent`, producing overly optimistic branch coverage figures for codebases that rely heavily on short-circuit defaults.

**Pattern 98** — Node.js `t.assert.snapshot()` with `--test-update-snapshots` for serialised output regression
```typescript
import { test, describe } from 'node:test';

function formatReceipt(items: { name: string; price: number }[]): string {
  const lines = items.map(i => `  ${i.name.padEnd(20)} $${i.price.toFixed(2)}`);
  const total = items.reduce((s, i) => s + i.price, 0);
  return ['Receipt', '--------', ...lines, '--------',
    `  TOTAL                $${total.toFixed(2)}`].join('\n');
}

describe('formatReceipt', () => {
  test('formats a two-item receipt', (t) => {
    t.assert.snapshot(
      formatReceipt([
        { name: 'Widget', price: 9.99 },
        { name: 'Gadget', price: 24.50 },
      ])
    );
  });

  test('formats empty receipt', (t) => {
    t.assert.snapshot(formatReceipt([]));
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Node.js 22.3+ `t.assert.snapshot()` stores snapshots in `.js.snap` files adjacent to the test file and integrates directly with the `node:test` runner without requiring an external snapshot library — but snapshot files are stored as raw serialised strings without pretty-printing for non-primitive values (unlike Jest's `pretty-format`), meaning objects with deeply nested structures produce single-line snapshot strings that are difficult to diff meaningfully in pull request reviews; for structured data, serialise explicitly to a formatted string (e.g., `JSON.stringify(value, null, 2)`) before snapshotting to produce diffable multi-line output.

**Pattern 99** — Vitest `describe.concurrent` with context-bound `expect` to prevent assertion cross-contamination
```typescript
import { describe, test } from 'vitest';

async function fetchUserScore(userId: string): Promise<number> {
  // Simulated async work with variable latency
  await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, Math.random() * 10));
  return userId.charCodeAt(0);
}

describe.concurrent('user score API', () => {
  test('alice gets correct score', async ({ expect }) => {
    const score = await fetchUserScore('alice');
    expect(score).toBe(97); // 'a'.charCodeAt(0)
  });

  test('bob gets correct score', async ({ expect }) => {
    const score = await fetchUserScore('bob');
    expect(score).toBe(98); // 'b'.charCodeAt(0)
  });

  test('concurrent snapshot does not bleed across tests', async ({ expect }) => {
    const score = await fetchUserScore('carol');
    expect(score).toMatchSnapshot();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Destructuring `expect` from the test context argument gives each concurrent test its own isolated assertion tracker, preventing the assertion-attribution bug where top-level `expect` calls are credited to whichever test happens to be active on the Vitest context stack at the moment of assertion — but context-bound `expect` does not support `expect.extend()` for adding custom matchers; custom matchers registered via `expect.extend()` are added to the global `expect` singleton only, so concurrent tests that require custom matchers must use the top-level `expect` import and accept the re-entry risk, or register the custom matchers inside a `beforeAll` that adds them to a locally-captured reference.

**Pattern 100** — Jest `projects` multi-config with per-project `displayName` and `testEnvironment` for layered test pyramid
```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import type { Config } from 'jest';

const config: Config = {
  bail: 1,
  maxWorkers: process.env.CI ? 2 : '50%',
  coverageThreshold: {
    global: { lines: 80, branches: 70, functions: 80, statements: 80 },
    './src/api/payments.ts': { lines: 100, branches: 100, functions: 100, statements: 100 },
  },
  projects: [
    {
      displayName: 'unit',
      testEnvironment: 'node',
      testMatch: ['<rootDir>/src/**/*.unit.test.ts'],
    },
    {
      displayName: 'integration',
      testEnvironment: 'node',
      testMatch: ['<rootDir>/src/**/*.integration.test.ts'],
      globalSetup: '<rootDir>/jest.global-setup.integration.ts',
      globalTeardown: '<rootDir>/jest.global-teardown.integration.ts',
    },
    {
      displayName: 'browser',
      testEnvironment: 'jsdom',
      testMatch: ['<rootDir>/src/**/*.browser.test.ts'],
      transform: { '^.+\\.tsx?$': ['ts-jest', { tsconfig: 'tsconfig.test.json' }] },
    },
  ],
};

export default config;
```
Tradeoff: The `projects` array maps directly to the three tiers of the test pyramid — node unit, node integration, jsdom browser — each with independent environment setup and teardown, making it possible to run only one tier (`jest --selectProjects unit`) without loading the other tiers' global setup overhead — but `coverageThreshold` is evaluated against the aggregate coverage of all projects combined, not per-project; a project with 100% coverage on critical paths can mask a second project with 30% coverage if their line counts produce an aggregate above the threshold, leading to false assurance that every tier of the pyramid is adequately covered.

**Pattern 101** — Playwright `page.route()` with `route.fallback()` for partial API mocking without disabling real endpoints
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('payment form shows error on card decline without mocking other endpoints', async ({ page }) => {
  // Intercept only the charge endpoint; all other API calls pass through to the real server
  await page.route('**/api/payments/charge', async (route) => {
    const body = route.request().postDataJSON();
    if (body?.cardNumber === '4000000000000002') {
      await route.fulfill({
        status: 402,
        contentType: 'application/json',
        body: JSON.stringify({ error: 'card_declined', code: 'insufficient_funds' }),
      });
    } else {
      // Let real requests through for non-decline scenarios
      await route.fallback();
    }
  });

  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.fill('[data-testid="card-number"]', '4000000000000002');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('payment-error')).toContainText('insufficient funds');
});
```
Tradeoff: `route.fallback()` allows a route handler to selectively intercept some requests while forwarding others to the real server, enabling integration tests that mock only the failure paths that are unsafe to trigger against production infrastructure while leaving all other API interactions real — but `route.fallback()` forwards the request through any remaining registered handlers and then to the network; if a second `page.route()` handler registered earlier (e.g., in `beforeEach`) matches the same URL pattern, the fallback will invoke that handler next rather than the network, creating an implicit handler chain that is invisible in the test body and produces confusing response behaviour when the handler order is changed.

**Pattern 102** — Playwright `locator.getByRole()` with `exact` and `name` options for resilient ARIA-semantic selectors
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('navigation contains all required accessible links', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');

  // Exact name match prevents false positives from partial text overlap
  const nav = page.getByRole('navigation', { name: 'Main navigation' });

  // Each link matched by its accessible name — survives CSS class and DOM restructuring
  await expect(nav.getByRole('link', { name: 'Home', exact: true })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(nav.getByRole('link', { name: 'Products', exact: true })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(nav.getByRole('link', { name: 'Contact', exact: true })).toBeVisible();

  // Assert count to catch accidental link duplication
  await expect(nav.getByRole('link')).toHaveCount(3);
});

test('submit button is disabled while form is invalid', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/contact');
  const submit = page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Send message', exact: true });
  await expect(submit).toBeDisabled();
  await page.fill('[name="email"]', 'user@example.com');
  await page.fill('[name="message"]', 'Hello');
  await expect(submit).toBeEnabled();
});
```
Tradeoff: ARIA role + name selectors are decoupled from CSS class names, element IDs, and DOM nesting depth, so they survive design system refactors that rename class names or restructure wrappers — but `getByRole` resolves accessible names by following the ARIA computation algorithm (text content then `aria-label` then `aria-labelledby` then title attribute) in that priority order; if a button's visible text and its `aria-label` differ (a common accessibility fix where the visible text is an icon and the label is descriptive prose), `getByRole('button', { name: 'Send message' })` will match the `aria-label` and not the visible text, which means renaming only the visible icon without updating the `aria-label` silently breaks the locator in a way that is not caught by accessibility linting tools.

**Pattern 103** — Jest `moduleNameMapper` with ordered patterns for ESM path alias and asset stub resolution
```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import type { Config } from 'jest';

const config: Config = {
  moduleNameMapper: {
    // Asset stubs — must come before alias resolution to prevent alias matching image paths
    '\\.(jpg|jpeg|png|gif|svg|webp)$': '<rootDir>/__mocks__/fileMock.ts',
    '\\.(css|scss|less)$': '<rootDir>/__mocks__/styleMock.ts',

    // Path aliases — ordered from most specific to least specific
    '^@api/(.*)$': '<rootDir>/src/api/$1',
    '^@components/(.*)$': '<rootDir>/src/components/$1',
    '^@utils/(.*)$': '<rootDir>/src/utils/$1',
    '^@/(.*)$': '<rootDir>/src/$1',
  },
  transform: {
    '^.+\\.tsx?$': ['ts-jest', { useESM: true }],
  },
  extensionsToTreatAsEsm: ['.ts', '.tsx'],
};

export default config;
```
Tradeoff: Placing asset stub patterns before path alias patterns in `moduleNameMapper` prevents the alias `^@/(.*)$` from matching `@/assets/logo.png` before the image stub regex can intercept it — Jest processes `moduleNameMapper` patterns in insertion order, so pattern ordering is a load-bearing semantic detail that is easy to accidentally reverse when adding new aliases — but the approach of listing patterns from specific to general breaks down if path aliases and asset patterns have overlapping prefixes; any future alias added with a pattern like `^@/(.*)$` that also matches image paths will shadow the asset stub if inserted in the wrong position, and Jest emits no warning about shadowed patterns, causing the module resolution to return source path strings instead of the stub.

**Pattern 104** — Jest `fakeTimers` with `doNotFake: ['nextTick']` for Promise-chain-compatible timer mocking
```typescript
// jest.config.ts (global fake timer configuration)
import type { Config } from 'jest';
const config: Config = {
  fakeTimers: {
    enableGlobally: true,
    doNotFake: ['nextTick', 'queueMicrotask'],
    timerLimit: 1000, // Prevent runAllTimers() infinite loop on self-rescheduling timers
  },
};
export default config;
```
```typescript
// src/poller.test.ts
import { pollUntil } from '../poller';

test('pollUntil resolves after condition becomes true', async () => {
  let ready = false;
  setTimeout(() => { ready = true; }, 5000);

  const resultPromise = pollUntil(() => ready, { intervalMs: 500, timeoutMs: 10_000 });

  // Advance past multiple poll intervals
  jest.advanceTimersByTime(5500);

  // Promise microtasks flush because nextTick and queueMicrotask are NOT faked
  await expect(resultPromise).resolves.toBe(true);
});
```
Tradeoff: Excluding `nextTick` and `queueMicrotask` from fake timers allows `Promise` resolutions and `async/await` continuations to flush normally between `advanceTimersByTime()` calls, preventing the common deadlock where a `Promise` chain awaiting a `setTimeout`-driven event never resolves because the microtask queue is blocked behind a faked tick — but `doNotFake: ['nextTick']` only affects Node.js's `process.nextTick`; in JSDOM environments, `Promise` callbacks are scheduled via the browser event loop simulation and are not governed by `nextTick`, so this exclusion has no effect in jsdom test environments and teams that share a single `jest.config.ts` across node and jsdom projects may be misled into believing Promise chains flush correctly in both environments when they do not.

**Pattern 105** — Jest `workerIdleMemoryLimit` with `maxWorkers` tuning to prevent OOM crashes in large integration test suites
```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import type { Config } from 'jest';
import os from 'node:os';

const isCI = Boolean(process.env.CI);

const config: Config = {
  // CI: fixed 2 workers to stay within container memory limits
  // Local: half available cores to leave headroom for IDE and build tools
  maxWorkers: isCI ? 2 : `${Math.max(1, Math.floor(os.cpus().length / 2))}`,

  // Recycle workers when they exceed 300 MB resident set size
  // Prevents test-order-dependent memory accumulation from module-level caches
  workerIdleMemoryLimit: '300MB',

  workerGracefulExitTimeout: 3000,

  // Explicitly shut down open handles rather than relying on --forceExit
  openHandlesTimeout: 2000,
};

export default config;
```
Tradeoff: `workerIdleMemoryLimit` recycles worker processes that exceed the configured RSS threshold between test files, preventing cascading OOM kills when integration tests load large fixture datasets or warm application caches that are never garbage-collected within a worker's lifetime — but worker recycling restarts the Node.js process, which re-evaluates all `setupFilesAfterEnv` hooks from scratch in the new process; if `setupFilesAfterEnv` performs expensive operations such as generating certificates or seeding a test database, worker recycling can increase total suite runtime more than the memory savings justify; profile the `--verbose` output's per-worker timing before enabling `workerIdleMemoryLimit` globally.

---

### Community Gotchas

**G256** — Jest `resetModules: true` in config silently breaks `jest.mock()` factory hoisting across test files
Why this matters: When `resetModules: true` is set globally in `jest.config.ts`, Jest resets the module registry before each test file, which is intended to provide clean module state. However, `jest.mock()` with a factory function relies on Babel/Jest transform-time hoisting — the mock declaration is physically moved to the top of the compiled file so it executes before any `import` statements. When `resetModules` clears the registry mid-suite, the hoisted mock factory is re-evaluated in the new registry, but any module-level variables that the factory closes over (e.g., a `let mockFn = jest.fn()` declared above the `jest.mock()` call) are not yet initialised at hoist time in the fresh registry. This produces the infamous "The module factory of `jest.mock()` is not allowed to reference any out-of-scope variables" error — but only in certain test file orderings, making it appear intermittent.
Fix: Never close over test-file-level variables in `jest.mock()` factory functions. Instead, declare all mock values inside the factory callback itself. To expose a mock reference for per-test configuration, use `jest.mocked()` on the imported module after the mock declaration: `const mockedFn = jest.mocked(module.fn)` and then call `mockedFn.mockReturnValue(...)` inside individual test bodies.

**G257** — Playwright route handler registered in `beforeEach` accumulates on retried tests, causing "route already handled" crashes
Why this matters: Playwright does not automatically deregister `page.route()` handlers between test retries. When a test is retried via `--retries`, `test.beforeEach` executes again on the same page object (unless the test uses the `page` fixture which creates a fresh page per test). The second call to `page.route(pattern, handler)` registers a second handler for the same URL pattern. Because Playwright executes route handlers in LIFO order, the newest handler runs first and calls `route.fulfill()`, completing the route. The original handler then also matches the same already-fulfilled request and attempts to call `route.fulfill()` a second time, throwing `Error: route.fulfill: Route is already handled!`. This crashes the retry pass, masking the original test failure entirely.
Fix: Always pair `page.route(pattern, handler)` in `beforeEach` with a matching `page.unroute(pattern, handler)` in `afterEach`, passing the same handler reference. Alternatively, use `page.route(pattern, handler, { times: 1 })` to auto-deregister after first use. For handlers that must persist across multiple requests within a test, store the handler as a named function reference on the test object and clean it up in `afterEach`.

**G258** — Vitest `vi.resetModules()` inside a test does not reset modules already evaluated by the fixture system before the test started
Why this matters: When using Vitest's fixture system, fixtures are evaluated before the test body runs. If a fixture imports a module at fixture-evaluation time (e.g., `import { config } from '../app-config'`), that module is added to Vitest's module registry during fixture setup. Calling `vi.resetModules()` inside the test body clears the registry snapshot at the test's start boundary, but modules already evaluated by the fixture during its setup phase are not in the snapshot — they remain in the Vitest module cache. Subsequent `await import('../app-config')` calls inside the test will return the fixture's already-evaluated version, not a freshly initialised module, silently defeating the purpose of `resetModules`.
Fix: Do not import environment-sensitive modules inside fixtures that are intended to be reset per-test. Instead, move the `vi.stubEnv()` + `vi.resetModules()` + dynamic `import()` sequence entirely into the test body where the registry state is fully controlled. Mark such tests with `@env-sensitive` in a JSDoc comment and add a CI lint rule that flags dynamic imports without a preceding `vi.resetModules()` in the same scope.

**G259** — Node.js `run()` with `concurrency: true` and `shard` together causes shard index to operate on the full unsharded file list when concurrency spawns sub-processes
Why this matters: When `run({ concurrency: true, shard: { index: 1, total: 4 } })` is called, Node.js splits the discovered test files into 4 equal shards and runs shard 1's file list. However, if `concurrency: true` causes the runner to spawn child workers and each child worker calls its own `run()` internally (a pattern used in some monorepo setups where a root runner spawns per-package runners), the child `run()` invocations discover the full file list for their package and apply their own shard logic independently of the parent's shard. The result is that shard 1 of the parent contains all files of all sub-runners' shard 1s, producing wildly unequal shard sizes and potentially running the same test file in multiple parent shards.
Fix: Shard logic must be applied at exactly one level of the process hierarchy. If using a root runner that spawns per-package `run()` calls, disable sharding in child runners and apply the shard logic only in the root runner's file discovery step by pre-filtering the files array before passing it to `run()`. Document the process hierarchy in a top-level comment in the runner script.

**G260** — Jest `coverageThreshold` aggregate masking: high-coverage projects hiding low-coverage projects in multi-project configs
Why this matters: In a Jest config with a `projects` array representing multiple test pyramid tiers (unit, integration, browser), `coverageThreshold` is evaluated against the combined coverage report of all projects. If the unit test project covers 95% of lines across 200 files, it can arithmetically mask an integration test project that covers only 25% of its 10 critical integration files, because the aggregate line coverage may still exceed 80%. Developers reading the CI coverage badge see a passing gate and assume all tiers of the pyramid are adequately covered, when the integration tier — which often covers cross-cutting concerns like database transactions and authentication middleware — is severely undertested.
Fix: Add per-path `coverageThreshold` entries for directories owned exclusively by the integration tier: `'./src/integrations/**': { lines: 90, branches: 85 }`. This enforces a per-directory floor independent of aggregate dilution. Alternatively, split the Jest config into separate configs run independently in CI (`jest --config jest.unit.config.ts` and `jest --config jest.integration.config.ts`) so each has its own threshold evaluated in isolation.

## Cycle 62 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 106** — Vitest `pool: 'threads'` with `isolate: false` for maximum throughput in stateless unit test suites
```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // Worker threads are faster than forked processes for pure unit tests
    // because they share the V8 heap and skip IPC serialisation of test results
    pool: 'threads',

    // Disable per-file module isolation when every test file manages its own
    // state explicitly — skips the VM context re-initialisation overhead
    isolate: false,

    // Each worker still runs files sequentially; parallelism comes from workers
    fileParallelism: true,

    // Limit thread count on CI to avoid CPU contention with other runners
    poolOptions: {
      threads: {
        maxThreads: process.env.CI ? 2 : undefined,
        minThreads: 1,
      },
    },

    // Enforce that tests actively opt out of isolation if they need shared state
    // rather than accidentally inheriting it
    sequence: {
      shuffle: true,
    },
  },
});
```
Tradeoff: Disabling isolation with `pool: 'threads'` removes the per-file VM-context reset, so any module-level singleton — such as an in-memory cache, a class registry, or a lazily-initialised Prisma client — that mutates state across tests will bleed between files in the same worker; the speed gain (often 30–50% on large suites) is only safe when every test file imports no shared mutable module-level state, and teams that later introduce such state will see order-dependent failures that only reproduce under `--no-file-parallelism` debugging, making root cause identification laborious.

**Pattern 107** — Vitest `projects` array with per-project `environment` for pyramid-tier-aligned multi-environment config
```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      reporter: ['text', 'lcov'],
      thresholds: { lines: 80, branches: 75 },
    },
    projects: [
      {
        // Unit tier: pure logic, no DOM, fastest pool
        test: {
          name: 'unit',
          include: ['src/**/*.unit.test.ts'],
          environment: 'node',
          pool: 'threads',
          isolate: false,
        },
      },
      {
        // Component tier: React components need jsdom
        test: {
          name: 'component',
          include: ['src/**/*.component.test.tsx'],
          environment: 'jsdom',
          pool: 'forks',
          setupFiles: ['./test/setup-jsdom.ts'],
        },
      },
      {
        // Integration tier: real DB, real network — process isolation required
        test: {
          name: 'integration',
          include: ['src/**/*.integration.test.ts'],
          environment: 'node',
          pool: 'forks',
          poolOptions: { forks: { singleFork: true } },
          globalSetup: './test/global-setup-db.ts',
        },
      },
    ],
  },
});
```
Tradeoff: Splitting pyramid tiers into Vitest projects gives each tier its own environment, pool, and setup lifecycle with a single `vitest run` command and unified coverage reporting — but `coverage`, `reporters`, and `resolveSnapshotPath` are root-only options that cannot be overridden per-project; teams that need different coverage thresholds per tier must run each project as a separate command with its own config file, losing the convenience of the unified invocation.

**Pattern 108** — Vitest `experimental.fsModuleCache` to persist transformed module cache across CI runs
```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
import path from 'node:path';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // Persist the Vite transform cache to the CI cache directory
    // so subsequent runs skip re-transpiling unchanged source files
    cacheDir: path.resolve(__dirname, '.vitest-cache'),

    // Experimental: persist per-file transformed module results to disk
    // Requires Vitest >=2.0; safe to disable if cache causes issues
    experimental: {
      // @ts-ignore — not yet in public types
      fsModuleCache: true,
    },

    // Verify cache does not hide coverage regressions by always
    // re-collecting coverage even from cached transforms
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      // Explicitly list source files to prevent cached runs from
      // silently omitting new files not yet in the transform cache
      include: ['src/**/*.ts', 'src/**/*.tsx'],
      exclude: ['src/**/*.d.ts'],
    },
  },
});

// In .github/workflows/ci.yml:
// - name: Restore Vitest cache
//   uses: actions/cache@v4
//   with:
//     path: .vitest-cache
//     key: vitest-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('src/**/*.ts') }}
//     restore-keys: vitest-${{ runner.os }}-
```
Tradeoff: Persisting the Vitest transform cache across CI runs eliminates repeated TypeScript compilation for unchanged files, measurably reducing suite startup time on projects with large dependency graphs — but the cache key must hash source files comprehensively; if the key only hashes `package.json` or lockfiles, a source-only change that does not touch dependencies will restore a stale cache and run tests against previously-transformed code, producing false positives that mask regressions introduced between cache primes.

**Pattern 109** — Playwright `storageState` with `setup` project for once-per-suite authentication in pyramid e2e tier
```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  projects: [
    {
      // Setup project runs first; saves auth state to disk once
      name: 'setup',
      testMatch: /.*\.setup\.ts/,
    },
    {
      name: 'chromium-authenticated',
      use: {
        ...devices['Desktop Chrome'],
        // Reuse the storage state produced by the setup project
        // so each test in this project starts fully authenticated
        storageState: 'playwright/.auth/user.json',
      },
      // Depend on setup completing before any test in this project runs
      dependencies: ['setup'],
    },
  ],
});

// tests/auth.setup.ts
import { test as setup, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';

const authFile = path.join(__dirname, '../playwright/.auth/user.json');

setup('authenticate', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/login');
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill(process.env.TEST_USER_EMAIL!);
  await page.getByLabel('Password').fill(process.env.TEST_USER_PASSWORD!);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('navigation')).toBeVisible();
  // Persist cookies + localStorage to disk for reuse
  await page.context().storageState({ path: authFile });
});
```
Tradeoff: Running authentication once in a `setup` project and reusing `storageState` across all test files eliminates redundant login round-trips, cutting e2e suite time proportionally to the number of authenticated tests — but the saved state encodes session tokens with a finite TTL; if CI queues delay suite execution long enough for the token to expire mid-run, every test in the dependent project will fail with an authentication error that is indistinguishable from a functional regression, so the setup project must include a validity assertion and suites exceeding the token TTL must re-authenticate mid-run or use long-lived API key credentials.

**Pattern 110** — Playwright `page.route()` with `route.fulfill()` for deterministic third-party API mocking in e2e tests
```typescript
// tests/checkout.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.describe('checkout flow with mocked payment gateway', () => {
  test.beforeEach(async ({ page }) => {
    // Intercept Stripe API calls before navigation so no real charge occurs
    await page.route('**/api.stripe.com/v1/payment_intents', async route => {
      if (route.request().method() === 'POST') {
        await route.fulfill({
          status: 200,
          contentType: 'application/json',
          body: JSON.stringify({
            id: 'pi_test_deterministic_1',
            status: 'succeeded',
            amount: 4999,
            currency: 'usd',
          }),
        });
      } else {
        // Pass through GET requests (e.g., status polling) to avoid masking
        // real polling logic that the test intends to exercise
        await route.fallback();
      }
    });
  });

  test.afterEach(async ({ page }) => {
    // Explicitly unroute to prevent handler accumulation on test retries
    await page.unroute('**/api.stripe.com/v1/payment_intents');
  });

  test('completes order when payment succeeds', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/cart');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Proceed to checkout' }).click();
    await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4242424242424242');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay now' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Order confirmed' })).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Intercepting third-party API calls with `page.route()` makes e2e tests deterministic and prevents accidental charges in staging environments — but `route.fallback()` silently passes unmatched request methods through to the real network; if the payment gateway changes its polling endpoint or adds a webhook confirmation step, tests continue passing against the mocked success response while the production integration is broken, so route mocks require a contract test or pact verification at the integration layer to catch upstream API drift.

**Pattern 111** — Playwright `locator.getByRole()` chained with `.filter()` for resilient scoped element selection
```typescript
// tests/data-table.spec.ts
import { test, expect, Locator } from '@playwright/test';

// Page Object encapsulating role-based locators — no CSS class dependencies
class DataTablePage {
  readonly table: Locator;

  constructor(private page: ReturnType<typeof test['info']>['page']) {
    // Locate the table by its ARIA role and accessible name
    // This survives CSS class renames and DOM restructuring
    this.table = (page as any).getByRole('table', { name: 'User records' });
  }

  rowByEmail(email: string): Locator {
    // Chain role locator with text filter — no brittle row index
    return this.table
      .getByRole('row')
      .filter({ hasText: email });
  }

  actionButtonForRow(email: string, actionLabel: string): Locator {
    return this.rowByEmail(email)
      .getByRole('button', { name: actionLabel });
  }
}

test('admin can delete a user row', async ({ page }) => {
  const tablePage = new DataTablePage(page as any);
  await page.goto('/admin/users');

  const deleteBtn = tablePage.actionButtonForRow('alice@example.com', 'Delete');
  await expect(deleteBtn).toBeVisible();
  await deleteBtn.click();

  // Confirm the row disappears from the table — web-first assertion retries
  await expect(
    tablePage.rowByEmail('alice@example.com')
  ).not.toBeAttached();
});
```
Tradeoff: Combining `getByRole()` with `.filter({ hasText })` produces locators that survive most UI refactors, because they depend on semantic ARIA roles and visible text rather than CSS structure — but tables that render thousands of rows via virtual scrolling only materialise a viewport-sized DOM slice; `getByRole('row').filter({ hasText: email })` will match zero elements when the target row is scrolled out of the virtual viewport, so this pattern requires the application to either provide a search/filter API that pre-positions the row in the viewport, or the test must trigger scrolling before asserting.

**Pattern 112** — Node.js `run()` with `testNamePatterns` and `shard` for per-tier parallel execution without a separate runner
```typescript
// scripts/run-tests.mts  (Node 22+, executed via tsx or ts-node)
import { run } from 'node:test';
import { spec } from 'node:test/reporters';
import { pipeline } from 'node:stream/promises';
import path from 'node:path';
import { glob } from 'node:fs/promises';

// Accept shard coordinates from CI environment variables
const shardIndex = Number(process.env.TEST_SHARD_INDEX ?? 1);
const shardTotal = Number(process.env.TEST_SHARD_TOTAL ?? 1);

// Discover all test files once in the root process — never in child workers
const allFiles: string[] = [];
for await (const f of glob('src/**/*.test.ts', { cwd: process.cwd() })) {
  allFiles.push(path.resolve(f));
}
// Pre-filter shard BEFORE handing files to run() to avoid nested shard logic
const shardFiles = allFiles.filter((_, i) => i % shardTotal === shardIndex - 1);

const stream = run({
  files: shardFiles,
  concurrency: Number(process.env.TEST_CONCURRENCY ?? 4),
  isolation: 'process', // Each file gets its own process for true isolation
  coverage: process.env.CI === 'true',
  testNamePatterns: process.env.TEST_PATTERN
    ? [new RegExp(process.env.TEST_PATTERN)]
    : undefined,
});

stream.on('test:fail', () => { process.exitCode = 1; });

await pipeline(stream.compose(spec), process.stdout);
```
Tradeoff: Pre-filtering shard slices in the root process before passing `files` to `run()` correctly prevents the nested-shard problem where child workers re-apply their own shard logic against the full file list — but the static `i % shardTotal` distribution assigns files round-robin by discovery order, which does not account for test file execution time; if fast unit tests and slow integration tests are interleaved by alphabetical order, one shard may run all integration tests while another runs only unit tests, producing wildly unequal CI job durations that inflate wall-clock pipeline time.

**Pattern 113** — Node.js `context.mock.module()` for ES module dependency replacement without Babel transforms
```typescript
// src/email-service.ts
export async function sendWelcomeEmail(address: string): Promise<void> {
  const { Resend } = await import('resend');
  const client = new Resend(process.env.RESEND_API_KEY);
  await client.emails.send({
    from: 'noreply@example.com',
    to: address,
    subject: 'Welcome!',
    html: '<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>',
  });
}

// src/email-service.test.ts  (Node 22+ built-in runner)
import { test, mock } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

test('sendWelcomeEmail calls Resend with correct address', async (t) => {
  const sendSpy = t.mock.fn(async () => ({ data: { id: 'mock-id' }, error: null }));

  // Replace the ESM module before the dynamic import inside sendWelcomeEmail resolves
  t.mock.module('resend', {
    namedExports: {
      Resend: class MockResend {
        emails = { send: sendSpy };
      },
    },
  });

  const { sendWelcomeEmail } = await import('./email-service.ts');
  await sendWelcomeEmail('test@example.com');

  assert.strictEqual(sendSpy.mock.callCount(), 1);
  assert.strictEqual(
    sendSpy.mock.calls[0].arguments[0].to,
    'test@example.com',
  );
});
```
Tradeoff: `t.mock.module()` in Node.js's built-in runner intercepts ESM imports natively without Babel transform hooks or `jest.mock()` factory hoisting, making it the correct approach for mocking ES modules in TypeScript projects using `--experimental-vm-modules` — but `t.mock.module()` only intercepts modules loaded after the mock is registered; static top-level `import` statements in the module under test are evaluated during module graph initialisation before any test body runs, so this pattern only works when the dependency is loaded via a dynamic `await import()` call, requiring the production code to use dynamic imports for mockable dependencies, which is an architectural constraint that may conflict with tree-shaking and bundler optimisation.

**Pattern 114** — Jest `--randomize` with `--test-random-seed` for deterministic reproduction of order-dependent failures
```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import type { Config } from 'jest';

const config: Config = {
  // Enable test randomisation globally to surface hidden order dependencies
  randomize: true,

  // Log the seed used so failing CI runs can be reproduced locally
  // The seed appears in the Jest output: "Randomized with seed: 12345"
  // Re-run with: jest --randomize --test-random-seed=12345

  // Pair with clearMocks/restoreMocks to ensure randomisation exposes
  // only genuine order dependencies, not mock-state bleed
  clearMocks: true,
  restoreMocks: true,
  resetModules: false, // Keep false unless needed — very slow per-test

  // CI: fail on first test suite error to get the seed from logs quickly
  bail: process.env.CI ? 1 : 0,
};

export default config;

// To reproduce a specific ordering failure:
// npx jest --randomize --test-random-seed=<seed-from-ci-logs>
//
// To pin ordering for debugging without disabling randomise:
// JEST_SEED=12345 npx jest  (if using jest-circus with seed env support)
```
Tradeoff: Enabling `randomize: true` in Jest's Circus runner shuffles the order of `describe` blocks and their `it` callbacks using a seeded PRNG, reliably exposing hidden dependencies between tests in the same file — but `randomize` only shuffles tests within a single file; cross-file order dependencies, which are a separate and equally common source of intermittent failures in suites that use module-level singletons, are not affected by `randomize` and require `--runInBand` combined with manual file-order rotation to diagnose.

**Pattern 115** — Jest `moduleNameMapper` with `identity-obj-proxy` and custom transform chain for CSS Modules and asset imports
```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import type { Config } from 'jest';

const config: Config = {
  moduleNameMapper: {
    // CSS Modules: return a Proxy that echoes class name lookups as strings
    // e.g., styles.container → "container" — prevents "undefined" class bugs
    '\\.module\\.(css|scss|sass|less)$': 'identity-obj-proxy',

    // Static assets: stub to a deterministic string so snapshot tests
    // do not embed filesystem-dependent absolute paths
    '\\.(jpg|jpeg|png|gif|svg|webp|ico|woff2?)$':
      '<rootDir>/test/__mocks__/file-mock.ts',

    // Path aliases mirroring tsconfig paths — order matters: more specific first
    '^@/components/(.*)$': '<rootDir>/src/components/$1',
    '^@/lib/(.*)$': '<rootDir>/src/lib/$1',
    '^@/(.*)$': '<rootDir>/src/$1',
  },

  transform: {
    // ts-jest with SWC transformer for fast TypeScript compilation
    '^.+\\.tsx?$': ['@swc/jest', {
      jsc: { parser: { syntax: 'typescript', tsx: true } },
    }],
    // Raw SVG imports as React components (SVGR pattern)
    '\\.svg$': '<rootDir>/test/transforms/svg-transform.ts',
  },
};

export default config;

// test/__mocks__/file-mock.ts
export default 'test-file-stub';
// Named export for modules that use: import { ReactComponent as Icon } from './icon.svg'
export const ReactComponent = 'svg';
```
Tradeoff: Mapping CSS Modules through `identity-obj-proxy` and asset imports through a stub transformer keeps Jest's Node.js environment free of JSDOM limitations with binary file loading and prevents tests from breaking when a stylesheet is refactored — but `identity-obj-proxy` returns every property access as the property name string, which means a typo in a CSS Module class name (`styles.conatiner` instead of `styles.container`) silently returns `"conatiner"` in tests while the component renders an unstyled element in production; snapshot tests that assert on className strings will pass regardless of the typo, so CSS Module correctness must be verified by visual regression tests or a separate `tsc`-based CSS Module type check using typed-css-modules.

**Pattern 116** — Vitest `vi.stubEnv()` with `vi.unstubAllEnvs()` in `afterEach` for isolated environment-variable tests
```typescript
// src/config.ts
export function getDbUrl(): string {
  const url = process.env.DATABASE_URL;
  if (!url) throw new Error('DATABASE_URL is not set');
  return url;
}

export function isProduction(): boolean {
  return process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production';
}

// src/config.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, vi, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { getDbUrl, isProduction } from './config';

afterEach(() => {
  // Restore ALL stubbed env vars after every test — prevents bleed
  // between tests that stub different variables
  vi.unstubAllEnvs();
});

describe('getDbUrl', () => {
  it('returns DATABASE_URL when set', () => {
    vi.stubEnv('DATABASE_URL', 'postgres://localhost/testdb');
    expect(getDbUrl()).toBe('postgres://localhost/testdb');
  });

  it('throws when DATABASE_URL is absent', () => {
    vi.stubEnv('DATABASE_URL', '');
    // Override with delete-equivalent: stub to undefined
    // Note: vi.stubEnv sets string values; use delete via unstub + delete pattern
    delete process.env.DATABASE_URL;
    expect(() => getDbUrl()).toThrow('DATABASE_URL is not set');
  });
});

describe('isProduction', () => {
  it('returns true in production', () => {
    vi.stubEnv('NODE_ENV', 'production');
    expect(isProduction()).toBe(true);
  });

  it('returns false in development', () => {
    vi.stubEnv('NODE_ENV', 'development');
    expect(isProduction()).toBe(false);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `vi.stubEnv()` overrides `process.env` values through Vitest's internal snapshot mechanism and `vi.unstubAllEnvs()` restores them atomically after each test, preventing one test's environment mutations from leaking into subsequent tests in the same file — but `vi.stubEnv()` can only set string values; setting a variable to `undefined` requires `delete process.env.VAR` directly, which bypasses Vitest's stub tracking and will not be restored by `vi.unstubAllEnvs()`, leaving the deletion visible to later tests until the module registry is reset or the worker process is recycled.

**Pattern 117** — Playwright `test.step()` for structured trace segmentation and failure localisation in long e2e flows
```typescript
// tests/onboarding.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('new user completes full onboarding flow', async ({ page }) => {
  // Steps appear as named segments in the Playwright trace viewer,
  // making it immediately clear which phase of a multi-screen flow failed

  await test.step('navigate to registration', async () => {
    await page.goto('/register');
    await expect(page).toHaveTitle(/Create account/);
  });

  await test.step('fill personal details', async () => {
    await page.getByLabel('Full name').fill('Alice Tester');
    await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('alice@playwright-test.dev');
    await page.getByLabel('Password').fill('Secure#Pass1');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Continue' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Verify email' })).toBeVisible();
  });

  await test.step('simulate email verification', async () => {
    // Intercept the token endpoint rather than waiting for a real email
    const tokenResp = await page.request.get('/api/test/latest-verification-token');
    const { token } = await tokenResp.json();
    await page.goto(`/verify?token=${token}`);
    await expect(page.getByText('Email verified')).toBeVisible();
  });

  await test.step('complete profile setup', async () => {
    await page.getByLabel('Job title').fill('QA Engineer');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Finish setup' }).click();
    await expect(page).toHaveURL('/dashboard');
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Wrapping each logical phase of a long e2e test in `test.step()` creates named timeline segments in the Playwright trace viewer and in JUnit/Allure XML reporters, enabling engineers to pinpoint the failing phase without replaying the full trace — but `test.step()` does not create test isolation boundaries; a failure inside a step stops execution of all subsequent steps in the same test, so a bug in the "fill personal details" step will always mask whether the "complete profile setup" step would have passed, requiring the team to either split phases into independent tests with shared `storageState` or accept that a single regression blocks visibility into multiple downstream steps.

**Pattern 118** — Node.js `t.mock.timers` with `Date` and `setTimeout` co-mocking for deadline-aware business logic tests
```typescript
// src/subscription.ts
export function isTrialExpired(trialStartedAt: Date, trialDays = 14): boolean {
  const expiryMs = trialStartedAt.getTime() + trialDays * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000;
  return Date.now() > expiryMs;
}

export function scheduleExpiryNotification(
  onExpiry: () => void,
  trialStartedAt: Date,
  trialDays = 14,
): ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> {
  const msUntilExpiry =
    trialStartedAt.getTime() + trialDays * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000 - Date.now();
  return setTimeout(onExpiry, Math.max(0, msUntilExpiry));
}

// src/subscription.test.ts  (Node.js built-in runner)
import { test, mock } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { isTrialExpired, scheduleExpiryNotification } from './subscription.ts';

test('isTrialExpired returns false during active trial', (t) => {
  // Freeze Date.now() at a specific point in time
  t.mock.timers.enable({ apis: ['Date'], now: new Date('2026-01-01T00:00:00Z').getTime() });

  const trialStart = new Date('2025-12-25T00:00:00Z');
  // 7 days into a 14-day trial — should not be expired
  assert.strictEqual(isTrialExpired(trialStart, 14), false);
});

test('scheduleExpiryNotification fires callback at exact expiry', (t) => {
  const startMs = new Date('2026-01-01T00:00:00Z').getTime();
  t.mock.timers.enable({ apis: ['Date', 'setTimeout'], now: startMs });

  const onExpiry = t.mock.fn();
  const trialStart = new Date(startMs);

  scheduleExpiryNotification(onExpiry, trialStart, 14);

  // Advance to just before expiry — callback must not have fired
  t.mock.timers.tick(14 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000 - 1);
  assert.strictEqual(onExpiry.mock.callCount(), 0);

  // Advance the final millisecond — callback must now fire
  t.mock.timers.tick(1);
  assert.strictEqual(onExpiry.mock.callCount(), 1);
});
```
Tradeoff: Co-mocking `Date` and `setTimeout` via `t.mock.timers.enable({ apis: ['Date', 'setTimeout'] })` ensures that both `Date.now()` and timer callbacks advance together with `tick()`, preventing the classic split-clock bug where `setTimeout` fires at real time while `Date.now()` returns a frozen value — but `t.mock.timers` only mocks the global `setTimeout`; code that imports `setTimeout` from a utility re-export or destructures it from a custom scheduler module will still use the real timer, silently defeating the mock and causing tests to pend indefinitely until the real timeout fires or the test runner's default timeout kills them.

**Pattern 119** — Vitest `onTestFinished()` inside fixture for guaranteed per-test cleanup independent of test outcome
```typescript
// test/fixtures/db-fixture.ts
import { test as baseTest } from 'vitest';
import { PrismaClient } from '@prisma/client';

interface DbFixture {
  prisma: PrismaClient;
  transactionId: string;
}

export const test = baseTest.extend<DbFixture>({
  prisma: async ({}, use, taskContext) => {
    const client = new PrismaClient({
      datasources: { db: { url: process.env.TEST_DATABASE_URL } },
    });
    await client.$connect();

    // onTestFinished runs after the test body regardless of pass/fail/skip
    // This is safer than afterEach which can be suppressed by early fixture teardown
    taskContext.onTestFinished(async () => {
      await client.$disconnect();
    });

    await use(client);
    // NOTE: do NOT disconnect here — onTestFinished handles it even if use() throws
  },

  transactionId: async ({ prisma }, use, taskContext) => {
    // Start a transaction and roll back after each test to keep DB clean
    let rollback!: () => Promise<void>;
    const txPromise = new Promise<PrismaClient>((resolve) => {
      prisma
        .$transaction(async (tx) => {
          resolve(tx as unknown as PrismaClient);
          // Hold the transaction open until rollback is triggered
          await new Promise<void>((res) => { rollback = res; });
          throw new Error('intentional rollback');
        })
        .catch(() => {/* swallow expected rollback error */});
    });

    const tx = await txPromise;
    const id = crypto.randomUUID();

    taskContext.onTestFinished(async () => { rollback(); });

    await use(id);
  },
});
```
Tradeoff: Using `onTestFinished()` inside Vitest fixtures guarantees cleanup even when the test body throws, when an assertion fails mid-fixture, or when `use()` is never called due to a setup error — but `onTestFinished()` callbacks execute after the test result is already recorded; if a cleanup operation itself throws (e.g., `client.$disconnect()` times out because the database is unreachable), the error is reported as a separate warning rather than a test failure, meaning a broken teardown will not fail the CI build and the resource leak will persist silently until the worker process is recycled.

**Pattern 120** — Jest `--coverage` with `collectCoverageFrom` scoped to pyramid tier via glob exclusion
```typescript
// jest.unit.config.ts
import type { Config } from 'jest';

const config: Config = {
  displayName: 'unit',
  testMatch: ['<rootDir>/src/**/*.unit.test.ts'],
  collectCoverage: true,
  collectCoverageFrom: [
    // Include all application source
    'src/**/*.ts',
    'src/**/*.tsx',
    // Exclude integration-tier entry points — their coverage is measured separately
    '!src/**/*.integration.ts',
    '!src/server.ts',           // Express app bootstrap — tested by integration tier
    '!src/db/migrations/**',    // DDL files — no unit test value
    '!src/**/*.d.ts',
    '!src/**/__generated__/**', // Code-gen output — not authored
  ],
  coverageThreshold: {
    global: { lines: 85, branches: 80, functions: 85 },
    // Critical business logic must be near-fully covered at the unit tier
    './src/pricing/**': { lines: 95, branches: 92 },
    './src/auth/**': { lines: 95, branches: 90 },
  },
  coverageReporters: ['text', 'lcov', 'json-summary'],
  // Write coverage to a tier-specific directory so integration coverage
  // can be merged separately in CI without overwriting unit coverage
  coverageDirectory: 'coverage/unit',
};

export default config;
```
Tradeoff: Scoping `collectCoverageFrom` to exclude integration-tier entry points and generated code ensures the unit tier's coverage gate reflects only code that unit tests can meaningfully exercise, preventing false positives from server bootstrap files that appear covered because integration tests happen to import them — but per-tier coverage directories require a merge step to produce an aggregate coverage report; if CI reports only the last-run tier's `coverage/` directory, the coverage badge reflects a partial view, and stakeholders may conclude that the project has lower overall coverage than it does, creating pressure to artificially inflate unit test count at the expense of the test pyramid balance.
