## Cycle 64 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 136** — Vitest `isolate: false` per-project override for stateless utility unit tests to eliminate per-file module re-evaluation overhead
```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    projects: [
      {
        // Unit tier: stateless pure functions; no singleton state
        // Disabling isolation removes per-file V8 context teardown/rebuild
        extends: true,
        test: {
          name: 'unit',
          include: ['src/**/*.unit.test.ts'],
          pool: 'threads',
          isolate: false,
          environment: 'node',
        },
      },
      {
        // Integration tier: keep full isolation to prevent DB connection leaks
        extends: true,
        test: {
          name: 'integration',
          include: ['src/**/*.int.test.ts'],
          pool: 'forks',
          isolate: true,
          environment: 'node',
          poolOptions: {
            forks: { singleFork: false },
          },
        },
      },
    ],
  },
});
```
Tradeoff: Disabling module isolation for the unit tier removes the per-file V8 context teardown and rebuild cycle, cutting total unit suite wall time by 25–40% on suites with 200+ test files that import shared utility modules — but any test file that mutates a module-level singleton (a cached config object, a logger instance, or a globally registered factory) will bleed state into subsequent files running in the same thread, causing order-dependent failures that only reproduce under parallel execution and disappear when files are run in isolation; auditing every unit test file for module-scope mutations is required before enabling `isolate: false` and should be enforced by a lint rule that flags mutable `let` declarations at module scope in test files.

**Pattern 137** — Jest `expect.extend()` with a typed `toMatchApiContract()` custom matcher that validates response shape against a Zod schema inline
```typescript
// test-utils/matchers/toMatchApiContract.ts
import { expect } from '@jest/globals';
import type { MatcherState } from 'expect';
import { z, ZodSchema, ZodError } from 'zod';

declare module 'expect' {
  interface AsymmetricMatchers {
    toMatchApiContract<T>(schema: ZodSchema<T>): void;
  }
  interface Matchers<R> {
    toMatchApiContract<T>(schema: ZodSchema<T>): R;
  }
}

expect.extend({
  toMatchApiContract<T>(
    this: MatcherState,
    received: unknown,
    schema: ZodSchema<T>,
  ) {
    const result = schema.safeParse(received);
    if (result.success) {
      return {
        pass: true,
        message: () =>
          `expected response NOT to match the provided Zod schema, but it did`,
      };
    }
    const formatted = (result.error as ZodError).issues
      .map((i) => `  • ${i.path.join('.')}: ${i.message}`)
      .join('\n');
    return {
      pass: false,
      message: () =>
        `Response does not match API contract:\n${formatted}\n\nReceived:\n  ${JSON.stringify(received, null, 2)}`,
    };
  },
});

// Usage in an integration test:
// const res = await request(app).get('/api/users/1').expect(200);
// expect(res.body).toMatchApiContract(UserResponseSchema);
```
Tradeoff: Embedding Zod schema validation inside a custom Jest matcher produces self-documenting assertion failures that list each field-level deviation with its JSON path and message, eliminating the need to manually decode `toMatchObject` diffs for deeply nested API shapes — but the matcher couples test infrastructure to the Zod version used in production source code; a Zod major version bump that changes `ZodError.issues` shape requires updating the matcher simultaneously with the production schema definitions, and teams that use different validation libraries (yup, valibot) cannot reuse the matcher without a library-specific wrapper for each.

**Pattern 138** — Playwright `test.use()` at `describe` scope combined with `storageState` snapshots to execute the same spec under multiple authenticated roles without browser re-launch
```typescript
// tests/e2e/dashboard.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'node:path';

const roles = [
  { name: 'admin',  storageState: path.resolve('.auth/admin.json') },
  { name: 'viewer', storageState: path.resolve('.auth/viewer.json') },
] as const;

for (const role of roles) {
  test.describe(`Dashboard as ${role.name}`, () => {
    test.use({ storageState: role.storageState });

    test('shows the summary widget', async ({ page }) => {
      await page.goto('/dashboard');
      await expect(page.getByTestId('summary-widget')).toBeVisible();
    });

    test('export button visibility', async ({ page }) => {
      await page.goto('/dashboard');
      const exportBtn = page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Export' });
      if (role.name === 'admin') {
        await expect(exportBtn).toBeVisible();
      } else {
        await expect(exportBtn).toBeHidden();
      }
    });
  });
}
```
Tradeoff: Scoping `test.use({ storageState })` to a `describe` block re-uses a pre-serialised authentication state for every test in that block, avoiding repeated login flows that each add 1–3 seconds of network and UI interaction time — but the `storageState` JSON files must be generated by a dedicated global setup script (`auth.setup.ts`) and committed or cached in CI; if the application rotates session tokens or changes cookie structure, the cached state silently becomes invalid and every role-scoped test will redirect to the login page, producing failures that appear as navigation assertions rather than authentication failures, which delays diagnosis unless a post-failure screenshot clearly shows the login page.

**Pattern 139** — Node.js `t.mock.timers.enable()` with `setInterval` and `tick()` for testing polling service intervals without real-time waits
```typescript
// src/polling-service.test.ts
import { test, describe } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { PollingService } from './polling-service.js';

describe('PollingService', () => {
  test('invokes the handler on each interval tick', (t) => {
    // Enable fake timers for setInterval and Date
    t.mock.timers.enable({ apis: ['setInterval', 'Date'], now: 0 });

    const handler = t.mock.fn<() => void>();
    const service = new PollingService({ intervalMs: 1_000, handler });

    service.start();
    assert.strictEqual(handler.mock.callCount(), 0, 'no immediate call on start');

    t.mock.timers.tick(1_000);
    assert.strictEqual(handler.mock.callCount(), 1, 'called after first interval');

    t.mock.timers.tick(3_000);
    assert.strictEqual(handler.mock.callCount(), 4, 'called 3 more times for 3 intervals');

    service.stop();
    t.mock.timers.tick(5_000);
    assert.strictEqual(handler.mock.callCount(), 4, 'no additional calls after stop');
    // Timers auto-restored at end of test via context-based mock API
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Using the Node.js built-in test runner's `t.mock.timers` API provides automatic cleanup when the test context is garbage-collected, which avoids the `afterEach(() => jest.useRealTimers())` boilerplate required by Jest — but `t.mock.timers.enable()` only intercepts timers created after the call; a `PollingService` constructor that creates an interval in its constructor body before `enable()` is called will use real timers, causing the test to hang; the service must use lazy interval creation (starting the interval in a `start()` method called after timer mocking is enabled) or the `enable()` call must be hoisted before the module is imported, which requires `t.mock.module()` combined with timer mocking.

**Pattern 140** — Vitest `vi.spyOn()` with `mockImplementationOnce()` chaining to simulate successive API retry responses without replacing the module permanently
```typescript
// src/api-client.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { fetchWithRetry } from './api-client.js';
import * as httpModule from './http.js';

describe('fetchWithRetry', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    vi.useFakeTimers();
  });

  afterEach(() => {
    vi.restoreAllMocks();
    vi.useRealTimers();
  });

  it('retries on 503 and succeeds on the third attempt', async () => {
    const spy = vi.spyOn(httpModule, 'get')
      .mockImplementationOnce(() => Promise.resolve({ status: 503, body: null }))
      .mockImplementationOnce(() => Promise.resolve({ status: 503, body: null }))
      .mockImplementationOnce(() => Promise.resolve({ status: 200, body: { id: 1 } }));

    const resultPromise = fetchWithRetry('/resource', { maxRetries: 3, backoffMs: 500 });

    // Advance fake timers to satisfy exponential-backoff delays
    await vi.runAllTimersAsync();

    const result = await resultPromise;
    expect(result).toEqual({ id: 1 });
    expect(spy).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
  });

  it('throws after exhausting all retries', async () => {
    vi.spyOn(httpModule, 'get').mockResolvedValue({ status: 503, body: null });

    const resultPromise = fetchWithRetry('/resource', { maxRetries: 2, backoffMs: 100 });
    await vi.runAllTimersAsync();

    await expect(resultPromise).rejects.toThrow('Max retries exceeded');
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Chaining `mockImplementationOnce()` calls models the exact sequence of responses returned by a retrying HTTP client, enabling precise assertion on call count and final result — but `vi.restoreAllMocks()` must be called in `afterEach` to restore the real implementation; if a test file mixes `spyOn` with `vi.mock()` at module scope, `restoreAllMocks` restores spies but does not undo module-level mocks, so test files that grow incrementally may accumulate both patterns and produce confusing state where some dependencies are real and others are permanently mocked throughout the file.

**Pattern 141** — Jest `test.each` with tagged template literals for property-based-style table-driven validation tests with descriptive failure names
```typescript
// src/validation/email-validator.test.ts
import { validateEmail } from './email-validator';

describe('validateEmail', () => {
  test.each`
    input                      | expected | reason
    ${'user@example.com'}      | ${true}  | ${'standard address'}
    ${'user+tag@sub.domain.io'}| ${true}  | ${'plus addressing with subdomain'}
    ${'USER@EXAMPLE.COM'}      | ${true}  | ${'uppercase domain normalised'}
    ${''}                      | ${false} | ${'empty string'}
    ${'@nodomain'}             | ${false} | ${'missing local part'}
    ${'nodomain@'}             | ${false} | ${'missing domain'}
    ${'double@@domain.com'}    | ${false} | ${'double at-sign'}
    ${'space in@domain.com'}   | ${false} | ${'space in local part'}
    ${'unicode@möbius.de'}     | ${true}  | ${'IDN domain accepted'}
  `('returns $expected for "$input" ($reason)', ({ input, expected }) => {
    expect(validateEmail(input)).toBe(expected);
  });

  test.each`
    input                    | errorCode
    ${''}                    | ${'EMPTY_INPUT'}
    ${'@nodomain'}           | ${'MISSING_LOCAL'}
    ${'nodomain@'}           | ${'MISSING_DOMAIN'}
  `('returns error code $errorCode for invalid input "$input"', ({ input, errorCode }) => {
    const result = validateEmail(input, { returnErrorCode: true });
    expect(result).toMatchObject({ valid: false, code: errorCode });
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Tagged template literal syntax in `test.each` produces human-readable test names that include the input value and reason column in the failure output, making it immediately clear which case failed without decoding an array index — but template literal tables must be maintained as raw source text; they cannot be generated programmatically from a JSON fixture or CSV file the way `test.each(array)` can, so suites with hundreds of test cases generated from external data sources must use the array form of `test.each` and accept less descriptive default test names unless a `name` column is added explicitly.

**Pattern 142** — Playwright `expect.poll()` replacing manual `waitForFunction` loops for assertion-first polling on slow asynchronous state changes
```typescript
// tests/e2e/job-status.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('long-running job reaches "completed" status', async ({ page, request }) => {
  // Trigger a background job via API (faster than UI interaction)
  const { jobId } = await request
    .post('/api/jobs', { data: { type: 'export', format: 'csv' } })
    .then((r) => r.json());

  await page.goto(`/jobs/${jobId}`);

  // expect.poll() re-evaluates the assertion every 500 ms for up to 30 s
  // without requiring a manual retry loop or a custom waitForFunction
  await expect
    .poll(
      async () => {
        const badge = page.getByTestId('job-status-badge');
        return badge.textContent();
      },
      {
        intervals: [500, 500, 1_000, 2_000],
        timeout: 30_000,
        message: `Job ${jobId} did not reach "Completed" within 30 s`,
      },
    )
    .toBe('Completed');

  // After status confirmed, assert the download link is present
  await expect(page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Download CSV' })).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `expect.poll()` integrates retry logic directly into the assertion call, producing a failure message that includes the last observed value and the assertion condition, which is far more informative than a generic `waitForFunction` timeout — but the `intervals` array is applied per-call and does not inherit the global `timeout` from `playwright.config.ts`, so tests that use `expect.poll()` with a longer timeout than the global default can silently extend CI run time if the polled condition never resolves; adding a test-level `test.setTimeout()` call that is at least 10 seconds longer than the `expect.poll()` timeout prevents the test context from being cancelled before the poll exhausts its timeout.

**Pattern 143** — Vitest `experimental.fsModuleCache` with a CI cache key derived from `package-lock.json` hash to persist transformed module cache across test runs
```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
import { createHash } from 'node:crypto';
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';

// Derive a stable cache key from the lockfile so cache is invalidated
// when any dependency is added, removed, or updated
const lockfileHash = createHash('sha256')
  .update(readFileSync('./package-lock.json'))
  .digest('hex')
  .slice(0, 12);

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    experimental: {
      // Persists Vite-transformed module cache to disk between runs
      // Reduces cold-start overhead on large dependency graphs by ~30-50%
      fsModuleCache: {
        enabled: true,
        cacheDir: `.vitest-cache/${lockfileHash}`,
      },
    },
    include: ['src/**/*.test.ts'],
    pool: 'threads',
  },
});
// In CI, cache the `.vitest-cache/<hash>` directory using the lockfile hash
// as the cache key. The hash suffix ensures automatic invalidation on
// dependency changes without requiring a manual cache-busting step.
```
Tradeoff: Persisting Vitest's Vite module transform cache to disk cuts the cold-start phase of large test suites with deep dependency graphs by 30–50% on subsequent runs, which is especially valuable in CI environments where the Node module cache is warm but Vite's transform cache is cold — but the `experimental.fsModuleCache` API is explicitly marked unstable, meaning it can be removed or have its configuration schema changed in a minor Vitest release without a deprecation period; projects that adopt it must pin the Vitest minor version and review release notes before upgrading, adding maintenance overhead that smaller teams may not be able to sustain.

**Pattern 144** — Jest `globalTeardown` with a typed `stopTestContainers` helper that reads container IDs from `global.__TEST_CONTAINERS__` set by `globalSetup`
```typescript
// test-infra/global-setup.ts
import { GenericContainer, StartedTestContainer } from 'testcontainers';

declare global {
  // eslint-disable-next-line no-var
  var __TEST_CONTAINERS__: StartedTestContainer[];
}

export default async function globalSetup(): Promise<void> {
  const postgres = await new GenericContainer('postgres:16-alpine')
    .withEnvironment({ POSTGRES_PASSWORD: 'test', POSTGRES_DB: 'testdb' })
    .withExposedPorts(5432)
    .start();

  const redis = await new GenericContainer('redis:7-alpine')
    .withExposedPorts(6379)
    .start();

  global.__TEST_CONTAINERS__ = [postgres, redis];

  // Inject dynamic ports as environment variables for worker processes
  process.env.TEST_POSTGRES_PORT = String(postgres.getMappedPort(5432));
  process.env.TEST_REDIS_PORT    = String(redis.getMappedPort(6379));
}

// test-infra/global-teardown.ts
export default async function globalTeardown(): Promise<void> {
  const containers = global.__TEST_CONTAINERS__ ?? [];
  await Promise.all(containers.map((c) => c.stop({ timeout: 10_000 })));
}
```
Tradeoff: Storing started container references on `global.__TEST_CONTAINERS__` in `globalSetup` and reading them in `globalTeardown` ensures containers are stopped even if tests fail midway, preventing orphaned Docker containers from accumulating on developer machines and CI runners — but Jest serialises and deserialises `global` state between the `globalSetup` and `globalTeardown` scripts using a snapshot mechanism that only preserves plain objects; if `StartedTestContainer` instances are not plain objects (they are class instances with methods), the references stored in `global.__TEST_CONTAINERS__` may be deserialised as empty objects in `globalTeardown`, causing `c.stop()` to throw a `TypeError`; the fix is to store only the container IDs as strings and reconstruct stop calls via the Docker API, or to use the `--runInBand` flag for the teardown step on CI.

**Pattern 145** — Node.js `--test-reporter=spec` with `--test-reporter-destination` piped to a TAP consumer for test result aggregation across heterogeneous runner processes
```typescript
// scripts/run-all-tests.ts
// Orchestrates unit (Vitest), integration (Node runner), and e2e (Playwright)
// using a shared TAP consumer for unified exit-code and summary reporting
import { spawn } from 'node:child_process';
import { createWriteStream } from 'node:fs';

interface RunConfig {
  label: string;
  cmd: string;
  args: string[];
}

const suites: RunConfig[] = [
  {
    label: 'unit',
    cmd: 'npx',
    args: ['vitest', 'run', '--reporter=tap'],
  },
  {
    label: 'integration',
    cmd: 'node',
    args: ['--test', '--test-reporter=tap', '--test-reporter-destination=stdout',
           'src/**/*.int.test.ts'],
  },
  {
    label: 'e2e',
    cmd: 'npx',
    args: ['playwright', 'test', '--reporter=tap'],
  },
];

async function runSuite({ label, cmd, args }: RunConfig): Promise<number> {
  const out = createWriteStream(`test-results/${label}.tap`);
  return new Promise((resolve) => {
    const proc = spawn(cmd, args, { stdio: ['ignore', 'pipe', 'inherit'] });
    proc.stdout.pipe(out);
    proc.on('close', resolve);
  });
}

const results = await Promise.all(suites.map(runSuite));
process.exit(results.some((c) => c !== 0) ? 1 : 0);
```
Tradeoff: Routing all three test tiers through TAP output enables a single TAP consumer (such as `tap-junit` or a custom aggregator) to merge results into a unified test report with consistent naming conventions, making it possible to track per-test flakiness across framework boundaries in a single CI artifact — but TAP output from Vitest, the Node.js built-in runner, and Playwright uses slightly different TAP versions and comment conventions, so a strict TAP 14 parser may reject output from one or more runners; using a lenient consumer like `tap-parser` with `{ strict: false }` is required, and the aggregated report will lose framework-specific metadata such as Playwright's video attachments and Vitest's coverage thresholds unless those are piped to separate artifact channels in parallel.

**Pattern 146** — Playwright `page.addLocatorHandler()` to dismiss dynamic cookie banners and modal interrupts without wrapping every test in a manual dismiss step
```typescript
// tests/e2e/fixtures/base.ts
import { test as base, expect } from '@playwright/test';

export const test = base.extend({
  page: async ({ page }, use) => {
    // Register a handler that fires whenever the cookie consent banner
    // becomes visible; dismisses it so it doesn't block test locators
    await page.addLocatorHandler(
      page.getByRole('dialog', { name: /cookie/i }),
      async (dialog) => {
        const acceptBtn = dialog.getByRole('button', { name: /accept all/i });
        if (await acceptBtn.isVisible({ timeout: 500 })) {
          await acceptBtn.click();
        }
      },
    );

    // Register a second handler for session-expiry modals
    await page.addLocatorHandler(
      page.getByTestId('session-expired-modal'),
      async () => {
        await page.getByRole('button', { name: /refresh session/i }).click();
        await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle');
      },
    );

    await use(page);
  },
});

export { expect };
// Tests import { test, expect } from './fixtures/base' instead of
// '@playwright/test' to get automatic interrupt handling for free
```
Tradeoff: `addLocatorHandler()` intercepts UI interrupts at the Playwright engine level without requiring each test to call a `dismissCookieBanner()` helper before every assertion, eliminating the most common source of timing-sensitive `ElementNotInteractable` failures on pages that show banners after navigation — but handlers registered via `addLocatorHandler()` fire asynchronously between Playwright's internal action steps and can trigger during a `waitForSelector` for a completely unrelated element if the banner appears at the same moment; on pages where the banner appearance is correlated with a specific navigation event (e.g., first-page-load only), a more targeted `page.once('load', dismissBanner)` handler is safer because it does not remain active for the entire page lifetime.

**Pattern 147** — Vitest `vi.mock()` with a factory returning a typed `vi.fn()` per export, combined with `beforeEach(() => vi.clearAllMocks())` for call-count isolation between tests
```typescript
// src/notifications/notifier.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach } from 'vitest';
import { sendWelcomeEmail } from './notifier.js';

// Factory-based module mock: each exported function is a typed vi.fn()
// so call counts, arguments, and return values are independently controllable
vi.mock('../email-client.js', () => ({
  sendEmail: vi.fn<
    [to: string, subject: string, html: string],
    Promise<{ messageId: string }>
  >().mockResolvedValue({ messageId: 'mock-id' }),
  getDeliveryStatus: vi.fn<[messageId: string], Promise<string>>()
    .mockResolvedValue('delivered'),
}));

import { sendEmail, getDeliveryStatus } from '../email-client.js';

describe('sendWelcomeEmail', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    vi.clearAllMocks();   // resets call counts; preserves mock implementations
  });

  it('sends exactly one email with the correct subject', async () => {
    await sendWelcomeEmail({ to: 'user@example.com', name: 'Alice' });
    expect(sendEmail).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
    expect(sendEmail).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
      'user@example.com',
      'Welcome to the platform, Alice!',
      expect.stringContaining('Alice'),
    );
  });

  it('does not check delivery status during the send flow', async () => {
    await sendWelcomeEmail({ to: 'user@example.com', name: 'Alice' });
    expect(getDeliveryStatus).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Calling `vi.clearAllMocks()` in `beforeEach` resets call histories between tests without restoring the mock implementation set in the factory, so tests within the same describe block start with clean call counts but retain the `mockResolvedValue` configured at the top level — but `vi.clearAllMocks()` does not reset implementations set via `mockImplementationOnce()` in a preceding test; if a test overrides the implementation for a single call and the next test relies on the factory default, the sequence must use `vi.resetAllMocks()` (which clears both call history and implementations) and re-apply the factory defaults in `beforeEach`, requiring more setup boilerplate per test file than `clearAllMocks`.

**Pattern 148** — Jest custom `testEnvironment` extending `jest-environment-node` to inject a per-test `AsyncLocalStorage` context for tracing test execution without global state
```typescript
// test-infra/traced-test-environment.ts
import { TestEnvironment } from 'jest-environment-node';
import type { EnvironmentContext, JestEnvironmentConfig } from '@jest/environment';
import { AsyncLocalStorage } from 'node:async_hooks';

interface TestTrace {
  testName: string;
  startMs: number;
  spans: Array<{ name: string; durationMs: number }>;
}

const traceStorage = new AsyncLocalStorage<TestTrace>();

export default class TracedTestEnvironment extends TestEnvironment {
  constructor(config: JestEnvironmentConfig, context: EnvironmentContext) {
    super(config, context);
    // Expose the storage on the global so production code under test can
    // record spans without importing the test environment directly
    this.global.__traceStorage = traceStorage;
  }

  override async handleTestEvent(event: { name: string; test?: { fullName: string } }) {
    if (event.name === 'test_start' && event.test) {
      traceStorage.enterWith({ testName: event.test.fullName, startMs: Date.now(), spans: [] });
    }
    if (event.name === 'test_done') {
      const trace = traceStorage.getStore();
      if (trace && trace.spans.length > 0) {
        // Emit trace to a local OTLP endpoint for developer observability tooling
        await fetch('http://localhost:4318/v1/traces', {
          method: 'POST',
          headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
          body: JSON.stringify(trace),
        }).catch(() => { /* non-fatal: observability must not affect test results */ });
      }
    }
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: Using `AsyncLocalStorage` inside a custom `testEnvironment` provides each test with an isolated trace context that is automatically bound to the test's async call chain — production code under test can record spans to `__traceStorage.getStore()` without any test-specific imports, keeping the source code clean — but `AsyncLocalStorage` context propagation is lost across `worker_threads` boundaries, so any test that spawns a worker thread (e.g., testing a Web Worker wrapper) will find `traceStorage.getStore()` returning `undefined` inside the worker; span recording must fall back gracefully to a no-op when the store is undefined, and the Jest config must set `testEnvironment: './test-infra/traced-test-environment'` globally, meaning the OTLP endpoint overhead is incurred for every test file even when no spans are recorded.

**Pattern 149** — Playwright `request` fixture with `extraHTTPHeaders` set to a per-test correlation ID for matching API calls in server logs during debugging
```typescript
// tests/e2e/fixtures/api-correlated.ts
import { test as base, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';

interface CorrelatedFixtures {
  correlationId: string;
}

export const test = base.extend<CorrelatedFixtures>({
  correlationId: async ({}, use, testInfo) => {
    // Derive a deterministic ID from the test title so the same test always
    // produces the same correlation ID in re-runs, aiding log correlation
    const id = `e2e-${Buffer.from(testInfo.titlePath.join('/')).toString('base64url').slice(0, 16)}`;
    await use(id);
  },

  // Override the request fixture to inject the correlation ID header globally
  request: async ({ playwright, correlationId }, use) => {
    const context = await playwright.request.newContext({
      extraHTTPHeaders: {
        'X-Correlation-Id': correlationId,
        'X-Test-Run-Id': process.env.CI_PIPELINE_ID ?? 'local',
      },
    });
    await use(context);
    await context.dispose();
  },

  // Override page to inject the same header into browser-initiated requests
  page: async ({ browser, correlationId }, use) => {
    const ctx = await browser.newContext({
      extraHTTPHeaders: { 'X-Correlation-Id': correlationId },
    });
    const page = await ctx.newPage();
    await use(page);
    await ctx.close();
  },
});

export { expect };
```
Tradeoff: Injecting a deterministic per-test correlation ID into all API and browser-initiated requests enables exact log filtering in structured logging systems (Datadog, Loki) to find every server-side event triggered by a specific Playwright test — but deriving the ID from the test title using base64url encoding produces IDs that silently change whenever a test is renamed, breaking historical log queries that reference the old ID; teams that rely on correlation IDs for post-incident test attribution should use a stable UUID seeded from the test's file path and title hash stored in a separate manifest, rather than deriving it inline, so renames are tracked explicitly.

**Pattern 150** — Node.js `t.plan()` combined with `t.test()` subtests to assert that a stream-processing pipeline emits the exact expected number of events without polling
```typescript
// src/stream-processor.test.ts
import { test, describe } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { Readable } from 'node:stream';
import { processEventStream } from './stream-processor.js';

describe('processEventStream', () => {
  test('emits exactly one processed event per valid input chunk', async (t) => {
    // t.plan() causes the test to fail if the number of completed subtests
    // does not equal the plan count, catching both over- and under-emission
    t.plan(3);

    const input = Readable.from([
      '{"type":"sale","amount":100}\n',
      '{"type":"sale","amount":200}\n',
      '{"type":"sale","amount":300}\n',
    ]);

    const processor = processEventStream(input);

    for await (const event of processor) {
      // Each emitted event spawns a subtest counted against t.plan(3)
      await t.test(`event amount=${event.amount}`, () => {
        assert.ok(event.amount > 0, 'amount must be positive');
        assert.ok(typeof event.processedAt === 'number', 'processedAt must be a number');
        assert.match(event.id, /^evt_[a-z0-9]{8}$/, 'id must match the expected format');
      });
    }
    // If the stream emits 2 or 4 events instead of 3, t.plan(3) fails the test
    // without requiring a manual assertion on a collected-results array length
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `t.plan()` combined with dynamically created subtests inside a `for await` loop provides a self-checking assertion that the stream emits precisely the expected number of events, which is impossible to express with a single `assert.equal(results.length, 3)` on a collected array because a stream that hangs after emitting two events would never resolve the array — but Node.js's `t.plan()` counts subtests rather than `assert` calls by default when subtests are present, so mixing top-level `assert` calls with subtests in the same test body requires careful counting to ensure the plan number reflects only subtests and not individual assertions; mixing both forms in the same `t.plan()` context is a common source of off-by-one plan failures.

---

### Community Gotchas

**G271** — Vitest `vi.mock()` hoisting causing TypeScript type errors when the mocked module's types are used in the same file before the mock factory is evaluated
Why this matters: Vitest transforms `vi.mock()` calls by hoisting them to the top of the module before any imports, which is required for the mock to intercept `import` statements. However, when a test file uses TypeScript types exported from the mocked module (e.g., `import type { UserService } from '../user-service'`) and also calls `vi.mock('../user-service', () => ({ ... }))`, TypeScript's language server resolves the types from the real module at type-check time, but at runtime the hoisted factory runs before the real module is ever evaluated. If the factory returns an object that is missing properties on the real type, TypeScript does not catch the shape mismatch because `vi.fn()` is typed as `any` by default; the type-safe version requires casting the factory return to `Partial<typeof import('../user-service')>` and using `vi.Mocked<UserService>` on the spy variables. Teams discover this gap when a real module property is renamed during a refactor — the mock factory continues returning the old property name, TypeScript finds no error because the factory is untyped, and the tests pass with a stale mock that no longer reflects the real interface.
Fix: Use `vi.mocked()` to wrap imports from mocked modules in test files, which applies `jest.Mocked<T>` typing. Configure a Vitest ESLint plugin rule that requires mock factory return values to be typed as `Partial<typeof import('...')>` or use `satisfies` to constrain the factory return. Add a CI step that runs `tsc --noEmit` with `strict: true` after `vi.mock` factories are introduced or modified.

**G272** — Playwright `toHaveURL()` matcher passing when the page has been redirected to an error URL that also contains the expected substring
Why this matters: Playwright's `toHaveURL()` matcher accepts a string, regex, or URL object and checks whether the current `page.url()` matches. When called with a plain string like `expect(page).toHaveURL('/dashboard')`, Playwright performs a substring match — not an equality check — so a redirect to `/error?from=/dashboard&code=403` satisfies `toHaveURL('/dashboard')` because the string `/dashboard` appears in the query parameter. Tests for successful navigation to protected routes appear to pass after a failed login because the error redirect URL contains the intended destination as a parameter. The failure mode is particularly insidious in test suites that run with reused `storageState` that has expired: all navigation tests pass the URL assertion while actually landing on error pages, and only screenshot-on-failure evidence reveals the discrepancy.
Fix: Use regex anchors in `toHaveURL()` assertions: `expect(page).toHaveURL(/^.*\/dashboard(\?|$)/)` to assert that `/dashboard` appears as the path rather than anywhere in the URL. For stricter enforcement, create a helper `assertPath(page, path)` that calls `expect(new URL(page.url()).pathname).toBe(path)` and use it in place of `toHaveURL` for all navigation assertions in the suite.

**G273** — Jest `--runInBand` silently causing `beforeAll` database setup to be skipped when used alongside `--testPathPattern` filtering that excludes the setup file
Why this matters: In suites that use a separate `db.setup.test.ts` file to run migrations and seed data before integration tests, `--runInBand` ensures all test files run sequentially in the same process, which is required for the shared database state set up in `db.setup.test.ts` to persist across subsequent test files. When a developer adds `--testPathPattern=user` to run only user-related tests during development, Jest filters out `db.setup.test.ts` because the pattern does not match the setup filename. The setup file is silently skipped, the database is uninitialized, and every test in the matching files fails with a connection or missing-table error. Because the same tests pass in CI (where the full suite runs without a filter), the developer assumes the failures are environment-specific and spends time debugging the database configuration rather than the test filter.
Fix: Move database setup into Jest's `globalSetup` rather than a test file so it runs unconditionally before the test runner applies `--testPathPattern` filtering. Alternatively, name the setup file with a prefix that sorts lexicographically before all other test files (e.g., `__setup__/db.setup.test.ts`) and document in `TESTING.md` that `--testPathPattern` must always include `__setup__` when filtering integration tests.

**G274** — Node.js built-in test runner reporting exit code 0 when all test files are filtered out by `--test-name-pattern` combined with a missing `--test` flag
Why this matters: Running `node --test-name-pattern="payment flow"` without the `--test` flag causes Node.js to treat the remaining arguments as a script name rather than a test pattern, silently executing no tests and exiting with code 0. On some Node.js minor versions the pattern flag is accepted but matched against an empty test registry, again producing zero tests run and exit code 0. CI pipelines that use `node --test-name-pattern` to run subset test re-runs after a failure rely on the non-zero exit code to detect missing test matches; when exit code 0 is returned for zero-test runs, the pipeline marks the re-run step as passed without executing any assertions, and flaky tests appear to have been verified when they were actually never run.
Fix: Always pair `--test-name-pattern` with the `--test` flag: `node --test --test-name-pattern="payment flow" src/**/*.test.ts`. Add a CI post-test step that reads the `tap` output from `--test-reporter=tap` and fails the build if the `# tests 0` line appears in the TAP summary, using a shell guard such as `grep -q '^# tests [^0]' test-results/output.tap || (echo "ERROR: zero tests ran" && exit 1)`.

**G275** — Vitest `coverage.thresholds` enforcement silently ignored when the `coverage.provider` is set to `'v8'` and the test run exits with a non-zero code due to a failing test before coverage is written
Why this matters: Vitest writes coverage data to disk only after all test files have finished executing. When a test file throws an unhandled error (not an assertion failure, but a module-level exception such as a missing environment variable or an unresolved import) early in the run, Vitest may terminate the worker pool before the coverage report is flushed, producing an incomplete `.v8` coverage file or no file at all. When `coverage.thresholds` is configured, Vitest evaluates thresholds against the written coverage data; if no data was written, the threshold check is skipped entirely rather than treating missing coverage as a threshold violation. CI pipelines that use Vitest's exit code to gate deployments receive a non-zero exit code from the test failure but not from a coverage threshold violation, so the deployment is correctly blocked — but subsequent coverage dashboards show a phantom 100% coverage (or no coverage at all) because the last written coverage data is from the previous successful run, misleading the team about actual coverage levels.
Fix: Add an explicit check in the CI pipeline that verifies the coverage report file exists and is newer than the test run start time before reading threshold results: `test -f coverage/coverage-final.json && find coverage -name 'coverage-final.json' -newer .vitest-run-start || exit 1`. Configure `coverage.reportOnFailure: true` (available in Vitest 1.4+) to force coverage report emission even when tests fail, ensuring thresholds are evaluated against real (partial) data rather than stale data.

## Cycle 66 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 150** — Playwright worker-scoped fixture for single-server startup shared across all tests in a worker
```typescript
// tests/fixtures/server.fixture.ts
import { test as base, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { createServer } from '../helpers/test-server.js';
import type { Server } from 'http';

type WorkerFixtures = {
  httpServer: { url: string; server: Server };
};

export const test = base.extend<{}, WorkerFixtures>({
  httpServer: [
    async ({}, use) => {
      // Worker-scoped: starts once per worker process, not per test
      const server = await createServer({ port: 0 });
      const { port } = server.address() as { port: number };
      const url = `http://localhost:${port}`;
      await use({ url, server });
      // Teardown after all tests in this worker finish
      await new Promise<void>((resolve) => server.close(() => resolve()));
    },
    { scope: 'worker' },
  ],
});

export { expect };

// tests/api-health.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from './fixtures/server.fixture.js';

test('GET /health returns 200', async ({ httpServer, request }) => {
  const res = await request.get(`${httpServer.url}/health`);
  expect(res.status()).toBe(200);
});
```
Tradeoff: Worker-scoped fixtures start the HTTP server once per Playwright worker rather than once per test, reducing startup overhead from O(n) to O(workers), but they prevent per-test server state isolation — any test that mutates global server state (registered routes, in-memory stores) will corrupt subsequent tests in the same worker unless the fixture explicitly resets that state in the `use()` body.

**Pattern 151** — Playwright `{ auto: true }` fixture for per-test request tracing without test signature pollution
```typescript
// tests/fixtures/trace.fixture.ts
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';
import { randomUUID } from 'crypto';

type AutoFixtures = {
  _traceId: string; // underscore prefix signals internal-only
};

export const test = base.extend<AutoFixtures>({
  _traceId: [
    async ({ page }, use, testInfo) => {
      const traceId = randomUUID();
      // Inject trace ID into all outgoing browser requests for this test
      await page.setExtraHTTPHeaders({ 'x-trace-id': traceId });
      // Write to test attachments for log correlation
      await testInfo.attach('trace-id', {
        body: traceId,
        contentType: 'text/plain',
      });
      await use(traceId);
      // No teardown needed — page context is discarded after test
    },
    { auto: true, scope: 'test' },
  ],
});

// tests/checkout.spec.ts — _traceId never appears in test signatures
import { test } from './fixtures/trace.fixture.js';

test('checkout flow completes', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  // All requests from this page automatically carry x-trace-id header
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay' }).click();
});
```
Tradeoff: Auto-fixtures inject cross-cutting concerns (trace IDs, authentication tokens, timing headers) into every test without cluttering test function signatures, but they are harder to discover during code review because the fixture is invisible in the test body — developers debugging unexpected header injection must search for `auto: true` fixtures in the fixture inheritance chain rather than inspecting the test's parameter list.

**Pattern 152** — Jest `moduleNameMapper` with ordered rules to stub static assets and path aliases without runtime errors
```javascript
// jest.config.js
const { defineConfig } = require('jest');

module.exports = defineConfig({
  moduleNameMapper: {
    // 1. Static assets: match before path aliases to avoid alias resolving .png
    '^.+\\.(png|jpg|jpeg|gif|svg|webp|ico)$': '<rootDir>/src/__mocks__/fileMock.js',
    '^.+\\.(css|scss|sass|less)$': 'identity-obj-proxy',
    // 2. Path aliases: must come after asset rules (most specific first)
    '^@/components/(.*)$': '<rootDir>/src/components/$1',
    '^@/utils/(.*)$': '<rootDir>/src/utils/$1',
    '^@/hooks/(.*)$': '<rootDir>/src/hooks/$1',
    // 3. Generic alias fallback: catches remaining @/ imports
    '^@/(.*)$': '<rootDir>/src/$1',
  },
  // src/__mocks__/fileMock.js exports: module.exports = 'test-file-stub';
});
```
Tradeoff: Ordering `moduleNameMapper` rules from most-specific (asset extensions) to least-specific (generic alias fallback) prevents Jest from accidentally resolving an SVG import through the `@/` alias handler and attempting to parse it as a module, but it requires maintaining a fixed rule ordering contract in the config — adding a new rule at the wrong position breaks resolution silently because Jest applies mappers in array order and stops at the first match, not the best match.

**Pattern 153** — Jest `mergeConfig` for environment-specific overrides without duplicating the base configuration
```typescript
// jest.config.base.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'jest';

export const baseConfig = defineConfig({
  testEnvironment: 'node',
  transform: { '^.+\\.tsx?$': ['ts-jest', { isolatedModules: true }] },
  coverageProvider: 'v8',
  collectCoverageFrom: ['src/**/*.ts', '!src/**/*.d.ts'],
  coverageThreshold: { global: { lines: 80, branches: 75 } },
});

// jest.config.ts (unit tests)
import { defineConfig, mergeConfig } from 'jest';
import { baseConfig } from './jest.config.base.js';

export default mergeConfig(baseConfig, defineConfig({
  testMatch: ['<rootDir>/src/**/*.unit.test.ts'],
  testTimeout: 5_000,
}));

// jest.integration.config.ts
import { defineConfig, mergeConfig } from 'jest';
import { baseConfig } from './jest.config.base.js';

export default mergeConfig(baseConfig, defineConfig({
  testMatch: ['<rootDir>/src/**/*.integration.test.ts'],
  testTimeout: 30_000,
  globalSetup: '<rootDir>/jest.integration.setup.ts',
  globalTeardown: '<rootDir>/jest.integration.teardown.ts',
  coverageThreshold: { global: { lines: 60 } }, // lower for integration
}));
```
Tradeoff: `mergeConfig` performs a deep merge where arrays (like `coverageThreshold.global`) from the override replace arrays from the base rather than merging them, which is the desired behavior for thresholds but means `collectCoverageFrom` patterns in an override silently discard any base patterns — explicit comment annotations are necessary to document which fields are intentionally replaced versus additive.

**Pattern 154** — Node.js `--test-global-setup` for one-time database container lifecycle outside the test worker pool
```javascript
// test-global-setup.mjs
import { GenericContainer } from 'testcontainers';

export async function globalSetup() {
  // Runs in the main thread before any workers start
  const container = await new GenericContainer('postgres:16-alpine')
    .withEnvironment({ POSTGRES_PASSWORD: 'test', POSTGRES_DB: 'testdb' })
    .withExposedPorts(5432)
    .start();

  const port = container.getMappedPort(5432);
  // Communicate the port to workers via environment variable
  process.env.TEST_PG_PORT = String(port);
  // Store reference for teardown — must be on globalThis in same process
  globalThis.__PG_CONTAINER__ = container;
}

export async function globalTeardown() {
  // Runs in the main thread after all workers finish
  if (globalThis.__PG_CONTAINER__) {
    await globalThis.__PG_CONTAINER__.stop();
  }
}

// Run with:
// node --test --test-global-setup=./test-global-setup.mjs src/**/*.test.mjs
```
Tradeoff: Node.js `--test-global-setup` runs in the main thread and can write to `process.env` before workers start, making the database port available to all test files through environment variables without any IPC channel, but the global setup file must export named `globalSetup` and `globalTeardown` functions — if the file uses a default export or misspells the export name, Node.js silently skips the setup without warning and tests fail with connection errors that appear unrelated to the missing container.

**Pattern 155** — Node.js `run()` API with `isolation: 'none'` and `concurrency` cap for fast in-process integration tests
```javascript
// scripts/run-integration.mjs
import { run } from 'node:test';
import { spec } from 'node:test/reporters';
import path from 'node:path';
import { glob } from 'glob';

const files = await glob('src/**/*.integration.test.mjs', {
  absolute: true,
  cwd: path.resolve(import.meta.dirname, '..'),
});

const stream = run({
  files,
  // isolation: 'none' runs all files in the same process — fastest but
  // module-level state leaks between test files
  isolation: 'none',
  // Cap concurrency to avoid database connection pool exhaustion
  concurrency: 4,
  timeout: 60_000,
  coverage: false, // coverage is computed in the separate CI coverage job
});

stream.on('test:fail', () => {
  process.exitCode = 1;
});

// Pipe to human-readable spec reporter
stream.compose(spec).pipe(process.stdout);
```
Tradeoff: `isolation: 'none'` eliminates per-file worker startup overhead (significant for suites with hundreds of files) and allows shared module-level state such as a single connection pool instance, but a module-level `import` side-effect in one test file that patches a global (e.g., `globalThis.fetch = mockFetch`) persists into subsequent test files executed in the same process unless explicitly undone, making test order coupling a constant risk that requires lint rules or a shared `afterEach` reset guard.

**Pattern 156** — Node.js `--test-random-seed` with deterministic replay for catching order-dependent test failures in CI
```javascript
// package.json
{
  "scripts": {
    "test:unit": "node --test --test-randomize src/**/*.test.mjs",
    "test:unit:replay": "node --test --test-randomize --test-random-seed=$SEED src/**/*.test.mjs"
  }
}

// .github/workflows/test.yml (excerpt)
// - name: Run randomized tests
//   id: unit-tests
//   run: |
//     SEED=$(shuf -i 1-999999 -n 1)
//     echo "SEED=$SEED" >> $GITHUB_OUTPUT
//     npm run test:unit -- --test-random-seed=$SEED 2>&1 | tee test-output.txt
//     exit ${PIPESTATUS[0]}
//
// - name: Save seed as artifact on failure
//   if: failure()
//   run: echo "Replay with: SEED=${{ steps.unit-tests.outputs.SEED }} npm run test:unit:replay"

// In test file — document order assumptions explicitly
import { describe, test, before } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

// Bad: implicit ordering assumption (breaks under randomization)
// test('create user', ...) — sets global user id
// test('delete user', ...) — reads global user id set by previous test

// Good: each test is self-sufficient
describe('UserService', () => {
  test('creates then deletes a user atomically', async (t) => {
    const { id } = await createUser({ name: 'Test' });
    const deleted = await deleteUser(id);
    assert.equal(deleted.id, id);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Passing `--test-random-seed` with a logged seed value allows deterministic replay of any CI failure caused by test ordering, converting a hard-to-reproduce Heisenbug into a reproducible run, but `--test-randomize` randomizes test file execution order within the runner rather than individual `test()` call order within a single file — intra-file ordering dependencies require `t.test()` subtests with explicit `await` chaining to guarantee sequence, not just top-level randomization.

**Pattern 157** — Vitest `pool: 'threads'` with `poolOptions.threads.singleThread` for CPU-bound transformation tests
```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // Switch from default 'forks' to 'threads' for tests that do CPU work
    // (parsers, compilers, data transformations) rather than I/O
    pool: 'threads',
    poolOptions: {
      threads: {
        // Use a single shared worker for tests that are not parallelizable
        // due to WASM module singleton or global registry initialization
        singleThread: false,
        // Limit worker count on CI runners with restricted CPU quota
        maxThreads: process.env.CI ? 2 : undefined,
        minThreads: 1,
        // Prevent worker from being reused across test files — trades
        // speed for stronger isolation of module-level side effects
        isolate: true,
      },
    },
    // Worker threads share memory; disable if tests use SharedArrayBuffer
    // without explicit synchronization
  },
});

// Example: CPU-bound test that benefits from thread pool
// src/parser/markdown.test.ts
import { describe, test, expect } from 'vitest';
import { parseMarkdown } from '../parser/markdown.js';

describe('parseMarkdown', () => {
  test('parses 10k lines without stack overflow', () => {
    const input = Array.from({ length: 10_000 }, (_, i) => `# Heading ${i}`).join('\n');
    const result = parseMarkdown(input);
    expect(result.headings).toHaveLength(10_000);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Vitest's `pool: 'threads'` uses Node.js Worker Threads which share a V8 heap within the process, making memory-bound test suites faster than the default `pool: 'forks'` (which spawns separate processes), but Worker Threads cannot safely use native addons that maintain C++ thread-local state (e.g., some database drivers, bcrypt) — those tests must remain on `pool: 'forks'` or be isolated with a separate Vitest project configuration.

**Pattern 158** — Vitest `test.dir` restriction combined with `include` glob to prevent accidental test discovery outside the source boundary
```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
import path from 'path';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // Restrict file discovery to src/ — prevents Vitest from scanning
    // node_modules, dist/, or generated/ directories for *.test.ts files
    dir: path.resolve(__dirname, 'src'),
    include: ['**/*.{unit,spec}.test.ts'],
    exclude: [
      '**/node_modules/**',
      '**/dist/**',
      '**/__generated__/**',
      // Exclude fixture files that happen to match *.test.ts naming
      '**/fixtures/**',
    ],
    // Explicitly set root to prevent config from resolving relative to CWD
    // when invoked from a monorepo workspace script
    root: __dirname,
  },
});

// tsconfig.json (aligned path root)
// {
//   "compilerOptions": {
//     "rootDir": "src",
//     "outDir": "dist"
//   },
//   "include": ["src/**/*"]
// }
```
Tradeoff: Setting `test.dir` to `src/` dramatically reduces Vitest's file system traversal time on monorepos with large `node_modules` or `dist/` directories, but it silently excludes test files placed outside `src/` (such as `tests/` or `e2e/`) without any warning — teams that place integration tests in a sibling directory to `src/` must either add a second Vitest project config or widen `test.dir` to the workspace root and rely solely on `include`/`exclude` globs for filtering.

**Pattern 159** — Jest `setupFilesAfterEnv` with `jest-extended` matchers and global `afterEach` timer reset guard
```javascript
// jest.setup-after-env.js
const matchers = require('jest-extended');
expect.extend(matchers);

// Global guard: reset real timers after every test to prevent fake-timer
// leakage from a test that calls jest.useFakeTimers() without cleanup
afterEach(() => {
  jest.useRealTimers();
});

// Global guard: clear all mocks after every test to prevent call-count
// bleed-through when a test uses jest.spyOn() without restoring
afterEach(() => {
  jest.clearAllMocks();
});

// jest.config.js
const { defineConfig } = require('jest');
module.exports = defineConfig({
  setupFilesAfterEnv: ['<rootDir>/jest.setup-after-env.js'],
  // Note: setupFiles (pre-framework) is for env vars and global polyfills;
  // setupFilesAfterEnv (post-framework) is for matchers and lifecycle hooks
});

// Usage in tests — jest-extended matchers available globally
describe('OrderService.calculateTotal', () => {
  test('returns a positive finite number', () => {
    const total = calculateTotal([{ price: 10, qty: 2 }]);
    expect(total).toBePositive();
    expect(total).toBeFinite();
    expect(total).toBeWithin(0, 10_000);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Placing `jest.useRealTimers()` and `jest.clearAllMocks()` in `setupFilesAfterEnv` as global `afterEach` hooks eliminates an entire class of cross-test timer and mock pollution bugs without requiring per-test cleanup, but `jest.clearAllMocks()` resets call counts and instances while leaving the mock implementation in place — tests that rely on `mockReturnValue` set in a `beforeAll` or `describe`-level setup will silently lose their return value if `jest.resetAllMocks()` (which also resets implementations) is used instead, causing the mock to return `undefined` and producing misleading assertion failures.

**Pattern 160** — Playwright `{ option: true }` fixture for per-project base URL and auth token configuration
```typescript
// tests/fixtures/options.fixture.ts
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';

type TestOptions = {
  apiBaseUrl: string;
  adminToken: string;
};

export const test = base.extend<TestOptions>({
  // Declare as option — value comes from playwright.config.ts projects,
  // not from the fixture setup function
  apiBaseUrl: [
    async ({}, use) => { await use('http://localhost:3000'); },
    { option: true },
  ],
  adminToken: [
    async ({}, use) => { await use(''); },
    { option: true },
  ],
});

// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  projects: [
    {
      name: 'staging',
      use: {
        apiBaseUrl: 'https://staging.example.com',
        adminToken: process.env.STAGING_ADMIN_TOKEN ?? '',
      },
    },
    {
      name: 'local',
      use: {
        apiBaseUrl: 'http://localhost:3000',
        adminToken: 'dev-token',
      },
    },
  ],
});

// tests/api/users.spec.ts
import { test } from '../fixtures/options.fixture.js';
test('GET /users returns 200', async ({ request, apiBaseUrl, adminToken }) => {
  const res = await request.get(`${apiBaseUrl}/users`, {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${adminToken}` },
  });
  expect(res.ok()).toBeTruthy();
});
```
Tradeoff: Fixture options centralize per-environment configuration (base URLs, tokens) in `playwright.config.ts` projects so the same test file runs against staging and local without modification, but fixture option values are not validated at config-parse time — a missing environment variable that produces an empty `adminToken` string passes TypeScript type checking and silently sends unauthenticated requests, requiring explicit runtime guards (`if (!adminToken) test.skip()`) in fixtures that need authenticated access.

**Pattern 161** — Jest per-path `coverageThreshold` to enforce stricter coverage on critical payment modules
```javascript
// jest.config.js
const { defineConfig } = require('jest');

module.exports = defineConfig({
  collectCoverage: true,
  coverageProvider: 'v8',
  collectCoverageFrom: ['src/**/*.ts', '!src/**/*.d.ts', '!src/**/index.ts'],
  coverageThreshold: {
    // Global floor: coarser enforcement for the whole codebase
    global: {
      lines: 70,
      branches: 65,
      functions: 70,
      statements: 70,
    },
    // Per-path strict enforcement: payment and auth modules require 95%+
    './src/payments/': {
      lines: 95,
      branches: 90,
      functions: 95,
      statements: 95,
    },
    './src/auth/': {
      lines: 90,
      branches: 85,
      functions: 90,
      statements: 90,
    },
    // Single-file threshold: critical validator must have full branch coverage
    './src/payments/card-validator.ts': {
      branches: 100,
    },
  },
});
```
Tradeoff: Per-path `coverageThreshold` enforces higher standards on security-critical and revenue-critical modules without requiring the entire codebase to meet the same bar, which unblocks teams that are incrementally improving coverage without gating on legacy modules — but per-path thresholds are evaluated against the collected coverage data only if the path pattern matches at least one file, so a renamed file (e.g., `card-validator.ts` → `card-validator.service.ts`) silently removes the 100% branch-coverage requirement without any CI failure.

**Pattern 162** — Node.js `/* node:coverage disable */` annotation to exclude generated boilerplate from coverage metrics
```javascript
// src/proto/generated/user_pb.js
// Auto-generated by protoc-gen-js — do not edit manually

/* node:coverage disable */
// Entire generated file is excluded from coverage instrumentation.
// Coverage of this file would be meaningless (it tests proto tooling,
// not application logic) and inflates uncovered branch counts.

export class UserRequest {
  constructor(fields) {
    this.id = fields.id ?? '';
    this.email = fields.email ?? '';
  }
  toJSON() {
    return { id: this.id, email: this.email };
  }
}

export class UserResponse {
  constructor(fields) {
    this.user = fields.user ?? null;
    this.error = fields.error ?? '';
  }
}
/* node:coverage enable */

// For inline exclusion of specific unreachable branches (not whole files):
// src/utils/exhaustive-check.ts
export function assertNever(value: never): never {
  /* node:coverage ignore next */
  throw new Error(`Unhandled variant: ${JSON.stringify(value)}`);
}
```
Tradeoff: `/* node:coverage disable */` is a Node.js-native V8 coverage comment (available from Node.js 22+) that excludes generated or unreachable code from branch and line metrics without requiring a separate `.nycrc` or Istanbul `/* istanbul ignore */` comment, keeping generated files out of coverage dashboards — but the annotation only works with Node.js's built-in coverage (`--experimental-test-coverage`); projects using Istanbul/nyc or Vitest's V8 provider must still use `/* istanbul ignore */` or `/* v8 ignore */` comments respectively, requiring dual annotations in codebases that run multiple coverage tools.

**Pattern 163** — Jest `globalSetup` with `jest-testcontainers` exporting connection strings via `process.env` for full-suite isolation
```typescript
// jest.globalsetup.ts
import {
  DockerComposeEnvironment,
  Wait,
} from 'testcontainers';

let environment: Awaited<ReturnType<DockerComposeEnvironment['up']>>;

module.exports = async function globalSetup() {
  environment = await new DockerComposeEnvironment(
    './docker',
    'docker-compose.test.yml'
  )
    .withWaitStrategy('postgres', Wait.forHealthCheck())
    .withWaitStrategy('redis', Wait.forHealthCheck())
    .up();

  const pgPort = environment.getContainer('postgres').getMappedPort(5432);
  const redisPort = environment.getContainer('redis').getMappedPort(6379);

  // Serialize connection info to environment variables for Jest workers
  process.env.TEST_PG_URL = `postgresql://test:test@localhost:${pgPort}/testdb`;
  process.env.TEST_REDIS_URL = `redis://localhost:${redisPort}`;

  // Store on globalThis for teardown — only accessible in same process
  (global as any).__TEST_ENV__ = environment;
};

// jest.globalteardown.ts
module.exports = async function globalTeardown() {
  if ((global as any).__TEST_ENV__) {
    await (global as any).__TEST_ENV__.down({ removeVolumes: true });
  }
};
```
Tradeoff: `jest globalSetup` with Docker Compose starts all dependent services once before the full test suite and passes port-mapped URLs through `process.env`, which avoids per-test container churn and ensures clean service state at suite boundaries — but `process.env` mutations made inside `globalSetup` are not propagated to Jest workers on Windows when using `jest-circus` with `--runInBand: false` because each worker is a separate child process that inherits the environment at spawn time, requiring the `globalSetup` to write connection strings to a `.env.test.local` file that each worker reads on startup via `dotenv`.

**Pattern 164** — Playwright `request` context fixture with typed API client wrapper for schema-validated API integration tests
```typescript
// tests/fixtures/api-client.fixture.ts
import { test as base, APIRequestContext } from '@playwright/test';
import { z } from 'zod';

const UserSchema = z.object({
  id: z.string().uuid(),
  email: z.string().email(),
  role: z.enum(['admin', 'user', 'viewer']),
  createdAt: z.string().datetime(),
});

type User = z.infer<typeof UserSchema>;

class ApiClient {
  constructor(private req: APIRequestContext, private baseUrl: string) {}

  async createUser(payload: Partial<User>): Promise<User> {
    const res = await this.req.post(`${this.baseUrl}/users`, { data: payload });
    if (!res.ok()) throw new Error(`POST /users failed: ${res.status()}`);
    return UserSchema.parse(await res.json());
  }

  async getUser(id: string): Promise<User> {
    const res = await this.req.get(`${this.baseUrl}/users/${id}`);
    if (!res.ok()) throw new Error(`GET /users/${id} failed: ${res.status()}`);
    return UserSchema.parse(await res.json());
  }
}

export const test = base.extend<{ api: ApiClient }>({
  api: async ({ request }, use) => {
    const client = new ApiClient(request, process.env.API_BASE_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3000');
    await use(client);
  },
});

// tests/users.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from './fixtures/api-client.fixture.js';

test('created user is retrievable by ID', async ({ api }) => {
  const created = await api.createUser({ email: 'test@example.com', role: 'user' });
  const fetched = await api.getUser(created.id);
  expect(fetched.email).toBe(created.email);
});
```
Tradeoff: Wrapping Playwright's `request` fixture in a typed API client with Zod schema validation turns API integration tests into both behavioral and schema contract tests — a response that changes shape (e.g., `createdAt` renamed to `created_at`) fails at `UserSchema.parse()` with a precise field-level error rather than a downstream `undefined` dereference, but Zod parse overhead on large response arrays (hundreds of objects) adds measurable latency to bulk-endpoint tests and may require `z.array(UserSchema).parse()` replaced with `z.array(UserSchema.partial()).parse()` for partial-response pagination tests.

### Community Gotchas

**G276** — Playwright `{ auto: true }` fixture teardown running after the test's explicit fixture teardown when the auto-fixture depends on a test-scoped fixture that is already torn down
Why this matters: When an auto-fixture depends on a Playwright built-in like `page` and performs teardown after `await use()`, its teardown runs in dependency reverse order — meaning it runs after all dependent fixtures have torn down. If the auto-fixture attempts to read `page.url()` or call `page.evaluate()` during its teardown phase (e.g., to log the final URL to an audit trail), the `page` object has already been closed by its own teardown and throws `Target page, context or browser has been closed`. The failure appears in the test report as a teardown error on a passing test, which confuses the team because the test body itself succeeded. The root cause is that auto-fixtures share the same dependency-order teardown sequence as explicit fixtures — they are not special-cased to run before or after explicit fixtures.
Fix: Move post-test page inspection into a `testInfo.attachments.push()` call inside the `use()` body (before `await use(value)`) using `page.on('response', ...)` listeners that accumulate data during the test, rather than inspecting page state in the teardown phase. If teardown must inspect the page, redesign the auto-fixture to depend on `testInfo` (a test-scoped fixture that remains valid during teardown) and store page state to `testInfo` during the `use()` phase.

**G277** — Node.js `--test-global-setup` silently skipping when the setup module uses a default export instead of named exports
Why this matters: Node.js `--test-global-setup` requires the target module to export named `globalSetup` and/or `globalTeardown` functions. A module that uses `export default { globalSetup, globalTeardown }` or `module.exports = async function globalSetup() {}` (a default-exported function named `globalSetup`) does not satisfy the named export requirement. Node.js does not throw an error or warning when the setup module is loaded but the named exports are missing — it simply skips the setup phase, starts the test workers with an uninitialized environment, and all tests that depend on the global setup (database containers, environment variables) fail with connection errors. Developers waste significant time checking container configurations before discovering the export shape is incorrect.
Fix: Always use explicit named exports in global setup files: `export async function globalSetup() { ... }` and `export async function globalTeardown() { ... }`. Add a CI validation step that imports the global setup module and asserts `typeof module.globalSetup === 'function'` before running the full test suite. Document the required export shape in `CONTRIBUTING.md` with a working example to prevent recurrence.

**G278** — Jest `moduleNameMapper` later rules never matching because an earlier broader pattern consumes all import paths first
Why this matters: Jest applies `moduleNameMapper` rules in the order they appear in the configuration array, stopping at the first match. A common configuration mistake places a generic alias rule like `'^@/(.*)$': '<rootDir>/src/$1'` before specific rules like `'^@/mocks/(.*)$': '<rootDir>/src/__mocks__/$1'`. When a test imports `@/mocks/db`, the generic rule matches first and resolves the path to `src/mocks/db`, ignoring the specific mock override entirely. The real module is loaded instead of the mock, causing tests to hit real database connections. Because Jest logs which module was resolved (only in `--verbose` mode), teams debugging connection errors in unit tests rarely think to inspect the mapper ordering and instead investigate the mock implementation itself.
Fix: Order `moduleNameMapper` from most-specific to least-specific: specific path prefixes (`^@/mocks/`, `^@/fixtures/`) before generic aliases (`^@/(.*)`). Add a Jest configuration linting script that checks for any `moduleNameMapper` entry whose regex is a prefix-match superset of a later entry — this can be implemented as a short Node.js script that runs on `postinstall` and reports ordering conflicts before they cause test failures.

**G279** — Vitest `pool: 'threads'` causing worker crash when tests import native Node.js addons compiled for the main thread's V8 context
Why this matters: Worker Threads in Node.js share the same V8 isolate as the main thread but each worker has its own JavaScript context. Native addons (`.node` files compiled with N-API or NAN) that store V8 handles in static C++ variables — a pattern common in older database drivers like `node-sqlite3` or certain image processing libraries — hold references tied to the main thread's V8 context. When Vitest spawns a Worker Thread and the test file imports such an addon, the addon's static initializer runs in the worker's context but accesses the main thread's cached handles, causing a segfault or `FATAL ERROR: v8::HandleScope::HandleScope Entering the V8 API without proper locking in place`. The failure crashes the worker process silently (from the test runner's perspective) and Vitest reports the test file as timing out rather than failing, making the root cause invisible.
Fix: Identify native addon dependencies with `node -e "const m = require('your-addon'); console.log(m)"` — addons that work without error in the main process but crash in worker threads indicate V8 handle caching issues. Move test files that import problematic addons to a separate Vitest project configured with `pool: 'forks'` (the default) while keeping CPU-bound pure-JS tests on `pool: 'threads'`. Add a comment in the project config explaining which addons require forks isolation to prevent future contributors from consolidating the projects.

**G280** — Jest per-path `coverageThreshold` silently disabling when the path pattern matches zero files after a module rename or directory restructure
Why this matters: Jest evaluates per-path coverage thresholds by matching the threshold key as a glob against the list of files in the coverage report. If a threshold key like `'./src/payments/'` is configured and the payments module is later moved to `'./src/billing/payments/'` during a refactoring, the threshold key no longer matches any file. Jest treats an unmatched per-path threshold as a non-issue and does not report a warning or error — the global threshold still applies to the files, but the higher per-path threshold is silently bypassed. A 100% branch coverage requirement on `card-validator.ts` configured as `'./src/payments/card-validator.ts'` becomes `0%` effective requirement after the file is moved, and CI continues to pass even when new uncovered branches are introduced.
Fix: Add a post-coverage validation script that cross-references every key in `coverageThreshold` (excluding `global`) against the list of files in `coverage/coverage-final.json` and exits non-zero if any threshold key matches zero files: `node scripts/validate-coverage-thresholds.js`. Run this script as a required CI step after `jest --coverage`. Alternatively, use path tokens like `<rootDir>` in threshold keys and enable a pre-commit hook that runs `grep -r 'coverageThreshold' jest.config.js` and prompts the developer to verify path matches whenever a file is moved.
