## Cycle 65 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 150** — Vitest `workspace` config with per-project `environment` to run browser and Node tests in a single `vitest` invocation
```typescript
// vitest.workspace.ts
import { defineWorkspace } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineWorkspace([
  {
    extends: './vite.config.ts',
    test: {
      name: 'unit',
      environment: 'node',
      include: ['src/**/*.unit.test.ts'],
      globals: true,
    },
  },
  {
    extends: './vite.config.ts',
    test: {
      name: 'browser',
      browser: {
        enabled: true,
        name: 'chromium',
        provider: 'playwright',
        headless: true,
      },
      include: ['src/**/*.browser.test.ts'],
    },
  },
  {
    extends: './vite.config.ts',
    test: {
      name: 'integration',
      environment: 'node',
      include: ['src/**/*.integration.test.ts'],
      pool: 'forks',
      poolOptions: { forks: { singleFork: true } },
    },
  },
]);
```
Tradeoff: A single `vitest` invocation runs all three environments in parallel and shares the module graph cache, reducing cold-start time by up to 40% compared to three separate `vitest --project` invocations, but the shared Vite dev server means a plugin error in one project config propagates as a startup failure to all projects in the same workspace run, making it harder to isolate which project caused the breakage without inspecting per-project logs.

**Pattern 151** — Jest `moduleNameMapper` with `__mocks__` directory co-location for auto-mocking third-party SDK calls without `jest.mock()` in each file
```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import type { Config } from 'jest';

const config: Config = {
  // Map the real AWS SDK clients to co-located manual mocks
  moduleNameMapper: {
    '^@aws-sdk/client-s3$': '<rootDir>/src/__mocks__/@aws-sdk/client-s3.ts',
    '^@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb$': '<rootDir>/src/__mocks__/@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb.ts',
  },
  setupFilesAfterFramework: ['<rootDir>/jest.setup.ts'],
};

export default config;

// src/__mocks__/@aws-sdk/client-s3.ts
export const S3Client = jest.fn().mockImplementation(() => ({
  send: jest.fn().mockResolvedValue({ Body: Buffer.from('mock-content') }),
}));
export const GetObjectCommand = jest.fn();
export const PutObjectCommand = jest.fn();
export const DeleteObjectCommand = jest.fn();
```
Tradeoff: Auto-mocking via `moduleNameMapper` eliminates the `jest.mock('@aws-sdk/client-s3')` boilerplate in every unit test file and guarantees consistent mock shapes across the suite, but when a new SDK command is added to the real library the manual mock silently omits it — tests continue to pass against the stale mock shape while production code throws `TypeError: client.send is not a function` for the new command, so the mock directory must be treated as a versioned contract and audited whenever SDK dependencies are upgraded.

**Pattern 152** — Playwright `route.fulfill()` with recorded HAR fixture for deterministic third-party API integration tests
```typescript
// tests/checkout.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';
import { join } from 'node:path';

test.describe('Checkout with mocked payment gateway', () => {
  test.beforeEach(async ({ page }) => {
    await page.route('**/api.stripe.com/**', async (route) => {
      const url = new URL(route.request().url());
      const fixtureName = url.pathname.replace(/\//g, '_').replace(/^_/, '');
      const fixturePath = join(__dirname, 'fixtures', 'stripe', `${fixtureName}.json`);
      const body = readFileSync(fixturePath, 'utf-8');
      await route.fulfill({
        status: 200,
        contentType: 'application/json',
        body,
      });
    });
  });

  test('completes a card payment and shows confirmation', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/checkout');
    await page.fill('[data-testid="card-number"]', '4242 4242 4242 4242');
    await page.fill('[data-testid="card-expiry"]', '12/26');
    await page.fill('[data-testid="card-cvc"]', '123');
    await page.click('[data-testid="submit-payment"]');
    await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="confirmation-banner"]')).toBeVisible();
    await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="order-id"]')).toHaveText(/^ord_[a-z0-9]{16}$/);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Using static JSON fixtures via `route.fulfill()` makes checkout tests fully deterministic and runnable offline without Stripe test-mode credentials, but fixture files must be regenerated whenever the payment gateway changes its response shape — a divergence that is invisible until a production deploy surfaces a breaking API change that tests never caught because they were asserting against a stale recorded response.

**Pattern 153** — Node.js `mock.module()` with ESM `import()` lazy loading to mock modules imported inside function bodies rather than at module top level
```typescript
// src/notifier.ts
export async function sendAlert(message: string): Promise<void> {
  // Lazy import inside the function body — top-level vi.mock() cannot intercept this
  const { SESClient, SendEmailCommand } = await import('@aws-sdk/client-ses');
  const client = new SESClient({ region: 'us-east-1' });
  await client.send(new SendEmailCommand({ /* ... */ }));
}

// src/notifier.test.ts
import { test, mock, beforeEach, afterEach } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

let sendSpy: ReturnType<typeof mock.fn>;

beforeEach(async () => {
  sendSpy = mock.fn(async () => ({ MessageId: 'mock-id-001' }));
  // mock.module replaces the specifier in the ESM registry before the lazy import resolves
  await mock.module('@aws-sdk/client-ses', {
    namedExports: {
      SESClient: mock.fn(() => ({ send: sendSpy })),
      SendEmailCommand: mock.fn(),
    },
  });
});

afterEach(() => mock.reset());

test('sendAlert calls SES with the correct message body', async () => {
  const { sendAlert } = await import('./notifier.js');
  await sendAlert('disk usage critical');
  assert.strictEqual(sendSpy.mock.callCount(), 1);
  const [cmd] = sendSpy.mock.calls[0].arguments;
  assert.ok(cmd.input.Message.Body.Text.Data.includes('disk usage critical'));
});
```
Tradeoff: `mock.module()` intercepts ESM dynamic imports by replacing the module registry entry before the lazy `import()` resolves, which is the only mechanism that works when modules are conditionally or lazily loaded inside function bodies, but `mock.module()` requires `await` in ESM contexts meaning every test using it must be `async` and the module under test must be re-imported via a fresh dynamic `import()` inside each test body to pick up the mock — this breaks tree-shaking and can cause subtle state leaks if the module caches instances at import time.

**Pattern 154** — Vitest `vi.stubEnv()` with `unstubAllEnvs()` in `afterEach` for isolated environment variable testing without `process.env` mutation leaks
```typescript
// src/config.ts
export function getDatabaseUrl(): string {
  const url = process.env.DATABASE_URL;
  if (!url) throw new Error('DATABASE_URL is required');
  return url;
}

export function isProduction(): boolean {
  return process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production';
}

// src/config.test.ts
import { describe, test, expect, vi, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { getDatabaseUrl, isProduction } from './config.js';

afterEach(() => {
  vi.unstubAllEnvs();
});

describe('getDatabaseUrl', () => {
  test('returns the value of DATABASE_URL when set', () => {
    vi.stubEnv('DATABASE_URL', 'postgres://localhost:5432/testdb');
    expect(getDatabaseUrl()).toBe('postgres://localhost:5432/testdb');
  });

  test('throws when DATABASE_URL is absent', () => {
    vi.stubEnv('DATABASE_URL', '');
    expect(() => getDatabaseUrl()).toThrow('DATABASE_URL is required');
  });
});

describe('isProduction', () => {
  test('returns true when NODE_ENV is production', () => {
    vi.stubEnv('NODE_ENV', 'production');
    expect(isProduction()).toBe(true);
  });

  test('returns false when NODE_ENV is test', () => {
    vi.stubEnv('NODE_ENV', 'test');
    expect(isProduction()).toBe(false);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `vi.stubEnv()` snapshots the current `process.env` value and restores it atomically after the test making environment-variable tests safe to run in parallel without cross-test `process.env` pollution, but `vi.stubEnv()` can only stub variables to string values — it cannot stub a variable to `undefined` (it uses empty string as a proxy), so tests that exercise the "variable is unset" code path must adjust the production guard to treat empty string as absent, or use `delete process.env.VARNAME` manually with explicit cleanup, breaking the atomic restore guarantee.

**Pattern 155** — Playwright `expect.poll()` with custom `message` and `intervals` for asserting eventually-consistent server state without arbitrary `waitForTimeout` sleeps
```typescript
// tests/background-job.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { createApiClient } from './helpers/api-client.js';

test('invoice PDF is generated within 10 seconds of order placement', async ({ page, request }) => {
  const api = createApiClient(request);

  const { orderId } = await api.post('/orders', {
    items: [{ sku: 'WIDGET-001', qty: 2 }],
    payment: { method: 'card', token: 'tok_visa' },
  });

  // Poll with exponential back-off — no arbitrary sleeps
  await expect
    .poll(
      async () => {
        const { documents } = await api.get(`/orders/${orderId}/documents`);
        return documents.find((d: { type: string }) => d.type === 'invoice_pdf')?.status ?? 'pending';
      },
      {
        message: `Invoice PDF for order ${orderId} did not reach 'ready' status within 10 s`,
        intervals: [500, 500, 1000, 1000, 2000, 2000, 3000],
        timeout: 10_000,
      }
    )
    .toBe('ready');

  const { documents } = await api.get(`/orders/${orderId}/documents`);
  const invoice = documents.find((d: { type: string }) => d.type === 'invoice_pdf');
  expect(invoice.downloadUrl).toMatch(/^https:\/\/cdn\./);
});
```
Tradeoff: `expect.poll()` with a custom `intervals` array uses exponential back-off to reduce API call frequency as wait time grows, keeping network noise low during long operations, but the `intervals` array is consumed in order and then the last interval is repeated indefinitely until `timeout` — a misconfigured intervals sum that is less than the expected operation duration causes the poll to exhaust intervals early and hammer the API at the last interval's rate rather than backing off further, defeating the back-off intent.

**Pattern 156** — Jest `--shard` with a custom `testSequencer` using the LPT algorithm to produce balanced CI matrix shards by estimated duration
```typescript
// jest-shard-sequencer.ts
import Sequencer from '@jest/test-sequencer';
import type { Test } from '@jest/test-result';

export default class ShardBalancingSequencer extends Sequencer {
  /**
   * Distributes tests across shards by accumulated duration (LPT algorithm)
   * so each shard has roughly equal total estimated runtime rather than
   * equal test-file count.
   */
  shard(
    tests: Test[],
    { shardIndex, shardCount }: { shardIndex: number; shardCount: number }
  ): Test[] {
    const withDuration = tests.map((test) => ({
      test,
      duration: typeof test.duration === 'number' && test.duration > 0
        ? test.duration
        : 1000, // default when cache is cold
    }));

    // Sort descending so the largest tests are distributed first
    withDuration.sort((a, b) => b.duration - a.duration);

    const buckets: (typeof withDuration)[] = Array.from({ length: shardCount }, () => []);
    const bucketTotals = new Array<number>(shardCount).fill(0);

    for (const item of withDuration) {
      const minIdx = bucketTotals.indexOf(Math.min(...bucketTotals));
      buckets[minIdx].push(item);
      bucketTotals[minIdx] += item.duration;
    }

    return buckets[shardIndex - 1].map((b) => b.test);
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: The LPT bin-packing algorithm produces shards within ±15% of the mean runtime on stable suites, reducing CI wall-clock time by up to 30% compared to file-count sharding, but the sequencer relies on `test.duration` data from the Jest cache — on the first run after a cache clear all tests receive the default 1000 ms estimate and shards revert to file-count distribution, silently losing the balance benefit until the cache is rebuilt over one full run.

**Pattern 157** — Vitest `onTestFailed` hook with in-process structured log flushing and DOM snapshot capture for rich failure diagnostics
```typescript
// vitest.setup.ts
import { onTestFailed, onTestFinished } from 'vitest';
import { writeFileSync, mkdirSync } from 'node:fs';
import { join } from 'node:path';
import { testLogBuffer } from './src/test-utils/log-buffer.js';

export function setupDiagnostics() {
  onTestFailed((result) => {
    const dir = join(
      process.cwd(),
      'test-failures',
      result.task.name.replace(/\W+/g, '-')
    );
    mkdirSync(dir, { recursive: true });

    // Flush buffered structured logs captured during this test
    const logs = testLogBuffer.flush();
    writeFileSync(join(dir, 'test-logs.json'), JSON.stringify(logs, null, 2));

    // Persist a DOM snapshot if the test set one on globalThis
    if (typeof globalThis.__CURRENT_DOM_SNAPSHOT__ === 'string') {
      writeFileSync(join(dir, 'dom-snapshot.html'), globalThis.__CURRENT_DOM_SNAPSHOT__);
    }

    console.error(`[vitest] Failure artifacts written to ${dir}`);
  });

  onTestFinished(() => {
    testLogBuffer.clear();
    globalThis.__CURRENT_DOM_SNAPSHOT__ = undefined;
  });
}
```
Tradeoff: `onTestFailed` fires synchronously inside the worker process that ran the failing test, giving it access to in-process state (log buffers, DOM snapshots, in-memory caches) that a post-run reporter cannot reach, but writing to disk inside `onTestFailed` is a blocking synchronous operation — large payloads (multi-MB DOM snapshots or long log buffers) can cause the worker to appear hung to the main process, triggering a worker timeout that masks the original test failure in CI output.

**Pattern 158** — Node.js `--test-global-setup` module exporting `globalSetup` and `globalTeardown` for TestContainers lifecycle outside the test worker pool
```typescript
// test-global-setup.ts
import { PostgreSqlContainer, StartedPostgreSqlContainer } from '@testcontainers/postgresql';
import { execSync } from 'node:child_process';

declare global {
  var __PG_CONTAINER__: StartedPostgreSqlContainer | undefined;
}

export async function globalSetup(): Promise<void> {
  const container = await new PostgreSqlContainer('postgres:16-alpine')
    .withDatabase('testdb')
    .withUsername('testuser')
    .withPassword('testpass')
    .withExposedPorts(5432)
    .start();

  process.env.DATABASE_URL =
    `postgresql://testuser:testpass@${container.getHost()}:${container.getMappedPort(5432)}/testdb`;

  // Run migrations against the ephemeral container before any test worker starts
  execSync('npx prisma migrate deploy', { stdio: 'inherit', env: process.env });

  globalThis.__PG_CONTAINER__ = container;
  console.log(`[setup] Postgres container started on port ${container.getMappedPort(5432)}`);
}

export async function globalTeardown(): Promise<void> {
  await globalThis.__PG_CONTAINER__?.stop();
  console.log('[teardown] Postgres container stopped');
}
```
Tradeoff: Running TestContainers in `globalSetup` starts the container once per CI job rather than once per test file, reducing integration suite time by 60–80% on large schemas, but `globalSetup` runs in a separate process from the test workers so `process.env.DATABASE_URL` written there is not automatically visible to workers on Windows — it must be passed through a temp file or globalThis coordination object read during `setupFiles`, adding platform-specific logic that silently breaks when the setup module is refactored.

**Pattern 159** — Playwright `test.step()` with `box: true` to collapse noisy helper sub-steps in the HTML report while keeping full trace detail
```typescript
// tests/helpers/auth-steps.ts
import type { Page } from '@playwright/test';
import { test } from '@playwright/test';

/**
 * Performs a full login flow as a boxed step — the HTML report shows
 * "Login as admin" as a single atomic entry; the trace viewer expands
 * each sub-action for debugging.
 */
export async function loginAsAdmin(page: Page): Promise<void> {
  await test.step('Login as admin', async () => {
    await page.goto('/auth/login');
    await page.fill('[data-testid="email"]', 'admin@example.com');
    await page.fill('[data-testid="password"]', process.env.ADMIN_PASSWORD ?? 'test-password');
    await page.click('[data-testid="submit"]');
    await page.waitForURL('/dashboard');
  }, { box: true });
}

// tests/admin-panel.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { loginAsAdmin } from './helpers/auth-steps.js';

test('admin can deactivate a user account', async ({ page }) => {
  await loginAsAdmin(page);
  await page.goto('/admin/users');
  await page.click('[data-testid="user-row-42"] [data-testid="deactivate-btn"]');
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="toast"]')).toHaveText('User deactivated');
});
```
Tradeoff: `{ box: true }` on `test.step()` collapses the step into a single line in the HTML report, reducing noise when login or navigation helpers are called in dozens of tests, but a failure inside a boxed step is attributed to the box step itself rather than the specific inner action that failed — the HTML report shows "Login as admin" as the failure point with no inline sub-step detail, requiring a mandatory trace-viewer round-trip to identify whether it was the `fill`, the `click`, or the `waitForURL` that timed out.

**Pattern 160** — Vitest Istanbul coverage with `/* istanbul ignore next -- @preserve */` and an ESLint rule enforcing justification comments on every ignore directive
```typescript
// src/feature-flags.ts
export function getFeatureFlag(name: string): boolean {
  const value = process.env[`FEATURE_${name.toUpperCase()}`];

  // This branch only executes in a live canary environment where the env var
  // is injected at runtime; it is untestable in the unit suite by design.
  /* istanbul ignore next -- @preserve */
  if (value === undefined && process.env.CANARY_MODE === 'true') {
    return fetchRemoteFlag(name);
  }

  return value === '1' || value === 'true';
}

// eslint-plugin-local/rules/no-bare-istanbul-ignore.ts
import type { Rule } from 'eslint';

export const noBareIstanbulIgnore: Rule.RuleModule = {
  meta: { type: 'suggestion', fixable: null },
  create(context) {
    return {
      Program() {
        const src = context.getSourceCode();
        for (const comment of src.getAllComments()) {
          if (
            comment.value.includes('istanbul ignore') &&
            !comment.value.includes('-- @preserve')
          ) {
            context.report({
              loc: comment.loc!,
              message: 'istanbul ignore comments must include a -- @preserve justification',
            });
          }
        }
      },
    };
  },
};
```
Tradeoff: Requiring `-- @preserve` on every `/* istanbul ignore */` directive creates an auditable trail of intentionally excluded branches and prevents naked ignore comments from silently masking coverage gaps, but the `@preserve` keyword is also required to survive esbuild's comment-stripping during the Vitest/Istanbul transformation pipeline — without it the directive is stripped before Istanbul's instrumentation pass, the branch is counted as uncovered, and thresholds fail in CI with no error message linking the failure to the stripped comment.

**Pattern 161** — Jest `workerIdleMemoryLimit` with `--logHeapUsage` flag to diagnose and cap memory-bloating test files without increasing CI runner size
```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import type { Config } from 'jest';

const config: Config = {
  // Recycle the worker process when heap exceeds 300 MB after a test file completes,
  // preventing a single memory-heavy file from OOM-killing the whole suite
  workerIdleMemoryLimit: '300MB',

  // Limit workers to 50% of CPUs to leave headroom for container memory pressure
  maxWorkers: '50%',

  // Increase the grace period for workers writing large snapshots
  workerGracefulExitTimeout: 5000,

  testEnvironment: 'node',
  transform: {
    '^.+\\.tsx?$': ['ts-jest', { isolatedModules: true }],
  },
};

export default config;

// To identify which test files bloat memory, run:
// jest --config jest.config.ts --logHeapUsage --runInBand 2>&1 | grep -E 'PASS|FAIL|heap'
// Files emitting heap > 250 MB should be split or have their large imports mocked
```
Tradeoff: `workerIdleMemoryLimit` recycles workers that exceed the heap cap between test files, preventing one memory-hungry file from accumulating heap across the suite and causing OOM kills on underpowered CI runners, but worker recycling clears the module cache and requires the next test file to re-require all dependencies from scratch — the cap should be set high enough to avoid unnecessary recycling rather than as low as possible, since excessive recycling increases suite runtime by 5–15%.

**Pattern 162** — Playwright multi-browser `projects` with `testMatch` to run the full suite on Chromium and smoke tests only on Firefox, WebKit, and mobile
```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  testDir: './tests',
  fullyParallel: true,
  retries: process.env.CI ? 2 : 0,
  reporter: process.env.CI
    ? [['html', { open: 'never' }], ['github']]
    : 'list',

  projects: [
    // Full suite on Chromium (primary development browser)
    {
      name: 'chromium',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] },
      testMatch: '**/*.spec.ts',
    },
    // Smoke-only on Firefox and WebKit
    {
      name: 'firefox-smoke',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Firefox'] },
      testMatch: '**/*.smoke.spec.ts',
    },
    {
      name: 'webkit-smoke',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Safari'] },
      testMatch: '**/*.smoke.spec.ts',
    },
    // Mobile viewport layout regression — smoke only
    {
      name: 'mobile-chrome',
      use: { ...devices['Pixel 5'] },
      testMatch: '**/*.smoke.spec.ts',
    },
  ],
});
```
Tradeoff: Running only `*.smoke.spec.ts` on Firefox, WebKit, and mobile reduces cross-browser CI time while still catching browser-specific rendering regressions on critical paths, but engineers must manually maintain the `*.smoke.spec.ts` naming convention — a new test added with `.spec.ts` that exercises browser-specific layout behaviour is silently excluded from Firefox and WebKit runs, allowing cross-browser regressions to reach production undetected.

**Pattern 163** — Node.js `t.mock.method()` with explicit `restore()` in a deferred cleanup for precise spy teardown in deeply nested test trees
```typescript
// src/cache.test.ts
import { test, describe } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { Redis } from 'ioredis';
import { CacheService } from './cache.js';

describe('CacheService', () => {
  test('get() returns cached value without calling Redis again', async (t) => {
    const client = new Redis({ lazyConnect: true });
    const cache = new CacheService(client);

    // Spy on Redis GET and control its return value per-call
    const getRedisSpy = t.mock.method(client, 'get', async (key: string) => {
      if (key === 'user:42') return JSON.stringify({ id: 42, name: 'Alice' });
      return null;
    });

    const first = await cache.get('user:42');
    const second = await cache.get('user:42');

    assert.deepStrictEqual(first, { id: 42, name: 'Alice' });
    assert.deepStrictEqual(second, { id: 42, name: 'Alice' });

    // The in-process cache should serve the second call without hitting Redis
    assert.strictEqual(
      getRedisSpy.mock.callCount(), 1,
      'Redis.get should be called exactly once — second call must be served from memory cache'
    );

    // Explicit restore for clarity in deeply nested suites
    getRedisSpy.mock.restore();
    await client.disconnect();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `t.mock.method()` binds the spy to the test context `t` and auto-restores when the test completes, eliminating the need for an explicit `afterEach(() => spy.mockRestore())` that is easy to forget in deeply nested `describe` blocks, but auto-restore fires only when the test context's cleanup queue is drained — if the test throws an unhandled promise rejection before `t.mock.method()` registers the cleanup, the restore is never called and the spy persists on the object across subsequent tests in the same module, causing call-count assertions in unrelated tests to fail with inflated counts.

**Pattern 164** — Vitest `pool: 'vmForks'` for integration tests that mutate module-level singletons without needing `isolate: false` trade-offs
```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // Default pool for unit tests: threads (fast, shared memory)
    pool: 'threads',
    workspace: [
      {
        test: {
          name: 'integration',
          include: ['src/**/*.integration.test.ts'],
          // vmForks: each test file gets a separate V8 VM context in a forked process.
          // Module-level singletons (connection pools, config caches) are re-initialized
          // per file, preventing cross-file state leaks without manual reset in afterAll.
          pool: 'vmForks',
          poolOptions: {
            vmForks: {
              // Limit concurrent forks to respect Postgres max_connections
              maxForks: 2,
              // Reuse the VM context within a file (shared state inside one file is intentional)
              reuseVm: true,
            },
          },
          env: { NODE_ENV: 'test' },
        },
      },
    ],
  },
});
```
Tradeoff: `pool: 'vmForks'` gives each integration test file its own forked process with a fresh V8 VM context, eliminating singleton state leaks without the `isolate: false` complexity or manual `afterAll(() => pool.end())` boilerplate, but forking a process has a 200–400 ms startup cost per test file versus ~5 ms for a thread worker — on a suite with 80 integration test files this adds 16–32 seconds to CI wall time, so `maxForks` must be tuned to balance connection pool saturation against parallelism rather than defaulting to the CPU-count ceiling.

### Community Gotchas

**G276** — Vitest `vi.useFakeTimers()` not advancing `setInterval` callbacks registered inside `useEffect` when the component is rendered before `vi.useFakeTimers()` is called
Why this matters: When a React component registers a `setInterval` inside a `useEffect`, the interval is created during the first render triggered by `renderHook` or `render`. If `vi.useFakeTimers()` is called after `render` (e.g., in a `beforeEach` that runs after the component has already been rendered in a describe-level setup), the real `setInterval` from the Node.js global was already captured by the component's closure before Vitest replaced it with a fake. Calling `vi.advanceTimersByTime(5000)` advances only the fake timer registry, which does not include the real `setInterval` handle held by the component, so the interval callback never fires. Tests assert that the component's state has updated after 5 seconds but find it unchanged, and the failure is attributed to the component logic rather than the timer setup order.
Fix: Always call `vi.useFakeTimers()` in a `beforeAll` or at the very top of the `beforeEach` that runs before any component rendering, and pair it with `vi.useRealTimers()` in `afterAll`. If `render` is called at describe scope in a shared fixture, restructure the suite so rendering happens inside individual test bodies where `vi.useFakeTimers()` is guaranteed to be in effect before the first render.

**G277** — Playwright `storageState` saved from one `baseURL` being silently accepted but ineffective when tests run against a different `baseURL` in a PR preview environment
Why this matters: Playwright's `storageState` serializes cookies with their `domain` attribute as recorded during the auth setup project. When `baseURL` is `https://staging.example.com` during the setup run but `https://review-pr-123.example.com` during a PR preview run, the saved cookies carry `domain=staging.example.com` and are not sent by the browser for requests to the preview origin. Playwright does not warn that the loaded storage state contains no cookies matching the current origin — the state is loaded silently, the session is unauthenticated, and every test that depends on auth redirects to the login page. Because the redirect happens before any `expect` call, the failure message is a URL mismatch (`/login` vs `/dashboard`) that looks like a navigation bug rather than an auth state issue.
Fix: Add a `test.beforeAll` in the auth setup project that asserts `page.url()` contains `baseURL` after loading storage state, failing fast with a descriptive message if the domain does not match. Alternatively, generate `storageState` dynamically in each CI environment by running the auth setup project with the environment-specific `baseURL` rather than committing a static state file to the repository.

**G278** — Jest `collectCoverageFrom` glob that omits newly added directories causing the global threshold to appear met when large untested modules are excluded from the denominator
Why this matters: If a new service module (`src/services/billing.ts`) is added but the `collectCoverageFrom` glob was written as `src/handlers/**/*.ts` (matching only the handlers directory), the billing module is silently excluded from the coverage denominator. The reported 85% branch coverage is computed only over files that are covered by existing tests, inflating the metric and allowing uncovered business logic to pass coverage gates undetected. Teams discover the gap only when a production bug surfaces in a module that tests reported as fully covered but was never included in the coverage calculation.
Fix: Set `collectCoverageFrom` to match all source files (`src/**/*.{ts,tsx}`) with an explicit exclusion list for generated files, test utilities, and type declaration files. Add a CI step that asserts `coveredFiles / totalMatchedFiles > 0.9` using the `json-summary` reporter output to catch cases where the glob silently excludes large untested areas.

**G279** — Node.js test runner `t.assert.snapshot()` generating divergent snapshot files when tests run on Windows and Linux CI due to `\r\n` vs `\n` line ending differences in serialized output
Why this matters: Node.js's built-in snapshot testing serializes test values to text using `util.inspect` and writes them to `.snapshot` files. On Windows, `util.inspect` output for objects containing strings with embedded newlines may produce `\r\n` line endings depending on the platform's `os.EOL` setting and the Node.js version. When a developer runs `node --test --test-update-snapshots` on Windows and commits the resulting `.snapshot` file, CI running on Linux compares the same serialized output (which uses `\n`) against the Windows-generated snapshot (which contains `\r\n` in embedded string values). The comparison fails with a diff that shows invisible `\r` characters, and the error `snapshot mismatch` gives no indication that the root cause is line ending normalization rather than a behavioral change in the code.
Fix: Add a `.gitattributes` rule `*.snapshot text eol=lf` to force LF line endings on snapshot files regardless of the committing platform. Alternatively, run `node --test --test-update-snapshots` exclusively in CI on Linux and commit the resulting snapshots from the CI environment, ensuring all snapshots are generated with consistent `os.EOL`.

**G280** — Playwright component testing `mount()` failing silently when a CSS module references a `url()` asset outside the CT bundle, causing intermittent pixel-diff flakiness on subsequent runs
Why this matters: Playwright's experimental component testing runner bundles the component under test using Vite. If the component's CSS module contains `url('./fonts/Inter.woff2')` and the font file lives in `public/fonts/` (served by the dev server at runtime but not copied into the CT bundle directory), Vite logs a warning but does not throw an error — the bundle is emitted with a broken asset reference. The `mount()` call succeeds, the component renders, and visual snapshot assertions pass on the first run. On subsequent runs on a different machine or in CI, the broken font reference causes an FOUT (Flash of Unstyled Text) that makes text metrics differ by a few pixels, causing pixel-level screenshot comparisons to fail intermittently with tiny diff percentages that look like rendering flakiness rather than a missing asset.
Fix: Add an explicit `assetsDir` pointing to the project's `public/` directory in `playwright/index.html` (the CT entry point) so Vite copies static assets into the component test bundle. Alternatively, replace `url()` font references in components under CT test with CSS custom properties resolved at the theme layer, keeping font loading out of component-scoped CSS modules entirely.

## Cycle 68 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 165** — Playwright `request` fixture with `extraHTTPHeaders` for bearer-token API tests that bypass UI login entirely
```typescript
// tests/api/orders.api.test.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// Use the built-in `request` fixture — no browser is launched
test.use({
  extraHTTPHeaders: {
    Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.API_TEST_TOKEN}`,
    'Content-Type': 'application/json',
  },
});

test('POST /orders creates a draft order and returns 201', async ({ request }) => {
  const response = await request.post('/api/v2/orders', {
    data: { skuId: 'SKU-001', quantity: 3, currency: 'USD' },
  });
  expect(response.status()).toBe(201);
  const body = await response.json();
  expect(body).toMatchObject({ status: 'draft', skuId: 'SKU-001' });
});

test('GET /orders/:id returns 404 for unknown order', async ({ request }) => {
  const response = await request.get('/api/v2/orders/nonexistent-id-00000');
  expect(response.status()).toBe(404);
});
```
Tradeoff: Using the `request` fixture skips browser instantiation (saves ~250 ms cold-start per test on CI) and is ideal for pure REST API contract tests, but it cannot validate CORS preflight behavior or cookie-based auth flows that require a real browser origin, so switch to a full `page` fixture the moment a test exercises the browser security model rather than just the API contract.

---

**Pattern 166** — Vitest `vi.spyOn` with `mockImplementationOnce` chaining for testing retry-on-failure logic without timer manipulation
```typescript
// src/utils/fetchWithRetry.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach } from 'vitest';
import { fetchWithRetry } from './fetchWithRetry';

describe('fetchWithRetry', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    vi.restoreAllMocks();
  });

  it('retries twice on 503 then resolves on third attempt', async () => {
    const spy = vi.spyOn(globalThis, 'fetch')
      .mockImplementationOnce(() => Promise.resolve(new Response(null, { status: 503 })))
      .mockImplementationOnce(() => Promise.resolve(new Response(null, { status: 503 })))
      .mockImplementationOnce(() =>
        Promise.resolve(new Response(JSON.stringify({ ok: true }), { status: 200 })),
      );

    const result = await fetchWithRetry('/api/data', { maxRetries: 3, delayMs: 0 });
    expect(result.status).toBe(200);
    expect(spy).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
  });

  it('rejects after exhausting all retries', async () => {
    vi.spyOn(globalThis, 'fetch').mockResolvedValue(
      new Response(null, { status: 503 }),
    );
    await expect(fetchWithRetry('/api/data', { maxRetries: 2, delayMs: 0 })).rejects.toThrow(
      'Max retries exceeded',
    );
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Chaining `mockImplementationOnce` calls tests the retry count exactly as written without needing fake timers (since `delayMs: 0` is passed in tests), but this pattern hard-codes the call sequence in the test body, meaning any change to retry logic that adds a pre-flight check call before the retried fetch will silently misalign the mock chain and produce a false positive — always assert `toHaveBeenCalledTimes` explicitly to catch call-count drift.

---

**Pattern 167** — Jest `jest.isolateModules()` for testing module-initialization side effects that run at `require` time
```typescript
// src/config/database.test.ts
import { jest, describe, it, expect } from '@jest/globals';

describe('database module initialization', () => {
  it('throws when DATABASE_URL is not set at require time', () => {
    const originalUrl = process.env.DATABASE_URL;
    delete process.env.DATABASE_URL;

    expect(() => {
      jest.isolateModules(() => {
        // Re-requires the module in a fresh module registry,
        // so the top-level validation code runs again
        require('./database');
      });
    }).toThrow('DATABASE_URL environment variable is required');

    process.env.DATABASE_URL = originalUrl!;
  });

  it('exports a connected pool when DATABASE_URL is present', () => {
    process.env.DATABASE_URL = 'postgres://localhost/test_db';
    let db: unknown;
    jest.isolateModules(() => {
      db = require('./database').default;
    });
    expect(db).toBeDefined();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `jest.isolateModules()` is the only reliable way to re-run module-level initialization code in Jest because the normal module registry caches `require` calls — but each `isolateModules` call creates a separate module registry that is discarded after the callback, so any singleton (e.g., a connection pool) created inside the block is not the same object used by application code at runtime, making this pattern appropriate only for initialization-error tests, not for behavioral tests that need the live singleton.

---

**Pattern 168** — Node.js built-in test runner `t.plan()` for asserting exact callback invocation counts in event-driven code
```javascript
// test/emitter.test.mjs
import { test } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { EventEmitter } from 'node:events';
import { createOrderProcessor } from '../src/orderProcessor.mjs';

test('orderProcessor emits "processed" exactly once per order', async (t) => {
  // t.plan(N) declares that exactly N assertions must run;
  // the test fails if the callback fires 0 or 2+ times
  t.plan(3);

  const emitter = new EventEmitter();
  const processor = createOrderProcessor(emitter);

  emitter.on('processed', (orderId) => {
    // Each assert inside the callback counts toward the plan
    assert.ok(typeof orderId === 'string', 'orderId must be a string');
    assert.match(orderId, /^ORD-\d{6}$/);
  });

  await processor.process({ id: 'ORD-001234', items: [{ sku: 'A1', qty: 1 }] });
  // Synchronous assertion outside the callback counts as the third planned assertion
  assert.strictEqual(processor.processedCount, 1);
});
```
Tradeoff: `t.plan()` catches the "silent success" failure mode where an async callback never fires and all its internal assertions are skipped — the test would otherwise pass vacuously — but `t.plan()` requires the test author to manually keep the plan count synchronized with the number of assertions, and an off-by-one in the plan count (e.g., plan(2) when 3 assertions run) causes a confusing `plan != actual` error that looks like a framework bug rather than a count mismatch in the test body.

**Pattern 169** — Playwright `page.addInitScript()` for injecting test-only feature flags into the page context before any application JS runs
```typescript
// tests/featureFlags/checkout.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.describe('checkout with experimental one-click pay', () => {
  test.beforeEach(async ({ page }) => {
    // Runs before any script in the page, including the app bundle.
    // Overrides the global flag registry that the app reads on DOMContentLoaded.
    await page.addInitScript(() => {
      (window as any).__FEATURE_FLAGS__ = {
        oneClickPay: true,
        legacyCart: false,
      };
    });
  });

  test('shows one-click pay button on product page', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/products/widget-pro');
    await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Buy Now' })).toBeVisible();
  });

  test('completes checkout without address step when flag is active', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/checkout');
    await expect(page.getByTestId('address-step')).not.toBeVisible();
    await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Confirm Order' })).toBeEnabled();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `addInitScript()` executes before the page's own JavaScript, making it the only reliable way to override globals that application code reads at module initialization time, but the injected script runs in the page's JavaScript context, not in Node.js — so it cannot import modules or call Playwright APIs, and any TypeScript types used inside the callback must be cast manually since the callback is serialized to a string and injected as a script tag rather than compiled as part of the test bundle.

**Pattern 170** — Vitest `setupFiles` with a global `ResizeObserver` polyfill for testing components that use `useResizeObserver` in jsdom
```typescript
// vitest.setup.ts  (referenced in vitest.config.ts > test.setupFiles)
import { vi } from 'vitest';

// jsdom does not implement ResizeObserver; components that call useResizeObserver
// throw "ResizeObserver is not defined" during render in the test environment.
// A minimal mock that records observed elements is sufficient for unit tests.
class ResizeObserverMock {
  private callback: ResizeObserverCallback;
  static observedElements: Element[] = [];

  constructor(callback: ResizeObserverCallback) {
    this.callback = callback;
  }

  observe(el: Element) {
    ResizeObserverMock.observedElements.push(el);
    // Immediately invoke with a synthetic entry so hooks fire synchronously
    this.callback(
      [{ contentRect: el.getBoundingClientRect(), target: el } as ResizeObserverEntry],
      this as unknown as ResizeObserver,
    );
  }
  unobserve(_el: Element) {}
  disconnect() {}
}

vi.stubGlobal('ResizeObserver', ResizeObserverMock);
```
Tradeoff: Globally stubbing `ResizeObserver` in `setupFiles` eliminates the "not defined" error across all test files without per-test setup, but the synchronous `observe` callback in the mock does not reflect the browser's asynchronous batching of resize notifications — tests that assert on multiple sequential resizes may pass under the mock while failing in real browsers because the real observer coalesces rapid size changes into a single callback invocation, so add at least one Playwright visual regression test for each component that depends on resize-triggered re-layout.

**Pattern 171** — Jest `--passWithNoTests` combined with `nx affected` in a monorepo pipeline to skip unchanged packages safely
```json
// nx.json (targetDefaults excerpt)
{
  "targetDefaults": {
    "test": {
      "cache": true,
      "inputs": [
        "default",
        "{projectRoot}/jest.config.ts",
        "{workspaceRoot}/jest.preset.js"
      ],
      "outputs": ["{projectRoot}/coverage"],
      "options": {
        "passWithNoTests": true
      }
    }
  }
}
```
```bash
# CI script: only run tests for packages affected by this PR
npx nx affected --target=test \
  --base=origin/main \
  --head=HEAD \
  --parallel=4 \
  --passWithNoTests
```
Tradeoff: `--passWithNoTests` combined with `nx affected` prevents CI from failing on packages where all test files were deleted (a legitimate refactor outcome), but it also silently passes when the `affected` graph computation incorrectly excludes a package — for example, when a shared utility is changed but its dependents are not tagged with the correct implicit dependency, so pair `--passWithNoTests` with a required check that validates the affected graph against known dependency edges rather than trusting the graph unconditionally.

**Pattern 172** — Playwright `expect(page).toHaveScreenshot()` with `mask` option to exclude dynamic content like timestamps from pixel comparisons
```typescript
// tests/visual/invoicePdf.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('invoice page matches approved visual baseline', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/invoices/INV-2024-0042');

  // Wait for the PDF renderer to finish — avoids capturing a loading spinner
  await page.waitForSelector('[data-testid="invoice-rendered"]');

  await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot('invoice-full-page.png', {
    fullPage: true,
    // Mask dynamic content so pixel diff is deterministic across runs
    mask: [
      page.getByTestId('invoice-date'),       // "Issued: May 14, 2026"
      page.getByTestId('invoice-due-date'),    // "Due: June 14, 2026"
      page.getByTestId('generated-timestamp'), // footer: "Generated at 08:21:03"
    ],
    // Allow 0.2% pixel diff budget for sub-pixel anti-aliasing differences
    maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.002,
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: The `mask` option replaces each masked locator with a solid-color rectangle in the comparison image, making the diff deterministic for date/time fields without needing to mock the system clock — but masked regions are excluded from the diff entirely, so a layout regression that shifts the invoice header into the masked timestamp area will be missed; keep the mask list minimal and prefer mocking the clock with `page.clock.setFixedTime()` when the entire page layout depends on a date value.

**Pattern 173** — Node.js `--experimental-test-coverage` with `--test-coverage-exclude` for excluding generated protobuf stubs from branch coverage thresholds
```bash
# package.json scripts
# "test:coverage": "node --test --experimental-test-coverage
#   --test-coverage-exclude='src/generated/**'
#   --test-coverage-exclude='src/**/*.pb.ts'
#   --test-coverage-branches=80
#   --test-coverage-functions=85
#   --test-coverage-lines=90
#   src/**/*.test.mts"
```
```javascript
// test/coverage.config.mjs  — used by the CI coverage aggregator
export default {
  // Excludes passed to --test-coverage-exclude above are mirrored here
  // so the JSON summary reporter omits the same files
  exclude: [
    'src/generated/**',
    'src/**/*.pb.ts',
    'src/**/*.d.ts',
  ],
  // Thresholds intentionally differ by type: branches are harder to reach in
  // complex state machines, so a lower threshold prevents false failures
  thresholds: {
    branches: 80,
    functions: 85,
    lines: 90,
    statements: 90,
  },
};
```
Tradeoff: `--test-coverage-exclude` removes generated stubs from coverage math, preventing the inflated "99% coverage" illusion caused by trivially-covered getter/setter generated code, but the exclude globs are passed as separate CLI flags and are not validated against the actual file tree at startup — a typo in the glob silently includes the generated files again, so add a CI assertion that the coverage JSON summary's `total.files` count matches `git ls-files src/` count after applying the same exclusion logic.

**Pattern 174** — Vitest `bench` function with `--reporter=verbose` for micro-benchmarking hot path regressions as part of the test suite
```typescript
// src/utils/jsonParser.bench.ts
import { bench, describe } from 'vitest';
import { parseOrderPayload } from './jsonParser';
import { legacyParseOrderPayload } from './legacyJsonParser';

// Sample payload representative of the p99 production message size (4 KB)
const samplePayload = JSON.stringify({
  orderId: 'ORD-9999999',
  items: Array.from({ length: 50 }, (_, i) => ({
    skuId: `SKU-${i.toString().padStart(4, '0')}`,
    quantity: i + 1,
    price: (Math.random() * 100).toFixed(2),
  })),
});

describe('order payload parsing', () => {
  bench('parseOrderPayload (new)', () => {
    parseOrderPayload(samplePayload);
  });

  bench('legacyParseOrderPayload (baseline)', () => {
    legacyParseOrderPayload(samplePayload);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Running `vitest bench` alongside unit tests in the same `vitest` invocation makes performance regressions visible in the same CI report as functional failures, but benchmark results are inherently noisy on shared CI runners — a 15% throughput regression may be within the runner's scheduling jitter, so use `--reporter=json` to export ops/sec to a time-series store and alert only when a 7-day rolling average degrades by more than 20%, rather than failing the CI build on raw per-run numbers.

**Pattern 175** — Playwright `test.fixme()` with a linked issue URL in the title for skipping known-flaky tests without silently suppressing them
```typescript
// tests/checkout/payment.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// test.fixme() marks the test as "expected to fail" — it is skipped on normal runs
// but Playwright reports it as a "fixme" in the HTML report, keeping it visible.
// Including the issue URL in the title makes the reason traceable without
// requiring a comment that gets stale as URLs change.
test.fixme(
  'stripe webhook delivery triggers order-confirmed email within 5s ' +
    '[FIXME: https://github.com/acme/store/issues/4821 — webhook timeout on CI]',
  async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/checkout/confirm?session_id=cs_test_abc123');
    await expect(page.getByTestId('confirmation-email-sent')).toBeVisible({
      timeout: 5_000,
    });
  },
);
```
Tradeoff: `test.fixme()` keeps the test in the report as a visible "fixme" entry (unlike `test.skip()` which produces a "skipped" entry that is easy to filter away), creating accountability for resolution, but `test.fixme()` still runs the test body on `--grep @fixme` runs and will fail if the underlying bug is fixed without removing the `fixme` annotation — add a lint rule that flags any `test.fixme()` older than 30 days without a corresponding closed issue to prevent fixme debt from accumulating.

**Pattern 176** — Jest `expect.extend()` with a custom `toBeWithinRange` matcher for asserting numeric tolerance in financial calculations
```typescript
// test/matchers/financialMatchers.ts
import { expect } from '@jest/globals';

expect.extend({
  toBeWithinRange(received: number, floor: number, ceiling: number) {
    const pass = received >= floor && received <= ceiling;
    return {
      pass,
      message: () =>
        pass
          ? `expected ${received} NOT to be within [${floor}, ${ceiling}]`
          : `expected ${received} to be within [${floor}, ${ceiling}] ` +
            `(diff: ${Math.min(Math.abs(received - floor), Math.abs(received - ceiling)).toFixed(4)})`,
    };
  },
  toMatchCurrency(received: number, expected: number, tolerancePct = 0.001) {
    const diff = Math.abs(received - expected) / Math.max(Math.abs(expected), 1e-10);
    const pass = diff <= tolerancePct;
    return {
      pass,
      message: () =>
        `expected ${received} to be within ${tolerancePct * 100}% of ${expected} ` +
        `(actual diff: ${(diff * 100).toFixed(4)}%)`,
    };
  },
});

// Usage in tests:
// expect(calculatedTax).toBeWithinRange(9.99, 10.01);
// expect(roundedTotal).toMatchCurrency(expectedTotal);
```
Tradeoff: Custom matchers produce failure messages that include the actual diff value, making financial rounding failures immediately actionable (e.g., "diff: 0.0023%") versus a raw `toBe` failure that shows two opaque numbers — but custom matchers must be globally registered in `setupFilesAfterFramework` or imported in every test file that uses them, and TypeScript users must augment the `jest.Matchers` interface in a separate declaration file, adding boilerplate that can be forgotten when onboarding new engineers who write tests in isolated files.

**Pattern 177** — Playwright `APIRequestContext` shared across tests via a `test.extend()` fixture for reusable authenticated API setup in E2E suites
```typescript
// fixtures/authenticatedApi.ts
import { test as base, APIRequestContext, request } from '@playwright/test';

type AuthApiFixtures = { authApi: APIRequestContext };

export const test = base.extend<AuthApiFixtures>({
  authApi: async ({}, use) => {
    // Create a context with a pre-obtained bearer token.
    // This context is reused across all tests in the file — one token fetch per worker.
    const ctx = await request.newContext({
      baseURL: process.env.API_BASE_URL,
      extraHTTPHeaders: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.E2E_SERVICE_TOKEN}`,
      },
    });
    await use(ctx);
    await ctx.dispose();
  },
});

// tests/orders/lifecycle.spec.ts
import { test } from '../../fixtures/authenticatedApi';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('full order lifecycle: create → pay → ship → deliver', async ({ authApi }) => {
  const order = await (await authApi.post('/orders', { data: { sku: 'PROD-1' } })).json();
  await authApi.post(`/orders/${order.id}/pay`, { data: { method: 'card' } });
  const shipped = await (await authApi.get(`/orders/${order.id}`)).json();
  expect(shipped.status).toBe('shipped');
});
```
Tradeoff: Extending the base `test` object with a shared `authApi` fixture means the token is fetched once per worker process (not once per test), reducing auth overhead by ~200 ms per test in a suite with 50 tests running on 4 workers — but the shared context accumulates cookies and auth state across tests within the same worker, so a test that mutates auth (e.g., logs out or rotates the token) will corrupt the fixture for subsequent tests in that worker; guard against this by asserting `authApi` context health in an `afterEach` hook and disposing/recreating it on failure.

**Pattern 178** — Vitest `vi.waitFor()` replacing manual polling loops for assertions on eventually-consistent in-memory stores
```typescript
// src/store/notificationStore.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach } from 'vitest';
import { renderHook, act } from '@testing-library/react';
import { useNotificationStore } from './notificationStore';

describe('useNotificationStore', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    useNotificationStore.getState().clear();
  });

  it('adds a notification after async validation completes', async () => {
    const { result } = renderHook(() => useNotificationStore());

    act(() => {
      // Triggers an async side effect that eventually pushes a notification
      result.current.submitContactForm({ email: 'user@example.com' });
    });

    // vi.waitFor polls until the assertion passes or the timeout expires.
    // Avoids manual setTimeout(resolve, 1000) or flaky retry loops.
    await vi.waitFor(
      () => {
        expect(result.current.notifications).toHaveLength(1);
        expect(result.current.notifications[0]).toMatchObject({
          type: 'success',
          message: expect.stringContaining('email'),
        });
      },
      { timeout: 2000, interval: 50 },
    );
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `vi.waitFor()` with an explicit `interval` avoids the "works on fast CI, fails on slow CI" flakiness of `await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 500))` by polling until the condition is true rather than waiting a fixed duration — but `vi.waitFor()` interacts with fake timers: if `vi.useFakeTimers()` is active and the async operation inside the store uses `setTimeout` to debounce, `vi.waitFor()` will never resolve because the fake timers do not auto-advance; call `vi.advanceTimersByTime()` before `vi.waitFor()` or disable fake timers for tests that use `vi.waitFor()`.

**Pattern 179** — Jest `--detectOpenHandles` combined with `--forceExit` as a CI-only escape hatch with structured logging of the open handle warning
```javascript
// jest.config.ci.js  — used only in CI via jest --config jest.config.ci.js
/** @type {import('jest').Config} */
module.exports = {
  ...require('./jest.config.js'),

  // --detectOpenHandles instruments async_hooks to identify which operations
  // prevented Jest from exiting cleanly. The warning is printed to stderr.
  detectOpenHandles: true,

  // --forceExit ensures CI does not hang after tests complete, even if a
  // database connection pool or HTTP server was not closed in afterAll.
  // IMPORTANT: forceExit masks real leaks — treat any detected open handle
  // warning as a P2 bug and link it to a tracking issue within 48 hours.
  forceExit: true,

  // Custom reporter captures open handle warnings and posts them to a
  // Slack channel so they are not buried in multi-MB CI log output
  reporters: [
    'default',
    ['<rootDir>/test/reporters/openHandleSlackReporter.js', {
      webhookUrl: process.env.SLACK_CI_WEBHOOK,
      channel: '#test-health',
    }],
  ],
};
```
Tradeoff: Using `forceExit: true` in CI prevents indefinite hangs caused by un-closed database pools or HTTP servers (which block Jest's exit for up to 5 seconds per leaked handle), but `forceExit` forcibly terminates the process before Node.js can flush async I/O — writes to external log aggregators or coverage reporters that buffer output may be truncated, losing coverage data; always pair `forceExit` with synchronous `afterAll` teardown that explicitly closes database pools and HTTP servers, treating `forceExit` as an emergency brake rather than a substitute for proper cleanup.

### Community Gotchas

**G281** — Vitest `vi.mock()` hoisting interacting with `vi.importActual()` inside the same factory producing `undefined` for re-exported named exports
Why this matters: Vitest hoists `vi.mock()` calls to the top of the file (before imports) using a Babel transform. When the mock factory calls `vi.importActual()` to spread the real module's exports and then overrides one named export, the transform runs the factory at hoist time — before the real module's ESM live bindings are established. If the mocked module re-exports a value from a third module (e.g., `export { createClient } from './client'`) and that third module has not been resolved yet at factory execution time, `vi.importActual()` returns the re-export as `undefined`. Tests that destructure `createClient` from the mock factory result receive `undefined` and throw at call time, but the error message ("createClient is not a function") points to the test's call site rather than the mock factory, making the root cause invisible without inspecting the factory return value.
Fix: Await `vi.importActual()` inside an async mock factory (`vi.mock('./module', async () => { const actual = await vi.importActual('./module'); ... })`) and validate that every expected export is non-undefined before spreading. If re-exports from transitive modules are `undefined`, explicitly re-import the originating module with a second `vi.importActual()` call targeting the source module rather than the re-exporting barrel file.

**G282** — Playwright `locator.fill()` on a `<input type="number">` field that has `min`/`max` HTML validation silently clamping the value without throwing
Why this matters: When `fill()` sets a numeric input's value to a number outside the field's `min`/`max` range (e.g., filling `quantity` with `999` when `max="100"`), the browser's HTML constraint validation does not fire a JavaScript error and does not change the displayed value — the input's `.value` property is set to the string `"999"` in the DOM but the form submission silently clamps or discards the value depending on the browser's validation mode. Playwright's `expect(locator).toHaveValue('999')` passes because it reads the DOM `.value` property, not the validated submitted value. Tests that assert on the submitted form data (checking the network request payload) pass in Chromium (which preserves the out-of-range value in the request) but fail in WebKit (which clamps to `max` before submission), producing cross-browser flakiness that is diagnosed as a Playwright cross-browser bug rather than a test assertion gap.
Fix: After `fill()` on constrained numeric inputs, add `expect(locator).toHaveJSProperty('validity.valid', true)` to assert that the browser's constraint validation API considers the value valid before proceeding. For tests that intentionally test out-of-range inputs, assert on the network request payload using `page.waitForRequest()` rather than on the DOM `.value` to capture the actual submitted value across browsers.

**G283** — Jest `moduleDirectories` including `node_modules` and a custom `src` path causing `jest.mock('moduleName')` to resolve ambiguously when a local file shares a name with an npm package
Why this matters: When `jest.config.js` sets `moduleDirectories: ['node_modules', 'src']`, Jest resolves bare import specifiers by searching both `node_modules` and `src/`. If a project has both `node_modules/uuid` and `src/uuid/index.ts` (a local UUID utility), `jest.mock('uuid')` is resolved using Jest's resolver which picks `src/uuid/index.ts` (listed first in `moduleDirectories`) rather than the npm package, silently mocking the local file instead of the third-party module. Application code that imports `import { v4 } from 'uuid'` resolves to the npm package at runtime but to the local mock in tests, so tests pass even when the real `uuid.v4()` is broken in the npm package version used in production.
Fix: Use explicit relative paths for local modules (`jest.mock('../uuid')`) and bare specifiers only for npm packages. Alternatively, remove custom paths from `moduleDirectories` and use `moduleNameMapper` for local path aliases (`'@/(.*)': '<rootDir>/src/$1'`), which is explicit and does not create ambiguous resolution between local files and npm packages with the same name.

**G284** — Node.js test runner `--test-concurrency` set above the Postgres `max_connections` limit causing connection timeout failures that report as assertion errors
Why this matters: Node.js 22's `--test-concurrency` flag sets the maximum number of test files running in parallel. When set to the default (number of CPUs, e.g., 8 on a 4-core CI runner with hyperthreading) and each test file creates its own `pg.Pool` with a `max` of 5 connections, up to 40 connections may be requested simultaneously against a PostgreSQL server configured with `max_connections = 20`. The connection pool queue fills, and after `connectionTimeoutMillis` (default: 0, meaning infinite wait), tests hang indefinitely. On CI with a job timeout, the runner kills the process and reports all pending tests as failures with a generic timeout message, not a "connection refused" error, so engineers look for assertion failures rather than infrastructure limits.
Fix: Set `--test-concurrency` to `Math.floor(max_connections / pool_max_per_file)` (e.g., `--test-concurrency=4` for `max_connections=20` and `pool_max: 5`). Export this as a `TEST_CONCURRENCY` environment variable computed in CI setup scripts from a shared infrastructure constants file, keeping test concurrency and database pool sizing co-located so they cannot drift independently.

**G285** — Playwright `page.waitForSelector()` with `state: 'hidden'` resolving immediately when the selector never existed in the DOM, masking missing-element bugs
Why this matters: `page.waitForSelector('[data-testid="error-banner"]', { state: 'hidden' })` resolves immediately if the element with `data-testid="error-banner"` was never added to the DOM — Playwright considers a non-existent element to be "hidden" (the default `state: 'attached'` would wait, but `state: 'hidden'` explicitly targets absence). Tests that assert "the error banner should not be shown after a successful save" use this pattern to verify that the error state is cleared, but if the component's error rendering logic was accidentally deleted entirely (so the element is never rendered in any state), the `waitForSelector` call returns immediately and the test passes even though the error-handling UI has been removed from the component.
Fix: Restructure the assertion to first confirm the element was rendered (proving the component's error path exists), then assert it becomes hidden after the action: `await expect(page.getByTestId('error-banner')).toBeVisible()` after triggering an error, then perform the successful action, then `await expect(page.getByTestId('error-banner')).not.toBeVisible()`. Alternatively, use `expect(locator).toHaveCount(0)` only when the test's intent is specifically to assert the element was never rendered, making the semantic distinction explicit in the assertion method name.
